New data compiled by a Bay Area anti-surveillance advocacy group shows that not only are American localities dropping cameras from Flock Safety, but they are doing it at an accelerating rate.
Communities from Lansing, Michigan, to Pflugerville, Texas, are ending their relationship with Flock, largely over concerns regarding out-of-control surveillance, unwanted data sharing, high expenses, and reports of police abusing the tool.
Secure Justice, an Oakland-based advocacy group, has recorded 214 cities and counties that have dropped Flock since 2021. Of those, 90 ended their relationship with Flock in August 2026 alone, a fourfold increase compared to the previous month.
Put another way: During the last 30 days, an average of three localities per day have halted contracts with Flock.
“Looking at that image, it’s gone parabolic!” Brian Hofer, the executive director of Secure Justice, told Ars.
Hofer, who until 2025 served as chair of the Oakland Privacy Advisory Commission for 10 years, recognized that while 210 remains relatively small, the momentum is growing rapidly.
“When you see that now 165 [cancellations] are just in the first almost eight months of this year… At that speed, if it goes another year, we’re talking serious money,” he said. “That number is going to get huge, fast.”
When presented with this data, Flock Safety did not express concern. “So far in 2026, new city partnerships have outpaced nonrenewals by approximately 10 to one,” emailed Courtney Terlecki, a company spokesperson. “That does not mean every community will make the same decision, and we understand that public safety technology deserves thoughtful public discussion and community engagement.”
She declined to say precisely how many new customers Flock has taken on this year, but the company has repeatedly said that its products are “trusted by over 5,000 communities.”
Criticism
After extensive criticism, Flock CEO Garrett Langley wrote in a recent blog post that Flock would reduce data retention defaults from 30 days to seven, among other privacy-minded changes.

The Maytag Man is one of the most enduring characters in American advertising, lonely because no one needs his help repairing a Maytag appliance. The Maytag brand, too, has endured—going back to the days when Frederick Maytag’s washers involved wooden tubs and cranks. Maytag was the first company to put an agitator at the bottom of a washing machine, a design still in use today, and it was the first to stack a washer and dryer, and one of the earliest adopters on smart appliances. But mostly, the brand has eschewed novelty and staked its claim on durability and reliability for its heavy-duty dishwashers, washers, dryers, refrigerators, and ovens. This is true even as Maytag folded into ownership by former competitor Whirlpool.
Maytag remains one of the few appliance companies to offer 10-year limited warranties on essential parts. But Maytag promo codes are a bit more ephemeral, offering short-term deals on appliances that will hopefully last a decade. Here’s how to get a Maytag coupon code and Maytag promo codes, and find closeout deals on last season’s Maytag appliances to save even more.
Save Big With Maytag Appliance Closeout Deals
One of the easiest ways to find a deal on Maytag appliances is to look at the overstock and closeout deals, which offer significant markdowns on last season’s items as Maytag looks to clear out space for the new models. These deals do not require a Maytag coupon code, but they do require knowing where to look. Go to the Maytag outlet site for appliance closeout deals. These deals generally last only until supplies run out.
Select Customers Can Get a Special Maytag Promo Code
Like many big companies, Maytag offers professional discounts for military, first responders, healthcare workers, students, and teachers. To receive up to a 15% discount for active military, veterans, and spouses, you’ll need to create a Maytag account and then verify your military status using the SheerID program. Maytag first responder discounts and healthcare worker discounts also require SheerID verification. There’s also a discount program for both students and teachers, including a teacher savings program and up to 15% off sitewide. Verified students are able to access pricing unique to students, when moving into their first off-campus apartment.
Work Smarter, Not Harder With Maytag Smart Appliances
Maytag is also offering deals on select smart appliances. As of early April, this includes a somewhat unique combination toaster-microwave that’s about $100 off MSRP, and a slide-in electric range with smart connectivity that’s on a steep discount to $1,260—hundreds of dollars less than even other recent sale prices. You can check out the special Maytag deals on connected and smart appliances by scrolling down to the bottom of Maytag’s smart appliance page.

Big-spending Tottenham crashed to a second successive Premier League defeat as Anthony Elanga and Yoane Wissa inspired Newcastle’s 2-0 win on Saturday.
Roberto De Zerbi’s side conceded twice in the second half in north London to extend its dismal start to the season.
Elanga put Newcastle ahead before Wissa killed off lacklustre Tottenham as its frustrated fans streamed to the exits long before the final whistle.
Newcastle manager Matthias Jaissle was able to celebrate his maiden Premier League win after a 2-2 draw against Liverpool in the German’s first game following his surprise appointment as Eddie Howe’s replacement.
It was another chastening result for De Zerbi, whose expensively assembled team suffered an embarrassing 3-0 defeat at Brentford in the opening game of the season last weekend.
Tottenham has spent over £300 million ($406 million) in the close season as De Zerbi overhauled a squad that narrowly avoided relegation on the final day of last term.
But for the first time since 1992-93, Tottenham has failed to score in its first two games of a league season.
Omar Marmoush, the latest new recruit, was handed his Tottenham debut after joining on loan from Manchester City this week.
However, the Egypt forward, who struggled to make an impact with City, was unable to spark Tottenham, who was without Savio, another recent signing from City, due to a muscular injury.
A 5-1 rout of Championship side Charlton in the League Cup second round in midweek proved a false dawn for woeful Tottenham.
- Tonali taunts -
Elanga nearly gave Newcastle the perfect start with a first-minute lob that Tottenham scrambled to safety just before it crossed the line.
That was the spark for a period of Tottenham dominance.
Mathys Tel’s curler from the edge of the area was clawed away by Newcastle keeper Lukas Hornicek.
Pedro Porro and Marmoush both volleyed narrowly wide in quick succession after Newcastle failed to deal with testing corners.
Hornicek kept out Andrew Robertson’s drive and Jan Paul van Hecke’s header.
Tottenham midfielder Sandro Tonali was taunted by Newcastle fans in his first appearance against his former club since his £100 million move in July.
The Italian squandered a golden opportunity to silence the Newcastle jibes when he scuffed wide from close range on the stroke of half-time.
De Zerbi’s side appealed in vain for a penalty after Malick Thiaw clipped Marmoush in the opening moments of the second half.
Tottenham paid for its profligacy in the 62nd minute.
After bagging his first league goal for Newcastle against Liverpool on Sunday, Elanga was back on the scoresheet, controlling Amar Dedic’s cushioned header with a superb turn before unloading a lethal finish from just inside the area.
Hornicek tipped Porro’s strike over the bar as Tottenham tried to vain to mount a response.
Wissa wrapped up the points for Newcastle in the 72nd minute, finishing with a clever over-the shoulder flick from close range after Nick Woltemade headed a corner towards the DR Congo forward.
Providing a fitting coda to a dispiriting afternoon for Tottenham, Tonali was hauled off with the jeers of the Toon Army ringing in his ears in the closing stages.
Hull beats Coventry
Coventry and Hull had played two goalless draws in the second-tier Championship last season, but this time Hull took all three points after Liam Millar scored the winner in the 82nd minute.
The goal came against the run of play from a Coventry corner, which was cleared before Mohamed Belloumi released Millar from inside his own half and the Canadian had only the goalkeeper to beat to silence the home crowd.
Hull, who beat Manchester United last week, has six points from two games and sits behind Manchester City on goal difference.

Trump’s oil deal riles both sides of Venezuelan political divide
U.S. President Donald Trump (L) and Venezuelan acting President Delcy Rodríguez (R). One potential advantage for Rodríguez in agreeing to grant the U.S. exclusive access to the country’s oil is that the deal could push the Trump administration to urge swift elections and help cement her grip on power.
| AFP-JIJI
Venezuelan hard-liners and opposition forces alike criticized acting President Delcy Rodríguez for agreeing to grant the U.S. exclusive access to the country’s valuable oil resources. She may be betting that the deal with Donald Trump is her ticket to a tighter grip on power.
One potential advantage for Rodríguez is if the deal to give the U.S. majority control over 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan crude hems in the Trump administration’s incentive to press for swift elections.
“I think it can benefit Delcy to the extent that it reinforces Trump’s commitment to working with her and thus probably diminishes incentives to move quickly to a new vote,” said Risa Grais-Targow, Latin America director at Eurasia Group. That “is precisely why the opposition is so upset,” she said.

Psoriasis (so-ri’a-sis, a word of Greek origin) is a chronic skin disorder in which red, scaly plaques appear on the skin. The knees, shin, elbows, naval, buttocks, lower back, ears and hairline, are most commonly affected. Some people suffer from pitting of nails as well. Dermatologists say patients have varying degrees of the condition -- from mild discomforting changes, to severe, debilitating forms.
Experts say that while psoriasis primarily manifests on the skin, it is defined as a systemic inflammatory condition affecting multiple systems in the body.
Understanding why psoriasis occurs
According to the National Psoriasis Foundation, a non-profit organisation based in the United States, psoriasis plaques occur because of an overactive immune system, resulting in faster skin cell growth. While normal skin cells grow completely and fall off in a month, in persons with psoriasis, skin cells pile up on the surface of the skin. Symptoms include flaky skin and raised, discoloured bulges on the skin, akin to boils. Some have blisters, itching and even bleeding. Some exhibit ridges along the nailbed. Some also have pustules, which break and leave scabs. It can occur in the palms, soles, scalp or elbows and in skin folds. Psoriasis is not a contagious condition, but results in low confidence in patient.
Krishnan* was diagnosed with psoriasis in 1991, when he was 20. “My father took me to a doctor who diagnosed my condition. It started as a scar on my bottom, spreading to my back and the armpits. It is persistent still, and flares up during winters,” he says. Mr. Krishnan was an active cricketer until the condition began to demotivate him. It also resulted ibn him avoiding a steady job. “I bathe twice a day. I have tried everything, from powder to lotion to ointments and even injectables,” he reveals, but psoriasis persists.
The condition can also run in families. His brother was diagnosed with the condition as well, Mr. Krishnan says. “But he leads an active life and does not have as many scars or episodes. He is a medical professional, and his condition is milder.”
More research needed
In an article ‘Psoriasis in India: Prevalence and Pattern’ publishedin the Indian Journal of Dermatology, Venereology and Leprology in 2010, the authors Dogra S. and Yadav S. of the Department of Dermatology, Venereology and Leprology at the Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research, Chandigarh, said the prevalence in India and the epidemiological characteristics are similar to that of the disease in the West. They maintained that in India, the prevalence varied from 0.44% to 2.8%.
The authors called for more research and a detailed prospective study to delineate the natural course of the disease, as it varied in different individuals. They also called for further research to identify risk factors to prevent the condition and pointed to lack of reliable information on time trends of the disease.
Current trends and treatment approaches
Much water has flowed under the bridge in the past 15 years, says U.R. Dhanalakshmi, a Chennai-based dermatologist. She has seen an increase in the number of cases of psoriasis in recent years. She points out that with an increase in the number of people with diabetes, psoriasis has also risen. While the mild conditions are treated using creams and over the skin applications, severe cases may need longer and more intense treatment. Co-morbid conditions such as hypertension, thyroid dysfunction and diabetes aggravate the condition making it difficult to control, she explains.
Unlike in the past, when the only treatment options were powders, creams and lotions, currently there are advanced methods to treat psoriasis. Patients with severe psoriasis are prescribed biological drugs. “The condition manifests in genetically prone individuals. It is not that the biological drugs will eliminate the infection. But they target overactive parts of immune system in order to reduce inflammation,” she explains.
Stressors such as work and family pressure are triggers. “It is a recurring disease as the person is exposed to the same work life and stresses. It can occur among people without any genetic load either, she says. Lifestyle modifications that help avoid triggers could play a role in managing symptoms, she adds.
A 51-year-old farmer from a suburb of Chennai discovered he had the condition in 2021. He was diagnosed after a bout of COVID 19. The condition, he says, flares up during monsoons and winters. Unlike Mr. Krishnan, this patient has managed to keep it under control, with maintenance drugs whenever there is a flare up.
Why are cases on the rise?
“Over the past seven years that I have worked in academic institutions and private practice, the number psoriasis of cases has gone up from 2 or 3 cases in a day to as many as 6 or 7 per day,” says Monisha Madhumita, an assistant professor in the Department of Dermatology, Saveetha Medical College in Chennai. “Increasingly a younger demographic is being affected,” she adds. In all her patients the metabolic syndrome has been impacted, she adds, indicating that it is a systemic condition similar to diabetes and hypertension.
Psoriasis may manifest as a skin condition, but, Dr. Monisha says, could cause heart attacks, fatty liver, and affect mental health as well.
Mental health is an aspect of the condition that may often go under-recognised: Mr. Krishnan, who continues to struggle with psoriasis is now resigned to his condition. He has tried every medication that is available, including Indian systems of medicine. He has also now been diagnosed with fatty liver. Lifestyle changes however are challenging for him.
“We have seen that obesity, exposure to microplastics, endocrine disrupting chemicals and personal care product use are also reasons for the rise in psoriasis cases,” Dr. Monisha surmises. “I see younger populations with more severe forms of psoriasis,” she adds.
The most common varieties she treats in her clinic are chronic plaque in elbows, knees or other parts of the body, and persistent infection in the scalp. There are also those with childhood psoriasis that can resolve as they grow older. Among the severe forms are psoriatic arthritis, and erythrodermic psoriasis where 90% of the body becomes red and the person sheds skin in large sheets, requiring to be hospitalised.
(R. Sujatha is an independent journalist based in Chennai. sujatha.raghunath@gmail.com)

AEW All In 2026 advertised a Meltzerian main event between Kenny Omega and Will Ospreay in Ospreay’s home country of London. The up-and-down build has led to some of the lowest and highest viewership of AEW Dynamite in back-to-back weeks. The go-home show garnered almost 800,000 viewers as ratings data once again gears toward a big shift. The true main event will pit top AEW star Mercedes Mone against Willow Nightingale in yet another women’s world title match that will not go on last. This will mark the 51st straight AEW main event without women headlining.
AEW has had a grand total of 51 pay-per-views in seven years.
AEW All In 2026 Preview And Surprises From Wembley Stadium
All In is expected to featured multiple surprises, including the imminent debut of the Kofi Kingston and Xavier Woods of the New Day. Tickets have been as slow as ever for AEW’s biggest show, with just over 44,000 tickets sold inside a 90,000-seat building. AEW did 72,265 for its Wembley Stadium debut, and paid ticket sales have exponentially declined every year since.
Many were quick to point out WWE’s last-minute surge in ticket sales for SummerSlam 2026, calling out “papered” seats and give-a-way tickets. The same scenario is playing out for AEW All In, except with less coverage from AEW’s state-sponsored media. It’ll be interesting to see how the final gate sales correspond to the tickets sold, and even more interesting to see how many AEW dirtsheet media stooges have the stones to cover it.
Last year, for AEW All In Texas, the Texas attendance numbers from the Texas government were far lower than numbers that were initially announced.

A Wildly Popular Movie Meets the Film World’s Most Revered Label
KPop Demon Hunters’ inclusion in the high-class cinema catalog may signal a changing tide.
Updated at 12:30 p.m. ET on Aug. 28, 2025
Over the past year, KPop Demon Hunters seems to have completely overtaken culture. Since premiering on Netflix in June 2025, the animated film has been watched nearly 650 million times and, according to Nielsen, accounted for some 20.5 billion viewing minutes last year. The soundtrack topped Billboard charts that fall; Spirit Halloween instantly sold out of licensed costumes.
But even the most ardent fans likely did not anticipate the mega-hit’s next big merch drop: a disc release from the Criterion Collection, home to some of cinema’s most distinguished titles. By some metrics, KPop Demon Hunters may be the most popular movie ever to be added to the collection. (Other new entries include David Lynch’s Wild at Heart and a Ukrainian folk romance from 1965.) It’s almost certainly the first Criterion inclusion to have its own flavor of McFlurry.
KPop Demon Hunters is an unlikely candidate for what’s come to be called “the Criterion treatment”: a painstaking transfer to disc, along with a making-of documentary and other special features, and a number printed on the box’s spine. Film buffs see this process as akin to an anointing; the trademark C, tucked into the upper-left corner of a plastic clamshell, signals a movie’s importance. Introducing a new title to the library can be fraught: James Kendrick, a professor of film and digital media at Baylor University, told me, “They’re always sort of risking diluting the power of that sign.”
Online, some of the label’s longtime devotees greeted the addition of KPop Demon Hunters with an eye roll, calling the move “substantially off-brand,” and a “cash grab.” The movie is so familiar to the general public that its release seems to go against the grain of Criterion’s reputation, which was built on bringing landmark works of film history to the masses. The company adds some 30 to 60 movies to its catalog annually, most of them lost gems of world cinema, festival-circuit darlings, or old Hollywood hits. In past decades, only one or two very new releases might have made the cut; canonization is usually a retrospective project of sifting through the past to see what art stands the test of time. Now the process seems to be speeding up: This year’s roster includes six movies from 2025 so far, many of them distributed by streaming companies.
Criterion has good reason to widen the net: Netflix, Apple, and Amazon make and distribute a significant share of films these days. A title that seems ubiquitous today could vanish tomorrow, evaporating from viewing platforms or even from personal digital libraries without warning. “We’ve lived kind of free and easy for the last couple decades, assuming these corporations would do that work for us,” Amanda D. Lotz, a media scholar at Queensland University of Technology, told me, “and that’s not in their remit, necessarily.”
Streaming services, unlike their traditional studio competitors, rarely produce physical media. “I suspect it is unclear that there is a market” for companion discs, Lotz said, despite the fact that, in her estimation, they could be a “nice little business niche.” (Signs are mixed: One by one, electronics companies have stopped manufacturing disc players, but the decline in disc sales seems to have slowed.) With more new films seeming transient—especially those whose rights belong to streaming studios—it makes sense for a label like Criterion to invest more in preserving them.
The decision to pick up KPop Demon Hunters also seems less surprising when you consider Criterion’s very early history. Back when the label was putting out movies on LaserDisc, in the 1980s, it was more inclined to pick up very new and popular titles, such as Ghostbusters. Some of that popcorn sensibility lived on in the brand’s DVD era, when it released Armageddon and The Rock, by Michael Bay.
Part of co-founder Bob Stein’s vision for the label was for it to distribute some titles that already had mass public appeal; Criterion, by offering a feature-packed disc to explore, could then deepen people’s relationship to those works and to the art form writ large. The brand has long been characterized by a high-low eclecticism: The literature scholars Mark and Deborah Parker told me that when they were working on their book about the history of the DVD, they visited Criterion’s office. Peter Becker, the president of Criterion, pressed a copy of a Japanese gangster flick into their hands; just down the hall, Mark told me, “they were doing the transfer of In the Mood for Love.”
The reasoning behind Criterion’s selections remains somewhat mysterious. (The company declined to be interviewed for this story.) Addressing an industry gathering in 2019, Becker said, “We let the movies carry the brand into the market place, so we don’t talk about the company very much.” But he did offer this explanation of what makes a work fit for Criterion: “It should be something we want to talk about, it should be a rich point of entry, but we try not to be snobby about what kinds of films can actually be exemplary.”
So what might KPop Demon Hunters exemplify? Its public reception has had a unique arc: a family-friendly fantasy that premiered on Netflix with little fanfare before becoming a word-of-mouth hit, then a critical darling, and finally an awards winner. As for its artistic properties, John Adkins, the lead writer for the newsletter Animation Obsessive, suggested to me that the film is “very tied to anime aesthetics and the slick, bright, Spider-Verse-type visuals that Sony Pictures Animation popularized” and that it could be taken to represent a modern-audience preference for an animation style with “a graphic or illustrative edge.” Tom Sito, a retired Disney animator and a professor emeritus at the University of Southern California, told me that the budding animators in his classes have adopted the movie the way he and his peers once did Yellow Submarine, the surrealist cartoon set to music by the Beatles.
That fervor might be enough reason to declare KPop Demon Hunters a contemporary classic and worthy of Criterion status. The revenue that it might bring in, which could then potentially fund more esoteric selections, is another. (Criterion, savvily, is releasing its edition just in time for holiday shopping, positioning it as an arty stocking stuffer.) Adding the film to the collection could be seen as part of a broader strategy to increase the company’s visibility, including through its “Criterion Closet” social video series, its mobile van, and a brick-and-mortar storefront during the Toronto Film Festival.
For many young fans of KPop Demon Hunters, who are more likely to pull up the “Golden” video on YouTube than pop a disc into a player, a souped-up Blu-ray might function mostly as a collectible—not so different from a Derpy Tiger plush or a Rumi singing doll. Some, though, may grow attached to the idea of physical media, or could even come to see home video as a vital technology rather than a nostalgia object. Cinema is a relatively young art form; the idea of owning a personal copy of a film is an even more recent invention. KPop Demon Hunter’s latest accolade is a reminder that the canon, too, remains far from fixed.
This article has been updated to reflect the nature of Criterion’s physical retailer.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Tuesday reported 17,180 confirmed cases of cyclosporiasis in the United States, an increase of 1,464 cases from a week ago.
Here are some details:
The CDC said it has received reports of 17,180 confirmed cases across 48 states plus the District of Columbia, with 922 hospitalisations and two deaths as of August 24. At least 11,844 additional cases may require further investigation and analysis, CDC said.
The data include the cases reported in the ongoing multistate outbreak linked to recalled iceberg lettuce, CDC said, adding that it is investigating multiple clusters of cyclosporiasis.
CDC and FDA are investigating at least six other clusters for which sources have not yet been confirmed, CDC said.
Michigan, the hardest-hit state, logged a slow 3% rise to 14,277 last week, hinting the outbreak may be easing.
The cyclosporiasis outbreak is one of the largest foodborne illness events in recent U.S. history. The illness is caused by the cyclospora parasite, which can lead to diarrhea, nausea and other gastrointestinal symptoms.
The outbreak has shaken U.S. consumers nationwide, causing many to forgo eating fresh produce or dining in restaurants.

The Trump administration plans to revoke up to 200,000 business and tourism visas held by people who've sought asylum in the U.S., AP first reported on Monday.
Why it matters: It would be the largest mass visa revocation in U.S. history and would likely trigger legal challenges.
What they're saying: "We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently," State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott told AP.
He wouldn't say how many visas might be revoked, adding, "as the process will be ongoing, the number of revocations remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis."
Representatives for the State Department and the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment.
Last year, the administration began "continuous vetting" of more than 55 million U.S. visa holders for potential violations that could lead to revocation or deportation.

26 ఆగస్టు 2026న నేపాల్, టిబెట్ ప్రాంతాల్లో సంభవించిన భారీ ఆకస్మిక వరదలు తీవ్ర విధ్వంసాన్ని సృష్టించాయి. భోటేకోషి, త్రిశూలి వంటి నదులు ఉప్పొంగడంతో పలు ప్రాంతాలు నీటమునిగాయి. ఎత్తైన పర్వతాలపై భారీ మంచు కొండ (Glacier), బండరాళ్లు ఒక్కసారిగా కుప్పకూలడం వల్లే ఈ విపత్తు ప్రారంభమైందని ప్రాథమిక అంచనా. ఈ విపత్తులో ఇప్పటివరకు వివిధ దేశాలకు చెందిన 160 మంది మృతి చెందగా, వందలాది మంది గల్లంతయ్యారు. ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, ఈ ఆకస్మిక వరదలకు సంబంధించిన దృశ్యాలంటూ కొన్ని వీడియోలు సోషల్ మీడియాలో విస్తృతంగా ప్రచారంలో ఉన్నాయి. వీటిలో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: 26 ఆగస్టు 2026న నేపాల్లో సంభవించిన ఆకస్మిక వరదలకు సంబంధించిన దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వీడియోలు ఆగస్టు 2026 నేపాల్ విపత్తుకు సంబంధించినవి కావు. ఇతర ప్రాంతాలకు చెందిన పాత వీడియోలు, ఆర్టిఫిషియల్ ఇంటెలిజెన్స్ (AI) తో సృష్టించిన వీడియోలను నేపాల్ వరదలకు ముడిపెడుతూ తప్పుగా షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.
వీడియో 1:
ఈ విపత్తుకు కారణమైన భారీ మంచుకొండ కుప్పకూలుతున్న దృశ్యాలంటూ కొన్ని వీడియో క్లిప్లు (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) ప్రచారంలో ఉన్నాయి.
వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఇదే వీడియో (ఆర్కైవ్) కనీసం ఆగస్టు 2025 నుంచి ఇంటర్నెట్లో అందుబాటులో ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. “లీ కోట్స్” అనే హెలికాప్టర్ పైలట్ ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్, యూట్యూబ్ ఖాతాల్లో దీనికి సంబంధించిన పూర్తి వీడియోలు (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. ఈ వీడియోలను అలస్కాలో చిత్రీకరించినట్లు అందులో పేర్కొన్నారు.
వీడియో 2:
నేపాల్ ఆకస్మిక వరదల్లో వాహనాలు, భవనాలు కొట్టుకుపోతున్నట్లుగా ఉన్న ఒక వీడియో ప్రచారంలో ఉంది.
అయితే, ఈ వీడియో (ఆర్కైవ్) 04 ఆగస్టు 2026 నుంచి, అనగా నేపాల్ విపత్తుకు కనీసం 22 రోజుల ముందు నుంచే ఇంటర్నెట్లో ఉంది. పైగా, ఈ వీడియోను పరిశీలించగా అందులో నీటి ప్రవాహం, వాహనాల కదలికలు అసహజంగా ఉండటాన్ని గుర్తించాం. ఈ వీడియోను Hive వంటి AI డిటెక్షన్ టూల్స్తో పరిశీలించగా, ఇది AI ద్వారా సృష్టించిన వీడియో అని వెల్లడైంది.
వీడియో 3:
భారీ వరద ధాటికి వాహనాలు కొట్టుకుపోతున్నట్లుగా ఉన్న మరో వీడియోను నేపాల్ విపత్తుకు ముడిపెడుతూ షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు.
ఈ వీడియో ఉత్తరాఖండ్లోని చమోలీ ప్రాంతంలో 10 ఆగస్టు 2026న సంభవించిన ఆకస్మిక వరదలకు సంబంధించినది. దీనికి సంబంధించిన మీడియా కథనాలను ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ చూడవచ్చు.
వీడియో 4 :
ఒక భారీ కొండ నుంచి కొండచరియలు విరిగిపడుతున్న దృశ్యాలున్న మరో వీడియోను నేపాల్ విపత్తుకు ముడిపెడుతూ ప్రచారం చేస్తున్నారు.
అయితే, ఈ వీడియో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) కనీసం 11 ఆగస్టు 2026 నుంచి ఇంటర్నెట్లో అందుబాటులో ఉంది. కొలంబియాలో 10 ఆగస్టు 2026న సంభవించిన భూకంపం కారణంగా ఈ కొండచరియలు విరిగిపడినట్లు పలువురు యూజర్లు పేర్కొన్నారు.
చివరిగా, ఆగస్టు 2026 నేపాల్ ఆకస్మిక వరదల దృశ్యాలంటూ సంబంధం లేని పాత వీడియోలను షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు.

I filed a request with McDonald’s earlier this month to access all of the personal data the fast food company collected about me, and I received a stunning 515-page report a few days later that detailed my app interactions in granular detail and predicted I would never stop eating there.
Under the California Consumer Privacy Act, I have the legal right to request access to information from large companies that collect personal data. So I was curious what others might have on me, and I spent the next week filing more than 100 requests.
The CCPA went into effect in 2020, and three of its key provisions are the right to opt out of the selling of personal information, the right to delete that info, and the right to request a copy for yourself.
I focused solely on the latter—access requests—to better understand what data is being collected. Most companies must list two ways for you to file. These are often via a web form, phone number, or email address, as designated in their privacy policy. After you submit a request, companies can take 45 days to complete it.
My experience placing these data access requests was incredibly time-consuming, from finding the right filing methods to verifying my identity multiple times. Most exasperating during this process were the companies that either responded to my access requests with messages concerning the deletion of information, which I explicitly said not to do, or refused to process the request through a method listed in their privacy policy.
Consumer advocates I spoke with were upset with how these requests were handled. “That’s crazy,” said Ben Winters, director of AI and privacy at the Consumer Federation of America. “That’s not an acceptable status quo.” Winters sees these examples as exhibiting the weaknesses of policy frameworks that rely on companies to act responsibly and in good faith.
In accordance with WIRED’s policies, I am disclosing that I used generative AI to draft bureaucratic emails and update my tracking spreadsheet as part of this report. I wrote the body of this article mainly by hand in my scratch notebook.

Dutch court sentences man to life over Rwanda genocide
- Published
A court in the Netherlands has sentenced a Dutch-Rwandan man to life for his involvement in the 1994 genocide in Rwanda.
The 66-year-old, named only as Eugene N, was accused, among other things, of throwing a hand grenade into a crowd of Tutsis who were seeking shelter in a stadium. He was convicted of war crimes and the crime of genocide, having acted with "genocidal intent", the judge said.
Rwanda had sought his extradition in 2014 but the authorities in the Netherlands then launched their own investigation into N, who had become a Dutch citizen.
In 100 days in April 1994, an estimated 800,000 ethnic Tutsis and politically moderate Hutus people were killed by Hutu extremists.
The court in The Hague heard N held an authoritative position in the community at the time of the massacre, overseeing around 1,000 people in Mbazi in southern Rwanda.
"The suspect was a man who was held in high regard and must have been aware of his role and the influence he had as a local administrator," the court explained, adding that he "committed multiple severe crimes".
At a football stadium, he instructed Hutus not to let any of the Tutsis escape. Trapped inside, they were pelted with stones, shot at and had hand grenades thrown at them.
Any who had survived, were killed with clubs and machetes, the court said.
Prior to the stadium massacre, N had watched on as people looted houses and set them on fire.
"Only a lifelong prison sentence does justice to the immense suffering that has been inflicted on the victims and the bereaved families," the court said.
As part of the Dutch investigation opened in 2020, more than 30 witnesses were interviewed. N was subsequently arrested in 2024.
N denied all the charges, the AFP news agency reports, alleging that he was a victim who had lost family in "those horrific events".
"The case has torn his scars open again. He is a broken man," his lawyers are quoted as saying by AFP. They had moved to seek acquittals on all accounts. N was acquitted of the incitement to genocide.
His defence team said they will "almost certainly appeal the charges", according to local news agency ANP.

Uranium supply deal, $5 billion annual trade by 2030: India-Uzbekistan strengthen ties during PM Modi's visit
India and Uzbekistan set a bilateral trade target of USD 5 billion annually by 2030, up from the present of over USD 1 billion.
India and Uzbekistan elevated their bilateral relationship to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership on Sunday following the talks between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev. Marking the 15th anniversary of the strategic partnership, the two nations set a target of $5 billion in annual trade by 2030, agreed to establish a framework for long-term supply of uranium from Uzbekistan to India, and more.
"Uzbekistan is at the heart of Central Asia and is at the heart of India's engagement in the region," PM Modi said.
"A stronger India-Uzbekistan partnership will be a powerful force for peace, progress and prosperity in Central Asia," he added.

Key outcomes of talks with Uzbekistan
PM Modi shared the key outcomes of the meeting with President Mirziyoyev in Tashkent in a post on X (formerly Twitter).
"Elevation of India-Uzbekistan relations to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership. Boost trade to over 5 billion dollars by 2030. Increase cooperation in infrastructure, DPI, AI, critical minerals, energy, space and more. Enhance market access, connectivity, banking and payments," the PM posted.
Trade expansion, payment systems, and more
India and Uzbekistan set a bilateral trade target of $5 billion annually by 2030, up from the present of over $1 billion.
Speaking about trade and investment, the Prime Minister said that matters including market access, connectivity, banking, and payment systems will be addressed in a structured manner.
The discussions between the two leaders focused on trade, investment, infrastructure, digital public infrastructure (including UPI), information technology, critical minerals, defence and security, education, pharmaceuticals, and agriculture, according to news agency PTI.

Long-term uranium supply, defence ties
The two nations agreed to establish a framework for long-term supply of uranium from Uzbekistan to India in line with cooperation in the civil-nuclear energy sector.
Following this, MEA secretary (West) Sibi George informed that “positive discussions” took place about the supply of uranium to India. He also noted that the two nations are close to signing an agreement.
“Positive discussions have happened on a long-term arrangement for the supply of uranium to India. We are close to signing an agreement very shortly. The level of bilateral ties between the two countries has been raised to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, which, as I mentioned, includes a Foreign Minister-level Coordination Group and raising the level of the Joint Commission Meeting, or the Intergovernmental Commission, from the Secretary level to the Ministerial level,” George noted.
"A Business Summit will be held to boost economic ties, and both sides will work on a long-term arrangement for the supply of Uranium. Both sides also set a target of bilateral trade of $5 billion by 2030. That is in the next three years," he added.
Both nations will promote direct linkages between their defense industries to pursue the co-development and co-production of military hardware.
"The close defence and security cooperation between our two countries reflects our deep mutual trust. In the future, we will promote direct linkages, co-production, and co-development between our defence industries," PM Modi said.
"We believe that terrorism, extremism, and separatism pose serious challenges to the entire region," he emphasised.
"Maintaining a policy of zero tolerance against these threats has been, and will continue to be, our shared resolve," the prime minister added.

Elevating ties between India and Uzbekistan
The leaders announced the elevation of strategic ties to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership to reflect the expanding scope and depth of bilateral cooperation.
A new coordination council at the foreign ministers' level will be created to direct cooperation across all sectors.
"We will establish a Coordination Council at the level of foreign ministers to provide direction to all aspects of our cooperation through close coordination," PM Modi also said.
Furthermore, he said that both sides will also elevate their existing joint commission from the level of secretaries to the ministerial level.
The two nations will also organise a bilateral business summit featuring industry leaders from both sides.
"Both sides will jointly organise a business summit featuring business leaders from both nations," he continued.
PM Modi at SCO summit
Prime Minister Modi landed in Tashkent on Saturday on a two-day visit to bolster ties with Uzbekistan.
Following this, the PM is scheduled to travel to Kyrgyzstan from Tashkent to participate in the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit.

As the Centre pushes to widen the role of AYUSH in India’s healthcare system — including through greater coverage, rural outreach and integration with mainstream health services — the country’s AYUSH medical education infrastructure has expanded rapidly. But government data suggests the expansion has been driven largely by non-government institutions.
Of the 541 Ayurveda colleges in April 2024, 467 were non-government — nearly 86% of the total. In Homoeopathy, 236 of 277 colleges, or about 85%, were non-government.
The pattern was similar in other systems. Of the 58 Unani colleges, only 16 were government-run; just three of 17 Siddha colleges and 15 of 71 Yoga and Naturopathy colleges were government institutions. The data clearly indicate that non-government institutions have become an important source of undergraduate medical education in AYUSH.
How has AYUSH education developed in India?
India’s push to expand AYUSH is not merely a recent revival of traditional medicine but an effort to integrate Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha, Yoga, Naturopathy, and Homoeopathy into the formal healthcare system.
Ayurveda has roots going back thousands of years, while Siddha developed in southern India and Unani became established in the subcontinent through centuries of interaction with the Islamic world. Yoga and Naturopathy developed along different trajectories, while Homoeopathy arrived from Europe in the 19th century and subsequently acquired a substantial following in India. The modern Indian state has therefore treated AYUSH not merely as folk medicine but as a collection of systems requiring institutions, education, regulation and research.
The institutional journey gathered pace after Independence, with the Government gradually creating structures for education, research and regulation. The decisive change came in November 2014, when AYUSH became a full-fledged Union ministry. Sowa Rigpa, the traditional Tibetan medical system, was subsequently added to the group.
Since 2014, the Government has sought to move AYUSH from the margins of the health system towards greater institutional recognition. Its agenda includes education, research, standardisation of medicines, hospitals and dispensaries, medicinal plants and the integration of AYUSH services into public healthcare. The expansion of medical education is now one of the clearest signs of this growth.
What is the current state of non-government involvement in India?
The number of AYUSH colleges rose from 789 in 2021 to 971 in 2024, while total admission capacity increased from 63,477 to 79,593. The permitted-seat capacity rose even faster, from 50,711 to 72,490.
But the most striking feature is who is providing this education. In Ayurveda, 467 of 541 colleges in April 2024 were non-government institutions. In Homoeopathy, the corresponding figure was 236 of 277.
There is also evidence of strong demand, particularly for Ayurveda. In 2024-25, 39,952 of 40,136 permitted Ayurveda undergraduate seats were filled. Across Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani and Homoeopathy, 60,890 students were admitted against 63,073 permitted seats. The expansion is consequently producing not just colleges but a growing pipeline of practitioners.
Yet this growth brings a new responsibility. More colleges and graduates do not automatically mean better healthcare. The quality of education, clinical training, regulation and employment will matter enormously — as will the way AYUSH practitioners interact with modern medical services.
The Government’s stated ambition is not necessarily to replace modern medicine, but to make AYUSH part of a broader healthcare system. That makes evidence, patient safety, proper referral and clearly defined professional roles crucial.
How is the AYUSH story moving?
The AYUSH story has moved through three broad stages — preservation of traditional systems, institutional recognition and now large-scale expansion.
“The next challenge is to ensure that this expansion produces competent professionals and useful healthcare rather than simply more seats and degrees,” said an official from AYUSH.

Flash floods at the Nepal-Tibet border have killed at least 543 people and more than 1,500 are missing. Hundreds were foreigners in the area to work, take guided treks or make pilgrimages.
Thousands have been rescued, with some of the injured taken to hospitals in Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu. The number of missing may vary because of progress in the ongoing rescue efforts and differences in how data has been collected and verified among agencies.
Here is how different countries have been affected.
Nepal
Nepal’s disaster management authority said on Friday the death toll in that country had risen to 538, with 977 people missing. The authority said 3,253 people had been rescued by helicopter, and more than 150 of the injured were taken to hospitals in Kathmandu and the districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading.
Local reports cited the National Emergency Operation Centre as saying on Thursday that the missing included 113 Nepali tourists, 85 personnel from the army and police, 161 residents from the Rasuwa district and one from the Nuwakot district.
China
State media reported on Friday that at least five people had died and 558 were missing in Gyirong County, Tibet. The state broadcaster CCTV reported that 260 of the 558 missing people were foreigners. In addition, nearly 100 Chinese citizens were missing on the Nepal side, China’s foreign ministry said.
India
India’s foreign ministry said 288 Indian nationals remained uncontactable, including 73 people who were working on a power project. Nepali officials said many Indian tourists were on pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus.
US
The US state department said 90 of its citizens were unaccounted for in China and Nepal, but that it was not aware of any US deaths. Three Americans have been rescued.
Malaysia
Officials said 51 Malaysians were missing.
Ukraine
Ukraine’s foreign ministry said 55 Ukrainians were missing. The number includes two tourist groups, of 47 and seven people respectively, in addition to one Ukrainian woman travelling with a foreign tour group.
Australia
The Australian government said 39 Australians were missing.
Britain
Officials said 33 of the missing were from Britain.
Canada
The Nepal tourism board (NTB) said 25 of the missing were from Canada.
South Korea
South Korean government officials said nine citizens working on the construction of a hydropower plant in Nepal were missing.
Singapore
Eight Singaporeans were missing, according to the NTB.
Germany
The NTB said eight tourists from Germany were missing.
Russia
The Russian embassy in Nepal said eight of its citizens were missing.
South Africa
The NTB said six South Africans were missing.
Latvia
The NTB said six tourists from Latvia were missing.
Japan
Japanese media said five Japanese tourists were missing, made up of a couple and their children.
New Zealand
Five people from New Zealand were missing, the NTB said.
France
The NTB said four French citizens were missing.
Belgium
The NTB said three people from Belgium were missing.
Spain
The NTB said three visitors from Spain were missing.
Others
The NTB said two people each from Italy, Kazakhstan, Portugal, Ireland and the Netherlands were missing. It said 10 others – one each from Belarus, Finland, Hungary, Israel, Lithuania, the Philippines, Bulgaria, Switzerland, Serbia and Sweden – were also missing.

The Sailors on the USS Abraham Lincoln Deserve Better
The treatment of those on board betrays the promise made by the 16th president himself.
When I was deployed at sea as a junior officer, I used milestones to track the passage of time. Each day counted toward something: a port call, when you get a break on land from the monotony at sea; the “crossing the line ceremony” when a ship crosses the equator (unfortunately, canceled at the last minute for my ship); and, eventually, the date I knew that, no matter what, I would be going home. Even on my worst days, that end point helped me stay focused on the mission and gave me something to be hopeful for.
The USS Abraham Lincoln left its home port of San Diego in November and was scheduled to return home in May. That did not happen. In the middle of this month, it surpassed more than 240 consecutive days at sea—one of the longest deployments on record—and had only a brief working port call early last month, where it appears sailors did not disembark, leaving them still at sea with land in sight. The 5,000 sailors and Marines on board have been working sustained combat operations, dealing with extension after extension and unreliable access to food, basic hygiene supplies, and mail.
The ship carries the name of a president who made a promise in his second inaugural address to care for people who have “borne the battle” and for their families. The treatment of those on board betrays that promise—and it is not limited to just this one ship on this one very long deployment. Rather, the crisis of the Lincoln has illuminated a pattern of callousness and cruelty toward military personnel, people who have sworn an oath to support and defend the Constitution of the United States of America. They have committed to going in harm’s way, but not to being neglected or treated with disrespect by the top of their chain of command.
The military used to understand that troops’ well-being was central to their ability to perform—and that improving the quality of life for those in the armed forces was not just a nicety, but a necessity. From 2021 to 2023, I served as acting director of force resiliency at the Department of the Navy, where I worked as part of an effort to support sailors’ and Marines’ mental health and reduce their suicide risk. Across administrations, both military leaders and career civilians have sought to foster a culture of respect throughout the armed forces. Some of that work was already ongoing during the first Trump administration: a shift toward prevention, building healthy command climates so that problems did not happen in the first place rather than being responded to only after the fact. Under the Biden administration, the Independent Review Commission on Sexual Assault in the Military produced ways to report sexual assault and harassment outside one’s chain of command, and provided independent investigators for those complaints. These efforts showed promise; sexual-assault and suicide rates have both fallen in recent years.
Sailors are resilient and try to make do with whatever they have. But that does not change the fact that on the Lincoln and elsewhere, they are at the mercy of poor planning, or no planning at all. Recent reporting from The New York Times and other outlets has shown that the Lincoln’s and other ships’ logistical issues could have been anticipated as far back as February, when the main base in Bahrain was damaged by an Iranian air strike, and resupply efforts were shifted to Diego Garcia, an island 2,200 miles from where carriers operate. This information was not made public, likely to save face and for operational security. Although Department of Defense leaders have had months to find alternatives, the administration does not appear to have planned for the conflict to stretch on this long.
The Navy needs more capable leaders; instead, an artificial leadership vacuum is being forced upon it from above. Throughout this year, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has been weakening the Navy’s leadership by blocking the promotion of nearly 20 admirals. He removed nine officers from the one-star-promotion list in May, and then seven more from the two-star list in July—by and large women and people of color who were selected by a board of their peers. Among those blocked from picking up a second star: Rear Admiral Amy Bauernschmidt, the first woman to command an aircraft carrier, by coincidence the USS Abraham Lincoln, which she led from 2021 to 2023. For the first time in more than a decade, no active-duty woman is likely to make admiral this year, and the subject is largely being ignored as a “woman problem” instead of being seen for the leadership crisis it is.
When families of the Lincoln’s sailors started talking with reporters, their complaints were met with contempt from the top. A Pentagon spokesperson, Sean Parnell, said that “legitimate challenges of a long combat deployment are being twisted into a false narrative,” and cited his own land-based combat deployment as evidence that the sailors needed to toughen up. Hegseth blamed “the reckless & shameless ‘American’ media.” The department’s rapid-response account answered reporting on food shortages by posting, twice, that sailors had ice cream. When asked whether the Lincoln’s deployment had gone on too long, President Trump’s response was to quip “not nearly long enough.”
I do not know what a junior enlisted sailor feels when they hear these comments. But there is a saying in the military that leadership sets the tone, and when the most senior leaders are flippant at best, and cruel at worst, many will understand that to be the permissible standard. The same leaders who so loudly demand that the country support the troops are not themselves doing so. And in June, this disrespect was put in writing: The Department of Defense issued a nonpublic memo on military equal opportunity and harassment that makes it easier for commanders to dismiss formal harassment complaints and retaliate against whistleblowers. Although service members do where they are told—and over the years, I have done many things while in uniform that I personally disagreed with—the respect of the commander in chief and military leaders is not supposed to be conditional. Most of their predecessors understood caring for those who go in harm’s way as a sacred obligation.
The USS Abraham Lincoln will come home. Another ship will relieve it. But homecoming is not just one day. For some sailors, the process will continue for the rest of their life. They will be expected to get back to business as normal: training, tending to the material condition of their ship, going to their new commands. They may also be moving to a new state (the Lincoln’s home port is planned to shift from San Diego to Bremerton, Washington), reconnecting with their families, and adjusting to a new pace of life. That is how the Navy operates.
The Navy’s SEAL teams have a cooldown period after deployment: time for family, therapy, whatever you need to be ready for next time. The rest of the Navy has no equivalent. Whether a sailor can tend to the home front or get counseling depends entirely on her immediate command, which is to say, on her boss. And for many, the check-engine light won’t show up for years. That was true for me. The PTSD from my three deployments and some traumatic noncombat experiences didn’t really show up until two years after I had left active duty, in part because I was no longer in the middle of it.
These sailors’ needs will then collide with yet another Trump-administration casualty: a weakened Veterans Affairs system. The VA eliminated nearly 30,000 positions last year. The War Horse reported on VA-medical-center policies that recommended discharging most patients from therapy after just eight sessions (far too few, according to many providers), an approach that the VA has denied adopting. The VA has lost more than 1,200 mental-health providers since the start of the administration, and demand is increasing. The department’s mission statement is President Lincoln’s promise itself. The bronze plaque outside its Washington, D.C., headquarters bears his words: “To care for him who shall have borne the battle and for his widow, and his orphan.” That’s not a promise the government is living up to today.

In August 2026, social media users circulated an apparent Truth Social post from U.S. President Donald Trump in which he floats the idea of renaming Lake Ontario to Lake America.
A screenshot of the purported post circulated on X and Threads. Here's what Trump allegedly said, in full:
The United States is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don't expect to be doing much business with Ontario any longer. Thank you for your attention to this matter! President DONALD J. TRUMP
Trump did, in fact, make the above Truth Social post on Aug. 25, which can be viewed on his account (archived). The White House also shared the screenshot on X (archived). As such, we have rated this claim as true.
The president later shared a map of the area, with "Lake Ontario" crossed out and replaced with "Lake America."
Trump's social media posts about renaming Lake Ontario came after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney walked away from negotiations over tariffs amid a contentious trade war between the United States and Canada.
"When the Americans go to the negotiation table first with the right attitude towards our industries and a true partnership, of course we'll come to the negotiation table," Carney said. "But an attitude that Canada is a subsidiary of the United States … that's not something we're going to accept."
Snopes previously confirmed that Trump said he wanted to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America, which he eventually followed through on via executive order.
As with the Gulf of Mexico, Trump is allowed to change Lake Ontario's name for official U.S. government use, but he can't dictate what other governments call it. Lake Ontario is a shared international waterway, and Canada and the United States jointly manage it through multiple agreements.
For more on the United States and Canada's relationship under Trump, we broke down the U.S. president's threats to annex the country's northern neighbor.

Laura Dern is set to give the Laudatio speech honoring George Clooney at Venice Film Festival where, as previously announced, he will be honored on Wed., Sept. 2, with a Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement.
Clooney – who is one of only three people to have been nominated in six different Oscar categories throughout his career (best picture, director, lead actor, supporting actor, original screenplay and adapted screenplay) – will be celebrated on the Lido on the evening of Sept. 2 during the festival’s opening ceremony in his triple guise as actor, director and producer.
Clooney is also being celebrated by Venice for the fact that the works he directed, and his public persona, also reflect his other vocation, “a commitment to social and humanitarian causes, making him a figure of absolute prominence in the universe of show business today,” according to a Biennale statement.
Popular on Variety
Dern in 2025 was part of the cast of Noah Baumbach’s “Jay Kelly,” alongside Clooney that competed in Venice. She previously attended the Venice Film Festival multiple times with “Haunted Summer” (1988) by Ivan Passer; “October Sky” (1998) by Joe Johnston; “Dr. T & the Women” (2000) by Robert Altman; “Inland Empire” (2006) and “Marriage Story” (2019) by Noah Baumbach, for which she went on to win the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress. More recently, Dern was in Venice with “The Son” (2022) by Florian Zeller. In 2006 Dern presented the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement to David Lynch.
Clooney is a Lido aficionado having strutted down the Venice Palazzo del Cinema red carpet several times over the decades with movies such as 1998’s “Out of Sight,” 2005’s “Good Night, and Good Luck,” 2024’s “Wolfs” and “Jay Kelly” last year.
The 83rd edition of Venice will run Sept. 2-12.

Before sunrise, Shameema slips on her worn rubber sandals and checks the insulated box – the ice packs inside must maintain the crucial cold chain at between 2C and 8C (35.6-46.4F). She hoists the container on one shoulder and steps out into the dark.
Tanzeela follows with her own pack, after quickly retying the laces of her canvas shoes. Both women live in Pulwama, a district where summer temperatures climb to 37C. Their destination lies higher, out of the valley where asphalt turns to dirt track and then to a barely distinguishable footpath along the floor of the mountain pine forests.
Shameema, 45, has worked as a vaccinator for more than a decade, while Tanzeela, 28, joined the programme three years ago. They form part of India’s army of 2.5 million frontline health workers – the human machinery behind the world’s largest immunisation campaign.
Shameema estimates she has administered polio drops to more than 3,000 children during her years as a vaccinator. She remembers a boy in her village who limped with a deformed leg, the legacy of a polio infection before India had fully eradicated it. It is this memory that keeps her going.
“I saw that child struggle to walk to school,” Shameema says during a pause near a stream. “His mother held him on her back until he grew too heavy. [People in] these mountains need protection too – the children here deserve the same health as those in the cities.”
This morning, they are walking towards Namblan, a meadow ringed by pine trees where nearly 50 dhokas, the seasonal mud-and-stone homes of Gujjar and Bakarwal nomadic families, are scattered over the hillsides.
Even before the paved roads end, the electricity lines stop far below these settlements. Horses are the primary transport for the families who spend the summer months with their livestock in these highlands.
The women climb more than 12 miles (20km) with the heavy insulated cool boxes, which hold vials of the oral vaccines, ice packs and the thick paper registers that document the day.
Tanzeela has given polio drops to about 800 children since she joined the programme. She wears the same shoes she uses for farm work. The soles have worn thin, but they grip the rocky paths better than the sandals of some colleagues, she says. One fellow worker walks barefoot for parts of the trail.
“The payment is small and the paths are steep,” Tanzeela says. “I think about my own nephews when I climb. The drops take seconds, but they change a life for ever.”
Their compensation is 125 rupees a day – about £1 – from the state government for the two-day vaccination campaigns, which happen four to six times a year during the national immunisation drives that target all children under five.
India’s polio programme represents a triumph of planning, vigilance and human endurance. The country has been certified polio-free since 2014 – with the final confirmed case in January 2011 in West Bengal – largely thanks to a surveillance network of 60,000 health workers, who monitor 40,000 reporting sites for acute flaccid paralysis, the signature symptom of wild poliovirus.
The oral polio vaccine uses a live but weakened form of the virus developed by a Polish scientist, Albert Sabin, in the late 1950s. The two drops placed on a child’s tongue stimulate antibodies in the intestinal lining that destroy the virus before it can enter the bloodstream and attack the nervous system.
The same gut immunity reduces viral shedding in infected children, ending the chain of transmission in communities where clean water comes from streams and springs. The oral formula creates communal immunity, protecting whole clusters of children who share courtyards and water sources.
This biological shield proves especially vital in the disputed region of Indian-administered Kashmir, where 73% of the 14 million population live in rural areas, with hundreds of thousands of children under six living in far-flung villages and mountain settlements.
Seasonal migration routes take the Gujjar and Bakarwal pastoral communities of about 1.2 million people far from clinics and hospitals during the summer. Reaching them requires coordination between state health departments, local panchayats (village councils) and the frontline workers who know the mountain trails.
The national immunisation effort targets 27 million children under five, and up to 1.7 million vaccinators can be deployed during a single day of a national immunisation drive. Those workers staff 750,000 booths, then fan out with mobile teams into forests, deserts and urban slums.
The scale of this operation dwarfs most military logistics exercises. Insulated boxes travel by foot, bicycle, boat and bus, but in regions such as Kashmir, the final leg of this journey is always down to women travelling on foot.
The dhokas sit miles apart, sometimes separated by ravines and streams that swell with melted snow. A mother might walk two hours to meet the vaccinators halfway, her baby strapped to her back. The workers record these encounters in their paper registers, marking the child’s name, age and the date of the dose.
Shameema and Tanzeela know the terrain and the communities, and time their ascent to reach the first dhokas as the families finish their morning prayers.
“The families welcome us with tea and bread,” Shameema says. “They know the value of these drops. Some remember the days prior to full eradication, when children in neighbouring villages fell ill.”
India’s greatest public health victory still depends on these health workers willing to make such critical journeys for little reward, dedicated to maintaining the country’s protection against the devastating disease.
By late afternoon, the final dhoka receives the vaccinators. A child opens their mouth, gets two drops on their tongue, another name goes on the register and the insulated box is a bit lighter as the women begin their descent down the same tracks they climbed hours earlier. It will be dark by the time they reach home.

President Donald Trump suggested referring NBC News anchor Kristen Welker for possible punishment by the Federal Communications Commission after the “Meet the Press” moderator made innocuous remarks about candidates the President has backed in the run-up to the nation’s midterm elections later this year.
Trump’s chilling diatribe, released via Truth Social, appeared to be misinformed. During a local segment in which Welker previewed her program with anchors on NBC’s Washington, D.C. station, WRC, she said that Trump had enjoyed “mixed results,” with some of the Republican candidates he’s backed losing in primaries, but also noted that Trump is “going to loom large over these midterms. There’s no doubt about that.”
Trump called for Welker to be “reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment.” The Commission can’t directly mete out condemnation to individual journalists, but it can put bumps in the path of the company that owns the station as well as NBC News. That would be NBCUniversal, currently a unit of Comcast that is slated to be spun off from its parent over the next several months.
Popular on Variety
“Kristen is one of the best in the business and we stand by her,” NBC News said in a statement Sunday afternoon. Welker did not utter any of the remarks that angered Trump during NBC’s actual broadcast of “Meet the Press” on Sunday.
Under Trump and Chairman Brendan Carr, the FCC has been more activist than at any other time in recent memory. The Commission is currently enmeshed in a legal tangle with Walt Disney Co and ABC. The FCC has ordered Disney to file for renewals for ABC’s eight owned-and-operated stations years ahead of schedule. In filings, Disney has said its applications were made “under protest in response to an unlawful, arbitrary, and unconstitutional order.” “The View,” which has thrived in recent years with discussion of politics, has also found itself in the administration’s crosshairs. The FCC has probed whether the program has violated so-called “equal-time” election laws following the appearance of political figures, launching its investigation after James Talarico, the Democratic Senate candidate from Texas, appeared on the show in February. The FCC issued new guidance in January that late-night and daytime hosts needed to give equal time to political candidates from various parties, claiming the programs might be working along partisan lines.
Disney and ABC have alleged in a suit filed in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia that the FCC is in violation of the First Amendment.
Trump’s relationship with Welker appears to run hot and cold. Many of the interviews he agrees to do with NBC News have been with her, and Trump has made a handful of appearances on “Meet the Press” to speak with her. But on Sunday, he called Welker “the Unpopular ‘Hostess’ of the once great Meet the Press, now considered Meet the Fake Press.”
To be sure, Welker’s analysis was accurate. Some candidates backed by Trump, including Randy Feenstra, a Republican candidate for the Iowa governor seat, and Mike Lindell, the MyPillow CEO who made a bid to run as the Republican candidate in Minnesota’s gubernatorial race, both lost in primaries. More recently, Senator Darline Graham, who has filled in on an interim basis for her late brother, former South Carolina Senator Lindsey Graham, won a primary for the Senate seat in her home state.

Researchers at the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition (ICMR-NIN), Hyderabad, have found that exposure to lead can significantly disrupt the natural waste-clearing and recycling system of nerve cells, providing fresh insight into how environmental factors may contribute to cellular changes associated with neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer’s disease.
Effects of lead and protein fragments associated with Alzheimer’s disease studied
The study examined the effects of lead and amyloid-beta (Aβ) peptides, protein fragments associated with Alzheimer’s disease, on human neuronal cells in the laboratory. Nerve cells rely on lysosomes, tiny structures within cells that act as a waste-disposal and recycling system. They break down damaged proteins and other unwanted cellular material, helping maintain cellular health and function.
Impact on structures that act as a waste-disposal and recycling system
The researchers found that exposure to either lead or amyloid-beta peptides individually impaired lysosomal function. However, combined exposure caused significantly greater disruption as it reduced cell survival, disturbed the acidic environment required for normal lysosomal function and damaged lysosomal structure.
In addition, lysosomal membranes became unstable and leaky, potentially allowing harmful enzymes to escape into the cell and cause further damage. According to the researchers, these findings suggest that environmental lead exposure may amplify the cellular stress associated with amyloid-beta and make nerve cells more vulnerable to injury.
ICMR-NIN’s Head of Cell Biology Suresh Challa, who led the research team, said, “Understanding these cellular changes can help us better understand how environmental exposures may influence neuronal health.” “The study highlights the importance of understanding the interaction between environmental pollutants and biological factors in maintaining brain health,” said ICMR-NIN director Bharati Kulkarni, according to a press release.
