Harlequins snap up Zimbabwe winger Sigauke
- Published
Harlequins have signed Zimbabwe winger Edward Sigauke.
The 22-year-old has played 12 times, scoring eight tries, for his country, having made his international debut in 2024.
Quins head coach Jason Gilmore said: "Eddie is a player we've been tracking and we're really pleased to get his signing over the line.
"He's got tremendous speed and footwork that makes him a real handful for any defence, and we believe he's got all the raw tools to become a weapon for us out wide.
"What excites us most is his potential - he's still developing as a player, and we can't wait to see how he grows within our environment as he takes the next steps in his career."
Sigauke will join his new team-mates from 1 September in preparation for the new campaign, which begins with a Prem Rugby Cup home game against Leicester on 5 September.
"This is a new chapter for me, and I want to make the most of it - working hard every day, learning from the players and coaches around me," he said.

The legal case against 
Lashkar-e-Taiba
 founder Hafiz Muhammad Saeed has acquired a fresh dimension in India. In July 2026, the National Investigation Agency named Saeed in a supplementary chargesheet in the 
Pahalgam terror attack
 case, charging him in his individual capacity and as the founder and chief of Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) and its active proxy, The Resistance Front (TRF). The NIA mentioned a cross-border conspiracy behind the April 22, 2025 attack, which killed 26 civilians. A special NIA court subsequently issued a non-bailable warrant against Saeed.
The development came as Mumbai Police separately began proceedings for a trial in absentia against Saeed and five other Pakistan-based accused in the 2008 Mumbai terror attacks. The proclamation covers Saeed, LeT operations chief Zaki-ur-Rehman Lakhvi, Sajid Mir, Abu Alqama, Asim alias Abu Qahafa and Major Abdur Rehman Pasha. The police have also approached the Union home ministry to facilitate service of the proclamation orders through Interpol.
The two cases, separated by 17 years, bring together different phases of LeT's history. One concerns an attack in Kashmir, the region that became the organisation's principal battlefield in the 1990s. The other concerns the Mumbai attacks, which demonstrated how far LeT's operational reach had expanded beyond the Kashmir insurgency.
But LeT did not begin in Kashmir, nor did 
Hafiz Saeed
 first emerge as a militant leader there. The organisation's institutional roots can be traced to the Afghan jihad of the 1980s, when Pakistan became a major centre for the mobilisation, training and movement of Islamist fighters.
LeT's major attacks
The Afghan war that created LeT's foundations
The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979 created an environment in which Islamist networks from Pakistan and other parts of the Muslim world expanded rapidly. Among the prominent figures associated with this mobilisation was Palestinian scholar Abdullah Azzam, who helped organise foreign volunteers for the Afghan jihad and promoted the idea of jihad as a broader obligation extending beyond a single battlefield.
It was in this environment that Azzam worked with Hafiz Saeed, a Pakistani Sunni scholar who had studied in Saudi Arabia. According to Bruce Riedel's 
Deadly Embrace: Pakistan, America, and the Future of the Global Jihad
, the two were involved in establishing Markaz-ud-Dawa-wal-Irshad (MDI), a religious organisation that combined missionary activity with support for jihad. MDI developed training infrastructure in Afghanistan, including in Kunar province, where recruits could gain battlefield experience. Riedel also records links between the organisation and Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI).
Lashkar-e-Taiba subsequently emerged as the military wing associated with this network. The US state department describes LeT as having formed in the late 1980s as the militant wing of MDI, an organisation originally established in opposition to the Soviet presence in Afghanistan. The Australian government dates LeT's formation as a military organisation to 1989.
The exact formation date therefore varies depending on whether the establishment of MDI, the creation of its military wing or the later formalisation of LeT is being referred to. What is clearer is the sequence: the Afghan jihad provided the organisation's early ideological, human and training infrastructure, while the end of the Soviet war opened the way for that infrastructure to be redirected towards other conflicts.
Why Lashkar-e-Taiba was established
LeT's early purpose was shaped by two connected objectives: participation in the Afghan jihad and preparation for jihad in Kashmir and India. Riedel describes MDI's objective as applying the experience of the Afghan war to Kashmir and India, including training Kashmiris alongside Afghan mujahideen so they could gain combat experience.
The changing situation in Afghanistan accelerated that transition. The Soviet withdrawal meant that the battlefield that had brought together thousands of militants was no longer the same. At the same time, violence in Jammu and Kashmir was rising sharply.
The Australian government's account of LeT's history says the organisation was originally formed to wage militant jihad against the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan and shifted its focus to the insurgency in Indian-administered Kashmir during the 1990s after Soviet troops withdrew. It identifies the organisation's stated objective as uniting Kashmir with Pakistan, while noting that its broader ideological objectives extended beyond Kashmir.
Kashmir thus became the next major theatre in which the organisation could deploy the personnel, training and networks developed during the Afghan war.
From Kunar to Kashmir
The shift towards Kashmir coincided with the rapid growth of the insurgency there. Riedel records that incidents of violence in Kashmir rose from 390 in 1988 to 2,100 in 1989 and nearly 4,000 in 1990. Against this backdrop, Saeed's organisation began establishing infrastructure in and around Kashmir while maintaining training facilities in Pakistan and Afghanistan.
LeT's emergence also coincided with changes among the various groups fighting in Kashmir. The Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front advocated an independent Kashmir, while Pakistan's security establishment increasingly favoured groups committed to the territory's integration with Pakistan. Riedel describes efforts to strengthen pro-Pakistan organisations and isolate the JKLF, which was regarded as too independent. Hizbul Mujahideen became a major pro-Pakistan militant force, while LeT developed its own network and capabilities.
By the 1990s, Kashmir had become LeT's principal operational theatre. The organisation developed training and recruitment networks and directed fighters towards attacks on Indian security forces. Stephen Tankel, in 
Lashkar-e-Taiba: From 9/11 to Mumbai
, describes Kashmir as the group's primary objective even as its connections to the wider global jihadist movement expanded.
This distinction is important. LeT developed relationships with al Qaida and other jihadist groups, but its core focus remained India and Kashmir. Riedel similarly distinguishes between the different objectives of the groups operating in the region, noting that the Afghan Taliban remained primarily focused on Afghanistan while LeT concentrated on South Asia. At the operational level, however, their cooperation increased.
Who is Hafiz Saeed
Hafiz Saeed - From cleric to terrorist
Saeed's prominence grew alongside the institutional development of MDI and LeT. He was not simply the leader of an armed organisation. The network around him combined religious propagation, education, charity and terror activity.
Riedel describes Saeed as a prominent Pakistani Sunni scholar who worked with Azzam in developing MDI. The organisation's combination of religious activity and military infrastructure provided the foundation for the later growth of LeT.
LeT's recruitment base was also closely connected to Pakistani society. Riedel writes that the organisation was predominantly Punjabi and recruited from many of the same communities and neighbourhoods as the Pakistani army and ISI. He also describes LeT camps located near army bases and the involvement of retired military personnel in training fighters.
The nature and extent of state support for LeT has remained a matter of dispute, but the organisation's relationship with Pakistan's security establishment became an important part of its history. The United Nations Security Council identifies LeT as a Pakistan-based organisation and records its links with al Qaida and the Taliban, as well as its use of Jamaat-ud-Dawa for financial, logistical and infrastructural support.
LeT survives Pakistani ban after 9/11
The September 11, 2001 attacks changed the environment for militant organisations operating from Pakistan. The United States designated LeT as a Foreign Terrorist Organisation in December 2001, while Pakistan banned the group in January 2002.
The ban, however, did not eliminate the network. The US state department says Saeed subsequently changed the group's name to Jamaat-ud-Dawa and expanded its humanitarian activities, while continuing to disseminate its message through JuD's media outlets.
Riedel similarly writes that although LeT was formally banned, it continued to operate and Saeed remained in charge. He describes the organisation's large facility at Muridke near Lahore, which included schools, dormitories, a garment factory, an iron foundry and a mosque.
This structure helped the network maintain a presence beyond its armed operations. Religious institutions, charitable activity, fundraising and recruitment provided a broader organisational base that could continue even when the LeT name itself faced restrictions.
The United Nations says LeT used JuD as a front through which it provided financial, logistical and infrastructural support for terrorist activity. It also records that an al Qaida operative, Abu Zubaydah, was captured in 2002 in a LeT safe house in Faisalabad, illustrating the organisation's connections to the wider jihadist network.
Four decades of evolution
From Kashmir insurgency to Mumbai
The years after 2001 saw LeT's operational reach extend beyond the traditional Kashmir battlefield. The United Nations records that the organisation conducted terrorist operations against military and civilian targets from the 1990s onwards, including attacks in New Delhi and Mumbai and the December 2001 Parliament attack, in which Jaish-e-Mohammed was also involved.
The 2008 Mumbai attacks represented the most significant expansion of that reach. Ten attackers carried out coordinated assaults across Mumbai between November 26 and 29, killing 166 people. The attack targeted several locations, including the Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus, the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel, the Oberoi-Trident and Nariman House.
The operation also demonstrated the organisational depth behind LeT's attacks. Riedel's account details the role of David Coleman Headley, who joined LeT in Pakistan and later conducted reconnaissance in Mumbai. Between 2005 and 2008, Headley travelled repeatedly to India, studying targets, recording locations and reporting back to LeT.
The Mumbai operation therefore represented more than an extension of the Kashmir insurgency. It demonstrated the organisation's ability to plan and execute a complex attack far from its traditional theatre while drawing on personnel, training and logistical networks developed over decades.
Why Afghanistan remained part of the network
The shift to Kashmir did not end LeT's involvement in Afghanistan. Instead, the two theatres became connected through overlapping militant networks.
Riedel wrote that LeT became increasingly active in Afghanistan, including operations against Indian interests and clashes with Nato forces. He also described growing operational links between LeT and the Afghan Taliban, particularly the Haqqani network.
The United Nations likewise records LeT's activity in Afghanistan and its links with al Qaida and the Taliban. The Australian government has documented LeT's continued presence in Afghanistan and reported that the UN estimated the group had close to 1,000 members operating there in May 2020.
Afghanistan therefore remained an important part of LeT's network even after Kashmir became its main operational focus. The relationships, training environments and infrastructure developed during the Afghan jihad continued to provide connections to other militant organisations.
Saeed's legal history and the Pahalgam case
Saeed's subsequent legal history illustrates the difference between Pakistan's formal action against LeT and the organisation's continued existence through associated structures.
Pakistan arrested Saeed in 2019 on terrorism-financing charges. He was convicted in several cases and received additional sentences in subsequent proceedings. The UN Security Council's current sanctions information says Saeed is in Pakistani custody serving a cumulative 78-year sentence following convictions in seven terrorism-financing cases.
India, meanwhile, has continued to pursue him over alleged involvement in major terror attacks attributed to LeT.
The latest development is the NIA's supplementary chargesheet in the Pahalgam case. The agency has named Saeed both individually and as the chief of LeT and TRF, alleging that he was part of the wider conspiracy behind the April 2025 attack.
The subsequent non-bailable warrant followed the NIA's request for Saeed's arrest and custodial interrogation. Meanwhile, Mumbai Police has begun the process for an in-absentia trial against Saeed and five other Pakistan-based accused in the 26/11 case.
From Afghan jihad to Kashmir
From Afghan jihad to Pahalgam
Lashkar-e-Taiba's four-decade history can be traced through a sequence of changing battlefields and organisational forms. Its foundations were laid during the Afghan jihad, when Hafiz Saeed and Abdullah Azzam helped build MDI and the networks around it. After the Soviet withdrawal, the organisation redirected much of its experience and infrastructure towards Kashmir, where it became a major Pakistan-based militant group.
The 2002 ban did not erase the network. It adapted through Jamaat-ud-Dawa and other associated structures, while maintaining religious, charitable and recruitment networks across Pakistan. Its links with militant groups operating in Afghanistan also survived, even as India and Kashmir remained its central focus.
The Mumbai attacks showed how far that network could project violence beyond Kashmir. The Pahalgam investigation has now brought the story back to the same region where LeT established much of its early operational identity.
The latest legal proceedings against Saeed therefore sit at the end of a history that began not in Mumbai or Pahalgam, but in the Afghan jihad of the 1980s.

A rumor (archived) that Disney bought Dolly Parton's Dollywood theme park circulated online after the beloved star's death in August 2026.
The Mouse Trap News Instagram account shared news of the alleged takeover, writing, "What do you think of Disney taking over Dollywood?!"
(@mousetrapnews, accessed via Instagram)
The story also appeared on Mouse Trap News' Facebook (archived) and TikTok (archived) accounts. Commenters across the platforms appeared to question whether the rumor was true. Snopes readers also contacted us to investigate its legitimacy.
The rumor about Disney buying Dollywood is not real. Mouse Trap News is a satirical news outlet covering the Disney parks. Profile descriptions on Facebook, Instagram and TikTok described the accounts' output as "100% Fake."
The outlet also posted a written story on its website, which describes its content as "100% made-up parody and satire stories about Disney Parks." Therefore, we find this claim was labeled satire.
Search engines such as DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo did not find any credible reporting to suggest Disney had bought Dollywood (archived, archived, archived). Because of both Disney and Parton's worldwide fame, reputable sources would have reported on such a takeover, if true.
Mouse Trap News shared the rumor on or around Aug. 28, 2026, three days after Parton's death.
The video that Mouse Trap News posted on its social media profiles used a combination of footage of Dollywood and Disney parks, as well as unrelated clips from two authentic videos. Some clips came from a video of Parton speaking about the "My Life of Many Colors Museum," which was set to open in the fall of 2026. Other clips came from a video of Dollywood Parks & Resorts President Eugene Naughton speaking about how the park would honor Parton's legacy after her death.
Remembering Parton as the park's "dreamer-in-chief," Naughton told viewers:
I know a lot of people are concerned that things are going to change without Dolly being present here and I want to assure you that it's not. Just know that we're all going to keep her alive here.
For further reading, Snopes has previously debunked stories from Mouse Trap News. For example, in June 2025, we alerted readers to another satirical story about Disney banning MAGA hats.
Since the effectiveness of satire is subjective, we use "originated as satire" or "labeled satire" ratings based on creators' description of their work. It's your call on whether you agree.

Google Maps renames Lake Ontario 'Lake America' in US - but not Canada
“It’s absolutely backwards,” Ontario Premier Doug Ford says after Google adopts “Lake America” for US users while Canada still sees Lake Ontario.
WASHINGTON: Google redesignated Lake Ontario as "Lake America" on maps seen by US users Sunday (Aug 30) after President Donald Trump announced he was renaming the body of water, with a Canadian official slamming the cross-border tensions as "absolutely backwards."
People in Canada will still see Lake Ontario, the Indigenous-rooted name used for the lake since the 17th century, on their devices and computers, the US-based tech giant said.
The shock nomenclatural spat erupted as the latest element of Trump's "America First" narrative, with longtime allies the United States and Canada ramping up a trade war that has seen Washington and Ottawa slap tit-for-tat tariffs on each other.
Apple's Maps app, which comes preinstalled on all iPhones, makes no mention of "Lake America" on its maps as of Sunday morning.
Google said it made its change in line with the US Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), the official federal database for geographic names.
"Since we update Google Maps to reflect name changes in official government sources, which is GNIS for the US, people using Maps in the US will see 'Lake America,' those in Canada will continue to see 'Lake Ontario,' and those outside of the US and Canada will see both names," Google said on its blog.
GULF OF AMERICA
The change mirrors Trump's unilateral alteration of the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America in January 2025 - a move Mexico has also rejected.
Ontario is the smallest by surface area of the five Great Lakes, which straddle the Canada-US border between Ontario province and the US state of New York.
The province's premier, Doug Ford, offered fresh criticism on Sunday of the trade dispute and Trump's lake-name change.
"It's absolutely backwards. It was like something out of (US comedy TV show) 'Saturday Night Live' when he signed a document saying - changed to 'Lake America.' No one's going to call it Lake of America," Ford told ABC talk show "This Week."
"It's just so disappointing."
"TAX ON AMERICAN PEOPLE"
Ford also warned that while a trade war would harm both countries, "it'd be definitely devastating on the US" given that Canada has been by far the largest purchaser of US vehicles. Should those buys dry up, US auto factories would be hit hard.
"A tariff on Canada is nothing more than a tax on American people," he said. "It's probably the worst move you could ever do."
Canada and the US have a deeply interconnected auto manufacturing sector, and a sizeable portion of parts for US vehicles are made in Canada.
Trump himself waded in Sunday to say Americans "want to make our own cars."
"Canada has been ripping us off for years - NO LONGER!" Trump posted on his Truth Social platform.

Antonio helps young Ghanaians chase Premier League dreams
- Published
In the heat of rural Leicestershire, the Samba Stars are chasing their dream.
Head coach Freddie Okyere has just finished a shooting exercise and allows the squad to catch their breath.
The teenagers from the Ghanaian academy, which is backed by former West Ham and Nottingham Forest forward Michail Antonio, have spent two and a half months in England with one goal - impressing clubs and earning a contract.
While scouts do visit west Africa, it is rare for academies to travel to the UK to put their players directly in front of professional clubs.
"The talent the lads have is incredible," said Antonio.
"We created Samba Stars Academy to give young players in Ghana access to elite coaching, shape them as players and create real avenues into the pro game and show how much talent Ghana has."
Based in Kumasi while building a new facility in Bompata, just over 100 miles north of Ghana's capital Accra, the Samba Stars' tactic has paid off.
Bournemouth, Everton, Manchester City, Charlton, Preston, Barnsley and Peterborough have all taken players on trial this summer.
"The first two or three weeks it hadn't sunk in, but then they saw the facilities we'd be [using] and the teams we were playing," said Okyere.
"They want to go and show what they can do. They are hungry, they really want it. I'm hoping there will be so much interest because we have so much talent here.
"With the facilities we will have in Ghana we feel we will be top two, top three [academies]. We hope we can bring the best of Ghana to Europe."
There are other success stories, with midfielder Listowell Lord Hinneh joining Middlesbrough in February after a trial., external
The 18-year-old has trained with the first team after swapping west Africa for England's north east.
"When I came in January, it was so cold. Experiencing something like that for the first time was tough," he told BBC Sport.
"Moving was a big milestone. It just makes me feel the dreams I've been having, thinking of trying to find myself in Europe to become a professional footballer.
"I feel the kind of dreams that I want, I'm on the verge. I'm on the way [to] becoming who I wanted to become."
Hinneh - whose sister Groovy lives in Leeds - met with the Samba Stars squad on their trip, offering advice.
"[I told them] what you've been dreaming about the future, it starts from here," he said.
"Don't just try, be so passionate. You need to play and enjoy it because you can have the success in whatever you're doing. You have to just put your heart in it."
'I'm seeing a different side of professional football'
All but one of the 20-strong visiting group initially had their visa application denied before eventually being admitted after re-evaluation.
Since arriving in the UK, they have been hosted by Brook House College in Market Harborough and trained at Harborough Town, who play in the National League North.
"The football [here] is very detailed," said 17-year-old goalkeeper Joshua Tetteh Tuwor.
"In Ghana we have the same passion but I'm seeing a different side of professional football.
"We are grateful to have such opportunities to train with elite coaches."
Rob Newman, formerly West Ham's head of recruitment and Manchester City's international scouting and recruitment manager, spent time with the academy in Ghana earlier this year and has helped coach them in Harborough.
"Hopefully clubs can see the potential," said the ex-Bristol City and Norwich defender.
"Nothing will give me greater pleasure in six months [than] going to see these boys playing in a first team in Europe. I believe they are two or three months away from being able to do that."
The Stars have played a series of games against youth teams from the EFL and non-league.
They started with a 9-0 thumping of Dorking Wanderers and also beat Under-21 sides from Sheffield Wednesday, Luton and Peterborough.
There were draws at Sheffield United and Barnsley while their only defeat came 3-2 against Preston's U21s.
Antonio watched them thrash Peterborough U19s 6-0 last month.
"You can see from what they've done since they've been in the UK - the results against top teams - that they have what it takes to play pro level," said the 36-year-old.
"It's great to help knock down barriers and give these lads a real chance."
'Back home everyone is depending on you'
Ghana have reached five of the past six Fifa World Cups - having never qualified before 2006 - and made the quarter-finals in 2010.
At this year's tournament, where they exited in the last-32 against Colombia, eight members of the squad were born overseas.
The Black Stars may not have come to rely heavily on diaspora talent, unlike some other African nations, yet the Ghana Football Association has made noises about widening its global search - something which could potentially impact home-grown talent.
"You have to have a tough mentality," said Sherif Mashud, an 18-year-old striker who has already had a trial with Hungarian top-tier side Zalaegerszegi thanks to his involvement with Samba Stars.
"Back home everyone is depending on you, everyone is looking up to you to succeed, to come and help them, your friends, your family. Everyone is praying for you."
The new English season has begun with six Ghana internationals on Premier League books: Mohammed Kudus at Tottenham, Antoine Semenyo with Manchester City, Brighton's Ibrahim Osman, Ipswich's new signing Abdul Fatawu and Coventry's Brandon Thomas-Asante and Caleb Yirenkyi.
The first to play in the English top flight was striker Nii Lamptey when he joined Aston Villa in 1994, while midfielder Michael Essien has made the most appearances, winning two titles with Chelsea.
Only two other Ghanaians have lifted the Premier League trophy - Jeffrey Schlupp and Daniel Amartey when Leicester stunned the world in 2015-16.
"Back home we've got people you grew up with and you might miss them, but that doesn't kill the dreams I'm here for," said Hinneh, who lists Kudus as his biggest inspiration and hopes to follow his heroes into the top flight after Boro missed out on promotion in last season's Championship play-off final.
"I'm trying to figure out what the reality is, what the future holds for me and then just chase the dreams."

Brentford sign £40m defender Diouf from West Ham
- Published
Brentford have signed West Ham defender El Hadji Malick Diouf in a deal worth up to £40m.
The 21-year-old Senegal left-back has joined on a five-year contract, with the club having an option to extend it by a further year.
The move sees Brentford paying an initial £35m for the player, with a further £5m in add-ons.
Diouf played in West Ham's Championship opener against Burnley, but was excluded from the matchday squads of the Hammers' following two games as a deal was worked on.
He was the Bees' priority defensive target in this transfer window, but discussions had stalled this summer before being reopened earlier this week.
Diouf is returning to the Premier League after suffering relegation with the Hammers last season.
And his sale represents a big profit for West Ham on a player they paid Slavia Prague £19m for a year ago.
Diouf played 34 times for West Ham last season, providing five assists.
"He's a player that fits our ideal age profile, with lots of room to still develop," Brentford head coach Keith Andrews said.
Diouf said Andrews had convinced him he could continue to improve at the club.
And when asked about his ambition upon joining his new club said: "Why not win the league?"
He is Brentford's fifth summer signing of the summer after the arrivals of striker Callum Wilson, midfielder Mamadou Sangare, centre-back Jannik Schuster and winger Jaidon Anthony.
After breaking into the Senegal side last year, Diouf played four times at the World Cup this summer.
While West Ham were relegated after finishing 18th last season, Brentford enjoyed an excellent campaign under Andrews, finishing ninth and just missing out on European football on goal difference.
Brentford began their season on Saturday with a 3-0 win over Tottenham Hotspur and play Leeds on Sunday in their next league game.

The two leaders were seen sharing a hug and handshake after PM Modi's arrival. The Prime Minister is expected to hold delegation-level talks with Uzbek President Mirziyoyev during the visit.
In his departure statement, PM Modi said the India-Uzbekistan Strategic Partnership had witnessed significant advancement in recent years.

For many young people dealing with stress, loneliness, family pressures, relationship concerns or fears about the future, the inability to speak openly can itself become a barrier to seeking help. Against this backdrop, anonymous peer-support platforms are emerging as a possible bridge between silence and support.
One such initiative, Let’s Talk Life, developed by mental health professionals at National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences (NIMHANS) and technologists at the International Institute of Information Technology-Bangalore (IIIT-B), allows young people to share their concerns anonymously and seek emotional support without fear of judgement.
A recent paper analysing 137 posts on the platform found that users commonly turned to it to express emotional distress, seek suggestions, make sense of their experiences, and receive validation. The findings were published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health.
The platform does not require users to disclose personally identifiable information. Responses are provided by trained peer volunteers and reviewed by mental health professionals before being posted.
Stigma, a barrier
“Many young people hesitate to approach formal mental health services because of stigma, fear of being misunderstood, or the belief that their problems are not serious enough. A safe, anonymous space can become the first point where they articulate what they are experiencing,” said Seema Mehrotra, Professor in the Department of Clinical Psychology at NIMHANS and Principal Investigator of the project.
Stress, loneliness
The study found that users discussed concerns ranging from academic pressure, family conflicts, and relationship difficulties to self-doubt, loneliness, anxiety, and depressive symptoms.
Stress, uncertainty, helplessness, loneliness, and feeling overwhelmed were among the prominent emotional states reported in the posts. Family pressures, relationship difficulties, self-esteem concerns, and mental health symptoms also featured frequently.
Users approached the platform for several reasons, including seeking practical suggestions, expressing emotions, sharing reflections, understanding their experiences, and seeking reassurance.
Peer support
“Peer support does not replace professional care. Its role is to create a bridge — helping a young person feel heard, understand their emotions better, and, wherever required, take the next step towards professional help,” Dr. Mehrotra said.
Researchers said young people often turn first to informal support systems, such as friends and peers, before seeking professional assistance. Digital platforms can make such support more accessible by allowing users to communicate anonymously.
Trained volunteers
Abhishek Karishiddimath, Scientist at the ICMR Centre for Advanced Research, NIMHANS, said the peer volunteers responding on the platform were themselves young people.
“They undergo structured training in empathetic, respectful, and solution-oriented responses. Every response is reviewed by mental health experts to ensure safety and appropriateness,” he said.
The platform is designed as a low-intensity support option rather than a crisis service or substitute for counselling. Responders are trained to identify signs of significant distress that may require professional intervention and encourage users to seek appropriate help.
First step towards seeking help
“Sometimes people do not immediately need advice; they need a space where they can express what they are going through without being judged. The experience of being heard, validated, and gaining a fresh perspective can be an important first step towards healing and growth,” Dr. Mehrotra said.
The researchers said such platforms could have a role in public mental health, particularly given India’s large youth population and widespread use of digital platforms.
They stressed that professional mental healthcare remains important for persistent or serious concerns, while moderated peer-support spaces could help young people articulate emotional struggles that might otherwise remain unspoken.
Future efforts should focus on strengthening such platforms and establishing clearer pathways to professional psychological support, they added.

Delhi police changes IO amid family raises concerns over a hit-and-run case
On August 2, Khanna, a local singer, was returning home to Uttam Nagar on his bike when an unknown vehicle rammed into his bike
Weeks after 35-year-old singer Jatin Khanna was killed in a hit-and-run accident on August 2, near the Mukundpur flyover in northwest Delhi, the Delhi Police on Sunday said they had changed the investigating officer (IO) after the family raised concerns about the progress of the probe and protested multiple times outside the Jahangirpuri police station.
On August 2, Khanna, a local singer, was returning home to Uttam Nagar on his bike when an unknown vehicle rammed into his bike. The accused managed to flee, police said.
According to police, they reached the spot within seven to eight minutes and rushed Khanna to a hospital, where he was declared dead.
Over the next weeks, Khanna’s family sought justice and a fair probe and raised concerns over the investigation. They also protested multiple times outside the police station.
On Sunday, during another such protest, police said they received the family’s complaint and subsequently changed the IO.
Khanna’s brother, Rohit Khanna, said the family had concerns about the response following the accident and the progress of the investigation.
“The accident took place at 4am. My brother was rushing home from a Mata Ki Chowki because it was his daughter’s fourth birthday. We didn’t know this would happen. He was killed by a car. When we reached the spot, we could see him alive but unconscious. Police was also there, but the investigating officer said only an ambulance could take him. My brother was alive. He could have been alive today. The delay in the ambulance’s arrival, which took around 20-30 minutes affected his chances of survival. His wife leaves the child at a relative’s home every day and we stage protests,” he said.
Rohit alleged that the family had not been shown any CCTV footage from the accident site so far.
“The policeman was rude and didn’t help us. When we asked about the accused, they said they hadn’t identified him. There are five CCTVs at the spot. How is it possible? We spoke to eyewitnesses, but the IO did not take their statements. It’s been almost a month now. We want answers. What happened with my brother that day?” he said.
Khanna’s wife, Navya, said the family has been travelling from Uttam Nagar every day to meet the station house officer and the IO.
“We want answers. Who killed him? It’s been a month now. We want to know why his brothers were not allowed to take him to hospital and why the CCTV footage has not been shown to us. Are hit-and-run accidents not a serious crime?” she said.
ACP Yogendra Khokhar on Sunday said the IO was changed following the family’s concerns and that efforts to trace the accused were continuing.
“We have received their complaint. They are not satisfied with the probe and have also levelled allegations against the IO. We have acted on it and the case is now being probed to catch the accused at the earliest,” he said.

Quick Answer
QuickLook brings macOS-style instant file previews to Windows 11. Install the free, open-source app, select a file in File Explorer, and press Space to preview images, PDFs, videos, archives, code, and more without opening another app.
If you are switching from a Mac to a Windows laptop or have already jumped ship, then among a bunch of cool things, there is a good chance that you might be missing that one tiny feature — tapping the Space bar to peek inside a file. On macOS, the file peeking feature has been around since 2007, and once you get used to it, selecting a photo, PDF, or video and instantly seeing what’s inside without opening a single app, going back feels like a step down. Windows, even with all the polish it has picked up over the years, never really bothered to catch up.
The Windows File Explorer still makes you double-click and wait for the right app to load, just to confirm whether you want that file or not. This is the gap that QuickLook fixes, as it brings the macOS-style press Space and preview feature to Windows 10 and 11 PCs. But it has more to it. Let us check it out.
Why does Windows File Explorer still lag?
No offense to Microsoft, but even after so many visual upgrades, Windows has never really implemented features that actually make a difference. For instance, it is not that Microsoft has never tried the preview feature. It has experimented with preview panes in File Explorer for years, and to be fair, the built-in Preview Pane (which you can enable through the sidebar from the View menu) does show images, PDFs, and a handful of document types. But it is quite slow and doesn’t support all file formats people actually deal with. On top of this, the preview pane needs a permanently open panel eating into your window memory. To put it in simple words, it was never designed to be instant but designed to be available if you go looking for it.
That’s a very different philosophy from what Apple built. Quick Look on macOS is designed so that you should never have to fully open an application just to look at whether the file is right or wrong. QuickLook for Windows brings that same philosophy and applies it system-wide, whether you are browsing on your desktop, a network drive, or even inside an Open/Save dialog box.
QuickLook is free and open-source
I love trying out new tools and software that bring more features and enhance the usage experience. QuickLook stood out because it is a free and open-source utility, and it has been actively maintained since 2017. One of the best parts about QuickLook is that it runs quietly in the background after installation, sitting in your system tray, waiting for you to select a file and press the Space bar. The moment you press the Space bar, a preview window pops open almost instantly; no loading spinner, no application splash screen, nothing.
What makes it genuinely useful rather than a gimmick is the long list of supported file formats it can preview. Out of the box, QuickLook handles more than fifty file types natively, including:
- Images (JPG, PNG, GIF, WebP, HEIC, RAW formats, and more)
- Videos and audio files, with actual playback controls inside the preview
- PDFs, rendered natively without needing Adobe Reader
- Source code files, with proper syntax highlighting for dozens of programming languages
- Markdown files, rendered as formatted text rather than raw syntax
- Archives like ZIP and RAR, letting you browse contents without extracting
- Fonts, showing a live specimen of how the typeface actually looks
- 3D model files, with the ability to rotate and inspect the model
Using QuickLook is straightforward
Once you are done with the installation, you can use QuickLook straightaway. All you need to do is click on any file, be it inside the File Explorer, your Desktop, or even inside a file picker, press the Space bar, and a preview window will open up, rendering the file’s contents without launching the actual application associated with it. Want to check the next file in the folder? Use the arrow keys to move your selection, and QuickLook updates the preview live, without you needing to close and reopen anything. When you are done, hitting Space again, pressing Escape, or clicking the close button dismisses the window immediately.
There is also a small but genuinely thoughtful touch. You can drag a file directly out of the preview window into another folder or application. This means that QuickLook does not just show you contents, but it can double as a lightweight way to move files around while you are inspecting them. For those who deal with folders full of similarly named files like screenshots, exported design assets, and scanned documents, this single feature removes an entire category of friction and saves a lot of time. Instead of opening five PDFs one at a time in a PDF Reader to find the right invoice, you tap through them in under two seconds each.
The plugin ecosystem is where it gets genuinely powerful
QuickLook’s native format support already covers most everyday use cases. But if you want to expand the list of supported file formats, the plugin system is what turns QuickLook from “a nice preview tool” into something closer to a universal file viewer. Community developers have built plugins that extend QuickLook to handle formats it doesn’t support by default. The best part is that installing one is refreshingly simple. You just need to download the plugin file, select it in File Explorer, press Space, and QuickLook prompts you to install it directly from the preview window itself.
Some of the more useful plugins in the ecosystem include:
- Office document viewers that render Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files without needing Microsoft Office or WPS Office installed at all
- ePub and comic book viewers, useful for anyone who reads digital books or manga and wants a quick way to confirm file contents
- PDF renderers built on WebView2, offering an alternative rendering engine for people who run into issues with the default PDF viewer
- SQLite database viewers, letting developers peek inside .db files without opening a separate database tool
- 3D model and CAD file plugins, handling specialized formats used in design and engineering work
It’s a similar philosophy to how tools like Winaero Tweaker approach Windows customization, where a small, focused core with optional extras layered on top, rather than a bloated all-in-one package.
QuickLook: Is this for you?
For anyone who regularly digs through folders full of screenshots, downloads, project files, or scanned documents, QuickLook solves a problem that Windows has quietly ignored for over a decade. It’s free, open-source, doesn’t collect telemetry, has no ads or premium tier hiding better features behind a paywall, and the entire project has stayed community-maintained since it first launched. Not only heavy file users, but casual users can also install it and use it in their daily lives, as it solves a core problem of having to double-click a file, use supported software, wait for it to load, and then preview the file. The setup takes less time than reading this article, and the payoff shows up the very first time you tap Space over a file and actually get what you expected, instantly.

Fears for communities near the great Colorado River as drought means future is uncertain
The severely depleted Colorado River is causing grave concern for those who rely on it
Located on the outskirts of Phoenix, a small town hugely reliant on the Colorado River has restricted development, reopened disused wells and negotiated new water agreements.
Yet Cave Creek Mayor Robert Morris fears these efforts will prove insufficient to sustain the desert enclave of roughly 5,000 residents long into the future. Furthermore, a recent federal initiative intended to tackle the worsening crisis across the river basin will offer no help.
Cave Creek draws almost all its supply from the river, which provides water to 40 million people across the US West but has been shrinking due to climate change, demand and excessive use. The town was compelled to reduce consumption this year and stands to lose even more under the new federal proposal.
Morris likened the situation to planning for a meteor strike.
“You can see it coming, but you can't get out of the way and you don't know what the damage is going to be,” he said.
The uncertainty stretches across seven U.S. states, tribal nations and Mexico. Farmers are deciding which crops are worth the investment. Phoenix could lose some municipal and industrial water for the first time and turn to backup supplies. And residents could face even more costly water.
Nevada raised the stakes this week by suing the Interior Department and the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, saying basic needs in the Las Vegas region will go unmet if the area has to absorb planned reductions of up to 70% of its Colorado River water in the next decade.
The bureau said Thursday it does not comment on litigation.
“The uncertainty is going to continue to build in the wrong direction,” said Tom Buschatzke, director of the Arizona Department of Water Resources.
Western reservoirs see record lows
In the U.S. West, water is stored primarily in reservoirs, aquifers and snowpacks. But a record snow drought means there's far less water to recharge those sources.
The two largest reservoirs in the country serve as barometers of health for the Colorado River system: Lake Mead and Lake Powell. Both hit record lows this month.
Eight other reservoirs operated by the Bureau of Reclamation recently recorded the lowest levels in at least the last 30 years. Among them is Elephant Butte Lake in New Mexico that's critical for supplying water for crops in southern New Mexico, Texas and Mexico. The Green Mountain Reservoir serves the western part of Colorado, and the Guernsey Reservoir in Wyoming funnels water to farmers in the eastern part of the state and western Nebraska.
Under the Bureau of Reclamation’s plan, California, Nevada and Arizona will collectively reduce water use by 1.25 million acre-feet (about 1.54 billion cubic meters) — enough to fill over 600,000 Olympic-sized swimming pools — annually in the next two years, with the possibility of larger cuts depending on conditions. Colorado, Utah, Wyoming and New Mexico are not required to make cuts for now but could voluntarily reduce water.
While El Niño could bring intense moisture to the northern Rockies and the Southwest in the coming months, it won't erase decades of drought.
“Drought is a slow-moving phenomena and it can take some time to come into it and also come out of it,” said David Mocko, senior research scientist who authored a recent U.S. Drought Monitor map.
Farmers are reluctant to plant
John Boelts grows vegetables, melons, durum wheat and other crops in Yuma, Arizona — a region that produces about 90% of leafy greens eaten in North America during the winter.
Farmers there have high-priority rights and may avoid cuts to their Colorado River supply over the next two years but, Boelts said, the reprieve isn't enough to make longer-term plans. That makes farmers reluctant to plant new acreage.
Citrus, date and other orchard crops that thrive in the region take years to become commercially productive, he said.
“There's no food that we grow in a hurry,” said Boelts, the Arizona Farm Bureau president. “Beef takes years to produce. The lettuce you eat today? A farmer was working on how they would grow that crop six plus months ago.”
Ray Martinez grows alfalfa on a reservation that's home to the Colorado River Indian Tribes. The tribe holds some of the river’s oldest rights, and while its Arizona allocation is huge, an old irrigation system and the lack of infrastructure have kept much of the water out of reach.
Martinez and the water department are concerned about having enough water to finish this growing season. He has left some fields unplanted for years to help prop up Lake Mead. If the reservoir keeps dropping, he said, surface water coming to him and neighboring farms will be further limited.
“Unfortunately, Mother Nature has its own way of doing things, and we have no control of that,” he added.

Zimbabwe minibus taxi carrying church members crashes, killing 27
A collision between a minibus taxi carrying church members and a haulage truck has killed 27 people in Zimbabwe
HARARE, Zimbabwe -- A collision between a minibus taxi carrying church members and a haulage truck killed 27 people Friday in Zimbabwe, a police spokesperson said, in the latest road disaster to hit the southern African country.
Paul Nyathi, the police spokesperson, said on Saturday that members of a popular indigenous African Christian denomination, known for wearing white robes, were traveling for a conference when the minibus taxi collided head-on with the truck Friday night. The truck was trying to overtake another vehicle when it crashed with the minibus taxi on a major highway near Chivhu town, 132 kilometers (82 miles) south of the capital, Harare, Nyathi said in a statement.
State-run broadcaster ZBC News, citing a provincial government minister, said 23 people died at the scene, while others succumbed to their injuries after being admitted to a local hospital.
The minibus taxi burst into flames and was reduced to a shell following the collision, according to local media, which published pictures of the wreckage.
Nyathi said both vehicles were carrying an “unspecified” number of passengers.
Road accidents involving crowded buses, minibus taxis and unregulated sedan taxis are common in Zimbabwe and are often blamed on dangerous driving and poor road conditions.
Zimbabwe is among the countries with the worst road safety records, with 94% of road accidents attributed to human error, according to authorities.
Across Africa, road crashes kill about 300,000 people annually, roughly a quarter of the global toll, according to the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa, which says the continent has the world’s highest road fatality rate. This is despite the continent of 1.5 billion people accounting for just about 3% of the global vehicle fleet.

Cyprus ferry incident latest: Seven reported dead after boat with more than 260 passengers capsizes
The catamaran-style boat was traveling from the port of Kyrenia, also known as Girne, to the Turkish port of Tasucu
At least seven people have died and many remain missing after a ferry carrying nearly 270 passengers capsized off the coast of northern Cyprus on Sunday.
Self-declared Northern Cyprus prime minister Unal Ustel confirmed the deaths to local media, saying a search was underway for another 23 people, while around 237 people had been rescued.
The catamaran-style boat was travelling from the port of Kyrenia, also known as Girne, in the breakaway north of ethnically divided Cyprus, to the Turkish port of Tasucu in Mersin province.
Mr Ustel said the ferry faced adverse weather conditions and began taking in water just 15 minutes after departure before a call for help was issued.
Footage of the incident shows people with life vests floating in the waters around the capsized vessel.
It has been reported that there were 267 people on board, including 259 passengers and eight crew.
Kyrenia mayor Murat Senkul said the ship belonged to the Filo Denizcilik ferry company and sank off the coast of Diana beach on Cyprus’ northern coast.
Helicopters and navy boats deployed in search for missing passengers
Several helicopters and Turkish Navy ships have been deployed to help rescue the passengers at sea, the interior ministry said.
At least 16 vessels and two helicopters belonging to the coast guard and navy have been dispatched.
“Search and rescue efforts are being carried out meticulously and in coordination among the relevant units,” it said.
'Utmost priority' is to reach 23 missing people, says self-declared PM
An urgent search is underway to find the 23 missing people, the self-declared northern Cyprus prime minister said.
In a statement shared to social media, Unal Ustel said all resources had been mobilised following the “tragic” incident.
“Our utmost priority at this moment is to reach the 23 missing individuals as soon as possible,” he said.
“Out of the total 267 people on board the ship, 237 have been rescued by our teams. Unfortunately, 7 individuals have lost their lives.
“I offer my condolences from Allah for those who have passed away, and wish patience and strength to their families and loved ones. I pray for a swift recovery for the injured.
“All institutions of our state are on the ground. We are continuing the search and rescue efforts with the utmost care and closely following developments.”
Capsized ferry belonged to Filo Denizcilik ferry company
The boat that capsized in northern Cyprus on Sunday was operated by ferry company Filo Denizcilik, Kyrenia Mayor Murat Senkul said.
Filo Denizcilik operates ferry services connecting Northern Cyprus and Turkey and goes between four different ports.
The ferry sank off the coast of Diana beach on Cyprus’ northern coast and was travelling from the port of Kyrenia, also known as Girne, in the breakaway north of ethnically divided Cyprus, to the Turkish port of Tasucu in Mersin province.
At least seven dead after ferry capsizes
At least seven people have died and several remain missing after a ferry carrying more than 260 people capsized off of Cyprus today.
Northern Cyprus prime minister Unal Ustel confirmed the deaths to local media, saying around 237 people had also been rescued.
He said an urgent search was underway for another 24 people.
The ferry faced adverse weather conditions and began taking in water just 15 minutes after departure. A call for help was issued shortly after, Mr Ustel added.

In a statement shared by local media, Unal Ustel, the prime minister of Northern Cyprus, said: “We are deeply saddened. There has been loss of life and there are injuries.

The Turkish ambassador to Nicosia, Ali Murat Basceri, also said there were some casualties, but did not specify how many, speaking to Turkey’s state-run TRT news channel.

The ferry was carrying more than 260 people and the search for others is still underway.

A Chinese rescue team has reached the all-but-obliterated Gyirong border crossing complex for the first time and found “nothing but ruins” as Nepal and China continue their arduous rescue operations in the flood-hit Himalayas.
Surveillance camera footage from the worst-hit Gyirong border crossing complex showed huge torrents of water and debris on Wednesday engulfing buildings and people trying to flee. Only on Friday were rescuers able to reach that area.
State media reported that the Chinese team of 21 rescuers and a search-and-rescue dog crossed mountains and valleys and used ropes to navigate forests and cliffs after roads to the complex, hemmed in by steep Himalayan slopes, were destroyed.
“There was no road … it was all virgin forest and sheer cliffs,” rescue worker Zou Mingqi said. At the complex, “as far as the eye could see, there was nothing but ruins.”
The glacier collapse which unleashed a deadly torrent through Himalayan mountain river systems has killed at least 579 people in Nepal and seven in China’s Tibet. The number of missing in Nepal has nearly doubled to 1,924, officials said on Friday. At least 558 were missing in Tibet’s Gyirong County, Chinese state media said. Among the missing are at least 540 foreigners, many of them Hindu pilgrims from India.
More than 90,000 people have been affected by the disaster, the Red Cross estimated.
Amid the deepening crisis, Nepal has now said it needs foreign help in specialised and technical areas in which it does not have expertise, but not in search and rescue.
Earlier on Friday, Nepal’s foreign ministry had said that Kathmandu could manage the rescue efforts on its own for now and declined foreign involvement.
The areas Nepal is seeking help include opening transport and communication services in places where bridges have been destroyed, identification of dead bodies, DNA testing and storing bodies for longer durations, foreign minister Shisir Khanal said late on Friday.
Asked about that stance of his government, Khanal said there was no need for assistance in general search and rescue which was being done by Nepali rescuers. “We think there is no need for repetition in this,” he said.
India and China, between whom Nepal is wedged, have been requested to supply bailey bridges to reopen transport and communication in an area where about two dozen bridges had been destroyed.
Nepal is continuing to monitor two barrier lakes upstream of the flood zone, with an official warning that flood risks will persist until both lakes fully drain.
Satellite imagery showed the second lake growing larger with no visible outlet, raising concerns that water pressure could still be building.
China’s state-run Xinhua news agency said that the first barrier lake was reducing in size, citing analysis by the water resources ministry. A Chinese government geo-hazards expert warned, however, that the lake may be unstable and that over 100 glacial lakes scattered throughout the area could pose a threat.
In Beijing, a politburo meeting chaired by President Xi Jinping called for stronger monitoring of glacier lakes and landslide risks, and for closer international disaster cooperation, Xinhua reported.
China’s Premier Li Qiang, the country’s No. 2 official, arrived in the area of Gyirong on Thursday afternoon, Xinhua said. The visit suggested Beijing was treating the disaster as a matter of the highest national priority.
In China, strict controls on the flow of information from one of its most sensitive regions are hampering the public’s understanding of events.
The BBC and NY Times have reported videos of the catastrophic floods, widely shared globally, have not appeared on Chinese social media sites.
Chinese state media has carried several broadcasts about the floods and dispatched their own journalists to the area, but reports have focused on the rescue efforts rather than the scale of the devastation. In one broadcast from a relief centre in Tibet, the journalist did not speak to any of the people sitting behind him.
Tibet, brought under Chinese control in the 1950s, is the most sensitive and tightly controlled region in the country.
The Gyirong border port plays a key role in China’s Belt and Road network linking the country to South Asia, with logistics zones and parking lots built there in the past decade.

EV maker Ola Electric has launched its new S1Z escooter range, powered by the company’s locally developed 46-series lithium iron phosphate (LFP) Bharat Cell technology, as it targets the mass-market electric two-wheeler segment. The S1Z will be available in two battery variants, with the 3.1 kWh version priced at an introductory ₹79,999 and the 5.1 kWh variant at ₹99,999 (ex-showroom). Deliveries of the 3.1 kWh variant are scheduled to begin in December 2026, while those of the 5.1 kWh version will start in March 2027. The 3.1 kWh and 5.1 kWh variants offer an IDC range of up to 179 km and 301 km, respectively. The S1Z is the first scooter range from Ola Electric to feature its 46-series LFP Bharat Cell technology. The battery technology has been developed at Ola Electric's Battery Innovation Centre and manufactured at its Ola Gigafactory. In an exchange filing, the EV maker said its in-house cell manufacturing had helped lower battery costs, enabling it to offer LFP technology at more affordable price points. In a post on X, chairman Bhavish Aggarwal said Ola Electric is setting a "new benchmark" as India's electrification accelerates. "More than just a metal body with a fancy name," he said, while highlighting the S1Z's 46-series LFP Bharat Cell. "The industry has always treated affordable scooters as stripped-down products: less range, less technology, more compromise. We've done the opposite," Aggarwal said. Aggarwal said Ola Electric has built the cell, motor, vehicle, software, and “every critical component” in-house and is passing the resulting technological advantage on to customers. The S1Z will run on MoveOS 5 and offer features such as cruise control, regenerative braking, GPS, over-the-air updates, ride statistics, and Easy Park. It will be available in four colours and come with 12-inch wheels. The S1Z will also be Ola Electric’s first scooter range to be sold through its new dealer-operated stores as the company expands beyond its company-owned retail network. The launch comes as Ola Electric looks to expand its product portfolio and strengthen its position in India’s competitive electric two-wheeler market. It also comes a day before rival Ather Energy is set to launch its new affordable escooter ‘Ather Konarc’. Amid falling sales, Ola Electric is also entering the energy storage segment while shifting to a dealer-led sales and service model. Earlier this month, it launched three battery energy storage systems (BESS) as part of its push into the energy solutions business. The portfolio comprises the second-generation residential Ola Shakti, the industry-focused Shakti Rack, and the utility-scale Mahashakti. The company also launched the Shakti Solar Charge Controller, which will be available in 3 kW and 6 kW variants from March 2027. On the financial front, Ola Electric’s net loss narrowed 22% YoY to ₹336 Cr in Q1 FY27 from ₹428 Cr a year earlier. Operating revenue fell 45% to ₹455 Cr from ₹828 Cr during the period. Sequentially, loss narrowed from ₹500 Cr in Q4 FY26, while operating revenue rose 72% from ₹265 Cr. Shares of Ola Electric ended today's trading session 3.5 % higher at ₹38.98 on the BSE.

Donald Trump may be preparing to announce sweeping new semiconductor tariffs at the absolute worst time, the tech industry fears.
On Thursday, Politico reported that a wide range of new semiconductor tariffs, which the tech industry expects will “doom” artificial intelligence innovation in the US, could be imposed in the coming “weeks or months.”
About eight people familiar with the Trump administration’s plans were granted anonymity to discuss how the tariffs might work. They suggested that the framework for tariffs may change as it becomes finalized, but one approach under consideration could “dramatically expand the number of tech products subject to the duties, hitting not just chips but potentially many of the goods made with them, such as gaming consoles or the servers that fill data centers.”
That scenario is the tech industry’s nightmare. Since Trump took office,trade groups have warned that imposing tariffs on both semiconductors and the many downstream products that use semiconductors—potentially even taxing used or refurbished products that contain chips—would be ruinous for the economy.
Most absurdly, given the priorities of Trump’s AI Action Plan, that tariff approach would cost the US about $90 billion annually in GDP losses and cause about 20 percent of data center projects planned through 2030 to be delayed or canceled, the Computer and Communications Industry Association (CCIA) estimated in June. The tariffs could even drive more data center development outside the US, the CCIA warned, which seems counterproductive, since Trump is imposing them in order to force more development into the US.
Beyond disrupting the momentum of data centers, the tariffs could have wide-ranging ripple effects if certain products aren’t exempted, the CCIA said in a May letter to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, which was cosigned by about 20 trade groups.
For consumers, prices of “everyday tools,” like smartphones, laptops, tablets, smartwatches, connected devices, and vehicles, could increase at a time when US households are already budget-strained. Tariffs could also limit technology choices for Americans by delaying new product launches, including devices featuring the latest AI technologies. And any dampened demand for popular tech risks further limiting innovation while seemingly working in lockstep with tariffs to slow AI adoption in the US, the letter warned.
“Consumer devices are the primary interface through which Americans access AI-powered tools. AI only delivers on its promise when people can actually use it—and tariffs that price consumers out of the device market would slow AI adoption at the very moment the United States is positioned to lead,” the letter said.
To shield AI firms, the Trump administration is mulling some tariff relief, but sources told Politico it would likely be tied to foreign firms investing in US chip manufacturing, like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Apparently, that’s the approach Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick favors most.
Perhaps mindful of the data center development timeline—and possibly the upcoming holiday season, as Trump previously has exempted goods from tariffs to avoid consumer backlash that negatively impacted his approval ratings—the administration may impose tariffs in phases to avoid the worst impacts hitting all at once.
Industry talks with Trump turn “negative”
The global data center buildout already has the tech industry broadly scrambling for access to high-end semiconductors, which are forecasted to remain in short supply well into 2027. Just yesterday, Gartner forecasted that due to the shortage that’s driving price increases, global semiconductor revenue is expected to reach $1.6 trillion in 2026—much sooner than expected.
Economists expect that tariffs would only further increase prices for chips, which Politico reported could “hammer US chip designers such as Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices, which rely on overseas manufacturers to produce their chips.” Tariffs could also hurt companies like Apple, which competes with foreign rivals overseas that wouldn’t have to deal with the tariffs. Chinese firms could benefit, Politico suggested, as chip suppliers potentially avoid tariffs by increasing business in China.
Politico’s sources confirmed that the tech industry is so panicked by the risk of semiconductor tariffs that it “launched a lobbying blitz” to guarantee that data centers at the very least would be exempted.
For the tech industry, the hope is that Trump will recognize an inherent tension at the heart of his semiconductor tariffs plan: Taxing data centers on chips during the key time they need to acquire as many as possible to scale AI infrastructure will not increase demand for chips produced domestically for a simple reason. Domestic chip plants take years to build, and the US can’t rush that timeline, so firms will remain heavily dependent on importing semiconductors. As a detailed report from The Next Web summarized the problem: “Taxing the imports in the meantime raises the cost of the thing the administration also says it wants, which is American AI infrastructure at scale. There is no version of the timeline in which domestic supply arrives before the buildout needs the chips.”
“This may be the single dumbest way imaginable to pursue American dominance in AI,” said one tech official who, Politico reported, is from a major industry group and also served in the first Trump administration. “It’s like kneecapping yourself at the starting line.”
However, even though industry representatives and lobbyists have met with Trump officials “with increasing frequency since the start of summer,” sources suggested that this time, the tech industry may not get the exemptions that they’re seeking. The talks have recently “trended in a negative direction,” sources told Politico.
Lutnick appears to be standing in the way. According to Politico’s sources, the Commerce Secretary thinks the US needs to apply the tariffs broadly to prioritize reshoring the domestic supply chain.
Four sources suggested that Lutnick plans to hold his ground and announce a system where the “US would let a set volume of chips enter the country duty-free, with the size of that allowance tied to how much companies pledge to produce on American soil.” Individual countries could also face different semiconductor tariff rates that Trump officials have weighed, further complicating the math for companies trying to guess how tariffs might shake up their supply chains.
Critics worry that the tariff structure Lutnick likes “risks widening the gap between the supply of tariff-free chips and the volume US companies need,” Politico reported. One tech representative suggested more exemptions would be needed, since “the volume they’re talking about granting duty-free wouldn’t cover the hyperscalers alone, let alone the rest of the industry. Those are chips we physically can’t buy here, because the capacity doesn’t exist yet.”
“The math literally just does not work,” that source said.
What does the tech industry want?
Earlier this year, Trump imposed a narrow set of semiconductor tariffs that pointedly exempted data centers. As recently as May, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said that “having semiconductor tariffs is important,” but they must be “on the right timing and in the right amount.” At that time, Greer said that the government wanted to ensure that “there are no immediate tariffs on companies that are producing semiconductors” and that the US “will allow companies to import an unspecified amount during that ‘reshoring phase.’”
It’s unclear what may have changed to shift the Trump administration’s position since then. However, The Next Web analyzed the upcoming phase of tariffs and noted that the Commerce Department submitted a report on July 1 that would determine if the data center exemption would survive. That report remains unpublished but is likely at the center of officials’ discussions with tech lobbyists.
The CCIA’s report suggested that the next round of tariffs could avoid the worst consequences by carving out exemptions for semiconductors used in AI servers and by lowering the tariff rate from a presumed 25 percent to 10 percent. That would supposedly ensure the “most fragile” projects aren’t disrupted and that GDP losses are minimized.
The best solution, their letter said, would be to avoid imposing tariffs on semiconductors and derivative products entirely. But if the administration must proceed, then trade groups hope they will consider applying tariffs in “a nuanced and targeted way,” their letter said.
That means perhaps excluding products from tariffs “with minimal semiconductor content or products whose semiconductor inputs are incidental to their principal use.” Or possibly setting a “de minimis” threshold where any product under a certain weight or value might be exempted. And at minimum, they should acknowledge that sellers of secondhand products may not have information on hand to establish the provenance of the chips contained inside. To ensure that there aren’t shipment bottlenecks, any tariff policy should only require paperwork that firms already have on hand, the letter said.
Finally, and likely the tech industry’s biggest ask: If tariffs are inevitable, don’t stack tariffs so that firms must pay a double tax on both the semiconductors within the derivative products and the products that contain them.
For the tech industry, the risk of tariffs coming at this key moment likely feels like Trump is adding a roadblock where he could be focused on cutting red tape that could expand US chipmaking capacity, data center development, and AI innovation.
Right now, investments in US chipmaking capacity are at a “historic high,” CCIA’s letter to Bessent said, and we need “policy measures that expand domestic capacity, accelerate permitting and infrastructure deployment, support advanced packaging and workforce development, and strengthen trusted supply chains [to] better advance US resilience without imposing economy-wide costs on downstream innovation.”
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

Chelsea has signed Argentina goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez from Aston Villa in a deal worth £7.5 million, strengthening its goalkeeping options in the ongoing season of the Premier League.
The 33-year-old World Cup winner has agreed to a three-year contract with the Blues. The move brings an end to Martinez’s six-year spell at Aston Villa.
“I’m delighted to be at this football club,” Martinez said. "Coming to Chelsea, for me and my family, was an easy decision to make, and I’m just over the moon - I can’t wait to get started.”
“I want to be successful here. I’m someone who wants to win at everything I do, and I want to bring that here to this football club because it’s a football club that wins titles, so I think it’s a good match... I’m all passion and I play with my heart. I will give 100 per cent every game, every training session to make the club, my teammates, and the supporters proud.”

As Gaza’s population of 2.1 million has been hemmed into an ever smaller slice of the territory, farmers are using every last remaining patch of unspoiled earth, no matter how tiny, in their struggle to survive.
With severe shortages of water, fertiliser and pesticide, and with more than 80% of greenhouses ruined, it has taken inventiveness and determination to clear land of debris and coax new seedlings into life. Moreover, venturing out into the open to tend to plants can be deadly.
Saqer Abu Rabee’s eldest son and brother were killed while at work growing food for their communities on their small agricultural plots in Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza. His son Yousef was 24 when he was killed by a drone-fired missile in October 2024. Abu Rabee was working in the fields 10 metres from his son when it happened.
“The missile was aimed directly at him and I have no doubt that he was the intended target,” Abu Rabee said. Yousef was well known locally as the driving force behind a collective first called We’ll Plant It and now simply Our Land, which brought together volunteers and encouraged farmers to go back to the land to restore agriculture in the area.
“They decided to target him directly,” said Abu Rabee, who stressed his son had no political affiliations. “Before his death, we received daily threats from the Israeli army. They shelled our area every day three or four times while I was working alongside the labourers.”
Abu Rabee’s brother Bilal was killed on 2 July after he went to retrieve some agricultural supplies from a destroyed building. His death came nine months into a partial ceasefire during which Israeli forces have killed more than 1,200 Palestinians. Abu Rabee is convinced farmers have become prime targets because of their role in sustaining Palestinian communities among Gaza’s ruins.
The Israel Defense Forces deny targeting farmers or any civilians, saying they have only responded to imminent threats from Hamas since the October ceasefire.
Despite the risks, Abu Rabee, 48, is still at work every day cultivating a 1.4-hectare (3.4-acre) plot in Beit Lahiya that was an orchard of orange trees before the war. He said the orchard was bulldozed by the Israeli army.
“We cleared it and rehabilitated it using only basic tools, manual labour and tremendous human effort. It took a great deal of time and hard work before it was ready for cultivation again,” he said.
Out of that scrap of land, Abu Rabee says his family have produced hundreds of thousands of aubergine, tomato and pepper seedlings. They raise cash by growing their own aubergines to sell to wholesale traders, while most of the seedlings are distributed to other farmers or to individual households to plant in patches of earth around their homes and tents.
He says the supply has transformed the local food market. Aubergines now cost less than two shekels a kilogram, compared with 40 shekels a few months ago. Peppers and mulukhiyah, a dark green leafy vegetable, are now selling at a tenth of their market price earlier this year.
“What has happened is that Beit Lahiya has regained a degree of self-sufficiency,” Abu Rabee said. “In my view, without Beit Lahiya, Gaza would face famine. Before the war, it was considered the food basket of Gaza Strip because of its fertile soil, fresh groundwater and light, productive land.”
Increased aid and commercial deliveries under the ceasefire have brought Gaza back from the abyss of last year’s famine conditions, but according to UN agencies there are still 1.4 million people – 67% of Gaza’s population – facing crisis levels of acute food insecurity or worse.
Much of the commercial inflows of food are of poor nutritional quality. The director general of the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), Qu Dongyu, has said the limited recovery will remain fragile without domestic food production.
“Food security in Gaza cannot recover unless local food production starts again and farmers, herders, fishers and other producers can rebuild their livelihoods,” Qu said in July.
Based on satellite data, the FAO estimates that little more than a quarter of Gaza’s total prewar cropland, 4,100 hectares, remains accessible, and only about 3%, 450 hectares, is undamaged, free of debris and ready for immediate cultivation.
Most of Gaza’s prewar farmland is under Israeli military occupation, and the proportion has grown as the army has pushed the “yellow line” steadily forward over the course of the ceasefire.
Using specialised satellite imagery, the human rights advocacy group Forensic Architecture carried out a survey of flora across Gaza as a measurable proxy for cultivable land. It found that nearly 68% of the territory’s flora was on the Israeli side of the yellow line and another 5% was inside a buffer zone declared by the army, delineated on maps with an orange line, where it is extremely dangerous for Palestinians to venture.
Bilal Abu Rabee, Saqer’s brother, was shot dead along with another man when they came within range of Israeli sniper positions. Their bodies were left out in the open for two days because it was too dangerous for their relatives to retrieve them.
The family’s old farm is now under Israeli control, so after the ceasefire was declared they came to Beit Lahiya to try to start again from scratch on leased land. Since last October the army has pushed the yellow line forward, swallowing up nearby farms in west Beit Lahiya.
“The expansion has had a devastating impact on the agricultural sector,” Abu Rabee said. “Fertile farmland that farmers had worked tirelessly to cultivate after spending everything they had or even borrowing money, simply it was seized just as it was ready for harvest, leaving them with nothing.”
On the remaining land, the challenges appear endless. With hardly any livestock left, there is little homegrown dung-based fertiliser, so the family are improvising by piling decaying vegetation under tarpaulins. Meanwhile, they are battling nematodes and other soil infestations and a chronic lack of water, all the time under the constant, unpredictable threat of death.
Abu Rabee said: “Stray bullets frequently reach this area and strike many places around us. Many people have also been wounded in the streets as a result of indiscriminate attacks. I fear for my own life simply because I’m a farmer.”
