RFK Jr blames media and ‘demagogic politicians’ as he downplays ‘so-called measles deaths’ amid outbreak fears
Measles cases surge to 35-year high as deaths in Pennsylvania spark clash between the governor and Trump’s health secretary
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has accused “fear-mongering” politicians and journalists of hyping up “so-called measles deaths” as he defended the Trump administration in the face of a historic spike in U.S. measles cases.
"In 10 years, there have been three measles deaths in America,” Kennedy said during Saturday’s town hall even on Fox News, after being asked if the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine should be mandatory, given two recent measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania.
“There are now about 1.2 million deaths every year from food-induced illness. The media and certain demagogic politicians are constantly trying to scare us about infectious disease,” he said.
Kennedy referred to the deaths in Pennsylvania, announced by public health officials on Tuesday, as “so-called measles deaths” and alleged “the governor has not been able to point to any child who died from measles in Lancaster County.”
Public health officials quickly took issue with Kennedy’s comments, noting that the low prevalence of measles deaths was a direct result of widespread vaccination.
“Measles deaths are rare in America for one reason: MMR coverage has been near-universal for decades,” Dr. Jake Scott, a clinical professor of infectious diseases at Stanford University, wrote on X. “Before the vaccine, this country lost 400-500 people to measles every year, with 48,000 hospitalizations. He’s citing the vaccine’s own achievement as evidence we never needed it.
Throughout the week, Kennedy has been locked in a war of words with Pennsylvania officials over whether the state had seen a spate of new measles-related deaths.
On Tuesday, the state health department said it had “confirmed” two measles-related deaths among people who were unvaccinated against the disease, the state’s first such deaths in 35 years.
Later that day, Governor Josh Shapiro said at a press conference he had pressed Kennedy in a phone call over his long history of vaccine skepticism, which included a 2021 visit to Lancaster County where he reportedly made light of his own childhood case of measles.
“I was very, very blunt with him,” Shapiro, seen as a 2028 Democratic presidential contender, said.
“[I] made very clear that his actions and the rhetoric that’s coming from this administration are having a negative impact on communities across America, particularly right here in Pennsylvania,” Shapiro said.
Kennedy responded, claiming on social media that Shapiro’s administration may have “fabricated” the cases for political gain, though the state said it reported the cases to the CDC on Tuesday.
Lancaster County Commissioner Josh Parsons has accused state officials of withholding information from the public and potentially announcing the cases prematurely.
Under the Trump administration, measles cases have surged to their highest level since 1991, and three unvaccinated people died from measles last year, the first reported measles deaths in the U.S. since 2015.
During his town hall, Kennedy insisted the MMR vaccine was safe and blamed the outbreak on declining vaccination rates during the COVID-19 pandemic, a time when “a lot of people across the globe lost faith in the public health system.”
Prior to his time in office, Kennedy was a prominent anti-vaccine activist, and he has made various misleading and false statements about the MMR vaccine since being appointed, including that vaccines aren’t “safety tested” and that immunity from the vaccine wanes quickly.

A video is circulating on social media claiming that, on the occasion of Raksha Bandhan, farmers across the country will receive ₹4,000 under the Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi (PM-KISAN) scheme. Let’s verify the claim made in this post.
Claim: Farmers will receive a special ₹4,000 instalment under the PM-KISAN scheme on the occasion of Raksha Bandhan in August 2026.
Fact: No such announcement was made by the Government of India. Under the PM-KISAN scheme, eligible farmers receive a standard payment of ₹2,000 per instalment, not ₹4,000. The most recent ₹2,000 payout (the 23rd instalment) was released on 20 June 2026, and the government has not yet announced a 24th instalment. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
An internet search using relevant keywords did not yield any official announcements from the Government of India regarding such a payout. The official PM-KISAN website notes that the last instalment of ₹2,000 (the 23rd instalment) was released on 20 June 2026.
Moreover, addressing the viral video, PIB Fact-Check clarified that the Government of India has not yet made any official announcement regarding a 24th instalment, confirming that the claim is fake. Launched in February 2019, PM-KISAN is a centrally sponsored scheme designed to provide assured income support to landholding farmer families with cultivable land. Under this scheme, eligible families receive annual financial assistance of ₹6,000, which is disbursed in three equal instalments of ₹2,000 directly into Aadhaar-seeded bank accounts via the Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) mechanism.
To date, over ₹4.46 lakh crore has been disbursed to eligible farmer families across the country through 23 instalments. In July 2026, the Union Cabinet approved the continuation of the PM-KISAN scheme from 2026-27 to 2030-31, with a total approved financial outlay of ₹3.15 lakh crore for this period.
To sum it up, the claim that farmers will receive a ₹4,000 payout for Raksha Bandhan is false.

The Best Label Makers for an Organized Home
Featured in this article
There’s something oddly satisfying about a perfectly labeled spice rack or a pantry with bins that specify exactly what they contain—even if it’s plain as day that the “pasta” bin contains boxes of dried penne. Taking a label maker to the most clutter-laden corners of my home helps me feel organized. And frankly, feeling organized externally often helps me feel organized internally, too.
With that in mind, I researched, selected, and tested some of the top home label makers to see how intuitive different devices were to use and how well their labels stuck to my kids’ dresser drawers, toy bins, water bottles, and lunchboxes. Read on for my thoughts about the best machines for various needs. Just beware that household organizing with a label printer can get addicting and lead to joy-inducing clean spaces.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Also Tested
Nelko P21 for $22: This adorably pocket-sized, affordable, direct thermal label maker is easy to keep at the ready (or even in a tote bag for on-demand label-making emergencies), but actually using it is kind of a lot of work. Its companion app offers plenty of fun templates, but a lot of them are behind a paywall. I only discovered this when I printed a “Pasta” label for a pantry bin, and it came out with a watermark-like overlay. Once I made my own simple label, I struggled to calibrate the label tape to get the pre-cut stickers appropriately centered for my design. Even after I did figure it out, I realized I had to recalibrate the tape for each subsequent print. That’s because there’s no perforation or internal cutting mechanism, so you have to pull out the label tape a bit after it’s printed, which then moves the rest of the pre-cut roll of labels off-center. If you don’t remember to recalibrate, your next label will print off-center as well. I’m sure with enough trial and error, this process would become second nature, but the learning curve for the Nelko was nonetheless the steepest of all the label makers I tried.
FAQs
What Are the Different Kinds of Label Makers?
The top label makers I’ve included in the list use either thermal transfer printing or direct thermal printing. Direct thermal printing works by heating special paper, which is a process that yields labels that are less durable under various conditions and also more likely to fade over time. Thermal transfer printing works by melting ink from a ribbon cartridge onto a label. These labels tend to be more durable and longer-lasting. Thermal-transfer label makers also typically require slightly larger, more expensive machines.
Are Bluetooth or Traditional Label Makers Better?
Neither is inherently better, but each offers its own benefits. Traditional label makers have on-device keyboards where you type your label and customize font sizes, styles, symbols, and borders. Bluetooth-enabled label makers work by pairing the device with a mobile app on which you design your label, and then print it remotely. Often, these apps feature a wider variety of templates and font options than traditional label makers. Apps also typically show a more accurate preview than LCD screens on label makers themselves. Some label makers, like the best overall Brother PT-n25bt, offer both on-device and app-enabled designing.
Can You Use Label Maker Labels on Clothing?
It’s not recommended unless the label tape in question specifically mentions being able to work with fabric, like the TZe fabric label tape for the P-touch Cube Plus. Some label tape does claim to be heat-resistant and water-resistant, but even in this case, the label’s adhesive quality is likely to degrade after a bunch of cycles in the washer and dryer.
How I Tested These Label Makers
I considered popular options, and I received some testing units as samples from the company and bought others. I tested the functionality of each device by creating labels with an on-device keyboard, designing labels in a companion app and printing via Bluetooth compatibility, or both, depending on the label maker in question’s capabilities. I tested the durability of the top machines’ labels by sticking them on various surfaces, seeing if they could get wet and handle heat without fading or losing their adhesive strength over the course of at least one week, often longer.

Would Marmoush joining Tottenham be a masterstroke or risk?
- Published
Tottenham are looking to sign Manchester City forward Omar Marmoush, with talks between the clubs progressing.
No agreement has yet been reached, but the Egypt international could become the latest addition to Roberto De Zerbi's squad, with the north London club's summer spending looking set to exceed £300m.
Spurs have already spent £229.5m on centre-back Jan Paul van Hecke and midfielders Sandro Tonali and Mateus Fernandes.
And on Friday it was announced that they have agreed a £75m deal to sign Manchester City winger Savinho as they look to strengthen their attack.
Spurs forward Dominic Solanke has endured injury problems over the past 18 months, while team-mate Richarlison has entered the final year of his contract.
Marmoush's influence at City has diminished but the numbers suggest Tottenham would be getting a forward whose skillset differs considerably from their existing options.
- Spurs in talks to sign Man City's Savinho and Marmoush 
  - Published23 hours ago
From Frankfurt sensation to City understudy
Joining Eintracht Frankfurt in May 2023 on a free transfer from Wolfsburg, the then 24-year-old Marmoush found form in his first season with the German side scoring 17 times across all competitions.
He then scored 15 Bundesliga goals from 8.9 expected goals (xG) during the first half of 2024-25, while registering nine assists in 17 league appearances. Across all competitions before leaving Germany, he had 20 goals and 13 assists in 26 games.
Set-pieces were another notable part of his game. Marmoush became the first player in Europe's top five leagues since Lionel Messi in 2019 to score directly from a free-kick in three consecutive competitive matches. Manchester City then paid £59m for him in January 2025.
The early signs were encouraging. Marmoush scored his first career hat-trick against Newcastle, struck the winner in City's FA Cup quarter-final at Bournemouth and then scored from long range against the same opponents in the Premier League. It was judged to be the goal of the season.
But there were difficult moments too.
With City trailing Crystal Palace in the 2025 FA Cup final, Erling Haaland handed Marmoush the ball for a penalty. His effort was saved by Dean Henderson as City went on to lose at Wembley.
Former Manchester City defender Nedum Onuoha does not believe that moment should define Marmoush's spell at the club.
"When I see Marmoush, I don't see the penalty miss," Onuoha told BBC Sport. "I see the strength he has with some of the runs he makes in behind."
Why did his role shrink?
Marmoush has scored 16 goals in 62 appearances in all competitions for City since arriving from Frankfurt.
Eight of those came in 36 appearances in 2025-26, but his Premier League involvement fell considerably.
He started only eight league games and played around 700 minutes, fewer than he managed after joining midway through the prior campaign.
His league return was three goals and three assists, with his 3.53 expected goals figure close to his actual scoring output. The issue was therefore not simply finishing.
Marmoush found himself competing for minutes in a side built around Haaland, while City further strengthened their attacking options.
"All the positions Marmoush could play are being filled by people who are specialists in those roles," said Onuoha. "Haaland is essentially always going to be the number nine, while City also regularly play with number 10s and Guardiola likes his wingers to stay wide."
What would Marmoush give Spurs?
Marmoush is primarily a number nine, but he has rarely been confined to one role across the front line.
At Frankfurt he was used predominantly through the middle but also appeared as a second striker and from the left. City have followed a similar pattern, using him mainly as a central attacker while also deploying him from the flank and just behind another forward.
That flexibility could suit De Zerbi. His teams have often relied on forwards changing positions, dropping towards the ball and then attacking the space created when opponents are drawn out. Marmoush is comfortable doing both.
Onuoha sees the Egyptian as most dangerous when he is able to threaten the space beyond the defence.
"As much as he is good dropping towards the ball, I think he is better when he plays on the shoulder," he said. "He needs to be in a team that will constantly play balls in behind and force the opposition to run back towards their own goal. That's when you see a better version of Marmoush."
Opta's Premier League numbers from last season show he averaged 11.46 runs in behind per 90 minutes, almost identical to Solanke's 11.61 and ahead of Richarlison's 10.03. But he also offered considerably more with the ball.
Marmoush averaged 5.67 progressive carries per 90 minutes, compared with 3.24 for Solanke and 2.48 for Richarlison.
He also led both Tottenham forwards for shots, chances created, successful take-ons and touches in the opposition penalty area.
He had 3.86 shots per 90 minutes compared with 2.81 for Richarlison and 1.80 for Solanke, while Marmoush created 1.55 chances against 0.92 and 0.54 respectively.
He also produced 0.77 goals and assists per game, ahead of Richarlison's 0.69 and Solanke's 0.27.
The sample is smaller because of his limited league minutes, but the profile is clear.
Marmoush is more inclined to take opponents on and manufacture shooting opportunities for himself than Spurs' existing central forwards.
That could make him particularly useful when opponents sit deep and deny Tottenham the space to attack directly. Onuoha feels De Zerbi's style could suit him better.
"Sometimes the fit can simply be better," he said. "Marmoush's ability to run in behind and link the play could be huge assets for Spurs. They won't be shy about playing those passes into him and forcing opponents on to the back foot."
Alongside Solanke rather than instead of him?
Marmoush would not necessarily have to replace Solanke.
His experience playing off another attacker creates the possibility of using the pair together, with Solanke occupying central defenders while Marmoush moves into wider areas or drops between the lines.
That may be particularly attractive to De Zerbi because Marmoush can also accelerate into the spaces opened when Tottenham play through an opposition press.
"Solanke is different to Marmoush. He's got more of a physical presence," said Onuoha. "I could see the goalkeeper playing a flat ball into Solanke, Marmoush coming underneath him to receive it, and that becoming the start of the attack.
"The two of them could complement each other. Playing in a front two might bring out more of Marmoush's strengths."

Head teacher evacuated 900 children minutes before Nepal floods hit school

A headteacher has told how he saved 900 pupils' lives from the Nepal floods - by quickly evacuating them just 10 minutes before the waters hit.
Rajendra Dawadi, who is in charge of Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School in Nuwakot, told the BBC he had received four calls at 09:10 local time (03:25 GMT) warning about the disaster, which has now claimed at least 794 lives.
He quickly decided to evacuate, telling the children to run to higher ground and ordering buses full of students to turn around to flee the area.
Dawadi said: "If we didn't make a quick decision, if it was 10 minutes later, we all - including the students and me - wouldn't be able to speak to you today."

  - Published9 hours ago
The warnings had come from four different people in the space of minutes and helped him evaluate the impending danger.
"A parent came and told me that 'a big flood was coming, I am here to take my daughter, I will take her'," he added.
"Parents don't rush without a strong reason, so it was confirmed that I shouldn't waste a second to evacuate the children.
"I decided I shouldn't delay any more. Even if the flood was not coming, it was just a matter of a single day's classes.
"I feel proud that we saved so many lives."
The floods - which decimated parts of Nepal on Wednesday and have left at least 2,426 people missing - saw the school building buried under mud and debris.
Dawadi said the waters arrived so quickly that a hostel building about 100m (328ft) from the river was engulfed immediately.
At first, many students did not realise how serious the situation was.
Pupil Yunisha Amatya, 16, said she scrambled to safety with her friends just before the flood hit.
"I along with my friends survived by just 10 seconds only," she told the BBC.
"Just before the flood came, we were in the class studying. Teachers had gathered in one place and initially had no idea what had happened. After five minutes teachers came and informed us about the flood and asked us to go home."
She said one student fainted after hearing about the disaster, but many initially underestimated the danger and waited for classmates who were in a maths lesson.
Yunisha and her friends scrambled uphill through an escape route behind the school.
"I could not walk fast, and my friends helped me to climb uphill. We tried our best to be in the safer zones then. We escaped through a narrow ladder from backside of the school. Within no time, the bazaar was swept away in front of my eyes," she says, referring to the local market around the school.
"If there was no grip in my shoes I would have fallen and students and other people were jostling each other to reach the safer area while escaping. The people who choose to escape from another route are apparently swept away."
Students and teachers initially moved a few hundred metres uphill to safety before making their way to a neighbouring village.
With roads cut off and transport disrupted, many remained stranded for two nights before rescue efforts reached them.
The principal and Yunisha, who both live across the river from the school, were eventually airlifted back to their home village.
Meanwhile parents were desperately trying to contact their children and relatives.
Yunisha's mother, Sabina Kumari Shrestha, says she repeatedly tried to call both her daughter and husband, but neither could be reached.
Her husband, Yubaraj Amatya, immediately headed towards the school.
"Soon after the flood news spread, I tried my daughter's number, but she was not reachable, then I was afraid," he said.
"Within a few minutes I rushed toward my daughter's school and Trishuli Bazar was all swept by the flood, then I thought my daughter was no more. I was so horrified, stopped my scooter, there was flooding but I could not think of returning without my daughter."
For nearly an hour, he had no idea whether she was alive and kept calling her without success. Then the phone finally connected and Yunisha answered.
"Finally, my daughter received my call and I couldn't stop myself, broke out... two relatives that were with me also cried and hugged me," he said.
Yunisha appears tearful as she recalls that moment.
"After I had reached the top of the hill, I received a call from my father. He was tearful and I could not speak a word then," she said.
Back home, her family waited anxiously for her return.
"Even my younger daughter couldn't sleep. But I felt so good to see her after three days (Friday), I am so happy and relieved," her mother said.
Yunisha says she is now thinking about what comes next.
"Now I am worried about my further studies," she said.
"If I had to change my school, I would have to miss my old friends and will face difficulties to make new friends. I am sad about my further studies."
Head teacher Dawadi says better warning systems, including sirens and evacuation alerts, could have helped residents respond sooner.
But he believes his decision to act immediately prevented a catastrophe.
"Had I decided to close the school after the period, nothing might be left, only the bell would be ringing at 9:30."

Exclusive: US coaches Polish forces in a drone-focused drill based on lessons from Ukraine
Members of the Polish special forces are taking part in an exercise that simulates moving through enemy lines and launching a drone strike on a key enemy location
HOHENFELS, Germany -- On a moonless and rainy night, a group of soldiers emerged from a ramshackle building meant to resemble a church. The alpine terrain loomed over them as they quietly set off for the tree line of the German countryside a short distance away.
The soldiers are members of the Polish special forces and are taking part in an exercise designed only months ago that simulates moving through enemy lines, traversing miles of enemy territory and launching a drone strike on a key enemy location.
Initially designed by the Army's Green Berets for U.S. special forces, the exercise that began Friday is informed by and simulates many of the challenges that Ukrainian troops have experienced in their conflict with Russia. It is the first time a NATO ally like Poland has undertaken the training, and it comes at a time when tensions between Russian President Vladimir Putin and NATO countries have escalated.
“We’re using lessons learned from Ukraine,” an Army Green Beret officer assigned to the training complex said Thursday. “All of those effects that we’re seeing either Russia or Ukraine having to overcome — we’re doing our best to replicate.”
The Associated Press received rare access to both the training ground and the troops conducting the exercise, which has only been conducted twice before, both times this year, by two different Green Beret teams.
The drill highlights the focus that some parts of the U.S. military have on learning the latest techniques in drone warfare, pioneered by Ukraine during its 4 1/2-year effort to repel Russian forces. It also shows how the U.S., its NATO allies and Ukraine are working together to counter the threat of possible further Russian action in coming years even as the Trump administration has warned of troop drawdowns in Europe.
CIA Director John Ratcliffe went to Moscow this week to warn Russia not to attack NATO countries, The Wall Street Journal reported. Russia has the appetite to conduct sabotage and cyberattacks against NATO countries, but Putin wants to avoid a direct confrontation, according to three Western officials, who spoke Friday on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military matters.
During the exercise in Germany, a senior enlisted soldier familiar with the training scenario at Joint Multinational Readiness Center Hohenfels — about an hour's drive southeast from Nuremberg — said the plan is to run it several times a year. The officer said he expects most, if not all, of the 32 NATO nations to express interest in sending their troops to try the exercise.
Both spoke on condition of anonymity in line with the U.S. military's longstanding policy of not publicly identifying individual members of special forces units.
The scenario, which runs for several days, takes place on a large, 1,100-square-mile (3,000-square-kilometer) plot of land nestled in the Bavarian countryside.
Poland's special forces will be expected to sneak past a U.S. Army airborne infantry unit, whose soldiers will play the enemy. The U.S. airborne infantry unit will parachute into the closed-off training area at the Army's Hohenfels base and set themselves up into a front line.
Assuming the Polish forces can make their way past the U.S. Army, they must then move north — through about 60 miles (100 kilometers) of German countryside — to another training area in the town of Grafenwoehr, where they are expected to destroy a simulated target.
In between lie German farms and villages, private and government cameras, as well as the city of Amberg with a population of more than 40,000 people, all of which not only pose as obstacles but also create the potential for them to be spotted.
“We have them take off their military attire, go in as civilians so they can blend in — but blend in also means don’t get seen by civilians,” the senior enlisted soldier said.
German civilians in the area largely are not aware of the exercise and serve as a reasonable test of how well special forces can blend into the local population. If they fail, reports of suspicious people to police will make it back to the military, which will use them to pinpoint the team.
“This is supposed to be Russia and you’re going to stand out in Russia,” the enlisted soldier added.
Plus, the U.S. Army also will be looking for the Polish forces with drones of their own.
If they're spotted, “now you have the entire Russian arsenal coming at you,” the enlisted soldier said.
The U.S. Army can either send a military police unit to hunt for the Polish special forces with dogs or direct more drones to the area. In previous versions of the exercise, the U.S. Army had access to more than a hundred drones, the enlisted soldier said.
Troops are able to be “captured or killed” as part of the training.
While the exercise taps into drones and NATO teamwork, the message of collaboration and the value of drones has been somewhat mixed lately across the military.
President Donald Trump stirred confusion among NATO allies by going back and forth on drawing down U.S. troop levels in Europe, and the administration has launched a force review on next steps. And last week, the Army’s top officer shuttered a unit that specialized in drone warfare.
But overall, there is growing interest in tapping Ukraine for its expertise on modern warfare and, specifically, drones.
In March, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country was helping five countries in the Middle East and Gulf region counter Iranian drone attacks launched during the war with the United States, while the U.S. and European countries were among those requesting support.
Meanwhile, the number of mysterious drone incursions in Europe have grown, including as recently as this month, when a pair of drones were spotted over a German military base and a drone carrying explosives was found at a key cargo airport in Germany.

You know an inaugural festival has been a success when, after the temperature reached 95 degrees, humidity topped 80%… perspiration stains were so pervasive that it was the odd dry spots that looked like stains… constant 12-minute trudges back and forth between two action-packed stages threatened to sap what few excess pounds hadn’t been sweated off… and you realized that, amid those conditions, you had not sat down in more than 10 hours… and, sitting in a gridlocked lot waiting to get out, all you could think was:
How soon do we get to do this again?
Popular on Variety
The answer to that, at the end of the Daisy Chain Fields festival Saturday in Irvine, Calif., was some time around this year in 2027. Festival creator and headliner Olivia Rodrigo told the 45,000-strong crowd the words they wanted to hear: that this was not a one-off, and that we’d reconvene next year for another thrillingly curated, expertly executed and altogether spirit-rewarding all-female-led bill. (Flowery adjectives ours, not hers.)
Now if they could just find a way to schedule future editions of the festival at a more meteorologically reasonable time, some period of the year where it is reliably warm in SoCal yet not prone to insanely long heat waves, because climate change has abated and… well, never mind, fine … August probably is as good a time as any.
What a distraction from all that the 14-act bill (plus three guest stars) managed to provide over a 10-and-a-half-hour day of music, with one killer act after another representing a wide gamut of styles and eras, bearing a sold amount of diversity except for the very un-diverse main criterion for booking.
Of course it ended with Sarah McLachlan, the instigator of the obvious inspiration, Lilith Fair, taking the stage to implicitly give her blessing for carrying on the tradition, as she joined Rodrigo’s stage for duets of “Building a Mystery” and “Angel” (the latter dedicated to Dolly Parton, with permission given to cry, because McLachlan knows she’s good at that). Or not literally quite the end, actually, because it was inevitable when Stevie Nicks was announced as one of Rodrigo’s guests that you don’t follow that.
As an ambassador from the 1970s, Nicks was an outlier in this company, where nearly all of the acts were either fairly newly minted stars or heroines of the Lilith era. There was a case being made here, without stating it quite so bluntly, that the two greatest decades for women in pop music were the ’90s and the 2020s. History isn’t quite that simple, but for 10-plus hours Saturday, I was ready to jump in and readily make the case that the respective eras of Alanis Morissette (who also showed up as a surprise guest) and Rodrigo really were and are the greatest generations, whether it can be empirically backed up or not.
At the very least, the two climactic main stage sets, by Rodrigo and Chappell Roan, set out a pretty indisputable case that we are living in a golden era. Between the two of them, they are responsible for four of the dozen greatest albums of the decade (i.e., Roan’s lone effort so far and all three of Rodrigo’s, peaking with her best achievement to date, “You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love”). It would have been lovely to see them share a moment on stage together, and we didn’t get that. But it was enough to have them performing superb sets back to back in an effective coronation and celebration of these two as the greatest pop figures currently in their 20s.
But if you were looking for the secret heart of the festival, it might have been over on the second stage, where some of the artists who inspired Rodrigo as a nascent rocker got their moment to shine. It would be hard to imagine a more heartwarming moment than when Bikini Kill revved through some vintage punk and the entire crowd of young ‘uns in front was singing along. Kathleen Hanna was at least as agog as any of the rest of us at the realization the band was playing to a pretty full and definitely engaged field of (primarily) women, something that would have seemed like science-fiction in their heyday. Hanna said that when they played Orange County in the ’90s, they were lucky if three women showed up to one of their gigs (and then she brought out three Irvine-ites who did form their own band after getting into Bikini Kill). Not all good things come to those who wait, but occasionally poetic justice prevails.
The Breeders and Garbage kept the ’90s magic happening on the Marigold Stage, where, in the afternoon and late evening heat, everyone would have been very happy if Shirley Manson had actually been able to summon rain. Kim Deal and company were confident enough to put “Cannonball” right in the middle of their set and not save it for the end; they also provided the day’s sole quotient of country music, with vintage C&W homage “Drivin’ on 9.” Manson was as un-shy as ever when it came to passionate monologs between songs, speaking about how the band wrote songs about LGBTQ+ themes before they or the culture had discovered the language that now exists. But those songs hardly suffered for not yet having a common terminology to reference.
A danger in doing a festival like this is that 90% of the crowd may claim their spots in the main field — for the Dandelion Stage, as it was known here — and never budge for fear of losing their spots. So it was a pleasure to see (if not always so much to participate in) the mass migration that occurred between those two spaces every 30 or 40 minutes, and to see how many twentysomethings and even teens wanted to see the legends of ’90s women in rock. That stage was not strictly themed, though; the final act of the night over yonder was Not for Radio, the band formed by Marias singer Maria Zardoya, whose very chill style for this side project was perfectly timed for a post-dusk time slot, whereas it might’ve been too ambient for comfort in the heat of the day.
Back at the larger field, there could hardly have been a greater study in contrasts than seeing Mitski followed by Doechii, even if their mononym names feel phonetically compatible, and even if there was a shared excellence uniting them. Mitski was one of those acts who really would be better suited for a nighttime slot, but she was in her most energetic, stage-traversing mode, and ending on the greatest cat-lady anthem of all time, “That White Cat,” allowed for a ferocious finale. There were a lot of passionate female-forward statements made during the day, as is natural, but Mitski is the kind of artist who really represents women (and people) in all their complications; some of the songs she performed were about pure, unabated need, bordering on self-abasement at times… yet her stage persona is so powerful that you feel quite confident you’d come out on the wrong end if you ever really crossed her.
Doechii had the strongest and most delightfully outrageous look of the day (rivaled only by Roan’s attention-getting makeover). She and her four dancers appeared with body makeup that put them in various shades of red and pink — kind of like a flow chart as to how some in the audience might have been changing color as the day went on. Doechii was of a different ilk than most everyone else on the bill in terms of being the kind of artist who brings tracks, not a band. That said, she was very much in competition for the title of greatest show-woman of the day, on top of offering flavors that otherwise might’ve been severely missed in a more purely pop-rock-driven lineup. (Complaining about the heat, she asked “Irvine” if it was always like this, then noted that she’s from Florida, which might have helped explain why she didn’t sweat off all that crimson.)
Roan was all about the purple, shocking the audience with a head-to-toe different look that had her dressed in an outfit that looked like someone’s fever dream of what a TWA stewardess uniform should have looked like in the ’60s. Her hair is still red, but now straightened and shortened into a bob; the curly and queenly aura is now history in favor of something that is even h-o-t-t-e-r-t-o-go. Whether it had to do with the outfit or just where she’s at in between tours, Roan seemed more energized and physically on-point than she ever has on stage — including some high kicks that could make a Rockette jealous — while also effortlessly mastering the demands of a “Good Luck, Babe” and other vocally challenging numbers. There were no surprises in her 40-minute set; “Only the hits today. It’s only the hits,” she warned the audience. But a new stylistic outlook did as much work as a new song might’ve, in helping keep an audience transfixed as she steamed through highlights of the greatest single-album catalog anyone has managed lately.
At an hour and 20 minutes, Rodrigo’s closing set was 40 minutes longer than anyone else’s, having less to do with the generous amounts of “You Seem Pretty Sad…” appearing in a set of hers for the first time than space built in for three guests stars. It was a nice touch that her guests were announced from the outset, rather than being held back as a surprise, allowing for their inclusion on the T-shirts, etc. That turned out to be a premature move, after all, when Karen O had to cancel her cameo because of an emergency, Rodrigo told the crowd. There was still a third guest, though, as the day’s one true surprise, Morissette, came aboard for an “Ironic” duet. Rodrigo-as-natural-pro came to the forefront here as her voice proved an easy and flawless harmonic complement to Alanis on that number, and to McLachlan on “Mystery” and “Angel,” and to Nicks on the closing “Landslide.”
Rodrigo’s set was preceded by the star bringing out Melinda French Gates to announce that the philanthropist was matching the $10 million already announced by Rodrigo as going toward the 10 charity beneficiaries with a dollar-for-dollar additional $10 million. Rodrigo does not require much to put an additional spring in her step, but her giddiness was at its peak, maybe not least of all because of having a successful and (most importantly of all) non-catastrophic first festival outing being extra wind beneath her rocker-girl wings. It’s hard to tell just how much of a preview this was or wasn’t of the tour that kicks off in Hartford next month, but getting in seven of the 12 tracks from “You Seem Pretty Sad…” — basically, all but the saddest ones — plus the newly released non-album song “Serena Joy” felt more than justified. If anything, you might’ve had mixed feelings about hearing singles as tried and true as “Good 4 U,” only because of knowing still another “Pretty Sad” song could have gotten its live premiere in that slot. All of which is beating around the bush on the way to say that the set was pretty unassailable for an abridgement of what is about to come on tour.
With the show over, Nicks didn’t want to leave the stage, even after Rodrigo did, not because she had a second song to sing, but because she had the same instinct almost every performer did Saturday — to speak the younger artist’s praises for pulling this off. These were merited accolades.
Truth be told, there’ve been other all-female lineups since Lilith Fair went out with a whimper instead of a bang in its early 21st century revival: Brandi Carlile has long put on an all-female-headliner festival in Mexico every year, though the travel factor makes the bar to entry high. More subtly and slyly, the All Things Go festival that takes place each year in three eastern cities has become an almost all-female thing; you jave to love how the D.C. edition coming up next month has dozens of fantastic women on the bill… along with Father John Misty and Ryan Beatty as hilariously token dudes.
But it takes a chart-topping superstar instigator to personally make phone calls for an annual event that will be an instant sellout, of the true FOMO variety, and — it feels like — an instant cultural touchstone. Even as Rodrigo’s and Nicks’ closing “Landslide” gave way to the landslide of 45,000 people trying to exit the gates, there was a communal bliss that not even one last Bataan march could spoil. Everyone seemed pretty elated for coming out of a festival that hadn’t toppled the patriarchy, but had proven again that, in 2026, women rule music in virtually every qualifiable way.

AstraZeneca detailed the surprise failure of a closely watched heart disease clinical trial, laying out how its experimental drug offered no additional benefits for patients who were largely already on another type of medicine, the latest twist in a multibillion dollar market, STAT explains. The study indicated that patients with a progressive condition known as ATTR-CM who received AstraZeneca’s drug, what’s called a silencer, saw no improvements if they were already taking another type of drug called a stabilizer, an effect so powerful that it tanked the whole Phase 3 study.
A U.S. appeals court ruled the Food and Drug Administration went through the proper process when it declared Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly’s diabetes and obesity drugs are no longer in shortage, Bloomberg Law notes. The order is a loss for the Outsourcing Facilities Association, which representing large-scale compounders and challenged FDA decisions in the last two years that shortages ended for Novo’s Ozempic and Wegovy and Lilly’s Mounjaro and Zepbound. That declaration restricted compounders from legally mass-producing versions of the drugs.

Uber, Eternal, and Porter have reportedly withdrawn from the Karnataka Platform-Based Gig Workers Welfare Board amid their legal challenges to the state’s gig workers law. The three companies were members of the welfare board constituted under the Karnataka Platform-Based Gig Workers (Social Security and Welfare) Act, 2025. They said they do not want to remain part of a statutory body created under a law they have challenged in the Karnataka High Court, ET reported. The HC has declined to stay the law but granted interim protection from coercive action to companies challenging it, including Eternal, Swiggy, Zepto, Urban Company, and Valmo Transportation. Uber also moved the Karnataka HC last month, challenging the constitutional validity of the law. The court subsequently extended the same interim protection to the ride-hailing major and directed that its petition be heard along with the existing challenges to the legislation. Amazon India, which is also represented on the welfare board, has remained a member as it is not involved in the ongoing litigation, the report said. The Karnataka government is now looking to fill the vacancies created by the exits. Delhivery, Namma Yatri, and Yulu have agreed to join the board, it added. Inc42 has reached out to Eternal, Porter, and Uber for comments on their reported withdrawal from the welfare board. The story will be updated on receiving a response. So far, only 15 platform companies, collectively representing about 7 Lakh gig workers, have registered with the board. The development comes as Karnataka labour minister Santosh Lad steps up the enforcement of the law. He reviewed its implementation yesterday and directed officials to issue notices to platforms that have not deposited the prescribed welfare fee with either the welfare board or the Karnataka HC. Why Platforms Are Challenging The Law At the heart of the dispute is the argument that Karnataka’s law creates a separate social security framework for gig workers despite the Centre’s Code on Social Security, 2020. Uber has argued that the state law overlaps with the central framework while imposing additional financial and compliance requirements on platforms. The company has also questioned the rules framed under the Act, saying they could leave platforms with obligations under both the state and central social security regimes. Karnataka notified the Platform-Based Gig Workers (Social Security and Welfare) Act in September 2025. The legislation provides for a welfare board and fund, social security benefits, and a grievance redressal mechanism for platform-based gig workers. A key provision of the law is the welfare fee payable by platforms. In February 2026, the state fixed the fee at 1% of each transaction, subject to category-specific caps. Food and grocery delivery platforms have to pay up to 50 paise per transaction. For ride-hailing platforms, the fee is capped at 50 paise for two-wheelers, 75 paise for three-wheelers, and ₹1 for four-wheelers. The levy is intended to fund benefits such as life and accident insurance, disability coverage, medical assistance, maternity benefits, and old-age protection for gig workers. Platforms have raised concerns about the additional costs and compliance burden. They also fear that similar laws in other states could lead to a fragmented regulatory landscape, requiring companies operating across India to comply with different welfare fees and rules.

Trump posts AI video of ‘Lake America’ being protected by an army of bequiffed ‘Donald Ducks’
The post came after the president signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario ‘Lake America’ amid a bitter tariff war with Canada
President Donald Trump on Saturday posted an apparently AI-generated video depicting an army of buff, bequiffed and heavily-armed “Donald Ducks” patrolling the shores of “Lake America.”
Hours later, while he was at his Virginia golf course, the president posted another AI-generated video, this time showing himself knocking over a “Welcome to Lake Ontario” sign and installing a “Welcome to Lake America” one in its place. He then dances to the Village People’s “YMCA.”
The posts followed Trump’s executive order renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America” amid a bitter tariff war with Canada, a longtime U.S. ally and trading partner.
Set to the theme song from Hawaii Five-O, a 34-second clip shows a squadron of Canada geese marching near the Great Lake. The birds have human arms, carry assault rifles and sport the president’s signature blond pouf of hair.
The geese then fire their weapons into the air as fireworks erupt over the skyline of a nearby city — which appears to resemble Toronto.
Earlier this week, Trump announced that the U.S. was giving “serious consideration” to rebranding Lake Ontario, which straddles the U.S.-Canada border. He also posted a TikTok video showing himself using a Sharpie to mark up a map of the lake.
“We’re gonna make a little change; we’re gonna call it something different than Lake Ontario,” the 80-year-old president said in the clip.
Any doubt that the effort was simply trolling evaporated Thursday, when Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to refer to Lake Ontario as “Lake America” in all official documents and records. The move echoed his similar effort last year to rebrand the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America.”
Although the president can direct how the federal government refers to geographic features, he cannot compel foreign nations, private entities or even U.S. states to follow his lead.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney responded to the missive in a Thursday post on X.
“The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big,’” he wrote. “The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America.”
“We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms,” he added. “Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always.”
Relations between the U.S. and Canada have deteriorated since Trump took office, including as a result of his repeated suggestion that Canada should become the “51st state.” Tensions escalated further this week over trade.
On August 22, the U.S. imposed 50 percent tariffs on about $20 billion worth of Canadian exports after last-minute talks between Ottawa and Washington broke down. The Trump administration has accused Canada of discriminating against U.S. businesses.
Carney, who has denied Trump’s accusations, likened the levies to an act of war. He retaliated with tariffs of up to 50 percent on a range of U.S. goods.
The trade war has also spilled into a war of words. This week, Trump singled out Ontario Premier Doug Ford in a Truth Social post, describing him as a blustering “flunky” who needs to “fall in line.”
At a news conference, Ford responded by calling Trump a “dictator,” a “bully” and the “king of bankruptcies.” He also told Trump to “kiss my a**.”

The Los Angeles Dodgers have spent another season searching for the right bullpen combination as they try to turn a talented roster into a third straight World Series championship.
While the relief group is deeper than it was a year ago, particularly after the addition of star closer Edwin Diaz, inconsistency has continued to force manager Dave Roberts and the front office to explore different options. Though the group has been fluctuating, it seems certain that the Dodgers will settle on a strong combination by October.
“While the bullpen issues are not nearly as drastic as they were last year, the Dodgers are also experiencing problems closing out games as the season comes to a close,” MLB.com’s Brent Maguire wrote. “In simpler terms, the Dodgers’ bullpen might be struggling right now — L.A. relievers had a bottom-10 ERA (4.44) since the All-Star break entering Wednesday’s games — but this group could look drastically different in the playoffs.”
That backdrop makes the latest development involving former Dodgers left-hander Caleb Ferguson particularly noteworthy. The veteran, who spent five seasons in Los Angeles, has now been designated for assignment by the St. Louis Cardinals after a short stint with the club.
Former Los Angeles Dodgers Veteran Sees St Louis Cardinals Stint Ends Very Quickly
Ferguson's Cardinals tenure lasted only nine games before St. Louis decided to cut him from the big league roster through a designation for assignment on Saturday, according to the official transaction log.
The decision comes after Ferguson failed to provide the production St. Louis was seeking in his very short run with the team. And he’s running out of time this season to join a new team.
“With Ferguson simply not performing, the Cards have chosen to utilize his roster spot on a fresher arm,” Mark Polishuk wrote for MLB Trade Rumors. “Since trades are no longer permitted past the deadline, Ferguson can only change teams via the DFA process if he is claimed off the waiver wire. Claiming Ferguson would put a new club on the hook for the roughly $750K remaining of Ferguson’s $4.5MM salary for the 2026 season.”
While Ferguson could potentially be an inexpensive reclamation candidate for a club needing left-handed depth, his struggles with the Cardinals might dissuade some potential suitors as well.
Long-Time Los Angeles Dodgers Reliever Has Plenty Of Experience
Dodgers fans will recall that Ferguson's best major league stretches came in Los Angeles, where he was a bullpen staple for several significant playoff series..
Originally drafted by the Dodgers in the 2014 MLB Draft, Ferguson climbed through the organization's minor league system before making his major league debut in 2018. He quickly established himself as a versatile pitching weapon, working both as a starter and reliever.
He went 7-2 with a 3.49 ERA in 29 appearances during his rookie season and was particularly effective in the second half. He also delivered three scoreless innings across six postseason appearances that year.
Ferguson later became a valuable bullpen piece again after recovering from his second Tommy John surgery. In 2022, he posted a 1.82 ERA across 37 appearances, then followed that with a 3.43 ERA over 68 games in 2023.
The Dodgers eventually traded him to the New York Yankees in 2024, beginning a stretch that took him away from the organization where he spent the first five seasons of his career.
Now DFA'd by St. Louis, Ferguson could once again become an intriguing depth option for a contender — including teams dealing with bullpen uncertainty. However, a reunion with the Dodgers appears unlikely.

Everton call off Armstrong sale after fan backlash
- Published
Everton have called off a proposed deal to sell midfielder Harrison Armstrong to Nottingham Forest following a backlash from the club's supporters.
Forest made a bid of £40m plus a potential sell-on clause for the England Under-19 international, who is regarded as one of the brightest prospects to emerge from Finch Farm in recent years.
The news enraged Everton supporters, who sang Armstrong's name throughout Saturday's draw at Bournemouth and said there would be a "riot" if he was sold.
Everton's board, led by chair Dan Friedkin, eventually decided to reject Forest's bid – with the owner at the forefront of the discussions.
- 'Supporters aren't always wrong' - Moyes on Everton fans' anger 
  - Published15 hours ago
- Are Moyes and Everton's owners on same page? 
  - Published2 days ago
Armstrong has made 24 appearances for Everton and played 87 minutes against the Cherries before he was replaced by Charly Alcaraz.
Speaking after the game Toffees boss David Moyes said he understood the fans' frustration and appeared to suggest the decision was out of his hands.
"I think you always have to consider supporters; supporters aren't always wrong," Moyes.
"But then there are also times where I've had people at clubs who are really powerful and make difficult decisions.
"Managers have to make decisions on players sometimes and they feel like huge decisions. But there are sometimes bigger decisions to be made and the club will, I'm sure, make what they think is the right one.
"If I'd say something to them (the fans), I'd say their manager's an Evertonian."
Moyes has been frustrated by the club's lack of signings and he made it clear he wanted reinforcements after the Carabao Cup second-round win against Preston on Wednesday.
The Toffees have signed Hayden Hackney from Middlesbrough for an initial £16m and fellow midfielder Christian Norgaard from Arsenal for £7m
Tyrique George and Merlin Rohl signed permanent deals after loan spells last season, while Brennan Johnson joined from Crystal Palace in a swap deal with Dwight McNeil.
Talks are ongoing and moving forward between Everton and Manchester City for Jack Grealish to return before the deadline, with another loan the most likely option at this stage.
However, the club have yet to sign a right-back to replace Seamus Coleman, though they have revived interest in Kenny Tete, who turned down the Toffees to sign a new deal at Fulham last year.
Analysis: Everton owners try to head off open revolt
Everton's decision to reject Nottingham Forest's offer for teenager Harrison Armstrong has headed off the possibility of open revolt against owners The Friedkin Group from a furious fanbase.
The revelation that Everton had received a £40m bid from Forest for the gifted 19-year-old, and it was under consideration, sparked an instant backlash from fans angry at the idea the club's best homegrown product for years could be sold.
Instead, after a day of drama on and off the field, Everton's board - led by chairman and billionaire owner Dan Friedkin - decided to unanimously reject Forest's approach and keep Armstrong.
Everton's fans made their feelings clear during the 1-1 draw at Bournemouth. The reaction was so loud, and toxic, that it is sure to have been heard by Everton's delegation at The Vitality Stadium and relayed back to the hierarchy in the United States.
It is highly unlikely to be coincidence that a deal that looked to be advancing was then stopped in its tracks.
And it will also pacify manager David Moyes, whose mood looked ominous post-match at Bournemouth, as he will now keep a young talent regarded as a key part of the club's future.

Srinagar, Aug 30: The National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS) successfully conducted the NEET-PG 2026 examination today, 30 August 2026, across the country with comprehensive logistical, technological, security and manpower arrangements to ensure a fair, secure and seamless examination process.
The examination was scheduled for 2,73,096 candidates at 1,111 examination centres across 339 cities, covering all 36 States and Union Territories. A total of 2,65,980 candidates appeared for the examination, with the examination successfully completed for approximately 2,63,535 candidates.
The nationwide examination was supported by extensive real-time monitoring and stringent security measures. A total of 2,527 faculty members were appointed as Independent Appraisers to oversee the conduct of the examination. In addition, more than 700 senior faculty members, including Deans, Directors, Medical Superintendents and senior professors, were deployed as Flying Squad members.
To strengthen coordination and monitoring, 16 NBEMS Regional Command Centres were made operational across the country.
The examination centres were also placed under live CCTV surveillance, which was continuously monitored from the NBEMS Command Centre at its Headquarters in Dwarka. A dedicated team of 190 personnel from NBEMS and TCS was deployed for real-time surveillance and monitoring.
At the dedicated Command Centre at NBEMS Headquarters, officials from NBEMS, Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, BEL, ECIL and TCS maintained close and continuous oversight of the examination process throughout the day.
As part of measures to further strengthen examination security and prevent impersonation, Aadhaar-based authentication of candidates was successfully undertaken at examination centres. Government agencies extended their full support towards the secure and orderly conduct of the examination.
While the examination was successfully completed for the overwhelming majority of candidates nationwide, an unforeseen technical disruption occurred at iON Digital Zone iDZ Sitapura Centres, Jaipur, Rajasthan (TC Nos. 41682 and 41683), where the examination could not be completed for 2,445 candidates due to internal power supply issues at the test centres, attributable to M/s TCS Ltd., the examination conducting agency.
NBEMS has expressed regret for the inconvenience caused to the affected candidates. To ensure that all affected candidates are provided a fair and equitable opportunity to appear in NEET-PG 2026, examination for these 2,445 candidates will be conducted on 05 September 2026 (Saturday) at 03:00 PM in Jaipur, Rajasthan.
The successful conduct of the examination across 1,111 centres in 339 cities reflects the extensive coordination among examination authorities, medical institutions, faculty, security agencies, technology teams and other stakeholders involved in the nationwide exercise.
NBEMS appreciates the cooperation, patience and trust of the candidates and acknowledges the dedicated efforts of all personnel and institutions associated with the conduct of NEET-PG 2026.

Abhijeet Dipke said that Mohan Bhagwat had earlier said that the protesting Gen Z should not be called anti-nationals but PM Modi came up with ‘dimagi naxal’.
Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke on Sunday said the BJP believes it has become bigger than the RSS. Dipke, who led the Jantar Mantar protest against alleged irregularities in the NEET exam, said the ruling party should heed what Sangh chief Mohan Bhagwat has been saying.
The former political communication strategist made the remarks in reply to a reporter's question about the RSS chief's statement in New York. Bhagwat had said that if any Hindu thinks that there should be no Muslims in Bharat, he will not remain a Hindu.
''I have been saying this from the beginning that the BJP should listen to Mohan Bhagwat. After being in power for 12 years and having so many agencies in its hands, the BJP is thinking that it has grown bigger than the RSS," Dipke was quoted by news agency PTI as saying.
He pointed out that Bhagwat had earlier said that the protesting Gen Z should not be called anti-nationals.
"But the PM (Narendra Modi) came up with a new word, 'Dimagi Naxal'. It clearly shows that the PM is not listening to Mohan Bhagwat,'' Dipke added.
The Boston University graduate said that while the RSS chief talks about inclusivity and not disrespecting children, the PM uses such words. “This doesn't look good," he said.
"They should at least listen to Mohan Bhagwat, who is their mentor... they (BJP) are in power because of the RSS,'' Dipke added.
Dipke on Sonam Wangchuk's ‘not saints’ remark.
Asked about activist Sonam Wangchuk's statement in an interview with a YouTube channel that, in his assessment, the CJP leaders have political ambition and are “not saints”, Abhijeet Dipke asserted that the statement was being distorted.

The language of fairness may be changing, but the desire for lighter skin has not necessarily disappeared in our country. As skin-lightening practices move into skincare, dermatological procedures and digital spaces, the health consequences are becoming increasingly harder to recognise and regulate.
What has changed
Skin lightening in India is changing. The fairness creams that once dominated advertisements are less visible today. The language around them has also shifted. Words such as ‘brightening’, ‘glow’, ‘de-tan’ and ‘even tone’ are now common across skincare products and digital platforms.
For dermatologists, this change is increasingly visible in clinical practice.
Patients may not come to the clinic saying that they have been trying to become fairer. They often present because something has already gone wrong. There may be acne, redness, thinning of the skin, increased facial hair, pigmentation or infections. Oral agents used with the expectation of achieving lighter skin are also being sought.
“We see patients because of the side-effects of what they have tried, and then work backwards,” says Rashmi Sarkar, head and director - professor, department of dermatology Vardhman Mahavir Medical College and Safdarjung hospital, New Delhi.
The profile is changing too. What was once viewed largely as a concern among women is now also seen among men, teenagers and transgender persons. This makes skin lightening an important skin-health issue, rather than simply a cosmetic concern.
Where treatment ends, lightening begins
Not all treatment that reduces pigmentation is skin lightening.
Melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation are common pigmentary disorders. They can be persistent and distressing, particularly in darker skin tones. These conditions may require treatment.
The important distinction, Dr. Sarkar says, is between treating a pigmentary disorder and attempting to lighten a person’s normal, constitutive skin colour.
This distinction is becoming less clear to consumers.
A product described as ‘brightening’ may be intended to reduce pigmentation, improve dullness or make the skin appear more even. The term itself does not explain what is being changed.
For clinicians, the focus should remain on skin health. Brighter-looking skin can follow better photoprotection, appropriate skincare, control of inflammation and improvements in general health and lifestyle. None of these requires changing a person’s natural skin colour.
The digital shift
The larger change is taking place online.
Skin-lightening messages are no longer limited to television advertisements or product packaging. They are increasingly delivered through influencers, e-commerce platforms, before-and-after photographs and social media.
Algorithms can amplify these messages. A person who watches one video on pigmentation may subsequently be shown repeated content around brightening products, supplements, peels or procedures. Filters and image manipulation add another layer. Photographs can be altered to make skin appear lighter, smoother or more uniform. Artificial intelligence can make these alterations increasingly difficult to recognise.
Dr. Sarkar believes public education, must therefore, also address digital literacy. People need to learn to recognise filtered or manipulated images and to question the aesthetic standards repeatedly presented to them online.
The impact is particularly relevant for younger users. Repeated exposure can gradually alter what is perceived as normal skin and what is considered a problem requiring correction.
When treatment becomes excessive
The growth of aesthetic skincare has also widened the number of places where people seek treatment.
Patients may move between dermatology clinics, aesthetic centres, salons, spas, social media and online marketplaces. The distinction between medical treatment and cosmetic marketing can become unclear.
Dr. Sarkar stresses that pigmentary disorders should be assessed by qualified dermatologists. Procedures also need to be selected carefully and patients should not be overtreated. This is particularly relevant in darker skin tones, where inflammation caused by aggressive treatment can itself lead to further pigmentation. The treatment can then become part of the problem.
There is also a role for clinicians in managing expectations. Not every variation in skin colour requires treatment. Unregulated over-the-counter skin-lightening products should be avoided and unrealistic expectations need to be addressed early.
The health consequences can be significant. The ILDS has warned that the misuse of potent topical corticosteroids in skin-bleaching products can contribute to treatment-resistant fungal infections, irreversible skin damage and systemic side-effects. The organisation has called for stronger regulation, clearer guidance and better public education.
Beyond the clinic
The response to skin lightening therefore also needs to change.
Traditional awareness campaigns remain important, but they may no longer be sufficient when much of the contemporary conversation is taking place online. This is a particular focus of the ILDS Strategic Working Group on Skin Bleaching. The group brings together international dermatology expertise to address harmful skin-lightening practices while also recognising the legitimate need for safe, evidence-based treatment of pigmentary disorders.
The message, says Dr. Sarkar, who is part of the Working Group, needs to reach people where these practices are now being discussed and promoted. “We need to leverage social media and amplify the message,” she says. This includes closer collaboration between the ILDS and national dermatology societies, as well as engagement with pharmacists, educators and credible public voices.
India has previously seen organised campaigns around inappropriate topical steroid use. These efforts included education of both patients and pharmacists. A similar approach is now needed for contemporary skin-lightening practices.
The ILDS initiative also has a wider aim: to move the conversation away from skin colour as an aesthetic hierarchy and towards skin health. The message is simple, but important. Healthy skin exists in every shade.
Patients, regulators need to be in step
For those experimenting with skincare routines, particularly skin lightening, it means understanding the difference between a pigmentary disorder and normal skin colour. It means recognising that medicines used without appropriate supervision can damage the skin. It means knowing that repeated procedures are not always better treatment. Increasingly, it also means understanding that the images seen online may have been filtered, lightened or otherwise altered.
Regulation will need to evolve alongside this change. Looking only for products explicitly labelled as ‘fairness’ products will miss part of the contemporary market. Claims, ingredients, digital advertising, influencer marketing and access to potent medicines all require attention.
But regulation alone cannot address the deeper issue.
Greater awareness has made overt fairness advertising less acceptable. Yet, as Dr. Sarkar points out, social perceptions around skin colour continue to persist.
The challenge is therefore no longer only the fairness cream. The language has changed. The platforms have changed. The people seeking these interventions are also changing. The response now needs to change with them.
For dermatologists, professional societies and public-health organisations, the opportunity lies in moving beyond treating complications after they occur. The focus must be on prevention, evidence-based care, digital education and a clearer understanding of what healthy skin actually means.
(Dr. Monisha Madhumita is a consultant dermatologist at Saveetha Medical College, Chennai. mail.monisha.m@gmail.com)

Lionel Messi scored a second half hat-trick, an assist, and finished Inter Miami’s 7-1 romp over CF Montreal with four goals in a Major League Soccer (MLS) league game on Saturday.
The Argentinian playmaker scored a goal either side of the first half before completing a hat-trick in the 83rd minute. He finished the game with his traditional free-kick goal in the stoppage time.
Miami began its torment over Montreal when Casemiro headed home in the 20th minute. But the visitor levelled 17 minutes later through Fabian Herbers.
However, Messi didn’t let Montreal settle and struck a low-curling free kick past goalkeeper Thomas Gillier in the 40th minute to take the lead back.
Messi then extended Miami’s lead shortly after half-time as the 39-year-old superstar’s momentum helped him weave through a cluster of Montreal defenders before drilling a shot into the bottom corner.
After a rather quiet 30 odd minutes, Messi assisted Luis Suarez in the 80th minute before 18-year-old Alexander Shaw found the back of the net soon to make it 6-1.
But there was still time for Messi to score a fourth as the veteran curled in a free kick from the edge of the area in the dying minutes of stoppage time.
The victory leaves Miami in second place in the Eastern Conference, seven points behind leader Nashville.

How to check if your TV is playing in 4K or not
You'd think everything on a 4K TV is displaying in 4K, but it's unfortunately not that simple.
If you have a 4K TV, along with a 4K video source like a premium streaming subscription tier or modern gaming console, then you should be watching everything in 4K, right? Unfortunately, this isn't necessarily the case. On your TV, streaming services, and any connected devices, you'll have to do a few checks to confirm if you're actually watching at the desired resolution.
The first step is to confirm that you even have a 4K TV. If you aren't sure, go to the main Settings page and look under the About or Info tab, where you should find model information. If the model has "4K" or "UHD" in its name, it supports this standard. Otherwise, look up the specific model name or number to check — if it's not in the menu, it might be printed on the back or front of the unit.
Once this is confirmed, you can move on to next steps, which involve confirming that your source devices, content and settings are all set up for 4K.
A few easy steps to check on your TV first
After establishing your TV is 4K, as long as you're playing 4K sources, the TV should display them as such. Virtually every 4K TV from brands like Samsung and LG automatically detects the resolution of what's playing and displays in its native resolution. There's no manual adjustment option. Many remotes have an Info or similar button that shows a banner indicating the current output resolution. You might also be able to see this by hovering over a source in your TV's menus.
With many TVs, you can adjust the picture size with options like 16:9, fit to screen, or custom if desired, though this is separate from resolution. LG TVs offer a feature called Super Resolution for image scaling, but this is for upscaling lower-res content on a 4K TV. Your 4K TV likely has different viewing modes like Cinematic and Gaming; swapping between these will adjust the picture and processing, but won't change the resolution itself.
Adjust your source device and streaming settings if needed
Your TV will only output what's being sent from the connected device. The best streaming devices support 4K, but some older or cheaper models only go up to 1080p. So if you're using a gaming console, streaming stick, or similar device, check its settings to make sure 4K output is enabled. Be sure you're using a modern HDMI cable that supports 4K, as well.
With most streaming services, you must subscribe to the highest tier to access 4K streaming, but may still need to enable this option. For example, for Disney+, go to the main Settings panel, then App settings. There's an option for data usage, under which you can choose Automatic to "stream in the highest quality available" (up to 4K UHD, which uses around 7.7 GB/hour). There are also Moderate (HD) and Save data (SD) options. As long as Automatic is selected and you subscribe to the appropriate plan, you should be streaming in 4K when available.
When using a service that lets you change the quality on-demand, like YouTube, set the quality of the current video to 4K (though not all videos are uploaded in 4K). Live TV services typically include "4K" in applicable channels' number labels, though this has caveats. Such channels may be lower-res content that's upscaled instead of native 4K. Live TV rarely streams in true 4K outside of special sports events.
Virtually all Apple TV originals are in 4K, but not every show or movie you can stream via Apple TV is. You'll see the available resolution in the information list under the title when you select it. Ted Lasso, for example, is available in 4K, but live sports may not be. Amazon Prime Video has 4K on offer, but it's now locked behind a higher-cost Amazon Prime Video Ultra tier that removes ads and adds 4K access for available titles.
All stars must align for 4K viewing
Provided you have a 4K TV and you're watching from a 4K source with the applicable plan, you should be watching in 4K. Though a show may be presented in 4K on a service like Netflix, if you aren't subscribed to Premium, it won't be streamed at that quality. When watching 1080p or even SD content, your TV may have an upscaling feature that improves the picture so it looks better, but it isn't truly 4K. It's similar with gaming: even though the PS5 supports 4K, some games will output at a lower resolution (which may be upscaled) to achieve a stable frame rate.
It's possible that a service could be downgrading quality to ensure you get a smooth viewing experience, rather than showing a constant buffering wheel because your network can't keep up. You can check if Netflix is downgrading your picture quality, for example. To avoid this, make sure you have a solid internet plan. 25Mbps is the minimum recommended for 4K streaming, though Dolby Vision content or watching on multiple devices at once will require more bandwidth.
As long as all parts along the train support it, your 4K TV will show 4K content from a 4K source. If not, you'll be watching at a downgraded resolution. Once you verify that you have a 4K TV, it all comes down to the source of the content.
