Salmonella is often linked to food poisoning, diarrhoea and typhoid. But the infection can range from mild gastroenteritis that gets better on its own to a serious bloodstream infection, and therefore, say experts, deserves more attention than it is currently being given. Typhoid also remains a major health burden in India. A Lancet study published this year, estimated 4.9 million typhoid cases and about 7,850 deaths in India in 2023. About 730,000 people were estimated to have been hospitalised, with fluoroquinolone-resistant infections accounting for 82% of these hospitalisations.
Salmonella is a group of bacteria that can cause different infections. Typhoid and paratyphoid or enteric fever, are caused by Salmonella Typhi and Salmonella Paratyphi. Unlike common food poisoning, typhoid can spread from the gut into the bloodstream, causing prolonged fever and, in severe cases, intestinal bleeding or perforation. It usually spreads through food or water contaminated with faeces The problem, however, is broader than typhoid. Non-typhoidal Salmonella infections, which often cause gastroenteritis, may go undiagnosed because many people recover without testing. At the same time, antibiotic resistance is making serious infections harder to treat.
Why infections turn serious
Non-typhoidal Salmonella commonly causes gastroenteritis, with diarrhoea, stomach cramps, fever and sometimes vomiting. It is often linked to poultry, eggs and other animal-based foods. Most healthy people recover with supportive care, but the infection can become serious and spread to the bloodstream, particularly in young children, older adults and people with weakened immunity.
“Salmonella should not be seen as only a cause of diarrhoea,” said Sweatha Kumar, associate consultant, infectious diseases, Rela Hospital, Chennai. “In some patients, especially young children, older adults and those living with other illnesses or weakened immunity, it can become invasive and life-threatening.”
Suresh Kumar D., senior specialist in infectious diseases, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, Vanagaram, Chennai, said the actual burden of non-typhoidal Salmonella is difficult to estimate as many mild infections are never diagnosed.
Contaminated water, food chain
Both typhoid and non-typhoidal Samonella infections spread through the faecal-oral route, but their sources are different.
For typhoid, humans are the reservoir. Someone with the infection, including someone who has no symptoms but carries the bacteria, can contaminate food or water. This makes safe drinking water, sanitation and hand hygiene central to prevention. Lack of access to safe water and adequate sanitation are major risk factors for typhoid.Non-typhoidal Salmonella has a wider ecology, involving animals, food and the environment. Poultry, eggs, meat and other animal-derived foods can be sources. Transmission can also occur when raw meat contaminates ready-to-eat food during preparation.
“Contamination can occur at multiple points, from farms, slaughterhouses and food processing to transportation, storage, restaurants and finally the household kitchen,” Dr. Sweatha said. “That is why Salmonella is very much a One Health problem involving humans, animals, food and the environment.”
Food handlers can play an important role in transmission, as those carrying the infection can contaminate food and potentially expose many people to the bacteria. But food safety cannot depend only on individual food handlers. The wider system needs better training, sanitation, refrigeration, monitoring and enforcement. While the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India has surveillance and testing systems, gaps remain, particularly in the large informal food sector.
At the household level, it is important follow: washing hands, using safe water, cooking poultry and eggs thoroughly, refrigerating perishable foods appropriately and keeping raw meat separate from ready-to-eat food.
Challenges and way forward
The major concern is the growing antimicrobial resistance in Salmonella.
India has seen a major shift in the resistance pattern of S. Typhi. A recent study in PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases said, culture-confirmed isolates from 1977 to 2024 found that fluoroquinolone resistance rose sharply, reaching 85% in 2015-19, and remains high despite a subsequent decline.
“The emergence and spread of extensively drug-resistant typhoid shows what can happen when resistance accumulates across multiple antibiotic classes,” Dr. Sweatha said, “It can leave clinicians with very limited treatment options.”
A study published in Indian Pediatrics found of an enteric fever outbreak in Thane between April and July 2025 found that 44 of 167 culture-proven cases 26.35% were resistant to ceftriaxone. Tanker-water supply was significantly associated with ceftriaxone resistance in the outbreak.
Researchers have also documented carbapenem-resistant S. Typhi carrying the blaNDM-5 resistance gene in India, highlighting the possibility of resistance emerging even to antibiotics generally reserved for difficult infections.
Experts say the answer is not to simply use stronger antibiotics. Blood culture is the main test for suspected typhoid and should ideally be done before antibiotics are started. The Widal test has limitations and should not be used alone to diagnose typhoid. For uncomplicated non-typhoidal Salmonella gastroenteritis, treatment mainly involves adequate fluids and electrolyte replacement. Antibiotics are usually reserved for severe or invasive infections and people at higher risk of complications.
“Giving an antibiotic for every fever is not harmless,” said J.S. Kumar, professor and head of general medicine, SRM Medical College Hospital & Research Institute, Chennai. “Unnecessary antibiotic use is one of the things that drives antimicrobial resistance.”
For typhoid, antibiotics are necessary, but the choice should be guided by the local resistance pattern and, where possible, culture and susceptibility results.
Prevention remains as important as treatment. The World Health Organization recommends typhoid conjugate vaccines for children from six months of age; however, this not yet part of India’s universal immunisation programme.
The challenge is to treat the infections that genuinely require antibiotics while preventing the infections that can be prevented in the first place.

Three years after a closely watched research misconduct investigation of Stanford’s then-president, Marc Tessier-Lavigne, led to his resignation, the prominent neuroscientist revealed new details this week from his research and travel in an attempt to refute allegations that he published fraudulent results and orchestrated a cover-up.
These allegations found new life this year with the release of “How to Rule the World,” a book by former Stanford Daily reporter Theo Baker, who presents Tessier-Lavigne as a case study in Silicon Valley’s culture of corner-cutting. A key part of that story revolves around a major paper on neurodegeneration that Tessier-Lavigne co-authored in 2009, while he was a top scientist at the South San Francisco biotech Genentech.
The former university head on Wednesday posted a more than 3,000-word response to the book on his Stanford lab website, alongside emails with former colleagues meant to bolster his defense of the study, published in the journal Nature.

FC Barcelona has reportedly agreed on a deal to sign Gabriel Jesus from Arsenal, with the Brazilian forward set to sign a two-year contract that includes an option to extend for an additional year, taking the deal through to 2029.
According to reports from the UK and Spain, his medical is scheduled on August 31 ahead of the permanent transfer.
Under the terms agreed upon, Arsenal is due to receive a 10 million euro package plus add-ons for the deal.
Gabriel Jesus made an immediate impact after joining Arsenal from Manchester City in July 2022, having previously worked under Mikel Arteta. He scored twice on his home debut, but a knee injury at the 2022 World Cup hampered his first season before he returned in April 2023 to net twice against Leeds.
In the 2023-24 season, despite having a knee surgery days before the Community Shield, he contributed eight goals and eight assists, shining in the Champions League with standout performances against Sevilla and RC Lens.
He also extended his remarkable record of never being on the losing side when scoring in a Premier League match (60 games: 55 wins, five draws at the start of the season).
In the 2024-25 season, Jesus hit form in December with five goals in four days against Crystal Palace, including a Carabao Cup hat-trick and two Premier League strikes. Another knee injury against Manchester United in the FA Cup third round, after scoring on New Year’s Day versus Brentford, ended his campaign early.

Sendai – It was January 2021 in Sendai, and the city was in a deep winter freeze.
A woman, in her 50s and out of work, had her water services shut off due to late payments, as well as her gas. Unable to cook at home or afford much of anything, and with public water faucets frozen solid, she spent a week eating raw eggs and drinking snowmelt before reaching out to a local food bank for help.
The woman’s case, recounts Saori Kasahara, a graduate student and volunteer with Food Bank Sendai, helped the organization realize that most of their beneficiaries were facing some level of energy poverty — forced to choose between “heat or eat” or, in many cases, unable to afford enough of either.
It also highlights a growing issue that, amid rising costs due to overseas conflicts and a weak yen, goes far beyond Sendai.
The European Union, where awareness of the issue is relatively high, describes energy poverty as occurring when a household must reduce energy consumption to a degree that negatively impacts health and wellbeing. There are other definitions as well, such as when a high percentage of household expenditure is spent on energy.
One primary factor that contributes to energy poverty is, understandably, low income. Roughly 15% of Japan’s population lives in “relative poverty,” according to the Ministry of Health, Labor and Welfare.
However, University of Osaka lecturer Hayato Koga points out that other factors, such as rising energy prices and housing conditions, also play a part. “Reducing the issue to just a matter of income downplays and oversimplifies the problem,” he says.
Being unable to meet the energy needs for a decent standard of living can negatively impact one’s mental health, opportunities for social interaction and performance at school and work, alongside serious health impacts, such as heat stress in the summer.
Energy poverty has been rising in Japan since the 2000s, spurred by the March 2011 triple disaster, the Russia-Ukraine war and the weak yen, according to research by University of Tsukuba professor Shinichiro Okushima. Based on his methodology, roughly 10% of households in Japan are in a state of energy poverty.
Currently, energy poverty is not named in Japan’s national policies, a step experts say would help raise awareness and galvanize action.
Existing measures — from welfare fuel allowances to energy-efficiency targets — indirectly address the issue to a certain extent. However, experts and advocates are calling for both improvements to existing systems and further measures to fully tackle energy poverty in Japan.
The vulnerable
Researchers and advocates have identified various trends in energy-vulnerable groups.
One such cohort is older adults living alone, a group that is expected to account for over 20% of households by 2050, up from 13.2% in 2020, according to a paper published earlier this year by Okushima and colleagues. Older adults tend to have lower income but spend more time at home.
“Since rural areas have increasingly aging populations and a larger proportion of people living alone in older homes, we could see energy poverty rise especially in the countryside,” Okushima says.
Those living in rural areas tend to depend on cars for transportation and often don’t have access to the cheaper city gas networks, which adds to their energy expenses, according to Okushima’s research.
Immigrants are another group potentially at risk, according to members of Food Bank Sendai, which was established in 2020 to serve those out of work due to the COVID-19 pandemic but which has expanded its scope since. About half of the food bank’s roughly 10,000 beneficiaries in 2025 were foreign nationals, primarily students from Asian nations attending Japanese school or a vocational school while working part-time jobs, says Shinsei Mori, the food bank’s director.
“With soaring prices and relatively low wages, many international students are struggling to make ends meet,” Mori says.
Kasahara adds that immigrants may face a language barrier if they fall behind on utility payments and need to find a solution. Even for those fluent in Japanese, the steps before a utility shuts off power due to late payments, and accessing avenues for recourse, can be opaque, she says.
Another key consideration when it comes to energy poverty in Japan is the lack of insulation in residential buildings, especially older ones, Koga notes. Low-income households often have no choice but to live in poorly insulated homes with inefficient heating and cooling systems, meaning they have to use even more energy if they hope to make the space comfortable.
Justice and rights
Climate change is making Japan’s summers hotter, raising cooling costs apace. However, Okushima highlights that it is also critical to ensure that climate change countermeasures, especially the transition to clean energy, do not inadvertently exacerbate energy poverty, too.
“If measures such as carbon pricing or renewable energy surcharges passed on to all ratepayers equally, regardless of economic status, place a heavier burden on low-income households, then their energy security could deteriorate,” he says.
One example of such a policy is Japan’s Feed-in-Tariff (FIT; a Feed-in-Premium system was also introduced in 2022), a renewable energy promotion framework in which renewable energy is purchased by utilities at a fixed price, with the surcharge borne by ratepayers. For fiscal year 2026, the economy ministry, which sets Japan’s energy policies, calculated that a household consuming 400 kWh of electricity per month would pay an annual ¥20,064 in FIT/FIP surcharges.
Energy prices are also easily impacted by world events due to Japan’s low energy self-sufficiency rate, which stood at 16.3% in 2024.
“Higher energy prices due to issues like the Ukraine war or the situation in Iran naturally have an impact” on energy poverty, Okushima says. “And with the weak yen, the bottom line is that if inflation occurs, energy poverty will of course worsen.”
In Mori’s view, another factor exacerbating energy poverty is the privatization of utilities, which he sees as an ongoing trend in Japan. “Private utilities generally don’t wait for customers who can’t pay. We’ve seen this happen many times with propane gas providers, in particular,” he says.
One food bank beneficiary, a woman in her 50s living on welfare, had her gas shut off by her utility even though she had told the company she would pay her bill with her next welfare allowance. A total of 557 households receiving support from Food Bank Sendai had a utility cut in fiscal year 2025.
“The essentials for human survival are being commodified, and if you don’t have money, you can’t use them,” Mori says. “I’ve come to think that energy poverty violates an individual’s right to life.”
Citizen-led initiatives
Among the various measures experts recommend to help alleviate energy poverty, square one is to simply name it — a step the Japanese government has yet to take.
For Okushima, a lack of recognition is a primary concern.
“Adopting an official definition of energy poverty has a pivotal role in recognizing the problem, making it visible and, finally, in adopting the necessary measures to counteract it,” Okushima and colleagues wrote in a 2022 book.
Still, even without using the term itself, some existing measures do partially address the issue. For example, “winter allowances” incorporated into Japan’s welfare system are intended to help cover heating costs, although Koga called current welfare levels overall insufficient to meet a basic standard of living.
“Many improvements could be made by tweaking the existing system,” he says.
In addition, in 2025 and 2026, the government stepped in to subsidize summer electricity and gas prices for all households, and did the same this past winter.
Another key recommendation from experts is to improve the energy efficiency of buildings and home appliances. Possible measures include mandating higher efficiency standards or providing subsidies, particularly ones targeting households experiencing energy poverty, to retrofit existing housing stock.
“Housing measures are considered some of the most important because they can reduce energy costs over the medium to long term,” Okushima explains.
Japan has set national targets for buildings to achieve net-zero emissions through a combination of high efficiency and on-site clean energy generation. Local governments, too, are establishing related measures, such as the Tokyo Metropolitan Government subsidizing part of the cost of high-efficiency air conditioners and other appliances, up to ¥80,000 for older adults and individuals with disabilities. In 2026, Tokyo and the city of Kawasaki also mandated solar panels on certain new-built homes, while Sendai set similar requirements regarding solar panels and thermal efficiency in new builds.
However, Koga points out that policies targeting homeowners may benefit the middle-class more than low-income households, as the latter often lack the financial means to buy and build homes. “The question of what to do about the existing, low-quality housing stock has not been institutionalized at all,” he says.
Citizen organizations can also address energy insecurity. For example, the HOME Project, run by Japanese climate campaign Power Shift, helps organizations tackling poverty switch their facilities to clean energy and promotes energy-efficiency improvements.
As another potential initiative, Koga raises the example of “energy advice” organizations in Europe and the U.K. These groups help improve households’ energy security in ways such as enhancing efficiency, switching utility providers and accessing public support measures. While often run as nonprofits, some municipalities provide similar support, such as London’s Islington borough, whose website encourages residents and local businesses to “Find out how we can help you save money by cutting down on your energy and water bills.” Although a handful of similar services exist in Japan, including part of Food Bank Sendai’s work, energy advice organizations dedicated to tackling energy poverty specifically are vanishingly rare.
Koga emphasizes that both citizen initiatives and greater government support are indispensable in addressing energy poverty.
“The voices of local citizens are truly important, through both community-rooted measures and changing the very structure of the system itself,” he adds.
Since beginning to engage with the issue of energy poverty in 2021, Food Bank Sendai and partner organizations have conducted surveys, staged a public protest, and requested that utilities serving the area provide more flexible support for late payments.
“While recognizing the importance of the role played by government agencies, we also need to build systems ourselves to protect our livelihoods,” Mori says, naming decentralized energy sources as one example.
These days, Kasahara says she is working with international students on initiatives such as farming and putting on monthly community meals, which also provide a space for people to connect.
“Although (the students) were initially receiving aid themselves, they have thrown themselves into these projects energetically,” she recalls. “They say, ‘I want to make a change myself.’”

Landslide disrupts Shimla-Kalka rail services, 4 trains cancelled till September 1
A landslide on the Shimla-Kalka heritage railway left a section of track hanging near Bridge No. 57 and forced train cancellations. More than 400 passengers and railway staff were shifted by road as services stay suspended till September 1.
A landslide on the Shimla-Kalka UNESCO World Heritage railway section disrupted train operations after heavy rain washed away soil beneath a portion of the track, leaving it suspended in the air near Bridge No. 57. Northern Railway cancelled train services on the affected section as a safety precaution and evacuated more than 400 passengers and railway staff by road.
The incident occurred on Saturday, August 29, near Bridge No. 57, between Koti and Ghumman stations on the Shimla-Kalka section in Himachal Pradesh.
The landslide caused soil beneath the railway track to wash away, damaging the track base and leaving a portion of the track unsupported. The disruption affected train movement on the route, which is part of the UNESCO World Heritage railway network and is used by tourists and passengers from across India and abroad.
Northern Railway said train services on the affected section have been cancelled until September 1 in view of safety concerns and the damage caused by the landslide.
FOUR TRAINS SHORT-TERMINATED
Following the incident, railway authorities curtailed the journeys of four incoming trains at designated stations to prevent passengers from being taken towards the affected section.
Train No. 52456 was short-terminated at Solan, while Train No. 52452 was short-terminated at Koti. Train Nos. 52460 and 52454 were short-terminated at Dharampur Himachal.
Officials coordinated the passenger evacuation and local arrangements.
SEVEN VEHICLES USED TO EVACUATE PASSENGERS
Northern Railway deployed a dedicated road fleet of seven vehicles, comprising five full-sized buses and two Tempo Travellers, to transport passengers from Solan, Koti and Dharampur Himachal to Kalka.
Around 391 passengers, along with 40 members of the train crew and IRCTC staff, were safely transported by road. Railway officials, including Vipin Paudwal and onboard travelling ticket examiner staff, escorted the convoy during the journey to ensure the safe movement of passengers.
The evacuation operation was carried out through road transhipment after train services were curtailed because of the damaged track.
FOOD, WATER ARRANGED AT KALKA
After the passengers reached Kalka station, railway officials arranged refreshments and basic assistance for them. Around 250 fresh food packets and water bottles were distributed.
While local passengers proceeded towards their respective destinations, around 120 passengers were accommodated on Train No. 13052. The train was specially rescheduled to depart at 1.30 am to provide onward connectivity to passengers who needed to continue their journey.
Railway officials said no passenger complaint or refund request was registered at Kalka station in connection with the disruption.
TRACK DAMAGE AFFECTS HERITAGE RAILWAY ROUTE
The Shimla-Kalka railway line is a UNESCO World Heritage railway section and is a major tourist attraction, with toy train services operating between Kalka and Shimla.
The damage caused by the heavy rain has disrupted movement on the route and could affect the travel plans of tourists and other passengers using the heritage railway service.
Northern Railway said passenger safety remains its top priority and that necessary measures are being taken to ensure safe train operations during adverse weather conditions. Train services on the affected section will remain cancelled until September 1 as restoration and safety-related measures are undertaken.

Every Love Island cycle produces the same predictable arc: a finale, a flood of brand deals, and a cluster of influencer careers that rise fast and often fade faster. Season 8 of Love Island USA is breaking that pattern. As the cast heads into Monday's reunion special, several Islanders have used their newfound platforms to build something more durable than a sponsored post, moving into media ventures, entertainment deals, and campaign work that reads more like a career launch than a victory lap. Here are the standout marketing moves so far.
Melanie Moreno’s Substack Launch
Of everyone to come out of the villa this season, Melanie Moreno has made arguably the most unconventional play. Rather than defaulting to the usual influencer route, brand partnerships stacked on Instagram, she launched a Substack. It is a choice that runs against the grain of reality TV monetization, and it is a smart one.
A newsletter lets Melanie build a direct relationship with her audience rather than renting attention on platforms she does not control. She owns the list. She owns the data. And she is not at the mercy of an algorithm change or a platform outage that could sever her from her audience overnight, a real risk for creators whose entire businesses live on borrowed real estate. It also lets her go deeper than a 30-second clip allows, giving fans a more intimate, long-form view of who she is beyond the villa edit. In an ecosystem where most contestants chase the same short-term influencer churn, Melanie's Substack is a bet on longevity over quick engagement, and it is the kind of move other reality alumnae should be studying closely.
Jen Terry’s Playfully Provocative Photoshoot With Gal
Jen Terry and Gal Tshnieder's Casa Amor connection fell apart almost as fast as it began, but the two turned their post-villa reunion into one of the season's smartest pieces of content. Rather than avoiding the drama or litigating it in interviews, they leaned all the way in: a cheeky, high-fashion photoshoot at Gal's coffee shop that played directly on their public breakup, complete with Jen tossing a drink in Gal's face and, in one shot, tying him to a surfboard.
The concept worked because it did double duty. It gave fans the closure and comedy they wanted around the storyline, while also positioning Jen as a legitimate style presence with real editorial range, someone who can hold a concept and a camera, not just a ring light. The post pulled hundreds of thousands of likes on TikTok, proof that turning a villa storyline into a controlled, stylized moment outperforms simply hoping the discourse dies down.
Gal Tshnieder's Coffee Shop Marketing
Gal's run in the villa was brief, but his marketing instincts back home have been the season's best case study in localized, community-first brand-building. His Venice coffee shop, Saba Surf and Coffee, became a pilgrimage site for fans within days of his elimination, and instead of treating the attention as a distraction, Gal and his team built directly on top of it: watch parties, free drinks tied to storylines from the show, and a dunk tank that let fans literally dunk him during the finale watch party.
It is a sharp example of how to turn reality TV infamy into foot traffic rather than just follower counts. Gal's approach shows how a physical, local business can ride a viral moment without losing its identity, treating fans as customers to welcome into a real space rather than just an audience to broadcast at. The result was lines out the door, a local political commendation, and a business that converted attention into revenue in a way most post-villa deals never manage.
Kenzie Annis And Dylan Wrona's Use Of TikTok
Kenzie Annis and Dylan Wrona's relationship played out almost as much on TikTok as it did in the villa, and that visibility has carried directly into their post-show run. Their content together, appearances, red carpet moments, casual clips of them out in Los Angeles, has kept fans invested in their story past the finale, extending the shelf life of a couple that could otherwise have faded once the season ended.
What makes their approach notable is the consistency. Rather than treating TikTok as a place to post the occasional sponsored plug, they have used it to keep their relationship narrative alive in near real time, which is exactly the kind of ongoing engagement that brands look for when deciding which Islanders are worth a longer-term partnership rather than a single campaign.
Trinity Tatum's Verizon Campaign
Trinity Tatum's Verizon partnership is the clearest example this season of what patience can do for a personal brand. Rather than taking the first offer that came her way after her win, Tatum, who signed with WME shortly after the finale, waited for a global brand with the scale and creative ambition to match her platform.
The payoff was "Queen of Cash," a campaign built around Verizon's new rewards program and directed by Warren Fu, known for his work with major music artists. The spot reimagines Tatum as a modern-day queen, an extravagant, cinematic concept that gave her room to actually perform rather than simply hold up a product. It let her flex real acting range while still tying back to the glamorous, fashion-forward persona that made her a standout in the villa. Verizon's chief marketing officer, Leslie Berland, called the partnership central to the brand's launch of Verizon Dollars, and the selectivity behind it is the real lesson here: Tatum treated her first major deal as a brand decision, not just a payday, and it shows.
What We’re Waiting For, Heading Into The Reunion
Taken together, these moves suggest Season 8's breakout stars understand something that earlier casts have not always grasped: attention is only valuable if you know what to do with it. A Substack, a coffee shop dunk tank, and a Warren Fu-directed ad campaign have little in common on the surface, but each represents a deliberate choice to build something that outlasts the news cycle rather than chase it. As the cast reunites Monday for the first time since the finale, it will be worth watching whether these early moves translate into the kind of sustained careers that Love Island has historically struggled to produce, or whether they simply set the bar higher for the next season's Islanders to clear.

'That trust isn't there' - how does Iraola get best out of Isak?
- Published
During Liverpool's negotiations with Paris St-Germain for Bradley Barcola, the Anfield hierarchy were determined not to pay more than the club-record £125m they spent on Alexander Isak last summer.
When the £123m deal for Barcola is completed over the coming days, the France winger will become the 10th £100m player in Premier League history.
None have cost more than Isak, so the expectation on the former Newcastle striker is understandable, to say the least.
Isak scored 44 Premier League goals in his last two seasons at Newcastle, but in an injury-plagued first campaign at Anfield the 26-year-old found the back of the net just three times in 14 top-flight appearances.
For Andoni Iraola, who has drawn his first two games as Liverpool manager, a major part of success at Anfield will be the ability to get the best out of Isak, who - despite scoring - was largely ineffective in their 2-2 draw against Nottingham Forest on Saturday.
Unlike last summer, Isak has looked sharp in pre-season after some impressive displays for Sweden at the World Cup, but struggled on his return to Tyneside last weekend.
For 45 minutes against Forest on Saturday, those struggles continued with just six touches, one accurate pass and zero shots.
"It is clear that Liverpool haven't worked out how to play with Alexander Isak yet," said ex-England goalkeeper Joe Hart, who is a pundit on Saturday's Match of the Day.
"At Newcastle everything flowed through him. That was down to a trust thing that they had built up over time - their midfield knew exactly where he was and they didn't even need to look up as he'd be there waiting.
"At Liverpool that trust just isn't there at the moment - no-one is feeling it and he isn't that central point, which is leading to him looking lost and isolated."

'There's no doubting Isak's quality'
It would have been intriguing to be a fly on the wall in the directors' box at Anfield.
Iraola's first home Premier League game was watched by incoming Liverpool vice-chairman Amit Bhatia, principal owner John Henry, and sporting director Richard Hughes, who was integral in getting the deal for Isak done last summer.
Thankfully for them - and Iraola - Isak got Liverpool on level terms after the break. He managed just seven more touches in the second half but centre-forwards deal in goals and the Swede timed his run perfectly to meet Cody Gakpo's delivery for his first goal of the season. His smile after told a story in itself.
"That's the job ultimately as a striker [to score goals]. I am very happy to score the first one and hopefully it just keeps coming," Isak told TNT Sports.
Former Liverpool captain Steven Gerrard described the goal as "big" - for both the striker's confidence and the team's.
But, in Hart's opinion, Iraola still has a major conundrum.
"Andoni Iraola has some big decisions to make," said Hart. "Does he base his team round him [Isak] or does he try to find a different solution within his squad? In my opinion he's got to commit to what the club have done by investing so heavily in Isak.
"There's no point signing these players if you aren't going to use them properly and play to their strengths. There's no doubting Isak's quality - they are just at a bit of a crossroads at the moment."
During Isak's struggles last season, the belief inside the club was that he was a long-term signing and judgement would be reserved for once he was fully fit.
Only Erling Haaland, Mohamed Salah and Ollie Watkins have scored more Premier League goals since Isak's first season in England and, with Salah now out of the picture, the onus is on Isak to deliver - particularly with Hugo Ekitike out injured.
Iraola's possession problem
Liverpool's first two games of the season have finished 2-2 despite Iraola's side enjoying 60% of possession against Newcastle last week and 70% against Forest.
In both games, they have found themselves trailing and are yet to be ahead in the Premier League this season.
That has inevitably made things trickier for Isak, who was such a force in a counter-attacking Newcastle side. Against low blocks, the proposition is different.
It is also symptomatic of a wider issue Iraola faces.
Last season, his Bournemouth side won just four of the 19 Premier League games in which they had the majority of possession. They won nine of the other 19.
The Cherries, who were known for their counter-pressing style and effectiveness in transition, also failed to win a game in which they had more than 58.8% possession.
In essence, his side were more successful when they had less of the ball - something that will rarely happen now he is at Anfield.
"As an attacking force it isn't flowing for Liverpool," said Hart. "With the physical nature of the Premier League and with them not 100% sure on what they are doing at the moment, teams are stomping all over them.
"It's going to take a whole lot of work from Iraola and his staff on the training pitch, but he is a top coach and they have top players."
Asked about whether he sets targets for the season, Isak said: "Not really. I think every striker wants to score [in] every game he plays. Obviously that's difficult but [we take] each game at a time."
That is one way to look at it, and this was certainly an improvement on his showing against Newcastle, but deep down Isak will know he can - and must - do better.

Deaths reported after ferry carrying nearly 270 passengers capsizes off Cyprus
More than 172 people have been rescued, Northern Cyprus PM says.
BODRUM, Turkey -- At least seven people have died after a ferry carrying nearly 270 passengers and crew capsized off the coast of northern Cyprus on Sunday, Turkish media reported.
Some 237 people have been rescued, Northern Cyprus Prime Minister Unal Ustel told Turkish state-run TRT news channel. He said a search was underway for another 24 people.
Ustel said the ferry faced adverse weather conditions and began taking in water just 15 minutes after departure. A call for help was issued shortly after, he said.
The catamaran-style ferry was traveling from the port of Kyrenia, also known as Girne, in the breakaway north of ethnically divided Cyprus, to the Turkish port of Tasucu in Mersin province.
Kyrenia Mayor Murat Senkul said the ship belonged to the Filo Denizcilik ferry company and sank off the coast of Diana beach on Cyprus’ northern coast.
The ferry started taking in water about 7.5 kilometers (4 nautical miles) off the coast, TRT reported.
Video footage from the scene shows people with life-vests floating in the waters around the capsized vessel.

Global investment firm Alpha Wave has offloaded nearly 1.92 Cr shares or 7.78% stake in MSME-focused NBFC Aye Finance via bulk deals today, as per BSE data. Alpha Wave India I sold two separate tranches of 95.94 Lakh shares each at weighted average prices of ₹168.19 and ₹168.02 apiece respectively. The investor raked in a total about ₹322.6 Cr via the stake sale. The same entity had a 7.78% stake in Aye Finance, amounting to 1,91,88,604 shares, as of June 30, 2026. Hence, after today’s stake sale, the investor has exited Aye Finance. This adds on to the string of partial or complete exits that Alpha Wave is on of late. As per reports earlier today, the firm is looking to sell over 2 Cr shares of other portfolio company Lenskart for around ₹1,313 Cr. This would be the second instance of Alpha Wave offloading stake in Lenskart since the expiry of its lock-in period, selling 3.72 Cr shares in the company back in May. It also recently exited logistics major Delhivery with the sale of 72.2 Lakh shares, raking in about ₹665 Cr. Meanwhile, the shares offloaded by the investment firm were lapped up by Integrated Core Strategies (Asia), an associate of Millennium Management, Singularity AMC’s Singularity Large Value Fund III, among other buyers. Additionally, boutique advisory firm F3 Advisors also sold 74,505 shares at ₹173.88 per share, while buying 14.6 Lakh shares at a lower price, i.e. ₹169.23 per share. At the time of Aye Finance’s public listing in February, Alpha Wave held 11.2% stake in the NBFC. The global investment company had sold 23.25 Lakh shares worth ₹30 Cr via the public listing, bagging a 1.4X gain on its initial investment. Important to highlight that Aye Finance’s IPO was undersubscribed and the stock listed flat at the issue price of ₹129 on the bourses.. Since listing, it has made a turnaround of sorts, gaining nearly 42%. It closed today’s trading session 2.89% higher at ₹181.60 on the BSE. On the financial front, the NBFC’s net profit in Q1 FY27 jumped 144% YoY to ₹74.5 Cr, while revenue from operations rose 18%. However, on a sequential basis, profit and revenue declined 13.3% and 7.3% respectively. Aye Finance reported ₹7,324 Cr in assets under management (AUM), a net worth of ₹2,528 Cr and a capital adequacy ratio of 42.38% during Q1 FY27.

Sir Billy Boston - 'the world-class athlete, whose story deserved to be told'
- Published
When Sir Billy Boston was knighted in 2025, it was a unique moment for rugby league.
For the first time, this rebel sport from the north of England had been recognised in such a manner; one of its heroes had been acknowledged for their contribution to history through the game.
Sir Billy was a fitting recipient of the honour and a world class athlete, whose story deserved to be told.
You can tell the importance of someone by how many statutes have been erected in tribute, and Sir Billy Boston wasn't lacking.
His name was chosen as one of just five to grace Wembley's monument to rugby league's Challenge Cup, while years after his departure north, his home city of Cardiff also ensured his legacy remained cast-iron strong as he formed part of a three-man tribute along with Clive Sullivan and Gus Risman.
Unsurprisingly, Boston is also captured in bronze in his adopted home of Wigan; the place where his legend really came to life.
Born and brought up in Cardiff's ethnically-eclectic Tiger Bay district, he learned his rugby skills on the streets and with the talent factory-esque Cardiff International Athletic Club.
Like all Welsh lads he harboured dreams of playing for his local club Cardiff RFC and hopefully the national team.
Like others before and after for a time, Boston found those routes blocked, having to travel to Neath and Pontypridd to trial before his military service took him north.
It was here where the league scouts came calling, and Wigan persuaded Boston to turn professional in 1953, forever ending his union dreams in the time of 'sine die' penalties for liaising with league personnel.
The money was life changing.
£3,000 could easily buy a house at that stage, while it proved money well spent as he took to the new code like a duck to water, scoring with his first touch in a Wigan A team game.
This prime specimen of Welsh breezeblock had everything; he was quick, he could step and as former player and BBC commentator Ray French put it - his fend was like "being hit in the face with shovel".
The sepia footage and slow shutter speeds of the cameras that captured his magic during his playing days simply cannot dull his brilliance.
Whether it was bustling over for another try in cherry and white hoops at Wembley or crushing the Aussies at Sydney Cricket Ground, Boston was a blur of speed, footwork and power.
Having swiftly progressed to the first team at Central Park, he would go on to score 478 tries in 488 games for Wigan, and tales of his feats would be passed down through generations. There are very few down at the Brick Community Stadium these days who don't know of Sir Billy, young or old, his name carried a cache right until his last.
Great Britain gave him the international recognition denied to him by Wales, and he rewarded the selectors by racking up the tries, particularly against the Australians who would bear the brunt of his scoring ability.
He scored 36 tries alone on his maiden Great Britain tour, dazzling both Australia and New Zealand in 1954 under captain and fellow Welshman Dickie Williams.
Boston was a phenomenal rugby league player, but there is also a powerful message in how in post-war Britain a black athlete could become a hugely popular figure by communities adjusting to a new, more diverse world.
Others like Roy Francis beforehand, Johnny Freeman, and Colin Dixon, also became established names, but never quite sprinkled the same stardust as Sir Billy.
It paved the way for players such as Ellery Hanley and Martin Offiah to charm the public with their talents, while modern day talent such as Junior Nsemba and Kai Pearce-Paul continues to stand out in a sport which has broken down barriers for years.
Sir Billy had a unique unifying effect on a normally partisan and tribal rugby league community.
He was revered naturally in Wigan, his adopted home, but you won't hear a boo or jeer at mention of Boston anywhere - not even at sworn rivals St Helens where they appreciate a good footballer when they see one.
Still a regular visitor to Wigan games right up to his passing, it was always a beautiful moment when the cameras found him, the crowd spotting him on the screen bursting into cheer, and the realisation creeping over his face in the shape of a smile.
There was a photo of him and his wife Lady Joan, who had died just a few weeks previously, on her seat with flowers at Wigan's game with Wakefield last week. There is a poignancy that Sir Billy departed soon after her.
His seat will always be reserved at Wigan, and he will be dearly missed but certainly not forgotten.

A Peaceful Detective Mystery to Watch
Culture and entertainment recommendations including The Sheep Detectives, the Hold Steady, and more
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
Welcome back to The Daily’s Sunday culture edition, in which one Atlantic writer or editor reveals what’s keeping them entertained. Today’s special guest is Lily Meyer, a staff writer who has published stories about the wisdom of Holden Caulfield, why making America’s houses bigger may have been a mistake, and the Seinfeld theory of fiction.
Lily recommends watching The Sheep Detectives for a heartwarming mystery, listening to any song by the Hold Steady, and reading Brother of the More Famous Jack, by Barbara Trapido, if you want a good cry and a laugh.
— Stephanie Bai, senior associate editor
A good recommendation I recently received: My friend Eliza Brooke—a freelance culture writer who often covers movies—told me to watch The Sheep Detectives, which I had assumed was for children, but I trust her. I was absolutely charmed by the film and, at the same time, quite moved by its exploration of how we think and talk about death. Also, it’s a whodunit, and I love whodunits. Hollywood, could we please have fewer sequels and prequels and remakes, and more peaceful detective stories?
The upcoming arts event I’m most looking forward to: I can’t wait to see the Lee Krasner and Jackson Pollock show opening at the Met this October. I love abstract expressionism, and ever since I read Mary Gabriel’s Ninth Street Women—an exceptional group biography of five abstract expressionist painters, including Krasner—I’ve been fascinated by the arc of her career, which included creating government-sponsored public art during the Depression, making mosaics in the Long Island house she and Pollock shared during their marriage (meanwhile, he got an entire barn as a studio), and the flowering of her own painting practice after his death. Of course I’m excited to see the Pollock paintings at the Met too, but I’m most eager to see the Krasners.
An actor I would watch in anything: Greta Gerwig. I saw Frances Ha, the gorgeous, bittersweet ode to female friendship that she starred in and co-wrote, a few weeks after I graduated from college—that is, at a moment when I was heartbroken about no longer living with my closest female friends—and I imprinted on her like a baby duck.
The best work of nonfiction I’ve recently read: Vivian Gornick’s The Romance of American Communism. Gornick, a “red-diaper baby” raised in the working-class Jewish Bronx, set out to interview former Communist Party USA members and militants about what their political activity meant to them, years after the party had lost most of its following. The result is a surprisingly beautiful and often wrenching reflection on belief, belonging, self-delusion, and sacrifice.
An author I will read anything by: Too many to name, so instead, I’ll give you a translator. I try to read—and believe I have read—everything that Megan McDowell translates. Her taste is impeccable, her style is flawless, and she works with some of the greatest Latin American authors writing today: Mariana Enríquez, Samanta Schweblin, Alejandro Zambra, and many more.
A quiet song that I love, and a loud song that I love: “It’s Gonna Be Easy,” by the Texas outlaw-country singer Doug Sahm, is a soft, melodic lament for a relationship the singer wishes would be easier to forget. (A recommendation to go with it: Callie Collins’s novel Walk Softly on This Heart of Mine, whose protagonist is loosely inspired by Sahm. Like the song, the book is a gentle heartbreaker.)
A loud song is “Waiting Room,” by my D.C. hometown heroes Fugazi. My husband and I asked the DJ to play it at our wedding, and the resulting mini–mosh pit is one of my favorite memories of the night.
A musical artist who means a lot to me: The Hold Steady. I’ve been going to their shows since I was 14, and seeing them live is the closest I’ve ever come to a religious experience. Hold Steady fans are real diehards, and the band’s lead singer, Craig Finn, believes fervently that—as he shouts at every single show—“we are all the Hold Steady.” He’s right: We are.
Something I recently revisited: I’m revealing a lot about my high-school self here, but one of my absolute favorite novels as a teenager was Chang-rae Lee’s Aloft, whose hero, Jerry Battle, is a New Jersey dad hiding from his emotions about family and aging by flying private planes. I revisited it before reviewing Lee’s new novel, A Tender Age, and was relieved that I loved it even more than I did at 15.
A favorite story I’ve read in The Atlantic: I’m not sure if “favorite” is the right word here, but Spencer Kornhaber’s essay about the singer Lizzo and her downward mobility has been haunting me since I read it. Spencer, I want you to know that introducing me to the concept of the Khia Asylum was not nice!
Something delightful introduced to me by a kid in my life: My toddler recently became obsessed with the book Chirri & Chirra, written and illustrated by Kaya Doi and translated from Japanese by Yuki Kaneko. It is so delightful. Doi’s illustrations are lovely, and the heroines’ sweet little adventure through the forest is a dream day. At the end, Chirri and Chirra go to a forest concert, and my daughter loves to sing “La-la-la” along with me as I read—it’s the best.
The last thing that made me cry: Brother of the More Famous Jack, by Barbara Trapido. It’s a sharp, generous tale of yearning and innocence, and its descriptions are my favorite kind, economical and precise. Its plot twist made me cry, but so did the intensity and joy of its narrator’s longing.
The last thing that made me snort with laughter: Also Brother of the More Famous Jack. I’m telling you, you need to read this book.

The Week Ahead

- Season 2 of The Gentlemen, a crime-comedy series about an aristocrat and his partner expanding their criminal empire into Italy (streaming Thursday on Netflix)

Essay
We’re Living in the World Dolly Parton Built
By Spencer Kornhaber
Dolly Parton’s death at age 80 comes at a time when her influence seems at its peak. Country music is surging, female singer-songwriters are on top, and audiences seem hungry for honest idiosyncracy—for figures who, like Dolly, transmit their inner truth to mass audiences in a voice that’s clear yet scraggly. But Parton’s greatest legacy is existential in nature. Piling on wigs and feathers, she showed that you can be yourself while playing a character.

Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, has defended her government’s highly controversial energy deal with Donald Trump, insisting the South American country will maintain ownership and sovereignty over its massive oil reserves.
Rodríguez, who assumed power in January after Trump ordered the abduction of the president, Nicolás Maduro, took to the airwaves on Saturday to push back against criticism of what the US president has called “the biggest oil deal in world history”.
“The benefits are endless,” claimed Rodríguez, a former vice-president whom Trump backed after ordering Maduro’s capture during a special forces raid on the capital, Caracas.
During a six-minute television broadcast, Venezuela’s acting leader claimed the deal would help her resource-rich country develop its economy, earn revenues of more than $209bn (£154bn), and become “an energy powerhouse”.
Rodríguez said: “As everyone knows, our country has the biggest oil reserves in the world. But having resources underground isn’t enough. We need investment, technology, infrastructure [and] production capacity to convert this wealth into wellbeing for our people.”
She added: “It’s no use having our oil reserves underground, only to appear in statistics or bookkeeping … and for us not to be able to convert and translate them into development for Venezuela.”
Trump announced the “groundbreaking” deal on Friday, calling it a “historic transaction [that] more than doubles American oil reserves … while helping to continue to set Venezuela on a course toward Tremendous Success and Great Prosperity”.
On Sunday, Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform: “One of the things I am going to do with the Venezuelan Oil is fill up the Strategic National Reserves which, because of Sleepy Joe Biden, has been virtually emptied.”
Trump added: “The ‘topping out’ process will begin very shortly, and is a Gift from Venezuela to the People of the United States.”
Hours after seizing Maduro on 3 January, Trump warned Rodríguez she would face an even worse fate if she failed to toe the US line. “If she doesn’t do what’s right, she is going to pay a very big price, probably bigger than Maduro,” Trump said.
Details of the agreement – struck during months of secret talks – remain sparse but it will reportedly see Washington take control of 65bn barrels of Venezuelan oil reserves.
The South American country has the world’s largest proven crude oil reserves, with an estimated 303bn barrels, compared with Saudi Arabia’s 268bn and Iran’s 208bn. Rodríguez said the deal involved 17 “strategic oilfields” where it was hoped more than 1.5m barrels could be produced each day.
But the deal has provoked outrage, both among members of Venezuela’s opposition and within the Chavismo political movement of which Rodríguez is part.
Speaking on Friday, one prominent opposition figure, who asked not to be named, called the agreement “a massive land grab” by a “rapacious, mafioso United States”.
Writing on X, Rafael Ramírez, the former head of Venezuela’s state-owned oil company PDVSA, accused Rodríguez’s administration of “driving a dagger straight into the heart of the homeland” with the “neocolonial” transaction. “They are handing over 65bn barrels of our reserves to the United States. That has never happened in Venezuela, and I think nowhere else in the world,” Ramírez added in an interview with the newspaper El Nacional.
On Saturday, dozens of leftwing protesters marched through Caracas with banners reading: “We are neither a colony, nor a back yard” and “Yankees go home!”
Critics of the agreement shared an ironic meme on social media suggesting the state oil company’s name should be changed from PDVSA to “PDUSA”.
In her broadcast, Rodríguez, the daughter of a Marxist guerrilla who spent years denouncing “imperialist” attempts to snatch her country’s oil reserves, countered claims she was surrendering Venezuela’s natural resources to a foreign power. She thanked Trump and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, for striking the deal but added: “There is something that must be made absolutely clear: Venezuela retains the ownership and sovereignty over its resources.”
“We are thinking of Venezuela’s future,” claimed the politician, whose country was plunged into authoritarian rule and one of the world’s worst peacetime economic crises during Maduro’s 13-year rule.
The deal represents an astonishing U-turn from Rodríguez and the socialist, anti-imperialist political movement she and Maduro inherited from Hugo Chávez after his death in 2013.
In one 2024 speech, footage of which circulated on social media after Friday’s announcement, Rodríguez lambasted the Venezuelan opposition, accusing it of seeking to surrender the country’s oil, natural gas and gold reserves to its “masters” in Washington.
Last September, as the US tightened the screws on Maduro, Rodríguez told the New York Times: “The Pentagon always had a strategic objective of obtaining Venezuelan reserves.”
The deal will reportedly involve the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital, which channels funds into projects seen as important for national security. It will also involve a private company owned by Alejandro Betancourt, a controversial UK-based tycoon who has emerged as a key intermediary between the Trump administration and Rodríguez.
Opposition politicians fear the deal will scupper attempts to recover Venezuela’s democracy and hold fresh presidential elections. Maduro is widely believed to have stolen the last vote, in 2024, and Rodríguez has deflected questions about a future election, saying vaguely that it will happen “some day”. Trump has also said Venezuela is “not really ready” for elections.
Writing on X, the opposition leader Juan Pablo Guanipa, said: “The only way to truly reactivate the Venezuelan economy in the long term and make this agreement benefit both parties is through a free election that leads to a representative government, clear rules of the game, rule of law, and institutions that allow our resources to be managed transparently and for the benefit of the nation.”
Without that, the energy deal was like “a skyscraper [built] on pillars of clay”, Guanipa added.

WASHINGTON — Vaping company Juul Labs on Friday received federal permission to sell an updated version of its e-cigarette, which includes an optional age-verification system designed to prevent underage use.
The decision from the Food and Drug Administration allows the company to sell a new version of its top-selling vaping device for the first time since it launched more than a decade ago. In recent years, the company has had to lay off hundreds of employees while paying roughly $3 billion to settle government and private lawsuits over teen use of its products.
Juul plans to market the new device under the brand name Juul2, along with updated versions of its tobacco- and menthol-flavored cartridges. In 2019, the company discontinued several flavors, including mango, mint and creme, that drove most of its sales but were favored by teens.
In a statement Friday, Juul CEO K.C. Croswaite said the company plans to market its new system with “a portfolio of flavors — beyond tobacco and menthol — that are targeted to adult nicotine consumers.”
The latest announcement is not an approval or endorsement, and people who do not smoke should not use Juul or any other e-cigarettes, according to regulators. The FDA determination indicates that smokers who switch completely to Juul can reduce their exposure to deadly carcinogens and other chemicals found in traditional cigarettes.
According to company studies reviewed by the FDA, between 20% to 50% of smokers who used Juul products were able to stop smoking at the end of six weeks. The rates of quitting varied based on the flavors and nicotine strengths used.
The new device also gives users the option to require age verification via an online app before the e-cigarette can be unlocked.
The FDA has authorized a handful of e-cigarettes to help adult smokers quit or cut back on cigarettes. In May, the FDA OK’d the first fruit-flavored electronic cigarettes intended for adult smokers. The approval represented a major policy shift and came after months of appeals to President Donald Trump from the vaping industry.
Juul is no longer the top-selling e-cigarette brand in the U.S. and trails Vuse, which is sold by tobacco giant Reynolds American. Reynolds also makes Camel and Newport cigarettes.
Teens have shifted away from Juul as part of a wider drop in vaping, according to federal figures. Teens who continue to vape mostly use unauthorized disposable e-cigarettes imported from China, which come in fruit and candy flavors.
— Matthew Perrone

As backlash grows over Flock’s AI surveillance cameras, Texas Governor Greg Abbott has frozen state spending on them. The move came just ahead of the publication of a Texas Tribune investigation that revealed the state spent over $30 million on Flock cameras. That money was primarily raised by tacking a $1 fee onto insurance policies, allegedly to help fight catalytic converter theft.
Texas Governor Abbott blocks funding for more Flock cameras
As bipartisan backlash mounts, more politicians are turning against AI surveillance.
Flock cameras have increasingly drawn ire from across the political spectrum as they’ve become the subject of privacy concerns. There have been multiple incidents of officers being placed on leave or criminally charged for misusing Flock systems, including at least six in Texas alone. The company has also come under scrutiny for its data-sharing, the placement of some of its cameras near playgrounds, its own employees’ access to video feeds, unsecured video feeds, and its ham-fisted attempts to avoid transparency.
In recent months, cities around the country have been canceling their contracts with Flock, including many in Texas. Abbott’s Democratic opponent in the race for governor, Gina Hinojosa, has criticized him for expanding use of the cameras in the state. And Republican representative Keith Self recently posted on Instagram that, “From Flock cameras to kill switches, we will NOT surrender our Fourth Amendment rights to the growing surveillance state.” Cheering on the destruction of Flock cameras has even become a unifying pastime on the internet.

In Summary
- Instagram has announced a new feature for its app, called First Draft. Available only for iPhone users at the time of writing, it trims and blends selected videos, converting them into a reel within seconds.
- Although First Draft’s editing is on the basic side, it is nevertheless extremely useful for those newcomers (or even veterans) who are not comfortable with editing videos.
- Experts might find First Draft to be very basic, but its ease of use and speed make it perfect for content creators who feel held back by their lack of basic video editing ability.
Instagram has just rolled out a new feature, which it claims is going to make creating Reels easier. As its name suggests, First Draft basically gives users a quick “first draft” by turning all the video clips that they have selected into a quick Reel. The feature is an iPhone exclusive for now and only available on the main Instagram app, and not on Edits (the Reels editing app by Instagram), but an Android release is likely to follow soon.
Given all the AI hype and how much Meta is focusing on it, you might think First Draft is a new AI feature, but Instagram has confirmed that First Draft does not use Artificial Intelligence. Nevertheless, it has made people wonder if its ease of use could actually reduce the role of conventional, “manual” editing in the Reel world. Well, we have used the feature for a short while, and here is what we think.
How to use Instagram First Draft
Using First Draft is a pretty simple affair. Just follow these steps:
- Open the Instagram app on your iPhone (do remember to update it to the latest version), then tap on the “+” icon present on the top left side of the app to add new content.
- From there, swipe to Reels on the panel on the lower part of the app.
- Tap on the camera to record footage or select an existing video from your gallery, which will be displayed.
- Once you have selected all the clips you wish to add, look for the First Draft option, which will appear on the panel at the lower part of the app – it appears the moment you select a video. Tapping it will open a First Draft box, with a “Try it” button. Tap on this button.
- Hitting the button puts the selected videos into a processing phase where the app analyses the clips, identifies highlights, trims clips, and reduces the length.
- In a matter of ten seconds, the feature will present a pretty basic edited version of your videos, trimming them and cutting out awkward pauses, with preview frames beneath the result, which you can move back and forth to reorder.
- If you like the results, tap on the Next button in the bottom right corner of the app to go to the Instagram Reels posting page (you can also take your results to Edits), make more changes, if need be, and hit Publish.
How First Draft works
Instagram has stressed that the new editing feature is just a “starting point” on which creators can then build their final Reel. The social media platform says the feature can identify silences, awkward pauses, and other such moments. It then removes these moments, trims the video, and gives a first draft that highlights what it assumes are important parts of the video. It allows creators to select or record, edit, and share all without leaving Instagram.
Instagram has been ensuring that users know that all that is done by the feature is reversible, and does not come as an attempt to replace a creator’s creativity, but actually offers ‘early video trimming’ so users can move their focus from the technical part of editing to its creative part. Instead of using AI (which comes as a surprise), First Draft actually uses internal processing and audio detection to find moments of silence in selected videos. We have fiddled with the feature for a short while and can say that it actually works,serving up a very basic edit of videos (or of a single long video), even while leaving the “creative work” to the user.
Going by our first encounter with First Draft, it cannot really replace manual editing. It is not a very creative feature and only offers what can be termed as the ‘bare-bones’ of what your edited Reel might look like. We found the feature does eliminate pauses and silence, but when it trims videos, there seems to be no method to its madness, which basically means you can end up with some of the important bits removed from the video. In its current form, it might come in handy for people who create piece-to-camera video formats, but you would still need to revise and re-edit the whole thing on your own.
Also See: Instagram Edits vs CapCut: Best Video Editing App for You
First Draft: Who is it for (and who might not like it)
It is rather basic, but those who are new to creating videos and struggle with editing might find First Draft useful. It offers a very quick, hassle-free edit of videos. This can be helpful for creators who are not as skilled when it comes to editing their content, or are intimidated by the task. First Draft can be a very simple, quick-fix solution for them. But it is unlikely to appeal much to those creators who have been in the game for a while, are good at editing, and have their own style and flair in the editing field. We can already see them skipping this new feature.
But given that a large number of Instagram users do not really know much about video editing, First Draft seems to be an extremely handy tool, especially for those who do not want to get into the hassle of going through all their videos one by one and trimming out stutters and pauses. The fact that one can do so right from within Instagram, without having to open an additional app, is a huge bonus. As mentioned by the platform itself, First Draft is just a starting point and nothing more. Even in its current form (and we think it will get better in clip selection), it will help new creators start their content journey and feel more comfortable without getting knee-deep in editing hassles from the get-go.
Experts might shake their heads at how basic the feature is, but then remember how DSLR photographers shook their heads at 0.3 MP cellphone cameras? First Draft might be the first step to breaking down the editing barrier that holds back many content creators, and if it gets better (maybe with even options to automatically choose background audio or add subtitles in other languages, and so on), who knows, even experts might find it a handy tool to save them some time. But that’s in the future (and we bet AI will come into it at some stage). As for now, First Draft is mainly for Instagram newbies who want Reel creation with zero hassles. And that actually is a bigger deal than some of the pros might admit.

Australia’s far-right One Nation party has secured its first lower house seat in the state parliament of Western Australia, defeating the ruling Labor Party to win a special election.
The election was watched as an indicator of One Nation’s strength after the party surged in the polls over the past year. With 75% of votes counted, One Nation’s Luke Herdegen held 57%, while the Labor candidate had 43%, according to the state electoral commission late Saturday in state capital Perth. Broadcaster ABC called the by-election for Herdegen.
In last year’s election in the area south of Perth, longtime Labor lawmaker Paul Papalia won the seat with almost 47% of the primary vote, with One Nation trailing at slightly more than 8%. Papalia announced in July that he would retire as a family member was ill, forcing the special election.
