Rohingya refugees face fierce new wave of hostility in Malaysia
- Published
Not long ago, Malaysia's then-prime minister urged his country to protect Rohingya Muslims - a stateless minority that has fled violence and discrimination in Myanmar for decades.
"We must defend them, not just because they are of the same faith, but [because] they are humans, their lives have value," Najib Razak said in 2017.
Nine years on, a fierce new wave of hostility against the Rohingya is sweeping the nation.
So much so that "going to school has become a dangerous thing," says Irhan, a Rohingya refugee, who founded a school in northern Malaysia for children from his community aged six to 15. We have changed his name to protect his identity.
Because Rohingya children are barred from Malaysian public schools, they often attend unlicensed, community-run "learning centres", which are now especially vulnerable.
Irhan's school was raided last month, when eight uniformed police officers stormed inside, took photographs of the students and ordered some of them to go home.
"The students are just here to learn. Now their families are afraid," he says.
A school in Selangor in the west suspended classes for a month and reopened at the end of July with new instructions: students must not wear their uniforms to school and must go straight home after class, without lingering or hanging out in groups.
"We're keeping a low profile to protect our students from getting attacked," says Farooq, a Rohingya teacher.
Crackdowns are haphazard and often spurred by public sentiment. The uncertainty and fear have forced some schools to close in recent months. In some parts of the country, Rohingya have also been evicted from villages they'd been living in for years. Some local residents told Malaysian media that allowing them to remain could lead to "social problems".
After they were evicted from a fishing village near Penang, some120 refugees sought shelter outside the UN's refugee agency in the capital Kuala Lumpur - and were temporarily detained. More than half of them were children.
All of this has left a community that has long felt beleagured looking over its shoulder again.
"In the early years, the Malaysians were our friends. They cared for our children. But it's changed," Irhan says.
"I would leave if I could, but where else can I go? We are not wanted anywhere."
- What you need to know about the Rohingya crisis 
  - Published23 January 2020
- Landmark Rohingya genocide case against Myanmar heard at top UN court 
  - Published12 January
Fleeing Myanmar
The UN refugee agency estimates that more than 126,000 Rohingya have resettled in Malaysia, making it the second-largest host country, after Bangladesh, for Rohingya refugees. But some rights groups believe the actual number is far higher.
Rohingya Muslims are denied citizenship in their home country of Myanmar, a predominantly Buddhist state. Although Rohingya trace their roots going back centuries in what is now Rakhine state, successive Myanmar governments have claimed that they are illegal migrants.
Ethnic tensions with the local Buddhist population have flared repeatedly, displacing tens of thousands of Rohingya. They ended up in camps within Myanmar, or fled across the border.
But the biggest exodus began in August 2017, after a brutal military crackdown. The Myanmar army massacred thousands of them, raped Rohingya women and burned their villages.
It was what the UN called "textbook ethnic cleansing" and former US president Joe Biden's administration determined as a genocide. Myanmar is now facing a landmark genocide case at the International Court of Justice, which saw deposed leader and Nobel Peace Prize winner Aung San Suu Kyi testify.
As Myanmar's leader at the time, she was sharply criticised for how her government responded to the killings, including by playing down what was happening or suggesting that the severity of the violence was exaggerated.
In 2017, more than a million Rohingya fled to Bangladesh. But overcrowded camps, violence and shrinking aid have prompted many to attempt perilous voyages across the Andaman Sea towards Malaysia. These journeys are on cramped, fragile fishing vessels, and thousands die en route.
As more and more Rohingya arrived on its shores, Malaysia's welcome has worn thin.
Although it has never formally recognised asylum seekers – which means refugees have no right to housing, employment, and education – many Rohingya still see Muslim-majority Malaysia as a place of safety and economic opportunity.
Or at least that has been the case for a long time, when Malaysian leaders urged their people and Muslim nations to protect the community.
Surviving in Malaysia
During the pandemic, the Rohingya were accused of spreading the virus and competing with locals for jobs. Petitions calling for their deportations flooded social media, and authorities turned away hundreds of Rohingya asylum seekers who had been drifting at sea for weeks.
The vitriol has returned with greater intensity this year, inflamed again by social media.
In May, posts emerged online accusing refugees of not properly disposing of animals sacrificed during the Muslim festival of Eid al-Adha and quickly went viral.
These snowballed into unfounded and hyperbolic claims that the community is demanding automatic citizenship, seeking political power, and trying to "take over" Malaysia.
An online petition urging authorities to "Remove Rohingya from Malaysia" garnered more than 420,000 signatures before it was taken down following criticism from rights groups.
Karim, a Rohingya activist, says locals' hospitality had "made [him] feel safe" when he first arrived in 2003.
"Life as a refugee is tough. It's disappointing to be stuck working in construction all these years. However, I found Malaysians to be very friendly and kind, which made me feel safe," says the 45-year-old, who now lives in Penang.
"Now, however, life has become increasingly difficult. I am often afraid to go outside. I've been asked several times while on my commute, 'Why are you making a mess of our city? Why don't you go back?'"
Irhan, who came to Malaysia in 2001 as a teenager among an earlier wave of asylum seekers, feels the same.
Both say most Rohingya want to go back to Myanmar eventually, but at this point they would be returning to a country locked in a bloody civil war.
Their home state of Rakhine has suffered catastrophic destruction amid intense fighting between the military regime and the Arakan Army. For the displaced Rohingya, going home could also mean being forcibly conscripted to fight for the embattled junta, or becoming targets of the Arakan Army.
The UN released a report by an independent fact-finding mission this week detailing how the the plight of minories has "plummeted to a new low" in Myanmar.
The Rohingya are "suffering misery and cruelty on multiple levels and across the country that is heartbreaking", the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk said on Tuesday.
And Malaysia too has become less of a haven than they had hoped.
Some say they are being used as easy scapegoats for the rising cost of living, with the hostility concentrated on them because they form the largest group of asylum seekers.
"I'm not saying that all Rohingya are good. There are good and bad people in every community. So why should a few individuals' actions be used to typecast a whole community?" Farooq says.
"I escaped the genocide in Myanmar hoping to find safety. Instead, many Rohingya today continue to live with fear of simply being who we are," he adds.
During a campaign speech in July, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Myanmar had agreed to take back 5,000 Rohingya refugees from Malaysia, owing to "good relations" between the two countries.
Anwar added that he had warned the Rohingya not to disrupt the lives of Malaysians. "This is our country. Malaysia is our country. Let no one else interfere," he said.
It is perhaps a sign of how mainstream anti-Rohingya rhetoric has become.
Nurulhidayah Zahid, daughter of Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, for example, compared the community to "monkeys in the forest".
"Enough of using religious and humanitarian sentiments. Do good in moderation. Don't let the monkeys in the forest be fed, [while] the children at home die of hunger," she wrote in a post on Threads that includes a picture of Rohingya.
A former deputy police chief, Ayob Khan Mydin Pitchay, likened the influx of Rohingya as a "cancer" requiring urgent action.
The BBC has reached out to the Malaysian prime minister's office and foreign ministry for comment.
Some believe the hostility against the Rohingya will only intensify as Malaysia heads towards the general election, which must be held before February 2028.
"[Refugees and migrants] are once again being turned into convenient political scapegoats to divert attention from deeper domestic challenges," says Yap Lay Sheng, a researcher from the human rights group Fortify Rights.
"For years, the Malaysian government has sought to present the country internationally as a humane and compassionate Muslim nation. Its treatment of the Rohingya exposes the hollowness of that claim," says Yap, who is based in Malaysia.
Back in the industrial building that for several months served as his classroom, Irhan is concerned less about the shifting politics than about what comes next for his students.
"I don't know where to get help, or who can get us registered as a school," he says. "I hope the Malaysians can understand that the children just want an opportunity to learn."

Quite a few music artists are in their flop era right now. Think about it: Drake hasn’t been the same since Kendrick Lamar knocked him out in their 2024 beef. Katy Perry once dominated the charts, but her recent releases haven’t been fireworks. And there was once a point where it felt impossible to step foot in a workout class without hearing Lizzo, but her latest album fizzled out.
What makes a song flop?
From Drake to Katy Perry, sometimes a song just doesn’t hit.
Some examples, in other words, are obvious. But what does it really mean for a song to flop? According to Tom Breihan, executive editor at StereoGum and author of the book The Number Ones Twenty Chart-Topping Hits That Reveal the History of Pop Music, it’s all relative.
“There’s a million songs on Spotify that nobody will ever hear,” he told Vox. “Those songs are not necessarily flops because they did not necessarily come with expectations. When a major artist does not reach whatever benchmark they or their fans or their label expect for them, it can be embarrassing. People love to seize upon that embarrassment and take off running with it.”
Why do some songs flail while others succeed? And how does an artist bounce back from those unmet expectations? We find out that and more on this week’s episode of Explain It to Me, Vox’s weekly call-in podcast.
Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Breihan, edited for length and clarity. You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts. If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545.
Are the songs that flop bad? Is that why they’re flopping?
In some cases, yeah. You can definitely pick out a few and be like, “That wasn’t the one.”
A lot of it is just timing and luck. Sometimes an artist comes along at the exact right moment and builds up goodwill and puts out the right song for themselves. Sometimes they misread the room in sort of howlingly, clangingly obvious ways, and they end up not doing well.
It’s happened to plenty of great people. Plenty of stars have bounced back from having flops, but it does happen.
What are some really good songs that have flopped?
As an online indie music critic, my prototypical example is Emotion by Carly Rae Jepsen. She had had this gigantic global breakout smash with the song “Call Me Maybe.” The album that she put out after this is this brilliant, layered, excellent pop record that became, I would say, influential upon the idea that you could be a pop star who was a cult artist, like an indie rock band or an underground rapper. But it didn’t sell. It didn’t do numbers. So in its moment, it was a critically beloved flop.
How much of becoming a hit is about the music itself and how much of it is about virality and marketing?
Those things are so bound up with each other. A lot of the time, artists are making songs that are engineered to go viral, or they’re making songs that comment on their own public perceptions.
When someone like Lizzo comes along and puts out a record that doesn’t do well, it becomes a bigger story than just, “Oh, people weren’t feeling this song.” It becomes, “Oh, people don’t like this person,” or “This person has run out of goodwill.”
Like a Lizzo song: You hear her persona jumping through the speaker, whether the song does well or not. So the song and the artist become inextricable from each other. The song and the marketing become inextricable.
There is another example of an artist who has gone from really high highs to very low flops that I would love to get into, and that’s Katy Perry. I feel like we’ve come a long way from Left Shark at the Super Bowl. What happened there?
Katy Perry has had the career that pop stars used to have, where they have a crazy dominant stretch where they’re knocking out hit after hit after hit, and they’re unstoppable. Then everything kind of tails off over time. One album has five No. 1 hits. The next album has two No. 1 hits. The next album has no significant hits at all, but a couple top 10s.
She put out an album right at the beginning of the pandemic. You can say, “Well, that one didn’t do well, and that’s not her fault.” Then she spent a long time on American Idol as a judge; she spent a long time playing Las Vegas residencies. And then she was like, “That’s it. I’m quitting American Idol. I’m coming back. I’m being the pop star that you all want me to be.“
She made a bad album. She also reunited with Dr. Luke, who was the co-writer and producer of lots of her big hits but who, in the time since she stopped working with him, accusations were made. Kesha, who was friends with Katy Perry when she came up, was the person making those accusations. So there’s a lot for the internet to glom onto there.
“Especially now, a song can debut at No. 1 based on streams and conversation, and then it can disappear from the charts.”
That’s how a song goes from being a bad song to a notorious flop — when not only does the song not perform, it actually burns up a lot of the goodwill that this person has had.
What songs did everyone maybe expect to be huge, but then bombed?
It is possible for a song to be a No. 1 hit and still a flop. Especially now, a song can debut at No. 1 based on streams and conversation, and then it can disappear from the charts.
In 1996, Michael Jackson released “You Are Not Alone.” The song debuted at No. 1. It fell pretty quickly. The album didn’t do that well. The song ultimately is not remembered that well, and has really entered the notorious shadow zone over the years.
Are there examples of songs that critics hated initially, and then over time became classics?
So many. The songs that were hits and were universally regarded as irritating in their time have a great hit rate. People were annoyed by “MMMBop,” by Hansen, or “Wannabe” by the Spice Girls.
There were certainly critics who understood ABBA when they were popping off, but they were, I would say, widely regarded as a punchline. Now that is just an impeccable, beautiful, influential pop catalog.
A song like the Quad City DJ’s ““C’mon N’ Ride It (The Train)” was not a song the critics were really lining up to praise in the 1990s, but as a person who was a child then, I can tell you that song goes so hard and never stopped going hard.
What’s the biggest misconception people have about pop music success?
I think the biggest misconception is the idea that a label or a corporation can engineer a giant hit. They can observe trends. They can put their money into promotion. But you never know what people are going to actually grab onto and what they’re not.
There are things that they can do to create the impression that something is connecting, but you need to have real sustained success to have everybody be like, “Okay, no, this actually is huge.”
How do artists tend to respond if they’ve entered a flop era?
There’s a grand, beautiful history of artists who instead of trying the same thing over and over again, they become behind-the-scenes figures. They write songs for other people, or they produce, or they become managers.
Max Martin, who is now ahead of John Lennon, but behind Paul McCartney in terms of songwriters with No. 1 hits, he was the lead singer for a Swedish band in the ’80s that was trying to be Bon Jovi, and they never caught on. His band was called It’s Alive. You can look their songs up online. They’re not that great, but he wound up making all these incredible records with all these different people.
There’s a lot of that. That has happened many, many times throughout pop history. It’s certainly one way to deal with the flop problem.

Sunderland sign Ahoka from Royal Antwerp
- Published
Sunderland have signed midfielder Jules Ahoka from Belgian side Royal Antwerp for 10m euros (£8.6m).
The Black Cats said the 20-year-old DR Congo youth international has signed a long-term contract with the club.
"I am very happy and proud to join Sunderland," said Ahoka, who featured in both of Antwerp's league games this season.
"It is a big club with great ambitions, and I am excited to be here.
"I want to work hard, learn from my team-mates and the staff, and continue developing as a player. I will give everything for the club and I cannot wait to get started."
Ahoka becomes the Black Cats' third summer signing, following the arrival of Belgian left-back Thomas Meunier and French right-back Dayann Methalie.
"Jules is a player we have been following closely and he has shown some very encouraging qualities for his age," said Sunderland director of football Florent Ghisolfi.
"He has huge potential and we believe Sunderland is the right environment for him to continue his development."
Sunderland were beaten 2-1 by Ipswich in their Premier League opener on Saturday. Their next match is against Fulham on Sunday (14:00 BST).

Why Are So Many People Listening to a Podcast About Living in a Convent?
Dominican Sisters Open Mic has gone viral, in part because of its hosts’ unabashed joy.
At a convent in Ann Arbor, Michigan, the bell chimes every day at 5 a.m. Then the 40 or so women who live there year-round—Dominican Sisters of Mary, Mother of the Eucharist—head to the chapel.
Their day begins with an hour of prayer, followed by Mass. At 7 a.m., they have breakfast together, in complete silence. Many of them head off afterward to teach at nearby Catholic schools—sisters, unlike nuns, are not cloistered—while the novitiates stay behind to study at “the motherhouse,” as they call the convent. On some days, one of the women—Sister Miriam Holzman, who started living there 20 years ago—turns to a new item on her schedule: podcasting.
Back in February, Sister Miriam started hosting Dominican Sisters Open Mic, a weekly show in which she and her fellow sisters discuss topics such as scripture, the saints, and day-to-day convent life. Sister Miriam told me that when the podcast started, she hoped it would encourage listeners to “go deeper in their spiritual life, no matter what their background might be”—Catholic or not, religious or not.
The show seems to have resonated outside Catholic circles. Clips of the sisters playing the ukulele and describing an Ultimate Frisbee match have gone viral on TikTok. As of late August, their account on the platform has more than 275,000 followers and more than 8 million likes. The podcast has been featured in The New York Times and on the Today show. Listeners seem to be especially drawn to the sisters’ cheerfulness. They laugh frequently and have an easy way of interacting with one another. “Their laughter seems so stress free,” one commenter observed. Another said, “Sisters, I also want that regulated nervous system laugh.” In a post liked by more than 5,000 people, one listener asked, “Why does being a nun seems so fun even though I’m not religious?”
Sister Miriam said that the show’s popularity may be connected to the overall trend of people seeking wellness content online. “People are looking for balance, and so are we,” she told me. “We want wellness too.” Their fixed routine—prayer, study, work, fun—minimizes unnecessary distractions. But the sisters aren’t just offering wellness advice or preaching self-optimization. Their search for balance includes trying to become a particular kind of person in body and soul, and noticing traces of transcendence every day. In one podcast episode, Sister Miriam talked about how, when she struggles to focus or when obligations and to-do lists intrude on her mind, her consistent schedule reminds her that in that moment, she is precisely where God wants her to be. “Which is such a gift,” she said. “I don’t need to be planning the rest of my life.”
Resisting the pressure to multitask or worry about the future seems to help the sisters prioritize prayer, a pillar of their Dominican order. At midday, the sisters meditate on the essential Christian belief that the all-powerful God took on human form in the person of Jesus Christ. Later in the afternoon, they recite the Liturgy of the Hours, a set of reflections on the Psalms and Gospels. Many of the sisters have said that after years at the convent, these practices spill over into the rest of their life—when they pray for a passerby at the airport, perhaps, or let out a sudden “Come, Holy Spirit” or “Jesus, I trust in you” at difficult points of the day. Prayer, a sister concluded in one episode, “expands your vision of reality.” It has allowed her to notice “the dew on the grass, or the sunrise on the way to work.”
As evening approaches, the sisters return to the motherhouse. They pray the rosary and have dinner together as one of them reads aloud from a recent papal address or a biography of a saint. Then out come the Trivial Pursuit boxes and guitars, the bicycles and Frisbees. As with prayer, recreation time together is fixed in their schedule. It’s not optional. The sisters don’t watch TV during it, nor do they scroll on phones.
For all the joy that the sisters display on the podcast, they are also open about the sacrifices involved in convent life. They seldom see their families. Their daily lives downplay individuality: Their sleeping quarters, called “cells,” are designed to be interchangeable and are minimally arranged with a bed, a dresser, a table, an image of the Virgin Mary. Adjusting to the 5 a.m. wake-up call can take years. And like all of us, the sisters are prone to stress and worry.
The contentment that the sisters seem to have despite these challenges may be partly explained by the documented benefits of engaging in religious practices. Clay Routledge, a social psychologist who studies sources of meaning in people’s lives, told me that prayer’s “cognitive and motivational power” can make people more attentive. He added, “It focuses your attention on something; it takes you off of these other distractions and worries, and helps you pay attention to what you care about.” In a 2016 study, psychologists at Georgia State University found that prayer motivated very religious students to “invest a greater amount of mental energy in the performance of everyday tasks.” A study from 2012 found that praying for others made participants feel more satisfied about making sacrifices for others—about living, in other words, a less self-oriented life.
Starting at 8 p.m., after their evening prayer, the sisters spend the rest of their night in complete silence. Sister Miriam told me that during this time she likes to pray about both the difficulties of the day and the things she’s grateful for. Another sister said that she sometimes walks up a nearby hill, notices the twilight sky, and thinks of her Creator. Then she returns to the motherhouse, ready for the next morning’s bell to chime.

Russian attack on Kyiv region kills at least 38
Almost constant air raids in Ukrainian capital have now reached their 3rd day
The death toll from a Russian strike on a warehouse west of Kyiv, the war's deadliest attack so far this year, rose to 38 with four people still missing, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on social media Sunday.
The strike on Friday night on the warehouse — an ammunition storage facility, according to Ukrainian officials — sparked massive explosions and fires that swept through dozens of nearby homes and buildings.
Emergency workers continued to extinguish fires and identify and neutralize explosive devices at the site in the village of Myla, Zelenskyy said.
He said 20 people were injured, including two children.
On Saturday, Zelenskyy called the Myla attack "a terrible situation" and a consequence of "terrible negligence on the part of those who stored explosives right next to people." He said a probe was underway into how and why the ammunition came to be kept there.
Russia vows 'massive strikes' against energy sector
Russia's Defence Ministry said on Sunday it is preparing to launch "massive strikes" against Ukraine's energy infrastructure, following a Ukrainian drone campaign against a retailer dubbed "Russia's Amazon" as well as the country's oil and gas sector, which Kyiv says both funds and directly fuels Moscow's invasion of Ukraine.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov on Sunday vowed "an appropriate response" to what he said was Ukraine's "path of escalation" and targeting of Russia's civilian economy.

Iran has taken the first step towards criminalising contact with foreign media, in a move human rights groups have said attempts to “sever the entire Iranian society from the rest of the world”.
For journalists, researchers and even ordinary citizens, the proposed law being discussed by Iranian lawmakers this month could make speaking to international audiences and groups a potential criminal act and restrict coverage of events such as January’s mass anti-regime protests.
Even social media platforms that the regime considers to be “financed” by another country, such as Instagram and X, would fall under the bill, said Moein Khazaeli, an Iranian human rights lawyer at Dadban, a legal counselling centre for Iranian activists.
“It means any kind of interview, contact, or sending photographs to them [foreign media or organisations] could lead to six months to two years’ imprisonment. Not just the US and Israel, but any contact with foreign media in any country could be considered a crime if one doesn’t inform the intelligence ministry beforehand,” said Khazaeli.
Among the recent examples of the risks facing Iranian journalists is the case of Yalda Moaiery, an acclaimed photographerwho was sentenced this month to 15 years in prison in Tehran for documenting the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Although Moaiery was charged under the espionage law introduced after last year’s 12-day war between Iran and Israel, Khazaeli said the new bill signalled a broader effort to regulate and punish contact between Iranians and foreign media and institutions. “It could move [Iran] to a North Korea kind of situation,” he said.
Moaiery, 44, has spent two decades covering the harsh realities faced by people in Iran, including the nationwide Woman, Life, Freedom protests in 2022 and the anti-regime protests that led to thousands being killed in January.
She came to international prominence in 2019 after criticising Trump’s use of one of her photos of a woman at a demonstration near Tehran University, saying Trump’s sanctions were damaging Iranian lives, including those of her friends and family. “This image shows my people and is for my people, and shouldn’t be abused by these men in Washington,” she wrote.
Now, in a cruel irony, Moaiery said she had been sentenced in absentia for her work covering the US-Israeli war in Iran and accused of media activity deemed to strengthen and aid Israel and the US.
“I have been a critic of Israel and its policies all my life. I am not an Israel supporter, never, ever. And I have always been a critic of American politics. It was like something that you are against, and they want to stick it to you. So it’s hard. It’s super hard,” she told the Guardian.
 Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI), said the new law on media contact risked turning Iran into an “isolated black hole”.
“It is not simply an attack on journalists and citizen journalists; it is an attempt to sever the entire Iranian society from the rest of the world by criminalising the free flow of information itself.
“It sends a chilling message and threatens to turn ordinary academic, professional and civic engagement into a potential national security crime,” she said.
Moaiery was arrested and sentenced to eight years in prison in 2022, but later received an amnesty. This time, however, she fears her sentence could be upheld and she might be jailed.
“Of course, I am scared,” she said. “The only thing that I’m worried about is wasting my life if I have to be there for 15 years. When I get out, I’ll be 60 years old.”
  She also criticised foreign journalists who travelled to Tehran to cover the funeral in July of the late supreme leader, Ali Khamenei.
“I have one word for them: shameful. They just want to say, ‘We were in Tehran.’ OK, but what did you do? They didn’t go and ask people about the economic situation or talk to the families of the thousands who died in January. Why were you here? To participate in their propaganda?”

The Jharkhand Health Department on Saturday (August 29, 2026) sounded an alert after at least eight people tested positive for H1N1 influenza, commonly known as swine flu, an official said.
In an advisory issued to all civil surgeons, medical colleges and district surveillance officials, the department asked them to remain vigilant, screen suspected cases and keep isolation wards ready at hospitals, he said.
“There is no panic situation so far. The alert has been issued only to spread awareness among common people and take up precautionary measures in advance,” state National Health Mission (NHM) director Shashi Prakash Jha said.
Mr. Jha appealed to people to take even a normal fever seriously and seek proper medical treatment.
“As many as 11 samples were examined, of which eight tested positive for the H1N1 virus at Ranchi’s Rajendra Institute of Medical Sciences (RIMS),” an official said.
Cases of influenza A (H1N1) and H3N2 seasonal influenza have been reported in several states, including Delhi, Karnataka, Kerala, Maharashtra and Rajasthan.
Under the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP), daily monitoring of ILI (influenza-like illness) and SARI (severe acute respiratory infections) cases across the state and reporting on the IHIP portal are being ensured, a release of the health department said.
Testing facilities for influenza A H1N1 and H3N2 have been made available at RIMS, Ranchi, and MGM, Jamshedpur.
“Instructions have been issued to designate an isolation ward with at least 10 beds in all district hospitals and medical colleges for the treatment of suspected and infected patients,” the release said.
The hospitals have been directed to ensure adequate arrangements for PPE kits, masks, triple-layer masks, essential medicines, oxygen equipment, and ventilators in hospitals.
Mandatory screening will be conducted for patients visiting hospital OPDs with symptoms of ILI and SAR, it added.
According to the health department’s advisory, the elderly, children up to the age of five, pregnant women, and individuals suffering from serious chronic illnesses are more susceptible to this infection and require special care.

The Limits of Yayoi Kusama’s Infinity
The visionary artist once challenged ways of seeing—until she was seen by everyone.
Years before the polka-dotted pumpkins, before the Instagrammable Infinity Mirror Rooms, Yayoi Kusama made art that was charged with oppositional energy. Her performances, in which she painted dots onto the naked bodies of her collaborators, were an expression of ’60s counterculture. They were protests against the Vietnam War, rebukes to the art market. Her Accumulations—soft sculptures of furniture or common household items covered in stuffed, handsewn penis shapes—were hilarious critiques of phallocentrism and early examples of feminist art.
Kusama was, in other words, part of the artistic avant-garde. Her death, at 97, is a cold reminder that the avant-garde no longer exists.
You could point to Andy Warhol, Jeff Koons, Takashi Murakami, or Keith Haring, but in many ways, no one epitomizes the collapse of the avant-garde more vividly than Kusama. I’m mostly a fan of her work. It’s very hard not to like her Infinity Mirror Room installations and playful gourds, and not to smile when you see Kusama’s endearing face framed by her signature brightly colored bobbed wig. But at a certain point, you can’t help but feel that she stopped being an artist and chose instead to become a highly profitable brand.
In death as in life, her name bestrides a tightly managed, commercially successful global enterprise with diverse revenue streams, including high-profile partnerships with luxury labels, licensed merchandise, and strictly managed intellectual-property protection. Kusama’s large-scale sculptures and immersive installations break attendance records at museums and galleries around the world, and her works regularly set records at auction. In her final years, she was one of the world’s top-selling contemporary artists.
Decades before all of that, though, Kusama was a creative maverick. After moving to New York from Tokyo in the late 1950s, she became a pioneer of both pop art and minimalism, then a key figure in performance art. She called her early breakthrough paintings—expansive, swirling fields of tightly packed dots—Infinity Nets. Before even Andy Warhol (although after Marcel Duchamp), she made her own persona an expression of her art, paving the way for such figures as Gilbert and George, the British-artist duo who made life itself a performance.
Kusama’s artworks had countercultural energy. They fought against cliché. They critiqued patriarchy. They broke down starchy inhibitions and wobbled magnificently on the edge of the rational. They tried, in other words, to open up new ways of seeing.
That was what the avant-garde was all about: It was an attempt to see the world afresh. For many of its leading figures, from the Impressionists in the 1870s to conceptual artists a century later, this also meant proposing new and better solutions to the problem of how to be and how to live together. These proposals, many times rooted in sympathy and love, were presented as alternatives to the political structures and market logic that had so often led to war, exploitation, hopelessness, and suffering.
Even when attempts to turn these imagined alternatives into reality failed—and often dismally—the avant-garde stood in a clear relationship to modernity’s traumas. It was like the whistle cap in the spout of a boiling kettle: both a release of suppressed pressures (psychic and cultural) and an alarm.
But society got sick of hearing the alarm. And the kettle got tired of whistling.
Kusama, having experienced a period of art-world success, had her own breakdown after returning to Tokyo permanently in 1973. Two years later, she checked herself in to a psychiatric institution, where she became a permanent resident from 1977 until her death. The institution was within walking distance of her multistory studio.
Her psychic travails had to do with her upbringing (she had an authoritarian mother and an unfaithful father), which left her afraid of sex and intimacy. She suffered from severe audiovisual hallucinations, in which she would see flashing lights, auras, and dense fields of dots. She fell into deep episodes of clinical depression and attempted suicide twice.
When Kusama reemerged as an active artist in 1989, she and her supporters presented her mental-health issues not just as an important aspect of her personal story but as part of the energy that fueled her artwork. All of this was healthy frankness, but it also undoubtedly enhanced her work’s reception. People could relate to the idea of creativity as a function of—and therapy for—mental illness.
Kusama and her promoters emphasized the link, tapping into narratives about the artist as a suffering visionary that went back to Van Gogh and even earlier artists (including such figures as Piero di Cosimo, Caravaggio, and Rosso Fiorentino) whose artistic brilliance was linked to their strange behavior and (perhaps) mental instability. In the 20th century, the idea of a connection between creativity and interior turmoil was taken up with renewed gusto, and the category of outsider art (or art brut) was established. Outsider artists could reconnect us to the amputated life of the emotions, re-enchanting a world diagnosed by Max Weber, in 1917, as disenchanted.
Kusama was one of many artists who swam with these currents. She talked about her repeating dots as an expression of an inclination toward “self-obliteration”—an urge to dissolve into forever-expanding patterns. The idea sounded at once mystical, therapeutic, and nightmarish. The idea that it might be all three only increased her appeal.
This second phase of Kusama’s art-world success far surpassed the first, proving, among other things, that you didn’t need to be in New York for your career to go gangbusters. She became one of the most popular artists on Earth. For museums struggling with attendances, she guaranteed box-office bonanzas.
Her zany, luridly wigged persona helped dismantle the intimidation factor that prevents many people from relating to art and museums. Her work’s upbeat vibes and instant recognizability (spotted pumpkins!) were huge factors in her popularity. They made it easy to let go of the idea that you had to have prior knowledge or be somehow “initiated” into art before you could enjoy it.
But the speed with which Kusama converted her popularity into massive commercial success was sobering, if only because it seemed to signal her total co-option by the market. A turning point came in 2012, when the luxury-goods brand LVMH, under the creative direction of Marc Jacobs, incorporated Kusama’s polka dots into its clothing lines, adorning stores all around the world with her designs. As Georgina Adam reported in her 2014 book, Big Bucks: The Explosion of the Art Market in the 21st Century, the collaboration caused sales of Kusama’s work to take off and exposed her to audiences she would have never reached otherwise.
From that point on, Kusama’s absorbing and fresh art, once charged by avant-garde energies, became more or less a meaning-free expression of market principles, an exercise in branding. She soon became a social-media phenomenon—the world’s most Instagrammable artist. Crowds waited in long lines just to spend 30 or 90 seconds in her Infinity Mirror Rooms taking selfies.
Kusama’s talk of self-obliteration sounds vaguely Buddhist or Taoist. But I suspect it’s more clearly seen, in the late phase of Kusama’s career, as pure capitalism at work—a function of the same logic relied on by Big Tech as it converts the liberating potential of the internet into addiction, polarization, and advertising revenue, and a drastic narrowing of human potential. You will no longer need an inner life, says this logic. You will no longer even be you. You will be data points and dollar signs. You will be ubiquitous, self-obliterating dots.
Kusama also achieved something that has eluded other artists who were co-opted by commerce and converted avant-garde energies into branding, including Warhol, Haring, Koons, and Murakami. The artist—an adorable maker of giant spotted pumpkins who lived in a psychiatric institution—became beyond criticism. You could no more criticize her than you could a grandmother giving a teddy bear to an orphan.
I have almost always felt delight when I’ve entered one of Kusama’s Infinity Mirror Rooms or encountered her pumpkins. But I smell something rotten behind their sameness and ubiquity. Successful branding is exactly what art at its best is not: a form of general seduction rather than specific engagement. I prefer the earlier Kusama, the artist of extraordinary boldness, who carved out thrilling new possibilities for art in a hostile, male-dominated field. For this, she paid a heavy personal price. But it didn’t stop her from making art that felt specific to her, art targeted directly at you and me.

Srinagar, Aug 30: The Department of Consumer Affairs has notified the Legal Metrology (Indian Standard Time) Rules, 2026 on 27 August 2026. The Rules will come into force 180 days from the date of their publication in the Official Gazette.
The Rules provide for Indian Standard Time (IST) as the common time reference across the country for legal, administrative, commercial and other official purposes. The 180-day period will allow Government departments, businesses, institutions and other organisations to make the required changes to their systems before the Rules come into force.
The need for a common time reference has increased with the growing use of digital and technology-based systems. Banking and digital payments, telecommunications, railways, power systems, computer networks and government records depend on accurate time and time stamps. Differences between time sources can affect the coordination and recording of such activities. The Rules are aimed at ensuring that important systems across the country use accurate and consistent Indian Standard Time.
The common time reference will support: Accurate time-stamping of banking and digital payment transactions; coordination of railways, airports and other transport systems; reliable operation of telecommunication and internet networks; accurate time-keeping in power systems; maintenance of government and legal records; and coordination of emergency and other time-sensitive services.
Use of Indian Timing Sources
The Government is developing infrastructure to disseminate accurate Indian Standard Time across the country through Indian institutions and Legal Metrology laboratories. The Rules also provide for the use of NavIC, India's satellite navigation system, and other approved Indian timing sources for reliable and secure time dissemination.
At present, several systems use foreign satellite-based time sources. The development of an Indian time dissemination infrastructure will provide additional options for critical systems and reduce dependence on external time sources.
White Rabbit Technology Demonstration
As part of the ‘One Nation, One Time’ initiative, a White Rabbit Technology-based Indian Standard Time Dissemination Demonstration Network was commissioned at the Regional Reference Standard Laboratory (RRSL), Bengaluru, in July 2026.
The system has demonstrated the dissemination of Indian Standard Time for sectors including banking, telecommunications, power, transportation and digital governance. The Department has also demonstrated secure dissemination of IST between RRSL Bengaluru and NSE Chennai, in collaboration with CSIR-NPL, ISRO, SEBI, NSE, BSNL and other stakeholders.
The 180-day period before commencement of the Rules will provide stakeholders time to review their existing systems, undertake necessary technical changes and prepare for implementation.The Legal Metrology (Indian Standard Time) Rules, 2026 will provide a common Indian Standard Time reference for time-dependent systems and official purposes across the country.

After funding struggles and a name change, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has been successfully launched. It will now make a three-month, one-million-mile journey to its orbit at the second Sun-Earth Lagrange point (L2) beyond the Moon.
The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launches to study dark matter and dark energy
The telescope will survey our universe 1,000 times faster than Hubble.
From this vantage point, Roman will conduct an unprecedented survey of the universe. Its field of view is 100 times larger than Hubble’s and, according to NASA, it can survey the sky 1,000 times faster using its 300-megapixel infrared camera. Roman also has a Coronagraph system that can block and mask glare from stars, allowing it to directly image exoplanets, even smaller, older, and colder planets orbiting close to their stars.
Roman will also conduct detailed 3D scans to help map the distribution of dark matter and narrow down the potential candidates for its makeup. Using the same 3D scans and gravitational lensing measurements, Roman will attempt to map how dark energy shaped the evolution of the universe.
Nicky Fox, associate administrator for the Science Mission Directorate at NASA, said in a press release that “Roman will be a discovery machine that will bring us closer than ever before to answering humanity’s most profound questions about our cosmic history.”

Congo on Thursday began vaccinating people against Ebola as health authorities work to slow the country's deadliest outbreak of the disease on record.
The vaccination campaign was officially launched in Kisangani, the capital of Tshopo province, in the country's east, Health Minister Roger Kamba said.
Health workers and other people working on the front lines of the Ebola response are among the first to receive the vaccine.
“We have decided to use the Ervebo vaccine to protect first those who are on the front line, therefore our health care providers, but also people who have been in contact with patients,” Kamba said.
The outbreak has so far affected six provinces in Congo, including Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Tshopo, Haut-Uele and Bas-Uele.
As of Tuesday, the country had recorded 5,713 confirmed cases, including 2,744 deaths, according to government figures. The overall death rate among confirmed cases was about 48%.
The outbreak in eastern Congo is spreading under extremely difficult conditions, fueled by insecurity, displacement, a health workers' strike and intense population movements. The World Health Organization has said it remains out of control and is on track to surpass the 2014-2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak, the deadliest on record, which killed more than 11,000 people, primarily in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
More than 50,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine have been received, according to Congo's state news agency.
The World Health Organisation said last week that 70,000 doses of Ervebo had been approved for use in Congo.
About 50,000 doses are intended for frontline and health workers, while another 20,000 will be used in a clinical trial to study whether the vaccine protects against Bundibugyo Ebola, the agency said.
The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo type of Ebola virus. Ervebo, however, is approved to protect against a different type, known as Zaire ebolavirus. There is currently no approved vaccine specifically for Bundibugyo Ebola.
The vaccine is being used under a compassionate-use program, which allows a medical product to be used in a serious disease situation even though it has not been specifically approved for that particular use.
Health authorities said Ervebo could offer some protection against the Bundibugyo virus because the two viruses are related. But whether the vaccine can actually prevent illness in people infected with Bundibugyo Ebola is still being studied.
Placide Mbala Kingebeni, Africa CDC's director for research, clinical trials and innovation, said data will be collected during the vaccination campaign to measure how well the vaccine works.
The campaign is expected to cover 14 health zones in Tshopo, Bas-Uele and Haut-Uele provinces.
Kamba strongly encouraged health workers to get vaccinated, saying the vaccine could protect them from the disease and help prevent them from carrying the virus into their communities.

The Dil Chahta Hai Reunion happened on August 28 at a suburban hotel in Mumbai. It was organized by Amazon Music and We Are Yuva. The event saw almost the entire team of the film – Aamir Khan, Saif Ali Khan, Dimpla Kapadia, Sonali Kulkarni, Farhan Akhtar, Ritesh Sidhwani, Javed Akhtar, Shankar Mahadevan, Ehsaan Noorani and Loy Mendonsa – get nostalgic on its 25 iconic years.
Reema Kagti scolded Aamir Khan for “4-5 hours” for landing up late on Talaash sets; actor had gone to attend Sachin Tendulkar’s party: “She hasn’t let me forget about it till today”
During the course of the discussion, Aamir funnily recalled that filmmaker Zoya Akhtar, who was the first AD (assistant director) on the film, once had a high temper and he advised her to cool down. While discussing her, Aamir said that he is still working on toning down the anger of filmmaker Reema Kagti, who was also an AD on Dil Chahta Hai and present at the event. Aamir recalled an incident, which he now looks at in a funny way, when Reema got extremely angry on him during the shoot of their film Talaash (2012).
Aamir said, “I was shooting with her for Talaash. I am a huge fan of Sachin Tendulkar. He was retiring. And Sachin and I are close friends. He is a national icon. Sachin said, ‘It’s my retirement party, so please do come’. I told him that I will definitely be there. That night we were shooting for Talaash; Ballard Pier, night shoot. I know how Reema is. I said, ‘Reema, this is a very important occasion. Sachin is retiring. I have to go and I will be late by one hour’. She was seething inside but she said, ‘Theek hai, come one hour late’.”
However, Aamir couldn’t leave the party on time as Sachin wanted him to wait. Aamir recalled, “Sachin said, ‘Please wait, I am waiting for someone to come and I want you to speak (to that person)’. I could not explain to him that Reema is on the other end. So I thought, ‘Aaj Reema se daant kha lenge. Sachin Tendulkar ke liye itna bhi chalega’.”
Although Aamir was expecting to get scolded by Reema, he was still unpleasantly surprised by how she reacted. Aamir said, “Shabana (Azmi, who was also present at the event), she has not let me forget about it till today. She fired me for some 4-5 hours. (She said), ‘How dare you come late? Is this your professionalism?’ Itna mujhe sunaya Javed sahab (referring to Javed Akhtar). I am still working on her (anger). We are getting there.”
It seems Aamir mixed up Sachin’s retirement party with the 2011 World Cup celebration party. Sachin’s retirement party happened soon after he retired in November 2013 while Talaash released in November 2012. The film’s shoot was wrapped up in November 2011. Hence, Aamir must be shooting for Talaash in April 2011 when the World Cup bash happened, as was evident from the look he had when he was in the stadium for the final match.

“The Dog Stars” couldn’t beat the heat during the dog days of summer and melted down over its opening weekend.
Disney and 20th Century’s “The Dog Stars” opened to just $8 million domestically from 3,330 locations for a fifth-place finish. The post-apocalyptic thriller, which cost more than $80 million to produce, has not sat well with critics or audiences, receiving a 40% on Rotten Tomatoes and just a “C+” grade from CinemaScore polls.
“The Dog Stars” is poised to lose tens of millions in its theatrical run, making it one of director Ridley Scott’s biggest misfires. The poor opening harkens back to Scott’s 2021 film “The Last Duel,” which opened to just $4.7 million in October of that year against a budget of about $100 million. The historical drama was also released by 20th Century, but it was received much better by critics. Scott, best known for classics like “Gladiator” and “Alien,” reached his box office peak in 2015 with “The Martian,” which grossed $630 million worldwide and earned seven Oscar nominations, including best picture.
Popular on Variety
“The Dog Stars” brings an up-and-down summer to an end for Disney. While the studio hit big with “Toy Story 5” ($1.12 billion) and “The Devil Wears Prada 2” ($692 million), it also fielded misfires like the live-action “Moana” ($308 million against a $250 million budget) and “The Mandalorian and Grogu” ($345 million against a $165 million budget). Hard to imagine Disney is worried, considering “Avengers: Doomsday” is waiting in the wings for what will surely be a box office blowout in December.
“The Dog Star” stars Jacob Elordi as Hig, a lonely apocalypse survivor with a canine companion. After he picks up on a mysterious broadcast signal, he is determined to track the source. Other cast members include Margaret Qualley, Josh Brolin, Guy Pearce, Allison Janney and Benedict Wong.
This weekend’s other major newcomer, “Coyote vs. Acme,” landed in third place after grossing an estimated $13.5 million domestically from 3,575 screens. The live-action-animation hybrid was abandoned by its original distributor, Warner Bros., for tax credits, enraging sectors of the film community. Ketchup Entertainment saved the title back in March of 2025 and slated it for a theatrical release.
“Coyote vs. Acme” sees “Looney Tunes” favorite Wile E. Coyote take the Acme Corporation to court after its products failed him one too many times in his pursuit of the Road Runner. Cast members include Will Forte, Lana Condor, John Cena, Tone Bell, Martha Kelly, Luis Guzmán, P.J. Byrne and John Early. Dave Green directs with a script from Samy Burch.
At No. 1, again, was Sony and Marvel’s “Spider-Man: Brand New Day.” It earned $22.2 million through Sunday, dropping just 44% from last week’s earnings. That figure pushes the superhero epic’s domestic total to a staggering $891 million.
“Brand-New Day” is on the cusp of two major box office milestones. After surpassing $936 million, it will become the highest-grossing movie of all time at the domestic box office. That record currently belongs to 2015’s “Star Wars: The Force Awakens.” When it clears that benchmark, “Spider-Man” will be on its way to becoming the first movie ever to hit $1 billion in North America alone.
Universal’s “The Odyssey” continues to impress. The Greek epic took second, earning $14.6 million through its seventh weekend at the domestic box office. That puts Chris Nolan’s blockbuster at a North American haul of $564 million.
Sony’s “Insidious: Out of the Further” made $10.1 million (a 60% drop) in its second weekend for a fourth-place finish. Those earnings put the horror sequel’s domestic revenues at $43 million. It’s a great start, considering the film only cost about $18 million to produce.

(Bloomberg) -- Federal immigration authorities said they deported right-wing provocateur and online influencer Milo Yiannopoulos after he was detained and accused of overstaying his visa.
Yiannopoulos was arrested at the Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport on Thursday after a federal immigration judge on July 22 ordered his deportation when he missed a court hearing, according to a statement from the Department of Homeland Security. 
The agency said Saturday that Yiannopoulos was deported on Friday.
A British media personality and former editor at the conservative outlet Breitbart News, Yiannopoulos had been a supporter of President Donald Trump’s 2016 campaign. Yiannopoulos claimed he helped broker a 2022 meeting between the president and the rapper Ye. More recently, he founded a public relations and management firm giving celebrities advice, according to the Hollywood Reporter.
Although Yiannopoulos entered the country legally in 2019, “he chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws,” the department said in its statement.  
The US is offering $3,000 and a free flight to people who self-deport as part of Trump’s overall immigration crackdown. The administration hit a high of nearly 50,000 arrests in July, according to information collected and published by the Deportation Data Project at the University of California, Berkeley and University of California, Los Angeles. As part of that arrest surge, immigration agents have been targeting foreigners as they pass through domestic airports, including people who say they are visa holders or green card applicants.
Laura Loomer, a right-wing online personality and Trump supporter who has clashed with Yiannopoulos, posted on X that she reported him to ICE and the FBI.

Kalshi today lost a major ruling over whether it can evade state gambling laws, as a federal appeals court found that Nevada can stop the prediction market from allowing sports bets. While the Trump administration is trying to help prediction markets avoid state regulation, a panel of three Trump-appointed judges unanimously ruled against Kalshi in today’s decision from the US Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit.
The Nevada Gaming Control Board today said the 9th Circuit “emphatically reject[ed] the view that the federal Commodity Exchange Act preempts application of Nevada’s gaming laws to sports-event contracts offered by Kalshi, Crypto.com, and Robinhood.” Nevada Governor Joe Lombardo, a Republican, said that “prediction markets offering sports-event contracts constitute gambling and must comply with Nevada’s gaming laws and regulatory framework.”
The judges affirmed a district court order that let Nevada enforce state laws against Kalshi’s sports-related event contracts.
“KalshiEX, LLC advertises itself as ‘the first app for legal sports betting in all 50 states,’” wrote Judge Ryan Nelson. “As the volume of activity on Kalshi’s ‘sports betting’ platform ballooned, the Nevada Gaming Control Board sent a cease-and-desist letter notifying Kalshi that it was violating Nevada statutes and gaming regulations. Kalshi sought injunctive relief, arguing that it is not a legal sports betting platform but a designated contract market under the Commodity Exchange Act (CEA) offering legal sports event contracts. Kalshi argues that the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has exclusive regulatory authority over its sports event contracts and, therefore, Nevada’s gaming regulations do not apply.”
Sports bets aren’t swaps, judges rule
As in other cases involving Kalshi and state gambling laws, the key legal issue is whether a sports bet on a prediction market meets the definition of a “swap” that can only be regulated by the CFTC. The 9th Circuit ruling conflicts with a 3rd Circuit decision against New Jersey, which found that sports wagers on prediction markets are swaps. The circuit split increases the likelihood that the Supreme Court will take up the issue.

A New Way of Seeing Alien Worlds
The latest telescope launch will be a major step toward finding extraterrestrial life.
Tomorrow morning, if all goes to plan, NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, its latest and greatest orbital observatory, will lift off from its launchpad and add a little rocket-booster light to the Florida sunshine. A lot is riding on this mission. If the Roman is successful, it could give humanity a new way to see the planets around other stars and a fresh understanding of the largest-scale objects that we know to exist. But if it fails, NASA’s science program, which is already fending off ruinous budget cuts, will need to seriously rethink its future. The Artemis mission to the moon was a big win for human spaceflight, and now the science side of the house badly needs one.
NASA’s engineers have spent more than a decade readying the Roman for this moment. Before the telescope arrived in Florida, it spent more than a year in NASA’s largest clean room at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. To get near it, you had to be mummified alive. When I visited in December, NASA staffers led me to a sterile, fluorescent-lit locker room. They tossed me a white jumpsuit and two sets of booties with tight-fitting straps. They told me to put on a beard net and hair net, and triple-wrapped the gap between my jumpsuit sleeves and gloves with blue tape.
The astronomers didn’t want my skin exposed in the clean room. Dry flakes of it could drift off and settle onto the telescope’s ultrasmooth primary mirror. “You’re going to be the dirtiest thing in here,” one of them told me, as we walked through a little chamber where more than 30 nozzles blasted us with air. I jotted down this remark on special mint-green paper that sheds fewer particulates than a regular notebook, and then stepped into a cavernous eight-story white space soundtracked by the hum of six school-bus-size fans. At its center, the Roman stood more than 40 feet high, and it was surrounded by more than a dozen people, all in identical jumpsuits. Half were standing in clusters, talking, while the other half were up on motorized lifts, fussing with the telescope, applying duct tape and making final adjustments. More than a thousand people have worked on this project, and those who are lucky enough to get close to the hardware seem to derive a physical pleasure from the experience.
The Roman has a pretty shady backstory for a scientific instrument. Its primary mirror was part of a surprise gift bestowed on NASA by the National Reconnaissance Office. The NRO is one of America’s most secretive government agencies, and it apparently had a Hubble-class spare just lying around. A cash-strapped agency can’t afford to be too choosy about provenance: NASA took this mirror that was supposed to point down at the ground, for surveillance, and will instead point it out at the stars.
The NRO’s spare mirror has also solved a bit of internal politics for NASA’s science program. The Roman is built to monitor the universe at the very largest scales, to map the cosmic superstructure of galaxy clusters that stretches out from us in every direction, to see how it has expanded over time. These observations might lead scientists to a more refined sense for gravity, and may even help them discover new physics. But the idea for a mission like this was originally conceived of around the early 2000s, shortly after the discovery of dark energy, and a survey of the large-scale universe seemed like the obvious next thing to do. When NASA was finally ready to build the telescope, in the early 2010s, the action in astronomy had shifted closer to home. Scientists were in the midst of discovering thousands of new planets around nearby stars, and they wanted to find more. Although the Roman’s original mission plan did allow for some planet-hunting, the new mirror would allow them to do it in a whole new way.
Finding a little world with its own atmosphere in the glare of a nearby star is tricky work. Even the very largest planets will be a billion times fainter than the suns they orbit. When I spoke with Dominic Benford, Roman’s program scientist at NASA Headquarters, he likened the challenge to spotting a firefly buzzing around a powerful searchlight from thousands of miles away. To make this possible, astronomers have lodged an exquisite new kind of coronagraph into the Roman’s metallic guts. Coronagraphs originally helped astronomers see the plasma flares emanating from our sun, by blocking out the far more brilliant light from the solar disk. In a sense, the device creates a brief artificial eclipse inside the telescope. The Roman’s coronagraph is designed to do something similar for more distant stars so that astronomers can see the planets that surround them.
When the telescope is trained on a star in our Milky Way, it will catch a lot of light, and then run it through the coronagraph’s system of barriers and mirrors. Two of the mirrors that it uses may be even more beautiful in their design than the ultrasmooth, eight-foot primary. Each is smaller than the average makeup compact, and has more than 1,600 actuators that can individually deform tiny portions of the glass in tiny increments, less than the diameter of a helium atom. Astronomers will employ hundreds of these warping movements, spread across the mirrors, to deflect a specific star’s glare, creating an image of the star within a ring of nearly pure darkness. Deformable mirrors like these have previously been used on the ground to help telescopes see through the warble and blur of Earth’s atmosphere. But no one has ever sent one of this complexity to space.
The Roman team believes that up there, where the viewing conditions are more pristine, the Roman will be able to deliver the first direct images of distant planets in visible light. Until now, most of the extrasolar planets that scientists have observed have been detected indirectly. In some cases, a planet’s existence is inferred from the gravitational force that it exerts on its host star, causing the star to wobble. Or astronomers might see a host star dim, repeatedly and predictably, as an orbiting planet passes in front of it. We have been able to get direct snapshots of only a few young planets that were still roiling hot and glowing brightly, and mainly in infrared. The Roman telescope’s coronagraph should be able to see worlds that aren’t glowing at all. Like Earth, they will be illuminated solely by the soft visible light of their host stars.
I asked Vanessa Bailey, the coronagraph’s instrument technologist, if there were any particular stars that she was excited to inspect. Because the coronagraph isn’t part of the telescope’s main mission, just three of the first 18 months will be set aside for its observations. Bailey said that the astronomers will use that time to look at previously detected planets that are only tens of light-years away. She mentioned the Epsilon Eridani system, where a Jupiter-size world is known to orbit an orange dwarf star. With the coronagraph, they’ll stare at it for many hours, letting photons from the planet slowly pile up. “It’s just going to be a little fuzzy smudge, just barely there,” Bailey said. “But we might be able to tell if it’s cloudy or clear, and we might be able to say whether it’s more like Jupiter or Neptune.”
All of this could go wrong. Bailey told me that the coronagraph has never been tested outside the lab, and in space, it may not work. If for some reason the mirrors are misaligned, or the instrument malfunctions, any planets would be lost in the astral glare. NASA’s long-running quest to find another living world in the universe would be set back, perhaps by a decade or more. But if the coronagraph does fulfill its mission, it will serve as a proof of concept for NASA’s next really big telescope, the Habitable Worlds Observatory, which the agency has been developing for more than a decade.
Roman’s coronagraph will be able to find only large planets—Saturn-size or ideally bigger—that circle their stars in chilly, distant orbits. NASA scientists want to place a much more precise one on the HWO. That mission will fixate on more than 100 nearby stars that share the sun’s rough age and brightness. Its coronagraph will cast a much tighter ring of near darkness around them, to see if any planets show up in the closer, warmer orbits that might be more hospitable to life—and it will even look for signs of life in the planets’ atmospheres. But the HWO won’t lift off until the late 2030s at the earliest. For now, the Roman has to prove out. It has to survive the violence of launch and fly a million miles from Earth so that its mirrors can catch the light of a nearby star and then surround it in darkness so deep that a faint alien world appears.

What triggered the mass migrant crossings into Ceuta?
Over the last 24 hours, the tiny Spanish territory of Ceuta - home to around 83,000 people - has seen an unprecedented surge in migrant arrivals.
An estimated 60,000 people from Morocco are believed to have crossed into the North African enclave that has long been a focal point for migrant attempting to reach Europe.
Dozens of people died while trying to make the crossing.
On Friday evening, Spanish officials confirmed that more than 48,000 of the migrants had voluntarily returned to Morocco.
BBC's Sarah Rainsford explains what may have triggered the surge in crossings and what happens next.

It took Cytokinetics 27 years to win its first regulatory approval. The second one could happen much faster than that.
The biotech on Friday unveiled the full pivotal study data of its drug aficamten in an inherited heart condition called non-obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, showing that the medicine improved how patients felt and their exercise capacity.
While some experts have described the benefits as limited, Cytokinetics plans to submit the drug to the Food and Drug Administration by the end of the year. If approved, it would be the first treatment specifically cleared for what’s known as nHCM.

2 sailors missing after a French trawler sinks near British port
French authorities say two sailors are missing after a French fishing trawler sank southwest of the British port of
BREST, France -- Two sailors were missing Sunday after a French-registered fishing trawler sank southwest of the British port of Plymouth, French authorities said.
The Maranello contacted another trawler, the Stradale, on Saturday to report a problem with its fishing gear. The Stradale managed to recover three of the five crew members before the Maranello sank, the French naval prefecture for the Atlantic said.
Two sailors remained missing despite a major search-and-rescue operation.
The two vessels were located approximately 26 nautical miles southwest of Plymouth, in an area under British responsibility. The Falmouth Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre took charge of the rescue operation in coordination with French counterparts.
A helicopter evacuated one of the three sailors recovered by the Stradale, who was injured, and transported him to Truro Hospital for treatment. The other two sailors were taken to Plymouth for medical attention.
The search, coordinated by MRCC Falmouth, is pressing on, the maritime prefecture said.
The French Navy’s Falcon 50, along with two British lifeboats and two British aircraft, has been deployed in the search.

Medical melodramas are a staple film genre in Japan. As a producer once told me, these narratives are a good box office bet because Japanese audiences love to cry.
But domestic films that address illness or disability can also be unblinkingly realistic and populated by characters who are flawed humans, rather than stainless victims or selfless saints. And if tears come, they are earned, not extracted.
The latest in this line is “Lives at Right Angles” by Syoutarou Kobayasi (as he prefers to romanize his name). The director sat down with The Japan Times for a wide-ranging interview about the development of the film and the experiences and ideas that guided his approach to its subject matter.

Drugstores say Medicare's $50 obesity drug program is catching on
Medicare’s $50 obesity drug program is proving popular, pharmacy chains say
Starting in July, Medicare began allowing eligible beneficiaries to get obesity drugs for $50 a month. Less than two months in, CVS and Walgreens tell NPR they've each filled around 100,000 such prescriptions.
The prescriptions were made possible as part of a pilot called the Bridge program.
By law, Medicare is barred from paying for weight loss drugs, but the administration came up with a workaround. Medicare will cover the drug, if a person meets certain conditions, such as having obesity combined with high blood pressure that's hard to control.
However, beneficiaries are ineligible if they have sleep apnea or Type 2 diabetes, because Medicare part D should already cover GLP-1 drugs for those conditions. The Bridge program is set to run through the end of 2027.
"We expected there would be uptake," says Walgreens' chief pharmacy officer Rick Gates, explaining that stores around the country stocked extra Wegovy, Zepbound and Foundayo to prepare for the July launch. "I think there's been a little bit more uptake than we even expected."
Walgreens pharmacies had to adjust a little as the program got up and running, but haven't run into any supply issues, Gates says. Around half of the patients Walgreens has served as part of the Bridge program had never taken GLP-1s before, he adds.
"That's the part where pharmacies naturally will lean in," he says, explaining that it's important to make sure patients don't stop therapy because of the initial side effects, such as nausea and diarrhea. "Those are the things that pharmacists can really help with."
CVS says it has filled more than 100,000 Bridge prescriptions as of mid-August. The pharmacy chain says it also has options for people who aren't eligible for the program. "CVS Pharmacy accepts a wide range of third-party prescription discount cards, manufacturer coupons, and manufacturer vouchers to help reduce out-of-pocket costs," the company wrote in a statement to NPR.
Walmart also serves as a pharmacy for many patients around the country. The store chain didn't provide a number for Bridge program prescriptions it has filled, but it did say that those prescriptions have been growing week over week. "Bridge prescriptions have now been processed at more than 5,000 Walmart and Sam's Club pharmacies nationwide," the company added in a statement to NPR.
Millions of beneficiaries could be eligible
Jeremy Shane, a nonresident scholar at the USC Leonard D. Schaeffer Institute for Public Policy & Government Service, says the numbers retail pharmacy chains shared with NPR show that seniors are making use of the temporary program.
"I think those are big numbers and they're encouraging about the demand for those medications," he says. "Before Bridge started, Medicare had estimated roughly about 4 million Medicare recipients might qualify for the program. And so if you figure this is 200,000 and, you know, there might be as many as twice as many that are out there through other chain drugstores and other prescription pharmacies. That's, you know, somewhere between 5% and 10% of the eligible population in just a short period of time."
The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services did not provide NPR with figures for how many people are taking advantage of the Bridge program. But CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz said in a video posted to the social media platform X on July 29 that 250,000 beneficiaries had signed up. It's not clear whether those people were able to get their prior authorizations approved, which is required to fill Bridge program prescriptions.
Weighing cost and value
The administration hasn't said how much the 18-month Bridge program could cost, but the nonpartisan health research group KFF took a stab.
It estimates that the bill could run between $1.3 billion and $10 billion, depending on how many of the nearly 4 million eligible beneficiaries participate. For context, KFF says that Medicare Part D spending on prescription drugs in 2025 was $181 billion.
Shane at USC says there's more to it than that. "I think that the Bridge program is actually a great opportunity to refactor how we think about the price of medications and cost," says Shane. "And my personal perspective is cost is the wrong way of looking at it."
He says it's important to look at the value of these medications over time.
Shane's colleagues published a research paper a few years ago that concluded expanding Medicare access to GLP-1s 10 years could reduce healthcare spending and improve quality of life. If people become healthier by taking GLP-1 medicines, society could spend less on other health complications, such as dialysis and hospitalizations.
"When you think about it, almost all of Medicare's costs are for people who have multiple chronic conditions and given age, they deteriorate over time," he says. "And so the value for Medicare is how can we stop or slow or prevent the progression of disease? And the longer they can do that, the bigger the value is at the end."
Correction Aug. 27, 2026
In the audio version of this story, as in a previous web version, we incorrectly say Jeremy Shane published a research paper on the potential benefits of expanding access to GLP-1 drugs under Medicare. Shane’s colleagues at USC published the paper.
