This past week, the top health story, without any doubt, is the huge crisis that is brewing out of proportions in Africa - the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo. It was first announced as an outbreak on May 15, this year.As per latest data, it has reached over 5,000 cases, making this the one of the worst Ebola outbreaks in history. The outbreak has clearly outpaced response efforts.
Data from Congo’s Ministry of Health showed the outbreak had so far recorded 5,021 cases, including 2,378 deaths as of August 16, 2026, as it rages in some of the most challenging conditions imaginable fuelled by insecurity, displacement and intense population movements. It has officially infected and killed more people at a greater speed than any other outbreak in history. Starting from the first detected case, it has spread about three times faster than an outbreak from 2014 to 2016 across West Africa, which was the deadliest Ebola outbreak on record with more than 11,000 deaths.
The dire situation was underlined as World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus announced: “We must be frank: the epidemic is far from being under control.” Safety concerns have limited the response as health workers are targeted, particularly in Ituri, the province that has been hit the worst by the outbreak. Residents recently attacked a health team in the territory of Aru after a suspected case was reported there. A mob set fire to an ambulance and damaged two other vehicles, according to Michael Wani, president of the Union of Cultural Associations for the Development of Ituri.
Meanwhile, more than 16,000 doses of the new Ebola vaccine Ervebo arrived in the DRC. WHO experts still do not know whether Ervebo protects humans against the Bundibugyo strain, but early data, notably from animal trials, suggest it could offer some protection.The Ervebo vaccine “has already been used several times, and in particular on a very large scale during the 2018-2020 outbreak”, Samuel Roger Kamba, the DRC’s Minister of Health, told the press.
The other big story in India was also about an infectious disease - H1N1. As the cases continue to surge, experts assure that there is no cause for alarm yet. However they do advise that a large number of children were being affected, and that children with asthma and other chronic conditions might require special intervention.
The H1N1 virus, commonly known as swine flu, is a subtype of influenza A, and can cause respiratory illness, with symptoms including fever or chills, cough, sore throat, a runny or blocked nose, headache, tiredness, and muscle or body aches. In some cases, patients may also experience vomiting and diarrhoea. Cases have been rising in Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Bengaluru and Kerala, and while there are a number of respiratory-like illnesses also about during this season, doctors have warned that early testing is key. Bindu Shajan Perappadan reports that union Health Minister J.P. Nadda reviewed the H1N1 situation, healthcare preparedness in Delhi.
With National Eye Donation Fortnight being observed across India every year from August 25 to September 8 to raise awareness about eye donation we did our bit to highlight issues relating to eye health a little ahead of schedule.
Athira Elssa Johnson writes about the Lazy eye in children, and about squints. In the former, she focuses on how many parents may miss lazy eye among their children. Often called lazy eye, amblyopia may have no obvious signs and can remain undetected during early childhood. Screening, timely treatment and sustained follow-up are important because visual development is time-sensitive. Squints are another condition that impact the development of vision, and therefore need to be addressed on time. Squint, medically known as strabismus, is a condition in which the two eyes do not align properly. It can affect children and adults and, when it develops during childhood, can interfere with the normal development of vision
In the modern age, the field of ophthalmology is among the earliest adopters of AI systems in health care, so here is an article on using AI systems in smartphones to help detect eye diseases. Kathleen Sherwin and Rishi Raj Borah make an impassioned case for more women to lead eye health care systems.
This week we looked at some little explored aspects of cancer care too. Shrabana Chatterjee writes an interesting story on a hardly-spoken about aspect- Navigating the challenges of fertility and breastfeeding after surviving cancer. This story has a positive message for women in this position - that with careful management and supervision, it can be done.
After a cancer diagnosis, women who have not yet started their families, must be given the option for fertility preservation, say doctors. Options such as embryo freezing before cancer treatment is begun may be considered under medical guidance. Other fertility preservations techniques including oocyte and ovarian-tissue cryopreservation may also be explored before treatment begins. When it comes to breastfeeding, doctors say that after surviving cancer it may pose difficulties, but it can be done under the right medical conditions and with guidance from doctors.
Dr. Siddharth Turkar turns the spotlight on sarcomas: Many soft-tissue sarcomas, which are rare types of cancers that form in fat, muscles and blood vessels, initially look like ordinary lumps. However, when a suspicious mass of this sort is removed without appropriate imaging, tissue diagnosis or oncological planning, the opportunity for the simplest and best-planned first operation may already have been lost.
This is by far the most important gene-based analysis that pertains to us, in India. Rupsy Khurana writes the truth: South Asians are missing from global health databases, and why this matters and what needs to change in this scenario. When scientists try to understand why diseases such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease affect South Asians differently, they often have to rely on genetic data drawn from European populations. Advances in artificial intelligence and machine learning are allowing scientists to mine vast amounts of genomic and health data to detect disease earlier, predict risk, monitor patients and tailor treatments to individuals. But at the heart of this changing landscape lies an old, constant problem – the data used to build these tools lack diversity, she points out.

After a month of celebrating Madras through its landmarks, neighbourhoods, changing building and the coastline that has watched the city through it all, there is still something to be said about the Madras that lives on through the memories of its people. A renowned artist who designed the Tamil Nadu state emblem in 1949, R. Krishna Rao, a native of Madurai, shared a close bond with Madras.
His son, Srichandar K., a resident of West Mambalam reminisces his late father’s works, especially one watercolour painting that had captured the people’s attention in the late 1940s or early 1950s. It was a painting of the Central railway station caught in its everyday glory. “It was an on-the-spot work and he did this painting sitting on the western bank of Buckingham Canal abutting the former Central Jail. He further added that the painting was sold away like hot cake in a group show he had participated in,” adds Mr Srichandar.
For Rao, it was the city that gave his artistic life a push that set things in motion. It also happened when he met K. C. S. Paniker in Madurai who pioneered The Madras Art Movement. “My father decided to pursue art after meeting Paniker. He got admission to the Government School of Fine Arts only the following year, but in the meantime, he worked at an architecture firm in Madras and spent his time painting the city’s landmarks on the spot,” he says.
The original painting is believed to be in one of the residences in Chennai, but all that remains with Mr Srichandar is a sepia-tinted print of the watercolour painting. “When my dad landed in Madras he was a raw and callow youth. He used to say he was “wet behind the ears”. It was Madras that moulded him, chiselling the artist in him. Through this painting of the Central Railway station, he seems to have tried to eternalise his love for this great city, the Vandaarai Vaazhavaikkum Madras,” he adds.

It’s safe to say Grand Theft Auto VI is the most anticipated game ever. Thirteen years after the last entry in the series, rampant fervor and speculation about what features the game will include have ratcheted up. Today, Rockstar Games divulged more details through an exclusive livestream event on Netflix called Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look. The spectacle was a 26-minute-long collection of gameplay, cutscenes, and game mechanics.
And boy, does this sure look like a GTA game. The trailer featured Lucia and Jason, the two main characters, driving around Vice City, GTA’s fictional version of Miami. It highlighted all kinds of violence and shenanigans your characters can engage in, and it looks good doing it.
The livestream follows a week of gameplay leaks and story spoilers by the hacker group Cyberleek, which Rockstar called “heartbreaking.” A bevy of other details about the game emerged just a day before the event in a story published by the British magazine Dazed. The piece chronicles the extraordinary level of detail and effort Rockstar has put into GTA VI, including how players control the characters and the unprecedented realism that Rockstar put into its satirical sandbox version of Miami.
It’s bound to be a massive game; today’s reveal shows just how much of a monster it will be. Here are the big takeaways from the livestream.
It Sure Is Pretty
GTA VI is gorgeous. The cityscapes, nightclubs, and lush natural parks shown all seem vibrant and awash in color.
There is a noticeable difference between cutscenes and gameplay, though, as the gameplay clips looked a little flatter and more desaturated than the cinematic cutscenes. That’s kind of a nitpick, though it’s worth noting that in the very first scene—in the dark basement of a crack house—the lighting is so dim it washes out the features of several Black characters around the table.
You Play as 2 Characters Simultaneously
The player can control two characters, Jason and Lucia, a Bonnie-and-Clyde-esque couple who seem to be working out some lingering tension in their relationship as they go about their various criminal activities.
The voice acting for the main characters and other non-playable characters (NPCs) feels tightly written, though that’s based on the select clips Rockstar showed. According to Dazed, the relationship between the characters can change over time, and the player’s actions can affect how that plays out. Keep that in mind if you’re hoping for a particular ending.
GTA VI offers a plethora of options for changing the two main characters’ appearances. Eating too much or too little food affects their weight. Working out can make them swole. The Extended Look also showed off characters eating and working out in minigames. It was a feature in 2004’s GTA San Andreas and in a smaller way in GTA V. Now, that reactivity will be much more fully realized in GTA VI.
There’s also an array of clothes you can equip your characters with, which Rockstar has apparently coordinated with real-life fashion designers to put in the game. Some of these, however, may only come with the $100 Ultimate Edition that people are very mad about.
Maybe Don’t Hit and Run
The NPCs in the game appear much more responsive and interactive than in prior games. According to Dazed, Rockstar has an entire studio in Los Angeles dedicated to working on NPC pedestrian behavior alone.
In the Extended Look, gameplay segments with car chases pointedly avoided streamrolling over pedestrians. But NPCs wore yoga outfits, rode scooters, and seemed to have more personality than the cut-and-paste crowds of past games.
Driving seems greatly improved. When driving, you have a minimap that looks like an actual GPS map guiding you where to go. A car chase saw the main characters running from the police. The player can switch between Lucia and Jason and choose to either drive or shoot at the pursuers. Shooting out tires can cause a car to flip, crash into the sidewalk, and cause environmental destruction.
At one point, a character also body-slams a cop through a wall, which hints at potentially more destructive environments indoors as well. GTA games have been iffy about destructible environments before, though. Sometimes in GTA V you can easily crash through a large light pole but then get instantly stopped by a volleyball net. So we’ll see how reactive everything gets.
So Much Room for Activities
Vice City and the surrounding areas seem absolutely massive. It’s also fully Florida, allowing your characters to fanboat around the Everglades, kayak on the rivers, or scuba dive and jet ski in the Gulf.
One scene from the trailer shows Lucia accidentally kidnapping a livestreaming influencer, then carrying him along through a car chase from the police. Many of the characters use phones and communicate via text. It’s clear that GTA VI has some satirical takes on social media, but we’ll see how relevant it feels in a constantly shifting era.
You Can Pet the Dog
A dog is in at least one scene of the game. Can you pet it? Yes. Yes, you can.
User-Generated Content
In 2023, Rockstar bought the modding marketplace Cfx and reworked it into an official place to share and purchase user-created mods for the game. That service, along with GTA Online’s Rockstar Mission Creator, which lets users make custom levels and modes, indicates that Rockstar has long realized that GTA is fertile ground for user creativity.
The Extended Look didn’t show anything suggesting it would advance those user-creation capabilities, but that’s likely because the game is being released as a single-player title before any multiplayer elements are added.

Voice AI startup Gnani.ai has unveiled Artha, an end-to-end sovereign AI stack aimed at Indian enterprises and public institutions. The platform was unveiled by India’s vice president CP Radhakrishnan in New Delhi today. Artha combines two of Gnani.ai’s core offerings – Evon v3.3, a 30 Bn-parameter open weight model trained natively across 11 Indian languages, and Plexus, the startup’s agentic AI platform. While Evon v3.3 provides the underlying language intelligence, Plexus enables organisations to build and deploy AI agents for specific workflows. Gnani.ai said the integrated stack will allow enterprises to use AI while retaining control over their data and technology infrastructure. The weights for Evon v3.3 are available upon request on AI model repository Hugging Face under an Apache 2.0 licence. Model weights contain the patterns and relationships learned by an AI model during training and determine how it interprets inputs and generates responses. Evon v3.3 is Gnani.ai’s first large language model launch, Gnani.ai cofounder and CEO Ganesh Gopalan told Inc42. The 30 Bn-parameter model has been trained on 2 Tn tokens, with a focus on reasoning and Indic-language performance. The startup now plans to expand the model family with 70 Bn- and 100 Bn-parameter models, depending on the complexity of use cases. Moreover, Gnani.ai is also looking to expand the model's language coverage from 11 to 22 languages in the near term. Gopalan said that the 30 Bn-parameter model has been developed with Gnani.ai’s upcoming speech-to-speech technology in mind, where low-latency reasoning will be critical. The startup has not disclosed a timeline for the launch of its speech-to-speech model. Nevertheless, it said that Evon v3.3 consumes around 40% fewer tokens for Indian-language workloads than comparable models, helping lower compute costs. Gopalan said the focus on efficiency is particularly important as Gnani looks to deploy its models in production rather than build them purely for benchmark performance. According to Gnani.ai, Artha has been developed to address three challenges faced by Indian organisations adopting AI – data sovereignty, the cost of deploying AI at scale, and the ability to work effectively across Indian languages and real-world use cases. Gopalan said Gnani.ai has started showing the model to select customers, with five of 20 enterprises that attended a recent customer meeting in Pune already expressing interest and beginning to build on top of Evon. Its potential use cases include underwriting, advertising and payments reconciliation, although these engagements are currently at the early stage and no deployments of Evon have gone live yet. While some voice AI workflows are already largely autonomous, Gopalan said regulated use cases such as underwriting and payments reconciliation will initially retain humans in the loop. He expects more routine tasks, such as document and data matching during loan onboarding, to become increasingly autonomous. Gnani’s Sovereign AI Pitch The launch comes as the Indian government is pushing for development of indigenous foundational models to reduce the country’s dependence on foreign AI systems. Gnani.ai was among the startups selected under the IndiaAI Mission in 2025 to develop homegrown foundational AI models. The startup was selected to build a multilingual, real-time voice AI foundational model with reasoning capabilities. In December 2025, it launched Vachana STT, a speech-to-text (STT) model for Indian languages trained on more than 1 Mn hours of real-world voice data. The model was developed under the IndiaAI Mission and was part of the startup’s broader voice technology stack. Founded in 2017 by Gopalan and Ananth Nagaraj, Bengaluru-based Gnani.ai offers voice AI products for enterprises. Its offerings include virtual assistants, tools that provide real-time guidance to customer service agents, and voice biometrics for fraud detection. The startup caters to enterprises and government bodies, with its products used across sectors such as banking, insurance, healthcare, telecom, and government services. Gnani.ai expects Evon and Plexus to contribute 20-30% of its business within the next year, even as its existing voice AI business continues to grow. Gopalan said the company is currently adding around 10–15 customers a month to its traditional voice business. Earlier this year, Gnani.ai raised $10 Mn in a Series B round led by Aavishkaar Capital, with participation from existing investor Info Edge Ventures. It said the capital would be used to expand internationally, strengthen its agentic AI capabilities, develop multilingual and industry-specific products, and expand its engineering and product teams.

The UK Foreign Office has been asked to intervene to secure the release of a British-Egyptian woman who it is claimed has been arrested in Cairo because of her sister’s political activism.
Eman el-Shazly, a 45-year-old based in Birmingham, was arrested on 16 August while visiting Egypt. Her lawyers say she has been detained in an attempt to silence her sister Mona, a relentless and harsh critic of the Egyptian government on her UK-based YouTube channel.
Her two brothers have already spent three years in jail and, in May, were rearrested. They were previously held in pre-trial detention, facing charges of “promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation on social media, as well as broadcasting false news harmful to state security”.
The UK Foreign Office has confirmed to the husband of Eman that she is being held in the Ramadan rehabilitation centre and her case has been given the same file number as that of her two brothers, Hassan and Eid.
The government of President Abdel Fatah al-Sisi has faced allegations that it frequently arrests relatives of political critics to put indirect pressure on the dissidents to end their overseas criticism of his rule or of state corruption. Much of Mona’s activism focuses on alleged cases of corruption inside the security services or public utilities, a highly sensitive subject in Egypt.
Arfan Rashid, the lawyer acting for Eman’s husband with whom she has four children, says that unlike Mona his wife has never been involved in politics, and had gone to Cairo two months ago to look after her ill mother after the arrest of her two brothers.
“There is ample evidence that Eman has been arrested to silence Mona,” Rashid said. He added that Eman had told the security officials she was no longer in contact with her sister, and that many family members had repeatedly asked her to stop her political activism in the UK, but to no effect.
Mona confirmed to the Guardian that she had been asked to halt her activism by other family members, including to take down her YouTube videos.
But she added: “I have done nothing wrong nor broken any law … I am a very strong woman, but it is very traumatic for me since 11 or 12 children are without their parents. It is a horrible situation, but the Egyptian government will not stop if I appear weak. The government is close to collapsing.”
Rashid said the UK government had recognised the practice of “punishment by proxy” in Egypt in its country profile policy and information note published in March 2026. Human Rights Watch and the House of Commons library warned in 2021 of an escalating pattern in which Egyptian family members of critics living abroad were being targeted.
Mona runs a YouTube channel in the UK that has 130,000 subscribers. She is also active on X, making specific and controversial claims about government officials.
The UK’s Foreign Office representation in Cairo has asked for access to see Eman but has not yet received a positive reply.
Eman’s husband, Zeesharn Moustapha, has said Egyptian police and security officers attended the family home where she was staying a few days before the arrest, and demanded that Eman tell Mona to stop publishing material against the Egyptian government.
On X, Mona has claimed as many as five members of her family have been detained or harassed by the Egyptian authorities. She wrote: “Kinship is something beyond my family’s will, and I invite them to disown me to save themselves from this despicable, illegitimate dictator. I am the one opposing Sisi, not five individuals from my family. This is a crime against humanity that does not lapse with time.” She has lived in the UK for 18 years.
Eman became a British citizen through marriage. Her lawyer has asked whether Alistair Burt, the UK’s new envoy on complex consular cases, should be asked to intervene by the Foreign Office. Burt was appointed a month ago and has been tasked with working to secure the release of British citizens held abroad.
Burt has already met Gurpreet Singh Johal, the brother of Jagtar Singh Johal, who has been detained by the Indian authorities for nearly nine years without a conviction.
The Foreign Office has been approached for comment.

Meta is testing robots that can plug in cables, reset servers, and handle other tasks inside its data centers, according to several current and former workers familiar with the projects. The ongoing effort, which has not been previously reported, may eventually allow Meta to operate its rapidly expanding data center footprint with fewer humans, keeping labor costs in check as its spending on AI infrastructure soars.
Meta is using robots and related hardware from several different vendors, including Watney Robotics, Kinova, and ABB, according to the same workers, who asked to remain anonymous because they weren’t authorized to speak to the media. Kinova and ABB declined to comment. Watney didn’t respond to requests for comment.
In one experiment, Meta is evaluating whether a Kinova Gen3 robotic arm could be used for power cycling or cutting off electricity to servers. The company is also testing a different robot to swap networking cables. One Meta data center worker estimates that if it’s successful, the bot could replace up to 80 percent of some people’s workloads. “We thought those of us performing the physical tasks were safe for a while, but not anymore,” says the worker. “It’s coming for us all, unfortunately.”
At some facilities, Meta quietly adopted another, relatively simple robot. It looks like a finger—or perhaps a pointy stick—that can press the power button on a Mac Mini or other device to restart it when remotely prompted by a human.
Meta declined to comment on the testing described in this story. Company spokesperson Francis Brennan said in a statement that Meta is investing heavily in training and hiring workers to build and operate its data centers. “America is in the middle of its biggest infrastructure boom since World War II, and there’s a major shortage of skilled workers to fill the roles; we need more workers, not fewer,” he said.
But at a conference last year, Eric Xu, senior manager for robotics at Meta, said the company’s “long-term goals” are to put robots in data centers, arguing they could speed up incident response, monitor the environment, and handle preventative maintenance. “We believe more collaboration and research will be needed, but we have to start, otherwise we don't have a chance to do this,” he said.
Until recently, robots largely weren’t well suited for the delicate work happening in data centers. They were expensive, and in earlier trials in the industry they sometimes crushed servers while attempting simple tasks, a person briefed on the experimentation says. But the hardware has gotten cheaper, and the AI models powering robots are now far more capable than they were a few years ago. Several startups are currently working to build commercial robots capable of assembling servers, swapping parts, and replacing wires.

Robots could offer more consistent output at a lower cost than human labor, especially in less populous regions where data centers are plentiful but qualified workers are scarce. Proponents also rally behind a pro-worker message: Like AI agents promise to do for knowledge workers, they argue robots could take on data center technicians’ most repetitive and dangerous tasks while freeing them to focus on more complex challenges. Longer term, getting workers out of the picture could make it more feasible to run data centers underwater, in space, or in other environments potentially inhospitable to living, breathing species.
“More and more of our customers are telling us ‘we want to run our data centers using humanoid [robots]’ because you can run them at higher temperatures, in the dark, and all these things,” says Paul Golding, who oversees so-called physical intelligence at the chipmaker Analog Devices.
The growing use of robots has received little attention from the activists driving a powerful nationwide movement against data centers. Tech companies often tout jobs for humans as an upside to the developments that can be used to justify tax breaks for them. In Altoona, Iowa, Meta operates what is now its largest data center campus, which employs hundreds of workers. The company opened the facility in 2014 and has several years left of a property tax break that allows it to save tens of millions of dollars annually, which the city has viewed as a worthwhile trade-off for having its cachet upped by having Meta jobs.
In Altoona, Meta worker group chats have taken on a demoralized tone, “saying we’re all going to be gone in a few years anyway because of the robots,” a person familiar with the discussions says. Even if adoption of robots proves slower than anticipated, some worry the quality of jobs available is trending downward. Two of the workers say that Meta is developing AI software and other technologies that they believe will allow it to hire lower-skilled—and thus, lower-paid—workers and centralize some roles in areas such as Denver, Colorado, that are more financially advantageous to the company.
“They no longer want people who can think independently, come up with creative solutions, or perform complex troubleshooting,” one Meta data center worker says. “They want ‘smart hands,’ people who are just capable enough to follow AI instructions and not mess anything up.”
Meta contends its need for skilled workers remains robust. This year, the company launched a long-term program to train thousands of people annually from any background in electrical, mechanical, and plumbing work at no cost to them. Meta is even guaranteeing employment in states such as Louisiana, Ohio, Indiana, and Texas for those who complete the training. It also partnered with building trade unions to fund apprenticeship programs.
But as communities rethink data center tax breaks and weigh putting new rules on the industry, the prospect of robots replacing at least some jobs may need to become a bigger concern. Altoona Mayor Dean O'Connor tells WIRED he hasn’t given much thought to robots taking jobs at Meta’s data center, though he frames automation as inevitable. “We will deal with it as it comes,” he says.
Tripping Cables
In a 2023 YouTube video, Meta touted that it was using a self-driving tugger robot to transport heavy server racks within its data centers as well as a wheeled, barcode-reading robot developed in-house to track inventory. The next year, Microsoft and Google unveiled separate investments in robots for their data center operations, and Amazon last year discussed using robots to help recycle parts at its facilities.
Pursuing robotics for “economically valuable tasks,” like “replacing a faulty server rack,” is “absolutely something we're looking into at Microsoft,” Ashley Llorens, a managing director for the company’s research accelerator, tells WIRED.
Meta’s tugger and inventory robots are now operating in a number of the company’s data centers, including in Iowa and Virginia, according to the people familiar with the projects. They say the robots generally work well, though there are limitations.
The inventory bot is now also being used for failure inspections, but it can’t differentiate between green and red indicator lights on equipment because its camera only detects grayscale, meaning human checks are still required to assess some breakdowns. The device also struggles with corners and traversing the cables that are often in the path of its wheels. Because there aren't that many of them, the robots need to be moved between buildings, which requires a door-opening human who maneuvers the robot with a remote control.
Two sources also describe the inventory bot as too slow. One says Meta previously explored using drones as a faster alternative, but ultimately didn’t pursue the idea.
Inside the Testbed
The Altoona data center campus is often where Meta prototypes new technologies. “What they do here in Altoona, they take to their other sites and put that in place there,” says O’Connor.
Since last June, Meta has been trying out a pair of dual-armed Watney robots for some cabling work at one of its Altoona buildings, according to one of the people familiar with the company’s efforts. The robots are supervised by humans and can’t work as fast as people yet, but they show promise.
After Watney launched in 2023, it put out a demo of a laundry-folding robot that it claimed could also handle janitorial work inside businesses. The San Francisco startup quietly pivoted to data center robots early last year, according to archived copies of its website.
Meta is testing additional robots in New Albany, Ohio, at the company’s newest data center campus known as Prometheus. Four-wheel robots “with a scissor-lift-style riser and a six-axis arm on top” made by the automation giant ABB are being used there to reseat parts and, eventually, they may take on other tasks with diminishing human oversight, a person familiar with the product says.
But the idea that robots will prevail over humans isn't guaranteed. “There's been a lot of pilots and demos, but no provable working solution,” says Helen Oleynikova, CEO of Exclaim Robotics, which is developing prototypes to replace broken parts and reset cables in data centers.
At Meta’s data centers, some workers have complained about the amount of downtime the robots need to recharge their batteries, according to the people familiar with the matter. Meta has also acknowledged internally that robots aren’t equipped for certain tasks, such as the intense cabling work required to run an Nvidia GB300 supercomputer. “Things have been designed for human hands forever to make everything a five-minute repair,” says one former Meta employee. “Redesigning everything will take time.” But the robots are getting prepared.

Claims that the Detroit Police Department issued a public service announcement warning about a rash of stabbings victimizing women circulated online in August 2026.
Facebook users claimed Detroit police said there was a "gang initiation going on in Detroit right now," and the stabbings were allegedly a part of the process. Multiple accounts that shared the claim urged women to "be aware of your surroundings at all times."
The claim that Detroit police issued such a warning was false.
The Detroit Police Department told Snopes via email that the posts were not accurate.
The DPD's website and social media feeds on Facebook, X and Instagram frequently posts alerts and warnings about specific police activity, curfews and community engagement events. Snopes' thorough search of the website and social feeds showed no posts warning about the alleged gang initiation stabbings.
A search of Bing, DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo revealed no credible reports of stabbings in Detroit linked to gang initiation, which would have been widely reported in the local media if the police had actually issued such a warning.
We found reports of two stabbings in local Detroit media in August 2026, neither of which mentioned suspected gang activity. The victim in one report was a male. The other report was about a teenage girl reportedly stabbing a man.
It's possible the August 2026 headlines were being misrepresented in social media posts that became an instance of copypasta — a copied-and-pasted piece of text meant to spur further shares — as users began to spread it online.
Snopes recently debunked another Detroit-related claim investigating the false claim that Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed ran a "dog slaughterhouse" in the city.

How 'Book Queen' Dolly Parton inspired millions of children with gift of reading
- Published
One child in Denver called her "The Book Queen".
Another in Alabama calls her "Ms Dolly".
Across the globe in Australia, a toddler with speech delays delighted her family with her first word - "orange" - after she and her twin sister received a free book in the post about colours. It came from Imagination Library, the literacy programme begun by late global superstar Dolly Parton.
Parton, who died this week aged 80, launched the philanthropic effort in 1995 to honour her father - whose difficult Appalachian upbringing never allowed him to finish school or learn to read and write.
"He was the smartest man I have ever known, but I know in my heart his inability to read probably kept him from fulfilling all of his dreams," wrote Parton in an open letter on Imagination Library's website.
"Inspiring kids to love to read became my mission."
Imagination Library sends one free book a month to children from birth to age five. It first launched in Tennessee's Sevier County, where Parton grew up, before expanding across the US in 2000. The programme, which partners with local organisations, launched in Canada in 2006, the UK the following year, then Australia in 2013 and Ireland in 2019.
By 2025, as Imagination Library celebrated its 30th anniversary, it had distributed more than 300m books - equating to one book mailed every 78 seconds, according to the organisation.
And for the families in receipt of the storybooks, the impact has been invaluable.

  - Published16 hours ago
"It just blows my mind that it's readily available for every family that lives in my borough," said London mother-of-two Harriet Anscombe, whose four-year-old daughter has been receiving Imagination Library books since she was three months old.
The free books helped Anscombe establish a reading-focused nighttime routine.
"I think that, if I didn't get those books, maybe I wouldn't have started doing bedtime stories till she was two - but because we were getting them so early, it embedded story time into our routine from when she was just a couple of months old," Anscombe said. "She probably doesn't remember a time when we weren't reading stories."
Imagination Library became part of the family routine for Ciara Fernandez Faber, too, after she signed up her son about eight years ago in Colorado. His favourite book for years was one written by Parton herself: I Am A Rainbow.
"We read it almost every night, and I never got tired of reading it to him," said Faber, 42.
"It's a book about different emotions, and so we would act out the different emotions, the different faces," she said. "At the back of the book, there's a little excerpt by Dolly talking about how everybody has a rainbow of feelings, and we would read that - and he would always point to her picture and say, 'There's the Book Queen.'"
Families like Faber's repeatedly remarked on how well curated the books were - detailing how topics helped their children not just with reading, but also with social and emotional development.
"There were themes that were addressed in a lot of the books that would have really helped us navigate issues," said Helen Cashell, of Dublin, Ireland.
She signed up both of her children, now aged seven and five, for the scheme. "Whether it was same-sex families or just different types of families, things about bravery, courage, bullying, things about different identities."
Author Selina Brown, whose book My Rice Is Best was selected for distribution through Imagination Library, noted how the plotline features a black protagonist.
The programme also helps promote authors like herself; because of the selection, it "means 14,000 copies of my book have been sent to children in the UK".
"To choose between gas, electric, food or a book, you're going to choose a core need - but with the Dolly Parton Imagination Library, you don't have to do that," she said.
In inner-city Sydney, Australia, first-time mum Paige Stewart was astounded as she watched her children's progress with the programme.
Her twin girls, now four, "had a speech delay and some learning difficulties" - but Stewart noticed a change after just the second book.
"Not only did they learn their colours from that book… it kind of set the tone for them speaking and their joy for books."
She's become a vocal advocate for the programme, telling others: "It's so helpful, honestly."
Alabama grandmother Kristina Hadley also promotes the programme to friends and family - even incorporating Imagination Library into baby gifts.
"I'll pull up the Imagination books website, and I'll print that, and I'll put it in a picture frame, and I'll get little newborn books and stuff like that, and I'll put it with that for like a suggestion for new mothers," said Hadley, 53.
She signed up her nearly three-year-old granddaughter, Eillie Elaine, "before she was actually born". Now the child has her own bookshelf in their shared household - "and one whole shelf is for her Dolly books".
"She likes to go to go to the mailbox, and she's like, 'Ms Dolly! Ms Dolly!' and I'm like, 'Well, let's go see if Ms Dolly sent you a book!'"
A lifelong Parton fan, Hadley chokes up while detailing how she was at work when a friend texted to say the singer had died.
Imagination Library, she says, "is going to keep her memory going with the younger generation, and I hope and I pray that this is something that goes on for years and years and years."
It's a legacy that Parton built quietly in the background as she presided over pop culture for more than six decades.
"The biggest thing that I like is the fact that she didn't do anything for recognition," said Geoff Blacklin, 67, of Manitoba, Canada.
He and his wife signed up their grandchildren for Imagination Library after a local doctor brought the programme to their region.
"She gave families more than books," Blacklin said. "She gave children a love of reading, precious moments with loved ones, and opportunities to learn and dream."
Such family stories and gratitude would undoubtedly have been music to Parton's ears; the expansion of the programme was truly a realisation of her own dream.
"In the beginning, my hope was simply to inspire the children in my home county, but here we are today with a worldwide programme that gives a book a month to well over 3 million children," she wrote on the Imagination Library site - also taking care to thank the partners "who have embraced my dream and made it their own".
At the centre of it, always, was her love for children - and her love for her father.
"Before he passed away, my Daddy told me the Imagination Library was probably the most important thing I had ever done," Parton wrote.
"I can't tell you how much that meant to me, because I created the Imagination Library as a tribute to my Daddy."

Thank you for joining us for our continuing coverage of the aftermath of Wednesday’s catastrophic flash floods in the Himalayan mountains near the Nepal-Tibet border.
Poor weather has hampered aerial rescue operations in Nepal as the search for thousands of people missing enters its fourth day.
Nepal’s finance minister says his country will need up to $5bn to rebuild after the floods, believed to have been caused by a melting glacier high up in the mountains that set off a deadly cascade of water into the valleys below.
Finance minister Swarnim Wagle told Reuters today those figures are “just an estimate” and that “loss and damage is being assessed”.
Here’s a summary of what we know so far:
Nearly 3,000 people are missing. Nepal’s disaster agency on Saturday said 2,426 people were missing on its side of the border, while China’s Xinhua news agency reports the total number of missing in Tibet is now 554.
The death toll in Nepal has now risen to 626, while China’s Xinhua news agency earlier today reported seven people confirmed dead in Tibet.
More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far but at least 93,000 people are estimated to have been affected by the disaster, according to the Red Cross.
At least 777 foreigners are missing, with Nepal’s disaster agency on Friday reporting 517 foreigners unaccounted for – which could include tourists and foreign workers – and Chinese officials putting the number of foreigners missing at 260.
India said it is increasing surveillance of glaciers and glacial lakes in its Himalayan regions bordering Nepal and China.
The deadly floods on the Nepal-Tibet border were believed to have been triggered by a glacial collapse that was detected as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event by geologists. You can read this explainer to find out more about how a collapsing glacier can generate a powerful flood, and whether the climate crisis is contributing to the risk.
Madan Kaushik, state disaster management minister in India’s Himalayan state of Uttarakhand, said: “Since we share a border with Nepal, as a neighbour, and also have a similar geographic situation … we have asked our department to monitor all the glaciers and known glacial lakes in the region.”
Uttarakhand is one of the most ecologically sensitive regions of India, with 1,266 glacial lakes. As glaciers melt, water can accumulate in lakes held back by natural barriers. If those barriers fail, vast volumes of water can be released suddenly, triggering devastating floods.
“We have asked our teams to be vigilant and monitor if a similar situation is emerging anywhere in the state,” Kaushik told AFP.
‘The flood took everything I have’: survivors grieve for relatives and homes swept away in Nepal
The Guardian’s south Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen and journalist Gaurav Pokharel report from the Nepalese town of Bidur, where rescue efforts are being coordinated. They spoke to survivors mourning loved ones and confronting the loss of their homes and livelihoods after devastating floods swept through their communities.
Among those caught in the floods was Sangke Dolma Tamang, who described the moment she watched her husband being swept away and returned to find her home and village destroyed:
Sangke Dolma Tamang, 61, had been cheerily cooking snacks in her village of Mailung in the Rasuwa district when the floods came without warning. The whole family ran uphill for safety, but as she grabbed for her husband, he slipped from her grip and was washed into the dark, fast-moving waters.
“Others tried to pull him to safety, but the flood swept him away,” she said, tears rolling down her weathered cheeks. There was, she said, nothing left of her village now. She had spent a night sheltering on higher ground, until an army helicopter arrived and brought to her safety at the barracks. Her son too was missing since the disaster, and she waited anxiously for any news.
“Now I have nothing left to live for,” said Tamang. “The whole house is gone. We couldn’t salvage anything.”
Nepal’s government has appealed for financial help as it faces the daunting task of recovering from the devastating flash floods and braces for the possibility of more flooding.
Entire communities have been swept away, leaving families homeless or sheltering in temporary facilities.
“Multiple bridges have been washed away and major roads disrupted, leaving some of the worst-affected communities extremely difficult to reach,” the Red Cross says.
At least 18 schools have been destroyed and another 20 damaged, leaving about 10,000 school-age children affected, according to the UN Children’s Fund.
The disaster comes just ahead of the anniversary of last year’s 8-9 September mass anti-corruption protests that toppled the government.
Nepal is now led by prime minister Balendra Shah, a 36-year-old rapper turned politician widely known as “Balen”. The former Kathmandu mayor swept March elections on a wave of euphoria calling for political change.
The risk of a lake formed after the glacier collapse bursting near the China-Nepal border where the devastating flood occurred earlier this week has decreased, Chinese authorities said today, as its size appears to have shrunk.
Satellite images from Thursday this morning suggest water in the lake – straddling the China-Nepal border at the confluence of two rivers – has been slowly flowing through, decreasing the reservoir gradually, state broadcaster CCTV reported, citing the water resources ministry.
The ministry said satellite imagery of the surface area of the lake at Purepu Tsangpo river showed it was 99,000 sq metres in size this morning – around the size of 14 football fields combined – having shrunk by 21,000 sq metres compared with images from Thursday.
Experts and authorities have warned of the extremely high risk of secondary disasters in the valley, especially from the lake that was formed by glacier debris, potentially endangering rescue operations downstream.
State-owned engineering and rescue enterprise China Anneng, which has been monitoring the lake since Thursday, dispatched a 15-member team on Friday with reconnaissance drones, portable satellite stations and mobile surveillance cameras to gather more data about the lake.
An overflow from the lake on Friday temporarily halted rescue work before further assessment deemed the risks manageable.

Worldwide, traditional medicine is used by billions of people for their health and well-being. At a signing ceremony in Geneva, the Government of India committed US$ 85 million over 10 years, 2022–2032, to support the programming of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre. India’s 10-year financial contribution will support a cross-sectoral program of work to strengthen the evidence base for traditional medicine by providing data and evidence on traditional medicine policies, practice, products, and public use.
The WHO-India donor agreement is part of a US$ 250 million investment from India in support of the establishment of the WHO Global Centre of Traditional Medicine in 2022, which includes financial support for the workplan of the Centre, interim premises and a new building. This support will scale up WHO’s capacities on traditional medicine across technical divisions and regions in the spirit of global collaboration and solidarity. Part of this substantial contribution from the Government of India will also be included in WHO’s Investment Round to resource WHO’s core work during 2025–2028.
Photo: WHO/Lindsay Mackenzie
“India’s commitment and leadership in expanding the evidence-based contribution of traditional medicine to the health and well-being of all people and the planet, comes at an opportune moment,” said Dr Bruce Aylward, Assistant Director-General of the Universal Health Coverage and Life Course division of WHO. “Traditional medicine, supported within national health systems, can allow us to reach those most often left behind. Integration of traditional practice and knowledge is critical to achieving health for all.”
“The signing of this donor agreement is a major milestone towards achieving the shared vision of Honourable Prime Minister of India Shri Narendra Modi and WHO Director-General Tedros for the development of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre at Jamnagar in India,” said Vice Minister Vaidya Rajesh Kotecha, Secretary of the Ministry of Ayush, Government of India.
“India remains committed to supporting WHO in its work to strengthen traditional medicine systems globally for achieving universal health coverage and serving the entire humanity, especially through this Global Centre in Jamnagar, which would help focus these efforts to benefit all Member States,” said Ambassador Arindam Bagchi, Permanent Representative of India to the UN and other International Organizations in Geneva.
The WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre is is a knowledge hub focusing on five inter-connected areas of work: research and evidence; primary health care and universal health coverage; Indigenous Knowledges and biodiversity; digital health applications; and the biennial WHO Global Traditional Medicine Summit and collaborations. The Centre is led by Dr Shyama Kuruvilla, Director a.i.
The first WHO traditional medicine global summit was held in August 2023 in Gujarat, resulting in the a multistakeholder action agenda, the Gujarat Declaration. The next WHO Global Summit is planned for November 2025, following up on the anticipated launch of the 2025–2034 Global Strategy for Traditional Medicine at the 78th World Health Assembly in May 2025.
India’s support for traditional medicine has been expressed through a variety of long-standing partnerships with WHO. In 2023, India signed a five-year agreement to support the technical work of WHO’s Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCI) unit. The unit is supporting the development of the Member State-requested new WHO traditional medicine global strategy (2025 - 2034), and publishes key benchmark documents, standardized terminologies, and other evidence-informed technical products to support the safe and effective integration of traditional medicine in national health systems.  
The Centre and TCI collaborate closely with teams across WHO to advance WHO’s multisectoral agenda on traditional medicine, including through regular meetings of the WHO Technical Expert Network, coordinated by the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre and TCI, to promote a One WHO approach on traditional medicine across headquarters, regional and country office.

South Africa accuses Israel of violating ICJ's legally binding provisional measures
South Africa has accused Israel of breaking legally binding orders issued by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) intended to protect Palestinians in Gaza, while calling on the international community "to take all necessary action to prevent and punish genocide".
In a statement issued by the Department of International Relations and Cooperation (DIRCO), Pretoria said that Israel has refused to comply with three separate provisional measure orders issued by the ICJ. This refusal "undermines their protective function and entails further destruction of the Palestinian group", the statement says.
"The Provisional Measures were not only ordered to protect the rights of the Palestinian people under the Genocide Convention, they also safeguard the administration of justice and the legitimacy of the ICJ itself, by ensuring that the rights the Court is called upon to vindicate are not destroyed before it renders its final decision."
The statement added: "The Court’s orders are binding on Israel, and the international community also has an obligation to protect the Palestinian people from genocide, including to take all necessary action to prevent and punish genocide."
Earlier this week, the South African government submitted a dossier of evidence to a dedicated committee of judges tasked with monitoring the court’s provisional measures.

Issued in 2024, the three provisional orders issued by the ICJ against Israel include the prevention of genocidal acts and incitement, ceasing military operations in Rafah and providing immediate access for Palestinians to humanitarian assistance and basic services in the Gaza Strip.
The provisional orders also mandated Israel to submit formal reports to the court detailing steps it has taken to comply, which it did in February 2024.
Under Article 11 of the ICJ’s Internal Judicial Practice, the committee examines information supplied by parties and recommends potential options to the broader court.
The South African government emphasised that the measures "safeguard the administration of justice and the legitimacy of the ICJ itself, by ensuring that the rights the Court is called upon to vindicate are not destroyed before it renders its final decision".
Pretoria’s dossier highlights the ongoing humanitarian catastrophe unfolding in Gaza, noting that as of August 2026, at least 73,407 Palestinians have been killed and 174,335 others wounded since 7 October 2023, representing more than 10 percent of Gaza’s entire population.
Among the survivors, an estimated 46,000 Palestinians, including children, are living with severe conflict-related conditions such as amputations and traumatic brain and spinal cord injuries.
The submission also notes that since the announcement of a ceasefire, the Israeli military has continued to kill an average of one Palestinian child every day and that the trauma and unbearable living conditions in Gaza's ever-shrinking territorial enclaves have caused Palestinian miscarriage rates to increase more than three-fold in 2026.
Palestinian rights organisation Al-Haq has welcomed South Africa’s submission to the ICJ documenting Israel’s non-compliance with the provisional orders.
"As the genocide continues, we call on the Court to act propio motu, including through additional Provisional Measures Orders," the organisation said.
Erasing the record
South Africa’s government emphasised that the ICJ’s orders are strictly binding and that the international community bears a collective obligation to take all necessary action to prevent and punish genocide.
"For almost three years, Israel has bombarded Gaza, killing and maiming tens of thousands of children, men and women," the DIRCO statement reads.
It noted that Israeli forces have arbitrarily detained and deported Palestinians to prisons and detention centres where they face torture, sexual and gender-based violence, and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment.
Pretoria also accused Israel of actively attempting to suppress evidence of its crimes by killing local journalists, barring foreign media and preventing UN-mandated investigative bodies from entering the besieged territory.
South Africa made history as the first country to formally file a genocide case against Israel at the ICJ in December 2023.
The August 2026 dossier is the latest in a sustained legal and diplomatic campaign by South Africa to seek Israel's full and immediate compliance on the global stage.
Pretoria previously submitted extensive public dossiers of evidence to the United Nations Security Council in May 2024, February 2025 and September 2025, urging member states to urgently act to prevent and punish genocide.
Similar dossiers focusing on the deliberate use of starvation were submitted to the UN General Assembly and the UN Economic and Social Council in October 2025, requesting urgent intervention under Article VIII of the Genocide Convention.

Lionel Messi produced one of the most spectacular individual displays of his Major League Soccer career on Saturday, scoring four times as Inter Miami dismantled CF Montreal 7-1 to end a five-match winless streak across all competitions.
It was the first time Messi had scored four goals in a single MLS game, with the 39-year-old also setting up another goal. His performance moved him to the top of the league’s scoring charts, with 18 goals this season.
Messi’s first goal of the night came just before half-time to restore Miami’s lead. He struck again in the 52nd minute before completing his hat-trick in the 83rd. The Argentina captain then saved his most eye-catching moment for stoppage time, curling home a free kick to complete the rout.
Inter Miami’s interim coach Guillermo Hoyos struggled to find words to capture Messi’s performance.
“There are no words to describe such footballing beauty,” Hoyos, an Argentine, said. “So much is going on that words simply fall short.

‘Trying to reach a safe location’: Missing UK couple's last message from flood-hit Nepal
The UK-based couple with Kolkata roots were in Nepal for Kailash yatra when the floods struck, leaving them out of contact with their family.
A UK-based Indian-origin couple with roots in West Bengal’s Kolkata have gone missing during a Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage through flood-hit Nepal, with the family holding on to a haunting last message from them.
Anal Kar is a chemical engineer, while his wife, Sanjukta Kar, is a teacher. They moved to the United Kingdom in 2001 and live there with their two children. The couple, fond of travelling with the Himalayas holding a special place for them, had undertaken another Himalayan trek a few months ago.
Track live updates on Nepal floods
Anal and Sanjukta reached Kathmandu on August 18 after meeting relatives in Kolkata. They were last traced to Timure near the Nepal-Tibet border, according to news agency PTI. The couple were travelling to Kailash Mansarovar when they went missing.
Deep Dive
The family last heard from them on August 26. Sanjukta sent photographs from the trip to her father, Ranjit Dutta, over WhatsApp on the night of August 25. The couple were scheduled to leave around 6 am the following morning to complete immigration formalities at the Nepal-Tibet border.

“My daughter had contacted me over WhatsApp on the night of August 25. They were scheduled to leave at around 6 am on August 26 for immigration formalities. Sanjukta had also sent several photographs from their trip,” Dutta was quoted as saying.
The final message
Ranjit Dutta said that Sanjukta sent her final message to a WhatsApp group of friends at around 8 am on August 26.
“She wrote that a landslide alert had been issued in the area and that they were trying to reach a safe location on foot as quickly as possible. After that, we have not been able to contact them in any way,” he said.
The family trying to trace the couple
The family contacted the travel agency handling the trip, but it could not provide any information about the couple’s location or condition.
Sanjukta’s aunt said the family approached the police the following day. A police team from Bhawani Bhavan subsequently visited their home and collected the necessary information.

Sumana* was an energetic child until she turned 11. Then she began complaining of tiredness, could no longer play as she previously used to, and fell ill frequently. Her appetite declined, and a paediatrician advised investigations.
A blood test that her parents thought was routine revealed the possibility of leukaemia.
It took her mother, Varalakshmi*, several months to come to terms with the diagnosis. By then, nearly a year had passed. Sumana had become increasingly weak and listless. When treatment intensified, she had to drop out of class 9. A year later, however, after the completion of her treatment, she was ready to return to school. Today, Sumana is a schoolteacher. She married a year ago, bringing immense happiness to her parents.
Sumana was fortunate. She lived in a metropolitan city with access to specialised healthcare; her parents ensured she completed treatment, and their financial circumstances enabled them to support her. She also had leukaemia, one of the most common and highly treatable childhood cancers.
Not every child is as fortunate.
Childhood cancer burden in India
India, home to about 380 million children below the age of 14, accounted for the largest share of childhood cancers in the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) region, according to a new study published in The Lancet Regional Health Southeast Asia. The study,, estimates 37,716 new childhood cancer cases and 17,698 deaths annually across the region in 2022. India accounted for 25,939 new cases, or 68.6% of the regional total.
“Leukaemia was the most common cancer in all countries (35–50%), followed by central nervous system (CNS) tumours (approximately 12% of cases),” the study states.
GLOBOCAN 2022, produced by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), combines cancer-registry data and vital statistics with region-based modelling where registry coverage is partial or absent. The estimates, therefore, may not represent every case diagnosed in India.
Gaps in data
Oncologists say better reporting has increased the number of cases being identified as healthcare expands, but substantial gaps in cancer registration—particularly in rural areas—mean many cases may still go unrecorded.
Venkatraman Radhakrishnan, professor of paediatric oncology at the Cancer Institute, WIA, Chennai, and one of the study’s authors, points to earlier estimates by Ramandeep Singh Arora, published in Indian Pediatrics. Based on the 2011 Census, that study estimated that 52,366 children aged 0–14 and 76,805 children and adolescents aged 0–19 could develop cancer every year.
Narendra Agarwal, senior haematologist and transplant physician and head of the haematology unit at Rajiv Gandhi Cancer Institute and Research Centre, New Delhi, says the higher reported numbers may partly reflect better reporting as the country’s healthcare system expands.
“We are still struggling with the expansion of our healthcare systems. It is possible that the incidence per 100,000 population may genuinely be higher in some parts of India compared with other parts of the world, but there is no strong data to establish this,” he says, adding: “Facilities are expanding rapidly, which is one reason why more patients are now being treated and more cases are being reported.”
Many cancers are curable
The good news is that many childhood cancers have excellent cure rates, given early diagnosis and prompt, comprehensive treatment.
For leukaemia, cure rates can reach 80–90% in many children, Dr. Agarwal says. “Most of these children can lead a near-normal life after treatment.” About 10–15% may experience a relapse after completing treatment, while some may develop long-term effects, including problems with growth and persistent aches and pains.
The challenge, therefore, is not simply whether India knows how to treat childhood cancer. It is whether every child who needs treatment can reach it and complete it.
Why are cure rates uneven in India?
Despite the fact that the prognosis for many childhood cancers is good, cure rates continue to remain uneven in India. According to the World Health Organization, in high-income countries, where comprehensive services are generally accessible, more than 80% of children with cancer are cured. In most low- and middle-income countries, less than 30% are cured
Delayed diagnosis, advanced-stage presentation, treatment abandonment due to financial constraints, infections, malnutrition and limited access to specialised paediatric oncology services, all complicate cure and survival rates.
The Central government’s Ayushman Bharat scheme provides health cover of up to ₹5 lakh per family. Initial standard treatment in government hospitals is either free or heavily subsidised, while NGOs sometimes help bridge gaps in treatment costs at corporate hospitals, says Dr. Radhakrishnan. But costs can rise sharply if treatment fails or the cancer relapses.
“If the initial treatment fails or the child experiences a relapse, treatment is usually more expensive because some of the drugs used are costly,” says Dr. Agarwal.
Private treatment can also be expensive, not necessarily because of the drugs, but because of investigations, hospitalisation and other charges. For families required to sustain treatment over a prolonged period, the financial burden can result in treatment abandonment.
India does not yet know the full picture
One of the biggest gaps in childhood cancer care in India, points out Arvind Krishnamurthy, deputy medical director at Cancer Institute, WIA., is the absence of a cancer registry covering the entire population.
“This is not unique to childhood cancer. Registry coverage is around 15% of the population, and figures for the rest of the country are extrapolated based on those populations. Coverage is particularly limited in rural areas. Most cancer registries predominantly capture urban populations,” he says.
This makes it difficult to determine where childhood cancer occurs most frequently and whether apparent regional hotspots reflect genuinely higher incidence or simply better reporting. Dr. Agarwal says a national registry could help identify such geographical patterns. A comprehensive registry should record not just diagnosis but also the child’s geographical origin, staging, treatment and outcome, he notes.
At present, 17 of the 36 States and UTs in India have so far notified cancer as a notifiable disease in light of the recommendations made in a parliamentary standing committee report. The Supreme Court, August 11, 2026, directed the other 19 States and Union Territories to declare cancer a notifiable disease as well.
Apart from the numbers a registry would help immensely with other research into cancer, for instance, whether socioeconomic and environmental factors influence childhood cancer: Dr. Agarwal says children from poorer socioeconomic backgrounds may have a somewhat higher risk of certain blood cancers, partly because of greater exposure to infections. .
At present, Dr. Radhakrishnan is leading a paediatric registry effort at the Cancer Institute, WIA, but says the government must encourage hospitals to share data.
What’s ahead for India
India’s cancer treatment infrastructure is expanding rapidly. Almost every State now has a government-sponsored Regional Cancer Centre, while Tata Memorial Hospital-linked centres and oncology departments at AIIMS institutions have expanded access to specialised care.
The country therefore has much of the clinical expertise needed to treat childhood cancers. The challenge now remains in ensuring that children are diagnosed early, reach specialised centres, receive financial and social support, and complete treatment.
“Improving early diagnosis, access to specialised treatment, supportive care and ensuring that children complete their treatment will be important in improving survival rates,” says Dr. Krishnamurthy.
For children like Sumana, such interventions can mean the difference between a diagnosis that ends a childhood—and one that becomes only a chapter in a long life.

British Arabs urge UK government to impose binding restrictions on Israeli settlements
Dozens of prominent British Arabs have called on the UK government to move beyond condemning illegal Israeli settlements and put legally binding rules in place to stop British economic activity from supporting their expansion.
In a joint letter to Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, dated 24 August 2026, the signatories call on the government to act on the obligations it already recognises, "particularly the duties of non-recognition, non-assistance and differentiation between Israel and the Palestinian territory occupied since 1967."
The real question is no longer whether the Israeli settlements are unlawful, the letter says.
Rather, it is whether the UK's present combination of “voluntary guidance, tariff differentiation and targeted sanctions is sufficient in practice” to meet the country's legal obligations, including the duty identified by the ICJ to prevent trade or investment that helps sustain the settlements.
The letter calls on UK ministers to use the powers already available, together with other countries, to immediately stop British money or business from helping Israeli settlements grow.

The signatories include prominent figures from the British-Arab world such as Adnan Hmidan, chairman of the Palestinian Forum in Britain; Sabah Almukhtar, president of the Arab Lawyers Association in the UK; Dr Omar Abdel-Mannan, president of Health Workers 4 Palestine; Feda Shahin, secretary general of the Palestine Solidarity Movement; and many others from various sectors.
Mechanism to stop settler violence
Among the measures requested in the letter are binding restrictions on UK economic activity that benefits settlements, extending sanctions to individuals as well as companies, applying full differentiation across government procurement and public dealings, and working with international partners to prevent circumvention via third-country structures.
The letter notes that the Sanctions and Anti-Money Laundering Act 2018 already gives the government a domestic legal basis for such measures.
It also points to the UK's 2016 vote in favour of a UN Security Council resolution which found Israeli settlements to have "no legal validity", and to the ICJ's advisory opinion of July 2024, which ruled Israel's presence in the occupied territories unlawful and said all settlement activity must stop immediately.
Alongside the economic measures, the letter calls on the government to work with international partners to establish a mechanism to protect Palestinian civilians from settler violence, citing a 1994 UN resolution the UK itself co-sponsored.
Such a mechanism would include independent monitoring, documentation of violence and displacement, and protection for communities most at risk, the letter says.
"This is not a request for hostility towards Israel or Israeli citizens, nor for indiscriminate restrictions on lawful trade with Israel," it adds.
"Britain's commitment to the international rule of law should be demonstrated not only through statements of principle, but through consistent and effective implementation."
The joint letter remains open for additional signatures.
The UK government said earlier this month that it will announce new measures against Israel over settlement construction east of Jerusalem that could effectively split the occupied West Bank in two, thus threatening a two-state solution.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband criticised the E1 settlement plan, saying it poses a threat to a two-state solution and that he had told Israel to stop all settlement expansion.
He said Britain would set out broader measures in the coming weeks.

Meta Platforms and state attorneys general have discussed a potential mid-trial settlement of a lawsuit accusing the company of deliberately designing Facebook and Instagram to be addictive to young users, Bloomberg News reported on Tuesday, citing people familiar with the matter.
The report comes during a federal court trial in California over claims brought by 29 states, in what is one of the highest-profile tests of allegations that social media companies have harmed young users. Just days before jury selection began on August 12, a federal appeals court declined to halt the trial.
Meta and the attorneys general of California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey did not immediately respond to requests for comment outside of regular business hours.
Late Tuesday, several state attorneys general put out advisories notifying the media of plans for press conferences, including Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford, whose office said it planned to announce “a major consumer protection settlement involving a leading technology company.”
The claims are part of a broader wave of litigation brought by states, local governments, school districts and individuals alleging that Meta and other social media companies fueled a nationwide youth mental health crisis.
The federal court trial covered claims from the attorneys general of Colorado, California, Kentucky and New Jersey that Meta violated their state laws protecting consumers.
The trial also covered claims from 29 states that Meta violated the federal Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act by collecting personal data from users it knew were children without parental notification or consent and using the data to train machine learning and generative AI models.
Meta has denied the allegations, saying it has worked hard to protect children on its platforms. The company had argued it could not have misled consumers about whether its services were addictive because “social media addiction” is not a recognised psychiatric condition.
