Whenever a major music star passes away, people around the world head to streaming platforms like Spotify and Apple Music, as well as download sites such as iTunes, to mourn the loss and show their support by streaming and buying songs and albums from the late superstar. Sometimes all that attention is focused around one or two tracks that defined a career, while at other times, multiple releases connected to one recently lost talent become bestsellers at once.
Only a few days ago, Dolly Parton’s death rocked the world, as it came as a complete surprise to millions. The country legend’s catalog is far too vast for only a handful of titles to become quick top performers on download websites, but fan attention in the United Kingdom has largely centered around several collections. The biggest of the bunch, at least in the earliest days following Parton’s death, is The Very Best Of. The compilation returns to multiple rankings across the Atlantic and even scores the singer-songwriter her first leader on one tally.
Dolly Parton Scores Her First No. 1
The Very Best Of reenters the Official Album Downloads chart at No. 1. The ranking focuses only on the bestselling albums and EPs purchased on download platforms throughout the United Kingdom. As her compilation returns, Parton reaches the summit for the first time in her career.
The Very Best Of Had Never Even Reached the Top 10
Amazingly, The Very Best Of had never broken into the top 10 on the Official Album Downloads ranking before this week. The last time the compilation was seen on the roster was in February, when it climbed to No. 24 – only a few spaces beneath what was then its No. 21 career high – before disappearing again. Following Parton’s death, the collection rockets all the way to first place with only a few days of solid tracking activity behind its ascent.
Dolly Parton Nearly Ruled With Rockstar
Parton had come close to conquering the Official Album Downloads tally in the past, but never quite made it. Rockstar, her first full-length devoted to rock music, peaked at No. 2. Parton has accumulated just five top 10s on the ranking, with Blue Smoke – The Best Of, Pure & Simple and The Complete Trio Collection – the latter alongside Linda Ronstadt and Emmylou Harris – rising as high as Nos. 7, 8 and 10, respectively. Another release, A Holly Dolly Christmas, missed the highest tier by only one rung.
Dolly Parton Returns to No. 1 on a Country Chart As Well
The Very Best Of also reenters the Official Country Compilations chart at No. 1. The collection has now spent an incredible 426 weeks somewhere on the genre-specific roster, and 118 of those frames have been at the summit. That enormous figure includes the compilation’s first 16 weeks on the tally, beginning in the spring of 2007.
The Very Best Of Returns to Five Charts
The Very Best Of returns to all five U.K. rankings on which it appears at the moment. In addition to leading the Official Album Downloads and Official Country Compilations charts, the compilation reaches a new high of No. 12 on the Official Albums Sales roster. The project also reenters the Official Albums chart at No. 46 and the Official Physical Albums tally at No. 73.

Lake Ontario, Always: Canada hits back at Trump’s Lake America order with giant sign
Doug Ford unveiled a giant billboard along the Canadian shore bearing the message ‘Lake Ontario. Now and Always’
Canadian figures have met President Donald Trump’s command to rename Lake Ontario as "Lake America" with ridicule rather than anger.
On Saturday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford responded by unveiling a giant billboard along the Canadian shore bearing the message: "Lake Ontario. Now and Always".
Wearing a Team Canada soccer jersey, Ford posed for photos beside the structure near Grimsby, Ontario. Measuring 24 by 12 feet (7.3 by 3.6 metres), the display rests on 6-foot (1.8-metre) legs, reaching roughly 18 feet (5.5 metres) high — about two storeys tall. The text is duplicated in French.
The action follows an executive order directing US federal agencies to adopt the name "Lake America." It comes after months of tariffs, threats to make Canada the 51st US state, and personal attacks on its leaders, triggering a mixture of defiance and humour.
Ford noted that Trump sought the change because Ontario and Canada were "standing up for ourselves", declaring the original name would outlast the president.
“Long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario,” Ford said in a video posted on social media.
Canadians mock Trump
Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew compared Trump to an aging rock band trying to revive an old hit
“You know when a rock band is really over the hill and you see them like in a casino playing some song from like 50 years ago. I think that’s the part of Donald Trump’s presidency we’re at now, Like he thought they had a real hit, a real golden oldie, with the Gulf of Mexico,” Kinew said, referring to Trump's executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America. “And he’s trying to bring back that, and he’s trying to play the hits for his base. But I think everybody here thinks it’s a little sad and it’s not his best work.”
The mockery was not limited to politicians. Canadian historian Robert Bothwell was even more scathing.
“The greatest country on earth takes this moron seriously?” Bothwell said.
But Bothwell said the dispute was more serious than the jokes, arguing Trump’s broader aim was “to subordinate Canada and at best make it a colony, at worst absorb it into the United States.”
Nelson Wiseman, professor emeritus at the University of Toronto, said Trump “would like Canada to act like a vassal state, but it refuses to do so. That irritates him.”
Canada and the US trade barbs over collapsed talks
The dispute comes as relations between the longtime allies worsen over trade. Negotiations collapsed last week, both governments accused the other of making late demands, and Canada announced retaliatory tariffs set to take effect next month.
Trump’s order also came amid an escalating war of words with Ford. In an interview with The Associated Press earlier this week, Ford said Ronald Reagan would be “throwing up” over Trump’s tariff policies and “disgusted with President Trump.”
Trump fired back by dismissing Ford’s comments as “bluster,” calling him Prime Minister Mark Carney’s “flunky” and mocking him as the “less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother” of the late Toronto Mayor Rob Ford.
Trump continued promoting the new name Saturday, reposting a meme showing Canada geese with Trump-like blond hair firing rifles as they “protected” Lake America.
Trump has repeatedly used maps to make political points. A “Gulf of America” map was displayed for a time beside the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office, and Trump has posted images depicting Canada as part of the United States or as the 51st state.
Ontario name has Indigenous origins
The name Lake Ontario comes from the Huron Indigenous people’s word “oniatarí:io,” which means “lake of shining waters.” The Canadian province of Ontario, founded in 1867, took its name from the lake.
Wendat Nation Grand Chief Pierre Picard, whose people historically lived from the St. Lawrence Valley to the Great Lakes and whose language gave Lake Ontario its name, called Trump’s move an attempt to erase Indigenous history.
“I want to tell him that it is unacceptable for us, as a nation, to have a president who can eradicate our history, our culture and our identity,” Picard said.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney rejected the move, noting the lake’s Indigenous roots and that the name predates both Canadian Confederation and the U.S. Declaration of Independence. Trump cannot require Canada to adopt the new name.

Assam approves ₹600cr proton beam therapy unit for cancer treatment: CM Sarma
“Assam will be the first state in the country to have a proton beam therapy unit in the public health care sector,” said CM Himanta Biswa Sarma
The Assam cabinet on Sunday approved purchase of a proton beam therapy unit for cancer treatment at a cost of ₹600 crore.
Chief minister Himanta Biswa Sarma said that once the unit is set up at Guwahati Medical College and Hospital (GMCH), Assam will be the first state in the country to have this facility in the public healthcare sector.
“Proton beam therapy is one of the most advanced form of treatments for cancer. World Bank will provide us a loan of ₹315 crore for this and state government would spend ₹285 crore,” he said.
“Assam will be the first state in the country to have a proton beam therapy unit in the public health care sector. At present the treatment is available at two private hospitals in Mumbai and Chennai, but no state-run hospitals have that facility till date,” Sarma added.
He informed that at present there are only around 40 proton beam therapy units across the world. The technique, which uses proton beams for advanced radiation treatment is more precision-based than existing methods and has less chances of damaged nearby healthy tissues.
“Assam will join an illustrious list of places where this advanced treatment will be available. Once this treatment starts, we are hopeful of not just treating patients in our state but also attract medical tourists,” said the CM.
Also Read:Cancer cases in Haryana up 11% in 5 years
The cabinet also approved expenditure of ₹50,000 crore for a period of seven years beginning 2027-28 in different sectors with the aim of transforming Assam into a developed state.
“This amount will be spent for various development works like giving ₹7 crore each to 1,000 high schools for upgradation of facilities, opening 6,000 new ‘anganwadi’ centres, setting up two women markets and a stadium in each constituency, new road network etc,” said Sarma.
“For this we will take a loan of ₹30,000 from NABARD (National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development) and spend ₹20,000 crore from state’s enhanced revenue collection,” he added.

The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier is set to make a temporary stop in Thailand next week as it heads back to the United States, Thai navy officials said, after spending more than 250 consecutive days at sea supporting US operations against Iran amid recent reports of poor living conditions and low morale onboard the vessel.
The Lincoln left the Middle East several days ago after being relieved by the USS George Washington, and is now heading home to San Diego. A Thai navy official told Reuters this week that the carrier was expected to make a brief port visit in Thailand next week for the crew to rest and recuperate before continuing their journey home.
“The stop is a routine port visit intended to allow personnel to rest and recuperate … as well as to receive logistical support,” the spokesperson for the Thai navy said.
Earlier this week, the Thai navy said that three ships from a US navy carrier strike group would be making a brief port call in eastern Thailand to allow personnel to rest. No military exercises would take place during the visit, the statement added. The Thai navy did not identify the vessels or provide a date.
The planned stop comes as the Lincoln’s deployment has faced scrutiny in recent weeks amid reports of poor living conditions onboard among its crew. Family members of sailors have described shortages of supplies and water, plumbing problems, low morale, and worsening mental health among the roughly 5,000 personnel on the carrier. The Navy Times also reported that there had been several attempts by sailors to jump overboard.
On Wednesday, the wife of a sailor who jumped overboard told MS Now that her husband, who she said had since returned to the US, was now facing disciplinary action from the navy.
Charging documents viewed by MS Now reportedly accuse the sailor of violating Article 83 for “malingering”, which is defined as someone who, “with the intent to avoid work, duty, or service”, fakes “illness, physical disablement, mental lapse, or mental derangement” or “intentionally inflicts self-injury”.
The document also reportedly accuses the sailor of violating Article 86 for “absence without leave” which is when the service member, without authority, “fails to go to his appointed place of duty at the time prescribed”, “goes from that place” or “absents himself or remains absent from his unit, organization, or place of duty at which he is required to be at the time prescribed”.
The couple, both 19, have a three-year-old son and welcomed a daughter in February while he was deployed. His wife told the outlet that he had requested paternity leave but was denied.
The sailor is now reportedly facing non-judicial punishment, which MS Now notes is typically used by commanding officers to address minor rule-breaking without a court martial.
In a statement to the Guardian on Friday, a navy official said “our first responsibility following this incident was the Sailor’s safety and well-being”.
“He was safely recovered, medically evacuated from the ship and evaluated by medical professionals,” they said. “He continues to have access to appropriate care and support.”
They added that “medical care and administrative or disciplinary processes are separate, and one does not preclude the other”, and “the command has the discretion to address misconduct based on the totality of the circumstances”.
“Because this involves an individual Sailor’s protected medical information and an ongoing personnel matter, we cannot discuss the specific evidence, medical care or ongoing proceedings,” the navy added.
The Lincoln left San Diego on 21 November bound for the Pacific, but was redirected to the Middle East. It has since spent more than 250 consecutive days without a significant port visit.
Reports about the conditions onboard have prompted several Democratic lawmakers to demand answers from the Pentagon.

Unprecedented scenes have unfolded at one of India’s most prestigious engineering institutions — the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Delhi — over the past week, following the death by suicide of an MSc student.
Classes have been largely called off, and students have been holding a sit-in where the student died last week. Never has the institute witnessed agitation and student mobilisation at this scale.
“Every death is followed by a copy-paste e-mail from the administration, following which the campus is almost immediately expected to go back to normal, even as memorials are held for those who died on the campus,” said a student who wished to remain anonymous.
On the boil
This “pent-up frustration”, the student added, blew up when students who had seen the 31-year-old’s body were called for classes soon after in the Lecture Hall Complex, the very spot where the death had occured. A comment from an administrative official that the student was “beyond repair” further angered the students.
The administration responded by setting up an external probe committee, which was reconstituted following objections from the protesters, and providing financial assistance to the family, though the amount has not been specified. The institute is yet to comment on allegations over the “insensitive remarks” following the student’s death.
On Thursday, IIT Delhi said the academic load had been lightened significantly since 2025, with lower credit loads in the first semester, smaller classes to minimise stress, fewer weekend exams and flexible credit distribution.
To this, an IIT-D student, who wished to stay anonymous, said, “The academic pressure is intense. Families don’t understand why we can’t give them time. Many of us have to pull all-nighters and function on one or two hours of sleep.”
Mental health support
On the institute’s assertion that students’ well-being is supported by a 24x7 team of counsellors and psychiatrists, fully reimbursed external care and a swift emergency protocol, students said counselling is inaccessible or ineffective. “There has been no monthly roster of counsellors in the past year,” said another student. In addition, the student said that parents are involved in such cases, raising privacy concerns.
A source at the institute countered this, saying the counselling centre is accessible and only minutes away from the hostels.

Farmers and their families are actively gathering ripe walnuts from traditional orchards, As the harvesting season starts in the hilly regions.
The farmers in the regions use through natural farming methodsopf cultivation, cleaning and sun-drying harvested walnuts for five to six days before being sold in the market. Local farmers regard walnut cultivation as not only an agricultural activity but also a vital source of income and the culmination of year-long efforts.
Madan Lal, a longtime horticulturist who owns around 100 walnut trees mainly of the Hamdan and Suleman varieties, reported an annual yield reaching up to 50,000 walnuts. He stated that walnut farming has been a crucial livelihood for nearly 30 years. Madan Lal added, “I draw great inspiration whenever Prime Minister Modi speaks about farmers and horticulture; the Prime Minister’s words regarding farmers and horticulture, shared through the ‘Mann Ki Baat’ program, have encouraged me to move forward.”
Another cultivator, Adil, described his anticipation for the harvest each year, saying, “They eagerly await the time when the walnuts ripen on the trees, and harvesting can begin.”
He said the post-harvest process, including thorough cleaning and sun-drying for about five to six days prior to market sale. Adil expressed pride in walnut cultivation, calling it “the fruit of a year’s hard work and a reflection of my deep connection to the land.”
As per District Horticulture Officer Mohammad Shakeel, approximately 3,000 families in the Bani area of Kathua rely significantly on walnut production for their livelihoods.
He noted that a single walnut sells for around ₹3 in the market, but it takes considerable time for a sapling to mature and bear fruit. “Once a tree reaches full productivity, it can generate an income of approximately ₹15,000 to ₹20,000 per season,” Shakeel said.
He further emphasised the considerable potential for walnut farming in the region and stated that the Horticulture Department is actively encouraging farmers and promoting the sector. For the past two years, the department has focused on the ‘Chandler’ walnut variety, which Shakeel described as a premium-quality type offering promising prospects for the area’s farmers.

A Palestinian woman and an NBC News team are reported to have been attacked and injured by masked Israeli settlers in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on Saturday, amid worsening confrontations in the area.
Benjamin Netanyahu said he condemned the violence committed “by a handful of rioters”.
The attack occurred when four members of the news team were interviewing Aida Ahmed Abdullah and her family in the Palestinian town of Jalud, near Nablus.
Abdullah told the outlet that they had been driven out of their home by settlers, and the team was walking down a hill toward the house.
A car with Israeli license plates reversed up the hill toward them. At least four men with their faces covered leapt from the vehicle, hitting them with sticks and throwing rocks.
“They jumped out, beat us, then jumped back in the car,” said NBC News correspondent Matt Bradley. Bradley was hit twice in the arm and treated at a nearby clinic.
Abdullah, 51, was taken for medical care by the Red Crescent. Her injuries were not life-threatening. Three other members of the news team were also injured and treated.
“Suddenly a car came to us,” said producer Lawahez Jabari. “The settlers had sticks, I saw a gun, but they didn’t use the gun.”
Camera operator Khaldoon Eid said the team had not expected to be attacked in a village.
Several violent incidents in the area were reported on Saturday. Palestinian workers were pepper-sprayed in nearby Qusra by masked Israeli settlers.
Israeli security forces told the outlet they had received reports that “violent clashes had occurred, including stone-hurling toward Palestinians and additional civilians”.
They said “security forces identified dozens of rioters who had barricaded themselves inside a Palestinian home while Palestinian residents were inside”, the statement said.
“The security forces who arrived at the scene initially operated to remove the rioters from the home and separate the groups, in order to protect the residents inside. In addition, the security forces confiscated vehicles belonging to the Israeli rioters that were suspected of having been used to reach the area,” the statement said.
“IDF soldiers and Israel Border Police forces continue to operate in the areas of Qusra and Jalud to prevent further disturbances and restore order in the area,” it added.
Earlier this month, a group of settlers began blocking supplies from entering Palestinian houses on the outskirts of the village near Nablus, trapping residents inside and drawing strong criticism from the US ambassador.
Israeli forces continue to operate in the area while settlers still roam the surrounding hills.
Netanyahu, whose government has been accused of turning a blind eye to the settler attacks, condemned the “criminal acts of violence” and blamed “a handful of rioters who violate the law, cause enormous injustice to the law-abiding settler public, hinder the IDF in fulfilling its missions and harm Israel’s standing in the world”.
According to the United Nations’ office for the coordination of humanitarian affairs, Israeli forces or settlers killed 76 Palestinians in the West Bank in the year to 24 July. Three Israelis were killed over the same period.

Following a controversial circular saying “women should not be present on public platforms”, Islamic scholar Kanthapuram A.P. Aboobacker Musliar on Sunday said women should remain confined to their homes.
The Kanthapuram faction of the Samastha Kerala Jamiyyathul Ulama, the State’s premier council of Sunni-Shafi Islamic scholars, last week said religious celebrations and programmes should remain within prescribed boundaries.
In a recent circular, Samastha Kerala Jamiyyathul Ulama president E. Sulaiman Musliar and general secretary Mr. Aboobacker directed that women should not share stages with men or appear in public spaces alongside them. The circular drew criticism, with several women political leaders speaking out against it.
Reason behind purdah
Speaking at an Islamic conference in Kochi on Sunday, Mr. Aboobacker said bringing women onto public platforms would lead to “great destruction” and claimed that Islam prescribed purdah for women to prevent this.
“It is precisely recognising that bringing women onto public platforms in this manner causes great destruction that Islam mandated purdah for women. The Holy Quran states that women should live confined within their homes and must not make public appearances,” he said.
Mr. Aboobacker said such views had been taught by knowledgeable religious scholars, particularly leaders of Samastha, for the past 100 years.
“Therefore, you must understand that it is because all knowledgeable people, especially the leaders of Samastha, taught this here for 100 years that the women in this country have maintained their honour and dignity,” he said.
He said religious scholars who had studied the religion had an obligation to speak on the issue and would continue to do so despite objections.
“When this is said, if leaders of any other organisation or Samastha leaders object to or question it, we have studied the religion and therefore have an obligation to say it. We will say it and continue to say it. No one can make us stop,” he said.

It was a normal July morning in the Indian state of Assam. After finishing her chores and eating breakfast, Gitali Phukon, a resident of the town of Gaurisagar, left her home to buy groceries. After two days of rainfall that had made the unpaved roads muddy and slippery, the sun was shining.
But less than an hour later, she returned home to a nightmare: the Mitong River, which runs through the town, was overflowing and water was gushing through the streets.
“I could not believe my eyes. The water came with great force. It quickly rose to waist level,” she says. She had seen the surrounding paddy fields flood in the past, but never before on this scale.
As evening approached, flood waters entered most of the homes in her neighbourhood. The rain resumed, and darkness descended. Standing on her veranda with a candlestick in her hand, Phukon watched as her neighbours moved to their rooftops or the elevated highway to escape the rising water.
They waved at each other, signalling they had survived. No one slept that night. “We feared we would all be drowned,” she says. Along with mosquito bites, they had endured a foul smell emanating from the flood waters.
The next morning, the situation worsened. Most villages in Assam depend on wells. “People were thirsty; they were crying for water. But there was no water to drink as the groundwater was contaminated,” says Phukon.
“Thankfully, I had some stored water, and I shared that with my neighbours,” says Phukon. People ate biscuits and puffed rice for at least three days until the water started to recede.
People in the Sivasagar district of Assam, as well the neighbouring districts of Charaideo and Jorhat on the southern bank of the mighty Brahmaputra River, reported similar experiences.
The Sivasagar village of Nepalikhuti, about 60 miles west of Gaurisagar, lies in ruins. As far as the eye can see, there is thick mud and silt. Drowned cars, dead cows and the broken walls of a house demonstrate the scale of the calamity. There is no sign of any cattle, goats or other livestock, the main means of support for the residents.
At least 10 people from the village of 3,000 people have died, and many remain missing. Villagers say they have seen several unidentified dead bodies floating on the Dikhou River.
Assam, in the far northeastern corner of India, is one of the most flood-prone regions in the country. About 40% of its land is vulnerable to inundation from the Brahmaputra and Barak rivers and other smaller rivers, and it sees at least two or three major floods annually.
According to official figures, about 2,690 villages in 25 districts have been flooded this year, affecting more than 1 million people. As of 11 August, 101 people have lost their lives. The death toll is likely to rise, officials fear.
In 2025, the death toll due to floods and landslides was 36. The year before, when all 35 districts of the state were affected by floods, at least 110 people died.
According to Partha Jyoti Das, a specialist in water and climate hazards with the environmental organisation Aaranyak, the current disaster was inevitable. The climate crisis has led to heavier rainfall, and changes to the landscape made flooding more likely.
“It’s a much-abused landscape, turning into a burial ground,” he says. Had it been just flood waters, the damage would have been less, but the rain brought with it debris, mud, silt and soil from the hills of Nagaland.
“These areas have seen mining and quarrying, both legal and illegal, for several years. From coal, sand or boulder mining, everything happens in these places. The whole landscape has been changed by large-scale deforestation, encroachment and excavation,” he says.
By 11 August, flood waters had receded in several villages, leaving behind heavy layers of mud and silt. However, low-lying areas of Sivasagar, Jorhat and Charaideo districts are still flooded, including the well-known Jokaichuk paddy field, a vast stretch of agricultural land shaped like a jokai, or bamboo fishing tool, near Gaurisagar.
“The floods have ruined 95% of the farmland across Sivasagar,” says Himadrijyoti Dutta, who works with farmers in the district through his non-profit organisation, Krishak Nyas, and has been visiting different villages to provide relief materials.
“The flood waters have washed away all the hard work and financial investments of the farmers. They have all been left poorer and desperate.”
Kalyan Das, a geography professor at Guwahati’s Cotton University, says the latest disaster will trigger a wave of migration. “Assam is already witnessing a serious crisis of out-migration of people from every block. There are many factors – primarily land degradation – making farming unsustainable,” he says.
Employment-driven migration from Assam rose from 16.3% in 1991 to 24.4% by 2011, according to a 2022 study. In rural areas, floods and soil erosion were the primary causes, the study said. “The latest floods have destroyed homes and agricultural fields. The villagers will be forced to migrate in search of livelihood opportunities,” Das says.
Eight years ago, Mintu Hazarika, 30, left Kosumari village in Sivasagar district for the IT hub of Bengaluru (formerly known as Bangalore). He earns 25,000 rupees (£195) a month by working double shifts as a security guard in Bengaluru’s Marathahalli suburb and sends half his earnings home.
“My father is a farmer, so is my elder brother,” says Hazarika. “They tend paddy fields, but it is not financially viable. So they also work as daily wage earners in nearby urban areas to supplement the household income.
On 22 July, Hazarika received a call from his father. He was told that the floods had destroyed their family’s two-hectare paddy field. “I don’t know how my family is going to survive. My elder brother is planning to come to Bengaluru to find work. There are already so many men from Sivasagar and other parts of Assam working in Bengaluru,” he says.
Bitupan Raidongia, district president of Sivasagar for the Bharatiya Janata party, the ruling party in Assam, says the authorities are providing support for affected communities. “Our government is doing its best to rescue marooned people. We are also reaching out to affected families by providing them with food items, clothes and other essentials.”
Sivasagar’s district commissioner, Mridul Yadav, adds that the local administration was making a coordinated effort to address the flood situation. “Various departments are working together on rescue, relief distribution, and damage assessment. Health camps, essential medicines, drinking water, livestock fodder and relief kits are being provided. Several relief camps remain operational to support affected families and restore essential services,” he adds.
But the authorities’ response has been criticised as too little, too late. In a video that went viral, the Assam-based singer Nilotpal Bora said thousands more people would have died were it not for the intervention of local charities and individuals.
“You people [the government] had a delayed response in reaching out to the affected people. If common people had not distributed relief, at least 3,000 people from flooded areas would have died because of hunger and thirst,” he said in response to a comment from Assam’s chief minister, Himanta Biswa Sarma, that “the situation was under control”, and the public should not raise money to help flood victims.
Meanwhile, local groups and people are doing what they can to help. About 40 bikers from One Northeast Motorcycle Club are travelling to affected areas to distribute food, clothing, sanitary items, candles, matchboxes and other essentials. “It’s a heartbreaking sight,” says the club’s founder, Chow Sureng Rajkonwar.
“Hundreds of people across villages have become homeless. Their homes were destroyed and flattened to the ground. Those that remain are filled with polokh [alluvial silt or sediment left behind by flood waters]. All their belongings were destroyed or washed away with the water. It will take months to rebuild those houses,” he says, adding that people are living in tents made of plastic sheets and tarpaulins on roads or higher ground near their villages.
Phukon was one of the luckier ones. Although the water level was more than 1.5 metres (5ft) high in her courtyard, it did not enter her house, which is built on higher ground.
For almost a week now, she has been providing relief aid to flood victims after getting distress calls from family, friends and acquaintances. “I decided to leave my home and reach out to people who need food, clothing, and other essentials. Everyone I know has been affected by floods.”
Maitreyee Boruah is a contributor to the Migration Story, where this story was first published

Army Cheetal carries out evacuation of injured mountaineer at 18,600 ft in Ladakh
Army pilots land a Cheetal helicopter at 18,600 ft on a treacherous Ladakh slope to evacuate an injured JCO near the Nun-Kun peaks.
Two Indian Army pilots pushed their single-engine Cheetal helicopter to its limits to evacuate an injured mountaineer near the Nun-Kun peaks in Ladakh’s Zanskar range, landing at 18,600 feet with just one skid barely touching the treacherous snow-clad slope, officials aware of the matter said on Sunday.
The pilots braved extreme weather and unforgiving terrain to evacuate the injured junior commissioned officer on Saturday but, despite their efforts, the soldier succumbed to his injuries at an Army hospital in Kargil, the officials said.
The Leh-based HQs 14 Corps called it a “daring high-altitude casualty evacuation” while sharing mission details.
“Indian Army Aviation pilots evacuated a casualty from an extremely challenging slope with no landing space and strong winds. With the helicopter lightened by removing non-essential equipment and carrying limited fuel, the aviators executed the evacuation with exceptional precision, courage and determination, including a critical landing with one skid touching the slope,” the Corps HQs said.
The mission was undertaken during the last available landing window of the day, highlighting the skill and courage of the Army Aviation Corps, officials added.
The development came three months after a Cheetal crashed near Leh’s Tangtse area on May 20. The two pilots—a lieutenant colonel and a major—and the third occupant, Major General Sachin Mehta, General Officer Commanding of the Karu-based 3 Infantry Division, miraculously survived the crash with minor injuries.
Equipped with a modern and fuel-efficient TM333–2M2 engine, the Cheetal features an automatic back-up engine control system. The Cheetal project began about 25 years ago to enhance high-altitude operational capabilities, improve maintainability, and provide a mid-life upgrade for safe and reliable operations.
The Leh-based HQs 14 Corps, responsible for operations in the sector, operates around 25 Cheetals, a re-engined version of the workhorse Cheetah helicopter.
The Army is looking at a swift replacement of its ageing Cheetah and Chetak fleets, helicopters that were designed six decades ago. A string of crashes has led to scrutiny of the choppers’ safety record.
The Army will begin phasing out the fleets in a year or two and replace them with new light utility helicopters (LUHs) over the next eight to 10 years, as part of the Army Aviation Corps’ drive to modernise its capabilities. The planned two-pronged replacement approach involves inducting locally produced LUHs and leasing similar choppers as a stopgap to meet critical requirements. The Army needs around 250 new helicopters.
Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) licence-produced 625 Cheetah and Chetak choppers for use across defence services. It no longer builds them but is responsible for their maintenance and repair. In 1970, HAL signed an agreement with French aerospace firm Aerospatiale to produce Cheetahs, eight years after it partnered with another French firm, Sud-Aviation (now Airbus), to manufacture Chetaks.

What will Jackson bring to Villa with Watkins set for exit?
- Published
Aston Villa have completed the signing of Nicolas Jackson in a deal worth up to £65m, with Ollie Watkins looking set to join Saudi Pro League side Al-Hilal.
Unai Emery's Villa are undergoing a major overhaul this summer, with key players including Morgan Rogers, Ezri Konsa, Youri Tielemans and Lucas Digne having already departed.
Jackson, 25, joins a number of new additions including Johan Manzambi, Joao Gomes, Zion Suzuki and Matteo Ruggeri.
That level of squad disruption was evident on the opening weekend, when Emery's side slumped to a 4-0 defeat at Brighton.
With Watkins, 30, unavailable and both Tammy Abraham and 17-year-old Brian Madjo injured, Villa started without a recognised centre-forward - Emiliano Buendia led the line.
The arrival of Jackson - who overtakes Manzambi to become Villa's record signing - from Chelsea gives Emery a specialist striker to work with.
It also looks set to coincide with the end of Watkins' six-year spell at Villa, during which he scored 108 goals in 278 games and became one of the defining players of the rise under Emery.
However, the stats suggest Jackson is not just a like-for-like replacement for the England international - he is a different type of number nine.
More involved, more shots - but a smaller sample
On the surface, Jackson's numbers at Bayern Munich last season compare favourably with those of Watkins at Villa.
The Senegal forward scored 11 goals and provided three assists in 1,320 minutes across all competitions, averaging 1.0 goal involvements per 90 minutes. Watkins recorded 21 goals and five assists in 3,837 minutes, an average of 0.6 per 90.
Jackson also generated more attacking opportunities. He averaged 3.8 shots per 90 compared with Watkins' 2.6, and 2.2 shots on target to 1.2.
His expected-goals (xG) figure was also higher, at 0.7 per 90 compared with 0.5, while he averaged 8.5 touches in the opposition box to Watkins' 5.6.
That fits a pattern which predates his spell in Germany. Among players with at least 5,000 Premier League minutes since January 2020, only Erling Haaland has registered a higher non-penalty xG figure per 90 than Jackson's 0.55.
Getting into scoring positions has rarely been Jackson's main problem - it is his ability to finish chances which has attracted scrutiny.
During his two Premier League seasons with Chelsea, he scored 14 goals from 18.7 xG in 2023-24 and 10 from 12.3 xG the following campaign.
Jackson has converted 18 of 61 big chances in England so far, although Watkins has also missed plenty of high-value opportunities (scoring 24 of 73 since joining Villa in 2020).
Interestingly, last season's numbers suggest the gap between them was negligible. Jackson converted 19.6% of his shots and 40.9% of his big chances, compared with 18.9% and 43.2% respectively for Watkins.
There is, however, an important caveat.
Watkins started 43 matches and played almost three times as many minutes. Jackson started only 15 of his 34 appearances, and Opta says his relatively limited, substitute-heavy sample could make some of his per-90 figures look stronger than they might over a full season.
Are Villa getting a different type of striker?
Both players were predominantly used as centre-forwards last season, making the comparison reasonably fair.
Watkins played 100% of his 3,837 minutes as a striker, with 92% coming as the central striker in Villa's 4-2-3-1.
Jackson spent 95% of his 1,320 minutes up front, with the remaining 5% on the left. At Bayern, 86% of his playing time came as the striker in a 4-2-3-1.
The similarity largely ends there. Jackson averaged 46.6 open-play touches per 90, compared with Watkins' 29.5, and completed almost twice as many passes - 24 per 90 to Watkins' 11.6.
He was also considerably more involved in creating and progressing attacks. Jackson averaged:
- 1.6 shot-ending carries per 90, compared with Watkins' 0.8
- 1.6 successful take-ons per 90, compared with 0.82
- 2.5 passes into the penalty area per 90, compared with 0.7.
Opta's touch maps reinforce the difference. Watkins' involvement was concentrated more heavily around the centre of the final third and penalty area, while Jackson received possession across a wider range of attacking zones.
Among a sample of 1,577 top-five European league strikers over the past 10 seasons, Jackson ranked in the 85th percentile for chances created, 77th for progressive carries and 73rd for touches.
Watkins ranked in the 28th, 53rd and eighth percentiles respectively. That points towards Villa moving from a relatively low-touch focal point to a forward who is more comfortable becoming involved in attacks earlier.
Greater intensity without the ball
There is another possible difference when Villa lose possession. Jackson averaged 34 high pressures per 90, slightly above Watkins' 31.4, but the distinction becomes clearer in where possession was recovered.
Jackson won the ball 2.7 times per 90, compared with Watkins' 1.8, and regained it in the final third 0.9 times per 90 to Watkins' 0.6.
His percentile for possession won in the attacking third was 88th among the Opta striker sample, compared with Watkins' 43rd.
The two were almost identical for runs in behind, Jackson averaging 13 per 90 and Watkins 12.7, although the Englishman made slightly more runs which finished inside the penalty area.
Watkins also offered more aerially, winning 1.2 aerial duels per 90 compared with Jackson's 0.7, and carried the ball more directly towards goal. So Jackson would not necessarily reproduce every aspect of the player he is replacing.
Why Emery believes he can unlock Jackson
Villa's interest also comes with an element of familiarity. Emery worked with Jackson at Villarreal, where the forward made 27 appearances under him, scoring three goals and providing three assists in 1,195 minutes.
Jackson has subsequently credited Emery with transforming his understanding of the game.
"Unai taught me everything about football," he said,
Jackson has explained that, when he arrived from Senegal, he possessed natural dribbling ability but had much less understanding of how and when to move.
Emery helped turn that instinctive talent into a more structured game.
Jackson's development accelerated after Emery left Villarreal. During the 2022-23 La Liga season he produced 0.56 non-penalty xG plus xA per 90, a rate bettered by only seven players with at least 1,500 minutes, all representing Barcelona, Real Madrid or Atletico Madrid.
Jackson's ability to carry the ball was already evident too. Ten of his league goal involvements followed carries, fewer only than Vinicius Jr, despite Jackson playing substantially fewer minutes.
Chelsea subsequently signed him in 2023. He scored 30 goals and supplied 12 assists in 81 appearances for the club before spending last season on loan at Bayern.
His time in Munich was complicated by circumstances rather than simply performance.
Bayern's obligation to buy would have been triggered if he reached a demanding appearance threshold, but Harry Kane remained fit and prolific, while the displays of Luis Diaz and Michael Olise limited opportunities elsewhere across the frontline.
Jackson still produced 11 goals across all competitions, and only Kane recorded a better rate of open-play Bundesliga goals per 90.
Bayern coach Vincent Kompany publicly defended him when criticism resurfaced, pointing to the quality of the forwards ahead of him and saying Jackson had trained and performed well.
A replacement - but not necessarily a replica
Watkins has provided Villa with reliability, running power and goals throughout one of the club's most successful periods of the modern era.
Jackson arrives with a different profile. He is five years younger, gets more touches, carries the ball more frequently, creates more for others and, in limited minutes last season, generated shots and high-quality chances at an impressive rate.
There remain questions around whether those per-90 numbers would survive a heavier workload, while his finishing record at Chelsea explains why doubts have followed him.
But Villa are not buying an unknown quantity. Emery has coached Jackson before, knows the qualities he wants to develop and would be replacing a 30-year-old striker with a 25-year-old whose underlying numbers suggest there may still be considerable room to improve.
If Jackson joins and Watkins does depart, the Europa League winners will be doing more than just changing their centre-forwards.
They will be changing the way their number nine plays.

Just Like That: 50 years on, why Mukesh’s voice still still resonates today
Fifty years after his death, legendary singer Mukesh’s soulful voice, timeless songs and emotional depth continue to resonate with generations of listeners.
Fifty years after his death, Mukesh’s voice remains inseparable from the emotional memory of generations of Indians. Unlike singers celebrated for vocal virtuosity, Mukesh’s enduring appeal lay in the vulnerability, melancholy and warmth that made his songs feel deeply personal. From Awaara Hoon and Kabhi Kabhie Mere Dil Mein to Kahin Door Jab Din Dhal Jaye, his voice continues to resonate across generations.
Mukesh, whose full name was Mukesh Chand Mathur, was only 53 when he died of a heart attack in Detroit, America, while on a concert tour with Lata Mangeshkar on August 27.
What distinguished Mukesh was not the conventional grandeur of his voice. He did not possess the dazzling vocal virtuosity of Mohammed Rafi, the extraordinary range of Manna Dey, the sensual delicacy of Talat Mahmood, or the effortless versatility of Kishore Kumar. Mukesh's gift was different. His voice had vulnerability. It seemed to come from somewhere within us—from memories of first love, separation, loneliness, friendship, disappointment, hope, and that indefinable sadness which is inseparable from the human condition.
In many ways, my life—and I am sure that of millions of others—was entwined with his songs. As a college student, when I did my yoga, I used to often put on his seven-album rendering of the Ramayan, which even today has 6.6 million hits on YouTube. When I joined the Indian Foreign Service and went in 1976 to the National Academy in Mussoorie for training, every night after dinner, sitting in the lounge, I would ask Ram Lal, who was in charge of the record player, to play two songs sung by Mukesh: Woh subah kabhi tau aayegi, and Phir na keeje meri gustakh nigahi ka gila.
His song Kabhie kabhie mere dil mein khayal aata hai, could easily figure among the most romantic songs of Hindi films. I recall that one day, when I wanted Renu, my wife-to-be, to hear it, I did not immediately have the money to buy an EP album to play it. Surendra Singh, the cook in our home, lent me the money and went post haste to the market to procure it.
Mukesh’s advent into playback singing is itself an unlikely story. Born in Delhi on July 22, 1923, into a large family, he was not initially destined for the cinema. A music teacher who came to teach his sister noticed the young Mukesh listening from an adjoining room and imitating what he heard.
After a brief spell working in the Public Works Department, Mukesh left for Bombay in 1940, encouraged by his mother despite his father's reservations. In Bombay, his distant relative Motilal, the well-known actor, helped him. In those days, the distinction between actor and singer was not as clearly established as it later became. Mukesh therefore made his screen debut as an actor-singer in Nirdosh in 1941, opposite Nalini Jaywant. He sang in the film, but neither the film nor the song made an impact. The production company closed, and Mukesh was left without work. He tried several occupations, including selling dry fruits and film distribution.
There was another obstacle. Mukesh was deeply influenced by K. L. Saigal and, in his early years, imitated him. His first significant success, Dil Jalta Hai To Jalne De, from Pehli Nazar in 1945, bore the unmistakable imprint of Saigal. The story is almost legendary: Saigal reportedly heard the song and wondered when he had recorded it. But imitation could never become Mukesh's destiny.
His great partnership with Raj Kapoor firmly launched Mukesh. Mukesh became, in effect, Raj Kapoor's singing voice. From Awaara and Shree 420 to Sangam and Mera Naam Joker, he gave voice to Kapoor's screen persona—the romantic idealist, the vulnerable clown, the common man, the eternal wanderer. Mukesh reportedly sang more than a hundred songs for Raj Kapoor during his career.
Consider the astonishing range of his enduring repertoire. Awaara Hoon became an anthem of the wandering Indian, cheerful on the surface but carrying an undercurrent of existential uncertainty. Mera Joota Hai Japani combined innocence, patriotism and cosmopolitan self-confidence with remarkable ease. Dost Dost Na Raha gave friendship the poignancy of betrayal. Jeena Yahan Marna Yahan became almost a philosophical statement about the theatricality and transience of life. And songs such as Saranga Teri Yaad Mein, Sawan Ka Mahina, Kahin Door Jab Din Dhal Jaye, Ek Din Bik Jayega Mati Ke Mol continue to demonstrate how effortlessly Mukesh could move between romance, reflection and melancholy.
Then there are other songs that remain evergreen: Chandan Sa Badan, Jhoomti chali haws, Suhana Safar Aur Yeh Mausam Haseen, Jaane Kahan Gaye Woh Din, Kisi Ki Muskurahaton Pe Ho Nisar, and the hauntingly philosophical Kai Baar Yunhi Dekha Hai. For the latter, from the film Rajnigandha, Mukesh received the National Film Award for Best Male Playback Singer in 1974.
One of my great favourites is a ghazal sung by Mukesh, but not for films: Tere labon ke muqabil ghulab kya hoga. Fifty years is a long time in popular culture. Voices disappear, fashions change, musical conventions evolve and heroes are replaced. Yet, even now, when I hear Mukesh’s voice, I know his appeal will never diminish.
Pavan K Varma is an author, diplomat, and former member of Parliament (Rajya Sabha). The views expressed are personal

Stressed out about politics? It could be impacting your health
Major events can cause anxiety, loss of sleep, loss of appetite and even depression, researcher says
In downtown Toronto, it doesn't take long to find people with politics on their minds. 
"I think everyone is pretty stressed about politics right now. It's hard not to be," said Tonya Facey when stopped by CBC News. "Politics is a part of everyday life and there's a lot going on, politically."
Jamie Haynes, visiting from St. John's, said he too worries about politics.
"Especially with the war on the go with Donald Trump and Canada — it's quite concerning," he said.
The trade war with the U.S., an Alberta referendum and Quebec election this fall, global conflicts: these are the kinds of political events that can trigger stress, researchers say. Political decisions that impact people's daily lives, and political disagreements that cause conflict with others are also sources of worry.
Political stress is now an entire field of study that gained traction in the U.S. around the 2016 presidential election. Here in Canada, political scientists, psychologists and mental health experts are also investigating the toll this form of stress can take on someone's health.
"There has been a lot of documented evidence, particularly over the past 10 years, in looking at things like loss of sleep, loss of appetite, negative emotions, periodic depression — these sorts of things that people can tie to things like a major election or maybe a particular conflict that's happening in the world,” said Amanda Friesen, a Canada Research Chair in Political Psychology.
The professor of political science at Western University in London, Ont., launched the Body Politics Lab in 2022, where her team carries out studies investigating how people's bodies and minds react to politics.
One study gave 81 undergraduate students a ring-like device that measured their temperature, pulse and sweat level as they scrolled their TikTok accounts. Western University PhD student Samantha Jones said a key takeaway from the results was not so much the physical reactions to viewing political content, but the emotional ones.
"They were more likely to report feeling negatively afterwards, compared to other types of content," said Jones.
They were also more likely to engage with it — by sharing it and viewing the comments — and that informs the algorithm.
"So despite this content making them feel negatively," said Jones, "they are inadvertently saying they want more."
Finding a healthy balance
Friesen said these kinds of studies are aimed at understanding what stresses people out when it comes to politics, and what that stress can mean for their health — and the health of democracy.
"One of our projects right now is balancing democratic and personal health," she said.
If something is shown to harm someone's well-being, they're usually advised to avoid it. But politics trickles into people's everyday lives, and with social media and the 24/7 news cycle, it's hard to avoid. Plus, people need to stay engaged in politics in order to have a thriving democracy, said Friesen.
Noah Vanderhoeven, one of the Body Politics researchers, said he thinks a balance between staying informed and maintaining healthy habits can be struck.
Some people even respond to the stress in ways that are good for democracy, he said.
"These kinds of anxieties about politics in the world can also be addressed through political action and being involved and engaged as a citizen," said Vanderhoeven.
He's leading a study this fall tied to the Alberta referendum, which he said could be a stressful event for some.
Staying informed about politics in a healthy way can be a challenge for some Canadians, according to Dr. Allison Crawford, a psychiatrist at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health who leads Canada's national 9-8-8 suicide crisis hotline.
She said people are reaching out because of political stress.
"When political worry causes uncertainty in general, especially related to finances or people's sense of security or the safety of the world, we do often see that in our texters and callers," said Crawford.
People report losing sleep, feeling unsettled, overwhelmed and helpless, she said.
Recognizing symptoms is a good first step, said Crawford, then people should reach out to someone they trust for support.
"We do want people involved in our democracy and we want people to not disengage but there are things that we can control and things that we can't control," she said.
Time spent consuming news and social media is something that can be controlled, Crawford advised, and could be limited as a way to de-stress.
Trade war stress 'spike'
Recent news headlines in Canada are dominated by the trade war with the U.S. and Friesen said she believes Canadians’ political stress levels have "spiked" since U.S. President Donald Trump took office a second time and took aim at Canada.
"Suddenly there was this sort of external 'enemy' that pulled Canadians together but increased this stress," said Friesen. "I think there's this kind of element of uncertainty. Is this all posturing? What does this mean? And anytime there's uncertainty, that is going to cause anxiety.”
That’s exactly what Amélie Valois said she’s feeling.
"Politics do stress me out especially what's going on with the U.S. right now, and how it's going to impact our grocery bills, and business, and everything going forward," she told CBC News as she walked towards the Rogers Centre to take in a Blue Jays game. "It's stressful."

- Rockstar is tying money directly to the main story progression for both Jason and Lucia in GTA 6.
- Unlike Rockstar's previous titles, players can't play the next main mission after completing one.
- GTA 6 will require a certain amount of capital to keep the main missions moving forward through the story.
Money in GTA games is almost as important as in real life. Without it, you’re basically nothing in this game. You can’t buy good clothes, luxury cars, or many in-game purchases. Now, Rockstar is taking a step further with GTA 6’s money, tying it to the main story progression for our main dual protagonists, Jason and Lucia.
GTA 6 Makes Money Important to Main Story Progression
Rockstar intends for money to play a pivotal role in GTA 6’s main campaign. You cannot complete one mission after another like in your GTA 6 playthrough time, which, by the way, can exceed 80 hours. Sometimes, you will need a specific amount of money before you can continue the game’s campaign.
This key feature was revealed in the previews that dropped after GTA 6’s Extended Look showcase on Netflix. So, whether you’re playing with Jason or Lucia, or both, you now need money not only to buy new clothes, exotic cars, weapons, or engage in multiple activities in GTA 6, but also to progress the game’s main story.
Of course, GTA 6 will feature multiple ways to earn money, such as running heists with Jason and Lucia, robbing stores, holding up businesses, stealing cars, and more. However, these criminal activities also risk drawing the cops. Since GTA 6 will feature a 6-star wanted level system, it’ll be much harder to escape police pursuits.
Luckily, GTA 6’s car-trunk mechanic will let you change clothes, stow weapons, and avoid detection on the run. Even then, you still need money to buy new clothes, not to mention progressing through the game’s missions in a straight flow.
You might feel like Rockstar is limiting the chaos by tying GTA 6’s main missions to the money Jason and Lucia have, but it’s all to showcase consequences and drive home the fact that they are more than just in-game avatars.
Who knows, being broke might also put a strain on Jason and Lucia’s romantic relationship in GTA 6‘s campaign. So, remember to raise your in-game money when GTA 6 launches in less than three months.

Electric two-wheeler maker Ola Electric has secured a ₹95.81 Cr incentive under the government’s Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme from the Ministry of Heavy Industries. Under the PLI scheme, the MHI provides financial incentives of up to 18% on sales to boost domestic manufacturing of advanced automotive technology (AAT) products. The incentive secured from Ola Electric pertains to the fiscal year FY27, making it the third consecutive year that Ola Electric has received the incentive. The Bhavish Aggarwal-led company had earlier received a sanction of ₹73.74 Cr for FY24 in March 2025, followed by ₹366.78 Cr for FY25, announced in December 2025. “The sanction of ₹95.81 Cr under the PLI-Auto Scheme, for the third consecutive year, is a strong endorsement of Ola Electric's manufacturing capabilities and our commitment to building world-class EV technology in India,” an Ola Electric spokesperson said. Besides the PLI for AAT products, Ola Electric is also eyeing up to ₹7,240 Cr in battery cell PLI incentives. Notably, the MHI revised the timelines under the advanced chemistry cell (ACC) PLI scheme, giving Ola Electric’s battery subsidiary, Ola Cell Technologies Pvt Ltd (OCT), a five-year incentive window. Under the new window, the company can potentially claim cumulative incentives of up to ₹7,240 Cr, it said in a filing on August 12. The incentives come amid declining sales for the EV major. Ola Electric’s registrations fell 20% to 13,085 units in July from 16,249 units in June, with its market share slipping to about 7%. Amid falling sales, the EV major launched its new S1Z e-scooter range today, powered by the company’s locally developed 46-series lithium iron phosphate (LFP) Bharat Cell technology. To note, the company is also entering the energy storage segment while shifting to a dealer-led sales and service model. Earlier this month, it launched three battery energy storage systems (BESS) as part of its push into the energy solutions business. The portfolio comprises the second-generation residential Ola Shakti, the industry-focused Shakti Rack, and the utility-scale Mahashakti. The company also launched the Shakti Solar Charge Controller, which will be available in 3 kW and 6 kW variants from March 2027. On the financial front, Ola Electric’s consolidated net loss narrowed 22% YoY to ₹336 Cr from ₹428 Cr. Operating revenue was down 45% from ₹828 Cr in Q1 FY26. To note, delivery of scooters stood at 39,192 units, almost double the 20,256 units shipped in Q4 FY26.

Hello, and welcome back to This Is India.
For this week’s newsletter, I’m looking at India’s evolving relationship with Israel, and how it has deepened as conflict swept across the Middle East. Why is it that India has formed an even closer bond with a country that has faced mounting international isolation and backlash over a military campaign in Gaza that has left the territory in ruins and killed more than 70,000 Palestinians, – many of whom were children?
Under Narendra Modi, India’s ties with Israel have taken on a different character, for a country that once championed the Palestinian cause and led the Non-Aligned Movement. To better understand it, I turned to Stanly Johny, Indian foreign policy expert and the international affairs editor at the Hindu. He told me it isn’t just a political or diplomatic shift, “it’s also at the strategic and defence level”.
The evolution of India’s role was revealed in a recent Amnesty International investigation, which showed that India was now a key part of Israel’s weapons supply chain. This represents a fundamental change. For years, New Delhi had primarily been a major customer of Israeli weapons. But, through joint ventures and manufacturing partnerships, it is now a “significant contributor” to Israel’s weapons production, according to Amnesty, which offers the most extensive account so far of the scale of India’s involvement since the war in Gaza began.
Indian companies, including state-owned enterprises, have delivered drone warheads, artillery shell casings, small arms parts and military vehicle components to Israeli military suppliers despite the substantial risk these could end up in weapons deployed in Gaza, it added.
By examining publicly available shipment-level trade data, Amnesty said it traced hundreds of thousands of weapons components shipped from Indian factories to Israeli military suppliers between 7 October 2023 and 30 November 2025, including:
 390,516 small arms parts for military grade weapons
  564,970 parts of explosive ordnance
  298 components of military vehicles
Many western nations, including Britain, have restricted or banned arms supply to Israel over its conduct in the war, citing risks that the weapons could be used to commit or facilitate violations of international humanitarian law. (The United States accounts for the overwhelming share of major arms transfers to Israel.)
An independent United Nations commission of inquiry concluded in September that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, and earlier this year another commission found that Israel is continuing to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children. Separately, the international criminal court has issued an arrest warrant for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, accusing him of committing war crimes.
Yet, the Amnesty report hasn’t resulted in any large-scale public debate or political backlash in India, despite some scattered media coverage. Johny believes this is a result of the support for Israel by Modi’s voter base. “There is a clear ideological confluence between Hindutva and Zionism,” he said. In rightwing circles in India and elsewhere, he argues, Israel is increasingly seen as a bulwark against the expansion of Islam.
Hindu nationalists have long admired Israel, viewing it as a model of a nationalist state that can assert itself in a volatile neighbourhood. Author Pankaj Mishra chronicled this affinity in a 2017 essay, writing that his grandfather was among high-caste Hindus who saw Israel as an example of how to deal with Muslims “in the only language they understood: that of force and more force”.
The war on Gaza doesn’t appear to have significantly shifted views. A Pew Research survey published in June found that more Indians view Israel favourably (32%) than unfavourably (28%). This is in contrast to the decline of support for Israel in many western countries, including the United States, since the war.
Modi, for his part, has cultivated a personal rapport with Netanyahu. In 2017, he became the first Indian prime minister to visit Israel, and Modi’s visit to Israel earlier this year came just 48 hours before Israel and the United States launched their attacks on Iran. The optics of Modi hugging Netanyahu on the tarmac, coupled with New Delhi’s noticeably muted response at the outbreak of war, were a clear sign of where India’s political establishment stands. It has not gone unnoticed. In July, after the US vice-president, JD Vance, rebuked Netanyahu by calling the US Israel’s “only powerful ally” left in the world, Netanyahu shot back: “We have some other friends, like a small country called India. It has 1.4bn people, and boy, do we have tremendous support there.”
The government has previously declined to give a direct answer about weapons supplies to Israel. When asked in parliament in 2024, external affairs minister S Jaishankar said that information is not in public domain and that exports of military products are guided by “national interest”. Amnesty identified three state-owned Indian companies – Munitions India Limited, India Optel Limited and Advanced Weapons and Equipment India Limited – supplying Israel with weapons, which it said, could expose India to the hazard of “complicity in ongoing genocide in Gaza”. Foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal responded that India’s exports are governed by national laws and international obligations.
The pushback has largely come from human rights activists, student bodies, trade unions, India’s left-leaning parties and the Congress party. The courts have offered no recourse, either. In 2024, a group of civil servants, activists and academics petitioned the supreme court, demanding India suspend its military exports to Israel. The court dismissed the case, ruling that the matter fell within the discretion of the executive.
“In India, you don’t see any anger towards the government for its relationship with Israel, despite the allegations the Israeli government is facing,” Johny said. This, he believes, is a sign that foreign policy debates in India are being stripped of moral concern.
Weapons aren’t the only thing India has sent to Israel during this period. Thousands of Indian workers have also gone to Israel, in many instances to replace Palestinians barred from entering the country after 7 October 2023. Last year, the government told parliament that more than 20,000 Indian workers, in construction work and caregiving, had moved to Israel after an agreement signed in November 2023.
India, meanwhile, has shored up its own arms supplies from Israel. Between 2021 and 2025, New Delhi was Israel’s largest defence customer, accounting for 29% of total arms sales, according to Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
But for Johny, India’s growing closeness to Israel is beginning to come at a cost. The war in Iran threatens India’s energy security and could have wider economic repercussions across the Gulf, home to a large Indian diaspora. “India has to continue to stay engaged with Israel, but it is important to restore balance to its approach to west Asia,” he said, adding that it needs to forcefully defend its own interests.

CJP warned that it would launch a public agitation with local residents if the problems were not resolved within the stipulated period.
The Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) on Sunday inspected two government primary schools in the Shastri Nagar-Bhatta Basti area and alleged that both lacked basic infrastructure, giving the administration seven days to address the deficiencies.

“Children cannot be expected to study in such deplorable conditions. The administration must provide safe and adequate educational facilities at both schools within seven days,” the CJP said.

As data center developers compete for a cut of the hundreds of billions of dollars flowing into the artificial intelligence industry, the queue to join the UK’s power grid has become jammed with projects that will likely never get built. The snarl is exacerbating already years-long wait times for viable projects, and it's messing with attempts to forecast energy demand and plan grid expansions.
In July, the UK’s energy regulator, Ofgem, laid out a proposal meant to force phantom data centers out of the swollen queue. Under the plans, set to be finalized after an industry feedback process that ends in September, developers would be required to put down a steep, nonrefundable deposit that could balloon to hundreds of millions of dollars for the very largest data centers. Developers would also be required to line up customers in advance and prove they have the funding to complete their builds.
However, Ofgem faces a Goldilocks conundrum: The reforms must be burdensome enough to deter speculators but not so much that they drive legitimate data center projects to other shores, undermining the UK’s ambitions to meet the voracious demand for the compute required to run sophisticated AI models.
Data center developers face delays almost everywhere; similar grid congestion issues afflict the US and countries across Europe. But whereas the US is a highly desirable market, Ofgem’s reforms risk making the UK—already unattractive for the high cost of energy and dearth of land—one of the world’s most expensive places to build a data center, industry experts believe.
The frenzied data center buildout “is bringing a huge amount of capital investment into the UK,” says Alex Burgoyne, head of data centers at real estate consultancy Knight Frank. “We don’t want to shoot the golden goose.”
Ofgem says that it will take into account industry concerns before settling on a fee, but that differences between international energy markets make like-for-like comparison difficult. “We recognize data centers are a key part of the UK's AI ambitions and future economic growth. Enabling viable data centers to connect more quickly is an enabler of this,” Nathan Macwhinnie, deputy director of strategic planning and connections at Ofgem, tells WIRED in a statement.
The queue to join the UK grid began to balloon toward the end of 2024, around the time the government designated data centers “critical national infrastructure.” Between November 2024 and June 2025, the total energy demand of the projects in the connection queue increased from 41 gigawatts to 125 gigawatts, according to Ofgem. New data centers make up 73 gigawatts of that—equivalent to one and a half times the peak demand for the entire UK last year—and counting.
The government has said it believes much of that demand is a mirage. “It’s absolutely insane,” says Taco Engelaar, managing director at grid optimization company Neara. “No one really understands … what the real grid demand will be because of these phantom projects.”
The crowded queue is largely the product of an incentives problem. Because developers face a years-long wait for grid access, and it has previously cost only a few thousand dollars to join the queue, they might as well apply for power, even if they do not have a watertight plan to develop a site. It’s a no-downside bet that allows developers to hedge for a future in which demand for compute remains sky-high.
However, because grid operators have to account for the combined effect of large infrastructure proposals on network stability before granting individual connections, phantom data centers can exacerbate already-lengthy delays for viable projects. “They have to treat every project as serious when they try to study whether the system can handle them,” says Olivier Darmouni, associate professor of finance at HEC Paris Business School, who has published research on the impact of AI on power grids. “The more speculative projects are especially damaging because they make these studies more complex, more expensive, longer.”
A lengthy queue also attracts middleman developers who apply for power with the aim of later flipping land at a premium to data center companies, packaged with grid access. “It’s like scalping for concert tickets,” says Darmouni. “The congestion feeds on itself and gets out of hand.”
The UK has required all developers since 2024 to demonstrate they have at least secured land rights, submitted a planning application, and met other milestones that indicate they are likely to follow through on their projects.
The latest Ofgem proposal runs with that same logic, and in the most basic sense, it’s expected to work. “It’s going to pour water on a lot of the speculative data center applications,” says Burgoyne.
Eliminating phantom data centers from the queue will also make it easier for grid operators to plan upgrades and expansions, avoiding a scenario where money is wasted on parts of the network that don’t actually require extra capacity. “If there’s an accurate queue and we know exactly what the demand will be, where it’s going to be built, it will help potentially target more focused investment from a grid upgrade and building perspective,” says Engelaar.
There is some concern, however, that the reforms could have unintended side effects that undermine the UK government’s ambition to rapidly expand the country’s compute capacity.
One risk is that the steep new fees make the UK market less enticing for data center developers, already more attracted to the US and corners of Europe that can offer plentiful, renewable energy. “It’s a really difficult balancing act,” says Daniel Mewton, a partner at the law firm Slaughter and May who specializes in digital infrastructure. “If you don’t set [the fee] high enough, you don’t deter speculation. If you set it too high, you risk killing viable projects, because people are unwilling to put large sums of money at risk at the development stage.”
The plans could also force all but the very largest data center companies from the UK market, trampling a new generation of smaller, AI-specific data center operators that may be unwilling to cough up the fees. Some of those up-and-comers, like Nscale, have previously pledged to spend billions of dollars in the UK. “There are new players arriving all the time,” says Burgoyne. “It might have the unintended consequence that it stifles growth in the sector.”
But while the reforms may not improve the UK’s immediate prospects of riding the wave of AI infrastructure investment, some say that cleansing the queue of phantom data centers will give the country a better long-term chance of winning a cut of the hundreds of billions of dollars pouring into the sector.
“It’s about shaping the next five years to make sure you build the data centers in the right place, at the right size, with the right power supply,” says Darmouni. “It’s not going to be a gas pedal you can press on, and the car is going to accelerate immediately.”

Europe's summer drought threatens fish in rivers, lakes and farms
Extreme drought and heat have severely impacted the Danube River and surrounding regions
NOVI SAD, Serbia -- Small boats stand idle on cracked ground in a shriveled side channel of the Danube River in northern Serbia, where the water has receded into a couple of shrinking ponds under pressure from extreme drought and heat. Fish circle in the shallow waters.
“This is all we have, these two little ponds that are full of juvenile fish,” fisherman Dusan Jovanovic said. He said the fish are in danger because there is too little water and its temperature is over 30 degrees Celsius (86 degrees Fahrenheit).
“If they start to die, they will all die at once,” Jovanovic said.
Persistent drought and scorching heat this summer have ravaged ecosystems and businesses across the region, from a lake in Slovenia and the side channel of the Danube in Serbia, to fish farms in Bosnia, the Czech Republic, Romania and Hungary.
The fish industry has been hit especially hard, with damage estimated in the millions of euros (dollars). This is adding to the already high toll caused by problems with energy and water supplies, devastated crops, losses in river traffic and trade.
Finding themselves unprepared for this year's crisis, countries and businesses are now pondering ways to minimize the effects of future extreme weather events that scientists have tied to human-induced climate change.
Around 99% of Hungary’s lands are currently under severe or extreme drought conditions, according to the national meteorological service. Desertification, a process where vegetation recedes because of high heat and low rainfall, threatens much of the Great Hungarian Plain.
Among the most affected are Hungary’s roughly 27,000 hectares (67,000 acres) of fish ponds. The country’s Agriculture and Food Economy Ministry said last week that “persistent heat and water shortages” had led to 1,588 hectares (3,924 acres) of those ponds drying out, causing the deaths of nearly 280 metric tons of fish at 20 farms.
The estimated revenue loss from the damage was 1.3 billion forints ($4.2 million), the ministry said. Producers say replacing lost fish could take years. Sometimes, operators were forced to drain one pond and divert its water to save fish in another, the Hungarian Aquaculture and Fisheries Inter-branch Organization said in early August.
For fish farmers in Romania, especially those cultivating carp, this year’s blistering heatwave follows severe droughts in 2023 and 2024, the effects of which are still being felt, says Catalin Platon, president of ROMFISH National Association of Fish Producers.
In carp production, Platon said, the production cycle is three or four years.
“So what we lost in 2023 has (had an) impact every year since," he explained. Water-use policies that prioritized irrigation for agriculture during the previous droughts, “left us with no water for the fish,” Platon complained.
Fish farmers across the Czech Republic have taken various emergency measures: reducing or suspending feeding to reduce oxygen use, aerating the ponds or draining them when necessary.
The Czech Fishing Association officials say sustained rainfall could ease the immediate crisis, but long-term measures are needed to retain more water in the landscape.
Jan Sokolik, a technician at the Rybarstvi Trebon fishery, explained that “some ponds that were actually low on water have already been fished, but they were all marginal ponds.”
“Now we’re just starting to plan what to do with the big ponds,” he said.
Veljko Budjen owns a trout farm near Trebinje in southeast Bosnia. He said hot and dry summers have brought serious problems in the mainly mountainous country famous for its trout restaurants.
“Trout is a cold water fish, which requires cold water with a lot of oxygen,” he said. “So during the summer you are forced to reduce trout production and feeding so the business can just barely survive.”
One option, he said, is to add liquid oxygen to the water during summer months. Otherwise, he said, “you wait for the first rain.”
Emergency teams have been pumping water into Lake Pristava in eastern Slovenia, a favorite spot for fishermen, to try to prevent a mass suffocation of fish from lack of oxygen and water chestnut overgrowing to cover the lake surface.
Firefighters have pumped in 8 million liters (2 million gallons) of water but they still fear it's not enough.
"We are surprised that any fish has survived at all,” Danijel Fras, from the Pesnica Lenart Fishing Association, told public broadcaster RTV Slovenia.
In Serbia, fishermen said the only solution for the endangered fish in the Danube side channel in Novi Sad is to move them to another location.
“The temperatures this year are extreme,” Jovanovic, the Serbian fisherman, said. "No one can remember anything like this.”
