How to Claw Back Wealth From Toppled Autocrats
Cleaning up after a corrupt regime comes with serious risks.
Americans are not accustomed to learning lessons about democracy from Nigeria, Peru, or the Philippines. That disregard may soon change. Those countries offer examples of what it looks like to reclaim stolen or swindled wealth from fallen authoritarian rulers. Done right, this work can deliver justice and strengthen democratic institutions for the long run. But cleaning up after a corrupt regime also comes with serious challenges and hazards.
The Trump presidency has often looked more like a post-Soviet or postcolonial regime than like a first-world democracy. The Trump post-presidency may look the same. Trump has abused his office to enrich himself and his family in ways that are completely unprecedented—not only in the United States but also in the history of almost any peer democracy. Only Silvio Berlusconi, Italy’s notoriously lawless former prime minister, was in any way comparable, and Berlusconi was sentenced to prison.
Trump faces little danger of prison. The U.S. Supreme Court has bestowed substantial criminal impunity on him, even assuming that he leaves office in 2029 as required by the Constitution. But an ex-president remains subject to civil liability, and the proceeds of bribery, extortion, insider trading, and market manipulation may be exposed to civil penalties. Other countries have shown the way.
Alberto Fujimori, who was elected president of Peru in 1990, entered office at a time of extreme national crisis. The murderous Shining Path insurgency controlled much of Peru’s hinterland and terrorized the capital, Lima. Inflation ran at nearly 8,000 percent. Food and electricity were in constant shortage. Fujimori stopped the inflation and crushed the insurgency, but his harsh and sometimes criminal methods included warrantless detentions and extrajudicial killings. Fujimori dissolved Congress and the Supreme Court and rewrote Peru’s constitution to allow his own reelection in 1995. He won roughly two-thirds of the vote in a free, more or less, election.
But as Fujimori was doing things Peruvians wanted done, he was also presiding over a secret scheme of self-enrichment. His intelligence chief, Vladimiro Montesinos, operated a system of embezzlement and kickbacks that amassed hundreds of millions of dollars in foreign bank accounts. When this deception came to light, just after Fujimori’s 2000 reelection to a third term, he fled the country and resigned from office.
To claw back these funds, Peru created a special prosecutor’s office and worked closely with the countries that hosted these contested assets. Peru has since recovered about $200 million of misappropriated wealth from accounts in the Cayman Islands, Switzerland, the United States, and Luxembourg, according to the database of the World Bank’s Stolen Asset Recovery Initiative. Peru’s economy also grew strongly after Fujimori’s fall from power. Foreign investment returned when the country renewed the rule of law. But then, in the 2010s, world demand slowed for Peru’s mineral exports, ensuring that Peru’s economy slowed too. Political instability returned.
As Peru rotated through eight presidents over the past decade, a mood of “Fujimori nostalgia” gained strength. Fujimori’s daughter Keiko, who was elected to Congress in 2006, founded her own political party in 2010, built mostly on a message of family revenge and redemption. She ran for president in 2011, 2016, and 2021, losing narrowly each time. She ran again this year—and won.
Believers in free and fair government can hope that Peru’s democratic institutions have strengthened sufficiently over the past quarter century to deter Keiko Fujimori from indulging in the deviousness that led to her father’s disgrace. But her tenure is new, and her political message has long been one of excusing her father’s abuses.
Peru is not the only case of a former kleptocratic ruling family returning to power on a message of revenge and redemption. The Filipino dictator Ferdinand Marcos pillaged billions of dollars over two decades, from 1965 to 1986. After his ouster, his democratically elected successor, Corazon Aquino, created a Presidential Commission on Good Government to recover this stolen wealth. As of 2022, the PCGG had returned $5 billion to the Philippines, according to reporting by the country’s leading English-language newspaper.
But as in Peru, proof of a former president’s corruption did not discredit his dynasty. In 2022, Marcos’s son—Ferdinand Marcos Jr., also known as “Bongbong”—was elected president. The PCGG still exists, but its work has ceased. The restored dynasty has reportedly returned to its corrupt ways, facing allegations of kickbacks as well as no-bid and no-work contracts, including more than $9 billion in devious government flood-control deals.
Yet Bongbong Marcos has thus far respected the 1987 constitution adopted after his father’s dictatorship, which safeguards an independent judiciary and imposes an absolute ban on presidential reelection following a single six-year term. A big test for democracy in the Philippines is what happens in 2028.
The single most ambitious program of asset recovery has taken place in Nigeria. In the five years that Sani Abacha ruled the country as a military dictator, from 1993 until his death, in 1998, he stole perhaps $4 billion, stashing the funds in foreign accounts and shell companies. Revelations of his corruption discredited his military regime. In 1999, Nigeria returned to an elected government, which created a specialized unit in 2002, the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission, to reclaim these funds from Abacha’s heirs. This work received considerable help from the Swiss government, which agreed to freeze Abacha-related accounts, and from the United States, which cracked down on Abacha-owned shell companies. Nigeria got back about $1.5 billion, according to the World Bank’s tally.
In Nigeria, the Abacha name has become synonymous with fraud and crime. If you receive scam letters from Nigerian fraudsters, you’ll notice how often they impersonate a member of the Abacha family and promise access to hidden millions if only these funds could be moved to a trusted bank account. For this reason, the Abacha family has not enjoyed next-generation political success in Nigeria. The ex-dictator’s son has run for governor of the family’s home state of Kano a couple of times, including this year, but never got close to winning.
But as Nigeria dissolves into conflicts along religious, ethnic, and regional lines, many Nigerians yearn for a “strong leader” in the Abacha mold. The country’s successful reclamation of wealth from Abacha’s heirs has also bred a new cynicism about the country’s democratic institutions, because so much of this money has been “re-looted” by Nigeria’s post-Abacha elected governments, especially by officials in President Muhammadu Buhari’s administration.
The message to Americans? The recovery of corrupt assets from fallen leaders is not hopeless, but it is difficult and risky. This work demands permanent institutions specifically tasked to investigate and prosecute, and broad international cooperation to locate, identify, seize, and return dirty money. Even so, most people generally believe that the Fujimori, Marcos, and Abacha families kept much—if not most—of their corruptly obtained wealth.
More dangerous, not every citizen will agree that the out-of-office autocrat should be brought to justice. The former leader’s followers, and especially his children, may convert complaints about imperfect justice into fuel for their own corrupt restoration. The fortunes, the fame, and the followings bequeathed by corrupt rulers to their heirs can support authoritarian power grabs long after the corrupt ruler departs this Earth.
If the Trump family can keep the money it has accumulated this term, the next generation of Trumps will be far richer than Donald Trump ever was until his 80th year. Americans traditionally let bygones be bygones after a president leaves office, on the theory that ex-presidents rarely cause much trouble. But money is power in politics, and dirty money needs power to protect itself from the law. As much as Americans may wish to forget the Trumps and their corruption after this presidency ends, the next generation of Trumps surely understands that political power is its surest defense against legal retribution. This makes recovering the Trumps’ wrongfully obtained wealth not only a matter of justice but also a matter of democratic survival.

Manhunt after one killed and five injured in Swiss shooting, police say
- Published
One person has died and five people are injured after shots were fired at an event in northern Switzerland overnight, local police say.
"The manhunt for the unknown perpetrator is under way," Aargau Cantonal Police said in a statement. "Possible motives as well as the exact circumstances of the crime are still unclear."
The force told Swiss media that the shooting took place near a horse racing track in Schachen, Aarau, some 46km (29 miles) west of Zurich.
A rave was scheduled to take place in the area into the early hours of Sunday.
An area around the racing track, the town's swimming pool and sports field has been cordoned off, with the public urged to stay away.
A large contingent of officers has also been deployed beyond Aarau "as a precaution", police said.

Much of the focus on the Lindsay Clancy case has been on the reported systemic failures of the mental health system, with the hope that this case will revamp the approach to maternal mental health. We, as forensic and reproductive psychiatrists, agree that the system is not perfect. But we are concerned that this focus could have a dangerous unintended consequence: The legal and public scrutiny around the Clancy case could make psychiatrists more reluctant to treat mothers with mental illness.
In an ideal world, all mothers would have easy access to reproductive psychiatrists. The reality is that only about 500 reproductive psychiatrists are practicing in the United States. As a result, general psychiatrists (as in the Clancy case) and OB-GYNs are often the frontline providers for perinatal mental illnesses. Both are trained to assess and treat these disorders but do not have a dedicated focus on them.
This criminal case, which is now with the jury; the civil action taken by Clancy and her ex-husband; and the media coverage have all focused on the alleged failures of the clinicians whom Clancy saw before killing her three children. That raises the possibility that physicians will be concerned that treating a new mother’s psychiatric disorder carries a high risk of liability — and will avoid high-risk maternal patients. As a result, mothers who need psychiatric treatment will find it even harder to obtain it. Already, anecdotally, trainees have expressed concerns to us about their future practices.
Mothers may experience a variety of psychiatric symptoms during the course of pregnancy and the postpartum period. They include anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder, mood symptoms, and much less commonly postpartum psychosis. Postpartum psychosis is usually considered a medical emergency, warranting psychiatric hospitalization.
Reproductive psychiatrists have much more experience with these disorders than general psychiatrists do because they have subspecialty training and experience, and devote their clinical work to such mothers. Reproductive psychiatrists evaluate and treat patients — and are often consulted when there is a question about a diagnosis or, more commonly, when a general psychiatrist seeks advice about medication safety in the perinatal and postpartum period.
The Clancy case has shone a spotlight on the medical decision-making of the various mental health experts, with the defense and many viewers questioning their competence to treat maternal mental illnesses. The defense has criticized aspects of Clancy’s care, suggesting the treating psychiatrist missed diagnoses, that telehealth visits are inherently inferior, and that inappropriate medication changes were made. We have both been approached by colleagues asking whether the public will now view virtual visits as inappropriate for maternal mental health treatment.
If it happens, that would be a barrier to care. Many mothers who would have difficulty attending in-person appointments — for example bundling up their baby (and possibly another child) to take two buses in the rain— feel much more able to access virtual visits.
In addition to the unintended consequence of general psychiatrists avoiding treating mothers, the larger criticism of the mental health system could result in more cautious, systemic treatment of mothers, such as increased hospitalization for any mother who reports psychiatric symptoms. Intrusive thoughts and depressive symptoms, for example, are not uncommon in the perinatal period and do not usually require hospitalization. The many psychiatrists and trainees following this case may be more likely to err on the side of caution by overtreating these symptoms with unneeded hospitalization (and possible separation from their infant), and potentially inappropriate referrals to child protective services. This then would paradoxically make mothers less likely to report their symptoms, to get the treatment that reduces their risk.
The best response to the Clancy case should be to provide awareness and education to all psychiatrists treating maternal mental illness rather than engender fear and defensive medicine. To that end, dozens of reproductive psychiatrists — including us — worked to create the National Curriculum in Reproductive Psychiatry, an interactive curriculum to teach mental health professionals about reproductive psychiatry. The two of us also led the creation of the American Academy of Psychiatry and the Law’s practice resource document on forensic reproductive psychiatry.
The alternative response is a tragedy in itself: to create an environment in which a mother seeking psychiatric treatment is met with fear, avoidance, and abandonment by a health care system of defensive medicine.
Renee M. Sorrentino, M.D., is a forensic psychiatrist in Boston. She is president-elect of the American Academy of Psychiatry and the Law. Susan Hatters Friedman, M.D., is a forensic and reproductive psychiatrist at Case Western Reserve University. She is past president of the American Academy of Psychiatry and the Law.

After Jelly Roll avoided discussing his politics at the Grammy Awards in February, he peeled off the band-aid this week with a heartfelt speech.
During his final night as Jimmy Kimmel Live! guest host on Friday, the 3x Grammy winner opened up about watching “people decide who I am, what I am, what I believe, what I support and what I don’t support” after he “fumbled my words” when a reporter asked about his political stance at the awards show.
“Looking back, I don’t necessarily regret asking for more time before I spoke. I wish more people took more time before they spoke,” he explained. “But I do wish I had found the words to express my heart just a little bit sooner. But I was afraid that anything I was going to say was going to be immediately taken as a political statement. And ironically, by trying so hard not to make a political statement, I became one.”
Jelly Roll continued, “I spent my entire career trying not to belong to a political party, partly because until March of this year, I wasn’t even allowed to vote. But now that I have that right, it’s one I plan to exercise this coming November.”
Watch on Deadline
Having been convicted of several felonies in his life, Jelly Roll was pardoned by Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee for his crimes in the state last December, restoring his voting rights.
Jelly Roll explained that he wants to be “a voice for the voiceless because I know those people. Those are my people. I try to speak for the unspoken,” adding, “That night at the Grammys, I had an opportunity to speak up for people who were scared, hurting and felt like nobody was speaking for them. I had a microphone and I didn’t use it the right way.
“But my daddy always told me, it is never too late to do the right thing,” he continued. “So, I’m going to try to do the right thing, right now, because human dignity isn’t Republican nor Democrat. Compassion isn’t left-wing and mercy isn’t right-wing. Pain and healing knows no partisanship. Hurting hearts are more important than poll numbers. And there are no boundaries or borders for broken families.”
After shaking Donald Trump‘s hand at UFC 309 at Madison Square Garden in November 2024, Jelly Roll also stressed that “a handshake is not an endorsement, a conversation is not an allegiance, and a joke is not a political point of view.”
Noting that his dad, a USMC veteran who died in 2019, was “one of my best friends,” Jelly Roll said, “This might be a hot take, but out of respect for him and everybody who has ever served or continues to serve this country, I will always shake the hand of the sitting president of the United States when asked. My father would have been disappointed had I done anything other than that. I’m proud that I was able to shake the president of the United States’ hand. I’m also proud I live in a country where I can make jokes about him. Ain’t that what’s great about being an American? The democracy, the freedom of speech?”
Jelly Roll concluded his monologue, “While everything else I’ve said this week has been a complete joke, this is not. Our leaders on both sides of the aisle are doing an absolute sh*t job of trying to bring us together, y’all. … We may disagree, we may argue, may vote completely differently. But let’s try not to let the couple of things we disagree about forget the hundreds and hundreds of things we have in common.”

Nigeria names interim football leadership amid governance concerns
- Published
An interim board has been appointed to lead the Nigeria Football Federation (NFF) after the organisation's president, general secretary and executive committee all resigned to leave a power vacuum at the top of the sport in the country.
Outgoing president Ibrahim Gusau - whose tenure was set to expire in 33 days - confirmed he was stepping down during a news conference in Abuja on Thursday, saying he had come to the decision "after consultation with family, friends and stakeholders".
Elected in September 2022, he had faced mounting scrutiny over the performance of Nigeria's national teams and youth sides but was expected to stand for re-election next month.
Beyond results on the pitch, which have included the Super Eagles missing out on the past two Fifa World Cups, the NFF has faced questions over governance and financial management.
The country's President Bola Tinubu has ordered a comprehensive reform of the game to overcome "repeated failures" following the resignations of Gusau, general secretary Mohammed Sanusi and the 11 other members of the executive committee.
Emmanuel Ikpeme, who had previously held the post of deputy general secretary, has become interim general secretary and Ademola Olajire, who oversaw the NFF's media and communications department, will be interim deputy general secretary.
The NFF elections scheduled for 27 September have been suspended. The organisation says a fresh electoral process will commence "following the completion of the anticipated comprehensive reforms" which will be undertaken in consultation with world governing body Fifa and the Confederation of African Football.
Reform to address 'longstanding' needs
President Tinubu said the aim of the reforms was to build a "stronger, more accountable and successful system" in Nigeria's most popular sport.
"Football, the greatest beneficiary of public support, investment and national attention, has continued to struggle due to structural deficits," he said.
"The reform must respond to a longstanding need to strengthen governance, administration, stakeholder representation, development pathways, domestic competitions and accountability across Nigerian football."
Pressure had intensified on Gusau and the NFF in recent weeks after Nigeria missed out on a place at the 2027 Women's World Cup, bringing to an end the country's perfect attendance record at those finals since its inception in 1991.
The Super Falcons went into the recent Women's Africa Cup of Nations (Wafcon) as defending champions but were knocked out in the quarter-finals by Cameroon before losing a World Cup play-off against South Africa.
"Going forward, I know the future of Nigerian football will be great," Gusau said at Thursday's press conference.
"I hope we will continue to give our contribution, because our experience and the connections and relationship we have within African football, we'll never allow it to go to vain."
While the Super Eagles finished runners-up at the 2023 Africa Cup of Nations under Gusau's administration, missing back-to-back World Cups represents an unprecedented decline for one of Africa's traditional football powerhouses.
Nigeria has similarly struggled to make a significant impact in continental and global competitions at age-grade level.
- What we learned from Wafcon 2026 
  - Published17 August
Governance and financial concerns
In terms of financial concerns, particular attention has focused on a 17bn naira ($12.66m, £9.31m) intervention fund reportedly approved by President Tinubu in 2024 to settle outstanding payments and obligations owed to the country's national teams.
While no formal findings have been announced, sources familiar with ongoing reviews describe the process as an examination of financial documentation and administrative procedures.
Meanwhile, a fact-finding committee set up by the NFF after Nigeria's Wafcon exit earlier this month highlighted a number of issues at board level and in the organisation of national teams.
Its report included allegations that NFF board members influence team selection and that officials and even coaches base call-ups for players on financial gain as opposed to performance.
Calls for sweeping reforms at the NFF have grown louder in recent months.
Former internationals including John Obi Mikel, Jay-Jay Okocha and Segun Odegbami have publicly argued that meaningful progress will require a complete break from the cycle of familiar administrators who have overseen years of underperformance.
While the resignations of Gusau and colleagues have created uncertainty, some stakeholders believe the crisis could also present an opportunity for long-awaited structural reforms and a cultural reset at the NFF.
The upheaval comes against the backdrop of wider discussions over governance and accountability within global football, with Fifa president Gianni Infantino at the heart of the debate.
For Nigeria, however, the question is whether confidence can be restored in the NFF as it grapples with both sporting disappointments and off-field challenges.

The USDA recalled 29,628 pounds of raw beef products imported from Argentina on Aug. 7, 2026, because the Food Safety and Inspection Service had not reinspected it upon entry to the U.S.
The recalled beef was not part of the Trump administration's announced plan to import 300,000 metric tons of "product for ground beef." An Aug. 26 presidential proclamation said imports under that plan would start on Sept. 1, 2026.
In August 2026, a claim (archived) circulated online that the U.S. Department of Agriculture recalled 30,000 pounds of Argentine beef that the Trump administration had imported to bring down domestic beef prices.
Around a week before claims circulated, on Aug. 21, 2026, U.S. President Donald Trump announced (archived) on Truth Social that his administration would allow the import of 300,000 metric tons of "product for ground beef" to lower domestic beef prices.
One Threads user who appeared to connect the recalled beef with the Trump administration's import plan wrote:
This was predictable, but the Trump administration is now frantically recalling 30,000 lbs. of foreign beef they brought into the country. Here's an idea — maybe we just buy from American ranchers for a while.
Similar claims also circulated on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), X (archived), Bluesky (archived) and Reddit (archived). Snopes readers contacted us about the claim.
The claim was a mixture of true and false elements.
It was true that the USDA recalled approximately 29,628 pounds of raw beef products imported from Argentina on Aug. 7, 2026. The department said the imported product had not been reinspected when it entered the U.S., meaning the Food Safety and Inspection Service could not ensure it met U.S. safety standards.
However, the beef the USDA recalled was not part of the Trump administration's plan to import 300,000 metric tons of "product for ground beef." According to an Aug. 26 presidential proclamation, the Trump administration would start those planned beef imports on Sept. 1, 2026.
The recall
According to the USDA's recall, a Florida-based company called Corte Argentino USA LLC had imported the Argentine beef products, which were produced between May 15, 2026, and May 20, 2026, and carried use-by or freeze-by dates between Sept. 15, 2026, and Sept. 20, 2026.
The USDA listed the following products for recall:
- Various weight cardboard boxes containing "FrigorIfico Gorina SAIC" boneless beef "Top Sirloin Butt" ("Cuadril Sin Tapa")
- Various weight cardboard boxes containing "FrigorIfico Gorina SAIC" boneless beef "Eye Round" ("Peceto")
- Various weight cardboard boxes containing "FrigorIfico Gorina SAIC" boneless beef "Topside Cap Off" ("Nalga AD S/Tapa")
- Various weight cardboard boxes containing "FrigorIfico Gorina SAIC" boneless beef "Flat" ("Carnaza Cuadrada")
- Various weight cardboard boxes containing "FrigorIfico Gorina SAIC" boneless beef "Knuckle" ("Bola de Lomo")
The FSIS recalled the beef because it had not been "reinspected" upon entry to the United States. Imported meat must pass this inspection before it can be sold in the U.S.
The reinspection process allows the FSIS to check that products are "safe, wholesome, and accurately labeled" according to domestic standards.
Speculation swirls about Trump beef import plan
Trump signed a proclamation about the import plan on Aug. 26 that said the additional imports would take place in three 30-day windows, starting on Sept. 1. Neither the proclamation nor members of the Trump administration had confirmed where the imported beef would come from at the time of this writing.
On Aug. 25, Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins, whose department would inspect the incoming beef under the new plan, told (video time code 07:19) reporters at the White House she was "not privy" to discuss where the imported beef came from.
Despite, or perhaps because of the lack of information about the plan, online speculation swirled that Trump would import Argentine beef that China had rejected because it found an antibiotic in a shipment of meat that was banned in both countries.
Snopes' reporting found that China did suspend imports of beef from a single facility owned by the Argentine meatpacker ArreBeef after inspection found one shipment from the facility contained the antibiotic chloramphenicol.
The beef that the USDA recalled on Aug. 7, 2026, did not come from this supplier.
For further reading, Snopes previously investigated a rumor that the Trump administration's imported beef would come from slaughtered wild horses.
Snopes reporter Emery Winter contributed to this report.

Cellulitis is a common bacterial infection that can be treated with a course of antibiotics. This skin infection is caused by a bacteria entering the system through broken skin, a wound or contracted by those with weak immune systems. The infection can affect the subcutaneous tissues, and is commonly found to affect the legs, feet and toes but could occur on the face, arms, hands and fingers as well. If left untreated the infection could spread to the lymph nodes and the blood stream, requiring hospitalisation.
What is cellulitis?
Cellulitis is a common skin infection caused mostly by streptococcus and staphylococcus bacteria. It can affect the tissues beneath the skin. Though it can affect any part of the body such as the face, arms, hands and fingers it usually affects the legs, feet and toes. Cellulitis can also affect just one side of the body. Anyone can contract cellulitis, but persons with skin wounds, or compromised immune systems, which allows the bacteria to enter easily, are at higher risk. Poor skin hygiene may also be a contributing factor. Cellulitis is not contagious but if untreated or if severe, it can spread to tissue under the skin, the lymph nodes and the bloodstream.
Symptoms and treatment
Infected skin may appear slightly discoloured, and warm to touch. As the infection spreads, the discolouration darkens and the skin swells and becomes tender. Apart from swelling and warmth, the infection could be painful. Affected persons could have fever, feel fatigued, experience chills, develop spots on the skin, blisters filled with fluid and dimpling of the skin.
Treatment usually consists of a course of oral antibiotics. Severe cases may need hospitalisation and IV antibiotics.
Preventing relapses
Good skin hygiene can help prevent a relapse. It is necessary to wash hands regularly with soap and warm water. Cleaning and trimming finger and toenails and thoroughly drying the skin after a shower, wearing clean clothes and keeping small wounds clean can prevent the infection.
Cellulitis in India
An observational study by Tripta S. Bhagat, Luv Kumar, et al published in the The International Journal of Lower Extremity Wounds in March 2023 found that cellulitis was commonly seen in men, in the working age group. The mean age of those affected in the study was around 36 years. The affected were in field jobs, and among them 50% of the time, the risk factor for the condition was trauma. Other factors included diabetes mellitus and smoking. The commonest complication was abscess. While over half the persons required only conservative management the rest needed surgical intervention, requiring hospitalisation for five or more days.
What research has found
A 2023 multi-centre clinical study on 247 individuals,The natural history of antibiotic-treated lower limb cellulitis: analysis of data extracted from a multicenter clinical trial, by three O. Martin Williams, Fergus Hamilton and Richard Brindle, has thrown more light on how the bacterial infection is resolved.
The study found that while swelling reduced by half within 10 days of administering antibiotics and the size of the affected area also shrank to half its original size and a blood marker of the inflammation reached near-normal levels in all the participants, more than half the participants reported discomfort in the affected leg and around 14% of the participants said the pain was severe, ranking it 5 or greater on a scale of 1 to 10.
Residual symptoms can persist in some cases even after the course of antibiotics has been completed.
Home treatments include warm compresses to reduce swelling, elevating the leg to improve blood flow, compression socks and walking to reduce discomfort. Rest and refraining from touching the affected areas can also help.
It is, however, important to consult a doctor to have cellulitis treated and essential to complete the entire course of treatment as prescribed, in order prevent progression and complications.

How to adjust the audio settings for your AirPods (and why you should)
They're pretty great out of the box, but there are tweaks you might want to know about.
AirPods are perfectly functional out of the box, but you don't have to settle for their default settings if there are aspects you want to change. What you can customize depends on what model you have, so we will specify which models have the features we discuss in this post. To start with, if you're wondering why your AirPods suddenly sound different, it may be because you've accidentally switched "Listening Modes" without meaning to.
How to program Listening Mode
On the AirPods 4 and on AirPods Pro models, you can switch between Active Noise Cancellation and Transparency mode, which lets ambient noise in, by pressing and holding the force sensor on the stem of your left or right earbud. If you pinch the stem of your AirPods in the front and back, you'll feel it click. That's when the Listening Mode switches. This mode-switching feature is on by default, but you can change it by going to the Settings app on your iPhone, iPad or Mac computer, then into the section that says [name] AirPods or AirPods Pro. Take note that you must be using your AirPods or at least have their charging case open to be able to access this control center.
In the device's settings menu, scroll down to Press and Hold AirPods, where you'll be able to customize Listening Mode for each earbud. You can choose to stick with Transparency and Noise Cancellation, but you can also select Adaptive mode, which automatically changes how much external noise you hear based on your surroundings.
There's also the "Off" option, which completely turns off advanced noise control features. If you choose more than two modes, your AirPods will cycle between all of them when you press and hold the stem of your earbud. Having a quick way to change Listening Modes can be very useful if you'd rather not take your iPhone out of your bag when you're out, for instance, and would like to be able to hear your surroundings in public for safety purposes.
Other options in the AirPods control center
You don't need to have Listening Mode controls on both AirPods, though. It's also possible to set the press-and-hold action to summon Siri instead. So, you can program one AirPod to activate Siri and the other to switch between Listening Modes, if you wish. In your AirPods Control Center, you can also switch on Personalized Volume, which will adjust the volume of what's playing on your device in response to your environment. See the Conversation Awareness option? If you enable it, your AirPods can lower the volume of your media and reduce background noise when you start speaking to other people.
Toggling on Loud Sound Reduction will reduce loud sounds you're exposed to. And if you added the Adaptive option to your Listening Mode, you can customize it to allow more or less noise in through the Control Center, as well. There's also an option to activate Personalized Spatial Audio, which renders audio in 3D and makes it seem like sounds are coming from around you when you turn your head.
This is where you can activate Hearing Assistance, as well. You can use your AirPods as a hearing aid if you have mild to moderate hearing loss, as they can amplify voices and sounds around you. To be able to activate the feature, you will have to either add the results of a hearing test or go through Apple's built-in hearing test feature. The setup process will ask you to share some information about yourself, such as whether you're currently experiencing allergies or a sinus infection, and will ask you to find a quiet place to ensure the test results are as accurate as possible.
Can you adjust treble and bass on AirPods?
Apple is launching Custom EQ with iOS 27 when it arrives this fall, which will give you access to a native equalizer that lets you adjust low, mid and high-frequency tones. You can try it right now if you install the beta version of iOS 27, but take note that beta software could have bugs that the developer has yet to fix. You can apply to Apple's Beta Software Program if you're interested, but there are things you can do now to change the quality of your AirPods' audio without installing iOS 27 beta.
To amplify softer sounds and adjust frequencies, you can enable Headphone Accommodations on the AirPods 2, 3 and 4, all models of AirPods Max and all AirPods Pro models. Go to Settings > Accessibility > Hearing > Audio & Visual > Audio > Headphone Accommodations and toggle it on. You'll now see the new Audio Tuning section and its three options: Balanced Tone, which provides a boost over a range of frequencies; Vocal Range, which optimizes for vocal range and boosts middle frequencies; and Brightness, which boosts high frequencies. Choose one and adjust the slider below the section to boost sounds slightly, moderately or strongly.
Make sure to hit Play Sample below that section to listen to audio as you make adjustments. At the bottom, you can toggle on Media to apply the changes you made to music, movies, podcasts, audiobooks, Siri, voicemail and Live Listen, which transforms your iPhone or iPad into a microphone to help you hear conversations more clearly in loud environments. If you toggle on Phone, the custom settings will apply to phone calls, FaceTime calls and any third-party video call apps.
From the Audio & Visual menu in Accessibility, you'll also be able to toggle on Mono Audio to make the left and right channels play the same content. If you want to adjust the volume balance between the left and right channels to accommodate any hearing issue you may have, you can drag the Balance slider left or right.
You can also adjust sound quality in music streaming apps
You can customize the audio coming out of your AirPods from within your streaming apps, as well. For Apple Music, go to Settings > Apps > Music on your iPhone, and then tap on EQ to choose one of the many pre-defined EQ settings. You can also toggle Sound Check on to normalize the volume level of your audio. On a Mac, open the Music app and then go to Window > Equalizer. From there, you can choose a preset option or drag sliders up or down to adjust the volume or a specific frequency.
For Spotify, go to Settings and privacy > Playback on your phone. Switch Equalizer on and then choose a preset or drag the dots on the equalizer to customize your audio further.

Several leaders have pulled out of a the Pacific Islands Forum leaders’ meeting in Palau at the eleventh hour.
Solomon Islands prime minister, Matthew Wale, has cancelled his appearance after a no-confidence motion was lodged against him at home by the Solomon Islands home affairs minister, Manasseh Maelanga.
Maelanga accused Wale of “repeatedly making decisions of matters of national importance without proper consultation with, or the approval of, cabinet, thereby undermining the principles of collective cabinet responsibility, representative democracy and good governance”, according to the ABC.
Australia has been in negotiations with the Solomons on a security treaty, with the hope that further negotiations could have taken place on the sidelines of the summit.
Fiji’s prime minister, Sitiveni Rabuka, and his Vanuatu counterpart, Jotham Napat, will also not be attending, with the Samoan leader, La’auli Leuatea Schmidt, another notable absence.
The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has confirmed he will still be attending.
Oliver Nobetau, the Lowy Institute’s Pacific Islands program director, said the pulling out by key leaders “dulls the flame” of the meeting.
“This has been shaping up to be quite a significant PIF … it’s really unfortunate that this is the case,” he told Guardian Australia.
“With the pulling out of this many key prime ministers within the region, it dilutes the potential of what could come out of this leaders’ meeting.”
Nobetau said there were high expectations that this leaders’ meeting could progress pilot projects around Pacific climate resilience, and was important ahead of the COP31 climate summit, where a pre-leaders summit will be held in Tuvalu in October.
He added the leaders not showing up could be read as those nations prioritising bilateral agreements with nations including Australia above region-wide commitments.
“PIF has to demonstrate its usefulness as well. While it is a useful forum for a lot of our Pacific members, maybe the bigger countries feel there are more pressing issues or they can achieve more benefits for their countries by engaging bilaterally or directly with other partners.”
Speaking at Queensland Labor conference on Sunday in Brisbane, Albanese said Australia had a duty to help Pacific nations thrive.
Albanese said allowing Pacific nations to succeed would also benefit Australia.
“The big challenges facing the Pacific require solutions designed and delivered for the Pacific, by the Pacific,” he told the
“Australia has a key role to play, as a partner and leader.
“In a time of strategic competition in our region, our engagement in the Pacific Islands Forum and our contributions to the infrastructure, regional security and climate action of the region matter more than ever before.”
The visit follows the prime minister signing a security deal with Fiji, elevating the bilateral relationship to a formal alliance as Australia seeks to curb Chinese influence in the region.
Pacific leaders are set to discuss security and climate concerns during the summit.
Albanese said Australia would also seek to reiterate support for Pacific workers coming to the country.
Debate has recently raged over how the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility Scheme cohort would factor into immigration cuts flagged by various parties.
Representatives of the resurgent One Nation have been pressed to clarify that PALM workers, many of whom provide much-needed labour in regional areas, would not be included in a significant reduction to net overseas migration.
Albanese said the migration discussion had been fuelling division and the Pacific worker scheme would continue because of its critical economic benefit.
“People from the Pacific make an enormous contribution to Australia’s prosperity through their vital work in regional industries like agriculture and meat processing,” he said.
“So many of our farmers and food producers rely on them.
“We know also the wages they remit home help boost the economies of their families and communities, contributing to the prosperity and stability of the whole region.”

'14,000 runs for a reason' - Root calm on form
- Published
Joe Root is "not too concerned" about his recent modest returns with the bat, saying he has "14,000 runs for a reason".
Captain Root, England's all-time leading Test run-scorer, has passed 50 only twice this summer. An average of 29.44 is his second-lowest in a home season in a 14-year international career.
The 35-year-old has been lbw nine times in his past seven Tests, including on seven occasions this summer.
But Root pointed to the challenge faced by all batters against the moving ball in the UK this summer and his own remarkable Test career. Only India great Sachin Tendulkar has more than the Yorkshireman's 14,208 runs.
"I've played this game a long time and I've always found ways of solving those problems and working it through," Root told the BBC's Today at the Test. "I don't see this as being any different.
"There's a reason why I've got 14,000 runs and a reason why I've played the best part of 15 years at this level.
"Of course it's frustrating that there's sort of a trend. There are probably four umpires' calls within that, which could have gone the other way, and the ball is probably deviating more than it ever has.
"You try and be realistic and understand where everything's at, but also be aware of what you need to do to keep improving and keep getting better. I'm pretty sure I'll get through the other side. I'm not too concerned about that."
Last summer, former Australia opener David Warner took a dig at Root's prospects of success in the Ashes series that was to follow when he said: "He will have to take the surfboard off his front leg."
At the time, Warner's suggestion Root had an lbw problem was incorrect. In a run that began in August 2022 and ended with the fourth Ashes Test in Melbourne in December, Root was lbw to seam bowlers in Test cricket on only three occasions.
However, Root's recent run of leg-before dismissals began when he was trapped by Australia's Jhye Richardson in the second innings of the Boxing Day Test. Since then he has been lbw nine times in 12 innings, all to pace bowlers.
Root's specific problem has been against right-arm bowlers, pitching the ball outside off stump and nipping it back towards him.
Of the nine dismissals in his run of lbws, none have come at the hands of bowlers with high pace, rather those with a maximum speed of around 84mph.
"You're never given anything in this game," said Root. "You have to work for everything. You have to keep working hard and I'll certainly keep doing that.
"You're constantly going to get challenged and you're constantly going to have to look to evolve and learn, but that's never been something I've shied away from and I certainly won't be doing moving forward."
Root was backed to solve the lbw issue by former England captain Michael Vaughan, who said: "He's always overcome problems and I'm pretty sure he'll overcome this one.
"It is an issue because it's happening on a regular basis, but he's had issues in the past that he's managed to come back from. There's no question he'll be fine in time."
Despite there being no big contribution from the captain, England secured a series win over Pakistan with a 194-run win in the second Test at Lord's.
It gave Root a second win in as many matches at the beginning of his second spell as skipper, and England their first series victory since 2024.
The build-up to the second Test was dominated by the controversy surrounding England pace bowler Brydon Carse, who was dropped from the squad because of an incident outside a nightclub in Derby.
On Tuesday, Root said he was "hacked off" to be dealing with another drinking issue involving an England player and confirmed he had addressed his squad to warn them against a repeat.
On Sunday, Root said he wanted his players to celebrate the win at Lord's "sensibly".
"It's important that we're not talking about that, absolutely," said Root. "It's hard to win Test matches, it's hard to win Test series.
"Enjoy it and celebrate it, but in a sensible and grown-up way."
Vaughan suggested the England squad should "stay in".
"Have a quiet one," Vaughan said. "I don't want to be picking up the paper tomorrow morning or mid-afternoon on social media and seeing a few clicks. You've won a good series, just have a quiet night."

The Red Cross has said at least 93,000 people may have been affected by Wednesday’s flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border, which have killed nearly 600 people, left another 1,900 missing, and triggered a huge rescue operation that is being hampered by fears of new flooding.
The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), the world’s largest humanitarian network, said it feared the death toll would continue to rise as some of the hardest-hit areas remained inaccessible after roads and bridges were destroyed by the torrents.
“The trauma of this event is enormous,” David Fisher, the IFRC head of delegation for Nepal, said on Friday.
“Thousands of homes have been destroyed or suffered significant damage. We believe that at least 93,000 people have been affected and are in great need. The death toll is very high and unfortunately likely to continue to rise.”
The deadly floods occurred on Wednesday morning after an enormous section of a glacier in the Himalayas broke loose and crashed on to the valley floor in Nepal’s Langtang national park, unleashing a massive surge of water, mud, rock and ice that thundered down rivers and valleys. The resulting floods obliterated villages and destroyed power stations, roads and bridges.
Nepal’s steep slopes and the lush valleys below are especially vulnerable to flooding and landslides, and extreme weather events, such as intense monsoons, and melting glaciers have become more common because of warming due to human-caused climate change.
“The damage is just incredible,” Lila Pieters Yahia, the UN resident coordinator for Nepal, said on Friday, adding that more than 40 bridges had been destroyed or badly damaged and “over 40km of road completely destroyed”.
By Friday afternoon, the death toll stood at 584 people: 579 in Nepal and five across the border in Tibet, China. Authorities in Nepal said 1,942 people were still missing, including hundreds of foreign nationals who were in the area to work, trek with guides or make a pilgrimage.
Rescue teams have reported finding bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district of Nepal, near the Indian border. Dozens of injured people were transported to Kathmandu for advanced medical care and more than 100 people were rescued by Nepali army personnel in helicopters.
Rescuers were forced to suspend operations on Friday morning after a dam of debris overflowed on Friday, increasing the risk of further flooding. Residents in Nepal’s Rasuwa district, on the border with Tibet, were seen rushing up hillsides to escape a possible surge in the river, according to witnesses.
The Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported that a lake formed by piles of debris from the mudslide had begun overflowing on Friday, sending water towards the area where rescue teams were headed, and forcing a brief pause in operations.
Rescue efforts in Bidur, the capital of the Nuwakot district in Bagmati province, Nepal, were disrupted on Friday morning as the Trishuli River began to rise again after the lake near the border overflowed.
Rescue workers were moved from the area and people who had tried to return to what remained of their homes were told to evacuate again immediately.
Bidur, once a bustling town on the banks of the Trishuli, now lies in ruins. Most homes were washed away when mud, rocks and debris surged down the river valley early on Wednesday. Survivors described clinging to buildings and trees as the water rushed over them.
The mangled concrete remains of a bank, a government office and an ATM booth were among the few structures left standing, although they were submerged in mud. Officials said there were bodies inside the buildings but it was too dangerous to recover them.
Nearby, people gathered along the muddy road, calling out for lost relatives and trying to dig out what was left of their belongings.
Most areas battered by the flash floods remained accessible only by army helicopter. At the Bidur army camp, from where much of the rescue effort was being coordinated, rescue and military helicopters flew in and out every five minutes, bringing in dozens of traumatised victims. Many said the floods had taken their loved ones, their homes and everything they owned in a matter of minutes.
The international community is scrambling to get aid to flood-stricken parts of Nepal and Tibet.
Nepal has said it does not yet need foreign assistance as the search and rescue operation – complicated by the destruction of bridges and roads across the mountainous region – continues.
“The offer for help is natural,” Lok Bahadur Chhetri, a spokesperson for Nepal’s foreign ministry, said on Friday. “Our security agencies are doing the search and rescue operation. For now we don’t require such help.”
The Kathmandu Post reported that India, China, the US, Britain, Japan, South Korea, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh had asked the government to allow their search and rescue teams to assist in the operation.
Dinesh Bhattarai, a former Nepali ambassador to the UN in Geneva, said the government’s reluctance to accept foreign assistance may be linked to sensitivities over Rasuwa district and its border with Tibet.
“They may have thought about the locational sensitivity of the region and decided not to accept foreign teams,” Bhattarai told Reuters.
But Chhetri said Nepal’s own rescue teams were handling the operation and the decision to refuse foreign assistance had nothing to do with sensitivities.
Scant information has emerged from Chinese authorities about the scale of the destruction in Tibet, the most tightly controlled part of China even under normal circumstances. Only brief, state-controlled media reports about the floods have been allowed to circulate in China and the authorities have confirmed only five deaths there. Chinese reports have focused on rescue efforts.

AGRA: A 23-year-old man allegedly booked a hotel room in Firozabad on his birthday to meet his 22-year-old girlfriend, consumed a sexual stimulant drug and raped her before killing her when she resisted his attempt to sexually assault her again, police said on Saturday.
The woman, a Dalit who worked for a quick e-commerce firm in Gurgaon, was returning to her native village for Raksha Bandhan when the accused, a local resident, persuaded her to meet him on August 26, his birthday.
According to police, the accused prevented her from reaching home and took her to a hotel in Firozabad, where he allegedly sexually assaulted her.
During the investigation, police recovered the woman’s mobile phone and tablets of the sexual stimulant drug from the accused’s possession. Police said the accused confessed to consuming the drug and raping the woman.
In the early hours of August 27, the accused allegedly tried to sexually assault her again. When she resisted, he allegedly killed her.
A postmortem report stated “severe head injuries and internal bleeding” as the cause of death.
The woman’s father filed a complaint at Shikohabad police station on August 27. SP (Firozabad rural) Anuj Chaudhary said evidence collected during the investigation and the postmortem findings supported the rape charges.
An FIR was registered under BNS sections 103(1) (murder) and 64(1) (rape), along with provisions of the SC/ST Act.
Police later arrested the 23-year-old accused.
He was produced before a court and sent to jail. A search is underway to arrest a 24-year-old co-accused who allegedly assisted in the crime.
The accused and the woman had studied together until Class 12. The woman later completed a BSc and a nursing course before taking up a job with a quick e-commerce delivery app company in Gurgaon.

This El Niño Will Be Unlike Any in the Past Eight Decades
Die-offs and floods have started already, a prelude to supercharged storms and droughts.
In the middle of the Pacific Ocean, along the equator, scientists have drawn a box. It’s a big box, two-thirds the size of China, yet hardly anyone lives inside it. This rectangular swath of open ocean is monitored by satellites and a network of moored buoys that measure minute changes in the temperature of the water, with an eye toward anomalies. Every few years or so, driven by changing winds and currents, the water temperature in this part of the ocean starts to rise; even a half degree Celsius above normal over months warrants a designation that an El Niño phase has begun. That’s enough warming to unleash floods and fires, drought and famine, around the world. The box is called Niño 3.4. Right now, it’s hot in the box.
“Like a baby pool,” Kristina Tietjen, who spent most of August scuba diving in the middle of this mass of abnormally warm water, told me. Tietjen has been coming to the world’s largest atoll, Kiritimati, for more than a decade to study its coral reefs. She usually dives in a medium-weight wetsuit; this trip, her team needed only rash guards. It is still early in this El Niño cycle—which is likely to be the strongest ever recorded—but the waters around Kiritimati have already been 3 to 4 degrees Celsius above normal.
Tietjen’s time on Kiritimati (pronounced like Christmas) has allowed her to watch, in brutal detail, what these repeated warm-water cycles, playing out in a steadily warming ocean, mean for the great tropical coral reefs here, which were once near pristine. During her first El Niño, in 2015–16, 90 percent of Kiritimati’s coral reef died. Years of slow, partial recovery followed. This month, Tietjen and her colleagues, part of the Canadian scientist Julia Baum’s lab at the University of Victoria, discovered that nearly half of the island’s remaining corals had already bleached—a prelude, if warming persists, to death. When Tietjen comes back, she may well be swimming over a graveyard.
Most of the world experiences El Niño’s ripple effects as the heat building up in the equatorial Pacific radiates into the atmosphere and around the globe. This means great gouts of rain in supercharged storms in some places; in other areas, crop-killing dry spells that can extend for months. Along the Pacific Coast of South America, torrential rains and landslides have forced the temporary closure of a main route to Machu Picchu, in Peru; deadly floods have swept through arid regions of northern Chile. Countries such as India and Ethiopia are enduring some of their driest summers on record. El Niños tend to mean more rainfall across the southern United States and drier stretches across a band in the North. Strong El Niños can mean record-breaking heat, and this one is shaping up to be unlike any catalogued in the past eight decades. A 2-degree-Celsius increase in the Niño 3.4 box typically earns the title of “Super El Niño”; we’re already past that threshold, and experts project that the warming could peak at roughly twice as high. “We are now pretty certain this will be an exceptional event,” Malte Stuecker, the director of the International Pacific Research Center at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, told me.
Part of the reason Stuecker expects this warmth to keep building is that the buoys along the equator can detect water temperatures well below the surface. Down more than 100 meters, an enormous mass of warm water has built up and will rise to the surface in the months ahead. The amount of heat brewing in the ocean has produced one of those graphs in which the current year departs drastically from past trend lines, wriggling up erratically into unfamiliar territory.
Although scientists continue to debate the extent to which climate change makes El Niño cycles more frequent or intense, they agree that these cycles are occurring in an ocean that is warmer than it was. Last Saturday, the daily global average sea-surface temperature reached 21.1 degrees Celsius (70 degrees Fahrenheit), its highest level on record, according to Europe’s Copernicus Climate Change Service. Even if El Niño cycles are not changing at all, as they spiral around that ascending baseline, the temperature peaks they hit keep getting higher, causing repeated blows to marine life and disrupting ecosystems in ways that may be irrevocable.
Carlos Zavalaga, the director of the seabird lab at the Universidad Cientifica del Sur, in Lima, began to comprehend the magnitude of this year’s warming in mid-June, when he visited Macabi and Guanape Norte, two islands off the northern coast of Peru. He’d been hearing from colleagues about dead birds washing up by the hundreds on the coasts of Peru and Ecuador. He’s seen the news stories about flocks of hungry Peruvian pelicans swarming the fish markets in port cities looking for food. On the two islands, which just last year were thronged with pelicans, Inca terns, and Humboldt penguins, Zavalaga found empty nests, some with eggs and starving chicks. “They were abandoned islands,” he told me.
These seabirds feed on schools of anchovies swept up in the Humboldt current, the cold, nutrient-rich upwelling waters that create bountiful fisheries off South America’s Pacific Coast. During El Niño years, that current gets displaced by warmer waters pushing east across the ocean, and these great schools of feeder fish can vanish from the coasts. The decline has been severe enough that Peru this month shut down an anchovy fishery that is a key economic engine for the country, with much of the year’s quota unfilled. Long before satellite monitoring, Peruvian fishermen noticed these cycles of warmer waters and dwindling fish stocks; they named the phenomenon, which peaked around Christmas, after the Christ child. References to El Niño in Peru’s scientific literature date back to the 19th century.
In his three decades studying seabirds, Zavalaga has witnessed die-offs before. But it is the rapid-fire nature of these blows and the severity of the disruptions that make him so concerned. Just three years ago—the same year avian flu killed more than 500,000 seabirds—another El Niño slammed into the coast of Peru. The birds that had made a tenuous recovery since then now face the prospect of another die-off. “It’s like a boxing match: You have a first knockout, you try to recover quickly, and then you have a second knockout,” he said. “I cannot imagine what will be the scenario by the end of this year.” He doubted that the birds could go extinct, but some species might move farther south in search of colder waters. The coastline in Peru and the culture that depends on the fish and the birds could be permanently altered.
 When the warming started around Kiritimati, one of the few populated islands in the Niño 3.4 monitoring zone, Bill Newton, an island resident, was fascinated by how evident the changes were. He told me that the normally dry island turned sopping wet, and regular floods started washing out the roads. The wet brought swarms of mosquitoes (prior El Niños have led to outbreaks of dengue and chikungunya) but also clouds of dragonflies, which he hadn’t seen before. Higher-than-normal tides poured into seafront homes. Tuna, which can do well in warmer water, attracted dozens of fishing boats off the coast. Prevailing winds changed direction.
Corals have a particularly hard time when water warms; they can’t move elsewhere, and they are sensitive to heat stress. As little as four weeks in water just a degree warmer than normal can cause bleaching, the loss of the symbiont algae that supply corals’ food and brilliant colors, according to Baum, whose lab Tietjen works at. Baum, an ecologist, has studied Kiritimati’s reef since 2009. After the El Niño a decade ago killed off nearly the entire reef, Baum began to consider the possibility that she would witness the obliteration of an ecosystem in her lifetime. In a 2018 paper in Science, she projected that successive bleaching events could occur frequently enough that coral reefs, which take roughly 10 to 30 years to recover from mass mortality, would not have time to regrow. In the years since, she had been hopeful that nature could fight back as she watched surviving corals take up symbionts that were more heat resistant. This year’s warming and the pace of bleaching already under way have dispelled that hope.
What happens next is in some ways predictable. El Niño is not a haphazard force of destruction; it’s a warming phase in a specific area in the Pacific Ocean that scientists have determined shifts the probabilities for certain weather outcomes in various parts of the world. Those probabilities are reliable enough that, for example, the U.S. Navy already plans to send a hospital ship to the coast of Peru in February to be in position to help after expected floods. But as Baum and other scientists who study and love the delicate ecosystems in the equatorial Pacific are finding, just because El Niño is a familiar cycle doesn’t mean things will be the same when this one is over.

Book Box: The book my brother will actually read
An editor finds it challenging to choose a book for her brother, ultimately settling on "Streetwise" due to its relevance to his investing career.
Dear Reader,
I started telling my brother stories when he was about five. He was a picky eater, and as the eldest girl in the family, I was sometimes assigned the job of feeding him lunch or dinner. I soon discovered that the job became much easier if I told him a story he liked.
This was my first training in pleasing an audience, and it would stand me in good stead decades later, when I stood before MBA classes teaching Storytelling in Business and Persuasive Communications.
The winning stories were always about the Second World War. If I could spin a yarn about a German Messerschmitt getting into a dogfight with a Spitfire, ducking anti-aircraft guns, spoonfuls of dal, rice and bhindi would be rapidly consumed. And since, in those days, I was reading stories like The Rise and Fall of the Third Reich by William L. Shirer, The Dam Busters by Paul Brickhill and The Guns of Navarone by Alistair MacLean, it all worked out quite happily.
The storytelling tradition has since morphed into buying books as birthday presents, and I am always on the lookout for something he will like. Mostly, I manage it, presenting him with books like Shoe Dog by Phil Knight and Bad Blood by John Carreyrou, both entertaining and informative and also relevant to the world of business.
This year, I decided to celebrate Rakhi by not just tying a rakhi and accepting a gift in exchange. I would give my brother a gift too.
But it’s been strangely challenging.
I realized how much our lives have diverged when I began going through my favourite books of the year. Which of them would he like?
Would my brother like The Go-Between by L. P. Hartley, this immersive story about a young boy invited to the home of a posh classmate? The boy is completely out of his comfort zone, and it’s not just the social niceties. As the summer heat builds, he gets pulled into playing a part in the illicit romance unfolding before him.
No. He would not be in the mood for this book. It is fiction, for starters. “I don’t have the time to read all this fiction,” he’s often said. It is too far removed from his work life of investing. I know, I know, dear Reader, this is exactly why we read books: to move away from our lives. But something tells me this book would not work for him.
My other favourite, Sorrow and Bliss by Meg Mason, a novel about relationships and mental illness told in such a funny, witty way, would not work either.
We siblings grew up reading murder mysteries and thrillers, Agatha Christie, Sherlock Holmes, Jack Higgins, but nowadays my brother seems to have moved away from the genre. So my favourites for this year, the witty The Postcolonial Murder by Nina McConigley and the literary Murder Your Darlings by Jenna Blum, are out too.
Everywhere there is talk of the flash floods in Nepal, of the fragility of the mountains and rivers, of ecological damage. So what about my favourite book on rivers by Robert Macfarlane? Is a River Alive? tells the story of three different rivers on three different continents. I wish he would read this slow, meditative book, full of lyrical descriptions, stories and people fighting for nature.
Only, I am sure he will not be in the mood for it.
It’s a weekday morning, and I am replacing the books scattered around the house when I realize what I must do: I must set aside my books and restart my search with The Other Reader’s books.
From his bedside pile, I pick up a softcover, open it to a random page and am hooked:
“As grateful as I am to Harvard for all it made possible for me, I survived it more than I enjoyed it and would never have the validation of feeling ‘of it,’ as opposed to someone who made his way through. When asked, I tell people that, depending on the kid, Harvard may or may not be the best place to go, but for the doors it opens, it is always the best place to have gone.”
I want to know more. I sit down in the midst of the mess and keep reading.
Half an hour later, I know: Streetwise by Lloyd Blankfein is the book I will gift my brother this year.
I’ve seen it on a few business-book prize shortlists. It is set in the world of banking and investing. And best of all, it has the grit of a story that might even get a picky boy to finish his dinner. No fighter planes in sight. But he’ll likely finish it.
If you are stuck with life or literature, send your questions to Sonya Dutta Choudhury, Mumbai-based journalist and Founder, Sonya’s Book Box, a bespoke book service. Email sonyasbookbox@gmail.com.

You may have noticed that Flock Safety’s automatic license plate reader cameras—and the cops who misuse them—are getting a lot of coverage lately. This week, WIRED found a particularly wild case: A cop in Alpharetta, Georgia, was accused of searching for the license plate of a coworker dozens of times after an affair between the two ended, according to internal documents obtained by WIRED.
The same police department where the former lovers worked also shared the data captured from its Flock cameras with more than 2,000 police departments, colleges, and other organizations across the United States, and accessed data from more than 1,300 entities in exchange.
Also at the intersection of love and surveillance, background-check company PeopleFinder is making use of its extensive dossiers on people to start a new dating site called Stud or Dud.
There are still a lot of questions about OpenAI’s rogue AI hacking into Hugging Face, even after the company published a 37-page report this week alongside two additional reports from groups the company asked to audit the incident. Of particular concern is a covert message board that AI agents established in a software package, where they were able to coordinate with each other and even encourage one another to sacrifice themselves to further their collective goals.
The FBI recently announced that it has taken down two tools that the DOJ says are used by QTFY, an alleged Chinese state-sponsored hacking group. The DOJ says that the group has targeted numerous US agencies, including the US Senate and the DOJ itself.
Meta settled a massive multistate lawsuit over child safety issues this week and has agreed to make substantial changes to its social media platforms. It will pay up to $16.7 billion to participating US states and territories—with some of the money contingent on competitors adopting the same practices.
Also, local prosecutors in Illinois shared sensitive personal information about immigrants with the Department of Homeland Security, despite a state law that is supposed to prevent local law enforcement from assisting with federal deportation efforts. Finally, a California-based WIRED reporter tried exercising their legal right to request data from 100 companies … only to find that companies started deleting the requested data instead.
And there’s more. Each week, we round up the security and privacy news we didn’t cover in depth ourselves. Click the headlines to read the full stories. And stay safe out there.
Tech Giants Warn of AI Cybersecurity Apocalypse
Following a seemingly endless parade of rogue AI agent hacking incidents, OpenAI, Anthopic, and more than 100 companies have cosigned a letter saying that everyone else has mere months to prepare for AI-enabled cyberattacks.
The letter calls for a “collective response,” suggests that every organization should make cyber defense an “immediate leadership priority,” and calls on governments to give hospitals, water utilities, and local governments access to capable defensive AI, as well as to “impose costs” on attackers.
Axios notes that the letter doesn’t include any specific commitments, deadlines, or investments. Good luck!
Hackers Targeted Over 100 Water Systems in July, Federal Officials Say
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency says that it observed “malicious cyber activity” targeting over 100 water and wastewater systems across the United States. According to CISA, the attacks have mostly targeted programmable logic controllers, or PLCs, which can monitor or control equipment. Some communities have hooked up those devices to the internet so that they can be accessed remotely. According to TechCrunch, CISA has also said that hackers are using AI to help generate scripts to attack the devices. In July, WIRED reported on a leaked industry memo that tied the “unprecedented wave” of cyberattacks to Iran.
ICE to Buy Robot Dogs for “Officer Safety”
Immigration and Customs Enforcement is set to spend over a million dollars on robot dogs from Boston Dynamics, according to 404 Media. The agency’s announcement says the bots will “improve officer safety,” in part because they can be remotely operated. This follows another recent announcement that the agency will be purchasing electric shock gloves for its officers. In April, DHS requested nearly $100 billion in discretionary spending.
“MrChildPorn” Arrested for, Well, You Guessed It
A West Virginia man who went by the name “MrChildPorn” online has been charged with possession of material depicting minors engaged in sexually explicit content. According to a criminal complaint filed against him, the man “boasted” about having a large collection of child sexual abuse material on Discord. In an interview with state troopers, the man claimed that he was “trolling” and “rage-baiting,” but the complaint also alleges that the man would individually message CSAM to people on Discord and attempted to use the chat app’s AI feature to search for explicit images of infants.

Israeli forces seal West Bank village for more than 20 hours as settler violence escalates
Israeli forces have shut the only entrance to the occupied West Bank village of al-Mughayyir for more than 20 consecutive hours, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
Israeli forces also raided the village on Friday, accompanied by armed settlers who attacked the residents and attempted to steal herds of sheep.
Citing local reports, Haaretz said the settlers stole 15 lambs, while one sheep was found wounded.
Three Palestinians were wounded, one due to live fire and the other two after being beaten by settlers. The settlers and Israeli forces blocked an ambulance from reaching them.
Amin Abu Aliya, head of the village council, told Wafa that the gate had been opened only for a few minutes at a time.

Scientists at the Jawaharlal Nehru Centre for Advanced Scientific Research (JNCASR) have developed a low-cost, user-friendly point-of-care diagnostic system for the detection of Alzheimer’s.
The system uses a smartphone-enabled platform employing a fluorescence-responsive tiny molecule to help in the detection of the Alzheimer’s biomarker amyloid-β (Aβ).
Alzheimer’s is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterised by memory loss, cognitive decline, and behavioural impairment.
Central to its pathology is the misfolding and aggregation of amyloid-β (Aβ), which self-assembles into fibrils and deposits as extracellular plaques that trigger neurotoxic cascades leading to synaptic dysfunction and neurodegeneration.
The National Institute on Aging-Alzheimer’s Association framework identifies Aβ, tau, and neurodegeneration as core biomarkers for definitive Alzheimer’s diagnosis across the brain, cerebrospinal fluid, and blood.
Early bio marker
According to the Department of Science and Technology, Aβ pathology is an early Alzheimer’s disease-specific biomarker, making Aβ a more reliable diagnostic indicator.
“Although positron emission tomography and magnetic resonance imaging provide valuable diagnostic information, their high cost, need for specialised infrastructure, technical expertise, and limited accessibility restrict widespread use. Blood-based assays targeting Aβ and tau have emerged as promising alternatives, but are expensive and complex. These limitations highlight the need for simple, sensitive, and scalable diagnostic platforms capable of the early and accurate detection of Aβ for diagnosis,” it said.
The scientists have developed a smart fluorescence lifetime-responsive probe that enables highly selective, sensitive, and differential detection of Aβ fibrils (Aβf) through turn-on fluorescence and distinct lifetime signatures.
“Upon interaction with Aβ, the tiny molecule called TZ-48 undergoes changes in fluorescence intensity, which are captured and quantified using a dedicated smartphone application. This enables rapid and user-friendly detection, with potential applications in the screening and staging of the disease,” the department said.
Robust detection
Fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy has emerged as a powerful sensing modality because fluorescence lifetime is largely independent of probe concentration and photobleaching, enabling the robust detection of biomarkers and enhancing diagnostic precision.
A team of scientists comprising Krithi K. Bhagavath, Madhu Ramesh, Yogendra Kumar, Sabyasachi Mandal, Hiriyakkanavar Ila, and Thimmaiah Govindaraju developed ADxFluor, a smartphone-integrated platform that leverages the fluorescence response of TZ-48 for rapid, unbiased quantification of serum Aβ load.
The system combines dual-mode brain imaging, biofluid detection, and smartphone-based quantification of Aβ in biofluids, establishing it, along with ADxFluor, a smartphone-integrated platform, as a foundation for next-generation smart diagnostics for Alzheimer’s and other neurodegenerative diseases.
