Srinagar, Aug 29: Member of Legislative Assembly (MLA) from Lal Chowk constituency Ehsan Pardesi Saturday said the government has initiated measures to upgrade elementary level schools with a focus on improving infrastructure and creating a better learning environment for students.
Talking to Greater Kashmir on the sidelines of the Annual Day function of Government Girls Higher Secondary School (GGHSS) Srinagar, MLA Ehsan Pardesi said that Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) have already been prepared for several schools housed in old buildings, while the government was planning to construct modern school buildings at various locations in Lal Chowk constituency.
“The government has already taken initiatives to improve our elementary level schools. Modern infrastructure would provide students with a better ambience and environment for learning,” he said.
On the disproportionate pupil-teacher ratio in elementary level schools of Lal Chowk constituency, MLA Pardesi said that the government was already working on the “serious issue”.
“I hope that the staff gaps would be addressed in the future,” he said.
Pardesi, however, said that choosing between government and private schools remains the prerogative of parents.
He referred to his recent visit to KothiBagh School and said he was informed by the principal that several parents whose kids were earlier enrolled in private schools have enrolled them in the government school.
Earlier in his address at the occasion, MLA Ehsan Pardesi stressed the need to have dedicated funds to maintain the existing school infrastructure.
He said every school should have a provision for regular maintenance so that existing facilities do not deteriorate.
“Our Director School Education is here. I would request that some funds should be kept available with the school for the maintenance of the existing infrastructure,” he said.
He said the government usually constructs buildings without any provision for its maintenance. “A school should look like a school. It is important that any new infrastructure which comes up remains properly maintained,” he added.
He congratulated the faculty, management and students of GGHSS Amira Kadal, Srinagar for their performance and wished them success in the future.

President Donald Trump interrupted Nvidia’s all-hands staff meeting on Thursday morning when he called CEO Jensen Huang midway through, three sources who witnessed the interaction tell WIRED.
Nvidia’s all-hands meetings typically involve Huang presenting or answering questions, on stage, to in-person staff at the company’s Santa Clara, California, headquarters, while thousands of remote employees tune in to a virtual livestream. During the meeting on Thursday, Huang received a call on his mobile phone, which he stepped aside to take.
Staffers could clearly hear Trump’s distinctive voice through Huang’s onstage microphone, although they couldn’t make out what he was saying. Less than a minute later, Huang returned to the stage and resumed the company meeting.
A spokesperson for Nvidia declined to comment on the incident. But staffers were abuzz about the president’s inadvertent interruption.
In a post on social media later that day, Trump congratulated Huang on Nvidia’s "incredible" quarterly sales and rosy financial forecast for next year. On Wednesday, Nvidia had reported second-quarter revenue of $96 billion, up 106 percent from the same period last year.
Huang regularly jet-sets to Washington to lobby government officials on behalf of his company’s interests—selling chips and building AI infrastructure—and has been in closed-door meetings with Trump before. But the president’s direct call to Huang came at an interesting moment for Nvidia: Earlier on Thursday, the chip giant announced a new employee-funded political action committee, through which it plans to donate to federal candidates as debate around AI policy grows. Nvidia and the Trump administration haven’t always agreed on how to regulate open AI models and sales of advanced chips to China. Bloomberg Law first reported the news of the Nvidia PAC.
The Information recently reported that Nvidia has been in advanced talks to acquire the open-source platform company Hugging Face, which makes AI data sets, models, and development tools widely available to software engineers who are building AI. An acquisition could be valued at more than $13 billion, Business Insider reports, which would almost certainly require merger approval from US antitrust regulators.

Opening summary: race to rescue tunnel workers
Welcome to our continuing coverage of the aftermath of the deadly flash floods near the Nepal-Tibet border.
Rescuers in Nepal and China are still trying to locate thousands of people who are missing days after a wall of water and debris swept through the Himalayan region.
The combined toll in Nepal and Tibet rose to at least 750 dead and more than 3,000 people missing after China’s latest update on Sunday. Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 missing, while Nepali officials confirmed 734 dead and 2,498 people missing. There were reports of some dead swept downstream as far away as India.
China said 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries were missing on the Tibetan side of a border crossing with Nepal: the highest number was from Nepal at 104, while 49 Indian, 33 Latvian, 18 American and 15 British citizens were also unaccounted for.
In a breakthrough late on Saturday, the Nepali army was able to insert a pipe into a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydroelectric site where workers are believed to be trapped.
“We have already started sending air through the small opening, and we will now begin excavation work and send the rescue team inside,” said the home minister, Sudan Gurungd. More than 100 workers may still be alive and trapped inside such tunnels, with rescue efforts focused on the Trishuli 3A and 3B sites.
Here’s the other main developments:
- 
  Four days after the disaster, authorities said some bodies being recovered had decomposed beyond recognition. They would be buried after legal formalities because of health risks and a fear of disease outbreaks. “DNA samples will be collected, and the bodies will be buried in an open space,” the Chitwan district administration said in a notice.
- 
  The foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, said Nepal required specialist assistance to rescue people trapped in tunnels; restore transport and communication lines where bridges had been destroyed; identify bodies; conduct DNA testing; and store bodies for longer periods.
- 
  A team of Indian tunnel experts arrived in Nepal on Saturday, Khanal said. China’s Xinhua news agency reported Beijing had dispatched five tunnel experts to support rescue efforts, with four more due to join them.
- 
  The US will provide $3.6m in humanitarian aid to Nepal, “including up to three months of emergency food assistance to up to 10,000 flood-affected households,” the state department said in a post on X.

Newcastle, Australia – A 134-year-old former courthouse in Newcastle, Australia, is now a facility of Japan’s Nihon University, with its preserved courtrooms offering students a hands-on lesson in the justice system.
Completed in 1892, the former Newcastle Courthouse, distinguished by an arched entrance, is listed as a New South Wales cultural heritage site. After the court moved to a new building in 2016, Nihon University purchased and restored the property.
The university has used the former courthouse since 2024, along with classrooms and lodging facilities built on either side.
Courtrooms of different sizes, holding cells as well as rooms where defendants met their lawyers, remain in their original configurations. The defendant’s dock in the former Grand Courtroom is enclosed by a wooden railing, with a dedicated staircase connecting it to the cell directly below.
Students taking part in a study program in Australia in late August held a mock trial in the former Grand Courtroom.
The smaller courtroom was named the Yamada Room after Akiyoshi Yamada, a former Japanese justice minister and founder of Nihon University’s predecessor, Nihon Law School, which was founded in 1889.
The university and the former courthouse date back to roughly the same period.
“Preserving the site’s historical value is meaningful,” Takenari Shiba of Nihon University’s office for internationalization promotion said. “We hope it will help students learn from the past.”
Haruhisa Ikenaga, a second-year student of the university’s College of Law, said, “The courtroom felt authentic, and I gained a vivid sense of how it differed from Japan.”
Hana Harada, a second-year student of the university’s College of Humanities and Sciences, said: “I saw cells for the first time. Scars on the walls prompted me to imagine the emotions of people who had been incarcerated there.”

In late August 2026, U.S. President Donald Trump ordered that Lake Ontario, the easternmost of the Great Lakes, be renamed "Lake America" in government publications. Trump signed that executive order while he feuded with Canadian leaders over failed trade negotiations.
Some people on social media immediately claimed Trump wasn't even targeting a Canadian name in his apparent attempt at retaliation. One X user wrote (archived) that Lake Ontario was named by Indigenous tribes hundreds of years ago, and Canada's province of Ontario adopted the name later.
People made the same claim on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived) and elsewhere on X (archived).
Preserved maps from early explorers show the name "Ontario" for the lake long before the province was labeled with the same name, which aligns with the lake's and province's histories as described by museums and historians. Therefore, we've rated this claim true.
According to the Canadian Encyclopedia, "Ontario" is thought to have come from an Iroquois word meaning "beautiful lake" or "sparkling water." Ontario's provincial government says the Iroquois word is "kanadario."
Other sources transliterate the word differently. The National Museum of the Great Lakes, says "Ontario" derived from the Huron (also known as the Wendat, who spoke an Iroquois language) word "Ontarí'io," meaning "great lake" or "beautiful water."
Either way, "Ontario" was an indigenous word referring to a body of water, not a piece of land.
"Ontario" was first applied to the lake by Europeans in 1641, according to the Canadian Encyclopedia, and appears on maps of North America as early as 1656.
The lake's name in the 1650 was in flux, at least for French cartographers exploring the area. Maps from 1653 and 1656 refer to the lake as, translated into English, Lake St. Louis or Lake Ontario. Notably, the 1656 map referred to the lake as Ontario first and Lake St. Louis second. Similarly, a map from 1657 called it Ontario Lake with a mention of the St. Louis name beneath it.
None of those maps labeled the land north of the lake, the present-day province of Ontario, as Ontario. In fact, this holds true even in a 1775 French map and a 1777 English map, both of which refer to the lake simply as "Lake Ontario."
The province of Ontario came into being in 1867, according to the Canadian Encyclopedia, when Britain's North American colonies joined together to become the Dominion of Canada. Before then, the land that's now Ontario was known as Upper Canada and Canada West. Prior to 1791, it was part of a singular province of Quebec that included both today's Ontario and Quebec.
While neither the Canadian Encyclopedia nor Canadian government webpages explicitly state that the province got its name from the lake, it at the very least used the name after the lake had long been called Ontario by the people around its shores.
For further reading, we previously investigated a claim that Trump demanded changes to Canada's French-language rules as part of a trade deal.

The recently notified treated wastewater reuse policies for Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand offer an instructive example of what contextualised policymaking can look like. Developed through an extensive consultative process, these policies do not apply a one-size-fits-all template. They account for the stark geographical diversity within each State, the distinct needs of hill communities versus densely populated plains, and embed principles such as fit-for-purpose reuse approaches, integration with urban planning and river rejuvenation, community participation, blended finance and public-private partnership pathways, and digital monitoring systems that make reuse accountable.
However, examples such as these remain the exception rather than the rule. Every summer, Indian States make headlines grappling with water scarcity and yet, the story never seems to change. Rampant groundwater extraction, and the relentless tug-of-war between agriculture, industry, and urban demand have become a recurring script. The real question is no longer whether India needs to rewrite this narrative, but how much longer it can afford not to.
Hidden opportunity
Treated wastewater is an untapped resource waiting to be mainstreamed. For agriculture, industry, urban landscaping, and ecological restoration, it offers something increasingly rare: a reliable, drought-proof supply. India’s water future may hinge less on discovering new freshwater reserves and more on the intelligence with which the country recycles what it already has. National missions such as the Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation have done commendable work in scaling sewage treatment infrastructure, but pipes and plants alone do not close the loop. A treatment facility that discharges into a drain rather than feeding a farm or a factory is infrastructure without purpose.
What India needs is an ecosystem that converts capacity into practice: institutional coordination across departments, pricing signals that make reuse economically rational, quality standards that inspire confidence in end-users, and city-level roadmaps that translate national ambition into local action. The National Framework on Safe Reuse of Treated Water (SRTW), 2022 offers precisely the canvas India needs to navigate this transition. More than a guiding document, it represents a policy signal that reuse is no longer peripheral — it is a national priority. By mandating States to develop their own reuse policies, the Framework acknowledges that water solutions must ultimately be local, even when the vision is national. Several States have already responded, putting in place policies that set reuse targets and chart a path toward measurable milestones.
Treated wastewater, reframed correctly, is not a waste management problem; it is an economic opportunity. Its case rests on hard, computable value — building climate resilience, drought-proofing cities, reducing costly dependence on freshwater, enabling industrial and urban growth without straining existing supplies, and supporting low-carbon urban development at scale. Until this economic case is made clearly and credibly to State governments and planners, the policy will remain an aspiration.
Reuse succeeds only when utilities, urban departments, irrigation agencies, and industries stop working in silos and start working in an integrated manner. The financial momentum needed to hit reuse targets is rarely found in new budgetary allocations alone; it is unlocked by identifying synergies with existing schemes and convergence opportunities across programmes that are already funded and moving.
Need for awareness
There is one more constituency that cannot be overlooked: the public. Misconceptions about the safety of treated water run deep. The National SRTW Framework as well as the reuse policies for Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand have chosen to call treated water Apna Jal (our water), signalling something that no document can fully capture: that the shift India needs is not just infrastructural but psychological.
Experts working with State governments are witnessing a quiet shift in thinking — that the safe reuse of treated water is not just a policy consideration but a strategic imperative. Yet, several States remain on the sidelines. States that have not yet adopted a clear plan for water security through reuse are not just falling behind, they are running out of time to catch up.
Sonia Grover and Girija Bharat are water policy experts at Mu Gamma consultants

Fery beaten by Buse in Winston-Salem final
- Published
Arthur Fery missed out on his first ATP Tour title with a straight-set defeat by Ignacio Buse in the final of the Winston-Salem Open.
Fery, who was the talk of Wimbledon as he reached the semi-finals of his home major in July, lost 6-3 6-2 to Peru's Buse.
The 24-year-old was the first Briton to reach the final of the ATP 250 tournament in North Carolina and will rise to 33 in the world rankings as a result - overtaking Cameron Norrie as British number one.
Only eight weeks ago, before his astonishing run to the last four at the All England Club, he was ranked outside the top 100.
Little could separate Fery and Buse in the early stages of their match on Saturday, before the Peruvian took control with a break to love for a 5-3 lead.
Fery quickly fell further behind in the second set as Buse opened up a double break cushion with no reply, and while he pulled back one of those breaks, it proved to no avail as his opponent reeled off three straight games to seal the win.
For 22-year-old Buse, victory makes him the youngest ever winner of Winston-Salem and marks a second career title after he beat American Tommy Paul at the ATP 500 event in Hamburg in May.
With little time to reflect on his Winston-Salem run, Fery will now head to New York for the US Open, which starts on Sunday.
Set to play at Flushing Meadows for the first time, he faces a tough opening tie against Italian 13th seed Lorenzo Musetti.
Fery is one of nine British players set to feature in the main draws at the US Open, the final Grand Slam of the season.
Joining him in the men's draw are Norrie and Jan Choinski, qualifiers Toby Samuel and Harry Wendelken, and lucky loser Jacob Fearnley.
Katie Boulter is joined by qualifiers Fran Jones and Harriet Dart in the women's draw, but both Jack Draper and Emma Raducanu are missing through injury.

‘Not one complaint’: Tharoor praises govt’s Nepal flood rescue efforts in letter to EAM
The toll from flash floods in central Nepal rose to 669 on Saturday, with more bodies being recovered, even as more than 2,000 people are still missing.
Congress MP Shashi Tharoor on Saturday wrote a letter to external affairs minister S Jaishankar, “appreciating" the government’s rescue efforts regarding missing Indians in the Nepal floods while also giving suggestions.
Several Indians are still missing in the aftermath of the Nepal flash floods. The MEA’s own tally puts them at 287. In his letter, Tharoor asked the Narendra Modi government for a full NDRF contingent and heavy-lift helicopters for rescue operations. He urged the government to pull out all stops to rescue the stranded or those who may still be alive beneath the debris.
"Every hour that passes narrows the ground on which hope can still stand," the MP from Thiruvananthapuram said in his letter.
Deep Dive
"I am writing to you regarding the Indian nationals who remain missing following the flash floods that struck Nepal on 26 August. India's response has been swift and substantial. The Prime Minister's early outreach to Kathmandu, the four tranches of relief material, the eleven-member team of doctors, paramedics and tunnel rescue experts, and the control room and Embassy helplines have all made a difference," Tharoor said.
An ice-rock avalanche following a glacial collapse near the Nepal-Tibet border on Wednesday sent a torrent of water, mud and debris downstream, wiping out towns and villages, damaging crucial infrastructure and washing away hydropower stations through central Nepal.
The death toll from flash floods in central Nepal rose to 669 on Saturday, with more bodies being recovered, even as more than 2,000 people are still missing. Bodies were recovered from all eight affected districts as search and rescue operations continue on a war footing.
What Shashi Tharoor said in the letter to EAM S Jaishankar
In his letter, Shashi Tharoor noted that India's Ambassador to Nepal, Naveen Srivastava, and his team have worked around the clock.
"The return of the group from Tibet, whom you personally received at the airport, gave many families their first moment of hope in three days. The rescue of the Indian workers at Trishuli- 1 was a genuine triumph," the Thiruvananthapuram MP said.
"Families have noticed all of this. Several have asked me to convey their gratitude to you personally, and I am glad to do so. It is precisely because of this that I feel compelled to urge that our efforts now be matched to the scale and urgency of what has happened," he said.
According to the ministry's briefing, 320 Indian nationals remain uncontactable, including many of Indian origin, Tharoor pointed out. The latest figure from the MEA is 287.
"Hundreds more remain stranded on the Chinese side. Many were pilgrims on their way to Kailash Mansarovar, a journey some had waited their whole lives to undertake. Ground reports suggest that entire stretches along the Tibet-Nepal border and in other badly affected areas, including Timure and Rasuwagadhi, have still not been reached by any search party," he said, noting that there may still be people alive beneath that debris.
The window in which they can be brought out alive is narrowing by the hour, he said.
"I understand that Kathmandu has now agreed to accept limited foreign expertise for tunnel rescue, DNA testing and forensic work, and that our offer to send Indian teams is still awaiting a response. I would urge that we press, at the highest political level and without further delay, for the following: First, the immediate clearance and induction of a full NDRF contingent with its equipment, rather than a limited number of experts," he said in his letter.
The Congress MP called for the deployment of an army engineer task force with earth-moving equipment, along with the Bailey bridges that India has offered, to reopen the Pasang Lhamu Highway. He also called for the deployment of Indian Air Force heavy-lift helicopters for Rasuwa and Nuwakot to reach roads rendered inaccessible.
Tharoor also called for the use of ground-penetrating radar, thermal imaging, sniffer dog squads and satellite tasking to map the debris fields and establish search priorities. He asked the Centre for specific and sustained tasking for the Timure-to-Rasuwagadhi stretch.
"Since Wednesday morning, I have been hearing from families whose loved ones remain unaccounted for. Not one has come to me with a complaint. They speak first of their gratitude for what India has already done, before they speak of their own son, daughter, husband or wife," he said.
What these people have now is a fear that is difficult to put into words, the Congress leader said.
"Above all, they want to know that, whatever the eventual outcome, everything that India could have done was offered, and that nothing was held back," he said.
"With the greatest respect, and with the utmost urgency, I hope we can ensure that no stone is left unturned, and that whatever can be moved is moved now rather than after another round of evaluation. Every hour that passes narrows the ground on which hope can still stand," Tharoor said.

A retired American teacher has reunited with a Chinese farmer 26 years after their initial encounter, returning to the once-barren sandy landscape transformed by his generous donation into a lush green environment.
In 1999, Ronald Sakolsky, now 67, was teaching English in Luoyang, Henan province, central-eastern China, when he discovered Inner Mongolian farmer Yin Yuzhen’s efforts to combat desertification. Inspired by her dedication, he donated US$5,000 to support her mission.
The pair first met during a donation ceremony in the Mu Us Desert in 2000. Afterwards, Sakolsky returned to the US, while Yin used the funds to plant over 50,000 trees.
Today, vegetation covers more than 80 per cent of the Mu Us Desert, which is one of China’s four major sandy regions.
In May, Yin, now 60, reconnected with Sakolsky via video call and invited him back to China to witness the “green miracle” that his contribution had helped foster.

Protests against caste-based reservations were held in Delhi’s Jantar Mantar on 21 August and in Connaught Place on 23 August, 2026, under the banner of the online campaign ‘Reservation Hatao Andolan’ (here, here, here). Against this background, a video showing a massive crowd gathered is being widely shared on social media (here, here), claiming that it shows a huge turnout at an anti-reservation protest at Jantar Mantar in Delhi. Claim: The video shows a massive crowd gathered at Jantar Mantar, Delhi, in support of an anti-reservation protest.
Fact: The viral video shows devotees gathered during the Jagannath Rath Yatra in Puri, Odisha, on 16 July 2026, and is unrelated to the anti-reservation protest in Delhi. The claim made in the post is FALSE.
On performing a reverse image search using the key frames of the viral video led to an Instagram post uploaded on 18 July 2026 that carried the same video and identified it as visuals from the Rath Yatra in Puri. A comparison of the two videos showed identical visuals, including the massive crowd, the open space in the middle, and security personnel wearing blue uniforms.
The Puri Rath Yatra was held on 16 July 2026, while the anti-reservation protest at Jantar Mantar took place on 21 August 2026. Therefore, the viral video was available online well before the Delhi protest and cannot be footage from the protest.
Further, we found a video posted by ANI on 15 July 2026, a day before the Rath Yatra. The video showed security arrangements outside the Shree Jagannatha Temple in Puri ahead of the festival. The same open space and security personnel seen in the ANI video also appear in the viral video. A comparison between both visuals can be seen below.
To sum up, an old Puri Rath Yatra video is being shared as an anti-reservation protest at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar.

Pioneering Care After Crisis: It All Starts with the People
How CityUHK’s innovative Community Chilling Hub is reimagining human care in Hong Kong
[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]
When the devastating fire broke out at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po on 26 November, the response from City University of Hong Kong (CityUHK) did not begin with a strategy memo. “In fact, since the very beginning, it was not a strategy,” says Professor Cherry TAM, Associate Professor from the Department of Social and Behavioural Science (SS). “We viewed it as our expertise, our responsibility … our aim is to care for people and society.”
Within five days—by 1 December—the university had organised a public lecture on resilience, mobilised psychosocial support for affected primary school pupils and begun planning trauma-informed workshops for frontline professionals. What started as an instinctive response soon evolved into something more ambitious: the CityUHK Community Chilling Hub, an innovative model demonstrating the synergies among private and public sectors, academia, public health and social care in Hong Kong. At its heart, the new model demonstrated how crisis exposes the urgency of human care and how universities can help innovate the possibilities.
 
From Academic Department to First Responders
Tam resists the language of “strategy”. The response, she insists, was embedded in CityUHK’s DNA. “At CityUHK, we have the very important mission to engage with the community ... we generate knowledge and we need to contribute to society,” she says.
In this instance, that ethos translated into speed. The resilience lecture was held just days after the fire. Senior management, academic staff and technical support units worked across time constraints and boundaries. “This kind of interdisciplinary, cross-departmental collaboration … happened in a minute,” Tam recalls.
In governance terms, that agility matters. Complex crises rarely fit neatly into existing silos. CityUHK’s response showed how mission-driven institutions can act responsibly across established structures. 
Trauma Support Rooted in Humanity
Beyond public messaging, the department provided direct psychosocial support, particularly for affected primary school pupils. “When we provide professional services for this kind of traumatic experience, the very important first step is to understand, to listen,” Tam explains.
Her team, partnering with an NGO and the University’s senior management, invited students onto campus, offering distance from the disaster site and emotional breathing room. Using adapted cartoon storytelling, facilitators helped children externalise their fears. “Let them know that their reaction is common, it’s normal,” Tam says. Artistic drawing allowed quieter students to express what words could not: “Silence is a very, very important signal.”
This layered approach—listening, normalising, identifying and referring—demonstrates sustainable recovery at the human scale. Rather than imposing solutions, the team built support around lived emotional realities.
Hope, Tam emphasises, is central to recovery. “Hope is very important. Without hope, maybe they would keep declining.” Bringing children to campus was therefore symbolic as well as being therapeutic. 
“Even though university feels like it’s a long way off,” she says, “bringing them onto campus gives them hope for the future.” Exposure reframed identity not around trauma, but possibility.
It is understandable that the fire’s psychological impact extended beyond residents. “Even many helping professionals felt it was totally out of their capacity to handle such a big trauma,” explains Tam. By early January, the department launched a full-day trauma-informed workshop using a “train the trainer” model. The aim was not just immediate intervention, but strengthening the professional ecosystem.
“This kind of training is very sustainable,” Tam explains. “With more professionals equipped, when we have other issues they can take action more immediately.” Rather than relying solely on centralised emergency responses, the university invested in distributed capacity—networks of practitioners ready to respond to future crises.
From Fragmentation to Integration
The early initiatives made clear post-traumatic recovery after such an unprecedented fire was not short-term but challenging. Long-term and continuous support to guide affected people to overcome and develop post-traumatic growth is indispensable. With this mission—and made possible through the generous and timely contribution of China Hongqiao Group Limited—CityUHK established the Community Chilling Hub, drawing on interdisciplinary expertise in social work, counselling, psychology, criminology and sociology, as well as technologies in health screening, to offer longer-term and sustainable support for the affected communities in a welcoming, stigma-free space.
“The services nowadays in Hong Kong to handle mental wellness-related issues are quite fragmented,” Tam says. Many are limited by age or socioeconomic criteria. The hub aims to be different: “Without age limit, without economic limit. Anyone can come here. It is a very inclusive service.”
The hub’s model integrates physical health screening, mental health support, social services and spiritual well-being. “It’s a one-stop shop—physical, social, mental and spiritual wellness support,” Tam says. This integrated design aligns with sustainable development goals: breaking down silos, reducing inequalities in access and addressing well-being holistically.
Beyond the Medical Model
Central to the hub is social prescribing, first developed in the United Kingdom. Traditionally, mental health systems have been “very diagnostic oriented, very medical oriented”, Tam says, but after acute intervention, people need community and social support. Social prescribing connects residents not only to therapy, but to social resources through trained community link workers—volunteers drawn from university students and residents.
“We provide basic volunteer training,” Tam explains, linking them with families to co-design tailored “social prescriptions”. The volunteers also build social capital, becoming “the pool of resources in the community to serve in Hong Kong”.
If evidence demonstrates effectiveness, the university hopes to present the model to the government as a scalable alternative. “We can prove the model … and let the government have more alternatives to improve the existing services,” she says.
Enhancing Human Care Through Community
Innovating for better human care is often framed around digital platforms or policy reform. CityUHK’s Community Chilling Hub suggests another path: human care with community capacity, interdisciplinary collaboration and human dignity. “It’s in our DNA … to work with the community, to break through existing silos. Unfortunately, people fall through these cracks,” Tam reflects.
The hub is an attempt to close the cracks. If it succeeds, it may offer Hong Kong—and beyond—a blueprint for human care that is responsive, more inclusive and more sustainable because it begins where all sustainable development must: with people.

Tens of thousands mourn King Harald V in Oslo as Norway enters a new royal era
Tens of thousands of mourners have paid their respects to Norway's King Harald V, who died at 89
OSLO, Norway -- Tens of thousands of mourners paid their respects to Norway's King Harald V on Saturday, placing flowers and condolence cards outside the royal palace in Oslo a day after the monarch died at 89.
A sea of colorful flowers covered Slottsplassen, the square in front of the palace, as a steady stream of Norwegians filed past. A palace gardener removed some bouquets on the south side of the palace to keep pathways clear, Norwegian broadcaster NRK reported. Palace workers also collected cards soaked after a nightly downpour and dried them to preserve the mourners’ messages for posterity, NRK reported.
Across the country, churches and city halls opened specially on Saturday so people could light candles, write down their thoughts about the deceased king in condolence books.
The coffin arrived at the royal palace Friday evening from the National Hospital in Oslo where Harald died.
“It’s special, intimate, and lovely. I’m placing my right hand on my chest in gratitude to him and the royal family,” Roni Ervik, 46, told NRK as he paid his respects. He said he was also paying tribute to the late king on behalf of his family, who are from western Norway.
Harald V died Friday morning and his 53-year-old son, Crown Prince Haakon, became King Haakon VIII.
Haakon adopted the motto “All for Norway,” which dates back to his great-grandfather. His wife became Queen Mette-Marit, while his oldest child, Ingrid Alexandra, became crown princess and heir to the throne.
Haakon is well acquainted with his royal obligations. As his father aged and his health declined in recent years, he stepped in as the country’s regent on several occasions.
Later Saturday, a choir was expected to sing in the Royal Palace Square. The new king was also scheduled to hold audiences with the speaker of Norway’s parliament, the chief justice of the Supreme Court and the presiding bishop of the Lutheran Church of Norway, with Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra also expected to attend, NRK reported.
Haakon is expected to address the people of Norway in his first speech as king either later Saturday or in the coming days.
His tasks in the near future will include shoring up support for the monarchy following controversies over his wife’s past contacts with deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his stepson’s rape conviction.
A date for the funeral has not been set, but the country is officially in a state of mourning and some people decided to postpone celebrations such as weddings and baptisms until after the mourning period has passed, NRK reported.
Norway’s monarchy has old roots, tracing its origins to King Harald Fairhair in the ninth century. When Norway regained its independence from Sweden in 1905, three-quarters of voters in a national plebiscite approved restoring the monarchy. Today, the role is largely symbolic as power lies with an elected parliament, but the country’s royal family retains celebrity and a role in promoting the wealthy nation around the world.

SHIMLA: Ten trains on the Kalka-Shimla narrow gauge railway line, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, were cancelled on Sunday after heavy rain washed away soil supporting a section of the track in Himachal Pradesh's Solan district.
According to railway officials, soil slippage between Koti and Gumman stations left a portion of the track suspended in the air, prompting authorities to suspend operations on the affected stretch on Saturday night as a precautionary measure.
Shimla Railway Station Superintendent Sanjay Gevar said 10 trains running between Kalka and Shimla were cancelled on Sunday. Services will resume only after the track is secured and its safety is assessed.
A railway notification stated that soil around the track near Bridge No. 57 between Koti and Gumman stations had been washed away due to continuous rainfall.
The cancellation of the popular 'toy train' service caused inconvenience to passengers who had booked tickets in advance. The impact was visible at Shimla railway station, which remained quieter than usual on a weekend, with fewer tourists and travellers.
Train services on the Kalka-Shimla heritage line have faced repeated disruptions this monsoon season due to rain-related incidents and landslides.
The 96-km Kalka-Shimla railway line, known for traversing challenging mountain terrain, features 102 tunnels, around 800 bridges and 919 curves, making it one of the country's most iconic engineering achievements and a major tourist attraction.
Meanwhile, rainfall continued across parts of Himachal Pradesh, leading to the closure of 64 roads as of Sunday morning.
According to the State Emergency Operations Centre, 24 roads were closed in Mandi district, 16 in Kullu, seven each in Kangra and Sirmaur, four in Una, three in Shimla, two in Chamba and one in Lahaul-Spiti. In addition, 225 power transformers and nine water supply schemes were affected.
The Meteorological Centre in Shimla has issued an alert for heavy rainfall at isolated places across the state from August 31 to September 3.
Light to moderate rainfall was recorded in several areas since Saturday evening. Dhaulakuan received 38.5 mm of rain, followed by Ghaghas (30 mm), Palampur (23.8 mm), Murari Devi (22 mm), Kahu (11.6 mm) and Pandoh (10 mm). The weather office also reported thunderstorms and lightning activity in some regions.
Officials said that since the onset of the monsoon on June 30, at least 103 people have lost their lives in rain-related incidents across Himachal Pradesh. The state has also suffered losses estimated at Rs 1,184 crore during the period.

Russia says it helped to repel Niger attempted coup
- Published
Russia has said its forces helped to repel Saturday's attempted coup in Niger.
Explosions and gunfire rang out across capital, Niamey, early in the morning, including at a key military airbase and the presidential palace.
Hours later, Niger's authorities said the rebellion had been contained.
Nigerien forces had repelled the attack "with the assistance of servicemen of the African Corps of the Russian Ministry of Defence", the foreign ministry in Moscow said on Sunday.
The ministry also said it would continue to support Niger in its fight against "extremists", but that the situation was now under the control of the legitimate authorities headed by President [Gen Abdourahmane] Tiani".
Russia's African Corps has become a key security partner for multiple military governments in the Sahel, who have been struggling to contain long-running jihadist insurgencies.

The Alliance of Sahel States - composed of Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso - said the attempted coup was "a betrayal by a group of soldiers involved in an attempt at destabilisation".
The authorities have not said how many soldiers were involved in the attempted coup, nor how many casualties there were.
Niger's military ruler, Gen Tiani, who was sworn in as its president last year after he deposed its elected leader, has also not publicly addressed the incident.
The nation's state broadcaster showed footage of several alleged mutineers being arrested by the Presidential Guard.
On Sunday, Niger Press Agency reported that commercial activity was returning to normal, with petrol stations, shops and other businesses reopening.
Supporters of the government gathered at a public square in central Niamey in support of the security forces and Tiani's government.
Air Base 101, the military site attacked on Saturday, is part of the Diori Hamani airport complex.
It hosts Nigerien military aircraft and drones, as well as an Alliance of Sahel States counter-terrorism unit. Russian and Italian forces are also based there, according to news agency Reuters.
Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso are all military-ruled countries that have cut ties with Western partners and strengthened their co-operation with Russia.
But jihadist violence remains widespread in all three countries, despite the shift in alliances.
For Niger's government, Saturday's mutiny highlights that the military is dealing not only with an external insurgency, but also signs of discontent within its own ranks.
The airbase where the mutiny began had itself been targeted twice by jihadists this year – once by an Islamic State affiliate and later by an al-Qaeda affiliate.
Nigerien authorities say security forces have increased patrols around key sites in Niamey following the attempted takeover, including the main airport entrance and the presidential pavilion.

Footage of Tibet floods isn't being shown in China - and we know little about victims there
- Published
The dramatic footage was almost impossible to miss. A torrent of water tearing through Gyirong Port, one of the main border crossings between Nepal and Tibet, sweeping away all in its path as hundreds of people fled for their lives.
The scenes, captured by CCTV cameras, quickly spread on social media and onto screens around the world.
Except here, in China.
Only a single still-frame shot has been broadcast so far by the country's state-run flagship news bulletin.
It has also been difficult to find the video on China's heavily censored internet. It is just as hard to even find posts describing the flash flooding that has claimed hundreds of lives, with just as many still unaccounted for since Wednesday.
Beijing has launched a massive rescue operation involving hundreds of emergency workers, which is continuing, and President Xi Jinping chaired an emergency meeting with officials to co-ordinate efforts.
But when you compare the country's internet content to what much of the world has been seeing online these past few days, China's firewall becomes more visible than ever.
Tibet, which Beijing annexed in the 1950s, had long resisted rule by the Chinese Communist Party.
China has quashed protests over the years, sometimes violently, and has been accused of grave rights violations in the Buddhist region. It has labelled the exiled spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, a separatist.
That history means the very name Tibet draws China's censors. Beijing's sensitivities are especially apparent at times likes this.
There have been daily updates on the missing and the dead, and Beijing has also been posting updates on the rescue operations, as well as the dangers posed by a barrier lake that has been at risk of overflowing.
But there is little detail beyond that. There are no accounts from survivors in Tibet, and almost no user-generated footage showing the deadly moments or their aftermath.
We are yet to hear from anxious families of those missing. Trying to contact people there is near-impossible during regular times.
As a journalist who has covered North Korea, it has often been easier for me to contact interviewees in Pyongyang than it is in the Tibetan capital, Lhasa.
On Thursday night, as global headlines led on the devastation in a Himalayan valley, China's state broadcaster opened its main bulletin with the launch of Xi's new book, a selection of his "most important and fundamental works".
Foreign journalists cannot travel to Tibet without government permission. We have just a few hours to get as much information as we can on huge stories like this before videos are scrubbed and voices stifled.
Instead, we have to rely on state media, which has so far focused on incredibly dramatic rescue efforts.
Specialist search teams scaling mountains and cliff faces, or crossing raging rivers to try to get to the worst-affected areas. We don't yet know what happened afterwards, or who they were able to save.
This is not to say that Beijing is unconcerned. Rather, they are very concerned.
China's Premier Li Qiang was quickly despatched to the region, where he was seen inspecting debris removal - a rare visit by the country's second-most important leader so soon after a major disaster.
The reason for what the world might see as a muted response is to preserve the one thing Xi covets for his country: stability.
The Communist Party will fear that such a disaster could fuel discontent, either with the response or the lack of foresight to prevent it.
It may also fear the impact of a tragedy like this and its potential to be a rallying factor, especially in a community where faith has long played a central role.
Although the region has not seen protests in a long time, Tibetan groups abroad have expressed concern over increasing Chinese control, such as new education laws that they say aim to weaken the role of monasteries and the Buddhist faith.
Just hours after the disaster struck, the Communist Party machine tried to rally its grassroots to stem any signs of discontent of its handling of the landslide.
A notice came from the local party office urging members to step up and help in disaster relief efforts in their area and provide emotional guidance or psychological support to affected residents.
The key line instructs them to "make every effort to maintain social order and ensure stability and public confidence in the disaster areas". Those who perform well would be rewarded - and those who do badly "would be held accountable".
It is a warning that will not be taken lightly. Tibetans in the region can be detained or arrested for speaking to journalists or posting anything online that is seen as contrary to the government narrative, according to rights activists.
That is making it difficult for Tibetans outside the region to find out what has happened to their relatives.
The International Campaign for Tibet, while praising the work of first responders in the area, said Beijing had been removing videos and other first-hand information from social media. It called on Chinese authorities to "disclose complete and verifiable information about the damage and casualties".
To try to understand what life is like for Tibetans, the BBC travelled to a town that sits on the edge of the Himalayan plateau last year - just outside what China calls the Tibetan Autonomous region.
There, we spoke to monks at the Kirti monastery in Aba, or Ngaba in Tibetan, which was once at the heart of its resistance to Beijing. "We Tibetans are denied basic human rights," one monk told us.
They said they lived under constant surveillance and claimed the Chinese government oppressed and persecuted Tibetans. The conversations were brief because we could not be seen speaking to anyone for long.
Beijing denies it is violating Tibetans' rights, and points to the heavy investments it has made in the region to boost tourism and integrate it with the rest of the country.
Nevertheless, people in China will not know very much about what is happening in Tibet right now.

Authorities in Ecuador seize 32 marine iguanas at the airport and arrest a Russian woman
Authorities in Ecuador say they have arrested a Russian woman accused of trying to smuggle at least 32 marine iguanas from the Galapagos Islands out of the South American country
QUITO, Ecuador -- A Russian woman accused of trying to smuggle at least 32 marine iguanas from the Galapagos Islands out of Ecuador was arrested Saturday, authorities in the South American country said.
Police said on X that the iguanas were distributed in eight plastic containers inside a suitcase, adding that the woman was at the airport in Quito and was headed to Iceland.
Ecuador’s Ministry of Environment said the iguanas were feeble and dehydrated, and that a group of veterinarians transferred them to a conservation center, where they would remain until their health improves.
The Russian woman was not identified, but police said they expected to charge her with wildlife trafficking. If found guilty, she could face up to three years in prison.
The marine iguanas from the Galapagos Islands are an endemic species and considered vulnerable.
The archipelago was declared a National Heritage of Humanity in 1979 by UNESCO given its great biodiversity. It is located in the Pacific Ocean, some 620 miles (1,000 kilometers) west of Ecuador.

This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on falling robots and the US-China AI race, follow Robert Hart. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.
China’s robots race ahead
Bots were breaking records and breaking down at Beijing’s World Humanoid Robot Games.
China’s robots race ahead
Bots were breaking records and breaking down at Beijing’s World Humanoid Robot Games.
How it started
I’ve admitted my fondness for robot fail videos on Stepback before, and let me tell you the World Humanoid Robot Games did not disappoint.
The five-day event, which wrapped this week in Beijing, brought high drama, and brought it well. One robot, made by smartphone maker Honor, lost a leg mid-sprint, while others tripped in a flurry of sparks. Another finisher ran straight into a crash mat, bounced off it, and promptly burst into flames. In the weightlifting, one robot lost its balance beneath a modest barbell and toppled inexorably into the judges’ table, arms cartoonishly aloft. Robotic cheerleaders tumbled and stumbled through routines, while a separate bot fell off a platform in circumstances that, had it been human, might have looked suspiciously like it was gawking at the performers.
This was only the second World Humanoid Robot Games, though it was already far bigger than the inaugural event last year. Unlike this year, last year’s records were paltry. The winning 100-meter sprint was a glacial 21.50 seconds and the highest standing high jump was just 0.95 meters. In keeping with China’s habit of turning robots into public spectacle — from intricate dances at a Spring Festival Gala to demos at major tech events — both this and last year’s games were staged in Beijing’s National Speed Skating Oval, a former Olympic venue.
And a spectacle it was. At most sporting events, contestants losing limbs, careening into walls, catching fire, and regularly being carried away on stretchers — oh, and did I mention catching fire?! — would probably be grounds to stop proceedings. At the Humanoid Robot Games, it was par for the course.
Fire aside, the games were unusual in other ways too. Alongside familiar events like sprinting, football, boxing, and weightlifting were more unusual competitions in bed-making, parcel delivery, shelf stacking, clothes folding, and hammering nails. Aptly, there was a firefighting contest too.
These less standard offerings spoke to the real purpose of the games: getting robots out of the lab and into the messy real-world environments their makers hope they will ultimately work in. And China is making no secret of wanting to lead the way.
How it’s going
For all the spectacle and drama, the games show there has been massive progress in robotics in recent years. Records fell, with one humanoid running the 100-meter sprint in 9.39 seconds, beating Usain Bolt’s 2009 world record. Another bot reached 2.88 meters in a standing high jump, nearly half a meter above the human high-jump record that has stood since 1993. Those performances are almost unrecognizable compared to robotics competitions a decade ago, when even the most advanced machines struggled to stay upright.
But the games also show how far there is to go before humanoids are actually useful in the real world. The flashy, video-friendly sporting events were impressive, but the more mundane tasks were less thrilling — I don’t see picking up soybeans with tweezers, block-building, or powder-weighing becoming Olympic mainstays anytime soon.
While many events required robots to operate autonomously — including gymnastics, football, tug of war, table tennis, and some track events — others allowed for human assistance via teleoperation, albeit with a scoring penalty. The dexterity being displayed certainly points to genuine and impressive hardware improvements, but seems like there is still a long way to go before these machines can operate reliably on their own in places like factories or homes.
What happens next
Beijing has not yet confirmed a third Humanoid Robot Games, but given the government’s enthusiasm for the industry, it would be surprising to not get another installment. The city has already confirmed another humanoid half-marathon for April, and the country plans to open its first robot-run hotel next year.
China was the undisputed champion of the games, and the country looks well placed to stay in top position moving forward — both at future competitions and in the humanoid robot industry as a whole. The medal table was almost entirely a Chinese affair, dominated in particular by AgiBot and Tien Kung, each scooping up more medals than nearly every other competitor combined, excluding the other.
In part, that asymmetry reflected the lack of international competition. Although the games were framed as a global affair, 641 of 666 teams were Chinese, domestically representing 157 companies and 200 universities, according to state-run China Daily. While there doesn’t seem to be a public breakdown of entrants, the biggest US humanoid players like Tesla, Boston Dynamics, and Figure were conspicuous by their absence.
Nevertheless, the sheer diversity of Chinese institutions represented in Beijing was a show of force, and a sign of how quickly the country’s robotics sector is maturing, even amid growing concerns about circular investment, thriving companies that lack viable products, and a possible humanoid bubble.
It’s not clear a stronger US showing at the games would’ve changed much. The US still has an edge in frontier AI and advanced chips, but China has been rapidly closing parts of that gap, while also making embodied AI a strategic national priority. The same cannot be said of Washington, which has for years paid much less attention to robotics and now trails China in nearly every regard, including manufacturing, deployment, and hardware. Some reports even suggest that recent efforts to ban foreign robots, a general policy squarely aimed at China, could backfire, given how dependent domestic firms are on Chinese components.
Catching up to China will take serious and concerted effort, but given how quickly the technology is moving, there’s still time to make up ground. Washington is already treating other areas of AI as strategic priorities in its competition with Beijing; robotics could be one of them. There will be plenty of stumbling along the way, and, hopefully, plenty more robot fail videos too.
By the way
- DARPA still runs robotics challenges, but they drew far more attention a decade ago.
- When the US government banned foreign robots, it didn’t just ban humanoids and quadrupeds. It banned Roombas too, reports The Verge’s own Sean Hollister.
- “The brains may come from the US, but the body could very well be Made In China,” writes Business Insider’s Lloyd Lee in a report setting out how the US could do with bolstering its hardware supply chain.
- Unlike language models, you can’t simply scrape the internet to build an AI capable of interacting with the real world. A lot of that data has to be generated, which is why companies desperately want to film you doing chores, or send someone to your house to film them doing them.
Read this
- The Atlantic and the South China Morning Post both have great sets of pictures showing highlights of the games worth checking out.
- Why do we keep laughing when robots fail? An old but still good exploration of that shared joy in vintage Vice.
- You can learn a lot about a robot by kicking it, says Verge alum James Vincent in an excellent Harper’s feature outlining the state of play in the humanoid industry.
- I’m not only about robot fail videos. I can hate them in real life too, as I did with Casio’s fluffy AI pet thing, Moflin.

Body odour is a normal part of life. Contrary to popular belief, sweat in itself does not usually smell. The familiar odour develops when bacteria and fungi that live on the skin break down substances in sweat, particularly secretions from glands in the armpits and groin. In most cases, body odour is harmless and may vary depending on factors such as heat, physical activity, diet and hygiene.
However, a new or persistent change in body odour should not always be dismissed as a hygiene issue, doctors say. In some cases, an unusual odour may be linked to an underlying health condition and may need medical evaluation.
Heat, food and hormones
Several everyday factors can alter body odour. Hot weather and physical activity increase sweating, while tight or synthetic clothing can trap moisture. Garlic, onions, spicy foods, alcohol and certain medicines can also affect body odour.
Hemanath M. J., consultant, internal and family medicine, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, Vanagaram, Chennai, says the apocrine glands in the armpits, groin and scalp contribute more to odour than the eccrine glands, which cover most of the body. Stress can stimulate the apocrine glands and intensify odour.
Hormonal changes can also play a role. Puberty, menstruation and menopause may temporarily alter sweating and body odour. Puberty is one common situations in which changes in body odour are routinely seen. An overactive thyroid, which can cause excessive sweating, may also make odour more noticeable.
A change is more likely to be temporary when there is a clear trigger and the odour settles after the trigger passes. “If somebody develops an odour after eating a particular food, drinking a particular drink, starting a medication or strenuous exercise, or during a period of hormonal change, and it returns to normal after some time, the context helps explain the change,” says Narayanan A., consultant, dermatology, SRM Prime Hospital, Chennai..
Body odour as a health clue
A persistent or unexplained change can sometimes be associated with a skin condition or an underlying medical problem. Skin infections in the armpits, groin or other moist areas can alter odour. These may be accompanied by redness, soreness, itching, peeling or discharge.
“An infection in the groin or axilla (armpit) or excessive growth of bacteria or fungi can alter the odour,” says Dr. Narayanan.
Dr. Hemanath says conditions such as erythrasma and fungal infections can produce a distinct smell, particularly in warm, moist areas. Excessive sweating, or hyperhidrosis, does not itself cause odour but can provide more moisture for bacteria to act on.
Certain metabolic conditions have also been associated with distinctive smells. Uncontrolled diabetes can produce fruity or sweet-smelling breath because of ketone build-up. A rare condition called trimethylaminuria can cause a fish-like odour because the body is unable to break down certain compounds properly.
Odour changes have also been described in advanced kidney and liver disease. But doctors caution against treating these smells as diagnostic tests.
“Some distinctive smells have been described with complications of diabetes, liver disease or kidney disease, but these are clues rather than reliable diagnostic tests,” says Dr. Narayanan. The overall clinical picture, including symptoms, examination and biochemical investigations, is what guides diagnosis.
Need for evaluation
The first step when there is a change in body odour is to look for an obvious trigger. Regular washing, changing sweaty clothes, washing clothes properly and using an antiperspirant can help determine whether the problem responds to routine measures.
But a sudden change in body odour without a clear cause is reason to consult a doctor.The physician would first consider what changed at the same time as the odour. If there is no obvious trigger and the change persists or keeps recurring, a deeper evaluation may be required.
A sudden unexplained increase in sweating, night sweats without an obvious reason, or sweating that interferes with daily activities should also prompt medical attention. Experts list other warning signs such as unexplained weight loss, excessive thirst or urination, fatigue, swelling, fever, night sweats or skin changes. A fruity odour with excessive thirst, frequent urination, nausea, vomiting or confusion requires urgent assessment.
Depending on the symptoms, a doctor may conduct a physical and skin examination and consider tests such as blood glucose and HbA1c, kidney and liver function tests and a thyroid profile. Skin scraping or culture may be considered if an infection is suspected.
Doctors say, body odour should not be used to self-diagnose a disease. Most changes have an everyday explanation, but a smell that is new, persistent, unexplained or accompanied by other symptoms is worth discussing with a doctor

Ontario premier answers Trump’s ‘Lake America’ with giant ‘Lake Ontario’ sign
Ontario Premier Doug Ford has responded to President Trump’s “Lake America” decree with a billboard declaring “Lake Ontario
TORONTO -- Ontario Premier Doug Ford answered President Donald Trump’s “Lake America” decree Saturday with a billboard-sized message on the Canadian shoreline — “Lake Ontario. Now and Always” — as Canadian leaders met the move with ridicule rather than outrage.
Wearing a Team Canada soccer jersey, Ford unveiled the sign near Grimsby, Ontario, and posed for photographs. The 24-by-12-foot (7.3-by-3.6 meter) sign stands on 6-foot (1.8-meter) legs, putting its top about 18 feet (5.5 meters) above the ground — roughly two stories high. The message is repeated in French, one
The display followed Trump’s executive order directing U.S. federal agencies to call Lake Ontario “Lake America.” After months of tariffs, threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state and personal attacks on its leaders, the reaction in Canada has mixed defiance with mockery.
Ford said Trump was trying to rename the lake because Ontario and Canada were “standing up for ourselves” and argued the name would outlast the president.
“Long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario,” Ford said in a video posted on social media.
Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew compared Trump to an aging rock band trying to revive an old hit
“You know when a rock band is really over the hill and you see them like in a casino playing some song from like 50 years ago. I think that’s the part of Donald Trump’s presidency we’re at now, Like he thought they had a real hit, a real golden oldie, with the Gulf of Mexico,” Kinew said, referring to Trump's executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America. “And he’s trying to bring back that, and he’s trying to play the hits for his base. But I think everybody here thinks it’s a little sad and it’s not his best work.”
The mockery was not limited to politicians. Canadian historian Robert Bothwell was even more scathing.
“The greatest country on earth takes this moron seriously?” Bothwell said.
But Bothwell said the dispute was more serious than the jokes, arguing Trump’s broader aim was “to subordinate Canada and at best make it a colony, at worst absorb it into the United States.”
Nelson Wiseman, professor emeritus at the University of Toronto, said Trump “would like Canada to act like a vassal state, but it refuses to do so. That irritates him.”
The dispute comes as relations between the longtime allies worsen over trade. Negotiations collapsed last week, both governments accused the other of making late demands, and Canada announced retaliatory tariffs set to take effect next month.
Trump’s order also came amid an escalating war of words with Ford. In an interview with The Associated Press earlier this week, Ford said Ronald Reagan would be “throwing up” over Trump’s tariff policies and “disgusted with President Trump.”
Trump fired back by dismissing Ford’s comments as “bluster,” calling him Prime Minister Mark Carney’s “flunky” and mocking him as the “less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother” of the late Toronto Mayor Rob Ford.
Trump continued promoting the new name Saturday, reposting a meme showing Canada geese with Trump-like blond hair firing rifles as they “protected” Lake America.
Trump has repeatedly used maps to make political points. A “Gulf of America” map was displayed for a time beside the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office, and Trump has posted images depicting Canada as part of the United States or as the 51st state.
The name Lake Ontario comes from the Huron Indigenous people’s word “oniatarí:io,” which means “lake of shining waters.” The Canadian province of Ontario, founded in 1867, took its name from the lake.
Wendat Nation Grand Chief Pierre Picard, whose people historically lived from the St. Lawrence Valley to the Great Lakes and whose language gave Lake Ontario its name, called Trump’s move an attempt to erase Indigenous history.
“I want to tell him that it is unacceptable for us, as a nation, to have a president who can eradicate our history, our culture and our identity,” Picard said.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney rejected the move, noting the lake’s Indigenous roots and that the name predates both Canadian Confederation and the U.S. Declaration of Independence. Trump cannot require Canada to adopt the new name.

Azerbaijani regime ‘trying to break’ opposition leader by denying him safe water in prison, family warn
Exclusive: The family of Ali Karimli claims the regime is ‘deliberately trying to break him’ as they urged the UK to intervene in the pro-democracy leader’s case
The family of Azerbaijan’s detained pro-democracy opposition leader has claimed that the regime is “deliberately trying to break him” by denying him safe drinking water in prison, amid growing concern over his physical condition.
Ali Karimli, 61, faces life in prison on “politically motivated” treason charges after being arrested in November and accused of plotting to overthrow the government in a Russian-backed coup. He has vehemently denied the charges and is awaiting trial.
His family have raised concerns about his physical state after he spoke with international media from prison in June to appeal for Western governments to put human rights before trade ties with Azerbaijan.
Speaking at the Baku Court of Appeal earlier this month, Mr Karimli sought to replace his pre-trial detention status with house arrest and claimed that his conditions in prison had worsened in recent weeks, according to his lawyers.
He said that for two days he had been denied water that he could safely consume and that he believes the authorities are deliberately trying to make him ill and cause his death.
Mr Karimli says that he is unable to drink the tap water offered to him to due to a gallbladder condition.
Sezan Karimli, his daughter, told The Independent that her father has not been allowed direct contact with the family since June, has been denied food parcels from them, and has spent weeks without ventilation in 30-35C heat.
She said Mr Karimli has been deprived of sleep for weeks and is no longer allowed to exercise, to go outside or to read books or newspapers in prison. His rubbish has not been removed for weeks, she said.
“Since 10 June he has been denied all telephone contact and visits with his family. What motivated it is not complicated: he kept speaking, and this is the punishment,” she assessed.
Mr Karimli is a long-standing proponent of democracy in Azerbaijan and has continued to speak out against alleged rights abuses, including torture, under the government of Ilham Aliyev.
Rights groups say a focused crackdown has targeted Mr Karimli’s Azerbaijani Popular Front Party (APFP) since late 2025. That comes amid a wider silencing of dissent and free expression over the last decade that has seen the arrests of hundreds of journalists, activists and political opponents.
Giorgi Gogia, deputy director of the Europe and Central Asia Division at Human Rights Watch, told The Independent they have seen no credible evidence to substantiate the charge that Mr Karimli was involved in an attempt to violently seize power.
“His prosecution also cannot be viewed in isolation from the Azerbaijani government’s much broader campaign against its critics,” he said, adding: “What we do have is a well-documented pattern in Azerbaijan of government critics being arrested and prosecuted on unfounded or highly questionable criminal charges.”
He said the methods of repression were increasingly familiar: serious criminal accusations unsupported by credible evidence, a lengthy pretrial detention, restrictions on contact with family and lawyers, and other forms of pressure designed not simply to punish an individual critic but to intimidate those around them.
“In Karimli’s case, the deterioration in his detention conditions after he spoke publicly about his treatment is particularly disturbing. The reported sleep deprivation, isolation from his family, restrictions on telephone calls and access to information raise serious concerns about Karimli’s inhuman or degrading treatment.”
Mr Karimli’s lawyers have observed that he appears to have lost “significant weight” in recent weeks, is visibly distressed and has “a markedly yellow complexion and red eyes”.
“We believe the sleep deprivation, the heat without ventilation, and the denial of water and food are being used deliberately to break him physically, because they have not been able to break him any other way,” Ms Karimli added.
She said: “A government confident in its charges brings them to trial, whereas one that holds a man for eight months without trial while degrading his conditions is not building a case, it is applying pressure.”
The pre-trial detention has now been extended to November but no trial date has been set. Ms Karimli said the coming weeks are a “critical window” for her father, who faces a potential life sentence in prison.
“The time for international pressure is now, while he is still in pre-trial detention. Every week in these conditions is a week his life is at risk,” she said.
Ms Karimli urged the UK government – as Azerbaijan’s largest foreign investor – to make a public statement to the Azerbaijani government about her father’s treatment and to press for his release.
She said the latest communiqué to Azerbaijani foreign minister Jeyhun Bayramov regarding Mr Karimli’s detention came on 12 May, before the escalation in June.
Ms Karimli said: “Human Rights Watch said this week that Azerbaijan’s international partners should raise his case publicly and in bilateral meetings. We are asking the UK to do exactly that, urgently.”
A spokesperson for the UK foreign office told The Independent: “We have raised Ali Karimli’s case with senior members of the Azerbaijani government, including pressing them to follow due legal process and ensure necessary access to medical care in accordance with their international obligations and commitments.
"We continue to monitor this case closely, alongside the wider human rights situation in Azerbaijan, and raise concerns about the protection of freedoms directly with the Azerbaijani government."
Azerbaijan’s ministry of foreign affairs did not respond to a request for comment.

A common way to deal with emotions is through food, says Lakshmi Venkatraman, consultant psychiatrist and assistant director of Psychosocial Rehabilitation Services at SCARF (Schizophrenia Research Foundation). Dieting and restrictions on food are also culprits. The vicious circle begins when people tend to eat more, end up feeling guilty at their act, reduce their self-esteem, because of which they binge eat and feel more guilty.
Simple measures such as eating regular meals with all foods, including favourites in moderation, helps. “When we realise emotions are pushing us (to eat), finding ways to tackle the emotions will help,” Dr. Lakshmi explains. “Be mindful while eating, focus on what we are eating, take it quite slow while eating which helps to prevent binge eating,” she points out.
R.M. Anjana, managing director of Dr. Mohan’s Diabetes Specialities Centre, cites the various studies done by the Foundation at various intervals of time, to explain the importance of regulating “what we put into our mouth”. When a person finds that they binge once a week and this persists for three months then it should trigger an alarm, she says. “Diet and physical activity alone can prevent 50% of diabetes,” she said and cited studies that state that binge eating contributes to about 15 to 20% of type 2 diabetes.
A bariatric surgeon aims to moderate the gut hormones, says P. Praveen Raj, consultant and head of the Department of Minimal Access Bariatric and Robotic Surgery in the Department of Surgical Gastroenterology, GEM Hospital and Research Centre, Coimbatore.
The first step is to take a thorough history of the person’s issues. There are various hormones in the gut that regulate satiety, trigger appetite and aid digestion. An imbalance in any one of them could be the cause for obesity. The aim is to treat the cause, he explains. “You rule out the psychological reasons, and the pathological abnormality. Once this is understood we can start to treat it (the condition),” he adds.
The specialists were panelists at a webinar on “The Binge: Learning to handle addictive behaviours,” organised on Sunday by The Hindu. The webinar can be viewed at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Cl4wxf7_HRI

Meta is rolling out an obvious fix to make its AI glasses less creepy amid backlash over the glasses’ non-consensual recordings that have flooded the Internet.
On Friday, The Verge reported that Meta closed a loophole that made it easy for smart glasses users to cover up an LED light that is supposed to alert bystanders that the device is actively recording. Meta had previously deactivated recording if a user attempted to start capturing video after placing a sticker over the light, but people quickly learned that they could get around that by reversing the order of the steps and covering up the light after they started recording.
In a post on Threads, Meta’s executive vice president of wearables, Alex Himel, explained that an update would be rolled out soon that ensures that “the camera will now stop working if the light is covered during a recording.” That way “the capture LED can reliably alert bystanders when photos or videos are being captured for someone’s gallery,” Himel said.
According to Himel, “only a tiny minority of people try to get around these protections, and the fact they have to go to these lengths shows our efforts are working. We’ll keep improving and evolving our approach.”
However, bad actors may still be able to modify the glasses or tamper with the light without affecting recordings. And it’s unclear if popular bypasses, like using semi-transparent stickers that make the light less noticeable, would block recording under Meta’s new safeguard.
Data regulators in the European Union are currently probing privacy concerns with Meta’s glasses and have suggested that Meta may not have properly field-tested the LED light to ensure that the public would understand its safety functionality. Germany is considering banning the glasses after a nonprofit filed a criminal complaint alleging that they breach Germany’s strict privacy laws, Politico reported. And Germany is not alone, as many countries in the EU mull a crackdown on the technology, which they see as invasive and carrying a risk of expanding mass surveillance. Another Politico report confirmed that the European Data Protection Board will release a report later this summer to decide what actions should be taken to ensure no one in the EU is recorded without their consent.

Roberto De Zerbi apologised for Tottenham’s dismal 0-2 loss against Newcastle but insisted there’s no panic and that there is a plan in place on Saturday.
Tottenham loss extended its miserable start to the new Premier League season. That it hasn’t scored in two games now, conceded three and two goals makes this club’s worst start to a season in 52 years.
Bottom of the table Tottenham has lost its opening two matches of a league campaign without scoring for the third time in its history and the first since 1974-75.
“There is no panic. I know where we are going and what the plan is. I’m sorry for the fans for the result,” De Zerbi said.
“We have to improve. We have to work hard on the pitch and find the connection between the players.”
De Zerbi’s side spent USD 406 million to freshen up the squad that was nearly relegated last season.
Tottenham has already signed eight players since the end of last season.
De Zerbi hopes to make one more major signing before the transfer window closes on September 1, with Liverpool forward Cody Gakpo linked to the north Londoners.
On the evidence of Tottenham’s limp surrender against Newcastle, De Zerbi could do with adding even more new recruits.
“Disappointed for the result because until the first goal we conceded I think we played better than Newcastle,” he said.
“We lost ball possession in the first half because we didn’t defend in the right way, the distance between the defenders and attackers was too big. We can improve in the defensive phases but today was an unfair result.”
“We created many chances to score, we have to improve the last decision, because that will make a difference,” De Zerbi said.
“At the end we are disappointed for the result and our fans. We are working to be a great team. When we become a team, I think we can change the story of the last two seasons for Tottenham.”
