'This star is for Africa' - Angélique Kidjo on making Hollywood Walk of Fame history
- Published
Five-time Grammy award winner Angélique Kidjo, who made history on Tuesday to become the first African musician to get a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, has told the BBC she wants to dedicate the accolade to the continent of her birth.
"This star is for all the continent of Africa. Because if I was not African, would I be here?" said the 66-year-old musical icon from Benin.
She reiterated her message, made at the ceremony in Los Angeles to mark her four-decade career, about the importance of Africans to the world of music.
"Without the blues brought by the slaves in America, there's no R&B, there's no rock and roll, there's no soul music, there's no jazz. All of it comes from Africa."
- Angélique Kidjo's secret to success: Being hangry 
  - Published17 November 2023
Kidjo told BBC Focus on Africa TV that Africans themselves needed to appreciate what they had given the world, and nurture talent at home.
"Let's celebrate our artists in their own right on the continent. Let's give them visibility, strength, because music creates economy," she said.
Most African artists - besides mega stars who have a global fanbase - struggle to make a living as they rarely get paid the royalties they are owed.
"We need to recognise our artists and create a system for them to make money on their continent and to participate also in creating jobs."
As her illustrious career was immortalised in Los Angeles, Kidjo became emotional - wiping away tears.
"At that moment, I'm like, dad, mum, I wish you were here with me to see [this]" the songstress explained to the BBC.
"I couldn't take the emotion. They were not here to taste the fruit of what they've created. How they have nurtured my curiosity, my love for music."
Kidjo - who has taken African sounds to global audiences, blending influences from home with funk, jazz and pop - grew up in Benin and then went to Paris aged 23, citing oppression from the country's then-communist government.
At her Walk of Fame ceremony, she was joined by other family, friends and stars such as Hollywood actors Willem Dafoe and Djimon Hounsou, who is also from Benin, and Nigerian musician Adekunle Gold.
The gathering was filled with singing and dancing in celebration of her career, which has included collaborations with big names such as Burna Boy, John Legend, Bono and Alicia Keys.
Her latest album, HOPE!!, was released earlier this year with tracks produced by Pharrell Williams, and collaborations with Ayra Starr, Quavo, Nile Rogers and Diane Warren.
Kidjo has released 18 albums in total and has been nominated for 17 Grammy awards, which she has won five times.
She also won the 2023 Polar Music Prize, and two years earlier was named as one of Time's 100 Most Influential People.
"She is without a doubt the hardest working woman in showbusiness," Dafoe said at the ceremony.
"The first time I saw Angélique perform live, I thought her music, her dancing, her commitment were incredible."
The Spider-Man star likened her energy to that of soul singer James Brown, who he called the "hardest working man in showbusiness".
"She's not only an incredible performer... songwriter and musician, but also an incredibly kind and giving person and a real deal activist."
Kidjo is a Unicef and Oxfam goodwill ambassador, and is the co-founder of the Batonga Foundation, which helps vulnerable young girls and women in Benin.
At the Los Angeles gathering she was also praised by Harvey Mason Jr, the CEO of Recording Academy - the organisation that also oversees the Grammy awards.
"She's connected cultures, she's crossed borders, she's reminded audiences everywhere that while we may come from different backgrounds, her music unites in a way that few other things can," he said.
During her interview with the BBC, the musician's phone kept ringing with those wanting to congratulate her.
"Yesterday I received the call of the president of Benin," she said.
"Today I received the call of Chris Blackwell, the founder of Island Records, the producer of Bob Marley, the maker of U2 and so on and so forth."
Kidjo explained how fundamental Blackwell, who signed her in the 1990s, had been to her success - launching her breakthrough album Logozo.
"I said to him at that moment… 'Can I do the music I want to do and keep my cultural identity without anyone imposing any other music on my shoulder?' He said… 'It's no brainer.'"
Kidjo joins Charlize Theron, a white South African actress, in representing Africa on the Walk of Fame, which comprises more than 2,800 stars.
She said she was amazed to hear a year ago that she had been nominated for a Hollywood star, telling Focus on Africa she did not believe the news given to her by her husband until she said she had seen it on the BBC.
And when asked about the significance of becoming the first African musician with a star, she replied: "Changes that last take time."

Nepal-Tibet disaster: Death toll nears 800; more than 3,000 missing
On the fifth day of rescue efforts, 2,502 people in Nepal remain missing while 546 people in China's Tibet remain unaccounted for.
CHITWAN, Nepal: Rescuers in Nepal and China raced on Sunday (Aug 30) to find thousands of people missing after a glacier collapse unleashed a catastrophic mudslide across the Himalayas, as they faced challenging weather conditions and rising water levels.
Nepal authorities said on Sunday the death toll had risen to 781, with 2,502 people missing on the fifth day of rescue efforts.
Chinese state media earlier confirmed 16 dead in Tibet and 546 people missing following Wednesday's disaster, taking the overall toll to 797 dead and 3,048 unaccounted for.
The Red Cross has estimated that more than 90,000 people are likely to have been affected by the disaster, which China has linked to the effects of climate change.
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told his Nepalese counterpart during a Saturday telephone call that the mudslide was their "most severe cross-border disaster" in recent years and that rescue operations had risen to an unprecedented level of difficulty and complexity, state broadcaster CCTV reported.
Beijing said 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries were unaccounted for in Tibet, near a key border crossing with Nepal.
The scale of the disaster has complicated rescue efforts across the rugged Himalayan terrain.
Local police in Nepal told Reuters that residents and rescue workers had moved to higher ground after the Trishuli River's water levels rose in recent hours following fresh rainfall, raising fears of additional flooding.
Rescue operations have been suspended several times since Friday because of bad weather and concerns that a lake formed across the Nepal-China border by the disaster could trigger fresh flooding after it began overflowing into Nepal's Lhende Khola and Trishuli Rivers.
CCTV reported that the lake threatening downstream areas had been largely drained by Saturday evening. But drones detected a landslide late on Saturday that is 2.8km downstream of the lake, forming a new dam and a fresh pool of water.
In Nepal, rescue efforts have become more focused on hundreds of people believed to be trapped inside tunnels at hydropower plants damaged by the floods.
Lok Bahadur Chhetri, a spokesperson for Nepal's foreign ministry, said Nepal required international assistance in specialised areas, including tunnel rescue operations, DNA testing, refrigerated storage for bodies and forensic identification of decomposed remains.
Indian and Chinese experts were already working to help open tunnels and support rescue operations, Chhetri said.
MASS BURIALS OF DECOMPOSING BODIES
Days after desperate relatives moved between hospitals, morgues and relief centres searching for loved ones, authorities in Nepal began mass burials of hundreds of unidentified victims whose bodies had started to decompose.
In Chitwan district, which escaped the direct impact of the disaster, bodies swept downstream from the flood-hit Rasuwa region have been carried by the river system into the Narayani River.
Authorities are photographing the bodies, collecting DNA samples and recording identifying details in the hope that families may still be able to identify relatives after burial.
"Of the bodies we have recovered so far, more than half are beyond recognition," police officer Anil Thapa told Reuters.
"Many have no visible faces. In some cases, only hands or legs remain; in others, only parts of the body are available. In many cases, more than half of the head is missing."
After burying more than 100 unidentified bodies on Saturday, authorities were digging additional graves on Sunday for hundreds more.
LINK TO "LONG-TERM EFFECTS OF CLIMATE CHANGE"
The flood was "caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming", CCTV reported, saying it was a "new and prominent feature of cryosphere disasters" on the Tibetan plateau.
The mudslide from the Nepalese side took six to seven minutes to reach the Gyirong border crossing, CCTV said, citing the findings of Chinese scientists. Dramatic surveillance footage shared worldwide showed torrents of water and debris engulfing buildings while people tried to flee.
The state-run TV channel reported China has mobilised more than 2,100 rescue workers and allocated at least 220 million yuan (US$32.7 million) to support relief efforts and has been airdropping equipment and supplies to frontline rescuers, while its soldiers used life-detection equipment to look for the missing.

క్లెయిమ్: లోక్సభలో ప్రతిపక్ష నేత రాహుల్ గాంధీ “80 శాతం అత్యాచారాలకు మహిళలే కారణం. భారతదేశంలో అత్యాచారాలు జరుగుతాయి, కానీ ‘భారత్’లో అత్యాచారాలు జరగవు” అని అంటున్న వీడియో.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వీడియోను ఎడిట్ చేశారు. అసలు వీడియోలో రాహుల్ గాంధీ స్వయంగా ఈ వ్యాఖ్యలు చేయలేదు. ఆర్ఎస్ఎస్ చీఫ్ మోహన్ భగవత్, మాజీ హర్యానా ముఖ్యమంత్రి మనోహర్ లాల్ ఖట్టర్ గతంలో చేసిన వివాదాస్పద వ్యాఖ్యలను ప్రస్తావిస్తూ, వారి అభిప్రాయాలను రాహుల్ గాంధీ విమర్శించారు. అయితే, వైరల్ వీడియోలో ఆయన ఎవరి వ్యాఖ్యలను ప్రస్తావిస్తున్నారో చెప్పిన భాగాన్ని తొలగించి, ఆ వ్యాఖ్యలు రాహుల్ గాంధీ స్వయంగా చేసినట్లుగా చూపించారు. కాబట్టి, ఈ పోస్టులో చేస్తున్న వాదన తప్పు.
వైరల్ వీడియోలోని కీలక ఫ్రేమ్లను ఉపయోగించి రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, కాంగ్రెస్ పార్టీ అధికారిక యూట్యూబ్ ఛానల్లో 22 ఆగస్టు 2026న అప్లోడ్ చేసిన అసలు వీడియో మాకు లభించింది. అదే రోజు పుణెలో జరిగిన కాంగ్రెస్ “ఛాత్రోన్ కీ గూంజ్” కార్యక్రమానికి సంబంధించిన వీడియో ఇది. అసలు వీడియోలోని 1:00:12 టైమ్స్టాంప్ వద్ద వైరల్ క్లిప్లోని దృశ్యాలు కనిపిస్తాయి. అయితే, అసలు వీడియోలో రాహుల్ గాంధీ ఆ వ్యాఖ్యలను స్వయంగా చేయడం లేదు. ఆర్ఎస్ఎస్ చీఫ్ మోహన్ భగవత్, మాజీ హర్యానా ముఖ్యమంత్రి మనోహర్ లాల్ ఖట్టర్ గతంలో చేసిన వ్యాఖ్యలను ఆయన ప్రస్తావించాడు. అత్యాచారాలు “ఇండియా”లో జరుగుతాయి కానీ “భారత్”లో జరగవని మోహన్ భగవత్ చెప్పారని, 80 శాతం అత్యాచారాలకు మహిళలే కారణమని మనోహర్ లాల్ ఖట్టర్ వ్యాఖ్యానించారని రాహుల్ గాంధీ పేర్కొన్నారు. అనంతరం, ఇలాంటి వ్యాఖ్యలు తాము వ్యతిరేకిస్తున్నానని ఆయన తెలిపారు.
మోహన్ భగవత్, మనోహర్ లాల్ ఖట్టర్ పేర్లను ప్రస్తావించిన భాగాన్ని వీడియో నుంచి తొలగించారు. ఆ వ్యాఖ్యలను రాహుల్ గాంధీ స్వయంగా చేసినట్లుగా కనిపించేలా వైరల్ వీడియోను రూపొందించారు. దీంతో వైరల్ వీడియోను ఎడిట్ చేసినట్లు స్పష్టమవుతోంది.
తదుపరి, గూగుల్లో కీవర్డ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ) ఉన్న వీడియోలు లభించాయి. వీటి ప్రకారం, 4 జనవరి 2013న ఆర్ఎస్ఎస్ చీఫ్ మోహన్ భగవత్ అసోంలోని సిల్చర్లో పర్యటించిన సమయంలో అత్యాచార ఘటనలపై వివాదాస్పద వ్యాఖ్యలు చేశారు. “ఇండియా”లో ఇలాంటి నేరాలు ఎక్కువగా జరుగుతాయని, “భారత్”లో తక్కువగా జరుగుతాయని ఆయన చెప్పినట్లు వార్తలు వచ్చాయి. ఈ వ్యాఖ్యలు అప్పట్లో వివాదానికి దారితీశాయి. తర్వాత అప్పటి ఆర్ఎస్ఎస్ అధికార ప్రతినిధి రామ్ మాధవ్ వివరణ ఇచ్చారు. మహిళలను గౌరవించే భారతీయ సంప్రదాయాల గురించి మోహన్ భగవత్ మాట్లాడారని, ఈ విలువలకు దూరమైనవారు నేరాలకు పాల్పడే అవకాశం ఉందని ఆయన చెప్పినట్లు రామ్ మాధవ్ వివరించారు.
అదేవిధంగా, 2018 నవంబర్లో అప్పటి హర్యానా ముఖ్యమంత్రి మనోహర్ లాల్ ఖట్టర్ అత్యాచారం, వేధింపుల ఘటనలపై వివాదాస్పద వ్యాఖ్యలు చేశారు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ). వార్తా కథనాల్లో ఈ వ్యాఖ్యలకు సంబంధించిన వివరాలు ఉన్నాయి. అత్యాచారం, వేధింపుల ఘటనల్లో 80–90 శాతం వరకు ఒకరికొకరు తెలిసిన వ్యక్తులే ఉంటారని ఖట్టర్ అన్నారు. అలాగే, కొన్నిసార్లు చాలా కాలంగా సంబంధంలో ఉన్న వ్యక్తుల మధ్య వివాదాలు తలెత్తిన తర్వాత ఇలాంటి ఘటనలు జరుగుతున్నాయని ఆయన సూచించారు.
చివరిగా, అత్యాచారం, మహిళలపై రాహుల్ గాంధీ వివాదాస్పద వ్యాఖ్యలు చేసినట్లు చూపిస్తున్న ఈ వైరల్ వీడియో ఎడిట్ చేసినది.

New Zealand's government introduced legislation on Monday to ban under 16s from using social media, joining a number of countries seeking to keep youngsters off sites such as Instagram and TikTok.
Australia implemented world-first legislation banning children from social media in December, with the UK, France and others following suit.
Under New Zealand's proposed law, firms like Meta could be fined up to 10 percent of their global revenue if they fail to comply.
"We simply cannot accept the harm being done to a generation of New Zealand children," Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said.
"One in three children aged between 13 and 17 are now spending at least five hours on social media a day," he said.
"Social media is exposing them to harmful content, addictive technology and pressures they are not equipped to deal with, and it's affecting their family life, mental health, sleep and education."
Luxon specifically called out platforms Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat and Facebook, saying they would be required to take "reasonable steps to check users are over the age of 16".
They would have to use "existing account information, facial age estimation, digital ID services and formal ID" to verify age.
Platforms would also be required to assess the risks they pose as well as report on how those dangers are being reduced, with penalties slapped on companies that fail to comply.
Education Minister Erica Stanford said the Bill "places legal obligations on platforms".
"No penalties are proposed for children, their parents or caregivers," Stanford said.
It's unclear whether the bill will pass, as both National Party's coalition partners, the libertarian ACT party and populist NZ First, have said they oppose it.
In a statement, the populist NZ First said they could not support the law given the "colossal failure" of the legislation in Australia, while ACT said they believed the law "won't work" and that teenagers would easily get around the ban.
The main opposition party Labour has submitted a list of dozens of questions it wanted answered before deciding whether it would offer support, including how age verification will work and which platforms will be affected.
"We take this legislation very seriously," spokesman Reuben Davidson said.
"The safety of young people in Aotearoa New Zealand is at stake and the risks they face in increasingly complex online environments are significant," he added, using the Maori-language name for the country.
Australia banned under 16s last year from the likes of Facebook, Instagram and TikTok, in a crackdown designed to protect children from online bullying and "predatory algorithms".
A team of Australia-based researchers in a peer-reviewed study published in June found little evidence to suggest teenagers have turned away from social media as a consequence, however.

Former Indian cricketer Ravichandran Ashwin had another tough day as Edinburgh Castle Rockers defeated his side Dublin Guardians by four wickets in the eighth match of the European T20 Premier League 2026 at The Hague on Sunday.
Guardians skipper Ashwin won the toss and opted to bat first. However, his team was dismissed on 109 in 18 overs.
The 39-year-old Ashwin scored eight runs in 12 balls without hitting any boundaries.
In response, the Castle Rockers chased down the target in just 13.4 overs. Off-spinner Ashwin bowled an economical spell, conceding only 20 runs in his four overs, but he did not manage to pick a single wicket. He did help Josh Little remove Castle Rockers’ opener J J Smuts by taking a catch.
New Zealand’s left-arm spinner Mitchell Santner was named the Player of the Match for his figures of five for 16 during the Guardians’ innings.
On Saturday, in the Guardians’ 33-run loss to Glasgow Cosmic, Ashwin had conceded 43 runs in his four-over spell, which included the wicket of Moises Henriques. With the bat too, he disappointed with a two-ball duck.

About 1,600 federal employees who work at the General Services Administration have been forced to relocate from their office on F Street in Washington, DC, to the Theodore Roosevelt Federal Building, roughly two blocks away. Workers say the new building, which also houses staff from the Office of Personnel Management has mice, a caved-in bathroom ceiling, and drinking water that needs to be run for five to 10 seconds before it is clear.
The federal workforce has been rocked by changes made by Elon Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) since January 2025. DOGE effectively fired tens of thousands of workers and forced those who remained to commit to in-person schedules and, in some cases, zero-based budgeting. GSA, the agency in charge of the federal government’s IT services and real estate assets, was hit early by DOGE, and in addition to major workforce cuts also rolled out plans to sell hundreds of federal office buildings. A year after the cuts, GSA announced it planned to hire about 400 workers.
“We’ve all been through a lot, but this really made me finally understand that they don’t care about us,” says one GSA employee who asked to remain anonymous, as they aren’t authorized to speak to the press. “We’re left wondering what else is going to collapse or break—do we need to look at the ceiling before going to the bathroom? Can we actually trust the water is safe to drink?”
Photos obtained by WIRED show a toilet in a men’s room on the third floor covered in debris from the ceiling, a gaping hole in said ceiling, and a dead mouse caught in a trap. Workers said the mouse wasn’t “entirely shocking” since many federal buildings allegedly have vermin, but the ceiling pushed them over the edge. An additional sign in the office recommends workers filling up water bottles to “run the water without your bottle for 5-10 seconds and wait for the water to run clear.”
GSA and OPM did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
GSA leadership, including administrator Ed Forst, has told employees they should expect to work in the OPM building—which is slated for “accelerated disposition,” or a quick building sale—until December 2028. Their prior building, located at 1800 F Street, is undergoing extensive renovations. The initiative is part of a “government-wide effort to reduce underutilized space and fortify the federal real estate footprint,” according to a GSA press release.
While Musk himself has stepped back from his public role in the Trump administration, DOGE affiliates have continued working in government, embracing austerity measures and AI initiatives. Others have gone back to the private sector, working in AI, data centers, and manufacturing.

Things to know before using your MacBook outside
Keep an eye on the thermomoter.
Taking a MacBook outside is usually as simple as moving from a desk to a patio table, but outdoor conditions are much harder to control. Heat and direct sunlight can affect both the laptop itself and how comfortable its screen is to use. You don't need special outdoor gear, but you do need to know Apple's temperature limits and give the MacBook a dry, stable surface with room to shed heat.
Keep your MacBook within Apple's temperature limits
Apple recommends using its Mac laptops when the ambient temperature is between 50 and 95 degrees Fahrenheit, or 10 to 35 degrees Celsius. That's a wider range than most people will encounter indoors, but the upper limit is easy to approach on a hot summer day. Apple also specifically warns against leaving a MacBook in a parked car, where temperatures can climb beyond its recommended range.
The important word in Apple's guidance is ambient. The 95-degree limit refers to the air around the laptop, not how hot its aluminum enclosure might become while sitting in direct sunlight. Apple doesn't publish a separate direct-sunlight limit for MacBooks, so it makes sense to move into the shade rather than treating a temperature below 95 degrees as an all-clear for using one in full sun.
There's a longer-term reason to avoid excessive heat, too. Ambient temperatures above 95 degrees Fahrenheit can permanently reduce battery capacity, meaning the battery may not last as long on a charge afterward. Charging a device in high temperatures can cause additional damage.
Heat also matters differently depending on the MacBook you have. All Apple Silicon MacBook Air models use passive cooling rather than a fan, dissipating heat through the chassis. MacBook Pro models use active cooling for sustained, demanding workloads. Either way, giving the laptop shade and room around it to shed heat is preferable to making its cooling system work against direct sun.
Direct sunlight can make your MacBook's screen harder to use
Heat isn't the only reason to look for shade. Bright outdoor light and reflections can make a MacBook display much harder to read, which usually leaves you reaching for the brightness controls.
How much brightness you have to work with depends on the model. Current MacBook Air displays are rated for 500 nits of brightness, while current MacBook Pros can reach up to 1,000 nits of SDR brightness outdoors. A nit is a unit used to measure display luminance, so a higher figure generally means the screen can produce more light.
That extra brightness comes with a tradeoff when you're away from an outlet. Dimming a MacBook display to the lowest comfortable level helps you maximize battery life. However, if sunlight forces you to keep the display near maximum brightness, expect the battery to run down faster than it would at a lower setting indoors.
So, before pushing the brightness all the way up, try changing your position. Turning the display away from reflections or moving a few feet into shade can make the screen easier to see while allowing you to lower its brightness again. It also gets the MacBook itself out of direct sunlight, solving two outdoor problems with the same move.
Use a hard surface and keep your laptop away from moisture
Where you put a MacBook matters more outside than it does at a desk. Apple recommends placing its laptops on a stable work surface that allows good ventilation and specifically warns against using them on pillows, bedding or other surfaces that can interfere with airflow. A table or solid tray is therefore a better choice than setting the MacBook down on a blanket or cushion.
Weather presents the other obvious problem. Current safety guidance for both the MacBook Air and MacBook Pro says to protect the laptop, power adapter and charging cable from dampness, humidity and wet weather. It specifically lists rain, snow and fog. A light shower isn't something to work through just because the keyboard still looks dry.
If rain starts, disconnect the charger and other cables and move the MacBook somewhere dry. The same guidance applies to the power adapter, so an outdoor outlet or extension cord doesn't make charging a good idea when moisture is present.

There was a lot of talk at the Business Council of Australia's annual dinner last week about the need to improve Australia's poor productivity.
To achieve that, it was agreed, government and business must work together.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said: "My theme tonight is the need for a positive partnership between government, business and the community to keep our economy strong."
BCA president Geoff Culbert said: "The government and the business sector need to work together to explain why change is needed."
BCA chief executive Bran Black named all the ministers he has been working with, who were all present at the dinner, as it happens, and said: "It's clear there are many areas in which government and business can work together to make Australia a top-10 investment destination and lift living standards."
I was not there, but those who were tell me the whole event was a group hug between the Labor government and the business community, with the latter's teeth a bit gritted, perhaps, after the budget tax changes.
But there was an inconvenient elephant in the Wentworth Sofitel Ballroom on Tuesday night.
Bold economic reform is behind us
The period when all those present agree that Australia's productivity was great and reform was happening was not when government and business were working together, but when government and labour were working together.
That was the 80s and early 90s, when productivity grew more than 2 per cent a year versus the current decade average of 0.3 per cent, and minus 0.7 per cent in the 2024-25 financial year.
The self-appointed role of the then-newly formed BCA was to oppose reform, while the partnership that produced the reform and the productivity growth was between the Labor government and the ACTU, specifically treasurer Paul Keating and ACTU secretary Bill Kelty.
Looking back now on what he and Keating did, Kelty says they had to fix the economic system by opening it up. Wage growth was unsustainable, the top marginal tax rate was too high, and inflation was too high.
Keating says Kelty was smart and knew what was needed. Their ideas reinforced each other, and they both talk fondly about that dinner at India House in Melbourne on January 30, 1991, where 12 per cent superannuation was decided on, and mapped out.
There were only four people present: Keating, Kelty, Keating's chief of staff Don Russell and the assistant secretary of the ACTU, Iain Ross, who went on to be president of the Fair Work Commission and is now on the RBA's monetary policy board.
Keating amazed them when he said he would legislate 12 per cent super, and "knock off" the commission.
Three years earlier, Keating had cut tariffs to 10 or 15 per cent and then, in 1991, cut them further to 5 per cent across the board, at the same time as formalising enterprise bargaining.
The so-called "Australian settlement" — centralised wages coupled with industry protection — was dead.
Bold economic reform was in the air in those days, and it felt as if anything was possible; as a finance journalist and editor, you woke up every morning wondering what new excitement the day would bring.
Last week, I spent some time with a New York-based Australian banker who also lived through those years, and having spent a few weeks here, she thinks that the attitude now is all about hanging onto what we've got, not making it better.
Australia's policy mindset these days is defensive, she thinks, circling the wagons.
An obvious difference between now and the 80s and 90s reform era is that the ACTU is a shadow of what it was and is involved in the national discussion from the stands, not on the field of play.
Businesses milking the economy
The most powerful players in national policy are lobbyists, as Four Corners showed us last week, and they work for those who pay the most, which is businesses and their organisations.
A big part of the union movement's decline in influence is simply the decline in union membership, from around 60 per cent to around 10 per cent, and it is focused on government and service industries.
It means labour is no longer institutionalised to the same extent, so it is no longer possible for the political classes to easily speak to the working classes. Employers, on the other hand, are well-represented by lobbyists and groups like the BCA, who put on lunches and dinners, large and intimate.
The other big contributor to the demise of union influence is the evident corruption in the CFMEU, which has damaged the whole movement's credibility.
Kelty says that part of the foundation of strong productivity growth is rising real wages, because if workers are going backwards financially, they lose heart and do not care.
That was why he and Keating were so focused on keeping inflation down and wages growth up, with well-functioning safety nets, especially healthcare and super.
Business groups generally oppose every wage rise, then and now, and their members are responsible for price rises.
An important reason for the recent slump in productivity growth has been the decline in real wages, and the fact that per capita household income has been negative for years after inflation — it simply is not true that struggling financially spurs people to be more productive; the opposite happens.
What is more, the decline in productivity growth has coincided with a fall in the growth rate of business investment from 2.2 per cent in 2015 to zero in 2025, at the same time as the profit share of the economy has increased sharply while the labour share has fallen.
In other words, the evidence suggests that Australia's businesses have been milking the economy.
They have been using the collapse of union power to suppress wages while using their own oligopoly power to increase prices and spending the proceeds on fully franked dividends and buybacks to support share prices and executive salaries.
The result is declining productivity along with rising inequality, generational anger and political polarisation.
And right now the main, possibly only, basis for optimism about productivity — including in the speeches at last week's BCA dinner — is artificial intelligence.
There will not be a return to the reform excitement of the 80s and 90s, because the unions are out of the game and the players who are on the field now are bereft of ideas and are happy to play keepings-off.
But optimism about AI's capacity to improve productivity and living standards is a bit like hoping a bungee jump will fix your heart disease — maybe it will; maybe you'll have a heart attack and die.

'No plan to ease the entry into the AI era'
Last week, Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates published a 6,000-word essay on his website in which he warned about the risks to both white and blue-collar employment from AI, as well as the risk of bioterrorism, deepfakes and cyber attacks.
He called for global governance and taxes on AI and robots to both raise money to support the unemployed and delay the rush away from human labour.
Then there is the potential for a financial collapse and recession caused by the debt-funded data centre bubble.
Albanese agreed in his speech to the BCA dinner on Tuesday that AI is a big deal, but he is not too worried: "How we handle this global moment will have major consequences for our economy, our social harmony and our democracy … The answer lies in not elevating grievance and division. We must remain positive and optimistic."
In his essay posted a few hours later, Gates wrote: "I don't see evidence that leaders, experts, and communities are confronting the challenges adequately. There is no plan to ease the entry into the AI era."
Alan Kohler is a finance presenter and columnist on ABC News. He hosts the podcast That's Business with Alan Kohler in the ABC Business Daily feed on Friday. He also writes for Intelligent Investor.

Norwegians in emotional memorials remembering the late King Harald V
Norwegians have gathered for memorial services honoring the late King Harald V, who died at 89
OSLO, Norway -- Norwegians across the country lined up early Sunday in front of cathedrals and churches for memorial services held for the late King Harald V, who died at 89.
“This Sunday is different. His Majesty King Harald is dead. A family has lost their spouse, father, grandfather, father-in-law,” said Dean Pål Kristian Balstad as he opened the funeral service in Oslo Cathedral, Norway's public broadcaster NRK reported.
The royal family attended the service at Asker Church, southwest of Oslo.
Since Harald's death Friday morning, tens of thousands of Norwegians have expressed their grief by laying flowers, writing cards and lighting candles in front of the royal palace in Oslo, where the coffin arrived late Friday from the hospital.
A date for the funeral has not been set, but the country is in a state of mourning and some people decided to postpone celebrations such as weddings and baptisms until after the mourning period has passed, NRK reported.
Harald's son, who became the new King Haakon VIII, eulogized Harald on Saturday night. He expressed his pain over the beloved father's death and promised to lead the country with the same dedication.
“I’m going to miss him. I’ll miss his laughter. His good-natured way of dealing with people and situations,” Haakon said in his first speech as new king that was broadcast live on public Television.
Trying to hold back his tears, he vowed to give everything for the country in the future as its new king.
“That means — in the ultimate sense — being willing to risk everything, even one’s life, for Norway’s freedom and independence,” Haakon said.
The new king adopted the motto “All for Norway,” which dates back to his great-grandfather. His wife became Queen Mette-Marit, while his oldest child, Ingrid Alexandra, became crown princess and heir to the throne.
His tasks in the near future will include shoring up support for the monarchy following controversies over his wife’s past contacts with deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his stepson’s rape conviction.
Norway’s monarchy has old roots, tracing its origins to King Harald Fairhair in the ninth century. When Norway regained its independence from Sweden in 1905, three-quarters of voters in a national plebiscite approved restoring the monarchy. Today, the role is largely symbolic as power lies with an elected parliament, but the country’s royal family retains celebrity and a role in promoting the wealthy nation around the world.

I’m on record declaring James Cameron’s Terminator 2: Judgment Day (1991) to be The Best Damn Sequel of All Time, and I stand by that assessment. August 29, the fictional date (in 1997) of the franchise’s original nuclear holocaust, is fast approaching, and Judgment Day is celebrating its 35th anniversary this year. So StudioCanal has decided to mark both occasions with a special theatrical rerelease of the film this weekend. What better time to revisit some of our favorite scenes from this seminal sci-fi action blockbuster?
(Many, many spoilers below.)
Nobody really expected 1984’s The Terminator to be a hit, but it racked up an impressive $78 million at the box office against its modest $6.4 million budget. Star Arnold Schwarzenegger was keen to do a sequel, but Cameron was busy with other projects, including Aliens in 1986 (another killer sequel). There were also legal complications over the film rights until Schwarzenegger convinced Carolco Pictures, the studio behind Total Recall (1990), to buy everyone out and hire Cameron to make Judgment Day.
Cameron wrote the script in about six weeks, diverging significantly from the stripped-down feel of its predecessor (which some have described as a “science fiction slasher”). Instead, Cameron chose to make his original Terminator the reprogrammed hero of the sequel, serving as a mechanical father figure to a young John Connor (Edward Furlong). Cameron likened the transformation to the Tin Man getting a heart in The Wizard of Oz. Linda Hamilton agreed to reprise her role as Sarah Connor, and this “found family” triad became the emotional core of the film. Hamilton worked out like a fiend for the role, and her resulting lean-yet-ripped physique made her an action heroine on par with Sigourney Weaver’s Ripley.
Released over the July 4th holiday weekend in 1991, Terminator 2: Judgment Day was a critical and financial smash hit, despite predictions that the film would bomb and lose its estimated $70 million production budget. It ended up grossing $520 million, which sadly was not enough to protect Carolco from other film losses. (The studio went bankrupt in 1995.) It’s the perfect sci-fi action film, expertly paced with well-drawn character dynamics, amazing special effects, emotional beats, and humorous touches to keep things from getting too grim. No subsequent film in the franchise even comes close.

The film also has one of the best villains in cinema with the shapeshifting T-1000 (Robert Patrick). Cameron actually had the idea for a Terminator made of liquid metal when he was writing the first film, but the technology available at the time wasn’t up to the task. Then Cameron made The Abyss in 1989, which featured a flowing, water-like alien at the very end created by Industrial Light & Magic (ILM). ILM made a major investment, expanding its staff and spending over $3 million on new equipment and specially designed software just for Judgment Day.
The gamble paid off. The T-1000 and other visual effects earned critical raves and an Oscar (the film snagged four in all) and helped usher in the golden age of CGI. Audiences loved the character, which had as much to do with Cameron’s expert pacing as the effects. The T-1000’s abilities are only gradually revealed. Initially, the slender Patrick seems no match for Schwarzenegger’s heavily muscled T-800, even if he can take on anyone’s form. Then we see its liquid metal form is impervious to bullet wounds, healing them instantly—even when a gunshot blast splits its head in two. Cameron keeps upping the ante, until one becomes convinced the T-1000 is well-nigh invincible.
“T2 was made for theaters, and our lovingly prepared 3D version, coming back to the big screen, is the absolute best way to see the film,” Cameron told Deadline Hollywood via statement. “I believe it’s safe to do spoilers after 35 years, so SPOILER ALERT: the good guys win against the AI super intelligence. And maybe that’s a message of hope we could use this summer.”
There is a staggered global rollout for the rerelease. It’s now available in Germany, Latin America, the Czech Republic, the US, Italy, and Poland. The film will be released in France on September 2; Australia, New Zealand, the Netherlands, Sweden, and Hungary on September 3; and the United Kingdom on September 4.
And now, we give you 10 of our favorite scenes:
The T-800 in the biker bar
Credit:
Paramount/Studio Canal
Credit:
Paramount/Studio Canal
Judgment Day‘s eye-popping special effects certainly provide plenty of highlights, but Cameron didn’t skimp on the story either. This is a prime example of how the director used touches of levity to make even the film’s more workmanlike segments entertaining. The T-800 arrives from the future naked as a jaybird and must acquire clothing, transportation, and weaponry. Naturally, he wanders into a biker bar—to the delight of the female patrons—finds a dude his size, and demands the biker’s clothes and motorcycle.
The biker thinks it’s a joke at first and refuses, extinguishing his cigar on the T-800’s bared pectoral muscle—with no effect. The outcome of the ensuing bar fight is a given. The T-800 walks away with cool leather clothing, a motorcycle, a shotgun, and a pair of stylish black sunglasses as George Thorogood and the Destroyer’s “Bad to the Bone” plays. The song’s been overused in films since then, but it was the perfect grace note for this scene.
Chase through the aqueduct
Credit:
Paramount/Studio Canal
Credit:
Paramount/Studio Canal
This is the first major chase sequence, with both the T-800 and the T-1000 trying to get to a fleeing John Connor first. John’s little motorbike proves no match for the large truck commandeered by the T-1000, which blasts through a cinder block wall at one point. The T-1000 never falters in its single-minded pursuit, but the arrival of the T-800 saves the boy. The truck eventually explodes, seemingly incinerating the T-1000. It’s only after the T-800 and John ride away that we see the T-1000 emerge from the flames and resume his police officer appearance.
The sequence was filmed over nine hours in LA’s San Fernando Valley. The T-800’s big stunt involved jumping a motorcycle 60 feet (at an altitude of roughly 15 feet) to the flood control channel below. Stunt coordinator Joel Kramer rigged up a support mechanism for the 750-pound motorcycle, since otherwise the jump was deemed too dangerous. The rigging and wires were erased during post-production.
The T-1000 emerges from floor tiles
Credit:
Paramount/Studio Canal
Credit:
Paramount/Studio Canal
This is one of those “upping the ante” moments. We’ve seen the T-1000’s amazing shapeshifting abilities, taking on the form of a policeman and John’s foster mother in quick succession. We’ve seen his arms transform effortlessly into weapons. We’ve seen him heal bullet holes instantly. When he arrives at the psychiatric hospital to take out Sarah Connor, he must briefly hide as a team of detectives exits. A lone security guard goes into the hall to get coffee from the vending machine. The T-1000 is nowhere to be seen—until it slowly oozes up out of the checkerboard hospital floor tiles right behind the unsuspecting guard.
The shot required a special bit of software capable of reshaping specific regions of a 2D image using 3D geometry, mapping a computer-generated replica of the floor to the actual footage. This was combined with animation of the T-1000 taking shape. As for the T-1000 taking on the guard’s shape—that was achieved the old-fashioned way, since the actor Don Stanton had a twin brother (Dan).
“Come with me if you want to live”
Credit:
aramount/Studio Canal
Credit:
aramount/Studio Canal
This is where flipping the script to make the T-800 John’s protector instead of the hunter really pays emotional dividends. Sarah Connor has reshaped her entire persona (not just her physique) in the wake of what happened to her in the first film. Everything centers on protecting John from the machines. Her obsession gets her locked up in a psychiatric hospital, and her odds of release are not good.
She’s in the middle of breaking out on her own—quite effectively—and has made it to the elevator, which opens to reveal the T-800, her former adversary, back (in her mind) to kill her and John. Horrified, Sarah flees back the way she came and is briefly subdued by hospital staff until the T-800 tosses them aside like rag dolls. She sees John is safe, and the T-800 reaches down and repeats the line her protector uttered in the first film: “Come with me if you want to live.”
Bonus: Sarah’s psychiatrist and everyone else who thought she was crazy rattling on about killer machines from the future must confront the fact that she was right all along, especially when the T-1000 shows up.
Sarah’s nuclear holocaust dream

Paramount/Studio Canal
Paramount/Studio Canal
Paramount/Studio Canal
Paramount/Studio Canal
Paramount/Studio Canal
This powerful dream sequence shows Sarah and the rest of Los Angeles utterly annihilated by a nuclear blast. It starts with children and their mothers—including a younger, more innocent Sarah Connor—on a playground, oblivious to the danger, as a distraught Sarah soundlessly tries to warn them by banging on the chain-link fence. Then the blast hits, burning Sarah alive (actually a full-sized puppet) and reducing those children to ash.
It took a ton of special effects work to pull off the sequence, combining practical effects, miniatures, and CGI enhancements. The team built a mini-Los Angeles based on the live-action footage, including skyscrapers and an overpass. Some of the model buildings stood 5 feet tall, and many were designed to break away to mimic the effects of a blast. The nuclear fireball was actually a backlit, 8-foot plexiglass column. The most powerful visual effect is the ashy remains of the playground victims, still intact—until a shock wave scatters the ashes to the wind.
That arm scene
Credit:
aramount/Studio Canal
Credit:
aramount/Studio Canal
Sarah’s dream is sufficiently traumatic to compel her to leave John with the T-800 and seek out Miles Dyson (Joe Morton), Cyberdyne’s director of special projects and the scientist most responsible for developing what would become Skynet. Her plan is to kill Miles and stop Judgment Day from ever happening—hence the film’s catchphrase, “No fate but what we make.” But she can’t go through with it, even as John and the T-800 arrive to stop her.
To prove to Miles that Sarah is telling the truth—that his work will lead to humanity’s near-annihilation—the T-800 removes the skin from his hand and forearm, revealing the cyber skeleton underneath. As he flexes the mechanical fingers in front of a horrified Miles and his wife, the T-800 intones, “Now listen to me very carefully….” I’m sure Miles was hanging on his every word.
The Cyberdyne showdown
Credit:
aramount/Studio Canal
Credit:
aramount/Studio Canal
John, Sarah, and the T-800 enlist Miles’ help to break into Cyberdyne headquarters and steal the salvaged arm and computer chip left behind by the T-800 in the first film. They are working against the clock, since pretty much every law enforcement unit in the city arrives at the building to stop them. John’s hacking skills prove useful, as does the T-800’s extensive firepower—although per John’s instructions, there are zero human fatalities.
Ultimately, Miles sacrifices himself so that the others can escape, holding onto the detonator that sets off a massive explosion until his final breath. The filming site was an empty office building in Fremont, California, and the explosion was real; pyrotechnician Tom Fisher used hundreds of gallons of gas to create that giant fireball. Respect.
T-1000 vs. liquid nitrogen
Paramount/Studio Canal
Paramount/Studio Canal
Paramount/Studio Canal
Paramount/Studio Canal
Paramount/Studio Canal
Paramount/Studio Canal
The carefully orchestrated high-speed chase down a highway that immediately precedes this scene deserves its own spot on the list, just for the ingenuity of the stunt design. That chase ends with a semitruck pulling a tank of liquid nitrogen overturning and skidding into an active steel mill, spilling liquid nitrogen all over the street. The T-1000 resolutely wades toward its targets anyway, only to start to freeze from the feet up, breaking its legs off at the knees and losing a hand before it solidifies, a look of shocked surprise on its face. The T-800 blasts it to smithereens with a well-timed, “Hasta la vista, baby.”
That should be the end of the T-1000, right? RIGHT? But within minutes the scattered shards start to melt in the heat of the steel mill and begin to coalesce yet again. “We don’t have much time,” the T-800 observes—and indeed, the T-1000 soon reassembles. The frozen shards were actually made of serabin, a material used as ballast for model railroad cars that resembles chrome when it’s polished. Frozen mercury didn’t work because it turned white. But globs of liquid mercury worked just fine to show the melting shards coming together, even though its toxicity meant the special effects crew had to wear protective gear over the two-day shoot.
The T-1000 has a meltdown
Spoiler alert: The T-1000 is not quite unbeatable. Sure, he recovers nicely from a hole in the head, courtesy of Sarah, and being cleaved in two by the T-800 wielding a piece of rebar—the former achieved with a mechanical head and shoulders replica of Patrick (“Donut Head”), the latter with a maquette sculpture (“Cleave Man”), both augmented with CGI. Just when things are looking dire for John and Sarah, the T-800 reboots on auxiliary power and shoots the T-1000 with a grenade launcher. The torso explodes and creates “Pretzel Man” (achieved with three full-sized puppets).
A teetering T-1000 then topples into a vat of molten steel and slowly melts into oblivion, running through each of the human forms it took on over the course of the film (foster mom, security guard, etc.) before vanishing in a howl. This was the most difficult sequence for the special effects team and took weeks to complete, matching carefully choreographed movements of all the actors in the live-action pit with splashing liquid filmed in a separate miniature version of the vat. The illusion of molten steel was basically water and mineral oil mixed with a little powdered sugar; creative lighting and heaters placed below the cameras—plus a few CGI sparks in the background—did the rest.
The result didn’t quite satisfy Cameron, but the rendering shots took so long that the director ran out of time, even with the production crew working 24-hour shifts. The final print wasn’t delivered to theaters until the night before the official release. But audiences were blown away. It was the perfect way to bring about the T-1000’s demise.
The T-800’s final sacrifice
Credit:
Paramount/Studio Canal
Credit:
Paramount/Studio Canal
After that spectacular special effects achievement, Cameron closed things out with an emotional, well-earned farewell. John drops the first T-800 arm and chip into the vat of molten steel to destroy them. But there is one chip left: the one in the new T-800’s head. Since it cannot self-terminate, Sarah is tasked with lowering the machine into the vat, against John’s anguished objections. It’s the final payoff to the relationship Cameron has painstakingly built between John and the machine—and the T-800 goes out in style, giving a gloved thumbs-up as its hand slowly sinks into the liquid steel.

Zambian opposition leader charged with treason
- Published
Zambian opposition leader Brian Mundubile has been charged with treason, his lawyer has said amid heightened political tensions in the country.
Mundubile was arrested on Thursday, after a deadly raid by the authorities led the opposition politician to go into hiding.
He had disputed the results of the country's recent presidential election, which saw incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema securing a second term.
The authorities then accused Mundubile's NRPUP party of planning an armed insurgency, which it denied.
On Saturday night, Mundubile's lawyer Milner Katolo announced that his client had been charged with treason. The opposition leader looks forward to answering the accusation in court, Katolo told the Zambian Eye, external.
The lawyer said 17 others, including Mundubile's running mate Makebi Zulu, had also been charged with treason.
Mundubile gained 38% of the vote in the 13 August election, while Hichilema secured 60%, official results show.
The day after the poll, security forces raided a property in the capital, Lusaka, linked to Mundubile, killing a former cabinet minister and arresting a number of other politicians.
Following the raid, Mundubile and Zulu took refuge at a United Nations building in the city. The pair were detained after the president put pressure on the UN to hand them over.
The opposition was unable to mount a legal challenge to the election outcome as the courts were sealed off by the authorities on Monday, the final day that a case could be filed.
Hichilema is due to be sworn in for a second term on 1 September.
Regional and international observers described the election day as largely peaceful, but Zambia's Human Rights Commission has called for accountability over people whose whereabouts remain unknown following arrests and security operations around the elections.

WATCH LIVE: NASA's newest space telescope launches today
NASA is set to launch a new space telescope Sunday from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida that will help scientists probe the nature of dark matter, dark energy, and other mysteries of the universe.
The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, which is about the size of a tour bus, is set to lift off at 7:26 a.m. ET on SpaceX's Falcon Heavy rocket. A weather forecast for the launch shows a 50% chance of favorable weather conditions. A backup window on Monday at 7:22 ET has better odds, with only a 30% risk of weather interfering with the launch.
The journey to Roman's new home
The new telescope is named for Nancy Grace Roman, NASA's first chief astronomer who was known as the 'Mother of Hubble' for her championing of the iconic Hubble Space Telescope. Her namesake observatory will have the sharpness of Hubble but a field of view that is at least 100 times larger, allowing it to image huge swaths of the sky at once.
Before it can do that, the Roman Space Telescope will have to get to its new home in the sky about a million miles away. Roman will live at the second Sun-Earth Lagrange point known as L2. There, the competing gravitational pulls of the Earth and the Sun help the telescope keep a steady orbit while using minimal fuel. The James Webb Space Telescope orbits at this point, which gives the spacecraft an unobstructed view of the sky.
"It takes us a good three-plus months to get out there, and we're spending that time checking everything out and doing a whole bunch of calibrations and making sure everything is working the way we know it can," said NASA's Jeremy Perkins, an integration and test scientist on the mission. "It's basically like our time to kick the tires and just make sure that the focus is right, the pointing is right."
Uncovering cosmic mysteries
Roman is on a kind of ghost hunt, searching for more evidence of dark matter — mysterious, invisible stuff whose gravitational influence appears to hold galaxies together and define the overarching structure of the cosmos. Roman will study how gravity subtly affects the path of light along great distances throughout a massive survey of the sky. By doing this, the telescope will help map both normal and dark matter, giving scientists a better understanding of just what this elusive substance might be.
Astronomers will also use Roman's observations to uncover dark energy, the strange force that is believed to drive the expansion of the universe. Scientists' understanding of dark energy comes from observations of a kind of exploding star known as a Type Ia supernova. These supernovas appear to shine at known and predictable brightness throughout the cosmos, giving them the nickname of 'standard candles'. By cataloguing even more of these supernovas, scientists hope to develop a better understanding of how dark energy works, which could fundamentally change the way astronomers view the universe.
Roman will also search for planets outside our solar system. Since astronomers confirmed their existence in the 1990s, more than 6,000 exoplanets have been identified. With Roman, NASA expects to identify more than 100,000 of them by identifying dips in starlight caused by a planet passing in front of its own star. The telescope also hopes to find some 1,000 through microlensing — a technique that searches for tiny changes in background starlight caused by the gravity of a far-off planet.
The spacecraft is also demonstrating technology that blocks out that starlight and actually takes a picture of the planet.
A deluge of data
The telescope will beam back 1.4 terabytes of raw science data each day, using a refrigerator-sized high-gain antenna. The data will be available immediately to scientists and the public.
"Roman's database at the end of its prime mission after five years is going to be bigger than your standard music streaming platform," Perkins said.
Because of the massive amounts of data, NASA is making it available to anyone through a cloud-based system called Roman Nexus. For Perkins, that's what makes this mission unique — anyone can look at the raw data and find new discoveries.
"It's all the things that we are not expecting to see," he said. "It's all these one-in-a-million things that we're going to be able to see with Roman that really excites me."

Reports that the US is preparing to claim a big stake in Venezuela’s massive energy reserves have sparked an outcry, with critics describing the move as “predatory” and a “rapacious” land grab.
Several media outlets this week reported that the Trump administration – which abducted Venezuela’s authoritarian president, Nicolás Maduro, in January and has steered the South American country ever since – hopes to secure long-term access to its oil and gasfields.
Venezuela has the world’s largest proven crude oil reserves with an estimated 303bn barrels, compared with Saudi Arabia’s 268bn and Iran’s 208bn.
On Thursday, the Wall Street Journal said Trump officials were in “advanced talks” with Venezuelan officials to take “a direct stake in more than a dozen oilfields” containing 90bn barrels, nearly a third of Venezuela’s energy reserves.
“This is real and being discussed at the highest levels of the US and Venezuelan governments,” a source told Reuters, which said the fields being negotiated were in the Orinoco Belt and Lake Maracaibo regions.
Axios claimed the deal would be “a legacy-defining moment for President Trump”, with one unnamed official telling the US outlet: “Calling this deal huge would be an understatement … It is massive.”
Bloomberg, citing sources familiar with the negotiations, said one deal under discussion was a 100-year lease on several oilfields.
The reports caused unease and anger among members of Venezuela’s opposition, who are already up in arms about Trump’s failure to bring about genuine political change after capturing Maduro.
“It’s a land grab – a massive land grab,” said one well-known opposition figure who asked not to be named because of the sensitivities of criticising the US. “It’s revolting because this is not the United States one would have [expected]. This is not the United States of the Marshall plan. This is a rapacious, mafioso United States,” they added.
Since January’s special forces raid on Caracas, Venezuela has been led by an interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, who was Maduro’s vice-president and minister of petroleum. Other key members of Maduro’s regime have also retained positions of power, including the interior minister, Diosdado Cabello, who has been collaborating with Trump officials – despite having a $25m (£18m) US bounty on his head for alleged drug trafficking. Meanwhile, the exiled opposition leader, María Corina Machado, whose movement is believed to have won the 2024 presidential elections, has been sidelined.
Ricardo Hausmann, an exiled former minister and opposition supporter, wrote on X: “An illegitimate interim government with an illegitimate hydrocarbons law has no legitimacy to strike this unconstitutional deal. It will be a fiasco for all involved.”
The economist Francisco Rodríguez urged Venezuela’s national assembly to reject what he called a “predatory deal”. “Handing over Venezuela’s oil wealth to the US contravenes the constitution and is not in the interest of the Venezuelan people – much more when it is done at gunpoint,” Rodríguez said.
Luz Mely Reyes, a prominent journalist and government critic, sarcastically called the “surrender” of Venezuela’s natural riches “the deal of the century”.
Gregory Brew, an energy historian and Eurasia Group analyst, anticipated “quite a lot of suspicion and rejection of any deal that would hand the United States government effective control over Venezuelan resources”.
Brew said the reported deal reminded him of how BP, then the Anglo-Persian Oil Company, controlled the oil resources of Iraq and Iran at the start of the last century.
“Anglo-Persian was given a concession by the shah of Iran in 1901 … in exchange for what was essentially a bribe to the Persian government, and it gave the company sweeping rights. The company was essentially in total control of any oil it found and would be able to retain virtually all the profits of any other oil it found and exploited and exported,” Brew said.
“From Trump’s point of view, the control over oil is something of an end in and of itself,. But if you do try to rationalise it, I think US dominance over Venezuelan oil reserves allows the US to regard Venezuelan reserves as its own reserves: a source of oil from which the United States can draw and that nobody else has access to. I think that’s how the administration is conceiving of this – excluding China, excluding Russia, but I think also excluding other potential customers for Venezuelan oil,” he said. “It sounds colonial, because it is.”
Venezuela’s post-Maduro conversion into what many call a US protectorate is the most dramatic play in Trump’s push to reassert Washington’s influence over Latin America as part of the so-called “Donroe Doctrine”.
That policy is a 21st-century adaptation of the 19th-century Monroe doctrine by which President James Monroe sought to keep European powers out of the Americas. Trump’s version is about countering China’s growing footprint in the region and imposing US will through economic and military pressure.
Maduro’s downfall has brought some change to Venezuela, with hundreds of political prisoners freed under Rodríguez and talks about reforming the regime-controlled supreme court taking place.
But no date has been set for a fresh presidential election and Machado has been unable to return from exile. “Delcy’s been doing a fantastic job,” Trump told reporters last month, claiming Venezuela was “not really ready” for a vote.

At least eight people have died and 18 people are missing after a ferry carrying nearly 270 passengers and crew capsized off the coast of Turkish-occupied northern Cyprus, local authorities said.
The territory’s prime minister, Ünal Üstel, told the state-run TRT news channel on Sunday that 237 people had been rescued. A search was under way for those who remained unaccounted for.
“Search and rescue teams are working very intensively to find them,” said the Turkish Cypriot leader, Tufan Erhürman. “If there are people still inside the vessel, reaching them does not appear easy at the moment. Efforts are being made using other technologies to reach them as well.”
The ferry had “completely sunk to a depth of 514 metres”, said Erhan Arıklı, the territory’s transport minister.
The catamaran-style ferry had been travelling from the port of Kyrenia, also known as Girne, in the breakaway north of divided Cyprus, to the port of Taşucu in Mersin province, Turkey.
The port area of Kyrenia is a popular holiday destination for local people and tourists. The private ferry was one of several daily shuttle services that link northern Cyprus with Turkey.
Mehmet Harmancı, the mayor of Turkish-held northern Nicosia, described the disaster as the worst in the more than 40 years since the territory proclaimed independence.
“We’ve not seen anything like this before. It’s by far the worst tragedy. There are 23 people still missing. We think most of the passengers were Turks and Turkish Cypriots,” he told the Guardian.
Hours after the ferry capsized, many details remained unclear. “We still don’t know how many have been injured or to what degree. All the injured are being brought to hospital here in [northern] Nicosia. I’m off to the hospital and am in the process of gathering warm clothes.”
Kyrenia’s mayor, Murat Şenkul, said the ferry belonged to the Filo Denizcilik company and had sunk off Diana beach. It started taking in water about 7.5km (4 nautical miles) off the coast, TRT reported.
Video footage from the scene showed people wearing life vests floating in the waters around the capsized vessel. When the ship capsized, passengers clung to its overturned hull.
The Cyprus Broadcasting Corporation reported the boat was new and that when it began taking in water four miles from the coast, the captain had told the passengers to put on lifejackets.
Erhürman told CNN’s Turkish channel he was “deeply saddened” by the loss of life.
He said: “The ship capsized. It has sunk in an area where the water is 514 metres deep. So far, we have reached 244 people.”
Speaking from the crisis centre set up in the area, he said: “There is a great sense of shock here. This is not something we have experienced before ... We are extremely saddened. Everyone is doing everything they can and making every effort.”
A source close to Erhüman said the ferry was a popular means of travel between the mainland and the island for Turks working in northern Cyprus.
“It’s much cheaper than the plane and only fakes a few hours. A lot of Turkish citizens use it to travel and see their families back home,” said one official requesting anonymity. “You could say that a lot of the passengers were poor. It’s all just so very sad.”
Four coastguard vessels and a civilian passenger boat were deployed to the scene, along with five Turkish coastguard vessels and two helicopters, local officials said.

A purported statement by Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke is circulating on social media. In the viral post, Dipke is quoted as saying, “We are demanding responsibility, not resignation from the chief minister (of Jharkhand), so that problems don’t arise regarding papers in the future.”
The apparent statement was shared by a verified Instagram handle named ‘indians’ on August 14. The post received has over 74,600 reactions till date. The page has around 9 million followers. (Archive)
The caption of the post reads:
“… Dipke said he does not want Soren to resign, but wants accountability to ensure such incidents do not happen again. His stand has sparked questions among citizens over why accountability is being sought instead of resignation in this case, while Dharmendra Pradhan faced demands to resign.”
After Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned following CJP’s Delhi protests, a similar protest erupted in Ranchi over alleged paper leaks and irregularities in Jharkhand’s government recruitment exams. Protesters, including students and activists, demanded chief minister Hemant Soren’s resignation.
It was against this backdrop that the quote attributed to CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke went viral. The viral posts reinforce the key BJP charge that CJP was comparatively restrained when allegations of exam irregularities emerged in Opposition-ruled states, particularly Jharkhand. BJP leaders have used this argument to accuse the group of selective outrage. In comments to the above Instagram post, many users replied saying Dipke’s stance showed his ‘hypocrisy’ or ‘double standard’.
The same quotation was also shared by Facebook pages named The Youth – India and Saale Dost Ko Thanks Bolta hai. The follower counts of the two pages are 141,000 and 4.9 million, respectively.
Fact Check
To find more on the purported statement by Dipke, we first went through his X timeline, since the CJP founder regularly posts about his media interactions and public statements on his X account. We could not find any post corroborating the viral claim.
We, however, found a post from August 2 where Dipke is speaking to the protesting students in Jharkhand on a video call. “The CJP stands with all the students in Jharkhand and support their demands,” he wrote. He makes the same point in the video as well.
Spoke to the students who are protesting in Jharkhand over irregularities in JPSC and JSSC recruitment exams.
The CJP stands with all the students in Jharkhand and support their demands. pic.twitter.com/lLSRhFVpv1
— Abhijeet Dipke (@abhijeet_dipke) August 2, 2026
Next, we performed a keyword search on Google, looking for news reports on the said statement. We used the keyword combination: “Abhijeet Dipke Jharkhand Hemant Soren resignation”.
We could not find a single report which mentioned that Dipke had said they were only seeking accountability and responsibility, and not the Jharkhand chief minister’s resignation. Instead, we found several reports on the CJP and its founder supporting the Jharkhand students’ stir. For instance, this report in The Hindu states that Abhijeet Dipke “was in touch with the protesters and supported their demands, and they will go to Ranchi to express solidarity.” Similar reports were carried by outlets like The Print and The Times of India.
None of the articles mentioned anything similar to what the purported quote claims.
We also found an ANI post containing Dipke’s detailed response to the Jharkhand situation. He says, “… We offer our full support. Our delegation has visited the area, and our people are distributing food there. We stand firmly with them and support all their demands… I, too, intend to go… Although, I am currently dealing with some health issues…”
#WATCH | Chhatrapati Sambhaji Nagar, Maharashtra | On students’ protest in Jharkhand, Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) Founder Abhijeet Dipke says, “We offer our full support. Our delegation has visited the area, and our people are distributing food there. We stand firmly with them… pic.twitter.com/R3XbAv5jaT
— ANI (@ANI) August 7, 2026
In another interview with PTI, Dipke said CJP would support demands for educational reforms, irrespective of which state was in question and which party was in power.
Alt News then reached out to Abhijeet Dipke and asked him whether he had made the statement shown in the viral posts. Dipke replied: “Never said this. These people (the social media pages) are running anything they want.”
To sum up, the viral post quoting Abhijeet Dipke as saying that they were seeking accountability but not Jharkhand CM Hemant Soren’s resignation is baseless. There is no credible evidence of the CJP founder having made such a statement. Dipke himself refuted the claim.

The journey of Orry aka Orhan Awatramani on Khatron Ke Khiladi 15 may have hit an unexpected roadblock. The internet media personality, who has been participating in the stunt-based reality show and taking on a series of challenges, has seemingly hinted at an emotional exit following an injury sustained during a task.
Is Orry exiting Khatron Ke Khiladi 15 after injury? Emotional post sparks speculation: “Sometimes you have to accept defeat”
Orry recently shared a video on his Instagram Stories in which he appeared to be helped by others after getting injured during a challenge. Alongside the video, he posted an emotional message reflecting on his stint on the show and his attempt to complete the task. Sharing the update, Orry wrote, “I gave it my all guys and I am sorry I don’t have more in me to give. Really wanted to do this for us all and for me. I never wanted to give up and I never aborted. I really did try but sometimes you have to accept defeat.”
His message suggested that he had pushed himself during the challenge but was unable to continue. Orry also appeared to indicate that his health would take precedence over his participation in the show. He added, “Health always comes before everything. Wishing everyone the best.”
The post has since led to speculation about whether the injury could mark the end of Orry’s stint on Khatron Ke Khiladi 15. While his choice of words, particularly his reference to accepting defeat and not having more to give, has left fans wondering if he has been forced to step away, Orry has not explicitly confirmed his exit from the show.
Orry’s participation in Khatron Ke Khiladi has also been closely followed by viewers, with the internet personality taking on physical challenges as part of his stint on the reality show. His latest update has therefore added an emotional turn to his journey.
The stunt-based format requires contestants to take on physically demanding tasks involving heights, speed, animals and other challenges under the supervision of host Rohit Shetty. Injuries are an inherent risk of such tasks, and contestants can sometimes be required to withdraw depending on their condition.
For now, Orry’s Instagram post remains the only indication that his journey may have been affected by the injury. Whether the message signals a temporary setback or his departure from Khatron Ke Khiladi 15 is yet to be officially clarified.
Until there is a confirmation from Orry or the makers of the show, his status in the competition remains unclear.

Greater awareness is needed to counter misinformation on social media and unproven products marketed for preventing or controlling myopia, experts said at a webinar organised by The Hindu on Sunday (August 30, 2026).
At the webinar titled ‘Excess Screentime: Is it Harming Children’s Eyes?’, Vasumathy Vedantham, ophthalmologist, vitreoretinal surgeon and paediatric retina specialist, Radhatri Nethralaya, and Vasudha Kemmanu, consultant paediatric ophthalmologist and public eye health specialist, Narayana Nethralaya, discussed the growing concern over myopia and refractive errors among children.
Dr. Vedantham highlighted the need for parents to be cautious about health information circulating on social media. She said misinformation and claims around various products and interventions for eye health were common online, and stressed that parents should rely on evidence-based medical advice rather than unverified products or remedies.
Dr. Kemmanu emphasised the importance of adequate time outdoors for children, noting that reduced outdoor exposure was a concern amid rising myopia. She said governments should introduce stronger public health measures to promote outdoor time among children and address the growing burden of myopia.
She said governments and schools needed to be part of efforts to create environments that support children’s eye health.
The experts also discussed the importance of regular eye screening, recognising early signs of vision problems and seeking timely evaluation, particularly when children develop difficulty seeing distant objects or show changes in their visual behaviour.
The session was moderated by Athira Elssa Johnson, Senior Reporter, The Hindu.
