39-inch display size is the ultrawide sweet spot. Excellent image quality. Good connectivity, including USB-C. Lower price than competitors.
TIRED
Design is tepid. Included monitor stand allows too much wobble. Refresh rate is just 165 Hz at native resolution.
Ultrawide OLED monitors are amazing, but they’re often a bit lacking in sharpness.
Your choice has been to either accept the lower resolution these panels come with or upgrade to a massive 45-inch 5K panel, which is way too large for most desks (and comes with a much higher price tag).
Alienware’s AW3926QW offers a solution. It has a 39-inch 5K2K panel that provides a roughly 30 percent improvement in pixel density over the 34-inch alternatives. It also ships at a more tolerable (if still not affordable) price near $1,100. While a few annoyances remain, the AW3926QW will definitely appeal to gamers who want a bigger, sharper OLED ultrawide.
Sizing Up
Size and sharpness are the AW3926QW’s most important traits. The monitor has other features, which we’ll get into, but these basic characteristics set the AW3926QW apart from most OLED monitors available.
Let’s talk size first. As a 39-inch ultrawide monitor, the AW3926QW is already unique. Thirty-four inches (measured diagonally) is the standard size for ultrawide monitors, and Alienware has been a pioneer in that space since the launch of the AW3423DW in 2022. Forty-five-inch models have been introduced, but they're reserved for those who really want something almost TV-like on their desk. The AW3926QW nestles right in between, though, with a 39-inch panel—still at a 21:9 aspect ratio. Gamers who want a big display but don’t have room for a 45-inch model aren’t going to be happy with a 34-inch alternative, which looks tiny by comparison. The AW3926QW fills that gap perfectly, still offering an impressively large screen to game on.
It’s not the first to use this size (a handful of 39-inch OLED monitors with 3440 x 1440 resolution exist), but in my mind, it's the first to do it the right way. The larger the screen, the more those pixels get stretched out. You need an actual increase in pixels if you want to retain the same clarity. And that's where the Alienware AW3926QW takes a big step forward.
The panel’s resolution is 5120 x 2160, and the latter of those two numbers is key. It means the AW3926QW’s vertical resolution is equivalent to a 4K widescreen with 3,840 x 2,160 resolution, which in turn means you can view 4K content at its full resolution. That’s not possible on an ultrawide with 3,440 x 1,440 resolution.
As mentioned, some 45-inch OLED ultrawides also offer 5K2K resolution. Because they’re physically larger, however, they’re not quite as sharp as the AW3926QW.
OLED Perks Apply
Size and resolution are the AW3926QW’s distinctive traits, but the AW3926QW offers many less distinctive advantages that, though shared with many OLED monitors of various sizes, are still impressive.
Contrast is fantastic across the board. The AW3926QW can hit a perfect minimum luminance of zero nits, which means it provides an essentially infinite contrast ratio. Dark scenes provide a deep, inky black level yet also display excellent shadow detail.
The AW3926QW has an RGB stripe tandem OLED panel produced by LG. At the moment, it’s one of just two ultrawide monitors to offer the panel, which is also available from LG’s UltraGear Evo GX9. I recently tested the 27-inch Asus PG27UCWM, another RGB Strip OLED that I was impressed by, but it's a standard 16:9 aspect ratio rather than ultrawide. RGB Stripe OLED panels use a different sub-pixel array to produce better color performance at high brightness and sharper text.
The AW3926QW is bright for an OLED monitor. It quotes a maximum SDR brightness of 300 nits, which my testing confirmed. HDR, meanwhile, is quoted at a peak brightness of 1,300 nits. I didn’t manage to hit that, but I did record a peak brightness up to 1,011 nits, which is at the upper end of what the best OLED monitors can deliver.
Color performance is excellent. The color gamut spans 99 percent of DCI-P3 and 93 percent of AdobeRGB. These are excellent figures and comparable to the best OLED monitors on the market. Color accuracy was high. The monitor’s color performance isn’t just excellent for games; many creative professionals will also find it sufficient for work.
Meanwhile, the AW3926QW’s price of roughly $1,100 isn’t inexpensive, but it’s a lot less than the LG Ultragear Evo GX9, which debuted at an MSRP near $1,800 and currently retails around $1,600. So, what’s the catch?
It’s not connectivity. The AW3926QW has two HDMI 2.1 inputs, one DisplayPort 2.1 UHBR20 input, and one USB-C input that also supports DisplayPort 2.1 and provides 90 watts of power delivery. All of the video inputs can handle the monitor’s maximum resolution and refresh rate.
The monitor has a lot of downstream connectivity, too. It includes three downstream USB-A ports with a 5-Gbps data rate. You’ll also find a single downstream USB-C port with the same data rate and support for up to 15 watts of power delivery. A 3.5-mm audio jack rounds out the connectivity options.
Some Cost Cutting
The Alienware’s lower price is more evident in the monitor’s look and build quality.
As I’ve put on record across multiple reviews, I’m not a fan of Alienware’s current design language. I think it’s too basic and demure for the Alienware brand. Aside from the AW3926QW’s curved design, which is noticeable even at a glance, nothing about the monitor stands out. Even the curve is not that remarkable, as most ultrawide monitors are curved.
While I don’t like the look of the monitor, it’s a stretch to say it’s a problem. You’re not going to open the box and gasp in horror at the hideous sight you behold. On the contrary, the monitor’s design is inoffensive. Even boring.
I have a nitpick about the stand’s operation, however. It offers up to 4.3 inches of height adjustment, which is useful. However, the stand is a little too flexible. It allows the display to slightly wobble and shake while typing, though only at the upper end of the monitor’s height adjustment. It’s not a deal-breaker, but it could be better.
Motion clarity is this monitor's other sore spot. The Alienware AW3926QW offers a refresh rate of up to 165 Hz at native resolution. That’s not bad, but most modern 34-inch ultrawides hit 240 Hz, and some can hit 360 Hz. Most are less expensive as well.
Don’t get me wrong. The AW3926QW’s motion clarity remains excellent if it’s compared broadly to, say, all monitors to have ever existed in history. Small objects are often legible, scenes maintain detail during quick camera pans, and motion blur is often easy to miss. But it would be incorrect to suggest there’s no meaningful difference between a 165-Hz and a 360-Hz display. I’ve reviewed many of them, and I find the difference is obvious. Does a 165-Hz OLED look crisp in motion? Yes. Is 360 Hz clearly, distinctly, obviously better? Yes.
Alienware tries to mitigate the problem with a trick that many high-end gaming monitors now support: a lower display resolution mode with a higher refresh rate. The AW3926QW can hit a refresh rate up to 330 Hz if you reduce the resolution to 2,560 x 1,080. Unfortunately, 2,560 x 1,080 resolution is terribly dull on a 39-inch display. It works out to a pixel density only a hair better than a 32-inch 1080p widescreen, which is dismal for any computer monitor sold in 2026.
Personally, I don’t mind the 165-Hz refresh rate despite the fact that I can notice the difference, but I usually play RPGs and strategy games. Players who enjoy competitive esports titles, or who otherwise want the best motion clarity and fluidity possible, could find the 165-Hz refresh rate too low for their liking.
Walking the Line
The year isn’t over, but the Alienware AW3926QW already looks like one of the best new monitors of 2026. That’s not because it’s a game-changing monitor on its own merit (though I do think it’s very good), but instead because it fills a gap in the ultrawide monitor market.
The existing 34-inch OLED ultrawides with 3,440 x 1,440 resolution are in many ways fantastic, but they’re not all that large or sharp. Forty-five-inch ultrawides deliver the immersion and sharpness that the 34-inch alternatives lack, but they’re often too large to fit on a conventional desk, and they’re extremely expensive.
Alienware’s AW3926QW walks the line between these options. It’s big but not too big. It’s sharp but not too expensive. And it otherwise retains the perks that gamers have come to expect from OLED monitors, aside from a small hit to the refresh rate. Highly competitive gamers should look elsewhere, but gamers looking for big-screen immersion should put the AW3926QW on their short list.

The day after Thanksgiving, I learned I'd have to move out of my beloved century-old, two-bedroom apartment in Kansas City.
My building had been taken over by a management company in another state.
Unfortunately, this wasn't the beginning of a Hallmark movie in which the protagonist unites with her neighbors to successfully push back against a corporate takeover (all while finding love along the way).
Instead, I found myself panicking about my next move while grieving the comfortable life I'd been so proud to have built over the seven years I'd rented that space.
A few weeks later, my parents suggested that my cat and I move back into my childhood home in the suburbs nearby. As much as living with mom and dad in my 30s felt like it could be embarrassing or a huge step back, it felt like the best choice. So, I did.
I planned to stay for just a few months, but it's now been four years — and leaving feels more difficult than I ever anticipated.
Financially, this setup has been a blessing
My parents live in a home that they have been paying a mortgage on for nearly 30 years. It's much cheaper than anything on the rental market, and my financial contributions aren't even close to what I'd be paying if I lived elsewhere.
It's also been freeing not to chase roommates down for their share of the rent. I've cut back on my expenses even more by no longer paying for WiFi or electric bills, and doing laundry at home instead of a laundromat.
My parents have always purchased enough food for a full household, even when they were empty nesters. This means food is rarely in short supply, and my grocery bill is less, too.
Luckily, they also stock up on some great snacks and subscribe to a weekly May through October Community Supported Agriculture (CSA) box full of organic produce that I cannot get enough of.
To further contribute to the household, I like to offer support through physical labor and chores. Personally, I love to cook, bake, and run errands for the family. I also run errands for my grandmother, who lives close by, which helps me check in with her more regularly.
Our dynamic has shifted, and I'm enjoying getting to enjoy my parents in a new way
Living with my parents in my 30s is very different from when I was a kid or even a teenager.
I had been away for a number of years, living in other cities and on my own, and that independence has earned me more of my parents' trust.
They now realize I am too old for rules — for the most part. In time, they have backed down on strict curfews and specific chore guidelines. We've also been able to have important conversations around expectations.
I've made it clear that respecting this household and keeping my parents informed about my plans is still important to me, but that it might look different now that I'm older.
For example, when I first moved back, my dad was constantly checking in on me. It was difficult to deal with, especially because I'm a freelance creative with a varied social life and shifting schedule.
Still, I can understand a father worrying about their kid. A brief chat about my age and level of responsibility helped us find common ground and build trust around checking in as needed.
Sharing a space with my parents as an adult has also helped me see them as they are now, from a perspective that is so different and less selfish than the one I had in my adolescence.
I have gotten to work alongside them and admire the career people they are firsthand. I enjoy their respective skills and hobbies, and even the lively debates we stir up while watching a new TV show.
I didn't plan to stay long, but now I worry about how difficult leaving will be
Moving back home wasn't such a step backward after all. I have been able to jump into the gig economy full force, contribute regularly to the household, and spend time with family.
My "few months" at home with my parents has turned into four years.
Although I have plenty of savings that would allow me to move out and live comfortably, I've taken my time finding a stable living situation that makes sense for me.
However, leaving home and all its comforts will be a lot harder than I thought this time around.
Still, no matter where I end up, I'll continue to connect with my parents, whether taking my mom to concerts or trying new burger spots with my dad. I will also still offer to pick up sticks from the river birches in their backyard that I made them promise not to get rid of.
Everyone's timeline is unique and circumstances are different. I feel lucky — not embarrassed — I've got family to fall back on. And my parents will (most likely) always be my favorite roommates.

During a visit to Johnson Space Center, President Trump on Friday signed an executive order to establish a new commission with the purpose of creating the first national space academy.
“It’s clear that we will need to educate and train an entire generation of skilled service members, engineers, and civil operators, and everything else to do what we have to do,” Trump said. “I will sign an executive order to begin the process of creating a new national academy. It’s called the US Space Academy. That’s a big deal.”
The proposed United States Space Academy would fall under the jurisdiction of NASA, and according to US space officials, is not intended be a traditional service academy in the sense that it educates and trains officers for the armed services, such as the Air Force Academy.
Trump signed the executive order as part of a ceremony in Houston during which he awarded the Congressional Space Medal of Honor to the four astronauts who flew on Artemis II earlier this year.
Seeking to modernize NASA
This initiative is being spearheaded by NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, who included the development of an “academy” to seed the future NASA workforce as part of his Project Athena plan to revamp US civil space efforts.
The goal is to create a top-tier educational institution with free tuition and, in return, graduating students to fulfill a service commitment of several years. Graduates will have the choice of going into the US Space Force, but the majority of slots will be allocated to NASA and civilian positions, according to people familiar with the project.
Isaacman has been seeking to modernize NASA and help the space agency find its way at a time when the US commercial space industry is taking an increased role in the types of activities—launch, crewed spaceflight, space stations, lunar activities—that were once the sole province of the space agency. Isaacman has sought to increasingly lean on the commercial industry where it is excelling and focus NASA resources on cutting-edge initiatives, like developing a base on the surface of the Moon.

Heavyweight Itauma handed harsh world-title lesson
- Published
Moses Itauma was still a schoolboy when he would turn up at boxing gyms in his uniform and give seasoned professionals a hiding.
On Saturday night at the O2 Arena, the 21-year-old was finally given an education, as the Briton ran out of gas and the granite experience of Filip Hrgovic carried the Croatian to the vacant IBF heavyweight title.
The referee waved off the fight as Itauma's corner threw in the towel in the ninth round. But for long spells, Itauma was the quicker, sharper and more assured fighter, repeatedly finding Hrgovic with the left hand and showing exactly why so many inside boxing believe he has the tools to reach the very top.
Yet what made the contest so compelling was the growing sense that, even while Itauma was winning rounds, he was drifting closer to defeat.
- 'Unbelievable' - Stephenson, Bellew & others react to Hrgovic's stoppage of Itauma 
  - Published57 minutes ago
- Wardley-Dubois rematch set for 17 October in London 
  - Published8 hours ago
His mouth opened in search of air and the spring disappeared from his legs. Hrgovic, hardened by the kind of difficult nights Itauma had never experienced, simply stayed there and waited for the younger man's body to betray him.
The sight afterwards was a sobering one as Itauma - who suffered a first defeat in his 15th pro fight - left the arena on a stretcher, before being taken to hospital.
"It's precautionary that he's gone to the hospital. That's what we always do to make sure because the most important thing is the boxer's health," promoter Frank Warren said.
"He's done something to his leg as well and he was quite tired. It was a high paced, fast fight for both the guys."
The remarkable night should not be remembered as the moment Itauma was exposed as incapable of operating at world level - his boxing showed the opposite.
What it exposed was the difference between possessing world-level talent and having the conditioning, experience and ring craft required to manage a 12-round world-title fight.
Where did it go wrong?
It would be too simplistic - and unfair - to say Hrgovic won the fight purely through mind games, but the 34-year-old had succeeded in making the build-up uncomfortable.
Hrgovic spent fight week repeatedly attacking Itauma's age, dismissing him as "just a kid". As the week wore on, Itauma looked increasingly irritated and eventually lost his composure at the weigh-in, shoving Hrgovic before the Croatian responded with a slap.
Itauma prides himself on being unusually cerebral for a heavyweight. He reads psychology and self-help books, talks openly about sharpening his mind and appears to spend far more time analysing himself than most 21-year-olds.
But there is always a danger that deep thinking becomes overthinking, something Anthony Joshua has been accused of repeatedly during the latter stages of his career.
Whether the pre-fight barbs played any part or not, Itauma's gameplan once the bell rang was clear; he wanted to end the night early.
"Someone said to me he doesn't feel like he'd win a world title unless he knocks him out. I didn't like that," promoter Frank Warren said afterwards.
That mindset was understandable because it had served Itauma extraordinarily well until now. But perhaps Hrgovic had been underestimated by almost everybody - Itauma, the media, pundits, former fighters and bookmakers who installed the Briton as a heavy favourite.
Hrgovic is an Olympic bronze medallist who went 12 hard rounds with the giant Zhilei Zhang, while against Daniel Dubois - the only defeat on his record - he was leading on two of the three scorecards before the fight was stopped because of cuts.
'El Animal' knew what it felt like to be hurt, to become tired and to remain in a fight when things were going badly. Itauma did not.
The eighth round summed up both Itauma's extraordinary talent and his lack of experience. He threw more punches than in any other round of the fight, pouring what remained of his energy into trying to remove a man who had already demonstrated that he was exceptionally difficult to remove.
"He was throwing too much. He was fighting like an amateur," Hrgovic said afterwards. "I knew I needed to endure it. I need to stay there. He will get tired and I'll get him in the later rounds."
There are questions about the Chatham fighter's preparation, too. Itauma - who had never gone beyond six rounds professionally - admitted before the fight that he had never even sparred 12 rounds.
His conditioning was clearly not where it needed to be for a championship fight and responsibility for that cannot rest solely with the fighter - it also falls on the experienced team entrusted with preparing him.
Educated, not exposed - will Itauma learn his lesson?
Itauma showed that many of the qualities which looked spectacular against lesser opposition still worked against a genuine world-level heavyweight.
He proved he can take a punch - there was no single blow that suddenly revealed a fragile chin. His hand speed troubled Hrgovic and he made the Zagreb fighter look slow.
So with those positives in mind, where does he go from here?
"Don't give up. Don't lose confidence. Get a few easy fights, easy wins. Build again and learn off these mistakes. You can't box like an amateur. It's a 12-round fight, you need to pace yourself," was Hrgovic's advice.
Warren remains convinced that Itauma is one of the most exceptional talents he has encountered, pointing towards two-time world champion Dubois as a prime example of a heavyweight who rebuilt successfully after painful setbacks.
But British boxing has seen the other side of that story too, of course - where fighters like David Price were once regarded as the country's next great heavyweight hope before successive defeats damaged an aura they never fully recovered.
Audiences will now scrutinise Itauma's every move, his breathing and how he paces a fight. That vulnerability may actually make him a more compelling fighter to follow.
The aura of untouchable perfection is gone. The schoolboy has been taught a lesson and now we will find out what he learns from it.

Trump cuts to science advisory boards have long-lasting consequences, researchers say
Netia McCray recalls how excited she was to join the federal advisory committee on long COVID in 2025. She had been diagnosed in the early days of the pandemic — and symptoms such as fatigue, heart palpitations and shortness of breath had become a frustrating but inescapable part of life.
By joining this group of doctors, researchers and other experts advising on the disease, McCray, 36, had hoped to channel her years of experience as a long-COVID patient into "something that could benefit so many individuals like myself and my community," she says. The work, she felt, could make her part of the solution for a debilitating condition that impacts millions of Americans.
But McCray had only been on the committee for a few months when she received an email notice that the group was terminated, "effective immediately."
McCray's advisory group is one of more than 100 science-focused federal committees that have been terminated under the second Trump administration, according to a news analysis in the journal Nature. As of March of this year, more than a quarter of the country's healthcare-related committees have been shut down, according to the advocacy group Public Citizen.
As a result, McCray is one of hundreds of experts who are no longer meeting to work on some of the most intractable and urgent problems around health and science in the United States. The losses linked to the demise of these groups are difficult to quantify, but participants and advocates say the impacts will reverberate across federal agencies for years.
A rare team of cross-functional experts
McCray — who runs a nonprofit helping high school students access opportunities in STEM — was joined on the committee by pediatrician Dr. Alexandra Yonts, at Children's National Hospital in Washington, D.C. Yonts, one of the few experts in the country who specializes in long COVID in children, was also eager to contribute to the advisory group. Patients often travel long distances to be seen in her clinic. She has frustratingly few options.
" We need new therapeutics," says Yonts.
Twelve other experts from a cross section of relevant fields including public health, pulmonology, and critical care joined this group to think together about how to galvanize new solutions.
But the committee never had a single meeting.
A hallmark of American government
The U.S. has long relied on a system of gathering outside experts from a range of backgrounds in order to advise federal agencies on complex issues. It was formalized in 1972, when Congress passed the Federal Advisory Committee Act, or FACA. The committees are composed primarily of volunteers, and draw from across fields of relevant study and practice.
Today, the list of science-related issues that these committees are convened to explore is vast and ranges from astrophysics to public health to biomedical research — advising on questions such as when and which vaccines children should receive, how often people should be screened for cancer, or how best to prevent asteroids from hitting the Earth.
" The beauty of FACA is that it brings brilliant minds together for issues of the day, and allows them to openly adjudicate and to prioritize with limited resources how to get to next steps," says Michael Abrams, a health researcher at the group Public Citizen who published a report on these terminated committees and describes them as a kind of connective tissue that helps facilitate good government.
The Union of Concerned Scientists – an advocacy group for researchers and scientists – now counts 150 advisory committees at science agencies terminated in 2025 alone.
Officials from the White House did not respond to requests as to why specific committees were terminated, but said in a statement that the dissolved committees "were found to be redundant, unnecessary, or ineffective."
Yet outside science advocacy groups worry that without them, important issues of science and research will be neglected and siloed within federal agencies. " What advisory committees can do is give a diversity of viewpoints and an independence of viewpoints that no one organization will ever have," says Russ Paulsen, President and CEO of the the science advocacy group Research!America.
Terminated committees include those devoted to topics such as managing fisheries and sustaining U.S. seafood resources; planning future NASA space science and astrophysics missions; and reducing preventable infections in hospitals.
No substitute for real world perspective
People with real-world experience working in healthcare, says infectious disease researcher Hilary Babcock, offer invaluable perspective to officials at federal agencies like the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — by helping them to put theory into practice. Babcock was on the Healthcare Infection Control Practices Advisory Committee, or HICPAC, before it was terminated.
"They don't need help necessarily knowing what the literature shows," says Babcock. "But what they don't do is work in hospitals and healthcare systems, so they don't necessarily understand intuitively what it means to try to operationalize findings from literature into guidance."
One example is the drug-resistant fungus Candida auris, one of many issues that Babcock and her colleagues were grappling with in their work on the committee.
Candida auris can live on surfaces in healthcare facilities and cause deadly infections in humans. Cases have risen sharply in recent years as clinicians have struggled to find interventions to treat it.
The fungus can spread between patients and resist some antifungal treatments. Babcock worries that the fungus is not getting the attention it deserves without the work of the committee. " There is some sort of interim guidance around Candida auris from the CDC, but we're not getting updated guidance," she says.
The fungus requires specific disinfectant practices in order to eradicate it..
Scott Roberts, an infectious disease doctor at Yale, has treated patients in the U.S. with Candida auris and worries that without a federal advisory committee to offer best practices on treating it, doctors like himself will be left with a patchwork of protocols, especially those at smaller or rural facilities. That patchwork, he says, could leave room for the fungus to spread.
"Losing a federal advisory committee on this is only going to make the problem worse," says Roberts.
Checks on authority
Other participants from advisory groups say these groups offer important checks on authority for officials inside the government.
"As a federal official, I found advisory committees to be really helpful to me in my thinking and policy development," says Carrie Wolinetz, who for years worked with advisory committees in her capacity as an official at the National Institutes of Health. Wolinetz now works outside government in healthcare policy and advocacy.
"They would bring up real-world issues that I — from within government — would not necessarily have thought of."
Juan Meza, a professor of applied mathematics at the University of California, Merced, has served on a number of advisory committees during his career. Meza recalls an occasion years ago when one committee he served on advised federal leadership at the Department of Energy against making an investment in supercomputers.
" The fact that we were supposed to be independent, I think gave us a certain amount of leeway to say, 'No. We've gotta go with what we think is right," says Meza. Reluctantly, he adds, leadership followed their advice.
Even when leadership does not take recommendations from committees, they create important transparency in government, says Kelly Holley-Bockelmann, a professor of astrophysics who until recently worked at Vanderbilt University. Holley-Bockelmann served on the Astrophysics Advisory Committee before it was terminated.
" There were a couple times where we offered expertise that was not listened to," says Holley-Bockelmann, "But nonetheless, we felt it was really important to get it down on record."
In a statement, NASA officials called the termination of the astrophysics committee a "restructuring," writing that they had merged several committees into one. The statement asserts that the agency "has remained committed to continuing to engage with the science community in a variety of ways."
But others who work in the NASA ecosystem say the previous structure of committees offered an important way to gather information from stakeholders at all levels.
The committees allowed the space agency's leaders to "hear almost directly from the community," says Amanda Hendrix, CEO of the Planetary Science Institute and a former member of another federal committee called the NASA Advisory Council.
That advisory group historically helped set the agenda for NASA priorities, she says, and pushed the agency to offer explanations as to why they made the investments they did for future years.
It's a rare tool of American government, says Hendrix, that provides this kind of accountability and window into decision making.
" I felt like the interactions with NASA folks at the different committee levels was very useful and important for the community," says Hendrix. "So it's really disappointing that that's all gone now."

England has experienced its driest July since records began in 1836, receiving only 6.5mm of rainfall – 10% of the country’s long-term meteorological average for the month. Wales also experienced its driest-ever July, while Northern Ireland recorded its eighth driest. Scotland was the only country in the UK not to set new records but still received only 69% of its average rainfall for July compared with the long-term average. Southern England faced the worst of the dry conditions with some areas, including the Sussex coast, receiving less than 0.2mm of rain in July. This resulted in widespread low moisture content within the soil, enabling temperatures to reach the high 30s celsius.
Looking ahead, despite notable spells of rain in the north, parts of southern England may receive only the odd shower for the rest of August. Throughout the summer, forecast models have hinted at more unsettled weather reaching the south-east of England at a 10-day range. However, as time edged closer the rain was largely confined to north-western parts of Britain, failing to reach the south-east with any significance. With much uncertainty within forecast models, the risk of this dry period persisting is not out of the question.
There is a disturbance in the Atlantic, approximately 1,000 miles east of the Lesser Antilles. The National Hurricane Centre has predicted an 80% chance of the cyclone forming in the next 48 hours as a short-lived tropical depression. If such a system does strengthen, it will become the fourth named storm of the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season and would be named Dolly. Regardless of any development, there will be a risk of gusty winds and heavy rainfall in Lesser Antilles on Friday night and into Saturday. This year’s strong El Niño is expected to play a significant role in lessening hurricane activity within the Atlantic.
In India, the monsoon continues to cause devastation, particularly in eastern regions where flooding in Assam has caused 100 deaths as of 10 August. Flooding caused by rivers overflowing has resulted in 700,000 people being displaced over the last month. This includes 300,000 displaced near the Brahmaputra, one of the largest rivers in Asia. The monsoon also brought significant lightning, which resulted in the deaths of 14 people in eastern India on the 4 August, including 10 in the district of Giridih. Many of the dead were farm workers, caught in open agricultural fields where there is a lack of shelter to provide safety when such storms arrive.

Somewhere in Japan this spring, a child who could easily read the blackboard in first grade began squinting at it by third grade. In just two years, the child’s myopia had roughly tripled. We have come to treat this as an ordinary part of childhood — a visit to the optician, a first pair of glasses, and life goes on. But it is not ordinary. Myopia is a disease, and much of it is preventable.
A career in ophthalmology and medical research has meant watching this epidemic advance in slow motion while arguing — in a book, newspaper articles and peer-reviewed research — that its seriousness has been badly underestimated. But this summer, for the first time in the nation’s history, the government acknowledged the problem. Japan’s Basic Policy for 2026, the blueprint guiding the country’s economic and fiscal course, now includes language on preventing childhood myopia. After years of advocacy, that is a genuine milestone.
But it is only a starting point.

Bishkek, Aug 30: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday arrived in Kyrgyzstan, where he is scheduled to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit and hold a series of bilateral meetings on the sidelines.
The prime minister was received at the airport by Kasymaliev Adylbek Aleshovich, chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers.
A traditional Kyrgyz dance performance was also held at the airport to welcome the prime minister.
Modi is visiting Kyrgyzstan at the invitation of President Sadyr Zhaparov to participate in the 26th SCO Summit on August 31-September 1.
The 10-member SCO is marking 25 years of the organisation.
It was founded in 2001 by China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan with India and Pakistan joining as full members in 2017, followed by Iran in 2023 and Belarus in 2024.
Modi is expected to hold bilateral meetings with SCO leaders, including with Kyrgyz President Zhaparov and Russian President Vladimir Putin, on the sidelines of the summit.
In his departure statement on Saturday, Modi said he looked forward to advancing India’s vision for the region, anchored in “security, connectivity and opportunity, and to working with fellow members for a region free from the scourge of terrorism, separatism and extremism”.
“I also look forward to meeting President Zhaparov and other SCO leaders,” he said.
He will also attend the opening ceremony of the 6th World Nomad Games.
The prime minister said this visit will strengthen India’s strategic partnerships in Central Asia, deepen its civilisational connect with the region, and advance a shared pursuit of peace, stability and prosperity.

How China’s liquor heartland traded old spirits for new energy
Home to one of the nation’s legendary baijiu makers, Yibin is racing to reinvent itself as a hi-tech manufacturing hub – though stark challenges remain
Wuliangye, China’s second-largest liquor producer, is a household name. But Yibin, the lower-tier city in Sichuan province home to the famous baijiu maker, has long flown under the radar.
So when I received an invitation earlier this month for a media trip to Yibin, the first question that sprang to mind was: where exactly is it?
Tucked away behind the hills of western China, we had to fly to Chengdu, Sichuan’s capital, followed by a bus transfer. And when we finally arrived, local officials were keen to show us everything the city had to offer – except the liquor.
“Wuliangye is old-fashioned,” local cadres said.
What followed was a tour of a prefecture-level city trying hard to redefine itself: from a sleepy backwater into a manufacturing hub, with many of the costs typically associated with breakneck development.
One of the first things that caught our eye was a 288-metre (about 944 feet), 57-storey skyscraper rising from a prime waterfront plot with sweeping vistas of the Yangtze River. The building, one of the tallest in Sichuan, is expected to house the province’s first five-star Westin hotel in 2027 after its developer signed a contract with America’s Marriott International.

I used to be an avid hiker and would try to go backpacking a few times a year. I always dreamed of thru-hiking the Appalachian Trail, but life kind of got in the way. (Turns out jobs, wives, and children aren’t thrilled with the idea of you disappearing for three months.) But I’ve been longing to reconnect with my love of the outdoors and just recently took my kids on their first camping trip. So I discovered A Trail Tale at a really opportune time. It’s an interactive trail journal created by Andy Moliski with help from his brothers Adam and Alex.
Vicariously hike the Appalachian in the gorgeous A Trail Tale
It’s an interactive trail journal inspired by Sierra point-and-click adventures and Oregon Trail.
The various segments of the trail are rendered in beautiful pixel art reminiscent of a ‘90s Sierra point-and-click adventure. Alex recorded an equally gorgeous original score that combines nature sounds, acoustic guitar, strings, and even what sounds like clarinet.
As you click through each day, you’re greeted with information about landmarks and a game-like UI that is partially inspired by titles like Oregon Trail. (Spoiler: nobody dies of dysentery in this one.) Clicking on Andy unfurls a menu of icons that offer details about the journey, his mental state, and even bits of poetry. There are even little icons for things that impact his fortitude and morale meters, like inclement weather or picturesque scenery.
It’s insanely easy to just get lost in Andy’s journey for hours. And it’s making me wonder if I should get back out there and start tackling some more of the AT myself.

The observance of Holy Mass was held on Sunday morning (August 30, 2026) at the St. Mary’s Cathedral Basilica in Keralam’s Kochi after a gap of four years, with the priest facing members of the congregation.
A sizeable share of priests and laity members of the Ernakulam-Angamaly Archdiocese had been demanding this mode of Mass, while opposing the Unified Mass that the Synod of the Syro-Malabar Church had been insisting on.
The Archdiocesan Movement for Transparency (AMT), which had been demanding the congregation-facing mass, said in a release on Sunday (August 30, 2026) that a consensus had been reached on the matter and that the Sunday service was held accordingly.
A communication shared by the AMT —dated 22 August and bearing the sign of Fr. Thomas Mangattu, Administrator of the Cathedral Basilica— said that a Unified Mass will be held on Sundays at 5 p.m.
The scheduled congregation-facing Mass will be held during the time of festivals, anniversaries, among other occasions. The same mode of mass would apply to marriage ceremonies being held on Sunday noon.
The consensus also spoke of church members taking swift measures to withdraw litigation they filed against each other in the wake of the dispute regarding the mode of Mass.
On Friday, clergy and laity members of the church who attended a protest meeting here, had given a call to boycott bishops, including the Major Archbishop, until they got ‘justice’ from the Synod. They had also warned of withdrawing from the consensus that had been reached, until and unless the Synod chose bishops from among the priests of the Ernakulam-Angamaly archdiocese.
They further warned that a lasting settlement would not be found, until a liturgical variant was permitted for the mode of Mass that they had been demanding.
Meanwhile, the executive committee of the One Church One Qurbana Movement has said that it would not agree with the ‘consensus agreement’ on the mode of Mass at the church.
The agreement was reached with a few persons who were not associated with stakeholders who have been seeking Unified Mass. The archdiocese must explain who entrusted these persons to be party to any such agreement, the movement said, in a release.

Why are there so few African players in the WSL?
- Published
Plenty of talent was on show during the Women's Africa Cup of Nations this month - but why do so few players from the continent play for clubs in England?
The Women's Super League is widely regarded as one of the best leagues in the world and Europe's top talent is flooding in.
Two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas joined London City Lionesses this summer - the latest figure from Spain's World Cup-winning squad to move to the WSL.
It follows past high-profile moves from foreign players, including Australia captain Sam Kerr who made 158 appearances for Chelsea before joining Gotham.
Some of the United States' biggest stars are in the WSL too, including Chelsea duo Alyssa Thompson and Naomi Girma, Arsenal's Emily Fox and Manchester City's Sam Coffey.
There has also been an influx of Asian talent in recent seasons, with Japan captain Yui Hasegawa becoming one of the WSL's best players at Manchester City.
BBC Sport explores why the WSL has just four African players - Chiamaka Nnadozie (Brighton and Nigeria), Aisha Masaka (Brighton and Tanzania), Rofiat Imuran (London City Lionesses and Nigeria) and Ines Belloumou (West Ham and Algeria).
- Why Michaely Bihina is the keeper making waves at Wafcon 
  - Published5 days ago
- Cameroon claim first Wafcon title with victory over Malawi 
  - Published4 days ago
- African quartet secure Women's World Cup places 
  - Published9 August
Where are Africa's biggest stars?
The small representation in the WSL is not because of a lack of talent in Africa.
National Women's Soccer League (NWSL) clubs in America have shown huge interest, spending big money on some of the continent's best players.
Zambia forward Racheal Kundananji became the most expensive women's footballer at the time in 2024 when she joined Bay FC from Madrid CFF for £685,000.
Her compatriot Barbra Banda, who plays for Orlando Pride, was voted the BBC Women's Footballer of the Year in the same year.
Cameroon's Wafcon player of the tournament Monique Ngock is at Washington Spirit, where six African international players currently reside.
Temwa Chawinga won the NWSL Golden Boot and Most Valuable Player awards in her first two seasons with Kansas City Current.
Her sister, Malawi captain Tabitha Chawinga, plays for European giants Lyon and helped her country reach the final of Wafcon last week, where they lost to Cameroon.
Michaely Bihina, who was a standout performer in the tournament for Cameroon, plays for Benfica.
Nnadozie, who notably became the first African goalkeeper to be shortlisted for the Women's Ballon d'Or award, joined Brighton last year. The Seagulls goalkeeper ended her season with an FA Cup final appearance at Wembley against WSL champions Manchester City.
What are some of the barriers?
A major barrier for WSL clubs hoping to sign African talent is the Governing Body Endorsement (GBE) criteria set out in the league's registration rules.
Foreign players must earn a minimum number of points in five categories to be eligible for a GBE visa.
The number of caps they have for their national team, appearances in the Women's Champions League and the ranking of their former clubs play a part.
WSL sides also have to compete with the wages and transfer fees being offered by NWSL clubs, who are targeting the best African footballers.
They have to use resources for scouting which, at the moment, is prioritised across Europe.
Another major issue is the lack of coverage given to the domestic game in Africa, as well as issues around Wafcon.
There was confusion in this edition when the Confederation of African Football (CAF) named Channel 4 as the UK broadcast partner, but no matches were shown live in the opening round as an agreement had not been formally reached.
The tournament had also been postponed just 12 days before it was set to kick off in Morocco, eventually taking place three months later.
Switzerland captain Lia Walti, who signed for Brighton this summer, told BBC Sport that, globally, coverage of women's football has room for improvement.
"I think you have to bring the game to the people. You kind of have to force people to watch it. I felt that was how it maybe started in England," she said.
"In a lot of other countries I think they have bad coverage. It's not shown at all, or if it's shown, from where they film the game [makes it look] really poor.
"It affects the way you watch a game. You don't really see the speed, the tactics or anything and you don't enjoy watching the game."
- What we learned from Wafcon 2026 
  - Published3 days ago
'Africa shouldn't be left behind'
Malawi's magical route to the Wafcon final ensured they will play in the Women's World Cup for the first time next year, alongside champions Cameroon, and semi-finalists Algeria and Morocco.
Tabitha Chawinga believed the Malawi side put their nation on the map and showed their quality.
Speaking to BBC's World Service following their final defeat by Cameroon, the Malawi captain said: "It's really the best. No-one gave Malawi a chance to be in the finals, no-one gave Cameroon a chance to be in the finals.
"But as you can see, we watched fantastic football. There was amazing football from both sides."
Nigeria goalkeeper Nnadozie paved the way in the WSL last year with her move to Brighton.
She told BBC Sport in October her Ballon d'Or nomination made a "big impact" in Africa and put the spotlight on some of the continent's best talent.
"We have so many good players and they just need the opportunity to show what they can really do," she said.
"Very soon, we will have more numbers [in the Ballon d'Or nominations] from Africa. Trust me, there are so many good talents from Africa.
"Some players have had the opportunity to come to Europe but some have stayed back home. I hope in the future, bigger competitions will come to Africa.
"The Under-17s World Cup is in Morocco. This is big evidence that they are doing a lot of great jobs over there. It is just a matter of time.
"Women's football is rising and Africa shouldn't be left behind."

New York housing block explosion leaves teenager dead as authorities link blaze to lithium-ion battery
The explosion set the building on fire
An explosion at a New York City housing authority building that left a teenager dead and set the building on fire over the weekend was linked to an e-bike’s lithium-ion battery, according to a report.
Fire officials said the blaze broke out around 7 p.m. Friday at the New York City Housing Authority Albany Houses apartment complex in Crown Heights, Brooklyn.
Sources told NY1 that they believe the fire was caused by a lithium-ion battery. It was not immediately clear where the e-bike was at the time of the fire.
At least 34 fire trucks and first responder vehicles responded to the public housing development, located at 162 Troy Avenue.
On their arrival, first responders found smoke and flames coming out of the building.
Authorities found an 18-year-old man unconscious inside an apartment in the building. He was taken to the hospital, where he died from his injuries.
Residents described the fire as fast moving.
“I was talking to the mother last week … we was having good talk about our kids. And that’s messed up how we both moved here young and our small children and for her to lose one … ,” a neighbor told Pix 11 about the victim’s family.
The victim’s identity has not been released by authorities and the cause of the explosion remains under investigation.
The blaze was put out by about 8 p.m., authorities said.
A resident told Pix 11 that it was the second fire at the location in two years.

Srinagar, Aug 29: Government Girls Higher Secondary School (GGHSS) Amira Kadal celebrated its annual day on Saturday with a blend of cultural performances, academic recognition and a tribute to the role of parents in shaping students’ achievements.
The annual function also witnessed the release of the school magazine “Uqaab”, which showcased the creative and academic contributions of the students.
Adding colour to the celebrations, students presented a series of cultural performances centredaround the theme of inclusiveness and social harmony.
The programme featured Ladakhi dance, Punjabi performance and the traditional Kashmiri Rouf which highlighted the diversity of India’s cultural landscape.
However, the most poignant moment of the function came when mothers of students who had excelled in the previous year’s JK Board of School Education (JKBOE) examinations were felicitated on behalf of their children.
The mothers of a few meritorious students attended the annual day function of the school and were felicitated on behalf of their kids, who were not present at the felicitation ceremony of their school
As the mothers walked onto the stage with pride to receive the honours, the ceremony turned into an emotional acknowledgement of the families behind the students’ success.
The moment made the gesture a special recognition of the mothers’ contribution and support.
In his address, Member of Legislative Assembly (MLA) Lal Chowk Constituency Ehsan Pardesi hailed the school administration, particularly the principal, for carrying forward the legacy of the institution.
Director School Education Kashmir (DSEK) Naseer Ahmad Wani, who was the guest of honour at the occasion, in his address stressed the need for strengthening ethical and social values among students.
He said that while technology has made access to education easier, values such as respect and responsibility cannot be acquired from online platforms alone.
“Students today have access to a wide range of educational resources through YouTube and other online platforms, but the responsibility of imparting ethics and social values rests with students themselves and their teachers,” he added.
“Respect for our colleagues, respect for our teachers and respect for our parents is very important,” he added.
He further urged the students to remain conscious of their responsibility towards society.
DSEK said the message emerging from the traditional Ladi Shah performance by a school student was the one that everyone should follow in their daily lives.
“Education should not remain confined to academic achievement but character-building and ethical conduct must form an integral part of a student’s development,” he added.
He congratulated the students who were felicitated during the function and appreciated their efforts across academics, sports and cultural activities.
He also lauded students for pursuing diverse career paths, including medicine, humanities and sports.
He said the Annual Day function is a special function as students look forward to the occasion throughout the year and work during the academic session to improve their performance, showcase creativity and earn recognition.
He also appreciated students who participated in academic, sporting and cultural events and congratulated the school management for organising the felicitation ceremony, release of the school magazine and cultural performances with coordination.
Chief Education Officer Srinagar Ghulam Mohiudin Bhat and Principal GGHSS Amira KadalNusratManzoor also spoke at the occasion.

The parents are calling for video cameras to be installed in classrooms at state special schools and in buses used to transport students to and from the schools.
A parents' group has asked the state government to conduct a review into the alleged abuse of 60 students at an eastern Victorian special developmental school, which they claim has been left unchecked for years.
Voices for Special Needs (VFSN) alleges extensive incidents of physical, mental and sexual abuse over an almost 20-year period at Latrobe Special Development School.
Allegations seen by the ABC and raised with Victorian premier Ben Carroll on Saturday include details of 15 alleged incidents of sexual abuse.
The allegations include student-on-student sexual abuse and inappropriate remarks and sexual assaults of students by staff.
They also include ongoing sexualised behaviours by students that allegedly ran unchecked by staff in what parents say is a pattern of secrecy and abuse.
The allegations are drawn from the alleged experiences of parents, students and former staff at Latrobe SDS.
Spokesperson for VFSN, Leanne Vella, said the faith and trust of parents whose children attended the school had been shaken.
As well as an independent investigation, the group wants video cameras installed in classrooms at special schools like Latrobe SDS and in buses used to transport students to and from the school to provide a layer of security and safety for students.
"For the life of me, I can't see why it's not just a given," Ms Vella said.
"They are our most vulnerable citizens. They have a right to have eyes on them."
The group has presented a timeline of the alleged assaults, said to have occurred between 2008 and 2026, to the premier and all state MPs.
Some of the victims in the timeline were withdrawn from the school after the alleged incidents, and their parents say they suffer from ongoing health impacts.
Abuse shocking, advocate says
Disability rights advocate Julie Phillips, who has been working with VFSN, has previously advocated for students in other special schools around Victoria, including in Bendigo and Sunshine.
"[Abuse is] more likely to occur in special schools probably because of the closed culture … so it's easier to hide an abusive culture," Ms Phillips said.
But she said she had been shocked by the alleged abuse perpetrated at Latrobe SDS.
"Latrobe probably has a greater number, to my knowledge, of the sexual offences student-to-student that haven't been dealt with than any other special school that I've come across."
In the timeline presented to the state's politicians, it's alleged that a particular student sexually assaulted children more than six times on school grounds over a seven-year period.
"A lot of [children] are withdrawn from the school situation as a result of what's [been alleged] and leaving the school system altogether,"
"Is that what we want?"
'No school, no school'
Former parent Carrie* said since leaving the school her son has been medicated for anxiety.
One day in 2014, when she picked him up from school, Carrie said her son let out a "deep howl".
"He just completely lost it in the car, he was inconsolable."
She said he showed signs of fear about using the toilet, backing into a wall and covering his genitals.
He would not let her help him to shower and refused to change his clothes for several days.
"He would cry before he got on the [school] bus, he would hide his bag, he'd repeat 'no school, no school' over and over," Carrie said.
Her son is non-verbal, so she has not been able to confirm what happened, but she believes he was sexually assaulted.
She felt staff did not take her concerns seriously.
Carrie removed her son from the school in 2020, feeling that she could go no further with her concerns.
Twelve years on he still has a fear of going to the toilet and pulls his pubic hair out when he feels agitated.
Family feels let down
A second parent, Monica*, said she took her concerns to the police after her daughter alleged she had been inappropriately touched by a contractor who worked at the school.
She said she explained to detectives the best way to communicate with her daughter, who uses sign gestures and PECS boards to speak.
She said detectives took her daughter's clothing for forensic testing and interviewed her using basic sign language, but not the resources her speech pathologist had offered to provide.
Monica said police would not allow her or her mother in the interview room for support, and an interpreter from Melbourne was not able to travel due to the COVID lockdown.
She told the ABC that police said her daughter would not make a good witness if the case went to court.
A Victoria Police spokesperson said the child's allegations had been investigated and found to be unsubstantiated.
"The investigation included forensic testing and an interview with the child," they said.
"At no stage whatsoever was the child denied access to their usual communication tools or the family told the child wouldn't make a good witness.
"The child's mother was present at the station during the interviewing process."
The police spokesperson said members used the Visual Audio Recorded Evidence model which is designed to support vulnerable witnesses and captures visual communication.
Former teacher speaks out
Former education support worker Anne*, who worked at Latrobe SDS for over two decades in education support, said she was left scarred by what she witnessed during her time there.
She alleges she approached senior leadership, but "you couldn't speak to them about what happened with the kids because they wouldn't listen".
A male student would regularly inappropriately touch students, Anne said, and she was aware of other incidents of sexual assault on the school grounds.
She said staff could be physically and verbally abusive, recalling one student being referred to as a "dirty little prick", and staff dragging students around or pushing them to the ground.
Anne said staff who complained or raised allegations of physical and sexual abuse at the school were bullied.
"If I said something nobody spoke to me,"
"I was excluded from everything.
"I was diagnosed with PTSD and depression … after this had happened."
She said other staff members told her they would not complain about what they witnessed out of fear of being excluded too.
She became suicidal during her time at the school.
During a meeting in 2022, Anne said she reported manhandling and incidents of sexual abuse to an education department official.
That official told her to go on WorkCover. Anne eventually took WorkCover and retired, saying she felt broken.
Signs of sexual abuse
Gippsland Centre Against Sexual Assault chief executive Jane Barr said young people with a disability could show signs of sexual assault in various ways.
She said parents would likely notice a change in their child's behaviour.
"They may be more isolated or more guarded, not willing to communicate as they once did," she said.
"Some [children are] not quite aware of what's happening to them at that particular point. They may seem more confused or less settled than they usually are."
Ms Barr said some victims may be fearful of being in contact with, or in the same space as, the person who assaulted them and may withdraw.
She said some young people may only report sexual assault after the incident when they're in an environment where they feel safer, so disclosure of the assault might take time.
Ms Barr said the Department Of Education had particular guidelines in place for educators with concerns around child safety, outlining what their legal obligations are.
"The Department Of Education has in place a PROTECT policy, which identifies the procedures, processes and supports for any victim within a school setting," she said.
"If there's incidents within schools, schools have an obligation through what's called their reporting pathways within the Department of Education, and they're focusing strongly on making sure that there's accessible pathways following disclosures.
"Specialist schools are a really high priority for us in terms of advocacy and reaching out and making sure that the people, not just the students, children and young people, but their families are well supported as well."
She said parents who are concerned their child has been a victim of sexual assault should seek independent legal advice.
"It doesn't mean always that once it's reported through a school principal, through to the Department of Education, that there's enough evidence to go and progress," Ms Barr said.
"That's a matter for policing."
Department says action taken
The Department of Education ordered a review of the school's culture, which was undertaken in 2021, and recommended 10 actions.
Based on the review the department then developed a plan of 34 actions.
The majority of these were completed by the end of term four in 2022, but three were deemed to be ongoing.
The ABC understands staff were able to provide feedback into the school's culture and the department has sought feedback from the school community following the review.
The department said it is not aware of any new misconduct claims made against the school since the review was conducted.
The ABC requested a copy of the review and its recommendations but the department would not provide a copy, citing confidentiality.
The ABC also contacted the Department of Education with an extensive list of questions related to the claims put forward by VFSN.
The department provided a short statement, saying the safety of students was its priority.
"We have worked closely with the leadership of Latrobe SDS to implement the actions established in the independent Culture Review completed in 2021,"
The spokesperson said security cameras at the school cover "all external school grounds, including in areas where staff supervision may not be continuous".
The ABC also contacted Latrobe Special Developmental School with a series of questions about the allegations but did not receive a response.
In late July, the Victorian government made a parliamentary apology to victims and survivors of child sexual abuse in Victorian government schools.
But Ms Vella said the parents involved in VFSN did not feel that the apology addressed their concerns or their trauma.
"My child was not safe at one of their Victorian special schools," she said.
"Abuses are still happening, they aren't historical, and the system in place is failing and has been for a very long time.
"It's just another announcement without any humility or integrity."
Member for Eastern Victoria Melina Bath, who has spoken with Voices for Special Needs about their allegations, raised their concerns in parliament in late August.
"The action I seek is for the premier to meet with representatives of Voices for Special Needs and affected Latrobe Valley families with a view to establishing an independent review of historical child safety complaints and concerns involving Victorian specialist schools and how they were handled," she told parliament.
She said the families had "spent years seeking answers about safety concerns involving students with disability".
"These families seek truth, accountability and confidence that every child attending a Victorian specialist school is safe, respected and protected."
* The ABC has used pseudonyms to avoid identifying alleged victims.

How to improve your audio quality on Android Auto
There are several things you should check.
If you already have a perfectly functional cable that supports Android Auto, upgrading to a 5Gbps cable isn't going to make Spotify sound like you rebuilt the stereo. Yes, a broken or poorly built cable can lead to dropouts, disconnects and other frustrations, but additional bandwidth won't improve an intact digital audio stream.
Google does recommend trying a high-quality or replacement cable when wired Android Auto is acting up, but that's basic troubleshooting, not some secret hi-fi upgrade. If you already have a stable connection, the best places to look for improvement are in the music, any processing your phone or app is doing and finally the car's audio settings.
Don't blame Android Auto first -- Check the music app
If your music app switches quality depending on the network, a weak cellular connection can result in poor streaming quality, and pre-downloading your favorite playlists or albums can be one of the easiest ways to eliminate this factor. Spotify's Automatic setting adjusts the streaming quality according to the connection, while YouTube Music gives Premium subscribers the ability to set a separate streaming quality level for downloads. That's worth doing if you frequently pass through areas where five bars drop to one with little notice.
Next, choose a higher download-quality setting, but don't necessarily set all the numbers to the highest. Android supports playback sample rates up to 192kHz, but Google doesn't provide a universal Android Auto output rate to confirm that your car is getting 192kHz audio. Bigger numbers here don't necessarily help.
You should pay more attention to your EQ and normalization settings. An earbuds-oriented profile with a bass boost can sound pretty weird in a car's completely different speaker configuration, especially if the car is adding its own bass boost, surround processing or EQ. Spotify is a great example (and sometimes an annoying one): On Android phones with a built-in equalizer, changes made through Spotify can also affect the sound of other apps.
Spotify's Loud normalization setting also applies a limiter, so temporarily flatten the EQ, set normalization to Normal or turn it off and play a familiar downloaded track. Add your preferred adjustments back one at a time. It's simple troubleshooting, but it's better than changing six things and finding nothing.
Use wired and wireless connections to narrow it down
Wireless Android Auto uses both Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, rather than simply sending music over a standard Bluetooth connection. The initial wireless setup pairs the phone and car over Bluetooth, with Wi-Fi also required for the connection. That makes going into Android's developer options to search for aptX, LDAC or some supposedly better Bluetooth codec a bad place to begin.
If playback is choppy, playback stalls or sounds obviously wrong, try the same downloaded song over wired Android Auto. If it sounds good, then you've isolated the connection without touching the music itself.
If wired playback fails as well, then the cable is finally a suspect. Always use a known, good cable and never use a hub or extension. What you don't need is a cable that you purchased simply because the packaging says it supports transfer speeds that your music will never even come close to using.
The last place to check is the vehicle itself. Turn off bass boost, surround mode or other enhancements, flatten its EQ and compare the same track again. There is no consistent menu path because each infotainment system handles these controls differently (some seem to hide them for sport). If the problem persists, it may also be worthwhile to check whether a firmware update is available for an aftermarket receiver. Wireless Android Auto does require a compatible phone with 5GHz Wi-Fi support.

Orangutan rescued from Borneo fire battles respiratory illness
Indonesia has intensified efforts to contain forest and land fires across six provinces in Borneo and Sumatra
On Sunday morning, Jais, a farmer in Ketapang, West Kalimantan on Borneo island – the province hardest-hit by raging forest fires – was en route to his farm when he found an orangutan writhing on the ground in a weak state on a palm-oil plantation near the fire site.
“It was very weak, then I gave it water,” said Jais, who only goes by one name.
Indonesia has intensified efforts to contain haze from forest and land fires across six provinces in Borneo and Sumatra islands after smoke triggered respiratory illnesses and forced thousands of schools to move classes online, including in neighbouring Malaysia.
Wildfires burned at least 202,010 hectares of land from January to July, according to Indonesia’s Forestry Ministry, increasing from 107,465 burned hectares from January to June.
After finding the orangutan, Jais and other residents immediately called for help.
Some two hours later, a wildlife foundation – Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia – arrived with a veterinarian to provide the animal with treatment. It had fainted by then.
The orangutan was then named Sampurna, after the village where it was found.

Trump’s new mass deportation target
The Trump administration is going after Haitian immigrants after ending deportation protections.
After ending legal protections for 350,000 Haitians living in the United States, the Trump administration is ramping up its efforts to deport them back to a country engulfed in violence — and bragging about it.
“Those with terminated TPS are in our nation Illegally,” the Department of Homeland Security X account posted on Thursday evening, alongside a video of chained Haitian immigrants set to cheery music. “They have two options: LEAVE IMMEDIATELY or be DEPORTED.”
Temporary protected status (TPS) is extended to immigrants for whom conflict, natural disaster, or another catastrophe means returning home would be unsafe, and Haiti certainly qualifies: The island nation has been in crisis since its president was assassinated in 2021, with armed gangs controlling most of the capital city; earlier this week, dozens were killed and kidnapped near the capital.
Despite all that, the administration first attempted to end TPS protections for Haitians living in the US last year, and succeeded after the Supreme Court gave its blessing in June.
Now, it’s sending them back to a country where the State Department warns Americans not to travel “for any reason” because of “crime, terrorism, kidnapping, unrest, and limited health care.” On Thursday, that effort included a deportation flight carrying families with young children born in the US.
Trump’s indiscriminate, record-breaking immigration crackdown
Haitian immigrants in the US aren’t the only people whom Immigrations and Customs Enforcement is targeting more aggressively. According to immigration data released this week by the Deportation Data Project at UC Berkeley and UCLA, ICE arrested a record number of people in two consecutive months this summer: first 43,000 in June, then nearly 50,000 last month.
As arrests surge, who’s being targeted is changing, too. More and more ICE arrestees don’t have a criminal record; in July, immigrants with only civil immigration violations made up a majority of arrests. Often, they also have active immigration cases pursuing asylum, a green card, or some other legal status, as the Seattle Times reported this week.
Overall, ICE detentions are also rising again, though they’re still lower than they were at the start of the year.
The pace of arrests reflects ICE’s growing size — 29,000 employees in June, according to the New York Times, compared to 21,000 in January 2025 — as well as its glut of cash after Trump’s reconciliation bill forked over $75 billion to the agency last year.
Nonetheless, the agency still wants more: As the New York Times reported in July, its internal target for arrests is 2,000 per day. That would mean a record of at least 60,000 people per month, the majority likely guilty of no crime at all.

Work on construction of Pushkar ghats along the Godavari in the historic temple town of Bhadrachalam began on Saturday ahead of the Godavari Pushkarams scheduled to be held in 2027.

Four armed men died in an exchange of fire with police during a naka-checking operation at Songsak in Meghalaya’s East Garo Hills early Sunday, with investigators probing their possible links to a recent businessman’s murder in a suspected abduction-for-ransom attempt across the interstate border, police said.
The encounter took place around 4am, when police conducting the naka allegedly came under fire from the four men as they approached the checkpoint for inspection, East Garo Hills superintendent of police Swapnil Pawar Vasantrao said.
