How much storage does a smart TV typically have?
It's a surprisingly low number.
Smart TVs have become pretty common across buildings and households the world over, and by the end of 2026, over 50% of all households globally are expected to own one, up from 34% in 2020. Smart TVs are popular for many reasons, including voice assistants, regular software updates and easy internet access, which allows viewers to stream their favorite shows without using a dongle or external device. But such beloved features need an OS (operating system) to run. And an OS needs storage space to occupy and operate in. Yet, most smart TVs ship with surprisingly little storage.
Typically, new smart TVs ship with around 8GB of storage, and the OS alone takes a huge chunk of that. On Samsung TVs, for example, system files can take up to 20% of the total storage.
What uses storage on your smart TV
Aside from the TV's OS, a number of things can also eat deep into your smart TV's storage. One of the most common culprits is pre-installed apps (bloatware). Most smart TVs come with apps already loaded into the TV right from the factory. Typically, these apps are popular streaming services like YouTube, Netflix, Prime Video and so on. Then there are the apps you personally install, which take their own space on top of what's pre-loaded.
Another silent storage eater on your smart TV is cache and temporary data. The apps on your smart TV tend to store temporary data to improve performance. For example, Netflix stores the thumbnails of shows you've recently viewed so it doesn't have to redownload the image when you go back to your watchlist. This cache builds and takes up more storage over time, especially if you use a lot of different apps.
How to free up memory on your smart TV
First things first: Clear out the app cache and temporary data. On most smart TVs, you can do this in the settings — how easy it is depends on your exact model. Clearing out the app cache is safe and doesn't remove the app itself. Do note that it's not always a permanent solution because as you continue to use those apps, the deleted data will rebuild itself over time.
A permanent option is to uninstall apps. Start with the apps that you don't use, especially the bloatware we mentioned above. Look through your app list, and any app you've not opened once in the last three months has probably fallen out of use and should be uninstalled. As for bloatware, depending on the TV's model and manufacturer, uninstalling them isn't always straightforward and is sometimes even disallowed by TV manufacturers. So you may need to look at your manual or use unconventional methods that we would never recommend but someone mentioned in a Reddit post seven years ago.
If all else fails or you don't just want to deal with all the technical jargon, a neat shortcut is simply to use a separate streaming device like a Fire TV Stick, Roku or Google TV Streamer. These devices come with their own storage, OS, app ecosystem and internet connection. All you typically have to do to get one running is plug it into your TV, set it up, download your preferred apps and you're good to binge.

FDA approves landmark pancreatic cancer drug that's shown to improve survival
The Food and Drug Administration on Wednesday approved a groundbreaking new drug for advanced pancreatic cancer, offering U.S. patients a more effective treatment against one of the deadliest types of cancer.
FDA officials gave expedited approval to the first-of-a-kind pill, called daraxonrasib, which blocks a mutated protein that fuels tumor growth in more than 90% of pancreatic cancer cases. It's an approach that previously eluded drugmakers for decades.
The daily pills will be sold by Revolution Medicines under the brand name Rasonque. A one-month supply would cost approximately $39,800, the company announced.
Patients taking the drug nearly doubled their survival time, with fewer severe side effects, in a study that randomly assigned them to receive the experimental treatment or more chemotherapy. The company-funded study enrolled 500 patients whose metastatic, or spreading, cancer had quit responding to prior treatment.
Patients getting the new treatment lived for a median of 13.2 months compared with 6.7 months for chemotherapy recipients. Side effects included skin rash, mouth sores, diarrhea and other digestive issues.
"This is one of the most anticipated approvals I can think of," said Dr. Andrew Coveler of the Fred Hutch Cancer Center. "This medicine is not a cure but a significant improvement."
Pancreatic cancer is among the most deadly forms in large part because it is hard to detect before it starts spreading to other organs. The American Cancer Society estimates about 67,000 new cases will be diagnosed in the United States this year and more than 52,000 people will die from the disease. The five-year overall survival rate is 13%.
The drug garnered public attention earlier this year when former Sen. Ben Sasse, R-Neb., described on CBS' "60 Minutes" how he has had less pain while taking it. A surge in public interest led the FDA to allow "expanded access," before the drug's official approval, for patients who met certain criteria.
FDA regulators noted on Wednesday that they approved the drug more than six months ahead of their target date.
"It is our fundamental duty to deliver more cures and meaningful treatments to patients as quickly as possible," the FDA's acting commissioner, Kyle Diamantas, said in a statement.
Unlike with other cancers that have benefited from a variety of chemotherapy alternatives, pancreatic cancer has been harder to tackle.
The new drug targets mutations in the RAS gene family that normally regulates cell growth. What are known as KRAS mutations are especially critical in fueling pancreatic cancer. But a structure that made it hard for drugs to stick to the mutated proteins meant this cancer driver was long considered "undruggable."
Doctors who treat pancreatic cancer hope the drug may usher in more new options for other forms of cancer, with scores of experimental drugs in development.
"I think this has opened doors for many other companies," said Dr. Pashtoon Kasi of City of Hope Orange County, a California-based cancer center. "Downstream I think there are going to be a lot more trials looking at this approach in other tumor types."
Revolution Medicines' drug uses what's essentially a molecular glue to bind with multiple KRAS subtypes. The Redwood City, California-based drugmaker is studying its technology for several other forms of cancer, including lung cancer.

Mari Katayama has spent years putting herself in front of the camera. Her photographs surround her with handmade sculptures, textiles and mirrors, turning her body into one element in complex, surreal compositions. It would be easy to call the work self-portraiture. Katayama would rather have you look beyond the body.
Her recent “tree of life” (2024-25) series offers one example. Katayama builds elaborate, almost otherworldly environments in which she appears among hand-stitched forms, gauzy garlands called “koilia” (after the Greek word for “stomach” and “inner feelings”) and other props, including tree branches and a fake crocodile head. Multiple mirrors fracture and repeat the scene, making Katayama’s body appear to multiply within a dense world of fabric, foliage and fantastical forms.
“Until now, my work has focused on the relationship between ‘you’ and ‘me’: between me and objects, me and my own body, me and society, me and institutions,” the 39-year-old artist says. “While building those kinds of relationships, I realized that I needed to think about the very stage, or structural system, that ‘me’ and whoever that ‘someone’ is are standing on.”

Judge finds mother with postpartum psychosis not guilty of murdering her two children in case echoing Lindsay Clancy trial
The NYC verdict comes as a Massachusetts jury deliberates in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial
A New York City mother was found not criminally responsible due to mental disease or defect by a Bronx judge Monday for the 2022 killings of her two young sons at a Bronx family shelter.
Dimone Fleming, 26, is accused of repeatedly stabbing her sons, Daishawn Fleming, 3, and Octavius Canada, 11 months, before submerging them in a bathtub inside an apartment in the Mount Hope area on November 26, 2022. She was 22 at the time of the killings and was initially charged with two counts of first-degree murder.
The prosecution ultimately agreed that Fleming should not face a conventional criminal trial because of the severity of her mental illness. Psychiatrist Dr. Eric Goldsmith determined Fleming was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis, including hallucinations and delusions, and was “grossly psychotic and out of touch with reality,” according to the New York Post. She will avoid prison but remain in custody for psychiatric evaluations.
Fleming believed killing her children was necessary to protect or “cleanse” them, according to a forensic psychiatrist report commissioned by the defense, the outlet reports.
The ruling comes as a Massachusetts jury deliberates in the case of Lindsay Clancy, who is accused of killing her three children in 2023. Like Fleming, Clancy’s defense has argued that postpartum psychosis left her unable to understand or control her actions. Her jury began deliberating this week and had not reached a verdict as of Friday.
Fleming had received psychiatric treatment in the months before the killings. She spent two months at a Queens hospital, where she was diagnosed with major depressive disorder and prescribed psychiatric medication. However, she did not take the medication as prescribed and instead used marijuana daily, which reportedly worsened her symptoms.
On the night of the killings, a shelter employee called 911 after noticing water and smoke coming from Fleming’s apartment. Police found Fleming “acting irrationally” and took her to a hospital for evaluation.
Officers initially did not realize the boys were dead. The children were buried under clothes in the bathtub, and a neighbor told police they were with their father.
Fleming’s then-boyfriend and Octavius’ father, Columbus Canada, later found the boys unresponsive inside the apartment and called police, according to The Post.
The mother allegedly confessed to killing her sons and made references to the “devil” while speaking with detectives, according to police sources cited by the outlet.
A finding of not guilty by reason of mental disease or defect does not necessarily mean immediate freedom, and Fleming could remain in a psychiatric facility for an extended period depending on her condition and subsequent court decisions.
Her next court hearing is scheduled for September 18, when the results of those evaluations are expected to help determine her future.

Milo Yiannopoulos, a British national known for his near-constant reinventions as a vizier within far-right American politics for more than a decade, has been detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Louisiana, according to the department’s records.
While it’s not clear which detention facility Yiannopoulos is currently being held in, the ICE directory instructs any family or legal representatives to contact the Enforcement and Removal Office in Alexandria, Louisiana, a processing center for the central part of the state, about 200 miles from New Orleans.
In an emailed statement, a spokesperson from the US Department of Homeland Security says that Yiannopoulos legally entered the country through New York City in May 2019. “He chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws,” the statement says. “Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an Immigration Judge on July 22, after failing to show up for his immigration hearing.” The DHS spokesperson says Yiannopoulos was detained on Thursday, August 27 and that “he will remain in ICE custody pending removal.”
TMZ first broke the news of Yiannopoulos’ detention. He has previously lived and worked in the US, allegedly on an O-1 visa, which is for individuals with extraordinary abilities in the arts, sciences, and other areas, including journalism—but he has never been a US citizen.
Yiannopoulos got his start in US politics at the right-wing website Breitbart, where he worked from 2014 to 2017. He left the job after his remarks about sexual intercourse between adults and young adolescent boys, which he said could be “perfectly consensual,” resulted in a backlash. He has dipped in and out of right-wing circles for years, and in 2022 claimed to have arranged an infamous 2022 dinner with Kanye West, white nationalist Nick Fuentes, and Donald Trump at Mar-a-Lago “to make Trump’s life miserable.”
Yiannopoulos married his long-term boyfriend in Hawaii in 2017 but in 2021 claimed he had become heterosexual and Roman Catholic, and announced plans to open a gay conversion therapy facility in Florida. He went on to work with Fuentes as well as former US representative Marjorie Taylor Greene.
Yiannopoulos also serves as spokesman for Kanye West, who is scheduled to perform at the Caesars Superdome in New Orleans on Friday night as part of his 2026 tour. The longtime provocateur joined West’s theoretical 2024 presidential campaign in late 2022, but walked away days after the rapper espoused Nazi beliefs and praised Adolf Hitler on conspiracist Alex Jones’ Infowars livestream. The two continually reunited and split over the following years, with Yiannopoulis claiming in a series of X posts in 2024 that West was addicted to nitrous oxide.
Throughout his evolution as a MAGA figure, Yiannopoulos has rarely shied away from highly public battles with enemies and rivals. Among the most outspoken is the Islamophobic conspiracy theorist Laura Loomer, who on Friday pinned a post on X announcing his detention by ICE—and appeared to take partial credit for it.
“I was the first person to report on the fact that Milo was in the US illegally where he incited violence against President Trump and worked for Marjorie Traitor Greene,” Loomer wrote. “Milo is going to be deported back to the UK where he can live among the Muslims he has recently chosen to embrace. Today is a great day for America.”
Last summer, Yiannopoulos endorsed a hardline anti-immigration stance on his own X account. “There is one concrete thing we must insist on this administration delivering,” he wrote. “We have got to deport millions and millions and millions of people. Without that, nothing else matters.”

Why does your Kindle even have Bluetooth?
How else do you expect to hear an audiobook?
Most people don't think of Bluetooth when powering up a Kindle e-reader for the first time. After all, most of what a Kindle does is grab new books to add to its internal storage, and they can do that via Wi-Fi or a wired connection to your computer. An internet connection lets you read Wikipedia entries, get more books and sync progress across devices. Why then do many Kindles support Bluetooth?
Keep in mind that only Kindles released in 2016 or later have Bluetooth connectivity. This feature lets you connect the ereader to wireless headphones or speakers to listen to audiobooks, or simply to have text read aloud since Amazon's newer e-readers don't have built-in speakers or headphone jacks.
Bluetooth also acts as a great accessibility feature alongside Kindle's VoiceView, which can read on-screen interface text and help vision-impaired users navigate menus. Here's how you can set your Kindle up to take advantage of this feature.
How do I get Bluetooth on my Kindle?
As mentioned, if your Kindle was made after 2016, it will already have Bluetooth connectivity. Pairing a Bluetooth audio device with your Kindle to listen to an audiobook is fairly straightforward. Here's what you should do:
- From the Home screen, tap the Library text and then press Downloaded. This will bring up all the content on your Kindle.
- Tap the audiobook you want to listen to. Pressing Play will prompt you to pair a Bluetooth device.
- Activate your Bluetooth device's pairing mode. This can mean pressing a dedicated button or holding a combination of buttons down for a couple of seconds.
- On your Kindle, tap the name of the device you want to use. Once it's paired, the audiobook will play.
You can skip back or go ahead, adjust the speed and switch between chapters on the Audible screen. To change the volume, open the Quick Actions panel by tapping the downward arrow at the top of the screen. If you aren't able to pair your regular Kindle or Paperwhite model to an audio device, try rebooting it or updating it to the latest software version.
Is there a Bluetooth page turner for Kindle?
No, Kindles don't grant page-turning functionality via Bluetooth. It would have been a neat convenience for people who find it difficult to tap the screen or press the Kindle Oasis' on-device buttons.
If you're wondering how third-party page turners work with Amazon's e-readers, they attach a clip to the screen that mimics the touch of a finger with radio frequency (RF) technology. The clip is controlled by a wireless remote. It's an interesting workaround though Amazon hasn't attempted to provide a first-party alternative. You cannot use Bluetooth to connect a keyboard or transfer files between your Kindle and smartphone either.
In addition to audiobooks, your Kindle can also use an audio device for its Assistive Reader text-to-speech feature that supports books obtained from the Kindle store. Its Bluetooth functionality might not let you turn pages right now, but it still comes in handy when you want to listen to an audiobook on Audible or have it read a book for you.

South Africa hold off All Blacks fightback to level series

'Rugby's Greatest Rivalry' series - second Test

Tries: Roigard, McKenzie, Carter, Savea Cons: Love 3
World champions South Africa delivered a powerful first-half performance as they edged past New Zealand and levelled 'Rugby's Greatest Rivalry' series at 1-1 with two Tests to play.
The All Blacks travelled to Cape Town knowing a win would write them into the history books as the first New Zealand team to win back-to-back Tests in South Africa since the 'Incomparables' of 1996.
But South Africa dominated the basics and showed a more clinical edge this week, even though the lively All Blacks again outscored them on the try count by four to three.
New Zealand's fightback ultimately came too late, captain Ardie Savea barging over on 77 minutes to get the game within a score, but on the All Blacks' final attack Boks replacement Cameron Hanekom won a superb turnover that settled the nervy closing stages.
As he did last week, Springboks wing Cheslin Kolbe took on the kicking duties over fly-half Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu, notching up 18 points in a player-of-the-match performance.
The first series in 30 years between these two mighty rugby nations is shaping into an epic, with the third Test back at altitude in Soweto, Johannesburg next Saturday.
Erasmus team tricks
The Springbok team that took the field at the Cape Town Stadium was markedly different to the one originally named by head coach Rassie Erasmus on Monday.
Fly-half Handre Pollard was fit and then injured and withdrawn in the week, while Kolbe was injured and then fit and eventually named on the wing.
On top of that, Erasmus switched around his whole front row in the hours before kick-off, with the starting trio dropping to the bench and vice-versa.
It meant there were five changes in all from the matchday squad announced on Monday and surely would have had the New Zealand management thumbing through the regulations of the tour agreement.
Boklash comes early
Despite producing a famous rearguard effort in the first-Test victory at Ellis Park, New Zealand boss Dave Rennie warned in the week his side would need to "go deeper" to cope with the inevitable Springbok backlash.
That South African onslaught came from the off.
Hooker Deon Fourie, at nearly 40 the oldest Springbok in history, found his target in the line-out, the South African maul powered into the 22, and lightning fast ball led to centre Jesse Kriel crashing over.
Kolbe added the extras as the world champions made the dream start.
But despite the fast start from the hosts, New Zealand grew into the contest, with referee Angus Gardner, himself a late call-up in place of Nika Amashukeli, presiding over a fast and fluent game.
Damian McKenzie made a clean break which almost put in Will Jordan, and while the Boks killed the ball from the ensuing breakdown, Eben Etzebeth got up to spoil New Zealand's five-metre line-out.
Despite their set-piece issues, the All Blacks came again. Intricate handling freed Jordan, who used his pace and strength to escape down the right and link with the outstanding Cam Roigard. Ruben Love levelled the scores from bang in front.
That score lit a fire in the Springboks, with Kolbe kicking a penalty and Damian de Allende barrelling over after another imposing maul as South Africa showed far more ruthlessness compared to a week ago.
With the Springboks dominating in the basics, the crowd in Cape Town smelt blood as the lead stretched to 17-7.
But with ball in hand, Rennie's crop are reminiscent of the great All Blacks side of old. Savea burst forward from a line-out, and perfect passing gave McKenzie a walk-in.
At 17-14 edging towards half-time the contest was in the balance, before a match-defining sequence just before the interval.
Kolbe forced a five-metre scrum, before which Erasmus brought on two of his strongest scrummagers in Malcolm Marx and Ox Nche, who immediately won a penalty.
From there, another scrum, another penalty advantage, and with the All Blacks back-pedalling captain Siya Kolisi crashed over for South Africa's third try and a 10-point lead after a pulsating first 40.
Boks withstand All Blacks fightback
New Zealand needed to score first in the second half, and they didn't, losing the ball when in Bok territory and then giving away a soft penalty which Kolbe kicked.
The All Blacks were on the ropes, Marx won a breakdown penalty, and Kolbe stretched the lead to 16 points with half an hour to go.
With the second half lacking the fireworks of the first, the All Blacks backs – led by Roigard - desperately tried to drag New Zealand back into the match.
After another McKenzie break led to nothing, some more beautiful handling resulted in Leroy Carter scampering into the left corner, a fabulous finish.
More excellent attacking play released Jordan down the right, and the recycled ball found skipper Savea, who crashed over to cut the gap to seven points with two minutes remaining.
But the Springboks held on, despite lock Lood de Jager being sent to the sin-bin for a high tackle.
Fittingly, it was a breakdown penalty that settled the game, with Hanekom winning the crucial turnover in an area South Africa dominated.
The All Blacks' impressive win in the first Test had temporarily shot them above South Africa in the world rankings, something Erasmus urged his side to rectify.
That they did, and with normal service resumed in the eyes of the Springboks supporters, South Africa travel back to the Highveld with the momentum.
But the All Blacks have played some wonderful rugby in the first two Tests, and will still believe they can join the legends of 1996.
The eyes of the rugby world now turn to Soweto.

Alpharetta, a prosperous suburb of Atlanta, Georgia, is home to about 67,000 people, served by about 120 local police officers. It also hosts several dozen cameras sold by Flock Safety, the increasingly controversial surveillance company that collects license plate data and other information and makes it searchable by police.
Data captured by those Flock cameras, WIRED has learned via public records requests, is accessible to more than 2,000 police departments, colleges, airports, and government agencies across the United States. These range from Morehouse College to Florida’s Fish and Wildlife Commission and include Medicare fraud investigators in Illinois, a drug task force focused on east-central Missouri, and the inspector general of a federal agency.
In return, Alpharetta receives Flock data from more than 1,300 entities, which span from the prosecutor’s office of Whitley County, Indiana, to the Metro Police Authority of Genesee County, Michigan.
The Alpharetta Police Department—which, as reported by WIRED, had an officer resign due to Flock misuse on August 5—also exchanges Flock data with several agencies that have been similarly rocked by recent incidents of officers misusing its technology, including Georgia’s Bibb County Sheriff’s Department, the Savannah Police Department, and the Dallas Police Department.
Alpharetta’s data-sharing network has expanded tremendously over the past year. Since June 2025, the number of entities receiving data from Alpharetta police has grown by about 42 percent, and the number of entities sending data to them has grown by about 125 percent. And, according to documents obtained via public records requests from several other cities around the country, Alpharetta is far from alone in having an expansive and complicated data-sharing system, providing a potent example of how pervasive Flock’s surveillance network has become.
One of Flock’s central selling points is its network of customers—mostly, though not entirely, law enforcement agencies. If a criminal suspect crosses city, county, or perhaps state lines, Flock tells its customers, a query can prevent them from falling through the cracks.
Data sharing across agencies is hardly novel. A police department can, for instance, share data from its automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) with state-run fusion centers, which centralize resources from law enforcement agencies in particular regions. They could also share it with a regional High Intensity Drug Trafficking Area (HIDTA) program. (Alpharetta police agreed to do just that in 2025, according to a memorandum of understanding that WIRED obtained.)
Whereas HIDTAs are federally funded public programs, Flock is a private company that manages a sprawling, interconnected ALPR network governed by rules and restrictions that vary wildly from city to city. And if police departments don’t closely supervise their settings for data requests and sharing within Flock’s interface, they can unwittingly become nodes in a much larger surveillance network than they necessarily know or understand.
This can lead to situations like that in Alpharetta, where citizens and visitors are embedded in a data-sharing network that has propagated to more than 2,300 nodes. So, how does it happen?
Setting Boundaries
To understand how cities like Alpharetta can build such expansive data-sharing networks with Flock, it’s important to understand how Flock’s interface actually works.
WIRED analyzed a cache of files on Flock’s website that are served by its login pages to anyone who loads them. Some of the code that WIRED analyzed illustrates what a Flock administrator might see in their own Flock interface—specifically, in their settings and sharing preferences.
An administrator can automatically share their agency’s Flock data with any organization within a custom radius, within their home state, or within one or more other states. Alternatively, they can individually choose organizations to share data with.
Administrators can also limit specific data that other organizations can receive, like live or archived videos. They can also limit which organizations can ask them for data. They could restrict this, for instance, to organizations based in the same state, or within a 50-mile radius.
Lieutenant Jason Hiott of the Alpharetta Police Department tells WIRED that per the city’s Flock settings, the department will “automatically approve” requests for its Flock data from law enforcement agencies within 500 miles. If they’re outside that radius, the police department has to individually request access to Alpharetta’s data.
Hiott was unable to say what the Alpharetta police department’s default settings were, whether it altered the default settings, or how long the radius has been set to 500 miles—though he did note that the department “does not share any live feeds, analytics, etc. with anyone.”
Flock spokesperson Jess Montejano claims that data sharing is turned off by default for new and onboarding customers—so no law enforcement agencies automatically get access to another agency’s data. Flock did not specify whether that has always been the case.
Paris Lewbel, another Flock spokesperson, adds that “historically,” its customers have been able to request data from other customers that are within the same state, or within 50 miles—the precursor to actually sharing data.
Coast-to-Coast
Flock’s network settings allow agencies to set specific limits on what Flock data it shares and receives, but in some cases, police departments have been caught off guard by how expansive the search settings were for their officers.
Often, the confusion has been tied to Flock’s Nationwide lookup tool, which the company introduced in 2021 and is available to customers that opt in, according to the company. It allows any Flock customer to query any other Flock customer in the country, as long as they have a specific license plate. (Flock disabled the tool for federal agencies following backlash to the company’s pilot program with Immigration and Customs Enforcement.) In several cases, Flock customers had no idea this tool was enabled.

Chris Shook is the city attorney in Reynoldsburg, Ohio, where two officers recently resigned after the police department probed their alleged misuse of Flock’s technology. He tells WIRED that in June, the city’s police department made an unexpected discovery while attempting to complete a public records request: Per the department’s Flock settings, the Nationwide lookup tool was active. Police leadership, however, had been under the impression that officers could only search cameras within Ohio.
Shook says that the police department immediately changed the settings to enable only in-state camera searches. But they had no idea when, or why, nationwide searches may have been enabled. Lacking answers, Shook turned to Flock.
According to emails reviewed by WIRED, Flock customer success manager Caroline Bush could only say that Nationwide lookup “was enabled at some point before February 2025.” Due to an “event-log limitation” prior to that month, she could not say exactly when. But she added that, upon checking the police department’s audit, she “found nationwide searches as early as 03/2023.”
This came as a surprise to Shook. If nationwide search was enabled, he said, there must have been an error, “but we are unsure of how that error could have occurred.”
“The most likely explanation is that the setting was enabled during initial account setup or onboarding,” Bush replied. She said Nationwide lookup “was a common default configuration for agencies at that time, before Flock introduced stronger in-product disclosures and tighter controls around this feature.”
In California, the Palo Alto Police Department had a similar experience. In a city council “study session” led by city manager Ed Shikada on June 1, he claimed that Flock activated Nationwide lookup “for all customers” in mid-2023. Flock says this is a “false claim,” based on research that found “agencies across the country that have never been in the Nationwide Network including in the state of California.”
Notably, California law forbids sharing ALPR data with federal or out-of-state law enforcement. Shikada said that Flock quietly “disabled” Nationwide lookup for Palo Alto police in October 2024, and for all California law enforcement by March 2025.
However, Shikada said Palo Alto police didn't know Nationwide lookup had ever been active until December 2025.
Meanwhile, Commander David Hart of Minnesota’s Beltrami County Sheriff’s Office tells WIRED that while his office didn’t have a debacle with the Nationwide lookup tool, he had to reel in the permissions that were set up when the county started using Flock in early 2024.
For the first few months, his officers could send and receive data requests to any Flock customer in the country. But toward the end of 2024, Hart says, he limited outgoing and incoming data requests to in-state agencies. No data requests are approved automatically. (Minnesota’s ALPR statute sets specific standards that agencies must meet before capturing or receiving ALPR data.) Hart tells WIRED that on principle, he doesn’t believe in using Flock casually for wide-ranging searches.
“It’s gotten to the point where people want to search more agencies just to be able to search more agencies, without a real reason behind it,” Hart says.
When examining Flock audit logs, it’s not always obvious why an officer would want or need to expand the scope of their search.
WIRED filed a public records request to the Reynoldsburg Police Department and received 549 pages that log every Flock query its officers made from January 2024 through April 2026. The records show that even from query to query, the number of probed Flock networks can vary significantly.
On January 1, 2025, for instance, a Reynoldsburg police officer queried 53 Flock networks. The officer’s “reason” for the search, according to the log, was a potential criminal offense coded “30.” Just 40 minutes later, the same officer cited the same criminal offense code but, for reasons the log does not specify, instead queried 5,392 Flock networks. Similar examples appear regularly throughout the log, though most of the searches WIRED reviewed had probed fewer than 100 networks.
Flock users, as illustrated in a recent video on the company’s YouTube channel, can customize the number of networks they want to probe in a single query. A police officer can probe every single camera network their department has access to—or they can limit their search to their state, or simply their own jurisdiction. That decision is left up to the officer.
“The particular officer can narrow the networks they want to search, but typically they don't,” Shook tells WIRED. “Typically, they search every network they have access to.”
Mixed Company
Alpharetta’s Flock data-sharing network shows that it sends data to and receives it from agencies that, along with being geographically distant, are a far cry from the local police departments and county sheriff offices that represent Flock’s prototypical customers.
It’s often unclear, outside of a fluke circumstance, what the agencies would gain from exchanging data.
For instance, it’s not obvious why the Office of Inspector General for the federal General Services Administration, Region G of the Alabama Drug Enforcement Task Force, or the University of North Texas’ Denton campus police would need to have a mutual exchange of Flock data with the police department of Alpharetta, Georgia. (None of these agencies responded to requests for comment.)
WIRED contacted more than a dozen agencies sending or receiving data with the Alpharetta Police that are neither a police department nor a sheriff’s office, and most did not respond to requests for comment. Just one answered specific questions about its use of Flock: Kentucky’s Louisville Regional Airport Authority, a nearly seven-hour drive from Alpharetta.
Natalie Ciresi Chaudoin, the airport authority’s director of public relations, tells WIRED that the Louisville Regional Airport Authority has 13 Flock cameras across its properties. She says that the airport shares data from its cameras with 2,240 federal, state, and local agencies across the country and receives data from 1,124 agencies.
Chaudoin adds that the airport’s Flock settings are configured to “automatically accept a request for data-sharing with in-state law enforcement agencies, while out-of-state agencies’ requests are manually accepted or declined following their review.”
When asked about Alpharetta, Chaudoin says that the airport was “aware that it received data from an agency” in the city. The airport has not shared its data in return.
Limiting Factors
Twenty-four states, as well as Washington, DC, have statutes covering ALPR use. The regulations they impose differ widely from state to state, with some being quite specific: Since 2023, it’s been illegal for law enforcement in Illinois to use ALPR data in criminal cases related to immigration or abortion.
The effects of California’s restrictions are visible in records obtained via public records request from the Northern California Regional Intelligence Center (NCRIC), which are published publicly on Muckrock, a public records request facilitator. According to the records, the fusion center shares and receives data from fewer than 400 agencies—a fraction of the agencies in Alpharetta’s network—and they’re all based in California. However, that fact alone doesn’t paint the whole picture.
According to an audit of searches run on the NCRIC’s Flock network, NCRIC member agencies ran more than 57,000 Flock queries in the single month between November 26 and December 26, 2025. Many of the queries probed thousands of Flock networks, and more than 96 percent of them probed at least 100.
In other words, the scope of the NCRIC queries tended to be significantly larger than those of the Reynoldsburg Police Department—the police department in a state with no ALPR statute, where officers had access to the Nationwide lookup tool until June and from which two officers recently resigned due to allegedly misusing Flock.
On August 13, Flock announced a set of changes to how its software works, seemingly in response to a surge in news coverage about police officers misusing the technology. The company said that it is now “recommending a 7-day ALPR data retention period,” a reduction from 30 days. But Flock customers can pay for extended data retention, according to documents obtained via a public records request from St. Petersburg, Florida.
Flock also says that law enforcement can’t run a Flock search without entering a criminal case code and that by the end of the year, all customers must activate its Audit Assistance tool, which scans for “defined criteria for abnormal behavior” and “automatically” suspends Flock access if detected.
In Alpharetta, according to Lieutenant Hiott, police chief Trent Lindgren learned about the Audit Assistance tool in July and promptly activated it. By July 20, the department had opened an investigation into one of its officers. On August 5, the officer resigned.

Vaccines took center stage at the federal autism advisory committee meeting Thursday, as committee members explicitly pointed to vaccines as a potential cause of autism, even though the link has been routinely debunked.
“We don’t want to close the door for any potential trigger, and that would include things like glutamate or aspirin, or a vaccination,” said Laura Cellini, the founder and CEO of Elucidate ASD, a nonprofit pushing for more medical treatments of autism. “We are quite open to investigating anything and everything. This plan closes no door.”
Vaccines are not mentioned in the committee’s new and already contentious strategic plan, which was the stated goal of discussion for the meeting. Multiple public members pointed to vaccines as possible culprits for their childrens’ “regression” into autism. None of the committee members challenged those statements — a sign that a new normal has been established on this committee, said Greg Robinson, director of public policy at the Autistic Self Advocacy Network.
“We are seeing right now the harms that come from misinformation around vaccines,” said Robinson, who is autistic, referencing the reports of two measles deaths in Pennsylvania. “We know how it has led to promoting harmful ideas about autistic people, about autism, and about supposed cures or remedies for autism for autistic folks that have been harmful or even deadly in the past.”
The committee members’ comments about vaccines are hardly surprising.
In January, health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. reshaped the Interagency Autism Coordinating Committee (IACC) with people who closely hew to his views on vaccines. This early brush with controversy has not faded, as autism researchers created a similarly named independent body to counter misinformation they expected from the federal counterpart, which has faced much criticism from the autism community because of its lack of transparency during its initial meeting, and as it has sought public comments about the new strategic plan to guide the federal approach to autism research.
The document radically reshapes the prevailing genetics-first approach to understanding autism, opting instead to fund research into areas with significantly less scientific evidence for their relevance, such as diet, inflammation, metabolic stress, and folate. The plan also calls for nearly doubling federal autism funding from $390 million to $747 million. Committee members voted to approve the plan, which will serve as nonbinding recommendations for Congress and federal health agencies.
“In every year this committee met [previously], roughly three of every four comments urged this committee to act. Urgency is not new. Acting is,” said IACC chair Sylvia Fogel during her opening remarks, to applause.
Fogel announced the 336-page plan on July 17, giving the general public just three days to read and submit comments. The backlash was swift. A slew of autism advocacy and research organizations put public pressure on Fogel to push back the date of the next meeting, which she eventually did, though not without a fight. The backlash resembled the committee’s first contentious meeting, during which some federal committee members and prior IACC members said the proceedings did not comply with federal advisory rules.
Researchers and advocates are thrilled that the committee wants to alleviate co-occurring conditions such as epilepsy and sleep, and some of them are excited with the shift away from genetics as the main tool to understand autism and autistic people.
“Recognition of motor issues and autism, recognition of communication — those are really important,” said Sam Crane, an autistic self-advocate and former public member of IACC. “Genetics is important, but it probably was overfunded.”
However, what Crane and others saw as bad in the strategic plan outweighed the good for many experts. The loss of early language skills and social engagement — sometimes called regression — receives significant attention in the plan, with the text suggesting that there are some immunological, metabolic, or infectious causes behind regression that are yet to be discovered. The plan also devotes significant attention to leucovorin and other folate-based therapies, despite the overwhelming lack of scientific evidence for their efficacy.
Robinson found it concerning that the plan did not address helping autistic adults secure employment or live independently.
“A lot of the life course recommendations that they have … are really pushing away from models that have really maximized our ability to be part of our communities,” he said.
Fogel used artificial intelligence to analyze the thousands of public comments the plan received. She says the analysis showed that 50% of commenters were “aligned” with the plan and 40% “mixed,” though she did not elaborate on how the software arrived at those conclusions. The comments included support for profound autism, increased communication access, and better caregiver and housing options.
Thursday’s meeting was largely devoid of conflict, but some committee members expressed frustration that they were not given a final suite of comments until hours before the meeting.
“We received yesterday afternoon more than 1,000 pages worth of additional public comments and additional revisions,” said Scott Robertson, a senior policy adviser at the Labor Department who is autistic. “The standard in other advisory committees … is several days to a week before. Less than 24 hours is infeasible for myself and others to adequately process the comments to help inform our engagement on the strategic plan.”
Robertson, who expressed concern about Fogel’s use of AI to analyze public comments, pointed out that the plan’s call to increase funding for autism research clashes with the committee’s appropriations outlined in the Autism CARES Act. He also asked to delay voting for the plan, noting a Wednesday statement from 13 advocacy organizations that pushed the committee to give members more time to review public comments.
“I can’t remember ever, prior to the adoption of a strategic plan, 13 awesome and significant disability organizations coming out and saying, ‘Please don’t rush through this kind of thing,’” he said.
Fogel remained undaunted, suggesting earlier that they can “energize” the community into more funding, and quickly shot down Robertson’s suggestion to delay the vote, saying the plan responds to “two decades of public comments” that did not receive enough attention.
“Some of those agencies who made that statement were well represented on this committee for two decades,” Fogel said. “We considered public comments more than ever in the history of this committee. … I, as chair, am moving to act.”
It could work. Kennedy has already taken suggestions from the committee, announcing last week the National Autism Missing and Endangered Person Alert initiative, which will connect various emergency management services to curb wandering and elopement, one of the main causes of injury and death among people with autism. Some committee members met with Kennedy and National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya and say the federal health leaders will soon adopt new initiatives around helping people with profound autism, in particular.
“The plan is not an ending,” Fogel said. “It does not close the door, it opens it.”
The committed officially adopted the plan — 26 yes, 1 no, 13 abstentions.

If you haven’t yet heard about how a certain fella is choosin’ a woman from Texas over Ella Langley, it’s only a matter of time.
A sad country song about Texas could become the biggest hit ever
Is “Choosin’ Texas” the song of the summer?
Langley’s massive hit, “Choosin’ Texas,” began dominating the Billboard Hot 100 charts a few months ago — and never looked back. It’s still sitting at No. 1 after 19 weeks, tied for the longest time spent atop the charts among non-holiday songs. In a few more weeks, Langley could shatter the all-time record and dethrone Mariah Carey’s “All I Want for Christmas Is You.”
It’s a runaway success for Langley, who is relatively new to country music but has quickly vaulted to a new tier of stardom. To break down how it happened, Today, Explained turned to Marissa Moss, a senior writer at Rolling Stone and the author of Her Country: How the Women of Country Music Became the Success They Were Never Supposed to Be.
Moss talked with Today, Explained co-host Noel King about where Langley’s success came from, what it means for women in country music, and why many fans don’t know what to make of Langley, who has maintained a low profile for a star artist.
Below is an excerpt of the conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
Tell me about “Choosin’ Texas.”
“Choosin’ Texas” is a song about a woman who is essentially losing her man in real time. She goes to a bar or a honky-tonk in Texas. She’s from Tennessee. She suddenly realizes that he sees his ex who’s from Texas and drifts away from her to this woman. It’s that feeling of knowing when you see it in someone’s face that they’re going to be leaving you and figuring out whether it’s worth it to hold on or to let go.
How big is this song, exactly?
It is huge. It is up there right now in competition with Mariah Carey’s “All I Want for Christmas Is You,” which owns the record for the most weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 with 22 weeks. Her only [other] competition is from Shaboozey and Lil Nas X, which are country-adjacent songs.
She really could blow by Mariah Carey. Of course you get a boost every time Christmas comes around, but we’re a little ways off from Mariah Carey declaring once and for all that it’s Christmas season. So I think Ella has plenty of time to catch up. And it could be the biggest song of all time, which is crazy.
You’re a music writer and you’re based in Nashville. How big a deal is Ella Langley in a place like Nashville and in the country industry?
She’s a big deal. And it’s exciting because she’s a relatively newish artist in terms of how long she’s been putting out music. She only released her debut album in 2024, called Hungover.
It’s really exciting because as a lot of people know, it can be really hard for a woman to make it in Nashville. Usually under 10 percent of songs on country radio are by women, so having someone like her out there and having so much country radio airplay and presence on the Hot 100 and breaking all these records, you really hope that it’s going to help influence people in Nashville to sign more women, platform more women, do all of those things to try to sort of flip this longstanding sexism that has existed in Nashville.
Not to put all of our hopes and dreams on one woman, because it’s not up to her to do this. It’s up to the industry to respond. But you sure have to hope so.
Was it a surprise that “Choosin’ Texas” became such a big hit?
I would’ve never predicted this. I loved the song when I heard it, but I don’t think I ever thought that something this country could be this popular.
“Despite the lyrical content, which may be a little bit of a bummer, the song does just feel so good. And it’s like a little bit of a brain weed gummy.”
And yes, country music is becoming so much more popular nationwide, worldwide. But it is also country music in a lot of ways that is a little bit more pop-leaning. Morgan Wallen is extremely popular, but he’s not putting out super-twangy tears-in-your-beer kind of country music songs.
“Choosin’ Texas” is kind of sad, but more than sad, I think it’s relatable. It taps into this feeling that a lot of people have, especially in the summer. If you’re thinking about a summer romance, of losing something that you once had, of letting go, of nostalgia, I think that’s something that we really want to feel right now.
And despite the lyrical content, which may be a little bit of a bummer, the song does just feel so good. And it’s like a little bit of a brain weed gummy. The second it comes on and you hear that little guitar lick it relaxes you. It gives you that summer feel of airy and fresh and a lot of people want to feel that way right now.
You’ve said she’s not a person who shares a ton about herself. Probably smart in this day and age. But country music often does get politicized. And I’ve seen that happening a bit around her and around this song. Tell me about the way she is being slotted into certain perspectives in the US, whether she wants to be or not.
One thing I’ve seen is a lot of people from the far right wanting to use her as an example of a return to sort of this anti-girlboss era. They like to take the fact that she speaks about her faith on stage and warp that into that being sort of her overriding agenda and that she wants this return to traditional values.
And then on the left, I’ve seen some people sort of play with the same. I personally think you could just as easily make a case that she’s a feminist who had Miranda Lambert produce her album and writes with women and takes all these women on tour.
So many people want this moment to serve their own narrative and want Ella Langley to stand for something on every side. And if you don’t give people a little, they’re going to go wild. But maybe that’s better than putting your personal views out there and having them ripped apart. I can’t say I really blame her, to be honest.

There is a moment before the camera begins rolling when the young Ukrainian commander says, "History is repeating itself for us in the Donbas. Unfortunately." Then he falls silent.
A few minutes later, the man, known by the call sign "Fleshka," takes a seat on a weight bench in the garden of a house in an eastern Ukrainian village, just a 30-minute drive from the nearest Russian troops. Every morning, he benches 80 kilograms here before returning to the screens where he coordinates the destruction of Russian assault units through the live feeds from his drone operators.
"I hope it will be a long fight. This is our land, and we will fight for every meter of it," Fleshka says once the camera is rolling. A few meters away stands his comrade "Sascha," another unit commander with the 33rd Brigade. "It's going to be a brutal meat grinder," he predicts, describing a bloody war of attrition. "But I'm glad to be part of it."
Fleshka, 24, and Sascha, 26, belong to a new generation of young Ukrainian commanders helping lead the defense of the last Ukrainian-held bastions in the Donbas. Both have spent years fighting on the front lines. They were involved in the drawn-out Battle of Bakhmut in 2023 and later took part in Ukraine's offensive in Russia's Kursk region at the end of 2024. Today, each man is responsible for more than 80 soldiers serving in a combined drone-and-infantry unit.
The Donbas is comprised of the Luhansk and Donetsk regions. Russia has captured almost all of Luhansk, while Ukraine controls just under one-fifth of the Donetsk region, an area of roughly 5,000 square kilometers, about five times the size of Berlin.
The question is increasingly not whether Putin's army will seize the remaining Ukrainian-held territory in Donbas, but when.
According to information obtained by WELT from conversations with representatives of a leading European intelligence service, Russian forces could reach the outskirts of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk by early 2027. The two cities form the center of the last major Ukrainian defensive belt in the Donbas.
Intelligence officials predict that Russian troops could complete the conquest of most of the region by next year. The human cost of that campaign, however, would likely be staggering. Hundreds of thousands more Russian soldiers could be killed or seriously wounded in the process.
Since the start of the war in 2022, Russia's military has suffered around 1.4 million casualties, according to estimates by analysts at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, including up to 450,000 dead and nearly one million wounded.
Military analyst Franz-Stefan Gady, author of Attack: When War Comes to Us, offers a somewhat more optimistic assessment for Ukraine. Russia's advance, he argues, is progressing at its slowest pace since winter. "At the current rate, Donetsk region would not be fully captured until the early 2030s," he says.
A slowdown, however, should not be mistaken for a stabilization of the front lines. In some sectors, Kyiv's military position is deteriorating. Russia enjoys local superiority in first-person-view drones on certain stretches of the front, in some cases by a ratio of 10 to one. Meanwhile, 3,000-kilogram guided glide bombs continue to inflict heavy losses on Ukrainian forces in front-line areas.
Gady believes it's possible that Russian troops could reach Kramatorsk and Sloviansk as early as spring or summer 2027, but only under one condition.
"Russia needs mobilization if it wants to sustain or increase the current pace," he says. "Moscow is unlikely to do this before the elections, and if it does, Ukraine has no equivalent response available."
According to Gady, Russia's General Staff estimates that newly mobilized troops need around four months before they can have a meaningful impact at the front. A mobilization this autumn could therefore begin to shape events during the first half of 2027.
Col. Markus Reisner of the Austrian Armed Forces says Russia's summer offensive has so far fallen well short of Kremlin expectations. Nevertheless, Putin's troops continue to advance "slowly but steadily".
The decisive factor in the battle for the Donbas, he argues, will be Ukrainian logistics.
"The single most important capability influencing the fight for the Ukrainian defensive belt around Kramatorsk and Sloviansk is the ability to supply the defenders in those cities. If Russian forces succeed in disrupting those supply routes, Ukrainian defenders will be able to hold out only for a limited period."
Already, much of the resupply effort relies on heavy multicopter drones and uncrewed ground vehicles. Russian forces are systematically targeting these systems while simultaneously attempting to prevent the reinforcement and rotation of Ukrainian troops.
Reisner's warning is stark: "If the Ukrainians fail to break this vicious cycle, the defensive belt will fall." Ukrainian brigade commanders also acknowledge that Russia ultimately possesses the resources required to conquer the Donbas.
"Of course, Russia has the potential," Vadym Krykun, commander of the Lubart Brigade, told WELT earlier this year. "It remains the second-largest army in the world. The question is how far Russia is willing to go, how much further it is prepared to mobilize its economy and its population."
Krykun has been fighting in Donbas for more than a decade. Russian troops first entered the region in 2014, and fighting has continued ever since.
As recently as last year, there were hopes that a settlement over eastern Ukraine might pave the way for a ceasefire or even peace. At the end of 2025, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy proposed withdrawing Ukrainian troops from parts of the Donbas as part of a peace initiative, on the condition that Russia also withdraw and that the area be converted into an internationally monitored demilitarized zone, or "free economic zone." The Kremlin rejected the proposal, which was also supported by the United States.
The troops led by Fleshka and Sascha operate heavy "Vampire" and "Nemesis" bomber drones in the Donbas that can strike targets up to 50 kilometers away. They are complemented by reconnaissance drones, drone-based mine-laying systems, and ground robots.
"Our primary focus right now is eliminating their drone operators," Sascha says. "We located the enemy, bombed the position, and mined the area around it. So I would advise them to leave their foxholes and get as far away as possible."
His soldiers, he says, are doing everything they can to keep Ukrainian infantry alive. "The longer the infantry survives, the longer the cities hold."
Fleshka explains that the so-called "death zone," the area in which soldiers must expect drone attacks at any moment, has expanded dramatically in recent months.
The kill zone now stretches 20 kilometers deep in some places, and up to 50 kilometers in others.
"When they use small groups and start moving, and we detect them, nobody wants to let them get away," Sascha says. "Our priority is to eliminate them. There are so many Russians that they simply do not care. I don't know, it's a complicated subject. We eliminate them without much difficulty, but there are just so many of them."
Sascha then describes the Russian tactic in greater detail.
"The enemy sends people forward one at a time. Ten groups essentially means ten individuals."
If one reaches the designated position, another ten groups are sent forward. Eventually, one gets through, then another, then another, until six soldiers have assembled and can continue advancing together.
"Well, let's put it this way: it's a good tactic. An interesting tactic. I haven't come across anything quite like it before," he says.
According to Gady, this method of gradual infiltration and attrition is central to Russia's approach. "Cities do not fall through breakthroughs or house-to-house combat. They fall through exhaustion."
Fleshka fears that Druzhkivka could be the next city to come under serious threat.
"They have shifted their focus toward Sloviansk. They are already fighting in Mykolaivka."
Sascha also expects a fierce battle for Sloviansk. He insists that his men are ready. "It will be like Chasiv Yar. But how long did they assault Chasiv Yar? About a year, if I remember correctly."
He points to the terrain surrounding Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. "The landscape here works in our favor and against theirs. We hold the high ground and have cover. It will be a brutal meat grinder."
Experts doubt that a complete Russian conquest of the Donbas would necessarily persuade the Kremlin to enter serious ceasefire negotiations. "Putin will adjust his war aims depending on the condition of Ukraine's defenders," says Reisner.
Russia is presently targeting what he describes as one of Ukraine's Achilles heels: the critical shortage of air-defense ammunition, particularly for Patriot systems.
"The first major attacks indicate that Putin plans to subject Ukraine to sustained large-scale strikes this winter. He is following a strategy of exhaustion inspired by Svechin, the well-known Soviet military theorist."
Gady argues that, from Moscow's perspective, the Donbas may represent only an intermediate objective.
"The Donbas is an interim goal, not the final one. Russia's strategic objective remains bringing Ukraine back into its sphere of influence. According to Ukrainian intelligence, planning already exists for future operations toward Mykolaiv, Kherson, and Odesa, even if no timelines have been defined."
A genuine de-escalation, he adds, is politically difficult for Moscow.
"It would require scaling back Russia's war economy and explaining to the population why the war is being brought to an end."
