Quick Answer
PowerShell commands such as Get-Help, Get-Command, Get-Process, Start-Process, Stop-Process, Get-Service, Stop-Service, Get-Content, Get-ChildItem, Copy-Item, Move-Item, Remove-Item, and Set-Location help you manage apps, services, files, folders, and system tasks faster on Windows.
PowerShell is a Windows program that simplifies system administration. You can use it to perform many system tasks efficiently and automate repetitive ones. However, to do either, you must know the right commands, or cmdlets (command-lets), as PowerShell calls them.
A typical PowerShell cmdlet follows the verb-noun structure, where the noun is the object you want to act on, and the verb is the action you want to perform on it. This makes them predictable and easy to remember.
Here’s a quick reference guide covering all the essential Windows PowerShell commands to help you get started with PowerShell.
Table of Contents
Essential PowerShell Commands for Windows
Get-Help
Get-Help is a handy cmdlet you can use any time you want to learn about a PowerShell concept or command. It shows information for everything from cmdlets and functions to aliases and scripts. Plus, it shows the exact syntax along with all the available parameters to eliminate the need for guesswork.
Syntax:
Get-Help
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Get-Help cmdlet:
- Get-Help Get-Process : Find out what the Get-Process command does
- Get-Help Get-Process -Detailed : Get a detailed description for the Get-Process cmdlet
- Get-Help Get-Process -Online : View a detailed explanation of the command with examples on Microsoft’s official documentation online
If Get-Help doesn’t return any result, try updating it by running:
Update-Help
Get-Command
Get-Command lists all executable commands installed on your computer, including cmdlets, aliases (or shortcuts that point to other commands), and functions (snippets or scripts that perform specific actions). It’s useful when you want to make sure the command you’re trying to use is supported by PowerShell and available on your system.
Syntax:
Get-Command
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Get-Command cmdlet:
- Get-Command -ListImported : Get a list of all commands in the current session
- Get-Command Get-AppLockerPolicy : View information about the Get-AppLockerPolicy cmdlet
- Get-Command -CommandType Alias : List all alias-type executables
- Get-Command *Service* : Get all the service-related executable elements on your system
Get-Process
Get-Process returns a table of all operating system processes (apps or executables) running on your computer locally. For each item in the table, you see the process name, ID, CPU consumption, and a few other details. This makes it really easy to identify which process is consuming significantly more resources, so you can act on it accordingly and free up system resources.
Syntax:
Get-Process
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Get-Process cmdlet:
- Get-Process -Name notepad : Get details about the Notepad process
- Get-Process explorer | Format-List * : Display detailed information about the explorer processes, including all its properties and their values
Stop-Process
Stop-Process allows you to stop one or more running processes on your computer right from the PowerShell window. To use it, you need the process name or the process ID (or PID), which you can identify by running the Get-Process command.
Syntax:
Stop-Process
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Stop-Process cmdlet:
- Stop-Process -Name notepad : Close the Notepad app
- Stop-Process -Name notepad -F : Force close Notepad
- Stop-Process -Id 3380 : Close the app with a PID of 3380
Start-Process
Start-Process is a PowerShell command that lets you launch one or more processes (or apps) on your computer. You can even open an executable file using it. Start-Process also gives you the ability to choose how you want to start a process. For instance, you may start a program as an administrator or open specific files with their default apps.
Syntax:
Start-Process
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Start-Process cmdlet:
- Start-Process notepad.exe : Launch the Notepad app
- Start-Process -FilePath “notepad” -Wait -WindowStyle Maximized : Open Notepad in a maximized window
- Start-Process -FilePath “sort.exe” : Start a process that uses the sort.exe file
- Start-Process -FilePath “powershell” -Verb RunAs : Open PowerShell as an administrator
Get-Service
Get-Service retrieves and gives you the status of all Windows services running on your computer. It’s useful when you want to identify the status of background services.
Syntax:
Get-Service
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Get-Command cmdlet:
- Get-Service -Name wuauserv : Check the status of the Windows Update service
- Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.Status -eq "Running"} : Filter services to only view the ones that are currently running
Stop-Service
The Stop-Service PowerShell cmdlet lets you stop a system service. You’d typically use it after you’ve run the Get-Service command and identified the problematic service running in the background.
Syntax:
Stop-Service -Name
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Stop-Service cmdlet:
- Stop-Service -Name wuauserv : Stop the Windows Update service
- Stop-Service -DisplayName “telnet” | Stop-Service : Stop a service using its display name
- Stop-Service -Name Spooler -Force : Stop the Spooler service along with other dependent services
Get-Content
Get-Content helps you read the contents of an item within the PowerShell window. You’d mostly use it to get the contents of a file. All you need to do is specify the file and its location. You can even mention the number of lines in the file you want to read, among other things.
Syntax:
Get-Content -Path
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Get-Content cmdlet:
- Get-Content -Path D:\Test\sample.txt -TotalCount 10 : Read only the first ten lines of the file
- Get-Content -Path D:\Test\sample.txt -Wait : Monitor a file and display new lines as they’re added and the file is saved
Get-ChildItem
The Get-ChildItem cmdlet allows you to view all the items (files and folders) at your specified location. Running it without any parameters returns items in your current location, but you can force it to find items at other locations, too.
Syntax:
Get-ChildItem -Path
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Get-ChildItem cmdlet:
- Get-ChildItem -Path D:\Test : Find files and folders in the Test folder in the D: directory
- Get-ChildItem -Path D:\Test -Name : Get the names of files and folders at a specified location
- Get-ChildItem -Path D:\Test -Filter *.txt -Recurse : Scan a directory and its folders for all text files
Copy-Item
Copy-Item lets you copy items (files and folders) from one location to another. You just need to specify the path of the file or folder you want to move along with the path of the location where you want to move it. The copied file continues to live at the original location.
Syntax:
Copy-Item -Destination
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Copy-Item cmdlet:
- Copy-Item D:\Test\sample.txt -Destination D:\Test2\sample2.txt : Copy sample.txt file to another location with sample2.txt name
- Copy-Item D:\Test\ -Destination D:\Test2\ -Recurse : Duplicate the Test folder along with all its subfolders and files to Test2
Move-Item
Move-Item is a handy cmdlet for when you want to move an item (file or folder) from one location to another. Unlike the copy command, it doesn’t keep the item at its original location after the operation. Instead, it moves it to the new location.
Syntax:
Move-Item -Path -Destination
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Move-Item cmdlet:
- Move-Item -Path D:\Test\sample.txt -Destination D:\Test2\ : Move the sample.txt file from the Test folder to the Test2 folder
- Move-Item -Path D:\Test\sample.txt -Destination D:\Test2\sample2.txt : Move the sample.txt file to the Test2 folder and rename it to sample2.txt
- Move-Item -Path .\*.txt -Destination D:\Test2 : Move all files with the .txt extension in the current directory to Test2
Remove-Item
Remove-Item allows you to remove or delete one or more items (files and folders) from a location. Remember that this cmdlet permanently deletes the item instead of moving it to the Recycle Bin for restoration.
Syntax:
Remove-Item -Path
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Remove-Item cmdlet:
- Remove-Item -Path D:\Test*.* : Delete all files with a dot (.) in their name
- Remove-Item -Path D:\Test*.* : Delete all files with a .doc file extension in the Test folder
Set-Location
Set-Location lets you change the current working location to your specified location. It’s quite handy when you’ve to perform multiple operations on different directories.
Syntax:
Set-Location -Path
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Set-Location cmdlet:
- Set-Location -Path D: : Set the working location to the D: drive
- Set-Location -Path D: -PassThru : Set the working location to the D: drive and display that location
You Should Also Learn Command Prompt
PowerShell is just one of the many powerful tools Microsoft bundles with Windows. You also have Command Prompt (CMD) — a command-line interpreter that lets you perform various system operations using commands. If you haven’t already, be sure to check out our essential Command Prompt commands cheatsheet, as that can help you use your Windows PC more efficiently as well.

There is much to be said for the extraordinary women living ordinary lives, who nonetheless shaped India. Women have changed public life in the country far more than their presence in formal politics would suggest.
And so, as India marked its 79th birthday over the weekend, I found myself reflecting on the multitude of people’s movements, big and small – as well as the women who helped shape them. During India’s struggle for freedom from British rule, women organised boycotts of British goods, made contraband salt and marched to confront the police, taking on roles usually dominated by men. In the 1970s Chipko movement, protesting deforestation, women put their bodies on the line, wrapping them around trees to stop them being felled, turning a local struggle into a national reckoning over environment and development. More recently, grandmothers in Shaheen Bagh sat to protest the citizenship law, which critics have denounced as discriminatory, creating space for dissent when many thought none existed.
Today, routes into public life for women have multiplied, with social media enabling people without political links to be in the public eye. But not all barriers have disappeared. Electoral politics remains notoriously hard to break into, especially for women. Almost half of all female parliamentarians and state legislators come from political families, while for men it is 18%, a 2025 analysis by Association for Democratic Reforms showed.
What makes a woman leading an ordinary life suddenly want to put her head above the parapet to change things for everyone? I spoke to women thrust into the spotlight in the recent student movement, who have stepped in front of vans, starved themselves and had abuse hurled at them in the process – to find out why they do it.
‘Politics is not just slogans and protests’: Neha Bora, 29
The president of the leftwing All India Students’ Association, Bora fasted for 23 days, demanding accountability over exam paper leaks and the resignation of the Education Minister during the Cockroach Protests. Now, she is touring the country as part of a Gen Z Rising outreach campaign on education reforms.
“I am a PhD student at Jawaharlal Nehru University in theatre and performance studies. My family’s political understanding is very different from mine. I ended up joining politics because that was the only way I could make sense of the times that I was living in – to not be … completely helpless in the decisions that are made for me, that should be made by me. To have a say in what I do, how I do it and what gets done around me. What is tolerable, what is good, what is injustice – all these definitions made sense to me through politics. Theatre was the first thing that taught me that politics is not just slogans and protests. Politics is the very language in which you talk to yourselves, the thoughts you formulate in your head, the relationships you have with your friends, family and peers. Student politics reaffirmed this idea.
Freedom as a student means the ability to study in a university where the model of education has not been turned into an opportunity for profit. Where education is something that helps societies move forward from dogmatism, conservatism and orthodoxy.”
‘Freedom for me is to have a voice – and not be ashamed’: Rhiya Ahir, 27
A model, actor and theatre artist from Mumbai, Ahir made the split-second decision to physically block a police van holding detained protesters – an act that exposed her to an organised hate campaign.
“I started doing theatre when I was four and a half. It taught me empathy and understanding other people’s pain, even people I don’t know. I’ve always been raised with the belief that if you see something wrong you have to step in.
Freedom for me is to have a voice, to put it across confidently and to not be ashamed. I was trolled for a photo in a swimsuit. But what about the uncles who wear chaddis at the Ganga ghat? My clothes are not my character. My clothes cannot overshadow the point or the fact that I was there, and I helped 20 students get back home safely that day. So, my clothes are just my clothes.
The hate did make me second-guess myself. The first two days [after the Mumbai protest] were very difficult because I was still trying to wrap my head around what had happened. They couldn’t find fault with my argument, so they started questioning my character. They went through my Instagram and found that I was a model. They talked about what I wear. They said she’s doing it for the camera.
When the hate started pouring in I was like, ‘What did I do to offend someone? Did I do something wrong?’ Then I realised this doesn’t change my reality. This doesn’t change who I am as a person. I don’t have to prove myself to anyone.”
‘The police have visited my ancestral village asking for information on me’: Danish Ali, 24
Ali was among the student activists on hunger strike at Jantar Mantar. A member of the Jawaharlal Nehru University student union, she faces a year-long suspension for dismantling a facial recognition system at the campus library. For her, freedom is deeply personal and rooted in her identity as a Muslim woman.
“I come from a very small town in Madhya Pradesh. No one in my family had even visited the city, so going to Delhi for higher education was almost like going abroad for education. Since the protest, the police have visited my ancestral village asking for information on me. They called my father, asking him to tell me to focus on my studies.
As a student activist, freedom means to be able to critique the government openly and say that we don’t like their policies. Freedom is being assertive about your individuality and not caring what the society would says, what your parents might say or what the state might do to you.
Freedom also means being an equal citizen in this country. Muslims in this country are being made to feel as if they are secondary and that they don’t have any right to express their religious or cultural identities. I am an equal citizen and I don’t want anyone to tell me otherwise.”
‘What used to work … won’t work with the youth’: Ratna Singh, 31
She traded a career in the law and journalism to join the Cockroach Janata party, where she now serves as the legal head. She felt drawn to the protests, seeing her work reflected in the students’ demand for accountability. Initially hesitant to become its public face, she stepped forward as spokesperson when they needed female voices.
“When I was in law school, most of my classmates would go to law chambers for internships but I would spend the summers teaching children at NGOs. Education has been something I have been very sensitive towards, and I believe every child should have access to it.
A lot of people were criticising us [and calling us] an impatient generation. We are impatient because we want to see change. We can’t be protesting and be OK with not getting answers from the government. We are also just done with divide and rule politics on the basis of religion. Political parties need to understand that what used to work for a certain mindset of people – it won’t work with the youth.
There are so many protests which have begun in different parts of the country. The fear of speaking up is gone. We are seeing a lot of leaders coming up in their own districts. They are starting their own initiatives. I think that’s giving us all hope to keep going.”
What else we’re reading about
Political promises | In his Independence Day speech, Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced a series of youth-focused initiatives, including an AI skills programme, free online coaching for competitive exams and a countrywide sport talent hunt. His call to identify “dimagi naxals”, or people aligned with Naxal ideology, referring to the armed guerilla movement in central India, was criticised by the Opposition as a threat to suppress critics and rivals.
Environment targets missed | The Green India Mission, for protecting and restoring the country’s declining forest cover, fell short of its target by 97% over the past decade, according to an audit report tabled in Parliament. New forest cover added was just 0.03409 million hectares, the report said, citing poor planning and inadequate funding.
Sister act | Two women of Indian origin adopted by separate Dutch families 40 years ago, who became friends as children, recently discovered they are sisters after a DNA test, Reuters reported. “It’s like a missing puzzle piece has been found,” one said.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Actor Imran Khan (@imrankhan) recommends: “Rang De Basanti is an extremely timely and relevant film for this moment; it follows a young English film-maker who befriends a group of Indian students. They set out to make a film about the Indian freedom movement. A tragic accident blurs the lines between past and present, throwing them into their own conflict against an unjust power structure. The film is funny but also heartbreaking. It celebrates the spirit of the great revolutionaries, and imagines what their modern counterparts might stand for. And the soundtrack gives us AR Rahman at his most audaciously experimental. It rocks.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
Two
Question hour in Lok Sabha functioned for 1% percent of its scheduled time during the parliament’s monsoon session, the lowest since 2019, according to PRS Legislative Research, a nonprofit that tracks the functioning of the parliament and state assemblies. The key forum for members of parliament to question the government saw two questions answered in nine minutes, PRS said.
Vibe check
For creator Maroof Umar (@maroofculmen), storytelling can change the way we see the world. And the stories he tells, rooted in heritage and culture through cinematically shot videos, can both break and mend your heart. Each has a person at its center but the stories also belong to the city and its communities. His short videos capture his (and my) hometown of Lucknow most frequently, but his latest work takes us to a sweet shop in Varanasi. In it, Ram Bhandar makes tricolor treats in a nod to the colors of the Indian flag, carrying on a tradition begun by his ancestors decades before, as they tried to spread patriotic fervor during the freedom movement.

Will India learn now at least?
Will it let Nepal speak to India through its agony what India has refused to hear ?
The Himalaya are not a series of silos — Afghanistan Hindu Kush Himalaya, Pakistan Himalaya, Indian Himalaya, Nepal Himalaya, the Himalaya in Tibet-China, Bhutan. To employ a powerful term I have heard Vadodara-based painter Gulam Mohammed Sheikh use for the Elephanta Caves, the Himalaya are one living rock, silently, broodingly, tense with seismic voltages, glacial stirrings and geological turbulence.
And they spell their uncoded thought in swipes no one can foretell. When, where exactly, with what ferocity, no one knows. And what disasters may radiate from them — through rivers plucked from their courses, rockfalls and landslides depositing mud and silt, turning human habitations into rubble and fertile farms into slime — no one can precisely envision.
Ask those who have heard from their parents and grandparents of the Nepal-Bihar earthquake of 1934 or the Assam temblor of 1950. They will speak of the nightmare.
The question of preparedness
The world has been told — India has specifically been warned — by seismologists of an impending earthquake of humungous scale with the potential of a cataclysm across a great swathe of northern India which lies under the quake-shadow of the Himalaya. It is not as if India’s government has declined to heed the warning. It has done much, as its disaster management agencies will rightly assure us, to be alert to the risk.
But after 26/8 what we need to ask and know is: should what happened in upper Nepal have happened in lower Nepal, and even lower than that, would our ‘preparedness’ have sufficed to save riverside habitations from instant death?
More pertinently, we need to ask and know whether the absolutely fearsome phenomenon of global warming triggered GLOFs (or Glacial Lake Outburst Floods), has led authorities to warn people living in potential GLOF-affected areas in India of the danger they face and advised them on how to face it.
We are, let us face it, in seismic, glacial, climatological and geological innocence.
By ‘we’ I mean we the people of India. Our earth scientists know it all but their jnana is clasped tight in their acharya-mushti-s (’knowledge kept in the teacher’s fist’).
What happened in Nepal on that stricken Wednesday is yet to be fully appraised. We will soon enough know whether it was an earthquake that caused the GLOF, or whether the GLOF resulted in the earth quaking and waterbodies swelling as they never have before.
Whatever happened, India must learn
Be the sequence as it may, the following lessons scream to be learnt by India.
First, the Himalaya, held sacred since memory has served, gestate ‘sure-shot’ danger.
Second, these dangers can now no longer be left to be unravelled in seminars and technical papers.
Editorial | Danger from above: On the Nepal flood
Third, they have to be made known on a war footing to us, the clear potential victims.
Fourth, and not just made known as in increasing our knowledge but made known as in making us part of a new safeguarding.
Fifth, our scholar-diplomat Shyam Saran has, in two timely and telling articles in The Tribune (“China’s hydel project bodes ill for India”, July 14, 2026) and The Indian Express (“From Nepal to Uttarakhand and China, the mountains are warning us”, August 28, 2026), explained how China’s construction of Medog, the world’s largest hydropower project, at the great bend of the Brahmaputra river just across the border and very close to the Paizhen Fault, could (should there be a major earthquake in the project’s vicinity), cause a massive discharge of floodwaters and debris into India’s northeast. India’s salutary initiatives to bring about a measure of mature civility on the borders with China must now include frankness about the ferocious danger that Medog poses.
Sixth, an urgent review of India’s own built hazards such as dams and reactors in the high risk zones followed by the dismantling of the real ‘baddies’ can no longer be postponed.
Seventh, and no less difficult but no less important, a calibrated but time-bound decongestion of human agglomerations in high-risk zones.
Eighth, if surgical strikes can be used with precision and without excesses against an external enemy to good effect, their civilian equivalent should be deployed to disable that which, though intended for our well-being, has become a danger.
Progress and danger
Marjorie Sykes was a British devotee of India, in the tradition of C.F. Andrews, Verrier Elwin and J.B.S. Haldane. I once heard her say with passion: “Dams are a damnation.” All dams may not be, but some, depending on their location, are. Likewise, some reactors can become rakshasas. And some commercial behemoths, predatory.
A big and great nation can learn from the experience of a small neighbour. Especially when both are perched on the same living rock that threatens to turn into a mass grave.
Gopalkrishna Gandhi is a former administrator who has held diplomatic and constitutional offices

Adding a distinctive charm to the beauty of the Western Ghats, a rare blue-violet flower resembling Neelakurinji has bloomed big along some trekking trails in the Kudremukh region of Chikkamagaluru district recently, attracting more trekkers and nature enthusiasts.
According to the Forest and Tourism Department officials, these flowers were seen in greater abundance in some of the hill regions of Kudremukh during 2022–23, earlier. They have appeared in limited numbers again this time. The blue-violet blooms scattered across the green hills are adding a unique attraction to the natural landscape of Kudremukh.
Sampath, owner of Namma Mane homestay near Kalasa in Chikkamagaluru, said that the bloom in 2022-23 had attracted big crowds to the region and they were expecting a similar jump in tourist traffic this season too.
Ram Prasath Manohar, Secretary, Tourism Department, said that the limited blooming of these blue-violet flowers in Kudremukh this year has generated special interest among trekking enthusiasts and nature tourists. “There is a need to present such natural phenomena through environmentally responsible tourism. Instructions have been given to the district Tourism Department officials to provide visitors with the necessary information, guidance and facilities without causing any harm to the flowers or their habitat,” he said.
He urged the visitors not to pluck the flowers and only watch them. “If they are plucked, then it disturbs the blooming cycle of these flowers. We have requested visitors not to damage the plants or litter the surroundings and help us preserve the natural environment,” Mr. Manohar said.
Tourism Minister K.J. George said blue-violet flowers like neelakurinji blooming in the hills of Kudremukh showcase the exceptional beauty of Karnataka’s natural wealth. “While visiting such natural attractions, tourists must adopt eco-friendly travel practices. Visitors should not only enjoy the beauty of nature but also understand their responsibility towards protecting it.”

When I walk into a suburban mid-century house with my sister, we're on the hunt for treasures that will make our customers happy — but we also like to marvel at the elaborate wallpaper in the bathroom.
We have time now to sift through the junk drawers and basement bookshelves. Within the last few years, we both were laid off from our jobs as writers and editors. While we continue to fling our résumés into the ring, we keep ourselves busy at estate sales and thrift stores.
We come from a family of thrifters and estate-sale lovers; our mother was an avid collector with an eye for beautiful and valuable antiques. She taught her three daughters how to find treasures in the junk —what to look for, how to bargain, and which cleaning potions worked best to restore items to their former glory.
I've always enjoyed the thrill of the hunt, but I never imagined turning our shared love for vintage into a small business.
My sister and I were laid off
I sensed a wave of layoffs coming in digital media before it happened. A strange mix of optimism and despair coursed through me as I tried to regroup. I quickly landed a new job, only to be let go from that role a year later.
Meanwhile, my younger sister had lost her job as part of mass layoffs at a major corporation. We were both reeling while grieving the loss of our mother and now also caring for our elderly father in our childhood home.
With the looming threat of AI, the job market looked bleak.
Layoffs disrupt and disorient. It's hard to know how to spend your time when there's suddenly so much of it. It's easy to sink into the couch and think your new job is just remembering to shower and watching every episode of "Love Island."
Facing job loss — and the grief of losing both of our parents within six years — my younger sister and I first reviewed our mom's epic collection for items we could sell. We also started hitting estate sales, thrift shops, antique malls, and garage sales more frequently.
Starting a business together was the answer
As we gathered more goods, I decided to make it official and established Travel Far Now Vintage, an Etsy shop, in 2023.
I handle most aspects of the business — packing, shipping, and accounting — and I rely on the keen curatorial eye of my younger sister, who can walk into any estate sale or thrift shop and score the most unusual vintage items hidden in the heaps.
Together, we found unexpected joy during some of the most challenging years of our lives.
There's no shortage of tasks to fill the time — from sourcing to cleaning, listing to packing, shipping to accounting, posting, and connecting with new clients — the business keeps us energized against the lethargy of layoffs.
Consistency is key. While we continue to search for meaningful full-time roles, running a vintage business keeps us alert, active, and curious about the objects we collect within an ever-changing marketplace.
Luckily, no two days are alike. There's always someone looking for that exact vintage object that connects them with the past.
The business has also helped us heal
Running a vintage business is the ultimate crash course in grief, with lessons on letting go at every turn.
There's an alchemy to this work. By giving abandoned objects a second chance at life, I've developed a deeper appreciation for the fleeting nature of time.
I've come to think of myself as a "memory merchant," dealing in nostalgia through vintage objects and the stories they tell about our lives.
When a client reaches out to me about an analog Sunbeam timer for sale, it's not just about the timer, but about connecting with a core memory in their childhood kitchen. Hearing these stories helps me connect with my own memories and make peace with the past.
Our vintage shop is an ode to our mother — the ultimate thrifter and sifter — who taught us the ropes. When we're out shopping, we always hear our mom's voice in the aisles.
"Do you know what this is?" she asks with a twinkle in her eye. "Yes, Mom, we know," we answer, and continue scanning the shelves for more unique treasures.
Operating this small vintage business with my sister has strengthened our bond as we remember our mom together. The search alone is therapeutic, but it's also immensely healing to know we can breathe new life into old things.

The small camera installed in Meta's AI smart glasses has become a problem for the company and the public.
Photos and videos captured by Meta glasses have proliferated on social media, and not all of them are consensual. Clips of content creators harassing women and recording their reactions covertly have become a trend, raising concerns about privacy.
"Are you a secret code?" one male content creator asked a woman in an Instagram video. "Because I'm trying to crack you." Some social media users have dubbed Meta's product "pervert glasses."
It's all a bad look for Meta. So the company is making moves to get ahead of the negativity. It has recently publicized new privacy settings for its glasses and has launched a PR blitz to explain them.
Meta Chief Technology Officer Andrew Bosworth posted an Instagram video on Friday, for example, in which he explained how the smart glasses' hands-free camera works.
"We designed this camera to be noticed by the people around you, so in every pair of glasses we make, there's a capture LED on the front, and it lights up when someone's taking photos or videos for the gallery," Bosworth said.
Bosworth said the camera has no off switch. It stops working if people try to cover or deactivate it.
"We took this issue all the way across Meta, and we've been taking down content and even whole accounts connected to people misusing the glasses," Bosworth said.
Alex Himel, the vice president of wearables at Meta, also attempted to calm nerves on Friday in a Threads post. He said Meta's smart glasses will not allow users to record if the camera's LED light is blocked before or during recording.
"We're going to keep rolling out updates like this to make sure the capture LED can reliably alert bystanders when photos or videos are being captured for someone's gallery," Himel said.
While the company has suspended accounts that use the cameras to harass people, Business Insider's Katie Notopoulos reported last week that it hasn't been able to catch them all.
Meta has taken strides to make their smart glasses a must-have accessory. The company has partnered with megastars like Kylie Jenner and Teyana Taylor, and it produced a star-studded Super Bowl LX ad to drum up hype.
As AI smart glasses become increasingly accessible, some event and venue organizers are taking a cautious approach with guests. Burning Man told attendees at the 2026 festival, which starts Monday, that they can bring smart glasses, but must get consent before filming anyone. New York City nightclub Basement updated its no-photo-and-video policy to include smart eyewear.
"Anyone bringing smart glasses into the venue, whether wearing them or carrying them in a bag, will be asked to leave and may be permanently banned," the venue said in an Instagram post on Friday.
Organizers for the DEFCON Hacking Conference told attendees in July that smart glasses and similar items are prohibited.
In his Instagram video, Bosworth urged users to watch for the LED light that indicates the cameras are recording.
"Please remember," he added, "the light is there for everyone."

Sudanese in Kordofan's Bara the latest civilians to be forced into battle
From the Sudanese war’s earliest months, civilians have been forced to take up arms to defend themselves.
In Darfur’s al-Geneina in the summer of 2023, members of the Masalit community fought back as the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and allied militias rampaged through the city.
Similarly, villages in al-Jazira state south of Khartoum fought off invading paramilitaries as communities around them were overrun.
And in el-Fasher, the North Darfur state capital that was under siege for over 550 days, residents helped keep the RSF at bay until the defensive lines finally collapsed in October 2025, precipitating the massacre of an estimated 60,000 people.
Since then, the focus of the war has shifted to Kordofan, the resource-rich region to the south.

Here, too, civilians have taken up arms, most often part of the Popular Resistance units fighting alongside the Sudanese Armed Forces, but also through non-violent means.
The Popular Resistance was established by army chief General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan in June 2023, with the SAF providing tens of thousands of civilians with weapons and training.
Its cadres include people from all parts of Sudanese society, including pro-democracy revolutionaries who previously opposed Burhan and his military rule.
However, Sumood, the bloc of civilian political parties led by former prime minister Abdalla Hamdok, argues that the Popular Resistance is dominated by religious conservatives who intend to use it to return figures from Omar al-Bashir’s era to power.
In North Kordofan, the scene of intense recent battles, Popular Resistance fighters say politics has taken a back seat when confronted with the danger of the RSF.
Mustafa Karam al-Din, a pharmacist from the city of Bara, joined the Popular Resistance under SAF command when the RSF killed his brother and ransacked his home last year.
“They raided our house, killing my brother and others in my neighbourhood, so I had no option other than taking up weapons to protect myself and my family and neighbours,” he tells MEE in el-Obeid, the North Kordofan state capital.
“The RSF was very brutal with everybody when they entered the city. That wasn't just against armed people but against all citizens, including the civilians.”
According to Karam al-Din, the RSF was out for revenge when they recaptured Bara, after the SAF briefly held the city last year, because its residents had celebrated the paramilitary's ouster.
“They had videos and lists of some people, including the agents of the Popular Resistance,” he says.
Karam al-Din says it became clear to civilians in Bara and elsewhere in Kordofan that they needed to protect themselves.
“They entered police stations and weapons stores and took up weapons. They also got others from the SAF. Then the Popular Resistance was organised, including in Bara, el-Obeid and other areas in Kordofan,” he said.
Bara, in particular, has witnessed extreme violence. The RSF and SAF have traded the city on Kordofan’s strategic Export Road several times over the past three years. Since July, Bara has been held by the army.
“Since October last year we have been fighting with the SAF against the RSF until we liberated our city, and I’m very proud of that,” Karam al-Din says.
The RSF has committed abuses across Sudan since the war broke out and has been accused of genocide in Darfur by the United States and several human rights groups.
'This conflict has become a war against the UAE’s foreign invasion, which is using the RSF as a tool'
- Mustafa Karam al-Din, Popular Resistance fighter
The group is backed by the UAE, which despite global outrage has supplied the paramilitary with weapons and mercenaries.
“This conflict has become a war against the UAE’s foreign invasion, which is using the RSF as a tool,” says Karam al-Din, who currently mans checkpoints on the frontline.
According to him, weapons and other supplies from the UAE were found in the hands of RSF fighters as the SAF retook Bara.
“We have also arrested mercenaries from Colombia, South Sudan and other countries fighting with the RSF in Um Syala and Gabrat al-Shiekh,” he says.
Godat Abdul Hadi, a leading member of the Popular Resistance, told MEE that it provides military training for hundreds of youths from Bara who were displaced to el-Obeid.
“The Popular Resistance in el-Obeid, Bara and other areas began at the start of the war and even before the SAF officially declared and expanded it under SAF command,” he says.
“The number was initially small, but it has hugely increased in response to the RSF invasion of the majority of North and West Kordofan and with the widespread atrocities it committed.”
Protection and risk
When the RSF attacked Bara last October, Mohammed Adam was sitting with his friends and neighbours, talking about the humanitarian efforts to help Bara’s people after the paramilitary’s last devastating assault.
Despite some of his friends and cousins carrying weapons, Adam, who is a pro-democracy activist and part of the Resistance Committees network that led the 2019 popular revolution against Bashir, was not convinced carrying weapons alongside the SAF was the right solution to the danger of the RSF.
When the RSF overran his city, any evidence that civilians were involved in armed resistance was a death sentence for people trying to flee.
“I can never forget that day. Some of the armed youths were with me in my house, and they were unable to join their units because of intensive RSF fire. So, we lay under beds for hours, and when the crossfire stopped, we realised the SAF had been defeated and RSF fighters were starting to attack civilians,” he recalls.
“We quickly decided to hide everything associated with fighting, including my friends’ Kalashnikovs and military uniforms. I gave them some of my normal clothes, and we decided to leave the city that day.”
Before they could leave, RSF fighters entered Adam’s house and threatened everyone there, accusing them of being "fulool", a term for people associated with the “deep state”. Despite searching the home, fortunately they did not uncover the guns and fatigues.
That night, Adam and his friends were able to escape Bara and head towards el-Obeid, which was still under SAF control.
“When we got out of my house, we saw a disaster. Dozens of dead bodies were in the streets, and wounded and displaced people were all along the route. The people of the nearby villages helped us with whatever they could provide: food, water and simple medical treatment,” he says.
“We endured difficult times at the hands of the RSF. One incident turned the people of Bara against them completely, when they killed one of our neighbours and then attacked the funeral ceremony the same day, killing many other people for no reason.”
Skeptics among the revolutionaries
Not all of Kordofan’s pro-democracy activists are so supportive of the Popular Resistance.
One member of the Resistance Committees network in Bara told MEE he believes that the mobilised units are dominated by religious conservatives and people linked to Bashir’s rule.
“Former regime associates are leading the so-called Popular Resistance in Bara and other places in order to pave the way for the old regime to exploit the war and return to power,” says the activist, who asked for anonymity for security reasons.
“This war has to be stopped by all means and concessions. It destroyed the country and enabled the old regime to come back through the SAF,” he claims.
However, Adam said many Sudanese, particularly the youth, don’t feel like they have a choice whether to take up arms and fight under SAF command or not.
“The RSF has attacked everybody: civilians or military, young or old, men or women. They take revenge on everybody in Bara,” he says.
“Those who took up weapons in self-defence were our brothers, cousins and neighbours. Any previous political disagreements are not an issue at the moment,” he adds.
“Let me tell you: I prefer not to carry weapons under the SAF, but I can’t tell those who have been attacked and humiliated by the RSF not to defend themselves by all means.”

India has met the fiscal consolidation trajectory set for 2025-26 and will work towards bringing the government’s borrowing down to 50% of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2030, said Union finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman on Sunday in the US. Speaking to members of the Indian diaspora in Chicago during her official visit to the US, Sitharaman said the government stayed on its planned path of fiscal discipline, with the country's fiscal deficit at 4.4% of GDP in 2025-26. “We have given ourselves a fiscal discipline path on the fiscal deficit as well. We have fulfilled the trajectory. The last mile that had to be reached by 2025-26, we have reached,” she said. She said the government had set a target of bringing borrowing down to 50% of GDP by 2030. “We have set ourselves a certain target, which is to bring the borrowing down to the 50% level of GDP by 2030. Therefore, I will be working on that path.” She contrasted India’s debt position with that of some advanced economies. “There are advanced economies whose debt is well over 200% of their GDP even now,” she said. Defending the government’s fiscal approach, Sitharaman said improvements in India’s credit ratings were not the result of cuts to social welfare spending. “The world has witnessed the fiscal prudence of honourable Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi when he was the chief minister of Gujarat and when he is the Prime Minister of the country. Our credit ratings are improving,” she said. “But that's not by cutting corners. That's not by stopping the resources which have to go for social welfare. It is through proper management of the economy,” she added. She also called for greater participation from the Indian diaspora, including through capital, ideas and talent, as the government works towards its 2047 target of making India a developed economy. “2047 is the target year set for achieving Viksit Bharat. It's hardly 20 years from now. So, the speed and scale with which the reforms are happening require a lot more support,” she said. “Lots more support from people who are talented and have exposure. Lots more support from people who can give ideas for us to carry it forward. And, above all, support in terms of capital, which is so required for a country to meet all its aspirations,” she added. The finance minister also highlighted how the government responded to disruptions in global supplies of fertilizers, crude oil and liquified petroleum gas, including higher shipping insurance premiums caused by geopolitical risks. “The fertilizer shortage was not felt in India because we managed to keep the markets informed about how much we would require,” she said, adding that global supplies had shrunk and challenges had increased across crude oil, LPG and fertilizers. “Ships going to procure these supplies were unable to secure adequate insurance cover. Risk premiums had gone up significantly,” Sitharaman said. She said the government had subsequently supported additional insurance premiums for shipping liners through a budget announcement. “Through a budget announcement, we made a pool of funds available so that any additional premiums paid by shipping liners due to the risks involved would be supported by the government. As a result, Indian farmers, Indian households and Indian logistics did not suffer,” she said. She said the government’s ability to track global uncertainties while assessing domestic requirements had helped India remain resilient. “By continuously keeping track of global uncertainties while understanding India’s own requirements, we have managed to stay resilient.” “Many countries have seen their calculations go haywire amid these uncertainties. Thankfully, despite our limitations, we have kept our citizens protected in this challenging environment,” she added. Sitharaman is on a nine-day visit to Canada and the US from 25 August to 2 September. During the visit, she is meeting investors and business leaders and is scheduled to represent India at the G20 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors’ meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, on 31 August and 1 September. Three hundred thousand metric tons of ground beef are on their way to the United States. There’s no easy way to visualize 300,000 metric tons of anything (for context, that’s about 12 times the weight of the Statue of Liberty). All of that beef could fill an important gap in the American market—but not everyone’s happy about it.
President Trump announced last Friday that he’ll be temporarily lifting some tariffs on beef and that, as part of an ambiguous deal, the imports will be sold at “25 percent below current market prices.” He was likely hoping for a political win here: Affordability has been a losing issue for Trump and his party ahead of the midterms, and increasing the beef supply in an attempt to lower prices could be one way of giving shoppers a reprieve. But industry leaders immediately condemned the move, warning that it will do little to address the underlying dynamics that have driven up prices in recent years—and their allies in Congress joined them in the revolt. Now Trump’s on-again, off-again relationship with ranchers is becoming the whole country’s problem.
There’s no great mystery as to why American beef is so expensive. The steaks we get from the supermarket represent the end product of a long, multiyear chain involving ranchers, auctioneers, feedlots, meatpackers, and grocery stores. But beef starts with cattle, and after years of drought, the number of cows now grazing on U.S. soil is the lowest it’s been in 75 years. The return of a certain flesh-eating parasite hasn’t helped things, either. This, combined with the fact that Americans are still hungry for beef, has created a basic supply-and-demand problem.
Economists told NPR this week that the president’s move, which was made official on Wednesday, may shave only a small amount off what shoppers are currently paying for ground beef at the grocery store. It’s too soon to tell whether this will actually happen—the government won’t release its August data for another few weeks—but Trump’s announcement did depress cattle prices somewhat, which suggests that traders at least think that beef could become less valuable, as the president intended. This is a problem for ranchers, who applauded last year’s restrictive Liberation Day tariffs. Most of the beef that Americans consume is produced in the United States, and the duties had been helping prevent foreign imports from undercutting domestic producers; without these protections, meat-processing companies are free to buy the cheapest option, wherever it may come from. In a joint letter to the president, the heads of four livestock-industry groups expressed “deep concern” that the plan would undermine beef producers by devaluing cattle and would prevent the rebuilding of the dwindling herd.
Ominously, the White House has declined to say where all of this beef will be coming from. When asked which countries will be supplying the beef, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins told reporters on Tuesday that she was “not part of any of those conversations” and is “not privy to talk about that.” Trump mentioned that “a few” different countries will be involved but hasn’t said which. (Thirty thousand pounds of Argentine beef were recalled earlier this month over concerns that it hadn’t been properly inspected; the White House declined to respond to my question about where the beef will be coming from but claimed, without elaborating, that the plan would reduce beef prices while allowing the U.S. cattle herd to grow.)
Despite being a core MAGA constituency, beef producers and ranchers have been periodically annoyed at Trump’s tariff changes over the past year. What’s more unusual is that high-profile Republicans have also been breaking with the president on this issue. At least 13 GOP senators have publicly criticized the tariff adjustment to varying degrees over the past week. “Beef prices are too high for a simple reason: Our cattle herd is too small,” Senator Tom Cotton wrote on X. “I have advised the President against this ill-advised action in the past and I now urge him to reconsider.” Others suggested that what Trump is doing is unfair, a way of rigging the market against American producers, who “simply want a fair marketplace,” per Senator John Barrasso. (Rollins seems to be supporting the current plan, though she reportedly opposed a similar tariff rollback in May.)
This isn’t the first time in recent months that the Trump administration—whose war with Iran has driven up consumer prices—has turned its attention to short-term solutions. As I’ve written, both Trump and Rollins have publicly praised business owners who have lowered their prices on certain goods, such as fuel and groceries. But these kinds of temporary cuts don’t amount to a lasting policy solution, and companies can’t be expected to shoulder this burden forever. The private-sector “commitment” to selling this imported beef below market price has a similarly short-term focus. The bigger issues remain unaddressed, and voters don’t believe that the administration has the economy under control.
The president attempted to make peace with ranchers this morning, writing on Truth Social that he’d give them the “right to PROCESS THEIR OWN FOOD”—a nod to long-standing complaints about what farmers say is a monopoly among the Big Four meatpackers. But this olive branch is effectively just a promise to disrupt a different part of the industry. In trying to please everyone, Trump may end up creating even more beef.

As the Centre pushes to widen the role of AYUSH in India’s healthcare system — including through greater coverage, rural outreach and integration with mainstream health services — the country’s AYUSH medical education infrastructure has expanded rapidly.
But the expansion appears to have been driven largely by non-government institutions, according to government data.
India must use the AYUSH opportunity
The number of Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha and Homoeopathy (AYUSH) colleges rose from 789 in 2021 to 971 in 2024, an increase of about 23%. Over the same period, total admission capacity grew from 63,477 to 79,593, or nearly 25%, while permitted seats grew from 50,711 to 72,490 — an increase of about 43%.
The 2021 figures cover Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha, Yoga and Naturopathy, Homoeopathy and Sowa-Rigpa. By April 2024, the Ministry registered 541 Ayurveda, 58 Unani, 17 Siddha, 71 Yoga and Naturopathy, 277 Homoeopathy and seven Sowa-Rigpa colleges.
Of the 541 Ayurveda colleges in April 2024, 467 were non-government — nearly 86% of the total. In Homoeopathy, 236 of 277 colleges, or about 85%, were non-government.
The pattern was similar in other systems. Of the 58 Unani colleges, only 16 were government-run; just three of 17 Siddha colleges and 15 of 71 Yoga and Naturopathy colleges were government institutions. Data clearly indicates that non-government institutions have become an important source of undergraduate medical education in AYUSH.
Additionally, the Ministry’s annual report for 2024-25 shows that 60,890 students were admitted against 63,073 permitted undergraduate seats in Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, and Homoeopathy (ASU&H).
Ayurveda had almost full utilisation, with 39,952 of 40,136 permitted seats filled, Homoeopathy accounted for 1,887 vacancies — more than 86% of the total. The Ministry has also begun collecting admission data from State and Union Territory counselling authorities, improving the availability of national-level vacancy data.
Spending rises from a low base
Central spending under AYURGYAN, the Centre’s scheme supporting AYUSH education, capacity building, continuing medical education, research and innovation, has also increased.
The allocation rose from ₹8.42 crore in 2021-22 to ₹10.5 crore in 2022-23, ₹14.66 crore in 2023-24 and ₹48.5 crore in 2024-25, according to Ministry data placed before Parliament.
This, however, is not an education-only budget as AYURGYAN also supports capacity building and continuing medical education, research, and innovation; from 2023-24, it includes Ayurveda Biology Integrated Health Research.

Not the GameCube, not the Wii U: This was Nintendo's most unsuccessful console
Nintendo’s worst-ever console was awkward to use and didn’t even sell a million units.
For as many massively successful systems as Nintendo has had (like the Game Boy, Nintendo DS, and Nintendo Switch), the company has also suffered through stumbles. Some of the minor missteps were limited to accessories, such as the clumsy e-Reader, or Nintendo 64DD that never released outside of Japan. But entire consoles have flopped too, which stings much more.
When you think of failed Nintendo platforms, the GameCube or Wii U might come to mind. During the sixth generation, the GameCube came in third place behind the wildly successful PS2 and newcomer Xbox. And the Wii U represented one of Nintendo's darkest periods, offering many mixed-reception games for confusing hardware that wasn't marketed well.
But the Nintendo console that had the worst run wasn't either of these. Rather, it was a short-lived system from the mid-1990s that didn't even last a year and sold just a fraction of the units. And as lambasted as it was, a recent comeback means it's easier than ever to try today.
The Virtual Boy was Nintendo's biggest disaster
You'll realize the Virtual Boy is unusual just by looking at it. Rather than a traditional home video game console that hooks up to a TV or a portable one you hold in your hands, the Virtual Boy falls into an awkward middle ground. It uses a viewfinder "binocular" design supported by a stand to guide you into the flagship feature: rudimentary three-dimensional visuals. The proper term for this is "stereoscopic 3D," where a different image is shown to each of your eyes to create the illusion of 3D. And while this technology sounds impressive for the time, it was really an underbaked mess fraught with problems.
Nintendo began selling the Virtual Boy in North America in August 1995, shortly after its Japanese release. This was before the Nintendo 64 or the Game Boy Pocket revision arrived in 1996, meaning Nintendo's hardware market had been quiet since the SNES's North American release in 1991. March 1996 saw the last Virtual Boy game released in North America (Tetris 3D), with Nintendo silently discontinuing the system not long after. Europe never even got it.
In June 1996, Nintendo reported that the console had sold 770,000 units. This makes it the worst-selling Nintendo console by far — the Wii U is next-worst, but still miles away at 13.6 million sold.
It was uncomfortable to use...
If you're wondering how you're supposed to comfortably play the Virtual Boy, you've happened upon the first major problem. Setting the Virtual Boy's stand on a table meant you had to lean forward to put your face inside, which wasn't a comfortable position to hold for long periods. Tilting the stand could help, or you could get creative with various angles like lying down. A strap would have been great, but Nintendo never released one. It's not a good sign when simply figuring out how to start using a system is a challenge.
For power, the Virtual Boy used six AA batteries in the back of the controller (or an optional adapter for a wall plug that slid onto the back of the controller instead). Its controller had a unique double D-pad design, which several games utilized. However, the A/B and Start/Select buttons having the exact same shape made it easy to forget which was which, since you couldn't easily look down to see them.
There were also complaints at the time about not being connected to the people around you while playing, since the Virtual Boy was a one-person experience. Others in the house couldn't watch you or easily pass the controller around. It clearly wasn't a portable console either; using this in a car would have been ridiculous.
...and the screen caused physical sickness
The Virtual Boy's discomfort doesn't end with getting your face into the device. Once you put your eyes up to the screen, another one of its huge issues becomes apparent: the screen is only in black and red. According to Nintendo, adding full color would have made production far too expensive. The color palette commonly caused eye strain and headaches, especially given how close your eyes were to the screen.
Aside from a boring single color, the Virtual Boy's 3D display technology made people feel nauseous. Internally, the system used oscillating mirrors to reflect a single-pixel-wide line of LEDs and create the images you see while playing (this video from The Slow Mo Guys illustrates it well). Because everyone's eyes are different, the unit had a slider on top to adjust the distance between the mirrors. I'm sure many people didn't do this properly (or at all), which contributed to the eye and head sickness.
Nintendo was aware of these problems, so the Virtual Boy had a built-in reminder to take a break every 15 minutes or so. The longer you went without stopping, the more likely you were to feel unwell. It's hard to get absorbed in an experience when you have to keep breaking the immersion.
The game library was limited and weak
Perhaps people would have forgiven the hurdles to using the Virtual Boy if the games had been worth playing. Unfortunately, almost all the system's titles were unremarkable. Many were hurt by the lackluster graphics of primitive wireframes and vast pools of black. Releases also fell into repetitive genres like sports, arcade, and puzzle. Plus, Nintendo's best-known franchises were largely absent; Zelda, Metroid, Kirby, and many others were nowhere to be seen.
A few Virtual Boy games were highlights, but hardly justified the price of the console. Teleroboxer had a lot of the same "puzzle-fighting" elements as Punch-Out!!, while the pack-in title Mario's Tennis was a good showcase for the 3D effects (and is the first game in the Mario Tennis series). But because of their short lengths and basic gameplay, nearly the entire library felt like tech demos instead of must-have releases.
Nearly everyone agrees Virtual Boy Wario Land is the best game for the system, featuring crisp graphics and a neat gimmick where you can swap between background and foreground layers. It's a brief experience, but a fun one — that's unfortunately stuck on Virtual Boy.
You can try a Virtual Boy today
Clearly, the Virtual Boy hit shelves in an incomplete state; it was rushed out so Nintendo could focus on the upcoming N64. Unlike the Wii, where everyone who tried one wanted their own, people trialing the Virtual Boy at a friend's house or through a Blockbuster rental promo realized how shallow it was. Its competition didn't help the situation, either. In North America, the PlayStation arrived a month after the Virtual Boy (in September 1995) and offered far superior 3D graphics.
Aside from a few minor references in other games, Nintendo was mostly silent about the Virtual Boy until September 2025, when it revealed Virtual Boy games would come to the Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack service. Place your Switch or Switch 2 into either a cardboard slot or a replica of the original Virtual Boy and you'll experience what the Virtual Boy was like. Two images are displayed on your system's screen, with lenses creating the 3D effect. Your Switch controller of choice is compatible, while an August 2026 update enabled changing the color to something other than red.
The Expansion Pack is $50/year (there's no option to pay monthly), with the replica model costing $100 and the cardboard version at $25. There's no option to disable the 3D effect, so you can't play these games on the TV. That's quite a cost to try such a limited library of games, but those curious about Nintendo's biggest flop should still have some fun with it.

Two mirrors, each small enough to fit in the palm of your hand, are set to change how we understand the cosmos.
The launch window for NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is about to open. The telescope’s primary instrument is due to inform practically every area of astrophysics, but also tucked inside the telescope is a specialized coronagraph, an experimental apparatus that will attempt to directly capture starlight reflected off a planet’s surface for the first time. It’s an ambitious project that NASA hopes will pave the way for a space telescope that can one day provide a glimpse of an Earthlike planet orbiting a sunlike star.
That’s a feat far beyond the power of current engineering—hence taking the basic technique for a spin on Roman. “We’ll test them in space for the first time, and we’ll understand what work still is left to go,” says Vanessa Bailey, an astrophysicist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory and instrument scientist for the coronagraph.
At its core, a coronagraph is just a science-minded sunshade that can block out the light of a bright star and reveal a fainter object otherwise lost in the glare. Such instruments have flown in space before—both the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes carry coronagraphs. But Roman’s is light-years more sophisticated than its predecessors, thanks largely to technology called adaptive optics, which deforms a telescope’s mirror to cancel out these light distortions. It still faces a monumental challenge, though: NASA compares the task of Roman’s coronagraph to photographing a firefly perched next to a floodlight—from across the country.
“Any little bit of starlight that gets in the wrong place could just destroy a whole portion of the image,” says Margaret Turnbull, an exoplanet scientist at the SETI Institute, a nonprofit research organization in California, who leads a Roman coronagraph science team.
The technology is standard on advanced ground-based telescopes, including the Very Large Telescope in Chile and Hawaii’s twin Keck Observatory. Here, adaptive optics monitors interference from the thick, shifting layers of Earth’s atmosphere that muddy starlight, allowing observatories to capture sharper images.
Space telescopes haven’t traditionally needed adaptive optics simply by dint of being beyond the atmosphere’s interference, but they’ve never even tried looking for old, cool planets illuminated solely by reflected starlight.
For Roman, the key to its success is those two palm-sized mirrors, each of which is rigged with approximately 2,300 tiny actuators that expand when a small jolt of electricity is applied, infinitesimally reshaping the mirror to reverse interference. It’s the agency’s first time ever flying active deformable mirrors in space.
But the mirrors can’t do much on their own. The system requires supersensitive detectors to amplify the signal from individual photons—a necessity given how few photons the instrument will catch from any given planet. Then there’s the heart of any coronagraph, the star shades—in Roman’s case, a set of exquisitely detailed masks that Bruce Macintosh, an astronomer who leads the University of California Observatories and a Roman coronagraph science team, calls “beautiful, complicated shapes” unlike anything currently in space. “The Hubble ones are just completely brute force, just literally a little piece of metal that gets in the way of the star,” he says.
During the Roman coronagraph’s operations, engineers will gather scads of test data to evaluate how well it works in space and any problems to address before similar technology flies again. Scientists will test the coronagraph by seeing if it can spot a handful of known exoplanets.
“If we go through the whole thing and we don’t see them, then we know something is wrong with the coronagraph, because those planets are there,” Turnbull says. The instrument will also target a few stars surrounded by clouds of dust or debris, gathering observations that could reveal gaps caused by planets that scientists can’t yet detect and give scientists a whole new perspective on how normal our solar system’s level of clutter is.
Everything about Roman’s coronagraph will inform future telescopes seeking ever-smaller planets, including the Habitable Worlds Observatory that NASA hopes to launch, perhaps in the 2040s, that will need a coronagraph up to 100 times more effective; a coronagraph armed with adaptive optics and nearly as sensitive as Roman’s is also due to fly on the planned Lazuli Space Observatory that ex–Google CEO Eric Schmidt’s research institution announced in January. Although seeing alien worlds is the most tantalizing application, coronagraphs could someday show astronomers binary stars or objects hiding near bright quasars.
Roman is a first, vital step toward this future—and the marvels it may show scientists along the way can support that future too, says Julie McEnery, an astrophysicist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland and senior project scientist for Roman.
“Obviously, the best way of demonstrating that something works is to do something interesting scientifically,” she says.

The wildest video game budgets can't hold a candle to GTA 6
The latest Grand Theft Auto is thought to be the most expensive entertainment product ever made.
When you think about the most expensive entertainment productions ever created, video games are likely not the first thing that comes to mind. Hollywood studios routinely spend hundreds of millions of dollars on a single movie that can have a multi-year production schedule. But video games have actually become just as expensive to produce of late, sometimes even surpassing major films. Case in point: Grand Theft Auto VI looks set to become the most expensive game ever created.
While Rockstar Games hasn't publicly disclosed how much it has spent so far, analysts peg the estimated budget at well over $1 billion, with some putting the current figure at around $1.5 billion. That puts GTA VI in rarefied territory, as it outpaces the known budgets of both major theatrical releases and other AAA games. So what has caused video game development to become so expensive and why is GTA VI's budget in particular eclipsing other big names?
How much is Rockstar Games spending on GTA VI?
A billion-dollar video game budget may seem surprising at first glance, but it starts to make sense once you consider that a modern game often has just as many moving pieces as a Hollywood production. You need actors, writers, programmers, animators, designers and composers among others to make an expansive open-world game. And short of a few outliers like the Avatar series, movies are typically in active production for a couple of years. GTA VI has been in active development for closer to a decade. Once a game is nearing completion, it usually goes through a rigorous testing process that requires yet another team.
Apart from a handful of indie breakthroughs, it's common for game budgets to quickly spiral into the double or triple-digit millions these days. Game development can also take several years, with hundreds of employees dedicated to a single project.
Development costs and timelines have been steadily rising, though. In 2023, court documents revealed that Sony Interactive Entertainment had spent $212 million on Horizon Forbidden West and $220 million on The Last of Us: Part II.
More recently, another court filing revealed that Activision's development costs for Call of Duty: Black Ops Cold War topped $700 million over the course of the game's life cycle. Modern live service games require constant development resources for additional maps, game modes, and new content in general. The initial budget for the base game was almost certainly lower than $700 million.
GTA VI is poised to break that threshold, based on even conservative estimates. And that's before you even consider its online mode, which, barring a huge surprise, will not debut alongside the single-player experience in November 2026.
So will it all pay off? Even though it's been over a decade since GTA V's Online mode released, leaked revenue data suggests Rockstar still earns millions of dollars in weekly revenue from microtransactions and GTA+ memberships.
With that much money on the table, it's perhaps not surprising that Rockstar and publisher Take-Two Interactive are willing to spend hundreds of millions of dollars or even billions on GTA VI. The single-player experience is expected to eventually sell hundreds of millions of copies and the online mode could have a loyal fanbase for the next decade and beyond. In 2013, GTA V generated $800 million in sales within a single day of its launch, with its total revenue now standing somewhere around the $10 billion mark.
How game budgets grew so big, and why it's a problem
There's one other billion-dollar game that often comes up in these discussions: Star Citizen. In development since 2011, its developer has raked in more than a billion dollars through crowdfunding and sales of in-game ships. Despite this impressive figure, though, Star Citizen has never reached a stage where it could be considered a finished game, even if it's technically playable. Its more-focused single-player game Squadron 42 was originally targeted for 2014 and is currently scheduled for 2027.
Rockstar Games has not escaped challenges either. It was forced to push back GTA VI's release date multiple times. Originally set to arrive in 2025, it was pushed back to May 2026 and then again to November 2026.
Feature creep in modern games has made development difficult, to the point where even skyrocketing budgets cannot save the day. Rockstar North co-head Aaron Garbut told The New York Times that GTA VI will ship with 600,000 animations, roughly double that of the studio's previous game, Red Dead Redemption 2. GTA V had just 55,000 animations, and was still widely praised for being one of the most detail-heavy games of the 2010s.
Implementing these complex details takes time and manpower, though, and this has had a direct impact on working conditions at major game studios. Around the time of The Last of Us: Part II's release, reports emerged that Naughty Dog employees had worked mandatory overtime and long hours, dubbed crunch. Simultaneously, many criticized the intricate animations for being extraneous given the human cost involved.
Rockstar Games' previous major game, Red Dead Redemption 2, also saw employees working 100-hour work weeks. GTA VI's development has seen controversies of its own, with employee allegations of intense crunch and late-night working hours. Rockstar also allegedly fired several employees involved in unionizing efforts, a claim the company denies.

By Priyanka Deb Barman, Agartala

A hostel warden on Saturday was awarded 20 years of rigorous imprisonment by a local court for sexually assaulting a minor student of a school in North Tripura district.
The court convicted him under Section 376(3) (rape of a minor under 16) and Section 506 (criminal intimidation) of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), and Section 4 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act.
The court also pronounced three years of rigorous imprisonment under Section 506 of the IPC and imposed a fine of ₹10,000 under Section 4 of the POCSO Act, failing which he would undergo an additional six months of simple imprisonment.
Police said that the convict sexually assaulted the 12-year-old girl several times and also used to threaten her since September 2022. The rape survivor fled the hostel on November 12, 2022, and returned home a day after the convict again sexually assaulted her.
She later narrated the entire incident to her guardian on November 21. A case was subsequently registered on the same date, and the convict was arrested.
The police, after investigation, filed a chargesheet against him on March 14, 2023. After the trial, the court found him guilty and sentenced him accordingly.

Gold custody, armed security, and bullion logistics are not core competencies of a Health Department, a government doctors’ association has pointed out, questioning the administrative burden and cost involved in implementing the Thaimaman Thanga Mothiram Thittam in Tamil Nadu.
In a district-level costing of the proposed hub-and-spoke model, the Service Doctors and Post Graduates Association (SDPGA) said the hospital-based arrangement could cost roughly three times the State-wide administrative norm prescribed in the Government Order, factoring in the expenses for dedicated vaults, armed security posts, and armoured transport.
The association recommended that the scheme be delivered through a bank channel — either direct disbursal against a PICME (Pregnancy and Infant Cohort Monitoring and Evaluation)-linked entitlement certificate or bank-run logistics under a Memorandum of Understanding using the infrastructure that banks already operate for their own bullion, currency-chest, and cash-in-transit business.
According to the G.O., the State government had allocated ₹750.83 crore — ₹17,000 each for 4,41,667 deliveries — for procurement of one-gram gold rings. An administrative cost at 0.66% of the total budget — five crore — was sanctioned for the scheme. The administrative cost included monitoring, transport, evaluation, consumables, software, and hardware.
In a letter to the Health Secretary, SDPGA president P. Saminathan said the G.O. envisages a hub-and-spoke framework under which government hospitals take custody of, secure, and physically transport gold rings from hub centres to spoke delivery points for handing them over to beneficiaries. At the district level, the Health Department had to build a parallel bullion-security apparatus that had nothing to do with clinical care, he said.
Among the costs that need to be factored in are dedicated Reinforced Concrete Cement strong room with double locking, fire-rated vaults and dual-custody protocol at the two district hubs, biometric access and CCTV at 27 sites, six-member armed police/home guard posts each hub, additional security for every spoke and armoured cash-in-transit vehicles under annual rate contract with a driver and two escorts.
A district-level costing of this model involving two hubs and 25 spokes, and 25,000 deliveries per year, was worked out by SDPGA. It estimated an annualised capital cost of ₹12.68 lakh for strong-room and vault infrastructure at the two hubs, CCTV and biometric access at the hubs and spokes, steel safes/almirahs, besides a recurring annual cost of ₹71.50 lakh for security personnel, vehicles, insurance and digital systems. With the annual value of gold procurement estimated at ₹42.50 crore (25,000 rings x ₹17,000), the combined annualised cost of ₹84.18 lakh works out to 1.98% of the gold value, nearly three times the 0.66% administrative cost norm prescribed in the G.O.
By contrast, SDPGA said that using the existing infrastructure of scheduled banks could reduce the administrative cost to a negotiated handling fee. Even a service fee in the range of 0.15%-0.30% of the value handled (₹42.50 crore/year) would come roughly to ₹6.4 lakh to ₹12.75 lakh/year, thereby saving substantial funds and allowing health staff to focus on patient care. “The bank model is a foolproof time-tested model. Earlier, the Revenue Department implemented the Thalikku Thangam Scheme through a bank model, and the same can be brought in for the gold ring scheme,” he said.

A decade's worth of Steam files totaling more than 12TB has leaked
The leak contains beta builds and finished games from Valve and third-party developers.
A treasure trove of Steam data has been leaked, which seemingly contains everything that was published on Steam between 2003 and 2013. The leak totals more than 12TB in scale and includes beta builds and completely finished games from Valve's own franchises, including Half-Life, Left 4 Dead and Portal. A GitHub catalog has compiled most of the titles, which also includes games from major franchises like Call of Duty, Fallout and Civilization, as well as those from indie developers.
Someone leaked 12 TB of Valve's internal builds and game assets from 2003 to 2013. This includes early versions of Portal 2, Left 4 Dead, CS:GO, F-Stop and potentially EP3. The community is still researching everything, so the next few days might be insane... There's a Weaponizer... pic.twitter.com/Sg7OqJjL2X
— Gabe Follower (@gabefollower) August 29, 2026
The sheer size of the leak means people are still combing through the details, but so far internet sleuths have uncovered details of the unreleased F-Stop game from Valve that features gameplay revolving around a camera that can manipulate real world objects. Of course there are hints of the long-rumored conclusion of the Half-Life franchise in the leak, but it references Half-Life 2: Episode 3, which was supposed to be the final game in the series but was later canceled. There are plenty of social media posts circulating about this Steam leak, but Valve hasn't commented on this yet so we should take all this info with a grain of salt.
