Arunachal Pradesh – A Living Treasure of Biodiversity
Arunachal Pradesh is one of India’s most biologically diverse states, where forests, rivers, wetlands, mountains and communities are part of one interconnected ecological landscape. Its extraordinary range of habitats supports thousands of plant and animal species, including several rare, endemic and threatened species.
The State’s biodiversity is shaped by its remarkable variation in altitude and climate. From tropical forests in the foothills to temperate forests, alpine meadows and high-altitude ecosystems, Arunachal Pradesh offers a continuous range of habitats within a relatively compact geographical area.
With more than 80 per cent of its geographical area under forest cover, the State plays an important role in maintaining the ecological balance of the Eastern Himalayas. It is also part of the Eastern Himalaya Biodiversity Hotspot, one of the world’s globally recognised regions of exceptional biological richness and conservation importance.
A Landscape of Remarkable Ecological Diversity
The geographical diversity of Arunachal Pradesh is reflected in its forests. Depending on altitude and climatic conditions, the State has tropical evergreen and semi-evergreen forests, moist deciduous forests, subtropical broad-leaved forests, pine forests, temperate forests, coniferous forests, sub-alpine vegetation and alpine meadows.
This remarkable transition from the warm foothills to the high Himalayas creates habitats for species with very different ecological requirements.
The State is home to more than 5,000 species of flowering plants, around 600 species of orchids, about 75 species of rhododendrons, 45 species of bamboo, 17 species of cane and hundreds of medicinal plants. Arunachal Pradesh is particularly renowned for its orchid and rhododendron diversity.
The forests also support a remarkable variety of mammals, including the tiger, leopard, clouded leopard, snow leopard, golden cat, marbled cat, Asiatic elephant, red panda, takin, hoolock gibbon and several other rare and threatened species.
A Paradise for Birds
Arunachal Pradesh is equally celebrated for its avian diversity. Its forests and mountain ecosystems provide habitats for hundreds of bird species, making the State one of the most important birding regions in India.
The Eaglenest Wildlife Sanctuary in West Kameng is one of the best examples of this extraordinary richness. Located within the Eastern Himalaya Biodiversity Hotspot, Eaglenest is home to a wide variety of hornbills, pheasants, kingfishers and other birds. The sanctuary is also known for the discovery of the Bugun liocichla, a bird named after the Bugun community that lives in the region.
Protecting Arunachal’s Wildlife
Arunachal Pradesh’s biodiversity is protected through an extensive network of national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, tiger reserves and other conservation landscapes.
The state is home to important protected areas such as Namdapha National Park and Tiger Reserve, Kamlang Tiger Reserve, Pakke Tiger Reserve, Mouling National Park, Eaglenest Wildlife Sanctuary, Sessa Orchid Sanctuary, Dibang Wildlife Sanctuary and Mehao Wildlife Sanctuary, among others.
These landscapes support an exceptional range of wildlife, from high-altitude species such as the snow leopard and red panda to tropical forest species including the clouded leopard, hoolock gibbon and numerous birds, reptiles and amphibians.
Recent wildlife surveys have continued to expand scientific knowledge of these ecosystems. A 2024 WWF-India survey in Arunachal’s high-altitude rangelands recorded six wild cat species, including photographic evidence of the elusive Pallas’s cat, marking the first such photographic record from the state. The survey used 136 camera traps across 83 locations, covering approximately 2,000 sq km.
The Orchids of Arunachal Pradesh
Among the many botanical treasures of the State, orchids hold a special place.
Arunachal Pradesh has one of the richest orchid assemblages in India, with hundreds of species occurring across its varied habitats. The Sessa Orchid Sanctuary in West Kameng was established in 1979 to conserve and study orchids in their natural habitats. The sanctuary has recorded a remarkable diversity of orchid species, including epiphytic and terrestrial orchids.
The Orchid Research and Development Centre at Tipi further strengthens conservation and research efforts. Its facilities include orchid species houses, natural orchidaria, a herbarium, tissue culture laboratory, museum and hardening units. These initiatives support both ex-situ conservation and the rehabilitation of orchids in their natural habitats.
Glaw Lake: Arunachal Pradesh’s First Ramsar Site
A landmark development came in August 2026, when Glaw Lake, located within the Kamlang Tiger Reserve in Lohit district, was designated as India’s 101st Ramsar Site and became Arunachal Pradesh’s first Ramsar Site.
Situated at an elevation of around 1,168 metres, Glaw Lake covers approximately 82 hectares and forms part of the catchment of the Kamlang, Lang and Lati rivers, which flow into the Lohit River. The lake is recognised by the State Forest Department as an important repository of aquatic biodiversity.
Its Ramsar designation gives international recognition to the ecological importance of the wetland and strengthens the focus on its conservation and sustainable management. The recognition is also significant for Arunachal Pradesh’s wider efforts to protect wetlands and the ecosystems and communities that depend on them.
A State Where New Discoveries Continue
Arunachal Pradesh’s biodiversity story is still being written.
Recent scientific discoveries demonstrate how much remains to be documented within the State’s forests and mountains. The rare plant Vaccinium piliferum, a relative of the wild blueberry that had not been documented for nearly 188 years, was rediscovered in Vijoynagar in Changlang district recently.
New orchid species have also been identified in different parts of the State, while researchers have recorded new cascade frog species from Arunachal Pradesh. In 2026, scientists also identified a new butterfly species, Euthalia zubeengargi, from Basar in Leparada district.
Such discoveries are a reminder that Arunachal Pradesh is not merely a repository of known species. Its forests and mountains continue to offer opportunities for scientific research and the discovery of life forms that may not yet be fully documented.
Biodiversity and Indigenous Knowledge
For generations, the indigenous communities of Arunachal Pradesh have lived closely with their natural surroundings. Forests provide food, medicinal plants, fibres, fuel and other resources, while traditional knowledge has helped communities understand seasonal changes, plants, wildlife and sustainable use of natural resources.
Today, this relationship is increasingly important to conservation.
A recent example comes from West Kameng, where indigenous communities are sustainably harvesting Zanthoxylum, locally known as Khagi, a wild Himalayan spice. The initiative has reportedly involved around 200 families while contributing to the protection of approximately 100 square kilometres of forest and generating livelihood opportunities.
Such efforts demonstrate that conservation and livelihoods can move together when local knowledge and sustainable practices are placed at the centre of biodiversity management.
Conservation: Protecting a Living Legacy
Arunachal Pradesh’s biodiversity is a natural asset of national and global importance. At the same time, ecosystems across the world are facing growing pressures from habitat loss, climate change, pollution, invasive species and unsustainable exploitation of natural resources.
Protecting Arunachal’s biodiversity therefore requires more than creating protected areas. It calls for habitat restoration, scientific research, responsible tourism, community participation, sustainable livelihoods and greater awareness among citizens.
The State’s protected areas, community conservation initiatives, biodiversity documentation programmes and institutions dedicated to research and conservation all contribute to this larger effort.
Looking Ahead
The story of Arunachal Pradesh is inseparable from its forests, rivers, mountains and wildlife. Its biodiversity sustains ecosystems, supports livelihoods, enriches traditional knowledge and strengthens the ecological security of the Eastern Himalayas.
From the orchids of Sessa to the forests of Namdapha, from the bird-rich landscapes of Eaglenest to the wetlands of Glaw Lake, every ecosystem adds another chapter to the State’s natural heritage.
The recent recognition of Glaw Lake as a Ramsar Site is an important milestone, but it is also a reminder of the responsibility that comes with being home to such extraordinary natural wealth.
Arunachal Pradesh is a living treasury of biodiversity and conserving it is not only about protecting nature today, but ensuring that its forests continue to breathe, its rivers continue to flow, and its remarkable species continue to thrive for generations.

Donald Trump and Canada continued a verbal duel on Saturday over the US government’s administrative renaming of Lake Ontario, with the country erecting a giant sign saying “Lake Ontario. Now and Always” – and the American president posting a video of him tearing down an avatar of that sign, erecting a replacement saying Lake America, and dancing to YMCA.
Rhetoric over the naming of Lake Ontario is the public face of an escalating trade dispute between the US and its northern neighbor involving a 50% US tariff on Canadian steel and retaliatory tariffs from Ottawa.
Trump’s order for the US government to refer to Lake Ontario as Lake America by Sunday had at least one prominent impact. Google Maps had changed Lake Ontario’s name to Lake America for US users to reflect the president’s executive renaming order.
Canada’s prime minister Mark Carney has flat-out rejected the renaming, explaining that Lake Ontario derives from an Indigenous Wendat word meaning “the lake is beautiful, the lake is great” that dates back more than 400 years.
With talks to resolve the trade dispute stalled, Trump issued an executive order on Thursday directing US agencies that the lake was now Lake America.
It revived memories of a dispute earlier in his second presidency with Mexico, which saw Trump direct US agencies to refer to the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.
“We’re going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario effective immediately to Lake America,” Trump told reporters before he signed an executive order renaming the body of water among US federal agencies.
In a statement explaining why it was acquiescing to Trump’s desired name for Lake Ontario, Google said its practice is to “reflect name changes in official government sources”. Trump’s order affects the US’s federal Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), “which sets the standard for official US maps”, the tech company said.
The Lake of Ontario’s name change “does not have any impact on Canadian naming conventions or how the rest of the world refers to the lake,” Google said in a statement. And it said “those in Canada will continue to see ‘Lake Ontario’” on Google Maps, “and those outside … the US and Canada will see both names.”
Google had done similarly in Trump’s executive order for the US government to refer to the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America. US Google Map users for now see that body of water named as the “Gulf of America”.
Meanwhile, on Saturday, the US president raised the volume again by resorting to the kind of AI-generated imagery for which he has shown a penchant.
He posted one such video of an army of Canada geese with Trump-like blond hair firing rifles in protection of Lake America. He published another of himself kicking over a Lake Ontario sign and replacing it with Lake America while he danced in his distinctive to a soundtrack of the Village People hit YMCA, which he has implemented into his public appearances for years.
Across the US’s northern border, Ontario premier Doug Ford replied with a two-stories high billboard declaring “Lake Ontario. Now and Always,” near Grimsby, Ontario. Ford said Trump was trying to rename the lake because Ontario and Canada were “standing up for ourselves”, and he argued the name would outlast the president.
“Long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario,” Ford said in a video posted on social media.
In an interview with the Associated Press earlier, Ford said the late Ronald Reagan would be “throwing up” over Trump’s tariff policies.
Meanwhile, Manitoba’s premier, Wab Kinew, said Trump’s Lake America provocation was akin to an aging rock band trying to revive an old hit.
“You know when, like, a rock band is really over the hill and you see them like in a casino playing some song from like 50 years ago, I think that’s the part of Donald Trump’s presidency we’re at now,” Kinew said. “Like he thought he had a real hit, a real golden oldie, with the Gulf of Mexico.
“He’s trying to bring back that, and he’s trying to play the hits for his base. But I think everybody here thinks it’s a little sad, and it’s not his best work.”
Wendat Nation grand chief Pierre Picard called Trump’s move an attempt to erase Indigenous history. “I want to tell him that it is unacceptable for us, as a nation, to have a president who can eradicate our history, our culture and our identity,” Picard said.
Lake Ontario is one of North America’s five Great Lakes, alongside Superior, Michigan, Huron and Erie. At 7,340 sq miles, Lake Ontario is the smallest of those in terms of surface area.

Which Dan Sullivan Will These Dan Sullivans Vote For?
The Alaska Senate race has become complicated by two candidates with the same name.
What in the Dan Sullivan is going on in Alaska? Senator Daniel S. Sullivan is running for reelection. Daniel J. Sullivan is one of his challengers. And former Anchorage Mayor Daniel A. Sullivan recently endorsed the senator, while also declaring himself “the OG Dan Sullivan.”
“It’s kind of hilarious,” Daniel K. Sullivan, a 33-year-old diesel mechanic and off-road fabricator from Wasilla, who is not running for Senate, told me.
“I got a chuckle out of it,” Daniel P. Sullivan, a longtime teacher from Nome, who is also not on the ballot, told me.
Control of the Senate could come down to a ranked-choice ballot that currently includes two Dan Sullivans (the Republican incumbent and the Republican challenger) and one Mary Peltola (a Democrat who was the state’s former at-large congresswoman). Republicans are worried that voters could be confused about which Dan Sullivan to select. Theories abound: Is this some sort of nefarious political plot by the Democrats? Or is it just that there are so many Dan Sullivans in the state that something like this was bound to happen?
To get at the question, I reached out to half a dozen Dan Sullivans who appear to live in Alaska.
I caught a second Daniel P. Sullivan, this one from Chugiak, while he was driving on a remote gravel road the other day. “The Dan Sullivan thing” has become a common topic of conversation, he told me, and his co-workers call him “the senator.” So many Dan Sullivans live in Alaska that his firearms purchases require a deeper background check. “So I don’t get mistaken for another Dan Sullivan,” he explained. (He said that he’s planning to move next summer so likely won’t vote for either of the Dan Sullivans: “Not really fair to vote when the outcome doesn’t affect me.”)
Daniel F. Sullivan, a registered nurse, called me back from Palmer. “I often joke that I’m the real Dan Sullivan, and those are all imposters,” he told me. He said he grew up in New York with another Dan Sullivan in his high school, who was a better student than he was: “My parents would sometimes get honor-roll letters in the mail. I always wondered if his parents got all the bad letters about skipping school.”
In Alaska, he found that his name had even greater benefits. A few years back, he had workers out to fix the electronic system in his hot tub, and the bill they promised to send never arrived. “I often wonder if the other Dan Sullivan got the bill,” he said. Whenever he’s part of a group going out to eat, the reservation is in his name in case it prompts VIP treatment. In this election, he said, he’ll probably vote but hasn’t settled on a candidate. “I won’t vote just because it’s a Dan Sullivan,” he said.
This is not the first time a ballot has featured multiple Dan Sullivans. In 2014, Dan S. Sullivan was running for Senate for the first time when Dan A. Sullivan, the mayor of Anchorage, was running for lieutenant governor (the Senate bid was successful; the lieutenant-governor one was not). Then, in 2016, the former mayor briefly ran for the state’s other Senate seat. Had he won, both of the state’s U.S. senators would have been named Dan Sullivan. Neither of those Dan Sullivans returned my messages.
The Dan Sullivan who has put the name into the news is Dan J. Sullivan, who lives in Petersburg, a small fishing village on an island where Sitka black-tailed deer outnumber the roughly 3,000 people. His father was named Dan Sullivan. So was his grandfather. At the moment, so is one of his sitting senators. Shortly before the June 1 deadline, he filed paperwork declaring his candidacy. “We need a Sullivan who stands up for Alaska,” his website says.
The only Dan Sullivans he personally knows, he told me in an email, are in his own family: three Dan Sullivans and four more Dans who are not Sullivans. “We all have nicknames,” he said. “Mine will never be divulged.” He says that his campaign strategy mostly consists of maintaining his website and posting on social media. “Maybe some travel, but I don’t have much money,” he told me. (He has $8,400 cash on hand in his campaign account. The other Dan Sullivan has nearly $7.3 million.)
His candidacy was immediately challenged by the National Republican Senatorial Committee, which referred to him as “Sham Candidate Sullivan,” and the Alaska Republican Party. Senator Dan Sullivan told reporters in Washington that it was “an insult” and that the challenger was “trying to trick my constituents to rig the election for Peltola.” “This is serious stuff,” he told CNN. “When people are going, Oh there’s two Dan Sullivans, isn’t that funny? No. It’s cheating.”
The senator and his allies pointed to similarities between the challenger’s logo and the senator’s: Both are navy and mustard-yellow and feature at least one gold star. They accused the other Dan Sullivan of being part of a partisan plot engineered by a Democratic consultant. The Sullivan facing those questions told me the consultant had helped set up his campaign site and provided “tips on communications and basic campaign functions,” but said “she is not currently working for me.” They questioned his party affiliation. (He was previously a member of the Alaska Independence Party, but when that disbanded late last year, he switched his affiliation to the Republican Party, which he said was in line with his conservative views.) The director of the Alaska Division of Elections, which is overseen by the state’s Republican lieutenant governor, determined in June that the newcomer’s declaration as a candidate was invalid because it had been “filed with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot’s fairness or neutrality.” The Sullivan in question appealed to the Alaska Superior Court.
“I am running because I am tired of sitting back and watching our current Senator routinely fail to represent the interests of ordinary Alaskans like me,” he wrote in his defense. “The fact that Senator Sullivan shares my first and last names adds insult to injury, motivating me to raise my hand as an alternative choice for Alaskans.”
Ultimately, the court determined that Dan Sullivan met all the requirements for making the ballot: It was his actual name; he did live in Alaska; he was over the age of 30. The whole experience, he told me, has been “daunting” because he feels unfairly singled out. “Typical of Sullivan to cry about it, make a nickname, and blame others,” he said, when asked about being called a “sham” candidate. Of the dozens of candidates running statewide in Alaska, he said, “only I have been accused of bad intentions (including one guy who is in jail). Seems unfair to me.”
Both Dan Sullivans were on the ballot in the nonpartisan primary earlier this month, after which the top four candidates advanced to the general election. Peltola, the Democratic candidate, got the most votes, leading the incumbent Sullivan by seven percentage points. Daniel J. Sullivan came in a distant third with 2.5 percent of the vote, qualifying him for the general election—and showing that he could be a spoiler in November.
His advancement angered Republicans, including the president. “The Crooked, Radical Left Dumocrats have put up another man named ‘Dan Sullivan,’ and they did this to take Votes away from our Great Senator of the same name,” Donald Trump wrote on social media. Senator Dan Sullivan’s early campaign ads have not mentioned the other Dan Sullivan, and when he talks in his speeches about an opponent, he references only Peltola.
But this is not the first time an election has featured similarly named candidates and accusations of political shenanigans. When John F. Kennedy ran for Congress in 1946 against a Boston city council member named Joe Russo, his allies helped recruit a janitor named Joe Russo to also run. In 2004, Representative José E. Serrano of New York was primaried by an unemployed former dockworker, Jose E. Serrano, who dropped out after being questioned about his legislative platform and not knowing what that was. In 2024, the governor’s race in Washington State featured Attorney General Bob Ferguson running against Robert Arthur Ferguson and Robert Benjamin Ferguson (the latter two Fergusons withdrew from the primary before ballots were printed).
The name Dan Sullivan is common enough. There was the offensive lineman for the Baltimore Colts in the 1960s. There was the race-car driver Danny Sullivan, who won the 1985 Indianapolis 500. There’s a theater and film director named Daniel J. Sullivan. Daniel was the ninth-most-common first name and Sullivan was the 107th-most-common last name in the United States in 2020, according to census records. There are nearly 5,300 Dan Sullivans in the country, according to the personal search aggregator Spokeo, and more than two dozen in Alaska.
In Anchorage, there’s the Sullivan Arena (named for the city’s longtime mayor, George M. Sullivan, the father of the Dan Sullivan who was the most recent mayor of Anchorage) and Sullivan’s Steakhouse (named after John Sullivan, a 19th-century boxer). “Sullivan just seems to be the big thing,” Dan Sullivan the Wasilla mechanic told me. “But I don’t know any benefits from it that I’m aware of. I don’t get any discount at the steakhouse or anything.”
The Dan Sullivan from Nome told me he would occasionally get random calls from people around the state confronting him about his campaign promises, especially when the Anchorage mayor and the U.S. senator were both Dan Sullivans. “I’d show my credit card, and they’d look at me and do a double take,” he said. “I got to meet all the Dan Sullivans. All the famous ones. I’m probably the least interesting out of all of them.” (He has since retired and has been traveling, and says he has not yet done his homework on which candidate he’ll support in the election).
For the Dan Sullivans, it can be a little disorienting when the political ads are blanketing the airwaves. “It’ll say, Dan Sullivan’s ruining the Alaska fisheries! Or Dan Sullivan voted to raise your health insurance! I’m like, No, I didn’t! It wasn’t me,” said Dan Sullivan the mechanic. “Or you’ll get an ad on the radio and it’s like, Dan Sullivan’s great for Alaska! Yeah, he is.” He’s not much into politics, so he says he’s unlikely to join the other Dan Sullivans in campaigning. He’s more conservative, so he plans to vote for the incumbent senator.
As if things couldn’t get more confusing, there’s also a Dan Sullivan who has run for Congress in Massachusetts. There are so many Dan Sullivans that, at times, my attempts to reach the ones in Alaska went awry. I messaged a Dan Sullivan I thought for sure was from Palmer, Alaska, but instead located one in Cleveland, Ohio. He politely responded that his origins are in Brooklyn and Massachusetts. “I am Daniel M. Sullivan. My dad was Daniel P. Sullivan,” he said. Although he won’t be voting in Alaska, the intrigue has caught his eye: “I have been following this story with interest.”
The Alaska race will be determined in November. At least in this election cycle, there’s room for only one Dan Sullivan in the Senate (and possibly none). But some other Dan Sullivans are getting ideas about future options.
“Maybe one of us needs to run for president,” Dan Sullivan the mechanic told me. Or perhaps two? “You can pick anybody you want. As long as it’s Dan Sullivan.”

The Great American Conflict, a 75-minute documentary produced by a Texas-based organization dedicated to converting Iran to Christianity, declares its goal right at the beginning: “to reveal the true Islam to all people, especially in the West,” Iran Alive Ministries’s founder Hormoz Shariat says. “This film is also meant to be a warning to America. There is a serious threat of Islam in our nation.”
Islamophobia is getting worse in Texas. One strange movie is helping drive it.
A documentary warns about a coming cultural conflict with Muslims in the US. It’s had surprising political influence.
Released at the start of summer and having premiered at a gathering of the Dallas County Republican Party, it’s an obscure film — you’ve probably never heard of it — but it has so far had a surprising political influence. It’s been shown at gatherings of local Republicans and conservative activists in Texas, where Islamophobic rhetoric and policy proposals have played a key role in activating the Republican base, candidates, and party leaders over the course of this year’s elections. The documentary is both a symptom and a cause of a larger trend unfolding in American politics in 2026 that is picking up steam now: the rise of a new iteration of blatant Islamophobia paired with Christian nationalist sentiment on the American right.
Iran Alive Ministries did not respond to requests for comment.
It’s no surprise who some of the backers and voices of this documentary are: Some members of this collection of right-wing, conservative, and evangelical activists are a throwback to early-2000s and 2010s Islamophobia, when some of the same figures spoke out against “radical Islamism” and “radical Islamic terror.” One of them, for instance, is the activist Brigitte Gabriel, the controversial founder of ACT for America, an early-2000s anti-Islamic extremism group. As the film makes clear, this latest version of Islamophobia in America has its roots in this post-9/11 era and borrows heavily from it, while making some modern-day tweaks.
What’s different now is how mainstream this stance is becoming in politics and how it appears to be getting only more mainstream.
“Islamophobia has passed the dinner table test. You can say things about Muslims with basic impunity today,” Nathan Lean, a researcher, assistant teaching professor at North Carolina State University and author of the book The Islamophobia Industry, told me. “And it’s institutionalized in the way that prejudice that targets other marginalized communities is not.” He pointed to the Sharia-Free America Caucus in Congress, which is composed of 68 elected members of Congress representing 25 states. He also pointed to efforts in Texas to make eliminating “sharia” law an official stance of the Texas GOP, and then the subsequent vote to recommend Gov. Greg Abbott “ban” it on the Texas 2026 primary ballot.
Now, politicians, content creators, and politically connected advocacy groups are using films like The Great American Conflict, selectively edited clips spread on social media, and investigative-style pseudo-documentaries to spread this sentiment further and wider, power more wins of right-wing candidates, and take aim in particular at Muslim candidates and politicians.
This is all playing out as antisemitism and Islamophobia are peaking during the 2026 midterm cycle, accelerated by demographic change across America, increased Muslim visibility and engagement in politics, including elections of Zohran Mamdani in New York City and the Senate campaign of Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, and more Republican politicians feeling comfortable using Islam as a scapegoat and cudgel, particularly in Texas. It all paints a worrying picture of what’s to come.
What The Great American Conflict argues is coming
As a cinematic project, The Great American Conflict isn’t much of an accomplishment; it can broadly be described as a collection of testimonials from evangelical Christians and former Muslims who’ve converted to Christianity who each make a case against Islam. Though poorly organized, it starts with some rough accounting of the rise of Islam in world history, lays out the case through interviews that Islam is an ideology and not a religion, then zooms in on specific Texan communities and examples of how Muslim politicians and activists are using democratic processes to achieve “domination.”
There are broadly three core themes that these speakers come back to:
- Islam is inherently violent and imperialistic: The documentary’s interview subjects argue that true believers seek to expand the faith and establish a cross-national Islamic state. They rely on some sketchy history of the prophet Muhammed and the contemporary history of Lebanon and Iran as examples of this “violence.”
- Islam is incompatible with the American Constitution and Western liberalism: Speakers also argue that, as opposed to other religions, Islam does not tolerate diversity of thought and seeks to enforce its rules and guidelines on nonbelievers. They claim that Islam rejects the separation between church and state, and that mosques can function as political or military centers.
- There is an ongoing effort by Muslims to infiltrate American politics and replace “Judeo-Christian” America: The rise of Muslim American politicians in Congress, in New York City, and at the state and local government level are all part of an effort to whittle away religious liberty and replace American values with “Islamic” values. Liberal and progressive allies are enabling this takeover. And they interpret public calls to prayer, halal food, school prayer rooms, Ramadan accommodations, mosque construction, and Muslim residential developments as evidence that American institutions are yielding to Islamic demands.
Interspersed throughout these testimonials are fearmongering compilations of social media clips of Muslim prayers and veiled women, and short selections of purportedly Muslim speakers making inflammatory comments about 9/11, about Jews and Christians, and about Islamic domination in the West, and violent clips of terrorist actions abroad.
And though the film’s main backer, Hormoz Shariat, says at the beginning of the film that his goal is not to inspire fear or hate, that’s precisely what the speakers seem to do for an hour.
For example, the Christian pastor Shahram Hadian, the founder of Truth in Love Ministry in Tennessee, repeatedly argues that America is at a turning point. “Western societies are right now at a critical decision point. Either they’re going to maintain, preserve, [and] fight for their Judeo-Christian values, or they’re succumbing,” he says.
And he takes a natalist turn, arguing that Muslims in the US are happy to continue to raise families as Western birth rates drop. “We continue to see the demise of Christianity, of our Judeo-Christian values, family values, family ethics, marriage — one man, one woman,” he says. “They’re just waiting us out. They’ll just wait us out. They’ll aid us in our own demise and destruction.”
To drill down on this, various speakers point to demographic change in Michigan and Texas as early signs of what they see as the capitulation of the United Kingdom and continental Europe to Islam. They point to self-segregating Muslim communities in Europe being mirrored in the US, particularly focusing on a housing development project in East Plano, Texas, centered around a mosque and Islamic center, that has been a focal point for Republican politicians.
Other speakers argue against accepting Islam as a religion at all, instead casting it as a political ideology that is seeking to take over American institutions. Some, like Gabriel, allege a coordinated strategy to “infiltrate” and “dominate the West and establish an Islamic government,” tracing this back to the Muslim Brotherhood, and a supposed decades-long plan to infiltrate political parties, schools, media, and churches to use democratic institutions to establish Islamic law. She points to Mamdani as an example of this, and ropes in Reps. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota and Rashida Tlaib of Michigan as being loyal to a foreign Islamic identity rather than to the United States.
And they contrast this all with an idealized “Judeo-Christian” America defined by constitutional government, traditional marriage, Christianity, and cultural assimilation. The final call to arms is to preserve and promote this Christian vision of America, on top of defending the Constitution, religious liberty, and “American” culture against what is a coming ideological and demographic conflict.
The danger of rising Islamophobia
Iran Alive Ministries itself doesn’t seem primarily dedicated to anti-Muslim American advocacy and activism. Most of its YouTube and internet presence is focused on digital Christian evangelism, particularly in Iran. It’s not entirely hard to see how a group focused on conversions would drift into Islamophobic preaching, but it does seem like a peculiar move, Lean told me.
“There is a group of people who form a faction of this sort of anti-Muslim movement in the United States who are, by their own description, evangelical Christians,” Lean said. “And it’s no surprise that a group like Iran Alive Ministries, that is formed on the basis of, as they say, transforming Iran into a Christian nation, one soul at a time, would go there.”
Emphasizing that Christian proselytism and evangelism are not inherently Islamophobic, Lean told me that there has been a more overt merging of religious convictions with Republican politics in recent years.
“The…driving mission of the group leads to a marriage of, we want a Christian world on the one hand, versus there are active agents in the world that are potentially preventing that. And who represents that biggest threat to that right now? Well, in the eyes of these people, Muslims do,” Lean said.
Lean told me that he expects to see this momentum build as midterms approach. At the local level, it’s most visible in Texas, where the New York Times recently reported on the stunning rise in Islamophobia and fearmongering across the state, and in Michigan, where cities like Dearborn and Hamtramck have seen white nationalist and anti-Islam demonstrations.
Lean said many of these lines of Islamophobic thinking sound like familiar tropes, smears, and lies of the last couple of waves of fearmongering around Muslims. Still, as opposed to the post-9/11 era, he noted a worrying difference: the scale of Islamophobia, given its increasing presence on both social and traditional media.
Much of the growth of these sentiments is happening online, too. Since Mamdani’s election as New York City mayor, and especially since El-Sayed’s victory in the Democratic Senate primary in Michigan, these kinds of views have surged online and in conservative media, while conservative activists and influencers have been pushing similar narratives of infiltration and under-the-radar Muslim “encroachment.”
A recent survey of internet discourse and activity by the research group Magnitude Media found something similar, centered on Dearborn: “Since the beginning of the month, there have been 690 posts mentioning Dearborn, generating 5.1 million engagements. Right-leaning accounts drove 88% of that engagement, compared to just 7% from left-leaning accounts,” the authors write. “The broader anti-Muslim conversation online has been substantial for months. Over the past six months, 68% of posts that either mentioned Islamophobia or contained common Islamophobic language came from right-leaning accounts. Dearborn appears less like the cause of a new Islamophobia conversation than the right’s newest focal point.”
So the documentary certainly isn’t the only cause for concern — but the fact that Texas Republicans have used it in official events, on top of strategists saying they are pivoting to “sharia” and fearmongering, suggests just how politically useful the party thinks these messages can be.
Which all suggests more ugliness to come. And as Lean told me, talking about a coming conflict and a threat to survival indicates an existential threat that should be fought by any means.
“Where does the logic of all of this take us? What’s the solution?” he said. “You can’t help but wonder when they’re issuing statements about fertility rates and these overtures are being kind of taken over, that this could very easily go to a dark place.”
Update, August 28, 11:45 am ET: This piece was updated to reflect Nathan Lean’s full job title.

Pegula foils Ruse to reach US Open second round
NEW YORK, Aug 30 : American Jessica Pegula cruised past Romania's Elena-Gabriela Ruse 6-3 6-2 to reach the U.S. Open second round on Sunday, taming early nerves as she opened the action on Arthur Ashe Stadium in her latest bid for a maiden major title.
The world number three squandered eight break-point chances early in the first set before hitting her stride with 26 winners to just 14 from her opponent, closing it out with an unreturnable forehand.
She will have two days' rest under the 15-day schedule the tournament rolled out last year, and will next play the winner of a match later on Sunday on Ashe between American wildcards Venus Williams and Sofia Kenin.
"I was so nervous today," she said. "(Now) I get to sit around the site and watch everyone else freak out."
Those nerves were apparent in a tricky opening set, where Ruse saved eight break points in a marathon third game but sent a shot wide to hand a break to Pegula in the fifth.
The Romanian held her arms aloft after surviving an entertaining cat-and-mouse exchange at the net to save break point in the seventh with a perfect backhand slice.
But Pegula took control of the match from there, cruising through her next service game before breaking Ruse with a forehand winner to close out the set.
Pegula sprinted through the next set, where she won all of her first-serve points and broke in the sixth and eighth games.

Toronto cinema says it was forced to cancel screenings over decades-old, unofficial 'zone' system
'Tony' screenings cancelled after distributor A24 withdrew the Carlton's access
A downtown Toronto cinema says it was forced to cancel screenings of a new movie after the film’s distributor unexpectedly withdrew access — citing a decades-old practice in Canada that limits which theatres can show movies first.
The Carlton had already sold tickets for its first week of screenings of 'Tony,' a new movie by Canadian director Matt Johnson, when it got word that distributor A24 would no longer be providing the film.
"They ended up telling us that they were pulling the film because of a clearance issue," said Stefan Kern, director of operations for Imagine Cinemas, which owns the Carlton.
Clearance, Kern explained, "typically revolves around the fact that another theatre is playing it in a close proximity geographically and so [the distributor is] going to hold that film and not provide it to us."
Independent theatres have long complained about the unofficial 'zone system' in Canada, in which distributors give only one theatre in a given area access to a new release.
This is far from the first time this has happened, Kern added.
"This was the third film that we've had recently that was pulled from us," he said.
A decades old system that 'privileges Cineplex'
According to Sonya Yokota William, director of the Network of Independent Canadian Exhibitors, the zone system has its roots in the pre-digital era, when studios would produce limited film prints of a movie, leaving theatres to jockey for who would get access first.
Now, she said, "this practice has lingered, and you'll find that it predominantly privileges Cineplex."
In Canada, Cineplex takes in about 75 per cent of the country’s box office revenue, she said. Of the country’s approximately 2,700 movie screens, more than half belong to the cinema giant.
Yokota William says that Cineplex’s market concentration has "twisted the incentives" for distributors deciding which theatres to prioritize for new releases.
"In some ways it's like it only makes good business sense for you to keep your number one customer happy," she said.
In 2024, her organization surveyed the independent cinemas that make up their membership, finding that more than half said they had to wait for a nearby Cineplex to have a complete run of a new release before they were given permission to play it.
As Vancouver’s Rio Theatre described it in a 2020 petition calling out the zone system, "this kind of underhanded business practice has made it very difficult for independently owned theatres to survive."
Cineplex says that film distributors hold the power
Cineplex, meanwhile, wouldn’t comment on the zone system in Canada or on the cancellation of the Carlton's 'Tony' screenings, writing to the CBC that "it is up to film distributors to decide where they play their films."
At present, the movie is playing at two Cineplex locations near the Carlton.
A24 did not respond to questions from the CBC about why it initially promised the Carlton access to ‘Tony’ — or what triggered its decision to pull the film.
Kern, too, did not name Cineplex in his interview or in a release put out by Imagine Cinemas about the 'Tony' cancellations.
Instead, the release encourages patrons to direct their comments to A24, film director Matt Johnson or to the Competition Bureau to "lodge a complaint about unfair business practices being used in theatrical distribution in Canada."
The Competition Bureau would not confirm whether it's reviewing any complaints related to the zone system, and said it has never issued any guidance in relation to theatrical distribution in Canada.
Though she supports looping in the Competition Bureau, Yokota William also hopes that raising awareness about the existence of the practice will help bring it to an end.
"I would love for filmmakers, producers, funders and the government to start making noise about this, even if they can't or don't make legislation," she said.

I filed a request with McDonald’s earlier this month to access all of the personal data the fast food company collected about me, and I received a stunning 515-page report a few days later that detailed my app interactions in granular detail and predicted I would never stop eating there.
Under the California Consumer Privacy Act, I have the legal right to request access to information from large companies that collect personal data. So I was curious what others might have on me, and I spent the next week filing more than 100 requests.
The CCPA went into effect in 2020, and three of its key provisions are the right to opt out of the selling of personal information, the right to delete that info, and the right to request a copy for yourself.
I focused solely on the latter—access requests—to better understand what data is being collected. Most companies must list two ways for you to file. These are often via a web form, phone number, or email address, as designated in their privacy policy. After you submit a request, companies can take 45 days to complete it.
My experience placing these data access requests was incredibly time-consuming, from finding the right filing methods to verifying my identity multiple times. Most exasperating during this process were the companies that either responded to my access requests with messages concerning the deletion of information, which I explicitly said not to do, or refused to process the request through a method listed in their privacy policy.
Consumer advocates I spoke with were upset with how these requests were handled. “That's crazy,” said Ben Winters, director of AI and privacy at the Consumer Federation of America. “That's not an acceptable status quo.” Winters sees these examples as exhibiting the weaknesses of policy frameworks that rely on companies to act responsibly and in good faith.
In accordance with WIRED’s policies, I am disclosing that I used generative AI to draft bureaucratic emails and update my tracking spreadsheet as part of this report. I wrote the body of this article mainly by hand in my scratch notebook.
One of the first errors came from Crunchbase, known for its database about tech startups. I emailed my access request to its privacy address on August 17. My message laid out the rights I wanted to exercise and included a direct request not to erase anything: “I am not requesting deletion at this time. Please do not treat this as a deletion request.” I received a reply two days later from a Crunchbase support representative.
“Thanks so much for your patience. Your account has been permanently deleted from Crunchbase. Please let me know if you need anything else!” the message read in full.
I followed up via email almost immediately, reiterating that I wanted data access, not data deletion. “Your Crunchbase user account was deleted. Other data located on Crunchbase was not deleted,” read the follow-up support response explaining what happened. If I wanted to have a Crunchbase account, I would have to reregister.
When I reached out to Crunchbase for comment, a spokesperson blamed the mistake on a “processing error” and said that the company would proceed with my original access request as filed. The spokesperson also claimed the misclassified response came from “a person on our customer success team” and not a generative AI tool.
My interactions with BeenVerified, a searchable database that gathers public records, also encapsulate my friction-filled experience placing these access requests.
I emailed BeenVerified’s dedicated CCPA compliance address on the morning of August 19. It laid out that I was a California resident placing an access request, not a deletion request. You’ll never guess what happened next.
Two days later, I received a message from a BeenVerified support representative about removing information. “It appears your person report has already been removed from our Person Search results,” read its initial response. “In addition, we have removed the requested phone number and email address from our search results. This change should be reflected within 24 hours.” Not at all what I asked it to do.
When I sent my next email explaining that I had submitted an access request, not a deletion request, the support representative followed up 15 minutes later, denying my claim and saying the company couldn’t verify my identity. That was perplexing, since it located some of my details earlier in the message thread and didn’t even attempt to explain what I might need to share for verification.
At my wit's end, I sent another email explaining how confused I was feeling by these responses. “Please be assured that we're able to process your opt-out request and have removed your information from our website,” read the support representative's response. If I wasn’t already bald, I would have pulled out the rest of my hair at that moment.
I found solace in chatting with an academic researcher who had previously helped place access requests with over 500 data brokers under the same California law and also encountered multiple misclassifications. “Sometimes I would make an access request, and the automatic answer was ‘We will opt you out’ or ‘We will delete your data,’” says Elina van Kempen, a PhD graduate from UC Irvine and coauthor of Consumer Beware! Exploring Data Brokers' CCPA Compliance. While some data brokers followed up with corrections, other times the researcher was left without any resolution.
When I reached out to BeenVerified for comment, Greg Hammond, senior counsel and senior director of compliance at its parent company, claimed via email that support agents receive annual privacy training, including how to process CCPA requests. “Unfortunately, despite the training, the agent who handled this matter was mistaken and misunderstood the request type,” he wrote. Hammond says the company now plans to provide refresher training on correct processing and to audit recent work.
My attempts to place an access request with Cash App, a money-sending service offered by Block, were equally frustrating, even without a deletion mistake. The company’s privacy policy, in bold, states that California residents can place access requests through Cash App’s website or by a toll-free phone call. I opted to test out the phone number.
The first time I called and explained that I was a California resident who wanted to place an access request, it was as if I had started speaking in a language from outer space. I was placed on hold multiple times before being told to check the privacy policy and call the number listed there, which I had just done to get to this point. My attempt to process an access request over the phone was being effectively denied.
“OK, sure, I'll call this number right back,” I said before I hung up, a bit of anger bubbling up in my voice despite my best efforts to remain professional. My interactions with the next customer support agent were similarly burdensome. After being put on hold, I was asked to call back later, so the support team would have more time to review their resources and understand how to handle my call.
“Customers can access or delete their personal information directly through Cash App, which allows us to more quickly verify identity before providing access to financial account information or deleting an account,” a Cash App spokesperson wrote over email when I reached out for comment. “Our phone support teams are trained to help customers understand how to submit these requests, and we also provide customers with instructions they can access through our online Help Center."
The spokesperson did not respond to follow-up questions asking why the phone number was explicitly listed in Cash App’s privacy policy as a way for consumers to exercise their data rights.
Experts I spoke with questioned whether companies are putting in enough effort to be legally compliant. “It shows how potentially little resources the companies are putting toward compliance and making sure that people can have access to their data,” says Mayu Tobin-Miyaji, a law fellow at the Electronic Privacy Information Center.
Both Winters and Tobin-Miyaji mentioned a beefed-up approach to “data minimization” as a potential better path forward for consumers. This would essentially mean companies can collect only the data they need to process standard business operations. For example, saving your credit card information in the app for future purchases might be allowed, but collecting personal demographic information to sell to brokers might be blocked.
Data minimization is a more holistic approach that shifts the burden away from consumers, who are currently forced to navigate a bureaucratic obstacle course just to see what companies know about them. Instead, by limiting what companies can collect about you in the first place, consumers can have more peace of mind without going through the headache-inducing process I endured.

How playing in a park helped these primary school students thrive
It is not every day that class takes place in the great outdoors, but one initiative is pushing the limits of what learning can look like.
The Greater Sydney Parklands's Bush School program takes young children in urban areas out with education rangers to help foster a love for the natural world.
Researchers, led by PhD candidate Alexandra Harper, followed a year 1 class from Middle Harbour Public School on Sydney's lower north shore in 2024.
The team observed the students as they spent two hours a week playing in the heart of Centennial Parklands.
Now, evidence from a study has suggested nature play can help boost education, wellbeing and development.
At Bush School, 25 children participated in immersive activities to learn about native animals and how to preserve the natural environment.
"It's learning in, through, and about the environment in a natural setting," Tonia Gray from Western Sydney University's School of Education said.
"For a lot of children, they're really switched on to that type of learning instead of computer screens."
Over 10 weeks, the students explored their surroundings, crafting stick cubbies, painting with ochre, and writing poems dedicated to the trees.
A recent research paper reflecting on the time found students experienced more joy, autonomy and a deeper connection to nature; helping them flourish.
Some even showed "significant improvement" in maths after taking part.
"It doesn't take away from time-compressed teaching, it actually adds to the learning environment ... it's like a catalyst for growth," Professor Gray said.
"Learning differently is just as important as learning through the mainstream ways."
From reserved, to 'at home' in nature
Reflecting back on Bush School, the cohort fondly remembered climbing trees, bush walking, and encountering items like seed pods.
"We saw lots of native wildlife including a water spider and a tawny frogmouth," participant Nate said, now in year 3.
"I got way more confident in things like balancing ... and right now I'm feeling more confident rock parkouring."
The students still bring up what they learnt in their outdoor adventures, even recreating games in the playground to share with their peers.
Middle Harbour Public School assistant principal Jenni Osborn said the children came to see the outdoors as an "extension of their own classroom".
"We were able to watch the kids go from being really reserved at first to ... becoming really at home in the environment," she said.
Teachers reported at the time that the Bush School students were more "engaged" in their explicit lessons, Ms Osborn said.
They also noted that despite being taken out of class, there was "no negative impact" on their curriculum learning, despite initial concerns from some parents.
Ms Osborn said students applied what they learnt to real-world scenarios.
The students would journal after each session, recount stories in literacy classes, and discuss challenges like how they got a DIY seesaw to balance in their maths lessons.
"Indigenous cultures have done this for centuries, children learn better on the land than in a box,"
"We need teachers to embrace it but we need teacher training institutions to upskill those educators to feel confident and capable to conduct outdoor lessons."
'Enjoying school a lot more'
The impacts have also been noticed at home.
School parent Andrew said the experience was "invaluable" to his son, Archie, and that he observed a "stark difference" in his behaviour afterwards.
"We could see he really started to expand not just his knowledge of the environment, but also his writing, his drawing, because he was interested in what was going on," Andrew said.
"He was more involved, he was really enjoying school a lot more.
"A lot of people don't have an understanding of the Australian bush, and it is unique, and I think it's really important we all start to understand the environment around us."
Rachel said Bush School gave her daughter Evie more confidence and helped her appreciate nature more.
"After each session they would bring it back to the classroom and talked to the other students about what they learnt and what they explored," she said.
Sej told the ABC that while jumping in mud may not be an activity "you'd associate with school", her son Hamish had "come into his own" in the couple of years since.
"He's got a real mind for science, nature, and history. So I have seen that grow and develop," she said.
"Every school in New South Wales should have this as part and parcel of the experience for every child."

Australia usually hosts the world's biggest cuttlefish mating event - not this year
- Published
Every winter, a sliver of the South Australian coast hosts the world's largest mating event for giant cuttlefish.
Some years, hundreds of thousands of the unique marine species endemic to Australia gather along the Cuttlefish Coast for the annual mating season, bringing their colourful, shape-shifting figures to the shallow waters and attracting thousands of keen divers.
But this year, the turnout was the lowest on record, sparking concerns of a "catastrophic decline" of the species.
Official figures released this month estimate just 1,811 cuttlefish turned up to mate this year, down from 63,000 last year - a 97% drop.
The state government says a toxic algal bloom that has ravaged the state's coastline for more than 18 months may be to blame for the sharp decline.
The low figures have also prompted calls for the species to be listed as endangered.
Adult cuttlefish typically die after breeding so each mating season is crucial for the species' future, but in recent months, just 440 eggs have been counted, instead of the millions that are usually laid.
Manny Katz, 28, was one of four divers who spent hours along the coast last month to observe the annual breeding event, having been tasked by South Australia's Department of Environment and Water (DEW).
"Because there have been so few cuttlefish, DEW thought it would be worth going out and trying to do an assessment of how many eggs there currently are around the coastline to understand what the population is going to be next year."
Over two days in July, his team did eight one-hour dives, exploring the undersides of rocky reefs to count the eggs.
"Along the eight kilometres (five miles) of coastline, there would normally be millions of eggs," he said, as each female can lay dozens of egg and tens of thousands usually turn up to breed.
"[We] pretty much looked under every single rock that we could have and we only found about 440 eggs."
Crucially, adult cuttlefish only live about 12 to 18 months, Katz said, "so the success of one breeding season is going to determine the population next year".
"Under our current circumstances, with there being so few eggs along the coastline, we don't know if the population is ever going to be able to recover."
Marine ecosystems in 'real big trouble'
While it's too early to tell what this means for the species' future, Katz said: "we will know that answer probably in the next year or two, whether or not this year has been a catastrophic decline."
His team also tracked adult cuttlefish numbers during the dive survey, and said the dozen or so they saw - when there should have been tens of thousands - appeared to be behaving differently.
"This year, they were all really skittish... hiding under rocks. Because there's so few cuttlefish hanging out at the moment, they don't have strength in numbers."
Katz said he wasn't shocked by the low numbers this winter given the devastating impact of the toxic algal bloom in South Australia since it was first detected in March last year.
The algal bloom - a rapid increase in the population of algae in water systems – is naturally occurring but is caused by ocean warming, marine heatwaves, and nutrient pollution - all exacerbated by climate change.
"Our marine habitats have been getting wiped out for the past year and a half now... this is an indicator that our marine ecosystems are in real big trouble - the canary in the coal mine, so to speak."
Last year's cuttlefish mating season was not impacted as the effects of the algal bloom had not yet reached the Cuttlefish Coast, Katz said, but since late last year, small concentrations of the toxic algae have been detected in the area.
This was particularly worrying as cuttlefish, along with other cephalopods like octopus and squid, are particularly vulnerable to the toxic algae.
Stefan Andrews, co-founder of the Great Southern Reef Foundation, is seeking to have the giant Australian cuttlefish listed as a threatened species given its "catastrophic decline" due to the algal bloom and the impact on the next generation.
"The harmful algal blooma is a leading plausible explanation and appears likely to have contributed, but the vailable evidence does not yet allow us to say definitively that it caused the entire decline," he said.
He said with so few adults and so little breeding activity observed, the number of young entering the population is likely to be very low.
"That will make the next breeding season especially challenging."
A spokesperson for South Australia's Department of Primary Industries and Regions said cuttlefish populations "naturally fluctuate" depending on environmental conditions.
Previous surveys have reported record lows of 13,500 in 2013 to highs of 247,000 in 2020.
"The cuttlefish population estimate rebounded to more than 100,000 just two years following the low numbers in 2013," the spokesperson said.
"While it appears likely the algal bloom has impacted cuttlefish numbers, researchers are working to determine whether this contributed to the reduced population or was just one of the potential impacts."
Prof Mike Steer, executive director of the South Australian Research and Development Institute which helped carry out the underwater surveys, said the unprecedented low estimate this year was "disheartening".
But he remained hopeful as "we know from the past that this population has the capacity to recover when conditions are favourable".
He said there were "positive signs" as adult cuttlefish were continuing to lay eggs and the population may recover "over coming years".

20 December 2024 was a crucial moment for Luxembourg in supporting WHO and strengthening global public health, to make progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals in 2025–2028. A Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) with the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs was signed amounting to €46.5 million – the largest-ever agreement WHO has had with Luxembourg. Furthermore, the first-ever multiyear agreement with the Ministry of Health and Social Safety €1 million was launched, as the country’s first voluntary contribution to WHO.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General greets with Luxembourg's Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety and Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. © MAE Luxembourg
“From now till 2028, this contribution will help finance priority areas in Luxembourg’s collaboration with WHO” said Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety during the bilateral meeting, “notably for sanitary crisis preparedness and response and the fight against health inequalities, with a special focus on gender.”
The amount of €46.5 million contains fully flexible and thematic funding, and allocations for the Universal Health Coverage Partnership, tropical disease research and polio eradication. The fully flexible funding enables WHO to allocate the money to the areas of highest need.
“By signing two new partnership agreements, we have reaffirmed Luxembourg's continued support for the WHO and its mission,” said Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. “This reflects our strong commitment to promoting global health and multilateralism. We launch these agreements with WHO because we believe the best way to avoid is to prevent.”
To support the achievement of WHO’s priorities, the strategic partnership framework with Luxembourg includes support for WHO’s core work to develop, deliver and implement high-quality technical products – the guidelines, norms and standards on which many countries rely.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, remarked how symbolic it was that the agreements were signed on the International Day of Solidarity. They are “a strong statement of solidarity by Luxembourg, not just with WHO, but with the people of the world”, said Dr Tedros.
Xavier Bettel, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and Martine Deprez at the signing ceremony. © MAE Luxembourg
WHO and Luxembourg continue their historical strategic partnership, collaborating to fulfill a shared mission to promote, provide and protect health.

Every summer evening, Gulshan follows the same routine. She washes the floor of her one-room home several times so it cools a little for her four children to sleep on. Last summer, the family saved enough to buy a desert cooler, which uses evaporation as a cheaper alternative to air conditioning.
The family uses the appliance cautiously to save on energy costs. But even when it is on, Gulshan, who does not use a surname, has to dampeneveryone’s clothes before sleeping. The 39-year-old and her children now have rashes and one has a skin infection from the wet cloth against their skin.
This summer, Gulshan started jotting down these coping strategies in a garmi khata, or heat registry. “I feel relieved that at least somebody might read my family’s experiences,” she says.
They are one of 40 households in Sunder Nagri, a slum in north-east Delhi, documenting their experiences of surviving the city’s increasingly longer and more frequent heatwaves.
Over the last few years, cities across India have begun drawing up heat action plans – agreements formulated by a municipality or district administration on how to prepare for and respond to extreme heat.
While some incorporate data such as satellite-derived land surface temperatures to identify heat hotspots, there are still significant gaps in information on people, making it difficult to understand how heat is experienced differently across communities.
Aravind Unni, an urban planner and researcher in Delhi, says: “Experiences of heat are vastly different depending on geography, income, occupation, gender, caste, class.
“While we have some meteorological data on heat, what’s absolutely missing is people, community – what they feel, what they experience.”
Most data collated in heat planning is usually just meteorological, such as air temperatures and heatwave thresholds.. The idea for the heat diaries was to “move beyond just the numbers”, says Nibedita Saha, a Greenpeace India researcher who worked on the project.
Aakiz Farooq, a senior campaigner at the group, says the team contemplated how best to encapsulate experiences and thought: “What if they become their own storytellers, they write their own evidence, they write their own testimonies?”
Arshi, 19, who lives in one room with five other family members, is a distance-learning student at Delhi University. She also works at home making decorative tassels for trucks.
She makes about 150 rupees (£1.17) working with her mother and sister for a day. “Sometimes I go to the college library just to sit in the air-conditioned space for a while. But I have to come back home so I can help my sister and mother,” she says. These experiences are part of Arshi’s diary.
The diaries, which ask about daily routines, work, home, mood and families, are intended to serve as comprehensive journals of residents’ daily lives.
Arshi’s small brick house is extremely humid, and while the temperatures are lower after rain, the combination of heat and humidity means everyone is sweating profusely.
The ambient air temperature insideis 29.3C (85F), but with relative humidity at 84.6%, the “feels-like” temperature is 36.3C (97F).
Raja, a 21-year-old street vendor, experiences temperatures as high as 45C during peak summer months as he sells vegetables from his pushcart. The fresh produce spoils quickly, leading to losses, and he has noticed a drastic drop in numbers of people on the street, which also reduces his income.
Every night, he returns to a home with limited ventilation and no cooling source beyond a ceiling fan. As the gap between day and night temperatures narrows year after year in Delhi, people in homes such as Raja’s get no respite, even after the sun sets. “I started sleeping out on the roof in May so I could feel some air,” he says.
Workers such as Raja, Unni says, could be better protected by public policy if the state knew of their experiences at a micro-level and establish systems to provide compensation.
When Sunder Nagri’s residents set out to map heat indices within their neighbourhood, they found that some streets, including where Raja sells vegetables, reflected temperatures on the ground of more than 54C (129F). The residents are attempting to find pragmatic solutions, such as shade, water sources or increased greenery.
This summer, satellite analysis found striking differences across Delhi. For instance, an analysis by the news magazine India Today found an average land-surface temperature of nearly 44C in the south-west district of Mahipalpur, by the airport, compared with about 37C just 2 miles (3km) away in the leafy, upmarket suburb of Vasant Kunj.
Unni feels the diaries and community heat mapping can help form urban resilience policy, but says a big stumbling block is that “Indian cities do not have the administrative capacity or infrastructure to have decentralised action”.
The diaries have now been submitted to India’s National Human Rights Commission, urging it to recognise extreme heat as a human rights issue and recommend measures to protect people.
Farooq says the team also plans to share the testimonies with ministries, policymakers and MPs to push for more targeted measures to protect people from extreme heat.
He says they are also working to develop the testimonies into evidence of impacts and injuries that could be used for lawsuits to increase accountability, given the supreme court’s 2024 ruling that protection from the most adverse impacts of the climate crisis forms part of the right to life.
On 4 August, India’s government added heatwaves to the list of nationally notified disasters, allowing states to access emergency relief funds.
Unni and Farooq say it “would be ideal” if the decision meant funds could support local action guided by community participation.
Arshi also feels more hopeful after the new guidelines. “Even if the government sees something as small as our rising medical and electricity costs and tries to help with that, it would feel like a win for me. At least they would have seen what we are going through,” she says.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi was conferred Uzbekistan’s highest state honour, the Order of “Oliy Darajali Dustlik”, by President Shavkat Mirziyoyev in Tashkent on Sunday, as the two countries agreed to elevate their relationship to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership and deepen cooperation across sectors including energy, trade and technology.
The award, presented during Modi’s visit to the Central Asian nation, marks his 36th international honour. Modi dedicated the recognition to the friendship between India and Uzbekistan and to the people of India.
“It is a moment of great pride for me to be honoured with Uzbekistan’s highest award,” Modi said.
Modi said the name of the award itself reflected the foundation of relations between the two countries.
He highlighted the meaning of “Dostlik”, which means friendship, and noted that Indians are also familiar with the word “Dost”, meaning friend.
Modi said the word “Dostlik” perfectly encapsulates the core sentiment underlying the relationship between India and Uzbekistan.
He added that the honour was not for a single individual but for all 1.4 billion Indians. On behalf of his fellow citizens, he expressed heartfelt gratitude to the people of Uzbekistan, the government and his friend, President Mirziyoyev.
The honour came during Modi’s fourth visit to Uzbekistan, where he received a ceremonial welcome and held delegation-level talks with Mirziyoyev at the Kuksaroy Presidential Palace.
The visit also produced a significant upgrade in bilateral relations, with Modi announcing that India and Uzbekistan would raise their strategic partnership to the level of a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership.
The development coincides with the 15th anniversary of the India-Uzbekistan strategic partnership and comes shortly before Uzbekistan marks its 35th Independence Day anniversary.
"In two days, you will mark the 35th anniversary of your Independence Day. I extend my advance congratulations and best wishes to you and the people of Uzbekistan on this occasion. It is a happy coincidence that this year we are also celebrating the 15th anniversary of our strategic partnership. I am delighted that, on this special occasion, we are elevating our ties to the level of a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership. We will move forward by setting concrete goals within this framework," he said.
The two leaders also discussed ways to expand economic engagement, with Modi welcoming Uzbekistan’s efforts to identify projects across key sectors and establish timelines for their implementation.
"I saw your book, in which you have identified projects across key sectors to advance our bilateral economic partnership and outlined a timeline for the way forward. I appreciate this initiative. I am confident that, by working together, we will make rapid progress on this," PM Modi said.
Among the decisions announced during the talks was an arrangement for the long-term supply of uranium to India.
The two countries also agreed to establish a Coordination Council at the foreign minister level to guide the broader relationship and strengthen coordination across areas of cooperation.
Modi said the existing Joint Commission would also be elevated from the secretary level to the ministerial level. India and Uzbekistan will additionally organise a business summit bringing together business leaders from both countries.
"We had a productive discussion over dinner last night and took several important decisions. Our teams are also aligned on these matters. We will establish a Coordination Council at the Foreign Minister level to provide direction to all aspects of our cooperation through close coordination. We will elevate our Joint Commission from the Secretary level to the Ministerial level. Both sides will jointly organise a business summit featuring business leaders from both nations," he said.
The agreements underline an effort by New Delhi and Tashkent to give greater institutional structure to a relationship that has expanded across economic, strategic and cultural areas.
During the delegation-level discussions, Mirziyoyev praised India’s economic progress and its growing international profile under Modi’s leadership.
The Uzbek president pointed to India’s economic expansion and progress in areas including digitalisation, information technology, artificial intelligence and space exploration.
He said India was achieving notable results across sectors while maintaining strong economic growth and implementing major projects. Mirziyoyev also said New Delhi’s voice and influence in global affairs had become stronger, adding that Uzbekistan welcomed the country’s achievements as a close friend.
Modi also spoke warmly about the reception he received in Tashkent, thanking Mirziyoyev for personally overseeing arrangements for a dinner hosted on Saturday.
He referred to the cultural performances and decorations across the city, saying the gestures reflected Uzbekistan’s close connection with India.
"I am especially grateful for the experience you curated for me during the meal yesterday; you were personally involved in every detail. Along with the delicious food, I also had the pleasure of witnessing songs and dances performed by talented children. It felt as though you had brought India itself to life here, as if you had awakened the spirit of my own Gujarat right here. Moreover, you adorned the entire city in the colours of the Indian tricolour. That, too, was truly touching. All of this demonstrates just how close India is to your heart," PM Modi said.
Earlier, Modi received a ceremonial welcome from Mirziyoyev and took part in engagements that included a visit to the Yangi Uzbekistan Monument and an interaction with members of the Indian community.
The Prime Minister also said he attended a yoga programme organised by the Yoga Federation of Uzbekistan in Tashkent.
Modi arrived in the Uzbek capital on Saturday and received a personal welcome from Mirziyoyev at the airport. The two leaders then travelled together by car to the presidential palace, where they held a dinner meeting before formal delegation-level talks the following day.
